Description:
## Overview

Darbar Abul Muali Qadri is an active Muslim shrine in Lahore, outside Mochi Gate of the old walled city. It is built around the grave of Hazrat Syed Muhammad Khair ul Deen, widely known as Shah Abul Muali Qadri, a saint of the Qadiri order of the Sufis, the mystics of Islam, who came to Lahore at the command of his master and uncle and taught there. The complex holds his tomb, a mosque and a graveyard in which members of the saint's family lie alongside ordinary and notable dead. It is cared for by the Government Auqaf Department, the department of religious endowments, together with the descendants of the shrine's hereditary custodians, and between 2,000 and 2,500 people come to it every day.

Visitors come to pay their respects, to pray, to seek healing and to share in the free food that is given out without pause. By the 1880s it was known as a famous and blessed tomb, and it is held to be a fountainhead of blessings. Its yearly *ʿurs*, the commemoration of the saint's death, is reported to draw 200,000 to 250,000 people, and construction work at the site is ongoing.

## The Saint

Accounts of the form of his name differ; the name the shrine keeps is Hazrat Syed Muhammad Khair ul Deen. Abul Muali, the name by which he is known, was his *kunyat*, an honorific name of the form "father of", and it is also reported that his title was Asadullah, the Lion of God. He was also called *zubdat al-arifin*, the choicest of those who know God. Other holy men bore the name Abul Muali, among them a Shah Abul Muali of the Chishti order and a Shah Abul Muali of a Gilani line, and the saint of this shrine is not to be confused with them.

Tradition holds that he was born on 10 Zil Hajj, the day of Eid al-Adha, in 960 of the Hijri, or Islamic, calendar, in Kirman in Iran; accounts of the year and place of his birth differ. He came of the Kirmani Sadaat, the *sayyids* of Kirman, descendants of the Prophet Muhammad, and he is reported to have been Hassani Hussaini and of the Ahl al-Bayt, the household of the Prophet. His father, Syed Rehmatullah Kirmani, was the son of Sayyid Fath Allah Kirmani. His father is described as a scholar and a poet in Urdu and Persian, who migrated from Iran and settled at Depalpur, in Okara. Two of his father's brothers are named: Sheikh Dawood Bandgi Kirmani, whose shrine is reported to be at Shergarh, and Syed Jalal ud Deen, whose shrine is reportedly in Sindh.

After his father's death, it is reported, he was taken into the care of his uncle Dawood Bandgi, who was also his father-in-law, and he studied with him until the age of thirty; accounts of the length of his training differ. Dawood Bandgi was his *pir* and *murshid*, his spiritual guide. The saint was the son of Dawood Bandgi's own brother, and he became his disciple, his son-in-law and his *khalifa*, the deputy who carries on a master's teaching, receiving from him the *khirqa*, the cloak, of *khilafat*, the authority to guide others.

Accounts of when he came to Lahore differ; the year the shrine keeps is 980 AH, when, at his uncle's command, he migrated from Depalpur to Lahore. There, near Mochi Darwaza, as Mochi Gate is also called, he established a mosque and a seminary, where he led the congregational prayers and taught. He made continuous and tireless efforts for the spread of the Qadiri *silsila*, the spiritual lineage of the order founded by Abd al-Qadir Jilani, and at Lahore he found great acceptance.

He is credited with having wells, mosques and *madrasas*, religious schools, built along his route, with writing books in Urdu and Persian, and with composing poetry, though his focus is reported to have been preaching. It is reported that he taught the Quran and had memorised it, that he possessed both the outward and the inward knowledge, and that he was a dervish and a perfect scholar. He is remembered as the learned man of his time, a *faqir*, a mystic who has embraced poverty, given to *zuhd*, the renunciation of the world, and to *riyazat*, spiritual discipline. He is counted, too, a man of *kashf*, inner unveiling, and of *karamat*, the miraculous gifts of a saint, with a passionate love for his own pir, and he is held to have stood at the degree of *fana fi al-shaikh*, the annihilation of the self in one's master.

Devotees relate that kings came to him with requests, that he never distinguished between rich and poor, and that he kept many *chillas*, retreats of forty days in seclusion, and nights of *dhikr*, the remembrance of God. Accounts of the number of his followers differ; devotees relate that millions pledged allegiance to him, and that because of him millions of people entered the fold of Islam.

He is said to have loved Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani and Mian Mir deeply. With Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani, honoured as Ghaus al-Azam, the greatest helper, he had a special *nisbat*, a spiritual bond, and a devotion to him beyond bounds. Among his teachings, he did not agree that the bond of love is useless after death: in his view love is lawful and proper in every state. On opposing the self, he held that the self's opposition is a good omen, as the call of a crow on the roof is good news that a guest is coming.

He married twice, it is reported. His first wife was a daughter of Dawood Bandgi Kirmani, who died some time after the marriage, and his second a daughter of the Emperor Shah Jahangir; the couple are said to have given her considerable wealth and lands entirely to charitable purposes. He is reported to have had eight sons, one of whom is said to have been martyred fighting in a war against the Sikhs. His eldest son was Shah Muhammad Baqir.

He died on 16 Rabi ul Awal, the third month of the Islamic year, in 1024 AH, at the age, it is reported, of sixty five. Accounts differ over the reign in which he died; the shrine places his death in the reign of Shah Jahan.

## His Books and His Verse

His most famous book is the *Tuhfat al-Qadiriya*, on the wonders and *karamat* of Ghaus al-Azam. Besides it he wrote the *Naghmat-e Daudi*, on the conditions of his own *murshid*, the *Munis-e Jan*, the *Zafran Zar*, the *Guldasta-e Bagh-e Iram* and a *Sharh-e Yazdah Bai'at* of Shaikh Abdul Qadir Jilani. By the 1880s many books of his composition still survived, and it is reported that many books have been written on his life and his *karamat*. It was at his insistence, it is said, that the commentaries on the *Futuh al-Ghaib* of Abd al-Qadir Jilani and on the *Mishkat* came to be written.

He was a poet too, and wrote under the *takhallus*, or pen name, Gharibi. By the 1870s a *diwan*, a collection of his poems, was in the possession of his descendants. In one couplet he acknowledges the favours of his pir, Shaikh Dawood, and names him:

بہ تخت فقر بنشینم چو حاصل گشت مقصودم
سلیمانی کنم کزجان غلام شیخ داؤدم

*A couplet acknowledging the favours of his pir, which names Shaikh Dawood.*

His death, too, was set in verse, in chronograms, verses whose letters, read as numbers, give a year. One line of them names him Maali Khair-e Din:

رحلتنش گفتا معالی خیر دین

*A line of a chronogram on the saint's death, which names him Maali Khair-e Din.*

## The Shrine

It is reported that when Shah Abul Muali came to Lahore he settled at this spot, and that during his lifetime the place became a centre where people received his spiritual blessings. Devotees relate that he was buried here after his passing, and that his tomb was raised on the site of his own seminary, where he had earlier built a mosque and taught.

The quarter around it, the *mohalla* of the Pirs, was settled in the time of the emperor Jahangir by the saint himself, who lived there. When the sultanate fell into ruin and the people scattered, his descendants moved inside the city wall and the quarter was left desolate; yet in the 1880s, among its old buildings, the *rauza*, that is, the tomb, of the saint still stood, built *pakka*, of solid and lasting construction. It had a very large graveyard and countless buildings belonging to it.

Accounts of who built the tomb differ, but most hold that the saint laid its foundation in his lifetime and that it was not yet complete when he died. His son Muhammad Baqir brought the building to completion. Under Sikh rule it was rebuilt by the people of the *sajjada*, the line of the shrine's hereditary custodians.

In the 1880s the tomb stood on a high platform built *pakka*. It was an octagonal building, its door for coming and going on the south, all of lime, plastered inside and out, with a roof of the kind called *qalbuti* under a grand dome. From outside it rose in two storeys, though inside it was of one, and its staircase lay on the west. In the nineteenth century its octagonal dome was white and decorated, a verse was set over the south door, the door had a green niche and carved latticework, and the tomb bore Arabic words saying that the friends of God do not die. Some of its stones had by then come to need repair, and its western staircase was unfinished.

In the 1880s four graves lay on the platform inside the tomb: those of the saint, of his eldest son Shah Muhammad Baqir, of Shah Muhammad Raza and of Haji Muhammad Fazl. Around the graves, on all four sides, stood a wooden lattice the height of a man.

Custodianship is reported to have passed from the saint to his sons and then to the hereditary custodians, reportedly termed *gaddi nashin*, those who sit on the saint's seat, the first of whom was Hazrat Haider Ali Shah, who is also buried in the shrine. It is said that "the kings of every era took care of this place", and in the present era the responsibility has passed to the Auqaf Department. In the nineteenth century the saint's descendants included Shah Sultan and Shah Muhammad Ali, and in the 1880s Imam Shah, Fazil Shah and Firoz Shah were among them, counted *safed-posh*, men of respectable standing. In the 1880s his grandsons and great-grandsons were countless; all of them lived in Lahore, and their livelihood rested on *piri-muridi*, the guiding of disciples, and on the income of the offerings made at the tomb.

The mosque was built by the saint in his lifetime and rebuilt under the Sikhs by a general of the artillery, and in the 1880s it still stood. In the nineteenth century the mosque faced east, its well had been built by the saint himself, and the well had a platform of red stone that had by then stood for twenty years.

In the nineteenth century the precinct held the graves of grandsons of the saint, of a *murid*, or disciple, named Muhammad Sufi, and of Muhammad Shah and Shah Hasan, with Hazrat Hasan Shah. It had *dalans*, open halls, among them the old *dalan* of Sayyid Imam Shah, and a room built by Sayyid Mehr Shah Sahib and Sayyid Alam Shah, with their *faqir*, besides many houses of the descendants and a graveyard. The room for the ritual washing stood west of the tomb. Many houses and *dalans* had been built for the saint's descendants, each of whom lived in his own house.

The graveyard was once a burial ground for the city. In the nineteenth century burials in the graveyard of the tomb, at Tila Shahid Ganj, were banned by order of the government.

## Devotion and Festivals

There is a press of visitors every day. The descendants of the custodians live at the shrine, and people travel from far away to receive *dum* from them, spiritual healing by breath and recitation. The mosque inside the shrine holds the five daily prayers. A gathering is held every day at which *naʿt*, devotional poetry in praise of the Prophet, is recited, and *langar*, free food from the communal kitchen, is given out without pause. Every Thursday drums are beaten, gatherings are held, lamps are lit and *niyaz*, consecrated offerings of food, is distributed. Devotees also recite the *Fateha*, the opening chapter of the Quran, at the graves.

Visitors come to pay their respects and to pray to Allah through the saint's intercession, and they are reported to say that their prayers are answered there. Whatever the worry or sorrow, they say, they find peace only here, because he had knowledge of the unseen; for them he was a *Wali Allah*, a friend of God, from whose door Allah never lets anyone go empty handed.

The *ʿurs* is held on 15, 16 and 17 Rabi ul Awal. Its programme includes the Chadar Poshi, the laying of the shroud; the Mela Chiraghan, the festival of lights; a *mehfil*, or gathering, of *naʿt* shareef; dhol drumming and *dhamal*, the ecstatic dance of the Sufis; *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis; the Ghusal, the ritual washing; and *langar*. Attendance is reported as 200,000 to 250,000 people.

In the 1880s the fair of both Eids was held at the tomb, and the people of the city went to it in complete faith and gave *nazrana*, offerings. The annual *ʿurs* was held as well, falling each year on the date of the saint's death. On its first night there was *chiraghan*, the lighting of lamps, and courtesans danced, and on the second day there was *qawwali*, to which the *fuqara*, the dervishes, listened. With the two Eid fairs and the *ʿurs*, there were, as it were, three fairs at the tomb in a year.

## Legends

Several incidents are told of the saint, and they are said to be widely known among devotees.

**The *majzub* at the roadside.** It is reported that, while he was still searching for a spiritual master, the saint set out for the house of a companion, Sheikh Hamid Karishmi, in Delhi. On the way he spoke with a *majzub*, one spiritually intoxicated and absorbed in divine love, who was sitting by the road. The *majzub* told him that the one he was wandering in search of was in his own home, and named his uncle, Dawood Bandgi Kirmani. Astonished, he returned to his uncle, who answered him with a verse to the effect of: "Wander and see the whole world, blister your feet, if you find anyone like us, then say." His request for allegiance was accepted, and after some days his uncle sent him back to Lahore with the instruction to spend his life in the path of Allah.

**The promised audience.** It is told that Shaikh Dawood learnt by *kashf* of his disciple's longing, and told him that today or tomorrow he would bring him into the presence of the holy and exalted one, and that he should wait for that hour. One night, between sleep and waking, his pir took him by the hand into the assembly of Ghaus al-Azam, where Abu al-Maali Iraqi sat on the right and his pir on the left. The moment the thought crossed his heart that the man on the right might outrank his pir, Ghaus al-Azam looked at him and said: "O Abu al-Maali, your shaikh is my heart, and the heart is on the left side".

**Dreams of Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani.** It is said that whoever pledged allegiance at his hands would see Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani in a dream that very night, and that this was due to his *karamat*.

**The rosary.** Tellings differ over who received the rosary, but the shrine tells the story of Dara Shikoh. It is reported that Dara Shikoh wrote that he once accompanied Shah Abul Muali to the court of his teacher, Sheikh Imam Niyamat Ali, where someone presented the saint with a rosary. Dara Shikoh silently wished that it might be given to him. On their return to the seminary the saint handed him that same rosary, telling him to recite *Darood*, the blessings on the Prophet, on it every day, so that the giver, the recipient and the saint would all share in the reward. Dara Shikoh is said to have been amazed that his unspoken thought was known.

**The white turban.** Here too tellings differ over who received the gift, and the shrine tells it of Dara Shikoh, who had never disclosed his love for Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani. One night, it is reported, the Sheikh came to him in a dream and gave him a white turban. In the morning, when he presented himself before Shah Abul Muali, the saint gave him a white turban, saying that Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani had asked that it be given to him.

**The rain at the Eidgah.** It is reported that during a drought at Lahore, when Hakim Afzal Agha was ruling, the Hakim gathered a very large crowd at the Eidgah outside the city, the ground for the Eid prayers, for congregational prayer for rain, and came to invite the saint. Shah Abul Muali excused himself, saying that he could not walk. The Hakim pressed him, saying that if the saint would not come, he too would remain sitting there. At last the saint told him to go, and said that it would certainly rain after two days. No rain fell for two days; on the third it rained heavily. When the Hakim returned to ask how he had known, the saint is said to have answered that had it rained on the day of the gathering, the arrogant among the worshippers might have taken it for their own wisdom, and it would later have become a cause of sin, and so Allah delayed it.

**Blessed halting places.** It is told that on his way towards Lahore every place where he halted became blessed and settled by the blessing of his steps, and that he stayed awake all night. Such, it is said, was his reverence for his pir, and for it he was raised to high rank. His miracles are said to be famous by the hundreds.

## The Setting

The shrine lies outside Mochi Gate, one of the twelve gates of the walled city of Lahore. In the nineteenth century the tomb served as a landmark for its quarter: a road ran to the saint's tomb, the tomb of a Shah Kamaita stood at its northwest corner, and the Khanqah of Abdi Shah, a Sufi lodge, lay west of its graveyard. The street on which it stands bears the saint's name, Shah Abul Muali Street, in Gowalmandi.

It is further reported that the land for Dyal Singh College in Lahore, close to the shrine, was given by the saint's descendants so that people could acquire education.

Name: Darbar Ghamkol Sharif (Zinda Pir)
Location: Ghamkol valley, near Kohat, Kohat District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
Events: Annual urs; large annual gathering
Description:
Darbar-e-Aliya Naqshbandia Ghamkol Sharif lies in a secluded valley a few miles outside the town of Kohat in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and is among the most important centres of the *Naqshbandi* Sufi order in modern Pakistan. It was founded in 1952 by the Naqshbandi master universally known as *Zinda Pir* (1912–1999), who was born in the nearby village of Jungle Khail. He had received spiritual authority (*khilafat*) around 1942 from his own guide, Baba Ji Muhammad Qasim of Mohra Sharif, who directed him to establish an independent centre; obedient to that instruction, Zinda Pir withdrew to the then-barren Ghamkol valley and there built, over the following decades, a great complex of mosque, seminary, and lodgings that grew into a thriving spiritual township. His following spread far beyond Pakistan, and the darbar developed an especially strong connection with the Pakistani community of Birmingham in the United Kingdom, where an associated mosque bears its name. Zinda Pir died on 21 March 1999 and is buried at the darbar, his tomb becoming a place of pilgrimage in its turn; his spiritual seat passed to his son, Pir Sayyid Badshah. Each year vast crowds of devotees gather at Ghamkol Sharif for the commemorative observances, making it one of the great living Sufi centres of the north-west.

Independent scholarly confirmation for the core outline comes from the anthropologist Pnina Werbner, who identifies the tariqa's specific branch name as *tariqa Naqshbandiyya Ghamkolia* and who, by the time of her fieldwork, found Zinda Pir's following grown into "a vast, transnational regional cult, stretching throughout Pakistan to the Gulf, Britain, Afghanistan and Southern Africa." She describes the lodge's daily rhythm — "truckloads of supplicants" arriving to seek the saint's blessing, swelling to "a veritable flood" on Fridays, holidays, and the *urs* — and the centrality of the *langar*, through which visitors are fed rather than asked for payment. Her fuller academic account appears in *Pilgrims of Love: The Anthropology of a Global Sufi Cult* (Hurst, 2004; Indiana University Press ed., 2016), the standard scholarly treatment of the darbar and its founder — though her 2009 conference paper on the subject dates the founding of the cult centre to 1948 rather than the 1952 given above, a discrepancy this entry has not resolved.

## Bibliography

- Pnina Werbner, "Transnationalism and Regional Cults: The Dialectics of Sufism in the Plurivocal Muslim World" (conference paper, Keele University, May 2009).
- Pnina Werbner, *Pilgrims of Love: The Anthropology of a Global Sufi Cult* (Hurst, 2004; Indiana University Press ed., 2016).

Neither source is reconciled here.

Name: Darbar Ghazi Ilm Din Shaheed
Events: Annual urs (31 October: chadar-changing, gusal, Mehfil-e-Naat, langar, collective prayer); Thursday-night Mehfil; daily lamp-lighting and vow-making
Description:
## Overview

In Lahore lies the shrine of Ghazi Ilm Din Shaheed, a young carpenter revered across Pakistan not as a Sufi master or spiritual guide but for a single act: the killing, in 1929, of the publisher of a book judged blasphemous against the Prophet Muhammad. The shrine is visited daily for prayer, vow-making and intercession, and devotees call him *Ghazi-e-Millat* and *Fakhr-e-Ummah* -- "warrior of the nation" and "pride of the community."

## Family and Early Life

It is reported that Ghazi Ilm Din was born on 4 December 1908 in Lahore to a family of carpenters (*tarkhan*); his father's name is given as Taleh Mand. He had two brothers, one a fellow carpenter and one a government employee. The family is said to have been widely respected by neighbours for its piety, with no history of dispute with anyone. Ilm Din received an early education at a neighbourhood madrasa before entering the family trade.

## The Blasphemy Case

The origin of the case is reportedly dated to 1928, when a Hindu publisher named Rajpal issued a book, *Rangeela Rasool*, that the Muslim community of the time considered blasphemous. It is reported that a British magistrate sentenced Rajpal to only six months' imprisonment -- judged far too lenient -- and that a further appeal, heard by a magistrate named Dalip Singh, secured Rajpal's release on bail, further inflaming public anger. Two earlier attempts on Rajpal's life are also reported: on 24 September 1928 a man named Khuda Bakhsh tried and failed, and was sentenced to seven years; later a man named Abdul Aziz, said to have travelled from Afghanistan, struck the wrong man (Swami Satyanand, not Rajpal) at Rajpal's shop, and received fourteen years.

Ilm Din is then reported to have overheard a public gathering recounting Rajpal's offence, and to have had a dream in which an elder rebukes him for sleeping while his Prophet is insulted -- a dream his friend Sheeday says he shared the same night. The two are said to have drawn lots three times to decide who would act, with Ilm Din's name emerging each time. On 6 April 1929, it is reported, Ilm Din went to Rajpal's shop and killed him, then walked to Anarkali police station and turned himself in without expressing regret.

## Trial and Execution

It is reported that Muhammad Ali Jinnah represented Ilm Din at the High Court, and advised him against confessing so a defence could be mounted; Ilm Din is quoted as refusing, calling the killing the one deed of his life he took pride in. The High Court passed a death sentence on 7 July 1929, which Ilm Din reportedly welcomed, preferring the gallows to imprisonment. Jinnah and Allama Muhammad Iqbal are said to have both sought clemency from the British government without success, and Ilm Din is reported to have been executed at Mianwali Jail on 31 October 1929.

## Funeral and Burial

It is reported that the body was brought from Mianwali to Lahore under tight security, with funeral prayers led by Qari Shams-ud-Din, Imam of the Wazir Khan Mosque, on Railway Auqaf land, attended by an estimated 600,000 people. Allama Iqbal and Allama Mehr-ud-Din Londkhori are said to have lowered the body into the grave, and Iqbal is quoted as saying, on that occasion, "this carpenter's son has surpassed us all." He was buried in Lahore's Miani Sahib Graveyard (Parvez Mahmood, “Miani Sahib: Resting Place of Heroes,” *The Friday Times*, 20 May 2022).

## Why the Shrine Is Venerated

It is reported that visitors regard Ilm Din's act as proof of a station high enough that Allah answers prayers made through his intercession (*waseela*). An account is also reported, attributed to elders who visited him in prison, that the Prophet appeared to him nightly to recite the Qur'an -- including an episode with the visiting scholar Pir Syed Meher Ali Shah, in which Ilm Din is said to have corrected a lapse in Meher Ali Shah's recitation of Surah Yusuf, prompting Meher Ali Shah to liken his imprisonment to that of the Prophet Yusuf.

## Devotion and Events

People reportedly come daily -- an estimated 400 to 600 visitors -- to light lamps, make vows (*mannat*), recite Fatiha and distribute langar; a space for two to three prayer rows sits beside the shrine. Thursday nights bring a dedicated Mehfil. The annual urs falls on 31 October (the date of the execution) and includes Mehfil-e-Naat, chadar-changing, ritual washing (*gusal*), langar, and collective prayer.

## Custodianship

The shrine is reported to be managed by a body called the Ghazi Ilam Din Shaheed Committee, with some matters handled by the Auqaf Department. It is also reported -- as a point some visitors raise -- that Rajpal was the book's publisher, while various accounts describe its author as an anonymous or pseudonymous figure, distinct from Rajpal himself.

- Parvez Mahmood, “Miani Sahib: Resting Place of Heroes,” *The Friday Times*, 20 May 2022 (first-hand account naming Ilam Din Shaheed's resting place at Miani Sahib, in the same passage as Wasif Ali Wasif and Tahir Bandagi) — cited here only for the shrine's location.

Name: Darbar Hazrat Khawaja Feroz-ud-Din Gharib Nawaz Chishti Nizami
Sufi Saint: Hazrat Khawaja Feroz-ud-Din Gharib Nawaz Chishti Nizami
Events: Annual urs (date not stated in the survey); recurring mehfil (zikr-e-Ilahi and Naat-e-Rasool) every few days; Thursday lamp-lighting (diyas) and vow-making (manatein)
Description:
## Overview

In the middle of Miani Sahib Graveyard in Lahore — one of the city's great burial grounds — stands the shrine of Hazrat Khawaja Feroz-ud-Din Gharib Nawaz Chishti Nizami, a Chishti Nizami Qadria saint remembered above all for a generosity so unstinting that he was called *Sakhi Lajpal*, "the generous one who never turns anyone away." The shrine sits within Miani Sahib's grounds, surrounded on all four sides by the graves that make up the wider burial ground.

## The Life of Hazrat Khawaja Feroz-ud-Din

It is reported explicitly that Hazrat Khawaja Feroz-ud-Din was his real name — not a title conferred later. His birthplace is given as Kandhari Bazaar, in the Rang Mahal quarter of Lahore, and his parents are named: his mother, Mehtab Bibi, described as an exceptionally devout woman who raised him carefully, and his father, Hassan Din, a poor and hardworking man already connected to the Chishti Qadria order, whose labour left him little time to oversee his son's education directly. His birth year is unclear: he is reported to have been "born in the latter part of the 1900s (19th century)" — a phrase that contradicts itself, since the 1900s and the 19th century do not refer to the same decades — and no other date for his birth is reported, so the year cannot be resolved.

Coming of age, he pursued the righteous path on his own initiative. At fifteen he pledged allegiance (*baith*) to Hazrat Khawaja Sheikh Muhammad Mustafa Chishti-Nizami — an event reported to have arrived through a dream, in which his future spiritual master appeared to him and said, "Your share is with us; come and take your share." He woke the next morning and travelled to his master's seat of learning on Barki Road, Lahore, to complete the pledge in person.

He never left his father's trade: he is reported to have worked as a shoemaker in Rang Mahal Bazaar for the whole of his life, making and selling shoes, while living with deliberate simplicity. His nights, from Tahajjud until Fajr, were given to the remembrance of Allah; his days to his shop and, increasingly, to the stream of people who came to him. His spiritual master at one point asked him to visit only on Fridays rather than daily, out of concern for the length of the journey Feroz-ud-Din was making to reach him.

## Pledge of Allegiance and Succession

It is reported that all of his religious learning came from his one spiritual master and guide, Hazrat Khawaja Sheikh Muhammad Mustafa Chishti-Nizami, whom he served closely for the rest of the older man's life. When Hazrat Khawaja Sheikh Muhammad Mustafa died in 1390 AH, he called Feroz-ud-Din to him in his final moments, conferred on him the cloak of succession (*khilafat*), and named him his spiritual successor. Thousands are said to have pledged allegiance to Feroz-ud-Din after he received this khilafat. He is said to have continued to mark his own master's annual Urs with honour throughout his life, without wanting elaborate invitation or attention drawn to the observance itself — a preference for a low profile that reportedly extended to his everyday manner: he asked disciples to visit on Fridays but treated anyone arriving on another day with the same humility.

He died suddenly of a liver ailment on Friday, 27 November 1981, and his disciples built his shrine at Miani Sahib, where a crowd of visitors is reportedly present at all times.

## The Shrine

The shrine itself is reported to have been built "very beautifully," using expensive marble and fine materials throughout its construction. Inside, it houses rare relics associated with sacred personalities from around the world, which his disciples are said to have brought back, preserved, and put on display over time — a detail reported as part of what gives the shrine its splendour, distinct from the devotional life described below. The wider graveyard surrounds the shrine on every side.

## Devotional Life and the Annual Urs

A spiritual gathering (*mehfil*) — combining the remembrance of Allah (*zikr-e-Ilahi*) with praise of the Prophet (*Naat-e-Rasool*) — is held every few days, together with free food (*langar*). Thursdays draw people specifically to light lamps (*diyas*) and make vows (*manatein*). Daily footfall is estimated at 750 to 1,000 visitors.

The annual Urs reportedly includes lamp-lighting, large-scale langar, the changing of the shrine's ceremonial cloth (*chadar tabdeeli*), ritual washing (*gusal*), further mehfilein, qawwali, and sustained zikr-o-azkar — drawing an estimated 175,000 to 225,000 pilgrims.

A reciprocal relationship binds this shrine to that of Feroz-ud-Din's own master: his disciples attend Hazrat Khawaja Sheikh Muhammad Mustafa's Urs in large numbers, and in turn the disciples of Sheikh Muhammad Mustafa take an active part in organising Feroz-ud-Din's own Urs — a link attributed to the scale of the following Feroz-ud-Din drew in in his own right after receiving khilafat.

## Custodianship

The shrine is reportedly maintained by his special disciples (*mureedeen-e-khas*) and their descendants, who took over its administration immediately after his death and continue to run it today; some workers are privately employed to attend to the shrine at all times.

Name: Darbar Hazrat Khawaja Shah Muhammad Sulaiman Taunsvi (R.A)
Events: Annual urs; qawwali and naat; daily langar
Description:
## Overview

At Taunsa Sharif, in the Dera Ghazi Khan region of southern Punjab, stands the darbar, or shrine, of Hazrat Khwaja Muhammad Sulaiman Taunsvi (c. 1770 to 1850), the great Chishti saint honoured as *Pir Pathan*. He is remembered as a chief reviver of the Chishti order in the Punjab, and his *khanqah*, the Sufi lodge where disciples gather, became one of the most important centres of Chishti learning and devotion in the nineteenth century. His darbar remains a major place of pilgrimage in the south west of the province.

He came to Taunsa at his master's command and began by living there in a hut, and gradually the town came to prosper. There he taught, founded a school, kept a great free kitchen and guided a vast following, and his disciples spread the order across the region. After his death the seat passed to his grandson.

## The Saint

Khwaja Muhammad Sulaiman, also called Shah Sulaiman and, after Taunsa, Taunsvi, came of a Pathan family, whence his title *Pir Pathan*. His great grandfather Umar Khan and his grandfather Abd al-Wahhab were Afghans of the Ja'fariya tribe, and his father was Zakariya Khan. He was born around 1770, in 1184 AH, in the village in the hills that was his original home, three *kuroh*, an old measure of distance, from Taunsa.

His father died when he was four, and he was brought up and taught under his mother's care. From his youth he gave himself to religious learning and the Sufi path. He read fifteen *paras*, or parts, of the Quran with Mulla Yusuf Jafar and the remaining fifteen with Mian Hasan Ali, completing the Quran, and from the same teachers he learnt Attar's *Pand-nama* and Sa'di's *Gulistan* and *Bustan*, among other books. He went on to read further Persian literature with Maulvi Wali Muhammad, and then went to Kot Mithan, where he entered the *madrasa*, the religious school, of Qazi Muhammad Aqil. There he finished the Arabic textbooks in a short time and completed his study of the outward sciences.

While he was living at Kot Mithan, Khwaja Nur Muhammad Maharvi came to Uch, and he went there to attend on him. At sixteen he was honoured with *bai'at*, the oath of allegiance by which a disciple is initiated into a Sufi order, at Nur Muhammad's hands. Afterwards he kept going to and from his master at Mahar, sometimes setting out on foot. His *pir*, his spiritual guide, trained him in austerities and spiritual struggle, in *zikr-e jahr*, the vocal remembrance of God, and in *pas-e anfas*, the watching of the breath, and taught him books of *tasawwuf*, the Sufi path, among them the *Adab al-Talibin*, the *Ashara-e Kamila* and the *Fusus al-Hikam*.

At twenty two he received from his master the *khirqa* of *khilafat*, the robe of succession, given, it is said, with the permission of the Prophet himself. After the death of Hazrat Maulana Fakhr al-Din Fakhr-e Jahan he went to Delhi and kept a retreat of forty days at that master's tomb, returning to Mahar after the *fatiha*, the prayers for the dead, said on the fortieth day.

He became the major successor of Nur Muhammad Maharvi and one of his renowned *khalifas*, the deputies a master authorises to carry on his teaching, and he rose to be among the foremost Chishti shaykhs of his age. Nur Muhammad, who died in 1790, was himself the fourth in the line of succession from Shah Kalim Allah Jahanabadi, and the chain of masters ran from Kalim Allah Jahanabadi through Nizam al-Din Awrangabadi, Fakhr al-Din Dihlawi and Nur Muhammad Maharvi to Sulaiman himself.

It was not his own choice to settle at Taunsa. His pir commanded him to live there, and in obedience to his master's word he settled in the small town, at first in a hut, and began the work of guidance and instruction.

He loved his pir with a passion and lived in a renunciation and detachment without equal. He owned nothing but a *lungi*, a length of cloth wrapped around the waist, and in his *hujra*, his small cell, a mat was spread on which he sat to worship. He was a scholar as well as a mystic, with mastery of the Quran, of *hadith*, the reported sayings of the Prophet, and of *fiqh*, Islamic jurisprudence. He loved *sama'*, spiritual listening to music, and was a man of longing and spiritual taste; at times, in dance and ecstasy, he wept.

Both his sons, Khwaja Gul Muhammad and Khwaja Darvesh Muhammad, died in his lifetime. Accounts of the year of his death differ; it is generally given as 1850, or 1267 AH, and he died in the month of Safar. He was buried at Taunsa Sharif.

## His Order and Disciples

He belonged to the Chishti order, the Sufi order founded by Moinuddin Chishti and prominent in South Asia, and to its Nizami branch, which descends from Shaykh Nizam al-Din Awliya, who died in 1325. In the Punjab the wider spread of the Chishtiya Nizamiya Fakhriya order came about through him. A further branch of the Nizami Chishtis, the Sulaymaniyya, is named after him, so that a master of that line is properly called a Sulaymani-Nizami-Chishti shaykh. He is credited with reinvigorating the Chishti tradition in the Punjab at a time of political upheaval, and the lines that led to Sial Sharif and Golra Sharif owe much to his *khanqah*.

His *khalifas* were many. Three were especially close to him, beloved and sharers of his secrets: Shaikh Muhammad Yar, Hafiz Muhammad Ali and Maulvi Muhammad Ali Thani. Mian Abdullah Shah was also among the most famous. Hafiz Muhammad Ali, known as Muharram Ali Khairabadi, was among his earliest *khalifas* and became one of his major successors, and his *khanqah* at Khairabad was a centre of learning. Through him, and through other disciples of the saint, the Nizami branch of the Chishti order expanded into the upper Punjab.

Muhammad Fadil Shah Mirpuri, author of *Za'faran* and *Nafi' al-rasikhin*, was another of his *khalifas*, and so was Muhammad Allah Bakhsh Tawnsawi, whose *Ghaza' al-muhibbin wa samm al-mu'anidin* was compiled by Nur Muhammad Mak'hadi in 1314 AH (1896 to 1897). Another disciple, Ahmad Ali Khayrabadi, wrote the *Qasr-i 'arifan*, a general history of the Sufi orders and of the Indian dynasties, which Muhammad Baqir translated into Urdu (Lahore, 1965).

Two of his *khalifas* are counted among the saints of Lahore, one of them Shaikh Haji Ramzan Lahori. His lineage travelled far. Sufi Saheb, who died in 1916, brought the Chishti Nizami Sulaymaniyya to South Africa.

## The Shrine

Taunsa lies on the west bank of the upper Indus, 40 *kos*, an old measure of distance, from Dera Ghazi Khan, and the shrine is remote and difficult of access. Today it is a large complex, richly built and kept by the saint's successors, and a busy centre of pilgrimage in southern Punjab. The town of Taunsa Sharif takes its name and its identity from the darbar, which has remained, through those successors, a seat of Chishti teaching and devotion. After the saint settled there, given to worship, austerity and spiritual struggle, Taunsa gradually came to prosper. His *mazar*, or tomb, at Taunsa is held to be a fountainhead of spiritual effusion and blessing.

He founded a *madrasa* at Taunsa, a *dar al-ulum* or house of learning, because many people were ignorant of the sciences of the *shari'a*, the religious law, and its aim was to teach them. He himself taught books of the mystical path to select students there, and little by little it grew into a considerable centre of Islamic learning. He consolidated the order by stressing learning through such institutions: besides the academy at Taunsa he established other religious schools throughout the Punjab, linking each to instruction in the mystical insights of the Nizami branch of the Chishti order.

A library was built up and kept at his principal lodge in Taunsa, a collection from which future scholarship stands to benefit. The shrine holds a manuscript calendar of the death anniversaries of the saints, compiled at the end of the eighteenth century and arranged by the months of the Muslim lunar calendar. It does not keep strictly to the direct chain of Chishti masters: it includes figures from outside the Chishti line, such as the first four caliphs, and some little known, undated figures related by family to the main Chishti shaykhs of the line. Books were copied at Taunsa too; a manuscript of the *Adab al-muridin* of Muhammad Chishti was copied there around 1790.

Because both his sons had died before him, the seat passed over a generation. After his death his grandson, Khwaja Allah Bakhsh Taunsvi, became his *sajjada nashin*, the hereditary custodian who sits on the saint's prayer carpet, and he still held the seat in the 1870s. Born in 1231 AH, he died in 1901 (1319 AH). Like his grandfather he was active in spiritual reform and training, and the splendour of the Chishti order in the nineteenth century has been credited to him.

Hereditary custodianship, under the title *gaddi nishin*, the holder of the seat, can be traced in variant forms from the principal Chishti shrine at Ajmer to branch shrines such as Taunsa. Here the succession was later contested. Two branches of succession from the saint came into conflict at the shrine, one linked to his grandson Allah Bakhsh, the other to Mihr Ali Shah, who died in 1937. The power struggles within the Sulaymaniyya have been traced to British manipulation and to the rivalry of local Sikhs, Hindus and Muslim reformers; but political contest is only part of the story.

## Devotion and Teaching

The shrine keeps up the daily prayers, *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, and *naat*, poetry in praise of the Prophet, and the free kitchen, the *langar*. Its annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, draws great crowds.

In the saint's own lifetime thousands of seekers of God were honoured in his service, and thousands of travellers, destitute and poor people ate two meals a day from his *langar*. He is said to have won such acceptance as no one else had in that age: more than a *lakh* of people, that is, over a hundred thousand, became his disciples, and hundreds of unbelievers and sinners repented.

He held strictly to a daily discipline and never let it change in any circumstance. After *tahajjud*, the voluntary prayer of the late night, came vocal *zikr*; after the dawn prayer, a short rest in his cell; then he went out to guide others. After the midday meal he always rested; after the noon prayer he recited the Quran; then came the afternoon prayer. After the sunset prayer he spent a watch of the night in vocal *zikr*, then took the night meal, said the *'isha*, the last prayer of the day, with the congregation, and rested in his cell.

His life passed in worship, austerity, guidance and instruction. He insisted that the purpose of human life is the worship of God, often reciting the Quranic verse that God created jinn and humankind only to worship Him. He held that following the Prophet is indispensable for advancement in this world and in religion. He urged his hearers to shun lying, backbiting, dishonesty, greed, envy, vanity and pride; he condemned the love of the world and taught that the company of worldly people should be avoided as far as possible; and he commended humility, that one should count oneself the lowest and worst of all. Among his sayings are that none can be accepted at God's court without following the *shari'a* outwardly and inwardly, that Muslims should keep away from what the *shari'a* does not allow, and that following it is altogether necessary for purity of heart and spiritual progress.

What marks him out above all is the combination of spiritual standing and political activism. He urged his followers to take part in what has been called "resistance against Sikh aggression in the Punjab", and so, apparently for the first time in Chishti history, spiritual biographies were drawn into partisanship for one political group, the Muslims, against another, those who were not Muslim. Yet he also worked to keep cordial relations with Punjabi Hindus even while he opposed their Sikh neighbours.

## Legends

A story is told about where the wealth of the *langar* came from. A merchant devoted to the saint used to travel to Hindustan, sell his goods and go back, and on his way back he would call on the saint, present an offering, ask for a prayer and leave. Once, seeing a great deal of offerings coming in, he thought that all this *langar* and giving ran on the rupees of worldly people, and that if the offerings stopped the whole work would come to an end.

The saint, it is said, knew the merchant's misgiving by *kashf*, inner unveiling, and answered it with a precedent. Sultan Ghiyas al-Din had once held the same suspicion about the *langar* and the largesse of Hazrat Nizam al-Din Awliya, and forbade anyone at his court to attend on Nizam al-Din or to bring him any offering. When Nizam al-Din learnt of it, he ordered the spending doubled and told his servant to take what was needed from the niche of his *hujra*.

Then the saint's prayer mat was fetched from his cell. The merchant lifted it and was amazed to see beneath it a river flowing in three currents, one of *ashrafis*, the old gold coins, one of rupees and one of jewels. The mat fell from his hand, and he came out and begged forgiveness. The story is counted among his *karamat*, the miraculous deeds and spiritual gifts of a saint.

Another story tells of an old woman who came screaming and weeping, saying that her only son was dead. A servant suggested that the boy might only be in a swoon. The saint found him dead, with no pulse anywhere, but at the servant's request he looked at him closely. Through the attention of his heart the pulse stirred; at a second look it was beating well, and the boy sat up. He lived for a long time afterwards, stayed on in the saint's service, and was given the duty of drawing water.

## Legacy

Khwaja Muhammad Sulaiman Taunsvi is remembered as one of the principal architects of the Chishti revival in the nineteenth century Punjab, though accounts differ over whether his work is best called a revival. Many count him a founding figure of the Chishti recovery, and his *khanqah* at Taunsa nourished a generation of saints. His shrine remains one of the great Chishti centres of southern Punjab.

His life was told in verse several times, and his death was marked in chronograms, verses whose letters give the year of an event. 'Abd al-Rahman Khayrpuri wrote a verse biography, the *Hilya-i mubarak*; Muhammad Husayn Pishawari told his life in seventy one verses in the *Raz-i Hazrat-i Khwaja Muhammad Sulayman*; Khuda Bakhsh Tawnsawi wrote a *Manaqib-i Sulaymani* in verse; and Musa Buzdar, whose master Hafiz Ghulam Shah Sadid al-Din Chishti died in 1960 (1379 AH), wrote the *Fayd-i Muhtawi*, also called the *Muraqqa'-i Sulaymani*, a *mathnawi*, a long poem in rhyming couplets. Even his robe of succession had its poem: Ishaq Afghan, of about 1875, wrote the *Qamis-i sharif* in verse on the pedigree of his *khirqa*, as well as a *Manaqib-i Sulaymani*.

He became the subject of numerous biographies, an example of how the Persian literature of the Chishtis went on multiplying late, right up to the end of the nineteenth century. They include Ghulam Muhammad Chhachari's *Manaqib-i Sulaymani*, compiled in 1256 AH (1840), whose manuscript at Bahawalnagar has an appendix of 1287 AH (1870) telling of the author's later visits to Taunsa and of the saint's death; Yar Muhammad's *Intikhab-i manaqib-i Sulaymani*; Nizam al-Din Ahmad Bada'oni's *Rahat al-'ashiqin*; Najm al-Din Nagawri's *Manaqib-i mahbubayn*, lives of the saint and of Nur Muhammad Maharvi, completed in 1278 AH (1862) and printed at Lahore; Khuda Bakhsh Tawnsawi's *Muntakhab al-asrar*, composed around 1870 to 1872; and a *Manaqib-i Sulaymani* by Nabi Bakhsh. Other works that tell of him include the *Khatam-e Sulaimani*, Muhammad al-Din Sufi's *Zikr-e Habib*, the *Manaqib-e Hafiziya*, Amir Bakhsh's *Anwar-e Shamsiya*, Din Muhammad's *Ahtiram al-Asfiya*, also called *Nishat-e Hafiziya*, and Khaliq Ahmad Nizami's *Tarikh-e Mashaikh-e Chisht*.

His sayings, his *malfuzat*, were gathered in several collections, among them a *Malfuzat-i sharif* compiled by Ghulam Haydar; the *Nafi' al-salikin*, compiled by Imam al-Din Ghulam Shah in 1267 AH (1851 to 1852); and the *Muntakhab al-manaqib*, compiled by Yar Muhammad Dhawqi ibn Taj Muhammad Pakpattani. In 1979 a modern study, Muhammad Husayn Lillahi's *Hazrat Khwaja Muhammad Sulayman Tawnsawi awr un ke khulafa*, a Karachi University doctoral dissertation, was published at Lahore by the Islamic Book Foundation.

Name: Darbar Hazrat Shah Gohar Peer
Sufi Saint: Hazrat Sufi Peer Syed Gohar Ali Shah (Syed Ali Gohar), known as Shah Gohar Peer
Events: *ʿUrs*, 19–21 Ramzan, with a fair; weekly Thursday *mehfil* with *langar*, *naʿt*, *qawwālī* and lamps; five daily prayers and Friday prayer at the adjoining mosque
Description:
## Overview
Darbar Hazrat Shah Gohar Peer is a Muslim shrine in Lahore, built over the grave of the
figure reported to be Hazrat Sufi Peer Syed Gohar Ali Shah, known to devotees as Shah
Gohar Peer. Its sect or *silsila* (Sufi order or lineage) is reported as "Ahl e
Sunnat - Ismaili Sadaat Uch Shareef", with a *shajra e nasab* (genealogy) traced to Hazrat
Imam Hussain. A mosque named after the saint stands directly in front of it, and a
residential area and graveyard surround the site. It is also reported that its dome is
the largest of any shrine in Lahore, and that he is the only member of his family whose
shrine is in Lahore, the rest lying at Uch Sharif.

## The Saint
It is reported that Shah Gohar Peer — given name Syed Ali
Gohar — was born on 11 Rabīʿ al-Sānī 729 AH at Uch Sharif. His father, Syed Ul Hassan
Kabeer, is described as a pious Sufi and a scholar of *dīn* (religion) whose disciples
included Shia, Sunni and people of other sects. He took his education and all his
spiritual knowledge from his father, and the oath of allegiance at his hand; seeing his
rising spirituality, his father bestowed *khilāfat* (the mantle of spiritual succession)
upon him and sent him out to bring non-Muslims into Islam. The family occupation, it is
said, was inviting people to Islam, and he was known by the title "Kuffar Shikan"
— the destroyer of disbelief.

He is said to have preached first in Kashmir. Travelling towards Uch Sharif he arranged a
stay at a place in Lahore reportedly known today as Mahmood Booti, but within days
changed his mind and camped permanently at the site of the present shrine. He is
reported to have been a solitude-loving worshipper, absorbed in *dhikr* (remembrance of God) and
possessed of *bāṭin* (esoteric) knowledge, outwardly a beautiful dervish, who did not
display his spiritual standing and moved constantly between locations; other saints
accompanied his mission from the beginning. He died, it is reported, on 21 Ramzan 825
AH, and a very large gathering assembled, including people from Uch Sharif. A grand shrine is
said to have then been built for him, attributed in one place to the King and
in another to Sultan Mahmud Ghaznavi, and known ever since for its grandeur and antiquity
(see the note below on that attribution).

## Miracles and Legends
Devotees relate that he was seen riding a lion and a snake, and it is by the lion and the
snake that he is still popularly known. Tradition holds that a canal at his camp site
dried up, or closed of its own accord, once he arrived. It is said that he would be seen
in one place and at the same moment far away. In another story he went to Delhi, had a
vision of Hazrat Ali Murtaza and carried the sacred footprints back on a snake; one is
said to have remained there and one to have been brought to Uch Sharif, where it is still
visited. Pressed with questions about such wonders, he reportedly adopted a
*Qalandarī* bearing so that people would take him for one lost in ecstasy. Emperors and
maharajas reportedly came to him for blessings, and Mughal emperors praised his
miracles.

Tradition also holds that he planted a tree with his own hands — named in one place as a
Sukh Chain (Pongamia) and in another as a banyan (*bor*) — on which writing formed by its
own branches is still visible, and that it yielded sugar long after his passing, as the
tree planted by his father at Uch Sharif is said to have given milk. Strikingly, it is
reported that according to books compiled about the saint, the graves immediately
adjacent to his own are those of the lion and the snake he rode. Devotees say that a
visitor need not state a request, and that prayers offered through his intercession
(*wasīla*) are still answered.

## The Shrine and its Devotions
Visitors come daily, but Thursday draws the larger crowd, when *mehfils* (devotional
gatherings) are held, *langar* (free communal food) is distributed, *naʿt* is recited,
*qawwālī* is performed and lamps are lit. The annual *ʿurs* (death anniversary observance)
falls on 19, 20 and 21 Ramzan, when a fair is held and very large numbers gather. Attendance is
estimated at 800 to 1,200 visitors daily, 2,000 to 2,500 on Thursdays and 100,000 to
150,000 pilgrims at the *ʿurs*. The mosque facing the shrine, built in 1983 and named for
the saint, hosts the five daily prayers and Friday congregational prayer; *niyāz* (food
offerings) is distributed in the surrounding streets.

## Condition and Custodianship
The Auqaf Department assumed responsibility for the site in 1972 and is recorded as its
current custodian. It is plainly reported that the shrine is gradually deteriorating
for lack of proper care, that the Auqaf Department is not carrying out its maintenance
properly, and that such arrangements as are made are made by local people and pilgrims who
love the saint. Shah Gohar Peer is said to have written no book himself, there
being no such custom in his time, though later saints and people who had seen him are said
to have written about him.

2026.

Events: Annual Urs (7th-9th Muharram): Mehfil-e-Naat and langar, deliberately without dhol or dhamal per the current custodians' account of the saint's own wishes. Weekly Mehfil-e-Naat and langar on Thursday nights and Fridays.
Description:
## Overview

The shrine of Hazrat Tahir Bandagi Qadri stands in the Miani Sahib Graveyard of Lahore, said to be the largest graveyard in Asia, and his tomb is the oldest seat within it. A scholar and teacher of the Qur'an, he built a mosque, a *madrasa*, or religious school, and a library on this ground in his own lifetime, and he was buried beside his mosque when he died in 1630. It is said that the graveyard grew up around his tomb over the following centuries, as generation after generation asked to be laid to rest near him. Visitors come every day to pray and to make their petitions, and in Muharram, the first month of the Islamic year, hundreds of thousands gather for his *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of his death.

The graveyard is reported to cover some 475 *kanals*, a local measure of land. Hazrat Tahir Bandagi is remembered as a Sufi, or Muslim mystic, of the Qadiri order, as a disciple of Hazrat Mujaddid Alf Sani, honoured as the renewer of the faith for Islam's second millennium, and as a man who lived by his pen and kept away from the rich.

## The Saint

He was born in Lahore in 1576, though accounts of where he came from differ. His father, Fazlullah, gave him his early education, and he went on to memorise the Qur'an. He is also known as Shaikh Muhammad Tahir Lahori.

For advanced learning he became the *murid*, the pledged disciple, of Hazrat Shah Sikandar, son of Pir Kamal Kaithali, under whom he first completed his training, and he became Shah Sikandar's *khalifa*, an authorised deputy. Accounts of his master differ, but Shah Sikandar is the master most often named, and he is credited with giving him the name Tahir Bandagi. Shah Sikandar is said to have told him, "you are meant for the spiritual reformation of people; simply remain devoted to the service of humanity at all times."

There was also, it is reported, a real trial in his life. For a period he became enamoured of a Hindu woman and stepped back from his religious work. Those who wished him well are said to have appealed on his behalf to Hazrat Mujaddid Alf Sani, Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi. He then returned to his path, formally became the Mujaddid's disciple as well, and later taught the Mujaddid's own children, among them Shaikh Muhammad Masum. The episode is told plainly, as part of his story rather than something to smooth over. It is told in more than one way, and one telling makes it a prophecy fulfilled. The Mujaddid, it is said, had foretold that one of those present would become a *kafir*, an unbeliever. Then, at Sirhind, Shaikh Tahir drew the *qashqa*, the forehead mark, and went and sat in a temple, having become a Hindu, until the Mujaddid prayed, his prayer was answered and Shaikh Tahir repented.

He attended the Mujaddid, who is also called the Imam-e Rabbani, gained great benefits from him and is counted among his *khalifas*, a man extremely strict in keeping the *shariah*, the religious law. The Mujaddid is said to have conferred on him the *qutbiyat* of Lahore, the rank of its *qutb*, the axis or pole of the saints and the highest spiritual station. It was at the Mujaddid's direction that he set about guiding the people of Lahore, and thousands reached high spiritual stations through him.

He is counted a Qadiri, a follower of the Sufi order founded by Abd al-Qadir Gilani, and he is remembered as the *qutb* of his age in the Qadiri *silsila*, the chain of spiritual descent from master to disciple. Most often he is counted a Naqshbandi as well, of the order founded by Baha-ud-Din Naqshband, in its Mujaddidi line, named after the Mujaddid, and the shrine's full name, Darbar Hazrat Tahir Bandagi Qadri Naqshbandi Mujaddidi, joins the two. He is also said to have initiated others into the Qadiri, Naqshbandi and Suhrawardi orders, receiving their *bai'at*, the oath of initiation into a Sufi order.

He was a worshipper of God, a man of *kashf*, insight into hidden things, and of *karamat*, miraculous deeds and spiritual gifts, and he was accomplished in the outward sciences too. It was said of him that no seeker, whether of faith or of the world, who came to his door went away empty. He lived by his pen: he copied out books of hadith, the sayings of the Prophet, and of *tafsir*, commentary on the Qur'an, and subsisted by presenting them. All his life he went to no rich man, nor admitted the rich to his own *darbar*, or court.

His nights passed in instructing his attendants and in worship. It is said that he spent them absorbed in *zikr*, the remembrance of God, rather than in the comforts that came with his following, that from time to time he fasted and denied himself for stretches of fifteen to twenty days, and that he never allowed the crowds who gathered around him to make him proud. In his later years he married twice, to Mah-e-Khanam and to Ismatullah, the daughter of an Afghan king. In the nineteenth century none of his descendants remained.

He died in the reign of the emperor Shah Jahan, on a Thursday, at the forenoon hour, on 8 Muharram 1040 AH in the Islamic calendar, which is 8 August 1630, and was buried beside his own mosque. Accounts of his age at death differ; the age the shrine keeps is 54, in keeping with his birth in 1576.

## His Disciples

Among his *khalifas* were Abu Muhammad Qadiri, Sayyid Sufi, Shaikh Adam Banuri and Shah Ghulan Sarmast, who has his own tomb in Lahore, outside the Mori Gate, inside the government garden. Shaikh Adam Banuri came to him on foot, walking from Banur to Lahore. In his own account, written in Persian, Adam Banuri told how he received from Shaikh Tahir the *nisbat-e jazba*, the spiritual bond of rapture, which had reached Shaikh Tahir through Shah Sikandar.

Within Shaikh Tahir's enclosure lies the grave of Hazrat Abu Muhammad Qadiri Lahori, his *murid* in the Qadiri *silsila*, whose family were *khadims*, or servants, of Shaikh Tahir. One line of Shaikh Tahir's spiritual descendants runs through three generations: Shaikh Muhammad Fazil Qadri Batalvi was the *murid* and *khalifa* of Shaikh Muhammad Afzal Kalanauri, who was the *murid* of Shaikh Abu Muhammad Lahori, who was the *murid* of Shaikh Muhammad Tahir Lahori.

Shaikh Tahir is said to have wished to visit the tomb of Shah Husain to seek his help, *istimdad*. A book, the *Tazkira-e Mujaddidiya*, whose author is otherwise unknown, has been ascribed to him by Muhammad Din Fauq.

## The Shrine

The land that is now the Miani Sahib Graveyard was given to him in his lifetime so that he could teach, and he settled there in the time of the emperor Jahangir. On it he built a mosque, a *madrasa* and a library, a *kutub khana*, and he taught the Qur'an there himself. He taught *fiqh*, Islamic law, hadith and *tafsir* to students free of charge, made many *murids* and gave instruction in *suluk*, the Sufi path. Because he was learned, accomplished and a perfect *faqir*, a mystic who has embraced spiritual poverty, thousands became his *murids* and pupils within a few years, and a magnificent settlement grew up around him.

The shrine's tradition tells of a raid in his lifetime, though accounts differ over when it happened. Sikh raiders, believing that gold was hidden inside boxes on the premises, broke in and found only books; on discovering this, they threw them back into the locality and left.

When he died, his resting place beside the mosque became his shrine, and the rulers and disciples of the period are said to have kept it under careful administrative care from the start. After his death the quarter stayed settled until the end of Muslim rule. By the 1880s the quarter that had grown up around him lay in ruins, but his tomb still stood, counted among the buildings outside the city, and some of the old fabric of his *madrasa* remained.

His enclosure was then the first and largest in the graveyard: a spacious wall of *pakka*, or fired, brick, inside which were thousands of graves, old and new. Within this great wall stood another large platform of fired brick, and on it his tomb, built of fired brick and plastered with lime.

The tomb has been rebuilt. The present tomb was raised by a Gilani pir, and it is said that when the old tomb was excavated for the new construction, it was found to have been built exactly in the style of the tomb of Hazrat Mujaddid Alf Sani.

His walled enclosure, the *chahar-diwari*, became a burial ground for others too. Sayyid Munawwar Ali Shah Naqshbandi Suhrawardi Lahori, who died in 1264 AH, lies inside it, and Shaikh Haji Ramzan Lahori Chishti lies near the tomb. In the nineteenth century other graves were located by his wall: one row adjoined it, another grave lay in its eastern corner and another to its north, and a neighbouring enclosure stood beside it.

## Keepers of the Shrine

The shrine is overseen today by its *Gaddi Nasheen*, its present custodians, and several people are formally employed as its staff; they are said to consider caring for the shrine all the year round a privilege rather than a job.

In the nineteenth century the office of *sajjada nashin*, the custodian who sits on the saint's prayer carpet, was disputed. Its holders in that century included Sayyid Mansur, *sajjada nashin* of Shaikh Muhammad Tahir's *khanqah*, the lodge where a Sufi's disciples gather, and Sayyid Shahsawar, *sajjada nashin* of his tomb. Sayyid Shahsawar came of a Gilani family whose line is traced to Sayyid Abd al-Qadir Lahori, son of Sayyid Jalal al-Din Baghdadi, who settled at Lahore in the reign of Akbar and married a daughter of Nawab Mir Kifayat Khan; one of the family, Bahadur, son of Chiragh Shah, was an engraver of seals. Accounts of the family's line differ. Later the office was held by Pir Sher Husain Tahiri, whose name Tahiri is taken from the saint himself.

## Devotion and Festivals

A mosque stands beside the shrine, where the five daily prayers are held, and visitors come both to pray and to recite the *Fatiha*, the opening chapter of the Qur'an, and to make their own supplications. Some families have come for generations, following their parents and grandparents before them. Daily attendance is put at 1,200 to 1,600 visitors. Every week, on Thursday nights and Fridays, the shrine holds *Mehfil-e-Naat*, gatherings for the recitation of *naat*, poems in praise of the Prophet, and *langar*, the free communal kitchen.

It is said that the shrine owes its continuing importance to answered prayer across generations: families who saw their petitions answered here return, and bring their children to do the same. Visitors describe Hazrat Tahir Bandagi as a *wali-e-kamil*, a "perfect saint", who was granted visions of the Prophet and of other venerable elders more than once, and devotees offer the presence of jinn, unseen spirits, and of other noble burials nearby as further evidence, in their eyes, of his spiritual standing.

His *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, falls every year on the 7th, 8th and 9th of Muharram, and an estimated 250,000 to 300,000 pilgrims come across the three days. The present custodians say that Hazrat Tahir Bandagi did not care for the *dhol*, a large barrel drum, or for *dhamal*, ecstatic devotional dancing to the beat of the drum, and the *ʿurs* is kept restrained accordingly, centred on *Mehfil-e-Naat* and *langar* rather than on music or dancing. In the nineteenth century his *ʿurs* was kept by the *sajjada nashin* and the graveyard's gravediggers in the first ten days of Muharram.

## Legends

Several traditions are attached to the shrine, and not all of them are agreed on even by today's visitors.

One holds that while he was leading the *Taraweeh*, the night prayers of Ramadan, the month of fasting, he was granted a vision of the Prophet Muhammad, who told him that whoever looked upon him, learned from him or was buried near him would enter Paradise; this is offered as the reason so many notable figures chose to be buried around his tomb. He himself, it is said, used to say that he had asked of God that whoever was buried within the enclosure of his tomb after his death should be of Paradise.

A second, more contested tradition concerns jinn. Graves near the shrine are popularly said to belong to jinn who watch over the site, and some visitors say they have seen figures in human form vanish before their eyes. Others do not accept this. They say that although the graves exist, they have never themselves seen any jinn or wild animal there, and they regard the stories of jinn as ignorance, pointing out, from their own study of his life, that Hazrat Tahir Bandagi never taught or endorsed such beliefs. Both views are held among visitors today.

## The Miani Graveyard

In the 1880s the Miani graveyard lay two miles south of Lahore. It had formerly been a village of the Miani people, that is, of *ulama* and *fuzala*, scholars and men of learning, and it was called Panj Pir Dhera, because five graves stood there before the village. The name Miani is said to come from the learned men who lived there, for in Punjabi a *maulvi*, a learned and accomplished man, is called *miana*. The place is also called Miani Sharif.

In the reign of Akbar, it is said, Miani was a village where only learned men lived. Its chief was Hafiz Jan Muhammad, father of Hazrat Abu Muhammad Qadiri, and after Hafiz Jan Muhammad's death Abu Muhammad was made its head. A dispute over a point of law later emptied the village, until a man appointed by the king settled there and it was peopled again. Shah Muhammad Muqim, travelling to Lahore, halted at the Miani graveyard, near the tomb of Shaikh Muhammad Tahir.

By the 1880s thousands of graves had been made there and many enclosures of fired brick built, and the unfinished enclosure of Rani Gul Begum, a woman of the courtesan caste, stood there too. For the ten or twelve years before, general burial had been stopped, and only those who had such enclosures still buried their dead there. The gravediggers, the *gorkans*, served the graveyard, and in the nineteenth century, whenever a body was brought, the family of the dead paid them their due and gave the *sajjada nashin* something besides, as they could.

## Legacy

Accounts of how the graveyard began differ, but Hazrat Tahir Bandagi Qadri's tomb is the oldest seat of the Miani Sahib Graveyard, and a Chishti and a Naqshbandi Suhrawardi saint lie beside him. By the 1880s all Muslims were said to acknowledge his greatness; the great family of his *silsila* was then at the town of Batala, with thousands of *murids* across the Punjab, and countless *karamat* of his were written in the lives of the saints.

His memory was kept in verse as well. A chronogram, a verse whose letters, read as numbers, give a year, was written on him as a quatrain, and it opens by naming him:

شیخ طاہر پاک باز و پاک دین
اوج عرفان پر تھے مثل آفتاب

Separately, the year of his death is drawn from a single word, *gham*, grief.
