Description:
## Overview

Darbar Malik Ahmad Ayaz is the shrine of Malik Ahmad Ayaz, the slave and beloved of Sultan Mahmud Ghaznavi and governor of Lahore, in Lahore's crowded Shah Alam Market, near Darbar Ali Hajveri Ganj Bakhsh. Ayaz is remembered as the man who rebuilt Lahore after Mahmud's conquest, and as a servant so devoted that, in mystical poetry, his king became "the slave of his slave". The shrine is an active Muslim shrine, visited by people from distant places, non-Muslims among them, and its *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of his death, draws tens of thousands.

He is also known simply as Malik Ayaz. In the nineteenth century he was honoured among the saints as Shaikh Ayaz Lahori, the slave and beloved of Shah Mahmud Ghaznavi, and it was said of him that God had given him both outward and inward wealth. The shrine follows the Ahl e Sunnat, the Sunni tradition, and names its *silsila*, its chain of spiritual transmission, as Ghaznavi.

## The Life of Malik Ayaz

Accounts of where Ayaz came from differ. Tradition at the shrine holds that he was educated in Georgia in 993 AD, and that when his country was attacked he was enslaved and taken for sale to the slave market of Baghdad, slave dealing being then the norm. Too weak to attract buyers, he was passed over until Mahmud Ghaznavi came by and asked his price. When the king's minister questioned the purchase, Mahmud answered that what he saw in the boy the minister could not see. His words raised greed in the seller's heart, and the price asked was ten thousand dinars; Mahmud paid it and enrolled Ayaz among his soldiers.

Though the Sultan had many thousands of slaves, Ayaz was the foremost of them. Mahmud made him the intimate of his private assembly and the companion of his select gatherings, and preferred him above all his servants and retinue. Tradition holds that the relation of master and slave turned into love, and that Ayaz spent his whole life in devotion to Mahmud, while the Sultan in turn was caught in the noose of his love.

In the story of the melon, the king cut a melon with his own hand and fed it to Ayaz, then tasted it himself and found it bitter, and asked why Ayaz had said nothing. Ayaz replied that, having had sweetness from his master's hand all his life, he had no cause to complain of one bitter piece.

The king's family and ministers are said to have mocked the closeness between the two. When the minister tested them by summoning everyone at midnight to eat, Ayaz alone appeared fully prepared, while the others arrived late, or intoxicated and asleep. Mahmud made him his minister, yet Ayaz always regarded himself as a slave. Each night he set aside his costly clothes and took out the old garments in which he had been brought for sale, so as to remember his past, sit alone and please his God. Mahmud is also said to have wished to hand his own place to Ayaz; Ayaz declined, asking that it go instead to one of his two sons, Saad, and the king relinquished his power.

Ayaz outlived his king. After Mahmud's death in 1030, Masud took the throne, and in his reign his son Majdud, then a young boy, was made governor of the Punjab; Ayaz was appointed his *atalik*, or tutor, and came with him. When Masud died and his son Maudud took the throne, Majdud rebelled and set up a separate sultanate in Hindustan. Maudud marched against him, and while Lahore was under siege, on the day of Eid, Majdud suddenly died, and Maudud established his hold over the Punjab.

Maudud tried hard to take Ayaz with him to Ghazni, but Ayaz would not go. He renounced the world and took to the company of *faqirs*, wandering mystics; he received complete *faiz*, spiritual grace, from the elders of Lahore, and gave away his boundless wealth to the *faqirs* and the poor for God's sake. The last ten years of his life, tradition holds, were largely given to *dhikr*, the remembrance of God.

He died in 450 AH, though accounts of the year differ, and was buried inside the city of Lahore. At the shrine it is told that he fell suddenly ill and died; it is said that he was poisoned out of resentment at the love shown him, though in some places it is said that he died a natural death.

## The Restorer of Lahore

When Ayaz came to govern Lahore, the city had been ruined by war, and its systems of livelihood, food, trade and wages were broken. By his intelligence, it is said, he gave it shape again and set it on its own feet. Tradition goes further and counts him the founder of Lahore. When Sultan Mahmud Ghaznavi attacked the city, Raja Anangpal, son of Raja Jaipal, was overthrown and fled to Hind, and Mahmud's army plundered Lahore; all its people left, so that not a breathing soul remained in it. Then Ayaz, taking the Sultan's permission, settled the city again, summoning people from far and wide to live in it.

After Mahmud's sack, the city stayed unpeopled for some years. When Malik Ayaz became *hakim*, or governor, of the Punjab by the king's order, he turned to peopling it again and obtained from the Sultan a *farman*, a royal decree, of permission. He went about the work with such zeal that within a few years the wilderness became a mine of *ulama*, religious scholars, and men of learning. Malik Ayaz, the favourite of the Sultan's eye and without equal in goodness and discernment, also raised a fort of baked brick, and the city was rebuilt. The tradition that he refounded Lahore is not universally accepted, and has been dismissed as "later writers' conjecture".

Three of Lahore's gates are tied to him. The settlement began from the *mohalla*, or quarter, called Lahori Mandi, and the gate there was built first of all and named the Lahori Darwaza. The Mori Darwaza is his monument of victory: Mahmud had breached the walls at that spot, and when Ayaz settled the city again he set up a gate there as a memorial of the victory. The Bhati Darwaza dates from his settlement too, for the Bhat community settled inside it after Ayaz had settled the city. Even after his settlement, Lahore remained now in a state of progress, now of decline. It was into this resettled city that Ali Hajveri, the saint of Data Darbar, arrived.

## The Shrine

Tradition holds that the tomb was built at this very place after the death of Malik Ayaz, that the Ghaznavi Sultanate built the Darbar, as the shrine is called, and that it was later kept in good condition by rajas and maharajas. It has since known loss. The water of the Darbar was polluted, and part of its ground was lost in the Sikh era and part to the surrounding market, so that the site is small today.

Beside the Darbar stands a mosque named after Malik Ayaz, where the five daily prayers are offered. The shrine is under the supervision of the Auqaf Department, the government's department of religious endowments, which is also the body responsible for its present condition.

The shrine stands in Shah Alam Market, said to be the largest market in Asia, and extremely crowded. Its *mazār*, or tomb, lies near Darbar Ali Hajveri Ganj Bakhsh, the shrine of Data Ganj Bakhsh, still a popular place of pilgrimage in Lahore and for the people of the Punjab. The congestion around the small site is said to keep many people from reaching it, so that both the fame of Malik Ayaz and the enthusiasm of his visitors have gradually waned. Residents of this densely populated neighbourhood are largely unaware of the life of the man buried there, though Allama Iqbal, Kaniya Lal and other writers are said to have written books about him.

## Devotion and Festivals

Visitors come from distant places. Non-Muslims visit too, some have made documentaries about Malik Ayaz, and his stories appear in books. Every day *diyas*, oil lamps, and *prasād*, consecrated food, are offered at the shrine, and some 700 to 800 people come each day.

The *ʿurs* is held on the 12th, 13th and 14th of Zil Hajj. Its observances include the lighting of lamps, the changing of the sheets, bathing, and the eating of food at the site, and it draws 40,000 to 50,000 people.

The place is held spiritually important because Malik Ayaz fought alongside the king, served the people, protected their lives and property and instilled the spirit of Islam in them; because after Mahmud Ghaznavi's death he left his residence; and because it was his habit to spend his nights in the remembrance of God. He is remembered as generous, intelligent, loyal, hasty, daring, brave, kind and honest, a soldier who was also a good and devoted man, and people were moved by the example he set of these qualities in his own life.

## Legends

Tradition at the shrine holds that Mahmud fought almost seventeen battles with Hindus, in which Ayaz played the role of the mastermind, and that his faith was so firm that the unbelievers could never sway him. In one such story the king, attacking the "Onkay temple", found its idol suspended in mid-air. Ayaz reasoned that a magnet in the temple held the clay figure up, and that if the walls were demolished it would come down of itself; and so, it is said, it did, to the king's satisfaction.

Another story tells of Ayaz's counsel at Somnath. There the amirs, or nobles, advised Mahmud to take the rajas' crores, sums of tens of millions. When Ayaz was asked, he held that breaking the idol was better, for the renown it would bring among Muslim kings, and that God would give more; and the Sultan broke it with his own hand.

The old clothes of Ayaz are the subject of an allegory by the poet Rūmī, counted among "the finest allegories ever written". In it Ayaz, Mahmud's favourite slave, would look at the worn-out shoes and shabby clothes he had worn before Mahmud chose him for himself, for he needed to remember his former lowly state so that he could appreciate the bounty his lord had bestowed upon him. The lesson Rūmī draws is that "man should likewise remember how weak he was created, and then he will recognize his nothingness before God".

Another story tells of the Huma bird, whose shade, in Persian tradition, conveys kingdom. One day the Huma passed over Mahmud's army, and everybody rushed to be touched by its shade; only Ayaz went into Mahmud's shade, for there was his true kingdom. In this, as one scholar of Sufism put it, he is "like the faithful, who does not seek glory and power from anything created but only from his eternally rich, beloved Lord".

One anecdote turns on obedience. Mahmud was a pious and God-fearing man, and "he wrestled much with his love for Ayaz so that he should not diverge" from the Path of the Law. At a carousal, with the wine affecting him, he looked at the curls of Ayaz and drew him to himself; but the 'watchman' of the Qur'anic verse warned him not to mingle sin with love. Fearing that he could not withstand the hosts of Ayaz's locks, he gave Ayaz a knife and told him to cut off his curls in the middle. Ayaz "doubled back his locks to get the measurement, executed the king's command, and laid the two tresses before Mahmud". This ready obedience became a fresh cause of love, and Mahmud gave him gold and jewels beyond his usual wont before falling into a drunken sleep.

Next morning Mahmud saw the clipped tresses and was seized by remorse. No courtier dared ask him why, until his Chief Chamberlain, the Hajib ʿAli ibn Qarib, sent the poet ʿUnsuri in to restore his temper. ʿUnsuri extemporised a quatrain, which in English reads in part:

*Why deem it shame a fair one's curls to shear, … When clipped the Cypress doth most trim appear* (translated by Edward G. Browne)

Mahmud had the poet's mouth filled twice with precious stones, and drank wine to those verses until nightfall, "whereby his melancholy was dissipated". The tale is told among stories of poets, and its moral is that "improvisation is the chief pillar of the Poetic Art".

## Ayaz in Poetry

In poetry the king and his servant became a model of love. The great warrior king of Ghazna, conqueror of northwest India, was transformed in literary tradition into the model of the ideal lover, praised for his close relationship with his officer Ayaz, who appears as the exemplar of the servant; but the king finally became the slave of his slave. In Persian the theme is known as *Shah i gada*, King and Beggar, and the word *niyaz*, humble supplication, is often used in the story of Mahmud and Ayaz for the sake of its fitting rhyme. Several epics have been devoted to the theme, and lyrics abound in allusions to Ayaz. As the same scholar of Sufism put it, "The story of Mahmud and Ayaz is a typical expression of this kind of love and shows, at the same time, how the poets of Iran used historical facts to point out eternal truth", though the romance itself has also been regarded as a literary growth of post-Seljuq times.

The tale of the Sultan's love and *niyaz* and of Ayaz's beauty and *naz*, graceful pride, is set down in most books, above all by Mawlana Zulali, who also gave it a dream version. Verses on this love are found in the *Mahmud-nama* and other treatises, and the Sultan himself is said to have composed them, bringing his inner burning and his hidden secret into view. At the court of love, it was said, king and dervish are equal, and in its presence master and slave are peers. Some poets wrote that Ayaz had no great outward beauty but was matchless in praiseworthy character, so that the Sultan's devotion was to his good disposition and not to his looks.

## Legacy

At the shrine it is said that what should be remembered is the bond between Mahmud Ghaznavi and Malik Ahmad Ayaz, "the love and romance" of king and slave: a slave who would sacrifice his life for his king, and a loyalty so complete that he could answer for it before God on the Day of Judgement. Poets and travellers of that era and of the present are said to have written of these qualities. He is remembered too as the man who gave Lahore a new shape, and he is known still because he "made a new map of Lahore". His settlement of Lahore has also been taken as the turn from which the city's later history runs.

In the words of the same scholar, "The complete surrender of the Turkish officer Ayaz, for whom only Mahmud exists, results in perfect love of the king, who becomes, in a wonderful transformation, the slave of his slave. Ayaz is the symbol of the loving soul".

His name also became a figure of speech. In the nineteenth century it was said of Raja Hira Singh that he was looked upon as an Ayaz, and called son.

Founded/Opened: 1416 AH (c. 1995–96 CE) — see note; not verified as a construction date
Sufi Saint: Hazrat Mian Qurban Ali Shah Sarkar
Events: *ʿurs* on 24, 25 and 26 Rabīʿ al-Thānī (dhol, changing of the chadar, *ghusl*, *langar*); weekly Thursday public gathering with *dhikr*, *naʿt* and *langar*; five daily prayers in the courtyard mosque; large door open Thursday, Friday and Sunday
Description:
## Overview
Darbar Mian Qurban Ali Shah is a Muslim shrine at Mint Stop, Lahore, dedicated to Hazrat Mian Qurban Ali Shah Sarkar. The site's *silsila* (Sufi order, and the lineage of spiritual transmission within it) is reported as Naqshbandī Mujaddidī, within Ahl-e Sunnat. A mosque named after the saint stands in the same courtyard as the tomb. The site has been in the charge of the government Auqaf (religious endowments) Department since 2005.

## The figure, as the tradition relates him
It is reported that Hazrat Qurban Ali Shah was born in 1341 AH in Malerkotla, India, that his given name was Qurban Ali, and that people later came to call him Mian Qurban Ali Shah in recognition of his learning. His father is named as Hazrat Mian Fazal Deen, said to have been a great religious scholar who held thousands of disciples in a relationship of *pīrī-murīdī* (spiritual mentorship) and who taught his son the whole of his education before instructing him to devote his life to preaching. Devotees relate that virtuous people and Sufis were repeatedly born into this family, and that its members kept the call of Islam alive throughout their lives.

He reportedly left his ancestral home in youth at his father's command, never returned, and preached along the way until he reached the Mint Stop area of Lahore, which he made his final abode. Tradition holds that people were drawn to his camp of their own accord; that he arranged food, drink and lodging for all who came, young and old alike; that thousands took *baiʿat* (the oath of allegiance to a spiritual guide) at his hand, often with their entire families; and that neither he nor his family ever compelled anyone's conversion, people entering Islam instead out of regard for his learning and character. Among those he brought into Islam, it is reported, were a large number of people named as "Marzaiyas (Ahmadis/Qadianis)". Devotees relate that he served people by day and spent his nights in *dhikr* (remembrance of God), and that although his bearing was that of a simple dervish he did not disclose his spiritual station. He is reported to have passed on the *gaddi* (spiritual seat) in the last part of his life, died on 25 Rabīʿ al-Thānī, and been buried at his camp.

## Reputation and *karāmāt*
It is reported that those seeking a cure for illness, the unemployed seeking work, and people caught in difficulty and worry would present themselves to him, that he would pray to God on their behalf, and that those prayers were granted without delay. Devotees still come to pray through his *waseela* (intercession) and say they do not return empty-handed. Those who met him in life are described as knowing his spiritual manifestations at first hand; others entered his allegiance on the testimony of their elders. His devotees hold that, having left the world while engaged in preaching, his standing is no less than a martyr's, and that martyrs remain alive.

## The site and its buildings
His camp itself reportedly became his shrine: after his death a shrine was raised over the burial place, and a mosque was built in his name alongside it. Beneath the tomb is a basement, closed to the general public, reportedly the room where he kept his nightly *dhikr*; it has been left in its original condition and is said to remain exactly as he left it. His special disciple is buried beside him. The Auqaf Department took responsibility for the shrine and mosque in 2005, but most maintenance and decoration is still carried out by devotees themselves. The shrine was reconstructed again in 2022. No graveyard is reported at the site.

## Regular observances
The five daily prayers are offered in the courtyard mosque. On Thursday, Friday and Sunday the large door of the shrine is kept open; on the remaining days the small door is open, and worshippers and pilgrims come throughout. Every Thursday there is a public gathering with *dhikr*, *naʿt* (devotional verse in praise of the Prophet) recitation and *langar* (free communal food); a set number of people is said to attend. No *qawwālī* is reported at the site.

## *ʿUrs*
The annual *ʿurs* (death-anniversary observance) is held on 24, 25 and 26 Rabīʿ al-Thānī. It includes drumming (dhol), the changing of the chadar over the grave, ritual washing (*ghusl*) and *langar*.

## Attendance and custodianship
Daily attendance is put at 500 to 600 people, and at the annual *ʿurs* at some 50,000 to 60,000 pilgrims. Residents of the neighbourhood around the shrine pay their respects there each morning before going to work. The custodian of record is the government Auqaf Department. It is also reported that the saint's successor in the *gaddi* was Haji Tufail, and that after Haji Tufail's death his sons hold the position of managing the site.

## Writings
It is reported that a disciple published a discourse on the saint's life a short while ago, that it became widely popular, and that readers subsequently entered the saint's allegiance in greater numbers.

## Bibliography
- Shrines Project field survey, Darbar Mian Qurban Ali Shah (surveyor: Saifullah), 14 July 2026.

Internal contradictions and gaps in the source. None of these are resolved in the public
prose above; none should be silently harmonised by a later editor.

1. FOUNDING YEAR vs NARRATIVE. Q6 ("year founded") = "1416 Hijri", c. 1995-96 CE. But Q8
   and Q9 both state the shrine was built after the saint's death, by others. 1416 AH is
   exactly 75 lunar years after the stated birth year of 1341 AH (Q9), and no death year
   is given anywhere in the survey — only the day, 25 Rabi-ul-Sani. The most economical
   reading is that the respondent answered the "founded" question with the death year.
   Flagged rather than resolved: the survey does not say so.

2. NO DEATH YEAR AT ALL. Q9 gives "25 Rabi-ul-Sani" with no year. The entry therefore
   carries a death day and no death year. The urs dates (24-26 Rabi-ul-Sani, Q13) do
   bracket the stated death day consistently — that is the one date check in this survey
   that passes cleanly.

3. WHO BUILT THE SHRINE — two different answers. Q8: "His disciples built a beautiful
   shrine, and alongside the shrine, a mosque was also constructed in his name." Q9: "The
   wealthy people of that era took responsibility for his shrine and constructed a
   beautiful shrine along with a mosque." Same building event, two different patrons
   (disciples / wealthy notables). The prose above attributes the construction to neither
   and says only that it was built after his death.

4. LENGTH OF RESIDENCE AT MINT STOP — two different answers. Q8: he "established his
   final camp at this location of Mint Stop, Lahore, where he spent the remaining part of
   his life." Q9: he "arrived at this area of Mint Stop in Lahore and stayed for a short
   while, but made this very place his final abode." A short stay and the remainder of a
   life are not the same claim.

5. SUCCESSION — singular vs plural. Q9: "he passed on his spiritual seat (gaddi) to his
   special disciples" (plural). Q16: "he passed on his spiritual seat (gaddi) to his
   successor disciple, Haji Tufail" (a single named successor). One or more successors is
   left open above.

6. CUSTODIANSHIP — two answers standing in tension. Q15 (custodian question): "Government
   Mehkama Auqaaf", flat. Q16: after Haji Tufail's death "his sons hold the position of
   managing it". Q8 adds that although Auqaf took charge in 2005, "most of the maintenance
   and decoration is taken care of by his devotees themselves". Both the Auqaf answer and
   the hereditary-management answer are reported above, side by side, without deciding
   which body actually controls the site. The devotee-maintenance detail is retained as
   given: it is the nearest thing to a maintenance-shortfall report in this survey, and
   has not been softened.

7. THE BOOK — asserted and denied within the same submission. Q16: "A short while ago, his
   disciple published a discourse on his life, which became a source of great popularity
   among the people." Q20 (upload a book or pamphlet): blank. Trailing export column
   "Column 1": "No book available". Reported above only as a claim of the tradition, with
   no title and no citation, per instruction.

8. "SHAH" — honorific or Sayyid descent? Q9 explains the name as an honorific earned by
   learning: "His original name was Qurban Ali, but later, on account of his knowledge,
   people began calling him by the name of Mian Qurban Ali Shah." Q19 instead attributes
   to him "spiritual majesty and nobility (Sadaat character)", i.e. implies Sayyid
   descent. The entry makes no descent claim and uses "Hazrat" throughout, never "Sayyid".

9. SILSILA UNSUPPORTED BY THE BIOGRAPHY. Q5 answers "Naqshbandi Majdadi - Ahl e Sunnat",
   but nothing in Q8, Q9, Q10, Q11, Q16 or Q19 mentions a Naqshbandi affiliation, a
   Naqshbandi chain, or any Naqshbandi practice. All spiritual authority in the biography
   descends from his father, Hazrat Mian Fazal Deen, whose own affiliation is never given.
   The silsila field therefore rests on the one-line Q5 answer alone. Note also that the
   Q5 answer mixes a silsila (Naqshbandi Mujaddidi) with a sect (Ahl-e Sunnat); the survey
   spelling is "Majdadi" and has been normalised to Mujaddidī in the entry.

10. MIGRATION UNDATED. Birth is placed at Malerkotla, India (Q9); life, death and shrine
    at Lahore. The survey never dates or explains the move, and no context has been
    supplied for it here.

11. WEEKLY ATTENDANCE FIGURE WITHHELD. Q12 says the Thursday gathering has "a specific
    number of people" participating but never states the number. Daily and urs figures are
    given (Q14) and are reported.

12. REGISTER NOTE, NOT A CONTRADICTION. Q19 is written in the second person, addressing the
    saint directly ("your father", "you became a scholar", "you included thousands"). A
    reader skimming the transcript could mistake these for statements about the surveyor.
    All Q19 material has been converted to third person above.

13. QAWWALI. Not reported at this site. Q12 lists mosque prayers, and a Thursday gathering
    with Zikr, Naat and langar; Q13 lists dhol at the urs. The absence is stated in the
    entry so that a later editor does not read it as an omission.

Name: Darbar Sakhi Shah Chan Charagh
Events: Annual urs; Muharram tazia procession (9 Muharram); commemorative mach bonfire
Description:
## Overview

In the crowded lanes of the old walled city of Rawalpindi stands the *darbar* of Sakhi Shah Chan Charagh, revered across the Pothohar plateau as the patron saint of the city. His very name — *Chan Charagh*, "the moon and the lamp" — carries the imagery of light that runs through everything remembered about him, and for generations the people of Rawalpindi have looked to his shrine as the spiritual heart of their town. It is a modest complex by the standards of the great Punjabi shrines, tucked among bazaars and old *havelis*, yet on the days of remembrance it draws crowds from the whole district, and its steady lamp-lit devotion has outlasted empires, partition, and the ceaseless rebuilding of the city around it.

## The Life of the Saint

The saint's given name is traditionally said to have been Shah Zaman, and he is remembered as a *sayyid* — a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad — whose lineage is traced through Imam Musa al-Kazim, the seventh Imam venerated especially in the Shia tradition. According to the accounts preserved by his devotees, his forebears came from the city of Mashhad in Iran and settled at Chakwal, in the Salt Range country south of Rawalpindi, before he made his way to the town with which his name is now inseparably linked. He is generally placed in the eighteenth century, in the twilight of Mughal power, though the datings given for him vary and the shrine is spoken of by some as being three to four centuries old; in the absence of firm documentary record these figures are best treated as traditional rather than exact.

He is said to have been the disciple of his own maternal uncle, Sayyid Shah Inayat, himself a celebrated *wali* or friend of God, and the sources describe him as a cousin or spiritual kinsman of the great Bari Imam of Islamabad, binding him into the web of saintly families that spans the Pothohar. The best-loved legend of his life tells that, on his arrival at Rawalpindi, he stumbled — or, in the more devotional telling, deliberately sat down — in a burning potter's oven, and there remained steadfast in prayer and penance amid the flames. It is from this episode that the shrine takes one of its most striking features: the great bonfire, known in the local speech as the *mach*, which is kindled at the site in commemoration and which pilgrims still gather around.

## The Shrine and its Devotional Life

The shrine complex today holds the marble grave-chamber of the saint together with the tombs of his descendants, companions, and adherents, and it incorporates an *imambargah*, reflecting the strongly Shia colouring of its devotion. The great commemorative bonfire remains a focus of ritual, and the calendar of the *darbar* is marked above all by the observances of Muharram: a *tazia* procession sets out from the shrine on the ninth of the month, and the site becomes a gathering place for the mourning assemblies that fill the old city in that season. An annual *urs*, the celebration of the saint's union with the divine, is also kept, drawing devotees who come to offer *fatiha*, tie threads of intention, and seek the *baraka* — the blessing — believed to linger about his resting place.

The saint's spiritual legacy is said to have been carried forward by a circle of disciples, among whom tradition names Sakhi Shah Raza, Qamar Ali Shah, and Sakhi Shah Sharaf; the most romantic of these stories concerns a figure remembered as Kochak Ali Sultan, described as a Mughal prince who, drawn by the light he had glimpsed in the saint, abandoned a life of ease for the path of the dervish. Such narratives, whatever their historical basis, express the enduring theme of the shrine: the exchange of worldly power for inward illumination.

## Legacy

For the inhabitants of Rawalpindi, Shah Chan Charagh is not a remote historical personage but a living presence and protector, his shrine woven into the ordinary rhythms of the old city — a place to bring newborn children, to pray in times of trouble, and to mark the turning of the sacred year. In a garrison city that has grown enormously in modern times, the *darbar* preserves a thread of continuity with the Rawalpindi of the pre-colonial and colonial past, when the walled town clustered close about its saints. It stands as a characteristic example of the small urban shrine that anchors civic identity across Pakistani Punjab, and of the particular devotional world of the Pothohar, where Sufi veneration and the mourning of the Prophet's household flow together.

## Bibliography

- *Rawalpindi District Gazetteer* (Punjab Government, colonial-era editions), for the topography and religious life of the old city.
- Reports in *Dawn* on the annual *urs* and Muharram observances at the shrine of Shah Chan Charagh, Rawalpindi.
- Local hagiographical (*malfuzat* and *tazkira*) traditions concerning Sayyid Shah Zaman "Chan Charagh" and his lineage.
- General studies of Sufi shrine culture and Muharram devotion in the Pothohar region of Punjab.

Name: Darbar Wasif Ali Wasif
Sufi Saint: Hazrat Wasif Ali Wasif Awan (born Muhammad Wasif Awan; "Wasif" was his pen name/takhallus)
Events: Annual Urs (12-14 January): chadar tabdeeli, ghusl, chiraghan, Mehfil-e-Naat Shareef, Mehfil-e-Mushaira
Description:
## Overview

Darbar Wasif Ali Wasif sits within Lahore's Miani Sahib Graveyard, in a plot set aside beside the wider burial ground — reported to be one of the largest graveyards in Asia, holding the graves of many well-known and pious figures alongside it. The shrine holds the grave of Hazrat Wasif Ali Wasif Awan, a twentieth-century Urdu poet and spiritual teacher. It was built by his son, Kashif Wasif, after his death in January 1993, and his family is reported to have maintained responsibility for the shrine since.

## Wasif Ali Wasif — life and career

It is reported that his given name was Muhammad Wasif Awan; "Wasif" was a pen name (*takhallus*) he took as an Urdu literary figure and poet, and he became known by the fuller form Wasif Ali Wasif. He was born on 15 January 1929 in Shahpur, Khushab District. His father, Muhammad Arif, was himself a teacher. His family reportedly belonged to the Khushab region and the Awan tribe, whose lineage (*shajra nasab*) is said — by the family's own account, as recorded here — to trace back to Hazrat Ali (R.A.); this is reported as stated, not independently verified.

He began his education in Khushab, passing his middle-school examination there in 1939. His father then sent him to his maternal grandfather in Jhang, a move described as transformative: his grandfather had been associated with the Muslim League and had spent time with Quaid-e-Azam. In Jhang, he passed Matriculation in 1944, Intermediate in 1946, and his B.A. in 1948, all from Government College Jhang and all in the first division. He went on to Government College Lahore for his M.A., and passed the Civil Services examination in June 1954. He is reported to have been offered a government post on the strength of this but to have declined it, turning instead toward writing and solitary devotion.

He founded an institution called "English College" in Anarkali, Lahore, which reportedly served as a gathering place for people of every background, where free food (*langar*) and offerings (*niyaz*) were continuously distributed, and where he began guiding visitors and devoting himself to their concerns. He later addressed large public gatherings — reportedly "over a thousand nights" of addresses at Lakshmi Chowk and Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore, taking questions on both spiritual and worldly matters.

## Writing and teachings

He is reported to have written more than 50 books, poetic compositions, poems, ghazals, and *na'at*, in both Urdu and English, among them: *Ghumnam Adeeb*, *Kiran Kiran Suraj*, *Qatra Qatra Qulzum*, *Harf Harf Haqeeqat*, *Mukalma*, *Dil Darya Samundar*, *Ba Say Baat*, *Dareche*, *Zikr-e-Habib (S.A.W.)*, *Guftagu*, *Shab-e-Chiraagh*, *Shab-e-Zaat*, *Baray Barwey*, and *The Beaming Soul*. One saying attributed to him is reported: "You and I are equal; we must please our Lord, and one day we all have to return." His teaching is described as combining devotion to the Prophet (recitation of *na'at*) with an explicit call to patriotism — that people owed a debt of gratitude for their homeland alongside their duties to God.

## Why the shrine is significant

It is reported that people regard him as a pious servant of Allah who gave his life to serving others, and who fulfilled requests made of him without exception. Both Muslims and non-Muslims are said to visit the shrine and study his books, and gatherings held in his name reportedly draw poets, scholars, teachers, and writers. Because he is said to have died in this devoted state, visitors reportedly regard him as a martyr (*shaheed*) in the sense of one who remains, in the words reported, "forever alive with Allah" — a status attributed to popular belief rather than to any formal religious ruling.

## Devotional life and the annual Urs

Free food (*langar*) is distributed daily, and visitors come to make offerings (*niyaz*), pray, and recite Fatiha for him; his books are kept at the shrine for visiting scholars to read. Gatherings called Mehfil-e-Mustafa (S.A.W.) are also held there. The annual Urs is observed every year on 12, 13, and 14 January, with the ceremonial changing of the shrine's cloth covering (*chadar tabdeeli*), ritual washing (*ghusl*), lamp-lighting (*chiraghan*), gatherings in praise of the Prophet (*Mehfil-e-Naat Shareef*), and poetry gatherings (*Mehfil-e-Mushaira*), attended by scholars and devotees; non-Muslim attendance at the shrine is reportedly also common. Daily visitors are estimated at 1,000-1,200, rising to roughly 150,000-200,000 during the Urs. Opposite the shrine is a private library where visitors gather to read and buy his books.

## Custodianship

The shrine remains under the management of Wasif Ali Wasif's family. It is reported that offerings (*hadiya*) collected there fund its ongoing upkeep and construction work, and that devotees take part in caring for it directly.

Name: Dargah / Roza Sufi Shah Inayat Shaheed
Events: Annual urs; Sufi music and remembrance
Description:
## Overview

At Jhok Sharif, in the Sujawal region of lower Sindh, lies the shrine of Sufi Shah Inayat Shaheed, a Sufi saint who died in 1718 and is remembered not only for his mysticism but for a remarkable social experiment and a martyr's death. He gathered around him a community that farmed the land in common, under the principle that the one who sows should eat, and this challenge to the entrenched order of landlords and rulers led, after a long siege, to his execution. He is honoured today as a saint, a martyr and, in modern eyes, a pioneer of social justice, and his darbar, or shrine, at Jhok is a place of pilgrimage and remembrance.

Shah Inayat of Jhok is famous as a Sindhi Sufi martyr. He wrote verse in Persian, and lines of it are quoted in the *Risalo* of Shah Abdul Latif, the great classic of Sindhi poetry. His *dargah*, the shrine complex at Jhok, is a living centre of initiation, custodianship and song, and most of the Hindu Sufis were in touch with Jhok, directly or indirectly.

## The Saint

Shah Inayat, a Sufi or Muslim mystic, belonged to the tradition of *wahdat al-wujud*, the mysticism of the unity of being, and was schooled in the Sufi currents of his age. He travelled in search of knowledge before returning to his native Jhok in lower Sindh, and there, in the early eighteenth century, he established a *khanqah*, a Sufi lodge where disciples gather. He is known as Shah Inayat of Jhok, or of Jhok Sharif, and by the epithet that the shrine's name also carries, *Shaheed* or Shahid, the martyr.

His own master was Sayyid Shah Mehmud Shah al-Qadiri, a Sufi master from Jhok Sharif who was buried at Bijapur, in Karnataka. The lodge at Jhok belongs to the Qadiri order, the Sufi order founded by Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani, and is tied to it through the holders of its seat. Among his own disciples was Rohal Faqir. Shah Inayat is not to be confused with an earlier poet of a similar name, Shah Inat, a Sindhi Sufi poet of the seventeenth century, also called Sayyid Inayat Allah Rizvi, who lived from 1623 to 1712.

## The Commune and the Martyrdom

Shah Inayat's community at Jhok is remembered as one that held and cultivated its land collectively and shared the produce, a way of life summed up in the Sindhi maxim *jeko kheré, so khaé*, "whoever sows, eats." Accounts of the commune differ, and how far he really aimed at a land reform in the modern sense of the word cannot be known; much that is told in his favour is strongly mixed with legend.

The poor and the landless gathered around him. His way of life, his spirituality and his justice attracted not only Sufi adepts, many of them from the mystical centres of the country, but also labourers, slaves and husbandmen from the neighbouring big farms and villages. The Sufi sheikhs and the feudal lords of the country lost large numbers of disciples and workers, while the dargah at Jhok flourished. After an unjustified attack on Jhok led by a group of Sayyids, descendants of the Prophet Muhammad, a considerable amount of land was distributed among his followers.

Such a gathering was an implicit challenge to the great landholders, the *zamindars*, and to the authorities the Mughals had appointed in the region, and it provoked their hostility. In 1717 he was persecuted under the pretext that he was trying to overthrow the established rule, and this was the first obvious sign of the struggle for power in the lower Indus valley. His adversaries denounced him at court and accused him of conspiracy against the Mughal throne. It was the easiest method of blackmail, for the throne had been in constant danger after Aurangzeb's death, and during the confusion in Delhi between the reigns of Farrukh Siyar and Muhammad Shah it was easy to sow mistrust.

Large armies, gathered from various places in Sindh and in Hind, or India, were sent against Jhok, and the Kalhora clan from upper Sindh, who soon afterwards became independent in Sindh, were particularly active in the struggle against him. Shah Inayat was besieged in his *khanqah*, and Jhok held out for four months. Accounts of how the siege ended differ; he is remembered as having been taken by treachery after that long resistance. He was executed by the Mughal governor in January 1718, and he has been remembered ever after as *Shaheed*, the martyr of Jhok. He was not the first mystical leader in Sindh, or elsewhere in the Muslim world, to engage in politics or social reform.

## The Shrine

The shrine of Sufi Shah Inayat at Jhok Sharif is a revered darbar of lower Sindh, drawing pilgrims who honour the saint and martyr. Jhok Sharif is a village in the far south of Sindh, the home of an important Sufi centre where the saint's *dargah* stands, though accounts describe its exact location in different terms.

The dargah is in the keeping of its *sajjada nashins*, the holders of the seat, and several of the Sufi masters at Jhok have borne the name Abdul Sattar. One of them, Sufi Abd al-Sattar Shah, initiated into the Qadiri path a disciple who spent many years at Jhok Sharif. He set the disciple to cleaning the stable of his master's mare, and when the disciple had reached the highest spiritual degree, that of salvation, he allowed him to give *nam*, the initiatory name, to disciples of his own. Sufi Hazrat Abdul Sattar Shah of Jhok Sharif spoke of *jam wahdat jo*, "the cup of unity". The seat has also been held by Sufi Ataullah Sattari, and Jhok Sharif has an official website in his name.

Three seats in Sindh, those of Daraza, Tando Jahaniya and Jhok Sharif, have *sajjada nashins* who still keep the lineages of Hindu Sufis now in India. A great Sufi poet is attached to each of the three: Sachal Sarmast, Qutub Ali Shah and Nasir Faqir. Nasir Muhammad Faqir, a Qadiri, was the disciple of the *murshid*, the spiritual master, of Jhok Sharif.

## Devotion and Song

The shrine's annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, gathers devotees for prayer, Sufi music and remembrance. The voluminous Sindhi verse of one Sufi poet, his *kafis*, short mystical lyrics, is still part of the main poetry sung at the *ʿurs* of Jhok Sharif. The *kalam*, or poetry, of Dalpat Sufi is sung in several dargahs of Sindh run by Muslim *sajjada nashins*, Jhok Sharif among them.

A performance tradition carries the saint's name. In the singing of Sindhi poetry, a style performed on the *capṛi*, the castanets, is known as the tradition of Shah Inayat of Jhok; it is not found in the poetry of Shah Abdul Latif, whose moods are more mellow.

Jhok was a place of initiation for many. At about the age of forty Rakhiyyal Shah adopted the Sufi path and went to the dargah of Jhok Sharif, where he stayed under the guidance of his master. The guru Asardas was a follower of the Sufi masters of Jhok Sharif, Dalpat Sufi was himself a follower of Jhok Sharif, and Bedil also visited Jhok Sharif and Daraza. The poetry of one disciple's own path tells that from his early childhood he had visions of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani, the founder of the Qadiri order, and that in one of them al-Jilani told him it was time for him to reach Jhok Sharif and take *nam* from the Sufi master there.

The Sufi centre of Jhok Sharif came to play a pivotal role: most of the Hindu Sufis were in touch with Jhok, directly or indirectly, often through their own Sufi master, and Daraza and Jhok were the two main Sufi traditions that were very popular among the Hindus. One Hindu Sufi path counts Shah Inayat of Jhok Sharif among the four masters whose death anniversaries, or *versi*, it keeps.

The dargah's reach crosses the border. After Partition, Molchand was worried that it had become difficult for Hindu Sindhi Sufis to visit the Sufi places in Sindh, now in Pakistan, and a search was made for the grave of Shah Inayat's master at Bijapur. Jhok's official website claims a dargah at Bijapur, that of Hazrat Soofi Abdul Malik, as affiliated with Jhok, and a yearly *melo*, or fair, is kept at Bijapur from the 17th to the 19th of Muharram, as it is at Jhok Sharif. This attempt at creating a Muslim Sufi pilgrimage from Sindh in India is unique, though it does not appear to have been very successful.

## Poetry

Shah Inayat wrote in Persian, and his verse is quoted in the *Risalo* of Shah Abdul Latif, a work with very few Persian quotations. The words *bar khez ba-dih sāqī*, half of a verse, come from one of his *ghazals*, or lyric poems, and a second Persian verse in the *Risalo* is also his. Shah Abdul Latif may have alluded to Shah Inayat's fate in some of his own verses, and he quoted a Persian line usually connected with Shah Inayat which, in English, reads:

*The head is sacrificed at the Friend's foot, / which is in order* (translated by Annemarie Schimmel)

Another Persian verse was tied to his martyrdom by a Sindhi writer, Qani. In his *Maqalat ash-shuʿara* he quoted, in connection with Shah Inayat, a quatrain on the 'kitchen of love' attributed to Sarmad, one of the Sufis in the succession of Hallaj, though the verse itself is much older.

Verse about him followed his death. His fate inspired many Sufi poets, Hindus and Muslims alike, to write touching poetry, and admirers of both faiths composed songs extolling him or describing his martyrdom. Among them was Janullah of Rohri, a mystic of the Suhrawardi order, founded by Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi, and one of the outstanding Persian poets of Sindh in the second half of the eighteenth century. For his death at the hands of the establishment, and for his overwhelming mystical state, Shah Inayat became 'the Hallaj of Sind'. The Sindhi poet Sachal Sarmast speaks of him too, and Sachal's litany of the afflicted tells of ʿInayat killed 'in the fighting arena'.

## The Setting

The epithet 'the Hallaj of Sind' draws on a long memory in the province. Hallaj traversed Sindh shortly after 900, and he is a very popular figure there; many Sufi poets mention his name in their verses, and illiterate folk musicians in remote corners of Sindh repeat it in ecstatic songs, claiming that he was the true lover who paid with his life for his love. Hindu writers of Sindh, too, composed poems in the imagery of the Muslims and devoted ballads to the fate of famous Sufi martyrs.

The Sindh in which Shah Inayat preached was a Mughal province in a time of change. Akbar had added it to the Mughal Empire in the 1590s, and although representatives of the Delhi court came there, the indigenous rulers enjoyed much freedom. The Kalhora ruled as governors from 1701.

The system of land tenure in Sindh, so far as is known, has always been feudal. The deference of the Kalhora to the priestly class led to an extraordinary reverence for *pirs*, the spiritual guides, for Sayyids and for holy men, which marked eighteenth century Sindh above all, and the social religion of the province was built round the reverence of the *murid*, the disciple, for the *murshid*. At the beginning of the eighteenth century a strong influence of the Naqshbandi order, founded by Baha-ud-Din Naqshband, changed the spiritual climate of southern Sindh to a certain extent.

## Legacy

Sufi Shah Inayat Shaheed holds a singular place among the saints of Sindh: a mystic of the unity of being whose commune of shared land and labour, and whose martyrdom in its defence, made him a saint of the poor and a byword for social justice. In the modern age writers, poets and social reformers have celebrated him as an early martyr for the rights of the peasant and the poor against feudal power, so that his shrine is honoured both as a place of mystical devotion and as a symbol of the struggle for justice. He has been called the first social reformer in Sindhi Islam, though progressive writers tend to read him, as they read Hallaj and Bishr al-Hafi, in the light of modern social ideals.

His darbar at Jhok Sharif keeps alive the memory of a holy man who joined the inward path to the cause of the landless, and who paid for it with his life. Jhok stands at the heart of a network that outlived Partition, for the invocation of Jhok Sharif contributes to the construction of a network of sacred territories which are all located in Sindh.

- Michel Boivin, *The Hindu Sufis of South Asia: Partition, Shrine Culture and the Sindhis in India* (London and New York: I.B. Tauris / Bloomsbury Publishing Plc, first published 2019).

Name: Dargah Fateh Pur Sharif
Location: Dargah Fateh Pur Sharif, Gandawah (Jhal Magsi District), Balochistan
Founded/Opened: 1359 (site/settlement); present dargah c. 1940 (after Syed Rakhyal Shah's death)
Sufi Saint: Syed Rakhyal Shah Sufi Al Qadri
Events: Annual urs
Description:
## Overview

At Fateh Pur Sharif — a small town in the Gandava plain of the Jhal Magsi District of Balochistan — stands the *dargah* of Syed Rakhyal Shah, the Qadiri Sufi poet-saint whom the people of the region remember simply as *Saeen Rakhyal*, "the Master Rakhyal." It is one of the principal shrines of Jhal Magsi, named in the district's own heritage listings alongside the *dargah* of Muhammad Ayub Shah Bukhari at Gandava and the shrines of Pir Lakha and Pir Chhatal Shah near Kotra. The shrine is inseparable from the verse its saint left behind — the multi-volume *Bahar al-'ishq*, "The Springtide of Love" — for Rakhyal Shah is honoured less as a miracle-worker than as a poet of divine longing whose words are still sung across the Baloch, Sindhi and Saraiki country that meets in this corner of the Kachhi lowlands.

## The Life of Saeen Rakhyal Shah

Rakhyal Shah is generally held to have lived from 1842 to 1940, a span of nearly a century across the colonial Indus frontier. Of Baloch origin and associated with the Qadiri tradition — the spreadsheet preserves his title as *Sufi al-Qadiri* — he devoted his life to the theme of *'ishq*, the love of the Divine, and became so beloved that, in the phrase of one modern scholar, "the poet himself grew to be the head of a cult." What most distinguishes him is his reach across languages: he is said to have composed in five tongues — Sindhi, Balochi, Saraiki, Urdu and Persian — a fluency that made his message intelligible to the mixed peoples of the Sindh–Balochistan borderland and that helped his fame outlast him. Around his person gathered a circle of *murids* (disciples) whose devotion would, after his death, give rise to the shrine that now bears his name.

## The Dargah and the Bahar al-'ishq

After Rakhyal Shah died in 1940, his followers raised a *dargah* over his grave at Fateh Pur, and the town — dignified with the epithet *Sharif*, "the noble" — grew into a place of pilgrimage. By local tradition the complex also preserves the memory of other holy men of Fatehpur, among them Cheezal (Chizal) Shah, whose name likewise appears among the venerated figures of the site. An annual *urs* marks the saint's death anniversary, drawing devotees who come to recite and hear his poetry; the *Bahar al-'ishq* remains the living heart of the shrine's devotional life, its couplets treasured as both scripture and song.

## Devotion and its Trials

Like many Sufi shrines of the early twenty-first century, the dargah at Fatehpur has suffered the violence of those who reject the inclusive piety it embodies. It was struck by a suicide bombing in 2005 and again, far more grievously, in October 2017, when an attack during the Thursday-night gathering killed some twenty worshippers as they performed *dhamaal*. That the target was a shrine whose saint preached love in five languages lent the atrocity a bitter irony widely remarked upon in the Pakistani press. Yet the *urs* has continued, and pilgrims have returned — an endurance that is itself part of the shrine's story.

## A Note on Dating

The dataset records a founding date of 1359 for this site. This is difficult to reconcile with the life of its principal saint: Rakhyal Shah belongs to the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and his *dargah* was built only after his death in 1940. The medieval date, if it is not simply an error, may attach to an older foundation or an earlier holy figure at the Fatehpur site rather than to the present shrine. Readers should treat the 1359 date with caution; the securely attested history of the dargah begins in the twentieth century.

## Legacy

Rakhyal Shah endures as one of Balochistan's most cherished mystic poets, and his shrine is among the rare centres of shared Baloch–Sindhi devotional culture in the province. In a region more often noted for its aridity and its hardships, the *dargah* at Fatehpur keeps alive a tradition of poetry, music and hospitality, and the saint's own vision — that love is the truest road to God — continues to answer, in the plainest way, the violence that has periodically sought to silence it.

Name: Dargah of Khwaja Muhammad Zaman (Luari Sharif)
Location: Luari Sharif, Shaheed Fazil Rahu Taluka, Badin District, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Annual urs
Description:
## Overview

Luari Sharif, some fifteen kilometres from the town of Badin in the far south of Sindh, is the *dargah*, the Sufi shrine complex, of Khwaja Muhammad Zaman (1713 to 1775), one of the most revered Naqshbandi Sufis and Sindhi mystic poets of the eighteenth century. Luari Sharif is counted among the oldest and most important Sufi sites of southern Sindh. His tomb and the vaulted chambers of his successors form the shrine, and every year his *ʿurs*, the commemoration of the saint's death, draws devotees from across the region.

The Naqshbandis are the order of Sufis, or Muslim mystics, founded by Baha-ud-Din Naqshband. The *khanqah*, the Sufi lodge, that Muhammad Zaman established at Luari became the foremost Naqshbandi centre of eighteenth century Sindh after Thatta, and from it his deputies carried the order's teaching across the province.

## The Saint

Muhammad Zaman was born into a family of the Siddiqi lineage, which claimed descent from the caliph Abu Bakr and had settled in Sindh in earlier centuries. His first teacher was his father, Shaikh Abdul Latif, a follower of the Naqshbandi order. He went on to study at Thatta, then the great seat of learning in Sindh, and there he came under the influence of the Sufi master Khwaja Abul Masakin, whose disciple he became. Tradition holds that he received from Abul Masakin the honorific Sultan al-Aulia, "master of the saints". He is also known as Makhdoom Muhammad Zaman Naqshbandi, and by the title Khwaja Kalan.

He settled at Luari, and the *khanqah* he established there became a place of study, from which his *khalifas*, or deputies, carried the order's teaching across Sindh. The *khanqah* is traditionally dated to 1737, though accounts of when Luari became a Naqshbandi centre differ. When the original settlement became uninhabitable, he founded a new town, also named Luari.

He was also a poet of note. A body of mystical verse in Sindhi is attributed to him, of which some eighty five poems are said to survive. He died in January 1775 and was buried at Luari.

## A Master of the Same Name

A Naqshbandi master of eighteenth century Sindh, called Makhdum Muhammad Zaman and Muhammad Zaman Lanwari, may be the saint of Luari, though the identification is not certain. The name fits, Lanwari may be a form of the place's name, and he lived in Sindh in the generation of Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit, as his younger compatriot.

He has been called "the famous saint", and the Sindhi scholar Abdur Rahim Girhori was his *khalifa*. Among his own masters was Mian Muhammad Thattawi. Girhori commented in Arabic on his master's sayings in Sindhi. Most of Girhori's own books were destroyed during the Afghan raids in Upper Sindh in 1781.

Shah Abdul Latif praised the eye-glass in his verse, but Muhammad Zaman Lanwari used the image the other way, explaining outward science as an eye-glass that stands between the eye and the goal of seeing. On a larger question of doctrine, the reality of the Prophet, *haqiqa muhammadiyya*, as mediator, he has been placed with Girhori and Dard, and Shah Abdul Latif outside them.

## The Shrine and Its Devotion

Muhammad Zaman was buried at Luari, where his tomb and the vaulted chambers of his successors form the shrine complex. Access to the complex has at times been restricted, and a police post has been maintained at its entrance since the 1980s. An annual *ʿurs* commemorates Khwaja Muhammad Zaman and draws devotees from across the region.

In the later twentieth century the trees near Sindhi shrines were still decorated with many pieces of cloth, preferably red, in the shape of little flags or tiny cradles, attached there for the sake of a vow, as is usual almost everywhere in the Islamic world.

## Luari Sharif and the Naqshbandis of Sindh

The Naqshbandi order came to Sindh from the sixteenth century onwards, with the Arghuns and the Tarkhans, two Central Asian dynasties that ruled the province. It had several important centres there, notably Luari Sharif, a village close to Badin in southern Sindh.

Naqshbandi scholars from Luari Sharif wrote treatises in Sindh, and the main author among them was Makhdum Muhammad Hashim (1692 to 1762), who was *qazi*, or judge, in Thatta. These scholars showed that the Muslims of Sindh did not know the Quran. They wrote paraphrases of it and then a Sindhi translation of the Arabic Quran, and they condemned some rituals, especially those labelled Hindu or Shia, as not Islamic. This came against a wider background: before the eighteenth century, few people in Sindh identified themselves as Muslims, probably because the name was restricted to the Sayyids, the descendants of the Prophet, and their dependants. Later Naqshbandi treatises on how to follow the rules of Islam led to the conclusion that the Sindhis, even when they were officially Muslim, did not practise "Orthodox Islam". Yet the official book devoted to the Naqshbandis of Luari Sharif was written by a Hindu follower.

In southern Sindh a strong Naqshbandi influence at the beginning of the eighteenth century changed the spiritual climate to a certain extent. Makhdum Muhammad Hashim and his relatives attacked the Sufis who defended the emotional side of religion, and this Naqshbandi group helped to promote a more sober mystical piety. The Naqshbandis of Sindh followed the reforming enterprise led by Shah Waliullah in Delhi, and in Sindh, as in Bengal, they tried to curb the overflowing emotionalism of the folk songs. Even so, many of the pious in Sindh kept "the marketplace of union warm" by reciting Rumi's *Mathnawi*, and stern Naqshbandis quoted Rumi's work as much as members of the more emotional orders did.

The order stands apart in Sindh in other ways too. Perhaps because of the hold of the Suhrawardi order on Sindh, the Chishti order could not spread there as it did in the rest of South Asia, yet music appeared very early in the Sufism of Sindh. The Naqshbandis are the exception: the majority of them in Sindh are strongly opposed to music and to the singing of devotional songs. Outside the Naqshbandis, Sufism in Sindh is dominated by poetry expressing *wahdat al-wujud*, the unity of being. A Hindu branch of the order is hardly found in Sindh, and the Sufis to whom Sindh's Hindu Sufis look all belong to the *wujudi* school, the school of the unity of being, which leaves out the Naqshbandis.

## The Setting

In the reign of Aurangzeb, Badin marked one edge of the Mughal province, or *suba*, of Thatta. The province ran two hundred and fifty *kos*, an old measure of distance, in length, from Bhakkar to Kech Makran, and a hundred *kos* in breadth, from the *qasba*, the small town, of Badin to the port of Lahari. It was bounded by Gujarat Ahmadabad to the east, Kech Makran to the west, Bhakkar to the north and the salt sea to the south, and it held four *sarkars*, or districts: Thatta, Siwistan, Nasirpur and Amarkot.

The greatest of its rivers was the Indus. Merchants from Multan and Bhakkar shipped goods by it to Thatta, and large armies rarely went by land, because of the jungle and the lack of water. The country depended for the most part on its boats, of which, great and small, there were forty thousand. The diet rested on rice, curds and fish; dried fish was shipped to the ports, and fish oil was used on the boats. Brahmanabad had once been a great capital whose fort had fourteen hundred towers, and Adpur became the seat after it.

Mirza Shah Beg Arghun came from Qandahar with an army and took Thatta, and Arghuns and then Tarkhans ruled until Mirza Jani Beg came to court with the Khankhanan, the holder of the title khan of khans, and the country was joined to the empire. Jani Beg was given the *jagir*, the revenue grant, of Thatta, and the port of Lahari, which lies on the side of Thatta, was made crown land. Sindh was part of the Mughal Empire from 1595, and although representatives of the Delhi court came there, its own rulers enjoyed much freedom.

The Sindh of Muhammad Zaman's lifetime was a province in upheaval. After Aurangzeb's death the native Kalhoro dynasty took over the rule, first in Upper and later in Lower Sindh, only to become the vassals of the invading Nadir Shah, who conquered Sindh and the Punjab before he reached Delhi in 1739. The Kalhoros were overthrown by the former disciples of their saintly ancestor, Adam Shah Kalhoro, and the Talpurs, who thus came to power in 1781, ruled the country until the British conquered it in 1843.

The holy men of that country held a place in its order. Before the British conquest most of Sindh's Sayyids were landowners, *zamindars*, but they were also *pirs*, spiritual guides. The *pirs* of Sindh were mediators between the tribes, and between the rulers and the governed, and their power grew in the eighteenth century, when the Kalhoras developed the irrigation system. The *darbar*, the saint's shrine, was the sacred ground on which Sufi culture was at work. The cult of holy men is particularly evident in the countryside, especially in the Punjab and Sindh, where great landlords and large concentrations of land are crucial features, and there the local *pir* represents the local landlord or is closely related to him. British policy, especially in the Punjab and Sindh, was to treat the hereditary saints in essentially the same way as landlords and tribal leaders.

Sindh's pride in its saints lives in a story told of more than one invasion. Diwan Gidumal, the minister of the Kalhoro princes, is said to have given an invader the most precious treasure Sindh had to offer, the holy dust of its saints. Sindh alone is said to have more than a hundred thousand Sufi shrines.

For all its upheaval, the eighteenth century can be called the most important period for the formation of mystical poetry and prose in Sindh. An Arabic saying was very popular there at the time: "Affliction is for saintliness the same as are flames for the gold". Shah Abdul Latif's verse speaks of the province itself. In his Sur Sarang the cloud of mercy rises from the desert of eastern Sindh, the Thar Parkar, and floats over the world, and the poet, coming home, prays:

*My Lord, be kind over dear Sind, / Friend! Sweet darling! You may make the whole world happy!* (translated by Annemarie Schimmel)

In a lament from the Marui cycle, the poet mourns the passing of the heroes and the holy men of Sindh. The lament has lived on in performance, and the singer Alan Faqir recited its line:

*Punnu is not in the Kec / Sind is not the amir*

Its second half means that Sindh is not in the position of leadership, or amirship. It is one of Alan Faqir's own political readings of the tales of women.

## Legacy

Luari Sharif is counted among the oldest and most important Sufi sites of southern Sindh, and Khwaja Muhammad Zaman is remembered as one of the most revered Naqshbandi Sufis and Sindhi mystic poets of the eighteenth century, whose *khalifas* carried the order's teaching across the province.

That legacy has two sides. Luari Sharif stands for the Naqshbandi scholars who paraphrased the Quran and translated it into Sindhi, and who condemned rituals they judged not Islamic; yet a Hindu follower wrote the official book devoted to its Naqshbandis. And the master called Muhammad Zaman Lanwari, if he is the saint of Luari, is remembered through his *khalifa* Girhori, who commented on his Sindhi sayings in Arabic, and through his image of outward science as an eye-glass standing between the eye and the goal of seeing, a counterpoint to Shah Abdul Latif's own verse.

Name: Dargah of Pir Muhammad Rashid (Roze Dhani), Pir Jo Goth
Location: Pir Jo Goth, Kingri Taluka, Khairpur District, Sindh, Pakistan
Sufi Saint: Pir Syed Muhammad Rashid Shah, "Roze Dhani" (founder of the Rashidi order)
Events: Hur gatherings on 27 Rajab and at fixed times; no public urs observed
Description:
The town of Pir Jo Goth — "the village of the Pir" — in the Kingri taluka of Khairpur District, Sindh, grew up around the shrine of Pir Syed Muhammad Rashid Shah (1757–1818), known by his honorific Roze Dhani, "master of the shrine," the founder of the Rashidi Sufi order and an ancestor of the line of Pir Pagara. A Qadiri–Naqshbandi saint of great influence, his teaching is said to have spread through Sindh, the Punjab, Balochistan, Rajasthan, and beyond. From his descendants issued the spiritual and temporal leadership of the Hurs, the community of devoted faqirs whose ancestors, under the later Pir Pagaras, waged a celebrated resistance against British rule in Sindh in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries; the present (eighth) Pir Pagara draws his authority from this shrine complex. The dargah is distinguished by an austere discipline unusual among Sufi shrines: devotees are required to enter only with the head covered, the Hur faqirs make pilgrimage at fixed times of the year, and the sacred date of 27 Rajab draws great throngs of mureeds — yet, in contrast to the festive urs kept at most Sufi tombs, the Rashidi tradition is said to observe no public urs here. The complex, entered through an imposing Shahi (royal) gate, remains the devotional and political heart of the Hur community and one of the most distinctive shrines of upper Sindh.

A separate compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints, Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, independently places the saint's shrine at Goth Reem Dino, also known as Pir Goth, Sindh, and confirms his descent within the Piran Pagara lineage — consistent with this entry's own account of Pir Jo Goth and the Pir Pagara succession. It also gives a fuller explanation of the epithet "Roze Dhani": tradition holds that as an infant he stopped nursing during the daylight hours of Ramadan, and that the name was later reinforced when a dome (*roza*) was built over his grave.

Name: Dargah Pir Ratan Nath Jee
Location: Jhanda Bazar, Peshawar, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: British colonial period (19th c.); no exact year
Events: Maha Shivratri
Description:
## Overview

The Dargah of Pir Ratan Nath, in the Jhanda Bazar of the walled city of Peshawar, is among the last living Hindu temples of that ancient frontier city. A shrine of the British colonial period, it is dedicated in practice to the Hindu god Shiva and centred on the veneration of Ratan Nath, a yogi and saint also called Baba Pir Ratan Nath. It belongs to the tradition of the Nath order of ascetic yogis, and it is one of only a small handful of Peshawar's temples still in regular use, alongside the nearby Kali Bari and the historic Gorakhnath temple at Gor Khatri. Its chief festival is *Maha Shivratri*, the great night of Shiva.

## Ratan Nath and the Naths

The temple's saint, Ratan Nath, belongs to the *Nath sampradaya*, the order of the *kanphata* yogis, named for their split ears. The Naths trace their lineage to Gorakhnath and, before him, to Matsyendranath, the founder of the sect, a figure partly of legend. They flourished across northern India, Nepal and the frontier lands of the north west from roughly the early medieval centuries. They practised a rigorous discipline of yoga and the austerity of *hatha*, the yoga of the body, and revered Shiva as the *adi-nath*, the first lord and archetypal yogi.

Peshawar and its region were an old stronghold of the order. The Gorakhnath temple within the Gor Khatri complex, and the ancient association of the nearby hill of *Tilla Jogian*, the hill of the yogis, across the Indus, with Gorakhnath himself, mark this as Nath country of long standing. From their centre at Peshawar the Nath yogis moved to all parts of Central Asia and Iran, at the same time influencing both the *qalandars*, the wandering dervishes, and the Sufis, the mystics of Islam.

Ratan Nath is remembered in tradition as a wandering seeker and teacher who carried the Nath message of peace, truth and compassion across the frontier lands. His veneration reaches beyond Peshawar to shrines in the wider region, including sites in Nepal. As with many figures of the order, the details of his life are wrapped in legend and cannot be fixed with confidence to a particular century: his story is sacred memory rather than documented biography.

## The Temple

In its present form the dargah is a temple of the nineteenth century, raised in the neighbourhood of Karimpura and the Jhanda Bazar, within the old walls of Peshawar, when the city's Hindu merchant community was numerous and prosperous. Its very name reflects the blended religious idiom of the frontier. *Dargah*, the word for a Sufi shrine, is borrowed from the vocabulary of the Muslim shrine, and on the frontier a Hindu yogi's shrine could be spoken of in the language of the Sufi tomb.

After the Partition of 1947, when the greater part of Peshawar's Hindu population departed, most of the city's temples fell silent or were turned to other uses. The Dargah of Pir Ratan Nath is remarkable for having survived as a functioning place of worship, tended by the small Hindu community that remained, and today it is reckoned one of the very few temples in daily use in the city, together with the Kali Bari.

## Devotion and Festivals

The temple's chief festival is *Maha Shivratri*, the great night of Shiva, when devotees gather for worship. Peshawar's Hindus have also kept the festival at Katas. Hindus from Peshawar came to Katas in 2010, and at Shivratri in 2011 Hindu pilgrims from Peshawar arrived there in two large buses, about a hundred people; the musical band had come from Peshawar too. Four marriages solemnised at Katas that Shivratri were, it was said, of girls from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and FATA, the Federally Administered Tribal Areas, who had suffered in the floods of 2010.

Diwali, the festival of lights, is the city's other great Hindu festival. It has been said: "If you want to see the lights of Diwali, go to Peshawar." Across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Hindu festivals are celebrated with much pomp.

## A Name with Many Identities

The name Ratan is borne by more than one figure, and it is not settled whether any of them is the saint of this temple. Among the Nath yogis was a Ratannath, one of the names associated with the Nath movement: a contemporary of Gorakhnath, and the subject of many miraculous tales.

A Muslim figure bears a similar name: Shaikh Baba Ratan, or Hajji Baba Ratan. Tradition makes him a man born before the birth of Muhammad who became a companion of the Prophet. Known by the honorific name Abu'l-Riza, he is said to have come from Tabarhinda or Bhatinda in the Punjab; his death is placed in 1300, and he lies buried in the Punjab. Baba Ratan Hajji has also been identified with Gorakhnath. The Hajji and the yogi Ratannath are sometimes joined into one figure, but there is no consensus that they are one, and Ratannath is also counted in his own right a very important figure of the Nath movement.

The name is also attached to a shrine in Delhi, a *dargah mandir* devoted to a Pir Baba Ratannath. The phrase calls one shrine at once a *dargah*, the Muslim word for a saint's tomb, and a *mandir*, the Hindu word for a temple. It has been counted among the 'paradoxical' terms of shrines that are at once Muslim and Hindu in name, and it carries the same meeting of Muslim and Hindu vocabulary as the Peshawar temple's own name. Whether the Delhi shrine honours the same figure as the Peshawar temple is not settled.

## Peshawar and the Frontier

Peshawar is an ancient city, known to earlier writers as Farshawar, Parshawar and Bagram. In Mahmud's first campaign, Raja Jaipal set out to meet the invader and gave battle at Peshawar. Five thousand of the raja's men fell to the sword in that fight, and Raja Jaipal was taken captive with fifteen of his sons, brothers and kinsmen and was put to death.

In Aurangzeb's reign three roads ran from Peshawar to Kabul. The first, the Nikshab road, had many hard defiles over a long distance, and armies passed over it with difficulty. The second joined the highway at Jalalabad, through narrow defiles and hard passes, with little water. The third was the road of Ali Masjid and the Khyber, which ran eighteen *kos*, an old measure of distance, from the spring of Jamshid, known as Jamrud, to a place on the bank of the Nilab. The Khyber was hard going for two *kos*, yet this road was easier than the others, and it was the one used by armies and caravans.

The district around the city, known as Peshawar, lay on the side of Hindustan. Its grapes, peaches and melons were like those of Turan, the lands of Central Asia, while its heat and cold, its seasons and its rain were like those of Hindustan. Its rice was better than that of Bengal, and crops and grain were plentiful. The district was the home of the Mahmand Afghans and others, who kept to the ways of paying revenue and of living as subjects. The city recurs in Mughal affairs: Dara sent robes of honour to the armies of Peshawar and Kabul, whose governorship Mahabat Khan held, and after the fort of Attock had been laid out the court set out for Peshawar, and from that stage a *farman*, a royal order, of counsel was sent to Hakim Mirza.

In the Janamsakhis, the traditional lives of Guru Nanak, the Guru comes to the city on his return from Baghdad, visiting Kabul before reaching Peshawar.

Peshawar has its place in the life of the Sufis too. Zauqi Shah, who moved between Agra, Jaipur, Bombay, Peshawar, Hyderabad, Ajmer and finally Karachi, began his *Sirr-i dilbaran*, a comprehensive encyclopaedia of Sufi terminology, in Peshawar in 1923. Compiled over a number of years, it was first published in 1951 and reached its fifth edition in 1985. In 2000 a woman disciple from Peshawar, speaking in Lahore, contrasted the shrines of her home region with Pakpattan: "In the frontier, we have so many shrines where you can walk into the saint's shrines. Women can go inside, we can touch the graves." At many places, she added, there is a separate side for the women; it is not like this at Pakpattan Sharif.

The boldest mystical verse of the Punjab and Sindh sees a oneness in which every boundary of birth and creed falls away. In that vision, as one scholar of Sufism put it, "the Sufi is no longer Arab, Hindu, Turk, or Peshawari".

Today Peshawar is a city on the western border of Pakistan. The elders of one Sikh man moved there from a village in the Khyber Agency for better economic opportunities, and Sikh refugees from the tribal areas moved to Peshawar, Hassan Abdal and Nankana Sahib and started living at gurdwaras, the Sikh places of worship, just like the migrants before them. After the attacks of 1971, one woman recalled, her family fled to Peshawar, where there was a considerable Sikh population, and stayed for a few months.

Since Partition, the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has been home to a large proportion of religious minorities, who have lived there rather peacefully. Hindus form the largest minority, and thousands of them are part of mainstream society, often visible in its economic and political fabric. At Partition the riots in the province were less intense than in the Punjab, and many Hindus and Sikhs stayed on in their ancestral lands because of the comparatively peaceful political situation. Earlier, during his reign, Maharaja Ranjit Singh had captured the Pathan regions of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the tribal areas, as a result of which several people converted to Sikhism.

Thousands of Nanak Panthi Hindus, followers of Guru Nanak, live in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab and Sindh, and the independent followers of Guru Nanak who refused the Khalsa, the order of initiated Sikhs, still exist in Sindh and in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

## Legacy

The survival of the Dargah of Pir Ratan Nath is significant out of all proportion to its modest size. In a city more often associated in the modern imagination with the Khyber Pass and the turbulence of the frontier, it preserves the memory of a deep and ancient Hindu and yogic presence: the Nath yogis whose austerities once echoed across these hills. As a shrine still in use, it is both a place of worship for Peshawar's remaining Hindus and a fragile monument to the religious plurality of the old walled city. Efforts to document and protect the temple, including its listing among the heritage sites of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, reflect a growing recognition of its value.
