Description:
## Overview

At Golra Sharif, at the foot of the Margalla Hills on the edge of Islamabad, stands the shrine of Hazrat Pir Sayyid Meher Ali Shah, who died in 1937. He was one of the most influential Chishti saints and scholars of modern South Asia, a master of both the inward path and the religious sciences. He is remembered as a great defender of orthodox Sunni belief, a renowned orator and author, and the founder of a living Sufi centre whose successors remain prominent to this day. His *darbar*, or shrine, is among the most visited of the Pothohar region and of the area around Islamabad and Rawalpindi.

It was here at Golra, in the early twentieth century, that Meher Ali Shah established his prominence. Today his shrine is a large and busy complex, kept by his descendants.

## The Saint

Meher Ali Shah was born at Golra in 1859, though accounts of the year differ, into a Sayyid family of learning and sanctity, descended from the Prophet Muhammad. He received a thorough classical education in the Islamic sciences at the seminaries of the age and became a scholar of the first rank.

On the Sufi path he was initiated into the Chishti order, the Sufi order prominent in South Asia that was founded by Moinuddin Chishti. He took spiritual allegiance in the line of Khwaja Shamsuddin Sialvi of Sial Sharif, his direct *pir*, or spiritual guide, who died in 1882. He was also affiliated with Muhammad Ali, one of whose disciples was Habib Ali Shah, who in turn was the master of Sufi Saheb, who died in 1916. It is through this second line that a branch of the Chishti order is traced as far as South Africa.

Combining deep mystical experience with formidable learning, he became a widely sought guide and teacher. In a conflict over the succession at Taunsa, the succession from Shaykh Sulayman divided into two branches, and one of them went to Meher Ali Shah. He is counted, with Khwaja Hasan Nizami and the Naqshbandi activist Pir Jama'at Ali Shah, among the notable Sufi masters of twentieth century South Asia who pursued reformist agendas. He died at Golra in 1937 and was buried there.

## Public Life and Disciples

Meher Ali Shah is especially remembered for his part in the religious controversies of his time, above all his prominent stand against the claims of Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian. He opposed them in debate and in writing, most famously in his work *Saif-e-Chishtiyai*. Haydar Ali Shah, too, opposed the Ahmadi movement, but Meher Ali Shah was said to be one of those most influential in marginalising and stigmatising Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian.

At the same time he was attracted to the Khilafat movement, which gathered around the largely symbolic figure of the Ottoman caliph, and he permitted his disciples to support it. The masters of Golra and of Jalalpur Sharif had different roles: Meher Ali Shah took on the historical persona of a Sufi *pir* thoroughly engaged in both the regional and the international politics of his time.

Among his disciples was Khwaja Hasan Nizami. At the age of 24, of his own will and believing he had a spiritual sign from Baba Farid, Hasan Nizami became a *murid*, a disciple pledged to a Sufi master, of Meher Ali Shah. Meher Ali Shah initiated him and in time made him a *khalifa*, one of his successors.

## Learning and Poetry

Pir Meher Ali Shah united the roles of scholar, poet and *shaykh*, or spiritual master. He wrote in defence of Sunni doctrine and on the love of the Prophet, and he was himself a composer of devotional verse: his Punjabi and Persian *naat*, poems in praise of the Prophet, are cherished by his followers and remain among the loved poetry of the tradition. His teaching held firmly to the union of the Sharia, the religious law of Islam, and the Sufi path, insisting that mystical devotion must rest on sound belief and on the example of the Prophet. He drew to himself a vast following, and the guidance he gave, sober, learned and centred on the love of God and His Messenger, shaped the religious life of the region.

His Punjabi verse is sung by *qawwals*, the singers of *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis. In their performances they move between the Persian verses of Jami, Hafiz and Rumi, the Punjabi poetry of Meher Ali Shah and Ghulam Farid, and the classical Hindi of Amir Khusrau, among others.

His memory is kept in homes as well as at the shrine. In Rawalpindi, the living room wall of Mama Ji carries popular prints of the saints Abdul Qadir Jilani of Baghdad, Pir Meher Ali Shah of Golra and Baba Lal Shah.

## The Shrine

The shrine of Meher Ali Shah at Golra is a large and busy complex. It is kept by his descendants, who have continued as its *sajjada nashins*, the hereditary custodians who sit on the saint's prayer carpet, and as noted religious figures. Among his successors at the shrine was Pir Ghulam Mohyuddin, known as Babuji, and the keepers who came after maintain the *darbar* and its teaching mission.

The shrine holds the five daily prayers, gatherings of *naat* and *qawwali*, and its *langar*, the free communal kitchen. Its annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, draws great crowds from across the Pothohar and beyond. As a centre of both pilgrimage and learning, Golra Sharif carries the saint's legacy of devotion joined to scholarship.

Golra Sharif also holds manuscripts. Two Persian works are recorded there as unique single copies: a biography of Hujwiri, and the *Albab-i thulatha* of Muhammad Chishti.

Golra Sharif is counted, with Nurpur Shahan and Pir Baba, among the Muslim pilgrimage places of northern Pakistan. Like Golra, the village of Nurpur Shahan and the shrine of Barri Imam stand on the outskirts of Islamabad, the federal capital of Pakistan, whose twin city is Rawalpindi.

## Legacy

Pir Meher Ali Shah stands among the towering figures of modern Sunni Sufism in South Asia, a saint whose combination of mystical stature, scholarship and public defence of orthodox belief gave him an authority felt far beyond his own region. Through his writings, his poetry in praise of the Prophet and the living line of his successors at Golra, his influence endures, and his shrine at the edge of the capital remains one of the great centres of Chishti devotion in Pakistan.

That authority reached to the controversy with Qadian and to the politics of the Khilafat movement, to his disciple and *khalifa* Khwaja Hasan Nizami, and, through a second line of affiliation, to a branch of the Chishti order traced as far as South Africa. His Punjabi verse lives on in the repertoire of the *qawwals*, and his picture on the walls of devotees' homes.

Name: Gorakhnath (Goraknath) Temple
Location: Gor Khatri area, Peshawar, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
Events: Diwali (principal annual opening)
Description:
## Overview

The Gorakhnath Temple, also written Goraknath, stands within the historic walled precinct of Gor Khatri, in the heart of the old city of Peshawar in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It is dedicated to Guru Gorakhnath, the great saint and *yogi*, a master of the ascetic discipline of yoga, who is venerated as the founder of the *Nath* monastic order, and it is one of the very few Hindu temples in the city still standing and in use. The present temple dates from the nineteenth century, but it sits atop one of the most storied and continuously sacred pieces of ground in the subcontinent, whose religious associations stretch back some two thousand years. Closed for decades after Partition, it was reopened for worship in 2011 after a legal campaign by Pakistan's Hindu community, and its revival has made it a symbol of the region's layered spiritual heritage.

## Gor Khatri, a Sacred Ground

The temple cannot be separated from Gor Khatri itself, an elevated mound in Peshawar's old city that has been held sacred, in various traditions, from the Gandhara period to the Mughal era. Its name is popularly taken to mean the grave of the *Kshatriya*, the warrior class of Hindu society, or of warriors, hinting at ancient associations with burial or with heroes. Excavation, notably the vertical digs begun by Professor Farzand Ali Durrani in the early 1990s, has revealed successive layers of occupation descending some fifteen metres and spanning many civilisations, from the Indo-Greeks of the second century BCE through the Hindu Shahi and later periods.

Gor Khatri is identified with Gorakhtari, a place in Peshawar whose name matches its own. The spot has been associated with "the tower of Buddha's bowl", and like other Buddhist sites taken over by yogis, it became a centre of their activity. Gor Khatri was long a celebrated resort of the *Nath* yogis. After his return from the Middle East, Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith, seems to have stayed in the Punjab, visiting Ajodhan, Multan and Gorakhtari from time to time. Babur, the founder of the Mughal dynasty, came to Gor Khatri during his forays into the region, drawn by curiosity about the *Shaiva* ascetics, the devotees of the god Shiva, who dominated the place, and he mentions the visit himself.

In the reigns of the emperors Akbar and Jahangir the place was an important centre of pilgrimage for the yogis. Near the city, Kor Khatri, the temple of the *jogis*, or yogis, was famous, and it was demolished in the reign of Shah Jahan.

Under the Mughals the site was transformed: in 1641 Jahan Ara Begum, the daughter of Shah Jahan, built a grand caravanserai here, the Sarai Jahanabad, an inn for caravans and travellers, together with a mosque, a bath and wells for their comfort. In the nineteenth century, during Sikh rule, the precinct served as the residence and headquarters of the Italian mercenary general Paolo Avitabile, governor of Peshawar.

## The Temple

The present Gorakhnath Temple was built in the middle of the nineteenth century, around 1851, within the Gor Khatri complex. At the Partition of British India in 1947 much of Peshawar's Hindu population departed, and the temple was left abandoned. It remained closed to worship for some six decades, its future in doubt amid changing custody of the site.

Its restoration came through the persistence of the Hindu community. In 2011, following a petition and litigation before the Peshawar High Court, the court ordered that the temple be reopened for worship and recognised as part of the site's heritage. The reopening, after roughly sixty years of silence, was widely reported as a significant moment for religious freedom and for the preservation of minority heritage in Pakistan, and Hindus could once again worship at the ancient shrine.

## Guru Gorakhnath

Guru Gorakhnath is one of the most influential figures of medieval Indian spirituality. He is traditionally held to have lived somewhere between the ninth and twelfth centuries, and he is revered as a *mahasiddha*, a great perfected master, and as the founder of the *Nath* order of yogis. He is remembered as the disciple of Matsyendranath. He is believed to have been born from the sweat of Shiva's breast, and it is told that he saved his master, in whose service he had earlier lost an eye. He is also believed to be an *avatar*, an incarnation, of Shiva. Much mystery and legend surround him, but he is known to have written treatises in Sanskrit.

The *Nath* tradition he shaped, with its emphasis on *hatha yoga*, the yoga of bodily discipline, on asceticism and on esoteric discipline, spread widely across the subcontinent and left a deep imprint on popular religion. The transmission of the Nath doctrine rests on a trinity, Shiva, Matsyendranath and Gorakhnath, and the Adi Nath, the First Lord of the Naths, is the Shiva of the Hindus. The Nath tradition venerates nine Naths and eighty four Siddhas, or perfected ones, though this does not mean that these figures are historical.

Gorakhnath is credited with founding the order of the *Kanphata*, the Split Ear Yogis, as the Naths are also called, and its framework has been taken to illustrate his remarkable gift for organisation and foresight. The order has its rite of piercing the ears, and its rite of initiation was still current in the late twentieth century. In Persian writing the chief Hindu figure is the *jogi*, a word usually used for the Nathpanthis, a Shaiva school of renunciants who followed Gorakhnath. The Naths lived in forests, wandered in towns and also founded permanent monasteries. Their goal was mastery of the body: in their teaching, the perfect yogi can transform his body at will and is therefore free of all disease and death. Siddhas such as the disciples of Gorakhnath are believed to have achieved this in the foothills of the Himalayas, and they came to be known as *jivan-mukta*, liberated while living.

Of his Sanskrit treatises the *Goraksha-Sataka* has survived and has been edited and translated into English, while the *Hatha-Yoga* has not. His disciples wrote treatises on magic, alchemy, left-handed occultism and *hatha yoga*. Generations of them also wrote verses in Punjabi and Hindi that are attributed to him, using the name Gorakhnath to establish a spiritual link with their master, the same borrowing of a master's name that is found in the verse attributed to Baba Farid. The *Goraksha-Bijay* of the seventeenth century, based on a Sanskrit work said to have been composed by Gorakhnath, was written by Shaikh Faizu'llah.

In his teaching, Ultimate Reality could not be conceived by logical reasoning; it was a direct experience, beyond the senses and the intellect, in the state of *samadhi*, or trance. He held the highest form of God to be Sat-Cit-Ananda-Murti, the One who reveals Himself as Being, Consciousness and Bliss, the self-manifestation of the Formless One, the Nameless One whose holiest names are Brahma, Shiva, Parmatma and Parmeswara. To Gorakhnath and the Siddhas the phenomenal world was not false or illusory. The *adhars*, in his teaching, are the main sources of the vital and psychical functions, which have to be controlled, and the Absolute Truth realised in the highest spiritual experience lies above *bhava*, existence, and *abhava*, its negation.

Peshawar and the wider north west kept strong *Nath* associations, and Gor Khatri, with its long yogic heritage, was a natural centre for devotion to Gorakhnath. The city also preserved other shrines linked to the tradition, among them the *Dargah*, or shrine, of Pir Ratan Nath in Jhanda Bazaar, a sign of the enduring presence of the *Nath* current in Peshawar's religious life.

## Legends of Gorakhnath

The yogis held Brahma, Vishnu and Mahesh to be both angels and disciples of Gorakhnath, and they claimed all the prophets and apostles as his disciples too. To the yogis the Prophet Muhammad was a pupil and disciple of Gorakhnath, a belief they kept hidden for fear of Muslim retribution. Baba Ratan was identified with Gorakhnath, and it was asserted that the Prophet had learnt yoga through him. Gorakh has also been seen as a counterpart of the awaited Mahdi of Muslim belief: a yogi becomes a Siddha only after meeting Gorakh, and both Gorakh and the Siddhas show the distinctive features of the Mahdi.

Gorakhnath has his part in romance and legend too. In the romance of Hir and Ranjha, Ranjha goes to the great yogi Gorakhnath for initiation and returns transformed from a herdsman into a yogi to win back Hir. In one version of the legend of Goga Pir, Gorakhnath sends an invisible army to help Goga Pir against Rai Pithora. In the Puratan Janamsakhis, early traditional lives of Guru Nanak, the account of the anointing of Guru Angad has Gorakhnath in conversation with Guru Nanak, though Gorakhnath lived and preached long before Nanak's time.

His name reaches as far as the cult of the goddess Hinglaj in Balochistan. Tradition has it that Hinglaj was very fond of the Nath community, and especially of Guru Gorakhnath, and that the goddess waited day after day in Thatta for him to come to meet her, with all the food she had prepared for his arrival. It is said that by a boon attributed to Lakhavat the piled *khichri*, a dish of rice and lentils, turned to limestone, and that anyone who returned from Hinglaj wearing a necklace of these limestone pebbles would be freed from the fetters of this world. In the valley of Hinglaj is the *dhuni*, or fireplace, of Guru Gorakhnath, which goes back to the long tradition of the Nath yogis who made the journey there, and two texts, the *Gorakh Caritra* and the *Gorakhpurana*, describe Gorakhnath's own pilgrimage to Hinglaj. Another story says that Gorakhnath himself brought a stone there from somewhere around Anil Kund.

## Gorakhnath and the Sufis

The Naths lived in continuous exchange with the Sufis, the mystics of Islam, and Peshawar had its place in that exchange. From the eleventh century the Nath yogis began to spread throughout northern India, and from their centre at Peshawar they moved to all parts of Central Asia and Iran, influencing both the *qalandars*, the wandering dervishes, and the Sufis.

The strongest sign of that exchange is the *Rushd-Nama* of Shaikh 'Abdu'l-Quddus, in which Gorakhnath's name stands for God. The Shaikh belonged to the Chishti order, the Sufi order founded by Moinuddin Chishti and prominent in South Asia. The work's verses refer six times to 'Gorakhnath', 'Shri Gorakh', 'Nath' or 'O! Nath'. In five places, as in many Nath texts, these words stand for Ultimate Reality and Absolute Truth, and in the sixth the Perfect Siddha, or Perfect Man. All the verses of Shaikh 'Abdu'l-Quddus on the simile of the mirror and the polishing of the heart rest on ideas expressed by Ibn al-'Arabi and Gorakhnath. In the words of Gorakh, the Shaikh also warned the yogis that wearing rings in their ears and rosaries of Eleocarpus ganitrus around their necks, or reciting *sakhi* and *sabad*, the poetry of the Naths, fails to make one a yogi. Some verses ascribed to Gorakhnath in the Hindi *Gorakhbani* challenge the *qazis*, the Muslim judges, for mechanically crying the name "Muhammad".

The Sufi poet Bulleh Shah, in his lyric of the lover turned yogi, names the authority that a *pir*, a Sufi spiritual guide, must satisfy:

*My Pir gains the approval of guru Gorakh.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

The city's own name appears in the mystical poetry of the Punjab and Sindh as one of the identities the lover leaves behind. In that vision, as one scholar of Sufism put it, "the Sufi is no longer Arab, Hindu, Turk, or Peshawari".

## Peshawar and the Frontier

Peshawar is an ancient city, which older books also write as Parshawar and Farshawar. In Aurangzeb's reign the district known as Peshawar lay on the side of Hindustan. Its grapes, peaches and melons were like those of Turan, the lands of Central Asia, while its heat and cold, its seasons and its rain were like those of Hindustan; its rice was better than that of Bengal, and crops and grain were plentiful.

Three roads then ran from the city to Kabul. The Nikshab road had many hard defiles, and armies passed along it with difficulty. A second road, joining the highway at Jalalabad, had narrow defiles, hard passes, little water and Afghan raids. The third, the road of Ali Masjid and the Khyber, was harder going for two *kos*, an old measure of distance, yet easier than the others, and armies and caravans used it. In the Janamsakhis, Guru Nanak, on his return from Baghdad, visited Kabul before reaching Peshawar.

Since Partition, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has been home to a large proportion of religious minorities, who have lived there rather peacefully. They are mainly Hindus, who form the largest minority, and Hindu festivals are celebrated in the province with much pomp. At Partition the riots in the province were less intense than in the Punjab, and many Hindus and Sikhs went on living in their ancestral lands after the creation of Pakistan.

Peshawar's Hindus have also kept the festival of Shivratri, the night of Shiva, at Katas. In 2011 Hindu pilgrims from Peshawar arrived there for it in two large buses, about a hundred people, and the musical band had come from Peshawar too; Hindus from Peshawar had come to Katas in 2010 as well. Of the festival of lights it has been said: "If you want to see the lights of Diwali, go to Peshawar."

## Legacy

The Gorakhnath Temple at Gor Khatri is at once a living place of Hindu worship and a window onto the astonishing antiquity of Peshawar, a city where Buddhist, Hindu, *Nath* yogic, Mughal and Sikh histories are stacked one upon another. It is one of the few Hindu temples in the region still in use and a rare survival of the *Nath* tradition in Pakistan. Its reopening restored a thread of continuity to a sacred ground that has drawn worshippers for two millennia, and it remains a cherished site both for devotees and for those who value the shared heritage of the frontier.

Name: Gori Temple (Gori jo Mandar)
Location: Gori village (between Islamkot and Nagarparkar), Tharparkar District, Sindh, Pakistan
Sufi Saint: Jain temple dedicated to Parshvanatha (23rd Tirthankara)
Events: Heritage site; occasional Jain/Hindu pilgrimage
Description:
The Gori Temple — *Gori jo Mandar*, the "temple of Gori" — is a marble *Śvetāmbara Jain* temple standing amid the desert near the village of Gori, between Islamkot and Nagarparkar in Tharparkar District, some fourteen miles north-west of the Viravah ruins. Built in 1375-1376 CE and dedicated to *Parshvanatha*, the twenty-third *Tirthankara* of the Jain faith, it is one of the most important surviving Jain monuments of the subcontinent's north-west. The temple, raised on a high stepped platform and built of marble, measures roughly 125 by 60 feet and is distinguished by its three *mandapas* (halls) and its remarkable array of some fifty-two domes, whose form blends Gujarati temple design with the regional architecture of the age. Its greatest treasure is its painting: the frescoes within the main dome — depicting princely processions, palanquins and coaches, riders, and elegantly robed figures in flowing Rajasthani dress — are reckoned to be the oldest surviving Jain frescoes in the northern regions of the subcontinent, a survival of extraordinary rarity. Long abandoned as a place of worship, the temple stands today as a monument of the once-flourishing Jain and Hindu culture of the Thar. It forms part of the group of Nagarparkar temples inscribed in 2016 on the UNESCO tentative list as the "Nagarparkar Cultural Landscape," and it remains a site of pilgrimage interest for Jains and Hindus and of growing concern for heritage conservation.

A heritage-preservation survey by the Endowment Fund Trust for the Heritage of Sindh records the temple's main structure as built of a Jodhpuri stone "much like marble," and notes that its last major repairs are recorded to have been carried out in 1715, attributing the damage the temple has suffered over the centuries to Sindhi troops, fire, and gunpowder rather than to the earthquake and British demolition reported elsewhere. Press coverage in 2016 has independently repeated the temple's dedication to Parshvanath and dated its construction only to "around the 16th century" — a looser dating than the 1375-1376 CE given above, which this entry has not reconciled with the more specific figure. The site was already known to colonial-era archaeology: Henry Cousens' 1929 survey of Sindh's antiquities indexes "Gori" among its subjects, though its descriptive passage on the temple itself was not retrieved in this research pass.

Name: Gurdas Ram Mandir
Location: Radhan Town, Tehsil Mehar, Dadu District, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Not documented
Description:
## Overview

In Radhan Town, a small settlement and railway stop in Mehar Taluka of Dadu District, Sindh, stands the Gurdas Ram Mandir — a Hindu temple named for a locally venerated Sant, Gurdas Ram, about whom almost no biographical or historical record survives. Pakistan's Evacuee Trust Property Board lists the mandir as currently functional; a separate Wikipedia listing of Hindu temples in Pakistan describes a "Bhai Gurdas Ram Mandir" in Dadu District as non-functional, a discrepancy that may reflect the same site under changed circumstances, or simply an outdated secondary source, and is noted here without resolution.

## An Undocumented Namesake — Distinct from Shikarpur's Bhai Gurdas

This mandir's eponymous Gurdas Ram should not be confused with the better-documented "Bhai Gurdas," an Udasi-Sevapanthi founder-figure associated with Shikarpur, some 150 kilometres away, whose career has been covered in recent academic and journalistic writing on Sindh's Nanakpanthi saints. No source connects the two figures, and the Radhan Gurdas Ram appears to be a separate, purely local namesake. The mandir belongs to the same wider cluster of small, similarly obscure Dadu–Mehar sant-shrines as the neighbouring Bhai Sant Thawan Das Mandir (Mehar) and the Sant Baba Bhagat Ram Darbar Mandir (Dadu), all ETPB-registered but lacking any preserved biography for their namesakes.

## Present State

Beyond its precise location and its listed (if disputed) functional status, nothing about the mandir's founding date, architecture, or present congregation has been documented in any source located for this entry. It is recorded here as an active, if little-known, site of Hindu worship in rural Dadu District, with its history awaiting a reliable local or gazetteer source.

Name: Gurdwara Babay De Ber
Events: Sikh pilgrimage; Guru Nanak Gurpurab
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Babay De Ber, the "gurdwara of the elder's jujube tree", also known as Gurdwara Beri Sahib or Babe di Ber, stands in the old city of Sialkot, near the ancient fort. A *gurdwara* is a Sikh house of worship, and this one marks a spot hallowed by the visit of Guru Nanak Dev Ji, the founder of the Sikh faith, during his travels through the north western Punjab. Its name comes from the *ber*, the jujube tree, beneath which the Guru is remembered to have sat, and a venerable tree, held by tradition to be more than five centuries old, still grows within the gurdwara's precincts as the sacred focus of the shrine. It is among the historic Sikh sites of Pakistan that have been restored and reopened for pilgrimage in recent years.

Tradition tells that the Guru sat beneath the tree to plead for the people of Sialkot, who lived in dread of the wrath of a Muslim holy man of the city, Hamza Ghaus. The gurdwara is held to be the place known in Sialkot as Baba Bair, "the shrine of the Berry saint", and the quarter in which it stands is known as the *mohalla*, or locality, of Baba Bair.

## The Guru and Hamza Ghaus

Tradition holds that Guru Nanak reached Sialkot in the course of his great journeys, coming by way of Jammu. He is said to have found the city gripped by fear, for it was believed to lie under threat of destruction on account of a broken promise made to a Muslim holy man of Sialkot named Hamza Ghaus, who had withdrawn in anger to meditate and whose wrath the townsfolk dreaded. The Guru seated himself beneath a *ber* tree close to the place where Hamza Ghaus was absorbed in his devotions, and began to sing aloud the divine word.

The sound is said to have disturbed the meditation of Hamza Ghaus, who came out and demanded to know who this was, and why he should intercede for a city of liars and promise breakers. The Guru is remembered to have replied that it was not just to punish a whole city for the fault of a single man, a teaching of mercy and proportion that, in the telling, moved the holy man and lifted the shadow from Sialkot. The episode belongs to the recurring pattern of the *sakhis*, the stories told of the Guru, in which his travels bring him into dialogue with the Muslim and Hindu holy men of the places he visits, and his words turn anger and division towards compassion.

The story is told in more than one way, and some tellings say more of the quarrel. Hamza Ghaus was a *faqir*, a Sufi mystic, and a Hindu man, it is said, had broken his promise to give him his firstborn son; the faqir told the people of Sialkot that he would pray for forty days and, when his prayers were done, destroy the city. In the *janamsakhis*, the cycles of tales told of the Guru's life, the Guru sets up his base at the foot of an old *beri*, or jujube, tree, the faqir pronounces his curse in the centre of the market square, and when the Guru leaves, almost the entire city is there to see him on his way.

The shrine of Hamza Ghaus lies in an old graveyard not far from the berry tree under which the Guru is said to have sat.

A similar story is told of Pasrur, about thirty kilometres from Sialkot. There the Guru is said to have humbled an arrogant Muslim Sufi named Mian Mitha, who had threatened to "churn" him. Mian Mitha came barefoot, touched the Guru's feet and became his devotee, and their exchange is held to be recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture.

## The Gurdwara

The shrine that grew up around the sacred *ber* tree was built, in its later form, by a man named Natha Singh, and the complex came to include a garden, a *sarovar* or pool, and residential rooms for pilgrims and attendants. The gurdwara was abandoned in 1947, at Partition, the division of the subcontinent. Like many Sikh shrines of Pakistan, it suffered in the disturbances that followed the demolition of the Babri Mosque in 1992, when a structure within the premises is said to have been pulled down by a mob.

In the years that followed, however, the gurdwara's fortunes revived. Access for Indian Sikh pilgrims was restored around 2012, and a board at the entrance recorded that the gurdwara was renovated in 2012 by the Auqaf Department, the department of religious endowments. After renovation the shrine was formally reopened for worship, an event widely welcomed in the Sikh world as part of a wider effort to restore Pakistan's Sikh heritage, though accounts of its condition differ.

Through all these changes the ancient *ber* tree has remained the heart of the site, a living link, in the eyes of the faithful, to the very afternoon on which the Guru sat in its shade. Pilgrims come to pay their respects before it and to make their devotions within the sanctum, where the Guru Granth Sahib is installed.

The gurdwara is reached through the narrow streets of its *mohalla*, though accounts of exactly where in the city it lies differ. The building was an open structure, with a veranda whose pillars held up the roof and a single room at its centre. The tree stood behind the building: a thick tree, bending towards the ground, that looked ancient, if judged by its size. Tiles in the floor carried the names of Sikh devotees who had contributed towards the initial construction of the gurdwara, and its walls bore pictures of Hindu deities.

Beneath the tree lay a long grave, covered with a red sheet bearing Quranic verses, and a red flag stood at the entrance. The grave was new: when the place had been visited earlier, there had been no such grave. A man who showed visitors round called it the grave of Pir Bairi, "the saint of berries". On a wall the invocations "Ya Allah" and "Ya Muhammad", O God and O Muhammad, had been scribbled with a piece of coal where the text in Gurmukhi, the script of the Sikh scriptures, had been wiped clean, and a mosque had newly been built next to the shrine.

## Guru Nanak

Guru Nanak was the founder of the Sikh religion and the first Guru of the Sikhs. Accounts of his dates differ, but they are most often given as 1469 to 1539. Accounts of how many journeys he made also differ, but his *udasis*, the long journeys of his travelling years, are most often counted as four, and they lasted more than twenty years. He travelled mostly on foot, east to Bengal, south to Sri Lanka, north to Kashmir, Nepal and Tibet, and west to Mecca. He preferred to stay on the outskirts of villages, and whenever he visited an area he would visit its religious shrines, Muslim, Hindu and of any other denomination.

Sialkot recurs in the janamsakhis. The story of the faqir falls on the Guru's second journey, and his third began and ended in the city: from Sialkot he trekked north into Jammu and Kashmir, to Sumeru, the legendary Mount Kailash, and to Ladakh, before returning to Sialkot.

He married Sulakhini, daughter of Mul Chand and Chando Rani of the town of Batala, on 24 September 1487, though accounts of the marriage differ, and his sons were Sri Chand, born on 8 September 1494, and Lakhmi Das, born on 12 February 1497. Lakhmi Das, it is said, was a worthy son, but spiritual wealth was not his portion, and the Guru passed him over. On his deathbed he appointed not his son but his most loyal student as his spiritual successor, a Khatri named Lehna, who became Guru Angad.

Nanak himself is held to have abhorred the association of miracles with religious personalities, yet the stories of his life are full of them. In one of them he tells Karori, who calls his cure a miracle, that "there is no such thing as a miracle". He was no unworldly mystic but a householder, and he brought a message of peace and harmony to the believers of Islam and Hinduism. His advice to Bhai Bala and Bhai Mardana was that "if one is a Muslim then one should be a good Muslim and if one is a Hindu then one should be a good Hindu".

Muslims have claimed the Guru too. Many Muslims acquainted with his teachings are devoted to him and visit his shrine, and to one Muslim painter, "Guru Nanak is like a Muslim Sufi Saint". A twentieth century Chishti Sabiri shaykh counted Guru Nanak, with Krishna, Rama, Sita and Lachman, among the spiritual luminaries outside Islam who believed in the one true God and had a "Divine connection", *nisbat*. The texts of the Sufi saint Baba Farid are revered among the Sikhs, for he is held to have influenced the founder of their religion, and in the Hinglaj valley there are the engraved footsteps of Guru Nanak. In his time, it has been argued, all literate Punjabis, Hindus and Muslims alike, were conversant with the Persian poets ʿAttar, Rumi and Saʿdi.

## Devotion and Verse

In Aurangzeb's time the followers of Baba Nanak, as the Guru was also called, lived at one with their friends and without strife towards their enemies, and their master's name was always on their tongues. The heart of their worship was the reading of his verses, which they sang. They counted the service of those who come and go as the highest worship, and whoever arrived at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name was treated as a brother and a friend and served, even a stranger, a thief, a highwayman or an evildoer. The Udasis, devotees of Baba Nanak who worship the Creator after their master's way, were counted then as a fourth class among the dervishes of Hind, or India. The tradition of *langar*, the free communal kitchen, is believed to have begun with Guru Nanak.

The Guru composed verses in Hindi on the truth of God, setting out the unity of God, and a singer named Mardana sang them and drew people into the snare of faith. His *bani*, devotional verses of supplication, entreaty, humility and reverence, was compiled as part of the Adi Granth, the first compilation of the Sikh scripture, by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, in 1604.

The Guru's verse is sung outside the gurdwaras too. The singer Abida Parvin has said: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak." In Sindh, Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the *banis* of Shri Guru Nanak and the *kalams*, the poems, of the Sufis.

Among the Guru's poems is the *Babur Bani*, a long poem that Nanak wrote at the time the Mughal Babur attacked the Punjab, destroying the cities of Eminabad and Lahore on the way. One of its lines reads:

ਆਵਨਿ ਅਠਤਰੈ …

*Coming in seventy-eight (1521 C.E)*

Lines from the Guru's other hymns, in English translation, give a sense of his poetry. His *aarti*, the hymn sung as lamps are waved in worship, has these lines:

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ
ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ …

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps*

On the oneness of God he sang:

ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥
ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One*

And again:

*God is One, / The Path is One*

His poem on the sacred thread, the *janeu*, runs:

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ
ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ …

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment*

Of washing he sang:

ਭਰੀਐ ਹਥੁ ਪੈਰੁ ਤਨੁ ਦੇਹ ॥
ਪਾਣੀ ਧੋਤੈ ਉਤਰਸੁ ਖੇਹ ॥

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white*

And in another song:

ਬਗਾ ਬਗੇ ਕਪੜੇ ਤੀਰਥ ਮੰਝਿ ਵਸੰਨਿੑ ॥

*The herons in their white feathers dwell in the sacred shrines of pilgrimage*

## The City of Sialkot

In the Guru's day Sialkot was a bustling city in the foothills of the Himalayas, inhabited predominantly by Muslims, with a powerful Hindu trading community. Accounts of its founding differ. Legend gives it to Raja Sela, the uncle of the Pandavas, the heroes of the Mahabharata, and its rebuilding to Raja Satya Vachan, when it became part of the kingdom of Kashmir. Its earliest recorded mention is in ancient Greek texts going back to 322 BC, where it is called Sagala, and it was famous for its silk.

The city stands in the Rachna doab, the land between two rivers, and was counted a city of the ancients. In former times it was the seat of government of the Punjab, its habitation stretching two or three *kos*, an old measure of distance. When Lahore lay in ruins in early times, Sialkot became the seat of government of the region, until the conquest of Sultan Mahmud and the rebuilding of Lahore by Malik Ayaz.

Sialkot passed into the Muslim Sultanate under Shahabuddin Muhammad Ghori, who repaired its old fort and left his army there; Khusraw Malik and the Khokhars besieged the fort for a time without success. Many Sufi missionaries settled in the region, making it predominantly Muslim and giving it a rich Sufi tradition, and the city was an important post on the trade route between West Asia and Delhi. Under the Mughal emperor Akbar, Raja Man Singh, military commander of Jammu and holder of the land grant of Sialkot, repaired the fort and improved the city; in Jahangir's reign Safdar Khan rebuilt the fort and its tower, and most later governors made repairs too.

In Aurangzeb's time Sialkot surpassed every other town of the province in population, and it was a city of crafts and learning. Its paper, the Mansinghi, the silk paper and the Khass-e Jahangiri, was white and durable and sent to other regions; its *karchikan* embroidery in silk and *kalabatun*, thread of gold and silver, went all over the world; and its *jamdhar* and *katari* daggers and *barchhi* spears were well made. Gardens surrounded the city, and the buildings of the *qanungos*, the keepers of the land records, and of some others were most pleasing and delightful.

A stream rising in the hills of Jammu flowed below the city. When it flooded in the rains, all the people of Sialkot, great and small, played in the water, naked but for a loincloth and carrying leather water skins, and anyone from the city who was far away remembered it with pleasure.

The city was a seat of learning and a gathering place of scholars, a mine of virtue and a home of the learned, and in the Mughal period it was one of the centres of Islamic scholarship, where Ahmad Sirhindi studied. Under Akbar, Maulana Kamal al-Din Husain left Kashmir, came to Sialkot in 971 AH and established teaching there; under Shah Jahan, Maulvi Abd al-Hakim spread the sciences, wrote glosses and drew students to his *madrasa*, his religious school. The saint Shah Daulah, whose first master lived in Sialkot, is said to have left the city after disputes with its people and, after some years, to have moved to Gujrat.

The Guru's own lifetime found the Punjab plunged into political crises. Babur invaded it a third time and reached as far as Sialkot, though accounts of what befell the city differ.

Today Sialkot has become one of the most important cities in Pakistan. Its business community financed its own airport, which handles international flights, and the highway. The city lies right on the border, and historically it gave the Punjab a connection to Kashmir. The author of the history *Tarikh Guru Khalsa* belonged to Sialkot.

Across the Pakistani Punjab, hundreds of temples and gurdwaras were taken over by refugees after 1947 and turned into houses, and several were taken over and destroyed by migrants. After the demolition of the Babri Mosque on 6 December 1992, well known Hindus living in the cities of the Punjab had to hide for several months.

## Legacy

Gurdwara Babay De Ber is one of several historic gurdwaras associated with Guru Nanak in the Pakistani Punjab that have drawn renewed attention as pilgrimage and heritage sites, and its story carries a particular moral weight. The story of the Guru's encounter with Hamza Ghaus, and of his plea that a whole community not be condemned for the sin of one, speaks directly to the ethic of compassion and shared humanity at the core of Guru Nanak's message. For the city of Sialkot, the shrine and its ancient tree are a reminder of a plural past in which, as tradition tells, the founder of the Sikh faith and a Muslim saint of the city met beneath the same sky; for pilgrims, it is a cherished station on the map of the Guru's travels through the land of the five rivers.

Everyone in Sialkot seemed to know where Baba Bair was, and the name itself is held to go back to Guru Nanak. Across Pakistan there are several sites where Nanak stayed or is said to have performed miracles, and the gurdwaras built there later by his devotees still stand tall.

Name: Gurdwara Babay Nanki
Sufi Saint: Bebe Nanaki (elder sister of Guru Nanak)
Events: Occasional pilgrimage; Bebe Nanaki commemoration
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Babay Nanki, also known as Gurdwara Janamasthan Bebe Nanaki or Gurdwara Bebe Nanaki, stands in Dera Chahal, a village in the Lahore district some twenty kilometres south east of the city, close to the present border with India. It commemorates Bebe Nanaki, also called Bibi Nanaki, the elder sister of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith; in Sikh tradition she was the very first of his followers, the first Sikh. Dera Chahal was the ancestral village of Guru Nanak's maternal family, and Nanaki is traditionally held to have been born here. Though far less frequented than the major gurdwaras, the shrine carries a particular resonance for pilgrims who wish to honour the family that nurtured Guru Nanak and the sister whose faith preceded even his ministry.

## Bebe Nanaki

Bebe Nanaki was born, by tradition, around 1464, and was older than her brother by some five years. Their mother, Mata Tripta, belonged to Dera Chahal. As the story is retold, Tripta, five months pregnant, went to her maternal home in that village, at a little distance from Lahore, and there, about six years after her wedding, gave birth to a daughter. The child's grandmother suggested the name Nanaki, since the child had been born in her maternal house, *Nanaka* in Punjabi. Tradition holds that she was born in a house that stood where the gurdwara now stands, and that Nanak was named after his sister.

From his earliest childhood she is said to have seen in Nanak a spiritual greatness that others overlooked, and she became his steadfast supporter and protector. In the stories of his youth she stands between the young Nanak and their father's displeasure. She restrains her father when he berates the boy, and in one telling she brings her father a glass of hot milk mixed with almonds and defends her brother: "He is a very sensible person." Sikh tradition holds her to be the first to recognise him as a teacher of divine truth, and so the first *Gursikh*, a disciple of the Guru. It also credits her with encouraging his devotional use of music, the practice of *kirtan*, the singing of hymns, which remains central to Sikh worship.

Nanaki married Jai Ram, a Khatri of the Palta or Uppal clan and an official in the service of Daulat Khan Lodi, the governor at Sultanpur, and moved to Sultanpur. It is told that it was she who arranged her brother's marriage, having already found a girl for him, Sulakhni. At the request of Nanaki and her husband, their father sent Nanak to Sultanpur, where he lived with them and took employment at Daulat Khan's *modikhana*, the government store. It was in this period, at the river Bein, that he is said to have received the revelation that inaugurated his mission. Nanaki's household at Sultanpur thus became one of the cradles of the nascent faith. Daulat Khan, Jai Ram's patron, later rose to become the governor of Lahore and the lands around it.

## Sister and First Believer

Nanaki holds a decisive place in the story of Nanak's call. When Nanak disappeared in the river, Daulat Khan and she alone believed that he was alive: "My brother will return safe," she said. Of the disciples who gathered round him at Sultanpur, the most ardent were his sister and her husband, Jai Ram.

She rejoiced at her brother's returns from his journeys, once together with Jai Ram. Though saddened by one of his decisions, she did not try to sway him; on another occasion, at her plea, he put off his departure. It is told that on one journey Nanak set out to visit his sister, her husband and his friend Nawab Daulat Khan at Sultanpur, stopping on the way at Dera Chahal, at Jaman and at one other place.

Nanaki also had a place in her brother's household after his marriage. It is told that she was particularly sympathetic towards Sulakhni, and that she decided to look after Sulakhni's eldest son, Sri Chand. Having no child of her own, she found it easier to adopt him for a time, and Sri Chand followed the spiritual pursuits of his father, encouraged by her.

One story of Nanak gives his sister the moment of discovery. In one storyteller's version of the tale of mud turned into sugar, it was his sister who opened the bags on the mules and found that the mud had been changed into sugar and *gur*, unrefined cane sugar.

Nanaki is believed to have died in 1518, at Sultanpur, in what is now Indian Punjab. She came down with a mysterious ailment and breathed her last, and Jai Ram, unable to bear the loss, died three days later. She died before her brother.

## The Gurdwara

Dera Chahal was the village of Guru Nanak's *nanake*, his mother's family, and the Guru is remembered to have visited it on more than one occasion. Later his followers built a gurdwara here to mark the spot. It honours the village as the *janamasthan*, the birthplace, of Bebe Nanaki, and stands within the settlement as a modest but cherished shrine. It is held to stand on the exact spot where the home of Nanak's maternal family used to be. When Maharaja Ranjit Singh became the sovereign of Punjab at the end of the eighteenth century, he spent large amounts of money on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras, this one among them, and attached vast tracts of land to them so that the revenues from the land could pay for their running.

The gurdwara was once one big hall, with a small balcony opening towards the centre of the hall from the first floor. Part of its grounds used to be the hall of the *langar*, the free communal kitchen; by the early twenty first century it had become a lawn with a few rooms around it.

Like the other sites of the Lahore region associated with Nanak, the gurdwara was largely abandoned after 1947 and passed into the care of the Evacuee Trust Property Board, the state body that administers the properties of communities displaced at Partition. Accounts differ over how far it stayed open to Sikhs in the years that followed, but it has continued to receive Sikh visitors, especially on pilgrimages that take in the great shrines of Nankana Sahib and Kartarpur.

After his book came out, the writer Iqbal Qaiser recalls, Sikhs living in Canada, England and America put a lot of pressure on the Government of Pakistan to renovate the gurdwara. Malik Meraj Khalid, a son of the village, was born in 1916 to a poor agricultural family of Dera Chahal. A politician of the PPP, the Pakistan Peoples Party, he was twice Speaker of the National Assembly, once Chief Minister of Punjab and, between November 1996 and February 1997, interim Prime Minister. One of his first orders as Prime Minister was the approval of funds to renovate this historical gurdwara in his village, though he was not a Sikh. The gurdwara was in a horrible state when he ordered its renovation, and even then only its external structure was spruced up.

## Devotion

For Sikhs, Bebe Nanaki embodies the ideals of insight, devotion and selfless love, and she holds a place of special affection as the woman who first understood the Guru's message. By the early twenty first century, pilgrims who came to Pakistan for festivals were allowed to visit her gurdwara, and on those occasions prayers were offered here.

A young priest, Daleep Singh, lived at the gurdwara. Inside, the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, was placed in a wooden *Thara Sahib*, a raised platform, and the priest bowed before it. Ghulab Singh, the first Sikh police officer in the revamped traffic police of Lahore, stayed at the gurdwara when he was in Lahore, and his official bike stood in its courtyard.

The gurdwara also has a tradition of its own. Bhai Bannu, sent by Guru Arjan to Lahore to bind the Adi Granth, the scripture of the Sikhs, is said to have come and stayed at this gurdwara, and to have prepared another copy here without the Guru's permission, adding verses that the Guru rejected. It is also said that one of the movements started from this gurdwara. The Kashmiri binders who once lived in Lahore were known for their meticulous binding.

## The Setting

Dera Chahal lies on the Bedian road, the old route to Amritsar. By the early twenty first century it was flanked by Phases Five, Six and Seven of the Defence Housing Authority, and around the old village stood the new houses of former farmers who had sold their land to developers. More generally, the Defence Housing Authority, the neatest and most expensive residential area of Lahore, sprawled across a vast tract of land, eating into the small historic villages of the area; congested and stricken by poverty, such villages were trapped within a wall after selling their land to it.

The white dome of the gurdwara could then be seen from afar. A saffron flag rose from behind the wall, a sign that members of the Sikh community were living here, and behind it lay a pool of water where buffaloes wallowed, once the sacred pool of this shrine. Next to the pool stood a mosque that was being expanded, and on one occasion a sermon from its loudspeaker drowned out a conversation at the gurdwara. Behind the pool lay agricultural land associated with the gurdwara, and from the gurdwara's window a new apartment block could be seen, one of those built recently to cater to the growing demands of urban Lahore.

That land became the subject of a legal fight. Ghulab Singh filed a case against the Evacuee Trust Property Board in the Lahore High Court over the alleged sale of agricultural land associated with the gurdwara. The Supreme Court of Pakistan took cognisance of the case and asked the construction companies to pay 986 million rupees as surety while the hearings proceeded. Daleep Singh alleged that documents proved corruption at the Board, and that its former head, Asif Hashmi, had earned billions in his tenure of five years. In April 2016 Asif Hashmi was arrested in Dubai.

In the early twenty first century it had become rare to meet a Sikh in Lahore, a city once ruled by a Sikh and the seat of Sikh political strength. After 1947 hundreds of temples and gurdwaras all over Pakistani Punjab were taken over by refugees and turned into households. Sikh architecture in Lahore, it has been said, draws inspiration from both Hindu and Muslim architecture, just as the Sikh religion picks up from both Hinduism and Islam, and Sikh builders made the domes of Muslim building smaller.

## Legacy

The veneration of Bebe Nanaki affirms the honoured place of women in the Sikh tradition from its very origin. The gurdwara at Dera Chahal is one of two principal sites associated with her, the other being at Sultanpur Lodhi in India, and it preserves her memory on Pakistani soil. Its continued existence within Lahore district adds to the region's remarkable concentration of sites tied to the life of Guru Nanak and his circle.

That memory has been under pressure and in renewal at once: the sacred pool given over to buffaloes and the gurdwara's former lands in dispute before the courts, but also a building restored on the orders of a Prime Minister born in the village who was not himself a Sikh, a priest in residence, the Guru Granth Sahib installed, and pilgrims admitted on festival days.

Name: Gurdwara Balila Sahib (Bal Lila Sahib)
Events: Guru Nanak Gurpurab (November)
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Bal Lila Sahib, also called Gurdwara Balila, stands at Nankana Sahib in the Punjab, some three hundred metres to the south east of Gurdwara Janam Asthan, the birthplace of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith. Its name, *Bal Lila*, "the play of childhood", marks the open field where, according to Sikh tradition, the child Nanak gathered his companions and passed the days of his boyhood. It is among the cluster of shrines that make Nankana Sahib, the Guru's birth town, the foremost place of Sikh pilgrimage in Pakistan, and it keeps the memory not of a miracle or a martyrdom but of the childhood of the founder of the faith.

The gurdwara stands across the road from Gurdwara Patti Sahib. Tradition holds that the ground was once an open field where Guru Nanak used to play as a child, and the gurdwara was built to mark the spot. Beside it lies a *sarovar*, a holy tank, called Nanaksar, whose waters pilgrims hold sacred.

## The Guru

In the Guru's day Nankana Sahib was the village of Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, held by Rai Bular Bhatti, the local landlord. Nanak was born there in 1469, though accounts of the date differ, and he spent his early years there. Accounts of his birthplace have not always agreed, but it is generally held to be Talwandi. The village was renamed Nankana Sahib in honour of the Guru, and because he spent his early years there it has several gurdwaras marking events from his childhood, all of which the pilgrims visit.

His father was Kalyan Chand Das Bedi, or Mehta Kalu as he was affectionately called, the accountant of the Bhatti family under Rai Bular, and his mother was Mata Tripta. Nanak belonged to the Bedi caste. Tradition tells that Mata Tripta had no child for a long time after her marriage, and that she would regularly visit an ancient Hindu temple on top of a mound not far from Talwandi to pray for a child; accounts of how his birth came about differ.

The *janamsakhis*, the traditional accounts of the Guru's life written by his devotees after his death, dwell fondly on his boyhood. They portray a child unlike his fellows: drawn to contemplation, indifferent to games for their own sake, and given to gathering the other children around him not merely to play but to sit in stillness and turn their minds towards the divine Name. Tradition holds that the field of Bal Lila was the scene of these gatherings, and there the young Nanak is remembered as a leader among his playmates and as a soul already absorbed in God. These stories fixed this patch of ground in the sacred geography of the *Panth*, the Sikh community, and a shrine rose to honour it.

In his early years, it is said, signs of spiritual unveiling and of wonders beyond the ordinary course of things appeared in him. The janamsakhis tell that the village astrologer foretold greatness for the child, and that at school he showed a brilliance never before seen in any child in Talwandi. At thirteen, in the same stories, he refused the *janeu*, the sacred thread, in his father's courtyard, saying that "it is our actions and our actions alone" that give a man his position among men. At sixteen, the stories go on, he herded cattle. They tell, too, that he became well acquainted with the dervish Sayyad Hussain and gained an intimate knowledge of the Sufi line of thought; accounts of the dervish's name differ.

Talwandi lay in the path of numerous mendicants, holy men and *sadhus*, as Hindu ascetics are called, who camped in a grove of trees on the outskirts of the village. It is told that when Nanak turned eighteen his father asked him to take up a trade and gave him twenty rupees, and that Nanak left the town with Bhai Mardana. The tale is remembered as the *Sacha Sauda*, the "true bargain".

From Talwandi he went to Sultanpur, around sixty kilometres away, as keeper of the stores of Nawab Daulat Khan. There, the janamsakhis tell, he vanished in the stream for a week and came out saying, "There is only one God. There is no Hindu, no Mussalman." He married Sulakhini, daughter of Mul Chand and Chando Rani of the town of Batala, on 24 September 1487, though accounts of the marriage differ.

He set out on long journeys, the *udasis*. Accounts differ on how many journeys he made, but together they lasted more than twenty years, and he travelled mostly on foot. Wherever he went he visited the religious shrines of the place, Muslim, Hindu or of any other denomination, and people came from every land in great numbers to become his disciples.

He came home between his journeys. The janamsakhis tell that when Nanak and Mardana returned to Talwandi in 1506, Mata Tripta felt great joy, and Mehta Kalu was a little in awe of his son. In the same stories, after Pak Pattan, he travelled back to Talwandi again; it was no longer an obscure little village but had become a place of pilgrimage, and he sat by Rai Bular, who was sick and failing.

Born into a Hindu household and educated in a Muslim milieu, he was neither a practising Muslim nor a Hindu, and his advice to his companions was that "if one is a Muslim then one should be a good Muslim and if one is a Hindu then one should be a good Hindu". He lived as a householder. Nanak himself is held to have abhorred the association of miracles with religious personalities, though the stories told of his life are full of them.

He spent a major portion of his life in what is today Pakistan: he was born there, and he eventually settled in a small village on the Pakistani side of the border. On his deathbed he appointed not his son but his most loyal student as his spiritual successor. His son Lakhmi Das, it was said, was worthy, but the Guru passed him over, and at the hour of his death he made Lehna his successor, with the title Guru Angad. Guru Nanak died on 22 September 1539, though accounts of his death differ.

## The Gurdwara

Tradition ascribes the original excavation of the tank, together with an early shrine, to Rai Bular, the Guru's own patron, who is remembered in Sikh devotion for the reverence he showed the boy Nanak. The present building is traditionally associated with the middle of the eighteenth century and the munificence of Diwan Kaura Mal, the influential minister of that era. In the early nineteenth century Maharaja Ranjit Singh is said to have had the shrine renovated, the tank enlarged and properly lined with masonry, and generous grants of land settled upon it for its upkeep.

As sovereign of the Punjab, Ranjit Singh spent large amounts of money on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras all over the province, and he attached vast tracts of land to them so that the revenues from the lands could support their running.

The shrines of Nankana Sahib were caught up in the great struggle of the early twentieth century to reform the management of the gurdwaras, which had passed into the hands of hereditary custodians known as *mahants*. Across the Punjab, as a result of sectarian divisions among the Sikh communities and the British takeover of the province, a large number of important Sikh gurdwaras were being administered by Hindu *mahants*. In February 1921 a peaceful body of reformers was massacred at Gurdwara Janam Asthan, in one of the defining episodes of the Gurdwara Reform Movement. In the aftermath, tradition records, the *mahants* of Bal Lila Sahib chose to hand over the shrine voluntarily to the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, the body that thereafter managed the historic gurdwaras, in exchange for a maintenance allowance for their families.

Since the Partition of 1947 the gurdwara, like its neighbours at Nankana Sahib, has stood in a land where few Sikhs remain, cared for by the Evacuee Trust Property Board and thrown open to the pilgrims who cross the border in their thousands each year. Kartar, whose family was one of the first to move to Nankana Sahib, remembered that no Sikh was left there after Partition and that the town's gurdwaras became barren and fell into a bad state. In the 1960s Giani Pratap came with a party of pilgrims from India and, seeing the dilapidated condition of the shrines, decided to stay and look after these holy buildings.

A Sikh community has returned to the town. Its people are not natives of the city but recent migrants from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where there is a considerable Sikh population. Families came following the alienation after the wars of 1965 and 1971 and the demolition of the Babri Mosque in 1992, and within about ten years the community grew to about two hundred households, though accounts of its size differ. Most of the newcomers were housed within the gurdwaras, in rooms generally reserved for pilgrims. Surjeet and Udam, whose families had moved to Nankana a few years before, spoke Urdu with a Pashto accent. Surjeet spoke of a cricket tournament arranged for the first time for the birthday of Guru Gobind Singh, and at one time he explained that the gurdwara was under renovation.

Several people at Nankana Sahib felt that the PSGPC, the Pakistani committee, was not representative of the Sikh community in Pakistan. Most of the town's Muslims had migrated from the other side of the border after Partition, and their attitudes are said to have been shaped by those experiences.

The town's gurdwaras have also known politics. Before the PSGPC existed, the staff of the Indian High Commission in Islamabad received the pilgrims at the border and arranged their stay inside the gurdwaras. At the Guru's birthday in November 1985, a year after Operation Blue Star, an American Sikh spoke for a separate Sikh state at one of the town's gurdwaras. During the speech the gate was closed, and two officials, Counsellor B. Jain and First Secretary K. K. Khanna, were attacked. The religious festivals at Nankana and in other cities of Pakistan went back to being religious festivals.

## Devotion and Festivals

The gurdwara is remembered for children's games. At Lohri, sports competitions are arranged for children within its premises, though accounts differ on how long and how regularly the custom has been kept.

Lohri is an ancient festival of the Punjab that commemorates the change of season. It is celebrated on the 13th of January, generally the last night of the month of Poh, with a village bonfire, dry fruit and folk songs; the children collect the wood, and *kheer*, a rice pudding, is left to cool overnight. After the creation of Pakistan this indigenous festival of the Punjab died down, and at Nankana it was being revived by a group of Pathan men living in the Punjab.

Most of the town's gurdwaras remained locked all year round, to be opened only at the time of the festival, and security guards were employed at the entrance to all of them. The great festival is the Guru's birthday, called Guru Nanak Jayanti or *Gurpurab*, and thousands of people come to Nankana Sahib for it from all over the world. Official estimates put their number at ten to fifteen thousand every year; in 2011, when the festival ran from 8 to 10 November, media reports counted only three thousand.

That year police stood in force at all the entrances to the city, no car was permitted inside, and devotees walked barefoot. Pilgrims from Delhi, Gujarat and Amritsar came by train and crossed the border at Wagah, where representatives of the Evacuee Trust Property Board and the PSGPC received them and a *langar*, the free communal kitchen, was arranged, and they stayed three days at Nankana. Three days of *Akhand Path*, the unbroken reading of the scripture, ended in the *bhog*, the closing rite, followed by the *Nagar Kirtan*, the procession with hymns. Richer pilgrims from Britain, America and Canada came by chartered plane and hired buses, and the posters of travel companies promised them "all" the gurdwaras in Pakistan. For those few days the whole city looked like a little India.

In Aurangzeb's reign the sum of the worship of Baba Nanak's followers, as the Guru was also called, was the reading of their master's verses, which they sang to melody. They counted service to those who come and go, the traveller and the guest, as the highest worship, and whoever arrived at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name they treated as a brother and a friend and served, even a stranger, a thief, a highwayman or an evildoer. The tradition of *langar* is believed to have begun with Guru Nanak.

The Guru's festival is kept far from Nankana too: at Manora, Jeeta Singh held a small festival every November, when the festival of Guru Nanak is celebrated at Nankana Sahib. At one of the shrines of Guru Nanak at Nankana Sahib, a picture of Baba Farid accompanied the picture of the Guru.

## The Guru's Verse

Guru Nanak's devotional verses are known as *bani*, verses of supplication, entreaty, humility and reverence. He composed verses in Hindi on the truth of God, setting out divine unity in clear words and shining metaphors, and a singer named Mardana sang his verses and drew people into the snare of devotion.

His poem on the sacred thread, the *janeu* that the stories say he refused as a boy, runs:

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ
ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ …

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment*

On the oneness of God he sang:

ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥
ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One*

And again:

*God is One, / The Path is One*

The *aarti*, the hymn sung as lamps are waved in worship, begins:

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ
ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ …

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps*

Of washing he sang:

ਭਰੀਐ ਹਥੁ ਪੈਰੁ ਤਨੁ ਦੇਹ ॥
ਪਾਣੀ ਧੋਤੈ ਉਤਰਸੁ ਖੇਹ ॥

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white*

And in another song:

ਬਗਾ ਬਗੇ ਕਪੜੇ ਤੀਰਥ ਮੰਝਿ ਵਸੰਨਿੑ ॥

*The herons in their white feathers dwell in the sacred shrines of pilgrimage*

A line of the *Babur Bani*, his verses on the invasion of Babur, dates the invaders' coming:

ਆਵਨਿ ਅਠਤਰੈ …

*Coming in seventy-eight (1521 C.E)*

The verse is sung beyond the gurdwaras. The singer Abida Parvin has said: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak." In Sindh, Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the *banis* of Shri Guru Nanak and the *kalams*, the poems, of the Sufis.

## The Setting

Talwandi lay between the rivers Ravi and Chenab, directly in the path of the armies that had set their eyes on Delhi. It is told that the village was destroyed thirteen times and thirteen times rose again from its ashes, like the fabled phoenix, and that its last rebirth came under Rai Bhoe, a Bhatti Rajput who had converted to Islam. In the same telling, Rai Bhoe's son was Rai Bular, and Shiv Ram, head of a Bedi family, was accountant to Rai Bhoe and was succeeded by his son, Kalyan Chand Das Bedi. In the time of Sultan Bahlul Lodi, when Tatar Khan was governor of Lahore, Rai Ram Deo Bhatti took the whole of the Punjab in farm from him, that is, the right to its revenue for a sum of money.

Behind Gurdwara Janam Asthan, away from the hub of the new settlement, rests an archaeological mound. A settlement once stood there; it was destroyed, after which Rai Bhoi di Talwandi was built within a boundary wall, so that Nanak was born in the new town. The young Nanak is said to have spent a lot of time on the mound in conversation with the yogis, *sadhus* and dervishes who passed through Talwandi, and it is believed that he began to frequent it in the six or seven years between the *Sacha Sauda* and his move to Sultanpur. The climb was steep, with no proper path, to a top at least twenty metres from the ground, covered with shrubs of *karir*, a thorny desert bush, with shards of broken pottery and other mud utensils underfoot.

Nankana Sahib lies about forty miles south west of Lahore, and it is counted among the holiest cities in the world for the Sikhs, because the founder of their religion was born there. From a rooftop one could see the minarets of mosques, the small white domes of the gurdwaras, and the remains of a few Hindu temples, cone like structures rising from houses abandoned at the time of Partition.

One main road ran through the entire city; the buildings were old, most of them from the late British or the early Pakistan era, and the road had potholes. In 2005 Nankana Sahib was separated from Sheikhupura and made an independent district, with the city as its headquarters. The city had a population of over a million. Guru Nanak was celebrated all over Nankana Sahib: there were a Guru Nanak High School, a Guru Nanak grocery store and a Guru Nanak cloth shop, all run by Sikhs, while the town's Muslims generally refrained from honouring Guru Nanak in this way.

## Legacy

Where other shrines mark the Guru's teachings, his travels or the sacrifices of the martyrs, Bal Lila Sahib, with its field and its tank, commemorates that the founder of the faith was once a child at play on this ground, and that even then, in the telling of the Panth, the light within him was already shining. For the pilgrim who has bowed at the Janam Asthan, a visit to Bal Lila Sahib completes the geography of Guru Nanak's beginnings. Across Pakistan there are several sites where Nanak is said to have stayed or performed miracles, and the gurdwaras built there by his devotees still stand. In Aurangzeb's reign Baba Nanak was called the caravan leader on the paths of truth and the torch bearer of the mystic way.

Devotion to the Guru reaches beyond the Sikhs. Many Muslims acquainted with his teachings are devoted to him too and visit his shrine, and to Nadeem, a Muslim painter, Guru Nanak was like a Muslim Sufi saint. Baba Farid, it is said, became an inspiration for Guru Nanak when Nanak visited his shrine on his travels, and Farid's texts are revered among the Sikhs, for he is held to have influenced the founder of their religion. A twentieth century shaykh of the Chishti Sabiri Sufi order described Guru Nanak, with Krishna, Rama, Sita and Lachman, among the spiritual luminaries outside Islam, as a believer in the one true God and a religious leader with a "Divine connection", *nisbat*. There is a growing similarity between the iconography of Guru Nanak and that of Jhulelal, and at the shrine of the goddess Hinglaj there are engraved footsteps of Guru Nanak.
