Location: Dabbi Bazaar, Walled City, Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: Sikh anniversaries; martyrdom commemoration of Guru Arjan Dev
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Baoli Sahib stands in the crowded Dabbi Bazaar at the very heart of the walled city of Lahore, where its precinct once adjoined the Loha, Kesera and Guru bazaars. It commemorates a visit to Lahore in 1599 by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Sikh Guru, and takes its name from the *baoli*, a roofed stepwell, that the Guru is remembered as having had sunk at this spot to provide water for the people of the quarter. Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth, the Sikh scripture, and was the first martyr of the Sikh faith; his principal memorial in Lahore is Gurdwara Dera Sahib by the Fort, and as a shrine tied to him, Baoli Sahib is a significant station on the map of Sikh Lahore. Today the site is also known as Baoli Bagh, its surroundings laid out as a garden.

The well is said to have been filled in during the turbulence of the eighteenth century. It was found again and restored in the reign of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, and by the 1880s the house of Baoli Sahib was the largest in extent of the famous Sikh places of worship in Lahore.

## The Guru

Guru Arjan was the fifth Sikh Guru and the son of the fourth, Guru Ram Das, who appointed him as the next Guru. He was born in 1563 and became Guru in 1581; accounts of the year of his death differ, but it is most often given as 1606. He was the younger brother of Prithi Chand, and it was the younger son whom their father chose.

Lahore stands at the root of that succession. It is told that Prithi Chand hid the letters Arjan sent from Lahore to Ram Das, and that Ram Das then disowned Prithi Chand and, a few days later, appointed Arjan as the next Guru. Sikh tradition finds the root of the conflict in Arjan's journey to Lahore and the machinations of Prithi Chand, who went on to approach the Mughal authorities for his share of the property; with this, it has been said, began the troubled relation between the Mughals and the Sikhs. Lahore was the birthplace of Guru Ram Das; Guru Arjan spent a lot of time in the city, and so did Guru Hargobind.

His great work was the scripture. In 1604 he compiled the Adi Granth, gathering into it the *bani*, the sacred compositions, of Guru Nanak and the writings of all the earlier Sikh Gurus and of other saints who were not Sikhs. Among them was the poetry of Baba Farid, which Guru Nanak had collected at Pakpattan. He himself has more hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib than anyone else.

The binding of the book was Lahore work. Guru Arjan sent one of his followers, Bhai Bannu, to Lahore to bind the Adi Granth, and the Kashmiri binders who used to live in the city were known for their meticulous binding. After the compilation the Guru was summoned to answer a charge that the book held anti-Muslim and anti-Hindu content; he sent Bhai Gurdas, who cleared up the misunderstanding. The Adi Granth played a significant part in the growth of a separate Sikh identity, and among the reasons given are rumours that Meherban, the son of Prithi Chand, was compiling a scripture of his own.

Other institutions are credited to him. He introduced the *daswandh*, the giving of a tenth of one's earnings to the cause of the Guru, and its collection through the *masands*, the Guru's appointed collectors, was a practice that began with him. He is credited with completing the Amrit Sar, the tank of nectar that his father had begun at Ramdaspur, after which the Harmandir Sahib was built there. In 1594 he founded Kartarpur, near Jalandhar, on land granted in the reign of Akbar, the third Mughal emperor.

A meeting between Guru Arjan and an emperor is also remembered. As the imperial camp left Lahore for the Deccan, the emperor crossed the Beas and came to the place where the Guru, the successor of Baba Nanak, had halted. The emperor was pleased with the meeting, and with hearing from the Guru's own mouth the Hindi verses that Baba Nanak had composed on the knowledge of God, and the Guru, counting it an honour, presented a fitting *peshkash*, a gift offered to a ruler. Then the Guru made a petition: while the imperial armies were in the Punjab grain had been dear and the assessment had been raised, but now grain had become cheap and the peasants could not meet it. At his request the officers of revenue were ordered to grant the peasants a reduction.

The Guru's name runs also through the Sufi tradition of the Punjab. It is said that the Sufi poet Shah Hussain travelled to Amritsar to have his poetry included in the Granth Sahib that Guru Arjan was compiling, and offered one of his *kafis*, short mystical lyrics, for inclusion. The friendship between Guru Arjan and Mian Mir is the subject of several folk tales. In Lahore the Qadiri order, the Sufi order founded by Abd al-Qadir Gilani, was represented by Mian Mir, who had come there from Sind, together with his sister Bibi Jamal, herself given to mysticism.

## The Guru's Death in Lahore

Guru Arjan died in Lahore. He was summoned to the city by the emperor Jahangir over his role during the rebellion of Prince Khusrau, the emperor's son; he appointed Hargobind as the sixth Guru, and was then martyred. Khusrau, it is told, had stopped at the Guru's *langar*, the free communal kitchen, in Amritsar and sought his blessing for victory, and the *tilak*, the mark on the forehead, that the Guru gave him was counted treason by the emperor. In his memoirs Jahangir wrote of "a Hindu named Arjan" in Goindwal on the river Beas, of how Khusrau "happened to halt at a place where he was", and of how Arjan made "a finger-mark in saffron which the Indians call Qashga". He called the Guru "this insignificant fellow", ordered his property handed to Murtaza Khan, and ordered that he be dealt with under the penal laws of the Yasa, the Mongol code of law, and put to death. Accounts of why he died differ, but his death is most often tied to Khusrau's revolt.

The revolt reached Lahore itself. Khusrau and Hasan Beg Badakhshi plundered along the road, burning *sarais*, the inns for travellers, and seizing horses, until they reached the city. Dilawar Khan, the governor of Lahore, would not meet the prince and made the fort fast, and however the prince tried, the fort did not fall to him. News of Khusrau's capture reached the emperor in the garden of Kamran Mirza at Lahore. From that garden to the gate of the palace the prince's companions were impaled in two rows, crowds came out of the city to watch, and Khusrau was led on an elephant between the stakes and imprisoned in the fort.

For five days, it is said, the Guru was tortured. In the walled city, near the Rang Mahal, there is a place with a well, and it is believed that Arjan was kept in a room next to this well, in what was the *haveli*, the mansion, of the Mughal Diwan of Lahore, and that he was immersed in a cauldron. Sikh belief holds that on the fifth day the Guru took a dip in the waters of the Ravi and did not emerge, having worked a miracle and passed into the other world, and that Mian Mir asked leave to bury his oppressors alive, but the Guru refused. Near Lahore Fort a small yellow structure is now called his *samadhi*, a memorial shrine, and it is believed that the Guru lost his life there. Accounts of his end differ.

His death has been called "the Karbala of Sikh history", and it is held to have given the Sikh community a cohesive motivation and to have precipitated the development of the Khalsa. He is counted the last of the Gurus who focused solely on spiritual matters.

## The Baoli

Accounts of how and when the well came to be made differ. In the tradition kept by the community, a devotee named Bhai Chhajju Bhagat, together with a Pathan merchant, laid a purse of gold *mohars*, gold coins, at the Guru's feet and asked that it be spent for religious purposes. The purse, it is said, held 282 *mohars* and had been in dispute, and the dispute was settled before the Guru. In that tradition, the Guru had a *baoli* sunk at this spot to provide water for the people of the quarter.

It is told, too, that the Guru set five Sikhs to guard his well, and that he himself sometimes stayed there. Immediately to the south, in a building of the bazaar that was as it were part of the house of the baoli itself, Guru Arjan's *langar* used to be held.

Accounts of when and how the well was lost also differ. It is said that the well suffered in the turbulence of the eighteenth century, when it was filled in and built over during the governorship of Nawab Yahya Khan, at the instigation of Diwan Jaspat Rai.

It was found again and restored in the reign of Maharaja Ranjit Singh. Accounts of how it came to light differ; it is most often told that the Maharaja, when he was ill, was advised by his astrologers to bathe in the baoli's water, and that the restoration followed his recovery.

In 1834 Ranjit Singh had a new building raised and a *sarovar*, a sacred tank, dug. The cost was borne by the state: the order came that one month's salary of the Khalsa, that is of the state, be deducted to raise this lofty building. The houses that had been built over the well were levelled, and shops, sitting places and *kothras*, rooms, were built. The work went on slowly and was still unfinished at the Maharaja's death. In 1927 the gurdwara passed under the management of the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee.

## The Gurdwara

By the 1880s the house of Baoli Sahib was counted among the famous places of worship of the Sikhs of Lahore, and the largest in extent of them all. It stood among the bazaars, the Lohati bazaar one of them, with the bazaar of the iron sellers to the east and the Kasera bazaar of the sellers of vessels to the south. Its great door was on the west.

An arched gateway with two *chaukis*, raised platforms, opened on *dalans*, halls open on one side, to the north and south of the *deorhi*, the entrance hall, with a *shah-nashin*, a raised alcove, above it, lit by three small windows. Beyond lay a very wide open court with a well worked by a wheel, sets of three *kothris*, small rooms, twelve upper *kothris* on the north, two *bel* trees and a *pipal*, the sacred fig. On the south stood the building of the Baoli itself, as it were three very wide *dalans* in one, with *shah-nashins* above.

In the third *dalan* stood a *takhtposh*, a wooden platform, with a small *palang*, a bedstead, on which the Granth Sahib was kept with great honour inside costly coverings. The stair of the baoli lay behind a door that was usually locked and opened when needed, and a second great door on the bazaar was always shut.

The descent to the water was long. One long flight of steps led down to an intermediate courtyard, and a second led on to the water, where an arched door of red stone was set in the wall of the well. Above, on the west of the upper courtyard, a small masonry tank with seven steps had long lain dry, and the wheel that once filled it from the well no longer turned.

The building passed through three hands. Maharaja Ranjit Singh gave it to Bhai Nihal Singh, with an annual *jagir*, an assignment of land revenue, of eight thousand rupees in return for its service. It then passed into the charge of Bhai Jawahar Singh Kartarpuria, who took the monthly rents of the shops. In the 1880s the building's serving officer was a Sikh with a white beard, Bhai Khazan Singh, appointed to its service and care.

The endowment was commercial. Shops belonged to the building, and the enclosure itself served the bazaar as a warehouse: the people of the bazaar had rented all the *kothris* inside it for their goods, cattle were kept within, and many kept their goods there under lock and paid rent. The building of the Roghan Mandi, the oil market, among its dependencies, also paid rent.

When Jawahar Singh's debts sank the income, the state provided a substitute. The government released a monthly sum for the servants' salaries, lamp wicks and *karah prashad*, the sweet offering blessed and shared at a gurdwara, paid each month from the Mahkama Khafifa, and all expenses, flooring included, were to be met from it. A further monthly sum went to the drummers who came every day at dawn to make the offering.

The offerings had dwindled. Those made to the Granth Sahib had once never been less than two rupees a day, and by the 1880s they brought no cash at all. What a raja or a *sardar*, a chief, offered was taken by Bhai Jawahar Singh, and the servants got nothing of it; but the sugar drops, sweets and coppers offered to the Granth Sahib were the right of the *pujaris*, the priests who served there.

## Devotion and Practice

In the 1880s the house of Baoli Sahib served as a place of assembly: whenever a gathering of any kind took place in the Hindu religion, this was the building chosen. A large *naqara*, a kettledrum, in the eastern *kothri* of the third *dalan* was played at two times of the day. The Granth Sahib lay in its coverings in the same *dalan*, *karah prashad* was paid for from the state's monthly grant, and the drummers came each dawn to make the offering.

The gurdwara is tied also to the scripture itself. It was here, at Gurdwara Baoli Sahib and not elsewhere in Dabbi Bazaar, that the original manuscript of the Adi Granth, the Kartarpur *pothi*, was kept in the custody of the Sodhi family. Under Ranjit Singh's patronage it was carried in grand procession to the Lahore Fort, and after the British annexation of 1849 it was restored to the Sodhi family.

The principal commemoration of the Guru's martyrdom in Lahore is held at the other shrine of his in the city, Gurdwara Dera Sahib.

## The Setting

In Aurangzeb's time Lahore was an ancient city on the bank of the Ravi. Akbar had built its fort, city wall and palace, Jahangir had raised buildings that still stood, princes and amirs had built mansions, and the city had grown further under Shah Jahan. It was a great and mighty city: craftsmen of every land lived there, and in every street and bazaar there were very many mosques. Jahangir's palace in the city, the imperial *daulatkhana*, was built of solid masonry.

In the province of Lahore the wells were worked by a wheel of three hundred and sixty pieces of wood and more than a hundred small pots, turned by a pair of oxen. Jahangir ordered along the highway from Agra to Lahore a tall *minar*, a pillar, at every *kos*, the old measure of distance on the road, wells of baked brick at intervals, and two rows of trees.

A Persian couplet is tied to a scene at the fort of Lahore. As an emperor, setting out on his second journey to Kashmir, crossed the Ravi below the fort, he asked about whom this verse had been written:

کلاه خسروی و تاج شاہی
بہر گل کی رسد حاشا و کلا

The well is said to have been lost in the turbulence of the eighteenth century, and the poets of that century in the Punjab wrote of the ruin of their land. Bulleh Shah wrote:

*The twelfth century has come with gaping mouth. The door of doom and torment has opened, and Panjab is in a bad state. It has been struck by fear of the pit of hell.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

The twelfth century of the Hijri era corresponds to the eighteenth century of the common era, and the poem's allusive verses appear to refer to a separation of Bulleh Shah from his master "due to the troubled conditions then prevailing in Panjab". Another of his poems says:

*Now hell has opened its bogs. / Punjab has gone to the dogs. / This hell is the nethermost hell.* (translated by Taufiq Rafat)

The full bitterness of that line, it has been said, comes through only against the backdrop of a province "being persistently rent by petty chiefs and marauders". Waris Shah, who dates his romance of Hir and Ranjha in the year 1180 of the Hijra, closes it with a lament for the land:

*Of all the wretched Punjab I am most concerned for Kasur.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

The Sikh Maharaja's Lahore is the setting of the rebuilding. When Maharaja Ranjit Singh became the sovereign of the Punjab at the end of the eighteenth century, he spent large sums on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras, and attached vast tracts of land to them so that the revenues from the lands could pay for their running. In 1799 he was greeted with enthusiasm by a population sick of the lawlessness of that time. The whole region of the Punjab came under his rule. He also built a mosque in Lahore, at a *mohalla*, a quarter of the city, called Gul Begum.

Of the city's Sikh buildings one historian has observed that "like the Sikh religion, which picks up from both Hinduism and Islam, Sikh architecture draws inspiration from both Hindu and Muslim architecture". In his view the Sikhs made smaller the domes that had first belonged to Muslim buildings, and Sikh shrines carry graphic depictions of the Sikh Gurus and also, in older buildings, sometimes of Hindu deities.

It is now rare to run into a Sikh in Lahore, a city once ruled by a Sikh and the seat of Sikh political strength. Across Pakistani Punjab hundreds of temples and gurdwaras have been taken over by refugees and converted into households, and in the country at large several gurdwaras and temples have been taken over and destroyed by migrants.

## Legacy

The well's later history is one of decline. Already in the 1880s its courtyard tank lay dry, though the well itself still held water at the foot of its two long flights of steps, behind its door of red stone. By 2015 the baoli had been reduced to "a mere small opening in an open space," with only a few traditional healers still drawing water from it as the water table fell, and by 2018 the demolition of the gurdwara structure itself stood as a grievance that had not been addressed.

What remains is the memory of a well sunk by the fifth Guru in the city where he would die, of a *langar* held beside it, of its loss and of a Maharaja who brought it back. As a shrine tied to Guru Arjan, the compiler of the Adi Granth and the first martyr of the Sikh faith, Baoli Sahib keeps its place on the map of Sikh Lahore, beside Gurdwara Dera Sahib by the Fort.

Name: Gurdwara Bhai Beba Singh
Sufi Saint: Bhai Biba (Beba) Singh (Sikh warrior; gurdwara from era of Guru Gobind Singh)
Events: Daily prakash; major Sikh anniversaries
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Bhai Biba Singh (also written Beba Singh) stands in the Jogiwara locality of the old city of Peshawar, one of the very few Sikh shrines in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to have survived into the present and returned to worship. A tall, richly ornamented building tucked into the labyrinth of the walled city, it is a rare surviving monument of the once-substantial Sikh presence in the Peshawar valley, and its reopening in 2016 after decades of closure made it a symbol of the small but resilient Sikh community of the frontier.

## Origins and Bhai Biba Singh

The gurdwara commemorates *Bhai Biba Singh*, a devout Sikh remembered in local tradition, and is popularly said to be around three centuries old, with its foundation traced by some accounts to the era of *Guru Gobind Singh* (the tenth Guru, died 1708). It took its enduring form, however, during the period of Sikh political power in the nineteenth century: after the armies of *Maharaja Ranjit Singh* brought Peshawar under Sikh rule in the 1820s, the city's Sikh community and its generals endowed and rebuilt places of worship, and Jogiwara — its very name evoking an older ascetic presence — became one of the quarters where the community concentrated. The precise date of the original foundation is uncertain and should be regarded as traditional; what is clear is that a Sikh shrine has stood on this site for well over a century and a half.

It should not be confused with the nearby Gurdwara Bhai Joga Singh in the Jogan Shah area of Namak Mandi, a separate Peshawar shrine associated with a different figure.

## Decline and Restoration

The Partition of 1947 emptied most of Peshawar's gurdwaras as the bulk of the Sikh population migrated eastward, and Bhai Biba Singh, like many others, fell silent and was left in the custody of the Evacuee Trust Property Board (ETPB), the state body that administers the properties of those who left. For the better part of six decades the building stood neglected and its use disputed. Restoration began around 2012, and after substantial public expenditure on repairs and renovation the gurdwara was formally reopened in 2016 and its management handed to the local Sikh sangat. Its revival was widely reported as a hopeful moment for the frontier's Sikhs, many of whom had migrated to Peshawar from the tribal districts in the preceding years.

## Architecture and Devotional Life

The gurdwara is admired as an architectural gem of the walled city. Rising through several storeys, its interior is decorated with mirror-work and painted ornament in the idiom of nineteenth-century Punjab, and its upper chambers command views over the rooftops of old Peshawar. Since its reopening the sangat gathers for the daily reading of the *Guru Granth Sahib* and for the major anniversaries of the Sikh calendar, and the building once again functions as a living place of worship rather than a mere monument.

## Legacy

Gurdwara Bhai Biba Singh stands as one of the most tangible reminders of Peshawar's layered religious past, when Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims shared the crowded lanes of the old city. Its restoration and return to use — negotiated between the ETPB and a community numbering only a few thousand — has given it significance well beyond its size, as evidence that the frontier's minority heritage can be preserved and honoured. For scholars of Sikh heritage in Pakistan it is an important case study, and for the community itself it is simply a home regained.

## Bibliography

- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Lahore: Punjabi History Board, 1998).
- SikhiWiki and Discover Sikhism, entries on the gurdwaras of Peshawar.
- Contemporary press coverage of the 2016 reopening (*The Express Tribune*, *Scroll.in*, SBS).
- Reports of the Evacuee Trust Property Board, Government of Pakistan.

Name: Gurdwara Bhai Joga Singh
Founded/Opened: Early 19th century (founded by Hari Singh Nalwa, Ranjit Singh era)
Events: Daily prakash; morning and evening worship
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Bhai Joga Singh stands in the Jogan Shah locality of the Namak Mandi quarter in the old city of Peshawar, one of the historic Sikh shrines of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It is dedicated not to a Guru but to a devoted Sikh, *Bhai Joga Singh*, a son of Peshawar who served in the presence of *Guru Gobind Singh*, the tenth Guru, and whose story of unhesitating obedience has made his name a byword for devotion. The gurdwara was founded in the days when Peshawar lay within the Sikh empire, and it remains a focus for the small Sikh community that still lives in the city.

## The Story of Bhai Joga Singh

Bhai Joga Singh, according to Sikh tradition, was a young Sikh of Peshawar who spent many years at *Anandpur* in the service of Guru Gobind Singh, devoted heart and soul to his master. When his parents came to take him home to be married, the Guru gave him leave to go, but on one condition: that he must return the instant he was summoned. The wedding was duly begun at Peshawar; but when Joga Singh had completed only two of the four *lavan*, the circlings of the sacred fire that solemnise a marriage, a messenger arrived bearing the Guru's letter of recall. Because the Guru had written the words "at once," Joga Singh rose from the very ceremony — deaf to the protests of his kinsmen and the entreaties of the moment — and set out immediately for Anandpur, leaving his marriage unfinished. The tale is cherished as a model of the obedience and single-mindedness that the Guru's Sikhs owed to their master, and it is this Bhai Joga Singh whom the Peshawar gurdwara commemorates.

## The Gurdwara

The shrine was founded by *Hari Singh Nalwa*, the celebrated general of Maharaja Ranjit Singh who governed the frontier when Peshawar was brought within the Sikh kingdom in the early nineteenth century, and it stands in the heart of the old city. Like the Sikh institutions of the frontier generally, it was abandoned at Partition in 1947, when Peshawar's Sikhs were scattered; but it was reopened in 1980 and has since served the city's Sikh families once more. In the mornings the *sangat* of Peshawar — at times joined by visitors from abroad — gathers for worship, and in the evening the *Guru Granth Sahib* is ceremonially installed, so that after a long silence the daily rhythm of Sikh devotion has returned to the shrine.

## Legacy

Gurdwara Bhai Joga Singh is a monument both to the reach of the Sikh empire, which under Hari Singh Nalwa extended to the Khyber, and to the endurance of Peshawar's Sikh community, one of the oldest and most resilient in Pakistan. In honouring a local youth rather than a Guru, it holds up the ideal of the ordinary devotee whose faith expressed itself in perfect obedience — the Sikh of Peshawar who left his own wedding at his Guru's word. Its reopening and continued use make it a rare living Sikh shrine in the region, a thread of continuity binding the modern city to its Sikh past.

## Bibliography

- "Bhai Joga Singh" and "Gurdwara Bhai Joga Singh (Peshawar)," in Sikh reference works and encyclopaedias.
- Traditional accounts of Bhai Joga Singh in the *Sikh* devotional literature of the era of Guru Gobind Singh.
- Histories of Hari Singh Nalwa and Sikh rule in Peshawar and the frontier.
- Reporting (e.g. *Scroll.in*) on the reopening and present life of Peshawar's gurdwaras.

Name: Gurdwara Chakki Sahib
Founded/Opened: Commemorates events of c. 1520-21; gurdwara built later
Events: Sikh pilgrimage, especially Guru Nanak's Gurpurab
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Chakki Sahib stands within the old town of Eminabad in Gujranwala District, the settlement known in Guru Nanak's day as Saidpur, and marks the place where a great millstone, or *chakki*, associated with the Guru was kept. A *gurdwara* is a Sikh house of worship, and this one commemorates one of the most dramatic episodes in the life of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith: his imprisonment, traditionally dated to around 1520 or 1521, when the Mughal emperor Babur invaded the Punjab and Eminabad was sacked and its people carried off. Since Partition it has had no resident congregation, but it is cared for as part of Pakistan's Sikh heritage, and pilgrims visit it on the great anniversaries, often together with the neighbouring Eminabad shrines of Rori Sahib and Bhai Lalo's well.

The present shrine, a simple building with a flat roof within a compound paved with brick, preserves the memory of the millstone and of the Guru's witness against the cruelty of war. The Guru's own lament on Babur's invasion, the *Babar-vani*, is the poem most closely bound to the town.

## The Captivity at Saidpur

Babur had opened negotiations with Ibrahim, without success, to annex the western Punjab to Kabul. After two minor raids in the region between the Indus and the Jhelum, he invaded the Punjab a third time and reached as far as Sialkot. Saidpur was sacked by his armies, and its people were carried off.

According to Sikh tradition the captives, Guru Nanak among them, were set to grinding corn with hand mills to feed the conquering army. It is remembered that the Guru's millstone turned of its own accord while he poured in the grain and sang the praises of the One God, the hymns lamenting the horrors visited upon the land that are preserved in Sikh scripture as the *Babar-vani*, the "utterances concerning Babur". The marvel is said to have astonished his guards and, when it was reported to Babur, to have brought the emperor himself to the Guru. Moved by his words, Babur is remembered to have sought the Guru's blessing and, at his urging, to have freed many prisoners. Accounts of their meeting differ, and it has been doubted that the two ever met. The encounter has also been taken to mark the beginning of the antagonism between the Mughals and the Sikhs, and Babur, the great grandfather of the emperor Jahangir, is remembered as having imprisoned Guru Nanak.

The story of the millstone that turned by itself is told in the *janamsakhis*, the cycles of tales of Nanak's life written by his devotees after his death. They are the primary sources for his life, and they survive in different versions; the earliest known janamsakhi dates from 1658, nearly 120 years after the Guru's death.

Not every telling of the captivity includes the miracle. Nanak himself is held to have abhorred the association of miracles with religious personalities, yet the stories of his life are full of them. In one of those stories, when a man who has been cured calls his cure a miracle, the Guru answers that "there is no such thing as a miracle".

In the janamsakhi telling the Guru came to Saidpur twice. The first time was early in the first of his journeys, when he came from Sultanpur by way of Talwandi. The second was on the way home from the fourth, when he came by Iran, Kabul, Peshawar, Kandahar, Hasan Abdal, Tilla Balnath and Katasraj to Saidpur and went on to Kartarpur; that return, the stories tell, fell at the time of Babur's third incursion into India, when the Guru took a south eastern route to the Punjab.

## The Gurdwara

In the late 1990s fourteen *ghumaon*, a Punjabi measure of land, were still attached to the shrine, and two rooms surviving from Babur's own time still stood within it. A fair was held here at Visakhi, the spring festival, with the *Nishan Sahib*, the Sikh flag, flying in the courtyard. From 28 February 1922 until 1947 the shrine was administered by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, the committee for the management of Sikh gurdwaras.

One visitor, travelling through Pakistan in the footsteps of Guru Nanak with a historian, was taken by him to a small house in the town, an ordinary structure with a small door and a few steps leading to it. From behind its walls rose a pole wrapped in saffron cloth, with a Khalsa flag on top, and the house was locked. The historian told him what the house had been: "This place was used as a prison at the time of Babur. Guru Nanak was imprisoned here and was forced to work on a stone grinder."

In 2017 the gurdwara's wooden door was locked, and the building was identified only by a small plaque reading "Gurudwara Chakki Sahib, Eimanabad."

## Devotion and Pilgrimage

Pilgrims come to the shrine on the great anniversaries, often in the same round as Rori Sahib and Bhai Lalo's well. To Pakistan's Sikh shrines in general, Sikhs living abroad came for festivals such as Visakhi and the birthday of Guru Nanak, which were attended by thousands of Indian pilgrims.

In Aurangzeb's time the sum of the worship of the followers of Baba Nanak, as the Guru was also called, was the recitation of their master's verses, which they sang to melody. Many of them had put away worldly ties; kin and stranger, friend and foe were the same to them, and they lived at one with their friends and without strife with their enemies. They counted service to the traveller, to all who come and go, as the highest worship, and whoever arrived at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name they treated as a brother and a friend and served, even a stranger, a thief, a highwayman or an evildoer. The Udasis, counted among the devotees of Baba Nanak, likewise made the singing of their master's verses the sum of their worship.

The tradition of *langar*, the free communal kitchen, is believed to have begun with Guru Nanak. Sikh hagiography has a favourite scene of the Guru's own worship, shown in several paintings: a serene Nanak listening to the songs of Bhai Mardana, his singer, who holds a *rubab*, a stringed instrument, while Bhai Bala stands behind them holding a fly whisk.

## Guru Nanak

Guru Nanak's dates are most often given as 1469 to 1539. He spent a major portion of his life in what is today Pakistan: he was born there, and he eventually settled in a small village that is now on the Pakistani side of the border. In Aurangzeb's time his descendants were still living at his abode on the Ravi, twelve *kos*, an old measure of distance, from Batala.

Accounts of how many journeys he made differ, but his *udasis*, the long journeys of his travelling years, are most often counted as four, and they lasted more than twenty years. He travelled mostly on foot, and whenever he visited an area he would visit its religious shrines, Muslim, Hindu and of any other denomination.

He lived as a householder, and he brought a message of peace and harmony to the believers of Islam and Hinduism; he taught that a good life rested on honest labour, compassion, selfless service and prayer. He offended both Hindus and Muslims by stating that there was no Hindu or Muslim. In the janamsakhis he is said to have declared, after vanishing for a week in the stream at Sultanpur, "There is only one God. There is no Hindu, no Mussalman." This teaching is said to have been questioned at Sultanpur, at Rai Bhoi di Talwandi and at the court of Malik Bhago in Eminabad. His advice to his companions was that "if one is a Muslim then one should be a good Muslim and if one is a Hindu then one should be a good Hindu".

He spoke vehemently against religious institutions and rituals. He associated with people of the lower castes, calling them people of God, and he criticised high caste landlords and government officials as exploiters. The movement that began with him has been called a spiritual reformation and a rebellion against institutional religion.

It has been argued that in Guru Nanak's time all literate Punjabis, Hindus and Muslims alike, were conversant with the poetry of 'Attar, Rumi and Sa'di, and that the Sufis of the Punjab in his day included Shaikh 'Abdu'l-Quddus Gangohi of Shahabad, his disciple Shaikh Jalal of Thaneswar, and the Qadiris, who had made the Punjab the main centre of their activities. Baba Farid is said to have become an inspiration for Guru Nanak when the Guru visited his shrine on his travels, and Farid's texts are revered among the Sikhs, for he is held to have influenced the founder of their religion.

## The Guru's Verse

Nanak wrote the *Babar-vani*, a long poem, at the time Babur attacked the Punjab, destroying the cities of Eminabad and Lahore on the way, and in it he lays the blame of Babur's wrath at God's feet. A hymn of Guru Nanak's preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, is read as evidence that he was himself present at Eminabad when Babur sacked it. One line of the poem, in English translation, gives its own reckoning of the invaders' coming:

ਆਵਨਿ ਅਠਤਰੈ …

*Coming in seventy-eight (1521 C.E)*

Lines from his other hymns, in English translation, give a sense of his poetry. On the oneness of God he sang:

ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥
ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One*

And again:

*God is One, / The Path is One*

His *aarti*, the hymn sung as lamps are waved in worship, begins in one translation:

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ …

*The sky the salver, the sun and moon the lamps …*

and in another:

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps*

His poem on the sacred thread, the *janeu*, runs:

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ
ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ …

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment*

Of washing he sang:

ਭਰੀਐ ਹਥੁ ਪੈਰੁ ਤਨੁ ਦੇਹ ॥
ਪਾਣੀ ਧੋਤੈ ਉਤਰਸੁ ਖੇਹ ॥

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white*

And in another song:

ਬਗਾ ਬਗੇ ਕਪੜੇ ਤੀਰਥ ਮੰਝਿ ਵਸੰਨਿੑ ॥

*The herons in their white feathers dwell in the sacred shrines of pilgrimage*

Other hymns of his open *O my merchant friend*, *Launch ye the boat of austere contemplation …*, *As a beggar goes a-begging …* and *His goodness cannot be priced or traded …*.

The Guru composed verses in Hindi on the truth of God, setting out divine unity, and Mardana sang his verses and drew people into the snare of devotion. His *bani*, devotional verses of supplication, entreaty, humility and reverence, was his sermon, and it was compiled as part of the Adi Granth, the first compilation of the Sikh scripture, by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, in 1604. The poems of the later Gurus are recorded not in their own names but in that of Guru Nanak. He brought into his verse several words that were not part of the Punjabi of his time, which is why, it has been said, his contribution as a poet to Punjabi is immense.

He is counted among the poets of devotion: the poetry of Kabir and Nanak in the fifteenth century led to the founding of Sikhism. Both poets used the *doha*, an old popular Prakrit and Hindi metre in which the two lines of a couplet rhyme, for their mystical poetry. The use of the local language for mystical poetry, in Sindh as in the Punjab, is traced back to the fifteenth century, and after 1800 Punjabi was used almost exclusively by the Sikhs as their literary medium, while the Punjabi Muslims turned to Urdu.

His verse is sung outside the gurdwaras too. The singer Abida Parvin has said: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak." In Sindh, Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the *banis* of Shri Guru Nanak and the *kalams*, the poems, of the Sufis, and a new edition of one Sindhi poet's *kalam* has kept Guru Nanak's poetry in it.

## The Setting

When Babur took over the city of Saidpur, he renamed it Eminabad, though accounts of how the town came by its name differ. The cone like spires of ancient Hindu temples rose among its houses, in contrast to the monolithic Muslim architecture that had come to dominate the town, and its dusty roads and worn houses showed that it had lost its economic strength. Once it was an important trading centre on the Grand Trunk Road, which connected with Lahore and then Delhi; the highway has since moved south, and Gujranwala, not far away, has replaced Eminabad as a trading centre.

One temple, abandoned in 1947, still looked sturdy. Temples such as these had been taken over by migrants from across the border after the creation of Pakistan, and after the destruction of the Babri mosque in 1992 no signs of attack on them were to be found. Much of the town's historical architecture had still been preserved.

Gujranwala lies in the heart of the Punjab, 75 kilometres from the provincial capital. Maharaja Ranjit Singh started from a small fief around it. When he became the sovereign of the Punjab at the end of the eighteenth century, he spent large amounts of money on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras, and he attached vast tracts of land to them, so that their revenues could support their functioning; he also allotted Baba Sahib Singh Bedi land around the cities of Gujranwala and Lahore. After the British took the Punjab, a large number of important Sikh gurdwaras were administered by Hindu *mahants*, the heads of religious establishments.

## Legacy

Gurdwara Chakki Sahib preserves the memory of the millstone and of the Guru's witness against the cruelty of war, and through the *Babar-vani* it ties Eminabad to the Guru's hymns lamenting the horrors visited upon the land. Across Pakistan there are several sites where Nanak stayed or is said to have performed miracles, and the gurdwaras built there later by his devotees still stand tall, though after the division of the Punjab several other gurdwaras and temples were taken over and destroyed by migrants. At Eminabad, the small house shown as the Guru's prison still stood, locked, under its Khalsa flag.

Muslim writers and singers have claimed the Guru too. Many Muslims acquainted with his teachings are devoted to him and visit his shrine, and to one Muslim painter, "Guru Nanak is like a Muslim Sufi Saint". A Muslim tradition, which the Sikhs do not accept, holds that Guru Nanak was born by the blessing of Baba Naulakh Hazari. A Chishti Sabiri shaykh of the twentieth century counted Guru Nanak, with Krishna, Rama, Sita and Lachman, among the spiritual luminaries outside Islam who believed in the one true God and had a "Divine connection", *nisbat*.

A growing similarity has been seen between the iconography of Guru Nanak and that of Jhulelal, revered by the Hindus of Sindh, and it has been suggested that *Bhakti*, the path of loving devotion, may have reached Sindh through the teaching of Guru Nanak. At the shrine of the goddess Hinglaj, the engraved footsteps of Guru Nanak connect Hinglaj with the traditions of the Sikhs and of the Nanak *panth*, or sect.

Name: Gurdwara Chhevin Patshahi, Chitti Gatti
Location: Chitti Gatti, near Mansehra, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
Events: Historically a Vaisakhi fair; not currently observed
Description:
Gurdwara Chhevin Patshahi stands in the small village of Chitti Gatti, in a garden by the roadside about eight kilometres from Mansehra in the Hazara hills of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Its name — Chhevin Patshahi, the "Sixth Sovereignty" — commemorates Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru of the Sikhs (Guru from 1606 to 1644), who by tradition is said to have visited the site during his travels through the region. The gurdwara is a handsomely built, domed structure, and it is remembered above all for an unusual arrangement of shared sacred use: a stone Shiv Ling was worshipped on the upper floor of the building while the prakash of the Guru Granth Sahib was installed on the floor below, with Hindu priests officiating — an arrangement that reflects the closely intertwined Hindu and Sikh devotion of the frontier, where the Guru was honoured by Hindus and Sikhs alike. A fair was traditionally held here at Vaisakhi, enthusiastically attended by the communities of the surrounding hills. The building stands beside the Shiv Mandir of Chitti Gatti (recorded separately in this dataset), the two shrines together forming a single sacred spot. Following the Partition of 1947 the Sikh and Hindu populations of the area departed and regular worship ceased, though the structure survives as a monument to the region's plural religious past.

This account rests on Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey, which describes the gurdwara as “beautifully constructed,” with a stone Shiv Ling still in place on the upper floor where it once shared devotion with the Guru Granth Sahib below; the site is also entered in the Department of Archaeology's 1962 register of Sikh shrines in West Pakistan as a “Gurdwara Chitti Chatti” in Hazara district near Mansehra, illustrated there by a photograph captioned “Gurdwara at Mansehra.”

Name: Gurdwara Chhevin Patshahi, Jhalian (Jhalian Dhilwan)
Location: Jhalian (Jhalian Dhilwan), near Barki, Lahore District, Punjab, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: Traditionally linked to a visit of Guru Hargobind (early 17th century); present structure colonial-era
Events: Historically an annual fair; not in regular worship
Description:
Gurdwara Chhevin Patshahi at Jhalian — a village of the Lahore District lying in the former Barki (Burki) police-station area, some five kilometres east of Barki town and close to the Lahore–India borderland — commemorates a visit by Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru (*Chhevin Patshahi*). The settlement is paired with the neighbouring village of Dhilwan, the two together being known as *Jhalian Dhilwan*. By Sikh tradition the Guru halted here and blessed the local *sangat*, and it was from this place, the accounts hold, that he afterwards travelled the short distance to Hadiara, where another gurdwara of the sixth Guru still stands (a separate entry in this dataset). The shrine at Jhalian is remembered as a modest but dignified building raised over the spot said to have been "touched by the feet" of Guru Hargobind: constructed in the manner of a colonial-era bungalow, with a verandah across the front and two rooms behind, and endowed by the villagers with some eight *ghumaon* of land for its upkeep. Like the great majority of gurdwaras on the Pakistani side of the 1947 border, it was maintained by the local Sikh community until Partition, after which the congregation departed and the building passed out of regular worship — such border-village shrines being frequently left empty or turned to other uses thereafter. Its history survives chiefly in Sikh pilgrimage literature and gazetteers rather than in independent record, and its present condition is not well documented. It should not be confused with the other shrines of the sixth Guru in the Lahore region — among them the *Chhevin Patshahi* gurdwaras at Mozang and inside Bhati Gate within Lahore city, and the one at Chitti Gatti near Mansehra recorded elsewhere in this dataset — each marking a different halt in Guru Hargobind's travels.

Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey adds that a refugee family from Ambala had settled in the Jhalian building, and that at Dhilwan a *Manji Sahib* — the seat marking where Guru Hargobind himself sat, reached from Jhalian after he had visited many other villages — stood east of the village, its former place of *prakash* now adjoined by a primary school. Independent record of the Guru's route between the two villages appears in the Department of Archaeology's 1962 survey of Sikh shrines in West Pakistan, which lists a “Gurdwara at Dhisalwan, Police Station Barki” under a variant spelling of Dhilwan.

Name: Gurdwara Chhevin Patshahi, Mozang
Location: Temple Road, Mozang, Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: 1619 (commemorated event); original structure raised under Maharaja Ranjit Singh (early 19th c.); present building rebuilt 1926 by Sardar Mehar Singh
Events: Annual Akhand Path around Guru Hargobind's Gurpurb (historic)
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Chhevin Patshahi stands on Temple Road in the Mozang locality of Lahore. It is one of several shrines in the Lahore area that commemorate a visit by Guru Hargobind, the sixth Sikh Guru, and its name, Chhevin Patshahi, means the "Sixth Sovereignty". In Sikh tradition the site is bound up with the memory of Mata Kaulan, also remembered as Bibi Kaulan, a devoted follower associated with the Guru, whose story is kept in the devotional literature of the Mozang gurdwara tradition. Since Partition it has been maintained as part of Pakistan's protected Sikh heritage.

Guru Hargobind, the son of Guru Arjan, was the first Guru to wear two swords, one for temporal and one for spiritual power, and he began the militarisation of the Sikh community. In the nineteenth century his building east of the village of Mozang was a spacious walled compound, and the Sikhs held it in honour.

## The Gurdwara

Tradition dates the Guru's coming to 1619. Accounts differ over how long he stayed; the gurdwara remembers a visit, one of several halts that Guru Hargobind made in and around Lahore. In the nineteenth century the place was known as the *takia*, the lodge or resting place, of Guru Hargobind Sahib. In the reckoning of the ten *patshahis*, or sovereignties, the sixth is Guru Hargobind's, and from it the gurdwara takes its name.

An original structure is said to have been raised under Maharaja Ranjit Singh in the early nineteenth century, and in Ranjit Singh's time the building was held in great honour. The building seen today was rebuilt in 1926 under the patronage of Sardar Mehar Singh.

In the nineteenth century the compound lay east of the village of Mozang and of the tomb of Hazrat Shah Abu Ishaq Sahib. Its enclosure was of brick, and its entrance was on the south. On the west stood four *samadhs*, memorial shrines; among those commemorated in them were Suba Singh and Sajjan Singh. There was a brick well, and a *musafir-khana*, a travellers' lodge. A brick *chaubara*, an upper room, with a stone floor and marble, was called the Darbar.

In the 1880s it was a very spacious enclosure of brick and lime. Within it was a second enclosure holding a brick well with a Persian wheel and a *sabil* for giving water, and beside it a small garden. There was a house of three storeys for the *mahant*, the head of the establishment; there were two *kothas*, or rooms, and an elaborate *chaubara* plastered with lime, which was the sitting place; there was a marble staircase; and there was a plastered brick platform three feet high.

Above the platform was an arched doorway with a railing, known as the Mandir Baba Sahib. On its walls were pictures of Guru Nanak and of other Gurus, and its vaulted ceiling was set with mirrors and painted. In the eastern *dalan*, or hall, two *Granths*, holy books of the Sikhs, were kept with all due reverence beneath a silken canopy. By then the building's income went to the *pujari*, the officiating priest, of Guru Arjan's *samadh*.

## Worship

Before 1947 the gurdwara sustained daily congregational worship, and every year it observed an *Akhand Path*, the unbroken reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, around Guru Hargobind's birth anniversary, his *Gurpurb*.

In the 1880s a gathering of Sikhs took place here on the fifth day of every moon. *Prashad*, consecrated food, was distributed, and there was *chiraghan*, an illumination with lamps.

## The Sixth Guru

Guru Hargobind was the son of Guru Arjan, his predecessor as Guru, and of Mai Ganga Sahiba. It is told that Guru Arjan's wife visited a holy man with gifts, and that he foretold a noble son and said that the child should be named Hargobind. He was born on the day Guru Arjan went to the village of Dawali. He was Guru from 1606 to 1644, and like his father he spent a lot of time in Lahore.

On 24 July 1606, after Guru Arjan had appointed him, he decided to give *darshan*, an audience at which his followers beheld their Guru. By then the Akal Takht, the Eternal Throne, had been prepared. He came dressed as a royal, in a saffron gown and *churidar* pyjama, close fitting trousers, with an aigrette, a necklace and two swords, and he refused to take up the religious symbols of Guruhood: "My rosary shall be the sword belt and on my turban, I shall wear the emblem of royalty". This was *miri-piri*: one sword stood for temporal power, the other for spiritual prowess. He was the first Guru to wear two swords.

When the news of his father's death reached him at Amritsar, it is told, he mourned and swore the most solemn of oaths to take revenge on Chandu Lal. Chandu Lal had been appointed Diwan of Lahore, a high office of state, by the Mughal authorities, and he had asked for Hargobind's hand in marriage for his daughter. The Guru ordered that no Sikh should speak Chandu Lal's name, and that whenever he was mentioned a Sikh should first say *phitkar*, a curse, three times. At the spot of his father's *samadhi* Guru Hargobind raised a small structure.

Known as the "soldier-saint", he began the militarisation of the Sikh community following the assassination of his father. He reared horses and encouraged his followers to keep arms in their defence. A saffron flag faced the Akal Takht; there was a large drum, and he kept a hawk as a pet. He had fifty two bodyguards and a force of *Sant Sipahi*, saint soldiers, five hundred to begin with, who were not paid a salary but were exempt from paying the required tribute. Through his *masands*, his appointed agents, devotees were told to offer arms and horses; the offering of weapons at the Guru's court was a practice he began, later reinforced by Guru Gobind Singh. To administer the Sikh community he created the concept of the *Sangat*, the congregation of followers, which was then put under a *masand*.

## The Guru and the Emperors

Jahangir imprisoned Guru Hargobind in Gwalior, and accounts differ over why. A story is told of it. Chandu Lal told Jahangir that the Guru was called the True King and had built a throne, and the emperor sent men to bring him; Bhai Gurdas stayed behind at Amritsar as one of his deputies. At Delhi Jahangir asked him which were good, Hindus or Muslims, and the Guru answered with a line of Guru Arjan's on the different names by which people call on God, some saying Ram and some Khuda. Its opening runs:

کوئی بولے رام رام کوئی بولو خدا …

When a Sikh came asking for his True King, Jahangir sent him on to the Guru. Chandu Lal then arranged that the Guru be held in Gwalior fort, and wrote to the *thanadar*, the officer in charge there, to keep him in hardship. Imprisoned rajas were held there too. The king had a dream in which a voice told him to release the Guru, and when Hargobind asked that these rajas be released as well, the king agreed. The Guru then claimed his father's rosary, and claimed *qisas*, retaliation, against Chandu Lal, who was handed over to him in chains; each Sikh was to give him five blows of a shoe.

In conflict with Jahangir at first, the Guru later came to a cordial relationship with the emperor, helping him in a couple of his military expeditions; some claims have him in Jahangir's employment, serving him in the Punjab and helping him to overcome Tara Chand of Nalagarh. Under Shahjahan three battles were fought, at Amritsar, Lahira and Kartarpur, and all of them were won by the Sikhs. Accounts differ over where he settled, whether at Kartarpur or at Kiratpur on the Sutlej.

The Sikh greeting is traced to him. It is told that the Guru ordered his Sikhs always to ask God for victory, and that in place of the greeting *salam* this phrase was fixed: *Wahguru ji ki fateh*, victory to the Wahguru.

His eldest son, Baba Gurditta, died in his lifetime, and he appointed Har Rai, the younger son of Baba Gurditta, who sat in the place of his grandfather. Following his grandfather's tradition, Har Rai too kept horses and a force of twenty two hundred fighters. Hargobind was the *pir*, the spiritual guide, of the seventh Guru and the father of the ninth, his younger son Tegh Bahadur, who followed in his father's footsteps and kept the sword of Guru Hargobind.

Opinion on him is divided. Critics saw his militarism as "a departure from the teachings of the early Gurus", and he was the first Guru not to compose a single hymn. He remains one of the most controversial of the Sikh Gurus, and yet he laid the foundations of the contemporary face of Sikhism.

## Bibi Kaulan

The story of Bibi Kaulan, as it is told, begins in Mozang. She was a maid employed by a Muslim trader who lived in Mozang and had bonded her against her wishes. Hearing that the Guru was encamped nearby, she pleaded to be rescued, and the Guru took her along with him on his horse. They rested for a while at a spot in the village of Amar Sadhu, inside the Defence Housing Authority of Lahore, before they went on to Amritsar. The gurdwara that stands there, built in honour of the memory of Guru Hargobind, is known as Gurdwara Bibi Kaulan.

In Amritsar, the story continues, she insisted that he marry her. The Guru could not marry her, and so he ordered a pool to be built near the Golden Temple and named after her, decreeing that visitors to the Golden Temple must first perform ablution at the pool of Bibi Kaulan.

## Mozang and Sikh Lahore

In the nineteenth century Mozang was a *mauza*, a village, east of which the Guru's building stood. It was a former settlement outside the city of Lahore, and one of the quarters of the city. Its settling is connected with Pir Shirazi Baloch, to whom Baloch people in Mozang came and went, and Miani lay to the west of the village.

Maharaja Ranjit Singh ruled the Punjab for forty years, and held Kashmir and the Derajat as well. When he became the sovereign of Punjab at the end of the eighteenth century, he spent large amounts of money on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras, and attached vast tracts of land to them so that the revenues from the lands could support their functioning. Later, with the divisions among the Sikhs and the British takeover of the Punjab, a large number of important Sikh gurdwaras came to be administered by Hindu *mahants*. In the nineteenth century the departure of Maharaja Dalip Singh from the Punjab, at the end of Sikh rule, was lamented in a *qita*, a short poem.

## Legacy

Since Partition the gurdwara has been maintained, like most of Lahore's Sikh shrines, as part of Pakistan's protected Sikh heritage rather than as a site of resident congregational worship. It remains distinguished among the city's several Chhevin Patshahi gurdwaras, including those at Chowmala/Bhati Gate and at Jhalian, each marking a separate halt in Guru Hargobind's travels.

In the early twenty first century, as one writer on Pakistan's religious minorities put it, "it is now rare that one runs into a Sikh in this city, a city which was once ruled by a Sikh and the seat of their political strength". Across Pakistani Punjab hundreds of temples and gurdwaras were taken over by refugees and converted into households, and several gurdwaras and temples were taken over and destroyed by migrants.

In the nineteenth century the place was a walled compound east of Mozang, with its *samadhs*, its well and *sabil*, its garden and lodge, the painted Mandir Baba Sahib, and the two *Granths* under a silken canopy, a place the Sikhs honoured as Guru Hargobind's.

Name: Gurdwara Choa Sahib
Location: Rohtas Fort (Talaqi gate), near Dina, Jhelum District, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: Reopened for pilgrims; Guru Nanak anniversaries
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Choa Sahib, the "gurdwara of the exalted spring", stands at the northern edge of Rohtas Fort near Jhelum, close to the fort's Talaqi gate; the great fort, built in the sixteenth century, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. A *gurdwara* is a Sikh house of worship, and this one keeps a tradition of Guru Nanak (1469 to 1539), the founder of the Sikh faith. Sikhs hold that the Guru, travelling with his companion Bhai Mardana, came to this waterless tract in the heat of summer after forty days at nearby Tilla Jogian, and that he brought forth a spring here. Long neglected after the Partition of 1947, the gurdwara was reopened for worship in 2019.

## The Guru at Rohtas

The gurdwara keeps the legend of the Guru's spring. Guru Nanak and Bhai Mardana, it is told, came to Rohtas in the heat of summer, after forty days at Tilla Jogian. When Mardana lamented his thirst, the Guru is said to have struck the ground with his staff and moved a stone, causing a natural spring to well up: the *choa* that gives the shrine its name. In the Guru's day there was as yet no fort at Rohtas, and the place must have been a desolate one; he and Mardana, it is said, sat here for days. In Aurangzeb's time Tilla was reckoned seven *kos*, an old measure of distance, from the fort of Rohtas.

A further Sikh legend tells that Sher Shah Suri, the builder of Rohtas Fort, three times tried to divert the spring uphill to supply his stronghold, and three times his engineers failed.

The gurdwara's tradition sets the visit on the fourth of the Guru's *udasis*, the long journeys of his travelling years. Accounts of how many journeys he made differ, but they are most often counted as four, and together they lasted more than twenty years. In the *janamsakhis*, the cycles of tales told of his life, the fourth journey, to the Arab lands, went by Multan, Sukkur, Thatta and Hinglaj and across the Arabian Sea. On it the Guru went dressed in blue robes, a colour considered sacred by the Muslims, carrying a staff, a prayer mat, the Quran and an ablution pot. After Mecca, Medina and Baghdad he came home by way of Iran, Kabul, Peshawar, Kandahar, Hasan Abdal, Tilla Balnath, Katasraj and Saidpur to Kartarpur.

Bhai Mardana, whose thirst, the legend tells, brought forth the spring, was the Guru's companion on the road; *Bhai*, brother, is a title of respect. He was a singer who sang the Guru's verses and drew people into the snare of devotion. The Guru's advice to his two companions, Bhai Bala and Bhai Mardana, was that "if one is a Muslim then one should be a good Muslim and if one is a Hindu then one should be a good Hindu". Mardana's own poetry stands in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, which contains the spiritual poetry of the Sikh Gurus together with that of other spiritual teachers such as Bhagat Kabir, Baba Farid and Bhai Mardana.

## The Gurdwara

The first commemorative structure here, with a *sarovar*, a sacred tank, and a place for the recitation of the Guru Granth Sahib, is attributed to Charat Singh. The present building dates from 1834 and was commissioned by Maharaja Ranjit Singh, who endowed the shrine with twenty seven *ghumaon*, a Punjabi measure of land, and 260 rupees.

Maharaja Ranjit Singh (1780 to 1839), crowned ruler of the Punjab in 1801, spent large sums on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras all over the Punjab, and attached vast tracts of land to them so that their revenues could support their functioning.

Under British rule, sectarian divisions among the Sikh communities and the British takeover of the Punjab left a large number of important gurdwaras administered by Hindu *mahants*, the priests in charge of religious establishments. After 1947 hundreds of temples and gurdwaras across the Pakistani Punjab were taken over and turned into homes, and several were taken over and destroyed by migrants; where the population was largely indigenous, such places were better looked after, though with exceptions.

Gurdwara Choa Sahib was long neglected after Partition. In those years the historian Iqbal Qaiser made what he counted the most difficult of his journeys, to this gurdwara. One June, with a friend, Ilyas Ghuman, he climbed a wall of the fort and saw the gurdwara just under the shadow of the fort's wall, then walked for hours through thorny shrubs; when the two reached it they fell on its steps and passed out. An old man who was working there brought them a whole pot of water, told them of a simpler route from the road, and warned them of quicksand and wild animals, and of dacoits, armed robbers, who had taken refuge in the forest.

Later visitors found the gurdwara abandoned. It was a building with a dome on top, unmistakably a Sikh gurdwara, and a black corrosive powder had collected on its walls. Close to, it was a beautiful three storey structure on top of a small mound, beside a forest at whose edge stood the fort, and one could climb to the top and walk around the dome. Facing the gurdwara stood a Shia shrine. Two men in black *shalwar kameez*, loose trousers and a long shirt, who had come by motorcycle to tend it, told the visitors to leave, since it was getting dark and the place was not safe.

The gurdwara was reopened to pilgrims around the time of the 550th anniversary of Guru Nanak's birth, in 2019. In January that year a delegation of the Walled City of Lahore Authority, led by its Director General, Kamran Lashari, inspected it together with the nearby site of Janam Asthan Mata Sahib Kaur, and directed the local administration to restore both. That August, seventy two years after Partition, the Evacuee Trust Property Board formally reopened Gurdwara Choa Sahib for worship, its chairman, Dr Aamer Ahmed, presiding over a ceremony open to Sikh pilgrims "whether they come from India or any other part of the world". From 2020 a Sikh organisation of the diaspora undertook its rehabilitation and restoration.

## Guru Nanak

Guru Nanak was the first Guru of the Sikhs and is held to be the founder of the Sikh faith. Accounts of his dates differ, but they are most often given as 1469 to 1539. He spent a major portion of his life in what is today Pakistan: he was born there, and he eventually settled in a small village that is now on the Pakistani side of the border. There are several sites across the country where he is said to have stayed or performed miracles. He preferred to stay on the outskirts of villages, and whenever he visited an area he would visit its religious shrines, Muslim, Hindu and of any other denomination.

It is said that he travelled through most of the world, then came to the town of Batala, married, and settled in a village of Batala on the Ravi, and that people came in their multitudes from every land to become his disciples. Passing over his son Lakhmi Das, who was held to be a worthy son, he made Lahna, a Khatri by caste, his successor, with the title Guru Angad: on his deathbed he appointed not his son but his most loyal student.

He lived as a householder, and he brought a message of peace and harmony to the believers of Islam and Hinduism. He taught that a good life rested on honest labour, compassion, selfless service and prayer. In the janamsakhis, after vanishing for a week in the stream at Sultanpur, he declares: "There is only one God. There is no Hindu, no Mussalman." He offended both Hindus and Muslims by stating that there was no Hindu or Muslim, and he associated with people of the lower castes, calling them people of God.

Nanak himself is held to have disavowed the miraculous, clearly and emphatically, and to have abhorred the association of miracles with religious personalities, yet the stories of his life are full of them. His genius, it has been said, lies in the poetic use of words and not in miracles.

Muslims, too, have claimed the Guru. Many Muslims acquainted with his teachings are devoted to him and visit his shrine, and to one Muslim painter, "Guru Nanak is like a Muslim Sufi Saint". A Muslim tradition holds that Guru Nanak was born by the blessing of Baba Naulakh Hazari, though the Sikhs do not accept it. Baba Farid, whose poetry also stands in the Guru Granth Sahib, became an inspiration for Guru Nanak when the Guru visited his shrine on his travels, and Farid's texts are revered among the Sikhs because he influenced the founder of their religion. In the Guru's time, it has been argued, all literate Punjabis, Hindus and Muslims alike, were conversant with the poets ʿAttar, Rumi and Saʿdi. A twentieth century *shaykh*, a Sufi master, of the Chishti Sabiri line counted Guru Nanak, with Krishna, Rama, Sita and Lachman, among the spiritual luminaries outside Islam who believed in the one true God and had a "Divine connection", *nisbat*. At the shrine of the goddess Hinglaj there are engraved footsteps held to be Guru Nanak's. In Aurangzeb's time the dervishes of Hind, its religious mendicants, were counted in classes, and the fourth were the Udasis, devotees of Baba Nanak, as the Guru was also called, whose worship was to sing their master's verses.

## Devotion and Verse

A fair was held at the gurdwara on the fifteenth of *Kattak Suddi*, the bright half of the month of Kattak in the Indian calendar. In Aurangzeb's time the sum of the worship of Guru Nanak's followers was the reading of their master's verses, which they sang to melody and song. They counted the service of travellers, those who come and go, as the highest worship, and whoever arrived at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name they treated as a brother and a friend and served, be he a stranger, a thief, a highwayman or an evildoer. They lived at one with their friends and at peace with their enemies. The tradition of *langar*, the free communal kitchen, is believed to have begun with Guru Nanak. In more recent times Sikhs living abroad came to Pakistan for festivals such as Baisakhi, the spring harvest festival, and the birthday of Guru Nanak, which were attended by thousands of Indian pilgrims.

The Guru composed verses in Hindi on the truth of God, in which he set out the unity of God. His *bani*, devotional verses of supplication, entreaty, humility and reverence, is sung outside the gurdwaras too. The singer Abida Parvin has said: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak." In Sindh, Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the *banis* of Shri Guru Nanak and the *kalams*, the poems, of the Sufis. The *doha*, a rhyming couplet, was a form in which poets such as Kabir and Nanak wrote their mystical poetry.

Among the Guru's poems is the *Babur Bani*, a long poem that Nanak wrote at the time the Mughal Babur attacked the Punjab, destroying the cities of Eminabad and Lahore on the way. In it, as it has been read, Nanak lays the blame for Babur's wrath at God's feet and challenges the divinity of the Divine. One of its lines gives its own reckoning of the invaders' coming:

ਆਵਨਿ ਅਠਤਰੈ …

*Coming in seventy-eight (1521 C.E)*

Lines from the Guru's other hymns, in English translation, give a sense of his poetry. His *aarti*, the hymn sung as lamps are waved in worship, has been read as placing God in nature. In one translation it begins:

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ …

*The sky the salver, the sun and moon the lamps …*

and in another:

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps*

On the oneness of God he sang:

ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥
ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One*

And again:

*God is One, / The Path is One*

His poem on the sacred thread, the *janeu*, runs:

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ
ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ …

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment*

Of water and washing he sang:

ਭਰੀਐ ਹਥੁ ਪੈਰੁ ਤਨੁ ਦੇਹ ॥
ਪਾਣੀ ਧੋਤੈ ਉਤਰਸੁ ਖੇਹ ॥

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white*

And in another song:

ਬਗਾ ਬਗੇ ਕਪੜੇ ਤੀਰਥ ਮੰਝਿ ਵਸੰਨਿੑ ॥

*The herons in their white feathers dwell in the sacred shrines of pilgrimage*

Other hymns open with the words *O my merchant friend*, *Launch ye the boat of austere contemplation …*, *As a beggar goes a-begging …* and *His goodness cannot be priced or traded …*.

## Rohtas Fort and Jhelum

The fort was founded by Sher Shah Suri while he was still known as Sher Khan. After the victory at Kanauj and the pursuit that followed as far as Lahore, he went into the country of the Gakhars, came back, founded a fort beside the hills and called it Rohtas, and he left ten thousand horse there to bar the road to the imperial army. Once the affairs of that country were in order he went to Agra, and he struck coin and had the *khutba*, the Friday sermon, read in his own name as Sher Shah. His successor, Islam Shah, brought the fort to completion.

Rohtas lay on the Gakhar border, between the Bihat and the Sindh. Sher Shah and Islam Shah raised the fort there on the frontier so that the Gakhars would be worn down and submit, but they made no headway at all, and in the end they made peace on condition that Sultan Sarang, the ruler of that country, came in.

Rohtas was the western end of Sher Shah's road. Along it, from Bengal to the Rohtas of the Punjab, stood *sarais*, inns for travellers, two *kos* apart, with two horses kept at each, so that news from Bengal reached Rohtas in two or three days. This was the Rohtas of the Punjab; there were other places of the name, among them a fort in Bihar held by Raja Chintaman.

In Aurangzeb's time the river Bihat passed below the town of Jhelum, and there it took the name Jhelum. In the Guru's lifetime the Punjab was plunged into a number of significant political crises. The region between the Indus and the Jhelum had seen two minor raids by Babur before he invaded the Punjab a third time, in 1520, reaching as far as Sialkot.

Jhelum has legends of its own. After his war with Porus, it is told, Alexander the Great was visited at Jhelum by an old Indian man who told him of two talking trees, one male and the other female, a little distance from Jhelum, and Alexander went to see them and indeed found them talking to each other. The tale comes from letters said to be Alexander's, though written after his death. A bodhi tree, the sacred fig of Buddhism, is said to grow near Jhelum, and another in Islamabad.

## Legacy

Gurdwara Choa Sahib keeps at Rohtas the memory of a spring, a thirsty companion and a Guru on the road. It once stood abandoned, a domed building with a black powder on its walls, reached through thorns and summer heat or at dusk beside a forest said to be unsafe. Its reopening in 2019, seventy two years after Partition, returned it to the pilgrims for whom it was built. Across Pakistan, the gurdwaras that devotees later built at the places where Nanak stayed still stand tall, though it has been asked whether Nanak's legacy, in its true essence, is slowly disappearing.

## Overview

Within the Chowmala mohalla of Lahore's Walled City, close to Bhati Gate, stands Gurdwara Chowmala Sahib, one of several sites in the city associated with a visit by Guru Hargobind, the sixth Sikh Guru. Sikh tradition holds that the Guru was received here in the seventeenth century by a resident named Bhai Jiwan, who converted his own house into a gurdwara following the visit; the hall is recorded as having been enlarged in 1915.

## Present State

As with several of Lahore's smaller, intramural gurdwaras, Chowmala Sahib's post-Partition history is thinly documented. Older sources record an annual fair once held around Basant Panchami, though whether this observance has continued is uncertain, and some reports suggest that the original structure associated with the site may no longer survive intact within the dense fabric of the Walled City. It is distinguished from Lahore's other Chhevin Patshahi ("Sixth Sovereignty") gurdwaras at Mozang and elsewhere, each of which marks a separate stop in Guru Hargobind's travels.
