Name: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib Kartarpur
Location: Kartarpur, Shakargarh Tehsil, Narowal District, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: Guru Nanak anniversaries; daily visa-free pilgrimage via the Kartarpur Corridor
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Darbar Sahib Kartarpur, also called Kartarpur Sahib, stands on the right bank of the River Ravi in Narowal District, in Pakistan's Punjab province, about two kilometres from the border with India. It marks the place where Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism, spent the last years of his life and where, in 1539, he died, which makes it one of the most venerated sites in the Sikh world and, in a real sense, the birthplace of the Sikh community as a settled, worshipping body. Its white domes, long visible across the fields from the Indian side of the border, became in 2019 the end point of the Kartarpur Corridor, a pilgrims' passage that needs no visa and that reunited the shrine with the devotees of a divided Punjab.

Kartarpur lies about 80 kilometres from Lahore, about an hour from the city of Narowal, and 180 kilometres by way of Lahore from Nankana Sahib, where the Guru was born. The shrine stands out, for there is no habitation around it, and the nearby railway station on the line from Lahore to Chak Amru, in Shakkar Garh, bears its name, Darbar Sahib Kartarpur. It is a different place from the town of Kartarpur about 15 kilometres from Jalandhar, which was founded in 1594 by Guru Arjan Dev.

## The Guru

Guru Nanak was born in 1469 at Nankana Sahib, earlier called Talwandi. His father was Kalyan Chand Das Bedi, the accountant known as Mehta Kalu. He married Sulakhini, daughter of Mul Chand and Chando Rani of the town of Batala, on 24 September 1487, though accounts of the marriage differ, and they had two sons, Sri Chand, born on 8 September 1494, and Lakhmi Das, born on 12 February 1497. Sri Chand became an ascetic and never married, and so the Guru's line is carried on through his younger son. The Udasi sect, which follows Sri Chand's tradition, is believed to have been founded by him, and the mainstream Sikh community did not recognise him as Guru.

He spent much of his life in what is today Pakistan, and it was there that he finally settled. Accounts of how many journeys he made differ, but his *udasis*, the long missionary journeys, are most often counted as four; they lasted more than twenty years and took him, mostly on foot, east to Bengal, south to Sri Lanka, north to Kashmir, Nepal and Tibet, and west to Mecca. Coming back from eastern India, he found the Punjab plunged into a number of political crises, as Babur invaded for the third time, in 1520, reaching as far as Sialkot. In the janamsakhis, the cycles of tales told of the first Guru's life, his last journey went by Multan, Sukkur, Thatta and Hinglaj, across the Arabian Sea to Mecca, Medina and Baghdad, and home by Iran, Kabul, Peshawar, Kandahar, Hasan Abdal, Tilla Balnath, Katasraj and Saidpur to Kartarpur.

## The Abode of the Creator

Guru Nanak is said to have founded the settlement of Kartarpur, "the abode of the Creator", around 1504, on land beside the Ravi; accounts of when he founded it differ. The janamsakhis tell that he came to the region between the rivers Ravi and Beas and chose land on the banks of the Ravi for his permanent home. A farmer of Pakhoke village, Ajit Randhawa, with a group of other farmers, pledged the land, and the foundations of the new settlement were laid. People of every faith and religion came, and the place soon took on the look of a pilgrim town, as Talwandi and Sultanpur had before it. His parents came to live there, and so did the parents of Mardana, the singer of his verses.

In the same telling, after a few months at Kartarpur the Guru set out on his journeys again, and it was at Kartarpur that the last of them ended. There he laid aside the pilgrim's clothes and took the garb of an ordinary householder. He settled at Kartarpur for the last years of his life, and by many accounts he spent some eighteen years there. His wife and children joined him. Here the wandering teacher became the founder of a living community. Setting aside the ascetic's road, he took up the life of a householder and farmer and gathered around him a *sangat*, a congregation, of disciples. Devotees moved there too, and from this base he travelled to the regions around. In his last years, the janamsakhis tell, he crossed the Ravi south east to Achal, a village near Batala in Gurdaspur district, for Maha Shivratri, the Hindu festival of Shiva.

It was at Kartarpur that the lasting institutions of Sikhism took shape. The Guru enjoined on his followers the threefold discipline still summed up as *kirat karo*, to earn an honest living, *vand chhako*, to share one's earnings with the needy, and *naam japo*, to remember the divine Name. He instituted the *langar*, the free communal kitchen, where all, whatever their caste, creed or station, sat together in a single row, or *pangat*, to eat, and he set the daily rhythm of shared devotion, the singing of hymns at dawn and dusk. Kartarpur is thus held to be the first Sikh commune and the model on which every later gurdwara has been built.

Three traditions took firm root there: *seva*, selfless service; *kirtan*, the singing of hymns; and the *langar*. The Guru's compositions were sung at the appropriate times of the day to the music of Mardana's *rabaab*, a plucked string instrument. In the kitchen everyone who could drew water, ground wheat, gathered wood, cooked, served and scrubbed, and people brought whatever they could for the evening meal.

By the end of the Guru's journeys the settlement had grown into a full township of people from different social backgrounds, castes and creeds, yet they were by no means a religious or monastic order: each went about an ordinary, everyday occupation. The Guru and his disciples worked the fields, and there were *sevadars*, volunteers in the community's service, with bullock carts. Disciples flocked to the *dera*, the settlement, and made their homes in it, and Duni Chand of Lahore was among its greatest contributors. Its people were of two kinds: the original inhabitants, who had come and settled when the Guru first marked out the site, and new settlers from the communities of his followers along the routes of his journeys.

## The Passing of the Guru

The Guru's successor came to him at Kartarpur. Bhai Lehna, a Khatri, became his disciple after the Guru had settled there; the janamsakhis tell that he was on pilgrimage to Jwalamukhi when he reached Kartarpur, and that he stayed on, working in the fields, on a building site and in the *langar*. Though he came from a rich family, as the Guru's disciple he was made to perform such humiliating tasks as carrying loads of wet grass. When a newly built wing of the *dharamshala*, the house of worship and shelter, nearly collapsed in the monsoon, it is told, Lehna led an overnight repair.

Before his death Guru Nanak set aside his own sons in favour of this devoted disciple, his most loyal student, renaming him Angad, "of my own limb", and installing him as the second Guru of the Sikhs, Guru Angad Dev. With this choice he founded the line of succession by spiritual merit rather than by birth that would run through ten Gurus. He asked Guru Angad to move to Khadur rather than stay at Kartarpur, to avoid the ire of his sons. Guru Nanak died at Kartarpur, by tradition on 22 September 1539; accounts of the date of his death differ.

A legend of the janamsakhi tradition surrounds his passing. His Hindu and Muslim followers, it is said, fell to disputing whether his body should be cremated or buried, but when the sheet covering him was lifted, only a heap of flowers remained. Each community, the legend goes on, took its share, the one to cremate and the other to bury, and each raised a memorial. The shrine is understood to hold both a *samadhi*, a memorial shrine, and a grave, side by side.

## The Gurdwara

Over the centuries the original memorial by the Ravi was threatened again and again by the shifting course of the river, which is traditionally said to have swept away earlier structures. The present gurdwara, with its white domes, dates from the early twentieth century and is said to have been built with the patronage of the Maharaja of Patiala; accounts of its building differ. At one time, because it lay so close to the border, the place was a centre for smugglers, and drug addicts too had settled there. The structure was renovated in 2001, and its keepers prepared their first *langar* there at that time.

Before the corridor opened, the roads of the border area were in a bad condition, and a mud track led towards the Ravi, which still flowed next to the shrine. On an earlier visit, one visitor had had to walk the three kilometres from the main road to the gurdwara through partly flooded rice paddies. Policemen sat at the gate on a *charpoy*, a woven string bed, drinking tea, and an old Muslim man and his wife from a neighbouring village walked in without any trouble.

A newly built wall protected the main shrine. Beside the parking stood what appeared to be a missile, kept in a glass case with a marble plaque, and next to it a well covered with marble, whose plaque said that it was the well Guru Nanak used to water his fields. Sugarcane grew nearby, and a peasant was working the fields. Visitors took off their shoes and covered their heads with skullcaps placed by the entrance. The main structure stood in the middle of a courtyard, with rooms around it for pilgrims. It was built around the *samadhi* of Guru Nanak, which lay behind a glass door, and the grave lay on one side of the building. "There is a grave of Nanak next to his samadhi," the *granthi*, the reader and keeper of the scripture, said. A *langar* hall and a pool were still to come.

At that time the *granthi* was Inderjit. His family belonged to a village in Faisalabad district and were not Sikhs but Nanak Panthi Hindus, Hindus who believe in the teachings of Guru Nanak but not in the Khalsa, the order of initiated Sikhs; he himself wore the garb of a baptised Sikh of the Khalsa. At Partition his grandfather, on his way to India, was stopped near the border by the Muslims of their village, who promised him security, and the family lived there peacefully until the war of 1965, when it moved to Nankana. Inderjit lived in a shed built with the help of the Sikh diaspora, furnished with a double bed, a sofa set and a television, and as a government official he lived under the government's protection.

The building's style was itself disputed. Inderjit said that Sikhs from England and Canada had complained that the architecture of the shrine was not, strictly speaking, Sikh: it had many features of Muslim architecture, and its arches were plain, a feature of Muslim architecture, where Sikh arches usually had three cusps.

The frontier lies to the east, across the river. The Ravi sometimes crossed into India and at other points came back to Pakistan, and otherwise it was parched throughout the year. Had the line drawn in 1947 erred by only a few centimetres, the shrine of Kartarpur Sahib would have ended up in India.

In the years before 2019 the complex was extensively restored and enlarged, its precincts widened to receive great numbers of visitors, and some count it among the largest gurdwaras in the world. Within, the *Guru Granth Sahib*, the Sikh scripture, is installed and read, and *langar* is served to all who come.

## Devotion and the Langar

The devotion at Kartarpur was not only Sikh. The old Muslim couple who had walked in at the gate prayed at the grave, and the woman touched it with her hand and passed the hand over her head, blessing herself. Local Muslims, the *granthi* said, came regularly and offered their *fateha*, the opening of the Quran recited as a prayer, just as they would at any Muslim shrine. Local people still came to the grave, brought offerings and cleaned the shrine as a service, a custom already followed before Partition.

The *langar* depended on the neighbours. Rich Muslim families of the neighbouring villages gave money to cook it, as their offering to the shrine, and the wood for its cooking was provided by the Rangers, the paramilitary force. At first Muslims were hesitant to eat food cooked by Sikhs, but in time more Muslims came to eat there than Sikhs.

In Aurangzeb's reign the Guru's followers counted service of the traveller, of whoever comes and goes, as the highest worship, and whoever arrived at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name was treated as a brother and a friend and served, even a stranger, a thief or a highwayman.

## Pilgrimage and the Corridor

The Partition of 1947 left Kartarpur in Pakistan and the town of Dera Baba Nanak, only a few kilometres away, in India. For years Indian pilgrims gathered at a raised viewing platform on their side of the border simply to gaze at the domes. Across the border, behind a fence, hundreds of people gathered every day to perform *darshan*, the devotional viewing of a holy place, looking at the shrine of Guru Nanak through binoculars.

The idea of a corridor was raised as early as 1999, but it was for the 550th anniversary of Guru Nanak's birth that it finally came about. Foundation stones were laid on both sides in November 2018, and the corridor was inaugurated on 9 November 2019, when a first *jatha*, a band of pilgrims, several hundred strong, crossed from India. The passage allows Indian Sikhs to visit the shrine without a visa and to return the same day, and it has been widely hailed as a rare gesture of goodwill between two often estranged neighbours.

## Legends

Several stories gather around the site. The plaque beside the parking said that the missile in its glass case "was dropped here by the Indian forces in 1971 but due to the miracle of Guru Nanak, it did not blow up". Among local Muslims there was a belief that the river floods every twenty odd years and comes right up to the shrine, and that this is the river paying tribute to the shrine of Nanak. The *granthi* spoke too of a giant snake, bigger than two men together, and said that snakes found in the fields are placed beside the shrine, and that after paying their respects they return, for all they want is a sight of the shrine.

The janamsakhis also tell stories of the early settlement. One tells of a Brahmin who came to the place where the *dera* was being built, and of his "kitchen" there: a cubit of consecrated ground was dug and bones were found, and the Brahmin relented and asked to share in the *langar*. In another, Moola Keer, one of the earliest settlers in Kartarpur, covered for a guest who had stolen his wife's jewellery, and the thief confessed after the *kirtan*.

## The Guru's Verse

The hymns sung at Kartarpur were the Guru's own. His sermon was his *bani*, devotional verses of supplication, entreaty, humility and reverence, which was compiled as part of the Adi Granth by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, in 1604. He composed verses in Hindi on the truth of God, setting out divine unity in clear expressions and shining metaphors, and the singer Mardana sang his verses and drew people into the net of faith. Like Kabir, he used the *doha*, a rhyming couplet in an old Prakrit and Hindi metre, for his mystical poetry, and he brought into his poetry words that were not part of the Punjabi of his time. In Aurangzeb's reign the sum of his followers' worship was the reading of their master's verses, which they sang with song and melody.

Lines from his hymns, in English translation, give a sense of the poetry. His *aarti*, the hymn sung as lamps are waved in worship, begins:

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ
ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ …

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps*

On the oneness of God he sang:

ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥
ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One*

And again:

*God is One, / The Path is One*

His poem on the sacred thread, the *janeu*, runs:

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ
ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ …

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment*

Of washing he sang:

ਭਰੀਐ ਹਥੁ ਪੈਰੁ ਤਨੁ ਦੇਹ ॥
ਪਾਣੀ ਧੋਤੈ ਉਤਰਸੁ ਖੇਹ ॥

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white*

In the *Babur Bani*, a long poem written when Babur attacked the Punjab, destroying the cities of Eminabad and Lahore on the way, Nanak lays the blame of Babur's wrath at God's feet.

The verse is sung beyond the gurdwaras too. The singer Abida Parvin has said: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak." In Sindh, Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the *banis* of Shri Guru Nanak and the *kalams*, the poems, of the Sufis.

## Legacy

For Sikhs, Kartarpur is where their Guru laid down the pattern of a whole way of life, of work, worship and shared bread, and where he closed his earthly journey. The opening of the corridor turned a shrine long visible but out of reach into a place of living pilgrimage once more, drawing thousands across the border and restoring Kartarpur to its central place in the devotional geography of the Panth, the Sikh community.

It was also a place shared across the line drawn in 1947, where Muslims from the neighbouring villages prayed at the grave, paid for the *langar* and ate at it. Many Muslims acquainted with the teachings of Guru Nanak are devoted to him; to one Muslim painter, Guru Nanak is like a Muslim Sufi saint. Baba Farid, it is said, became an inspiration for Guru Nanak when Nanak visited his shrine on his travels, and Farid's texts are revered among the Sikhs, for he is held to have influenced the founder of their religion. A twentieth century shaykh of the Chishti Sabiri Sufi order counted Guru Nanak, with Krishna, Rama, Sita and Lachman, among the spiritual luminaries outside Islam who believed in the one true God and had a "Divine connection", *nisbat*. Far to the south west, at the shrine of the goddess Hinglaj, the engraved footsteps of Guru Nanak are found.

Across Pakistan there are several sites where Nanak stayed or is said to have performed miracles, and the gurdwaras built there later by his devotees still stand tall. Nanak himself is held to have abhorred the association of miracles with religious personalities, yet the stories of his life are full of them. He lived as a householder, and it is the householder's life, of work in the fields and of hymns sung at the appropriate times of the day, that the janamsakhis place at Kartarpur.

Name: Gurdwara Dash Mesh Pita
Events: Not documented
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Dash Mesh Pita is one of the small number of Sikh institutions that survive in Sukkur, the city on the Indus in northern Sindh. Pakistan's Evacuee Trust Property Board lists it as a functioning gurdwara, a Sikh place of worship, on a plot of some 300 square yards. Its name honours Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru: Dashmesh Pita is a title of reverence for him, meaning roughly "father of the Tenth [House]".

It is a separate place from Sukkur's two much better documented gurdwaras, Sadhu Bela, on its island in the Indus, and Gurdwara Pehli Patshahi, or Jind Pir, near the bridge between Sukkur and Rohri, both with detailed histories tied to the travels of Guru Nanak, the first Guru. Of Dash Mesh Pita's own past little is known, but much is told of the Guru whose name it bears, and of Sukkur and the followers of Nanak in Sindh.

## The Gurdwara

When the gurdwara was built, who established it and what event or visit it commemorates are not known. Its name suggests some historical or devotional tie to the tenth Guru, but nothing more specific can be said. As with several of the smallest gurdwaras of Sindh, what is certain is what the Evacuee Trust Property Board's register gives: its name, its place in Sukkur and that it is in use. Its history, and the size and character of its congregation today, await a local or community account.

It should not be confused with the Dashmesh Darbar Singh Sabha, a separate gurdwara at Jacobabad, roughly 100 kilometres away in another district, though the likeness of the two names may have caused confusion in the past.

## The Guru

The life of Guru Gobind Singh is the history behind the gurdwara's name, not the history of the gurdwara itself. The tenth, the number in the gurdwara's name, runs through the names he is given: the tenth Sikh Guru, the tenth Guru Gobind Singh Sahib, and the last of the Gurus, who stands at the end of the line as the ninth incarnation of Guru Nanak. He was referred to as Sacha Padshah, the True King, and his court as Sacha Darbar, the True Court, and a book of his bears the name Daswan Padshah ka Granth, the book of the Tenth King.

He was born at Patna in 1666, the son of Guru Tegh Bahadur. Before heading to Delhi, his father appointed him his heir, and it was the young Gobind Singh who urged his father to aid the Pandits, the learned Brahmins. Tegh Bahadur was killed by the emperor Aurangzeb, and in 1675, at the age of nine, Gobind Singh became Guru. When Jaita recovered Tegh Bahadur's body, he brought it to Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur, a city his father had founded, and the Guru cremated it.

After his father's death the gravest threat came from his uncle Ram Rai, the disgruntled son of Guru Har Rai. Ram Rai approached the emperor Aurangzeb, and the chiefs of the Punjab surrounded the Guru's abode at Anandpur.

The Guru kept a royal court. He lived in a regal tent and kept a war drum, and he commanded a standing army whose weapons came from the offerings of devotees or from raids upon neighbouring villages. The offering of weapons at the Guru's court had been started by Guru Hargobind and was reinforced by Gobind Singh, and Hargobind's sword passed to him; he can be seen as the true descendant of Guru Hargobind. He loved war epics, hunted regularly and took an active part in military exercises, and he was adept in Persian, Arabic and Sanskrit. Much more inclined to arms than his father, he is known as a warrior and a poet.

Bhai Mani Singh and Gulab Singh were in attendance on him. Bhai Mani Singh, a Sikh scholar and martyr of the eighteenth century to whom one set of the janamsakhis, the tales of Guru Nanak's life, is supposedly attributed, had been his childhood companion.

## The Khalsa and the Granth

On the first of Vaisakh, 14 April 1699, the occasion of the spring festival of Baisakhi, thousands of Sikhs gathered at Anandpur Sahib, in East Punjab, India. The Guru asked for volunteers ready to give their lives, and five offered their heads. He led each of them away and came back each time with a blood soaked sword, but in reality all were safe, and the blood was a goat's. The five became the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, the first of the Khalsa, the Pure Ones.

The Khalsa gave the Sikh community its distinct attire and identity. The Guru made compulsory the five Ks, the five articles of faith whose names begin with the letter K: *kesh*, uncut hair; *kanga*, a comb; *kara*, a bangle; *kachera*, short breeches; and the *kirpan*, a sword, which he ordered his followers to keep with them at all times. He gave the men the surname Singh, lion, and the women Kaur, lioness, to dilute caste identities. The Khalsa order had a code of conduct, and only the official institution embodied by the Guru was held able to provide salvation, through following that code. Under him the Sikhs became a militant body, and they have a religious prohibition against shaving and smoking.

With the Khalsa came the end of the *masands*, the Gurus' agents among the congregations. The Guru abolished the Masand system when he established the Khalsa, because of the corruption that had seeped into it, and devout Sikhs believe that he thereby purged Sikhism of corruption. The *daswandh*, the offering of a tenth of one's earnings, on the other hand, was carried into the Khalsa.

He is credited with completing the compilation of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, and he bowed before the book. Sikh tradition holds that he ended the line of the Gurus by declaring the Guru Granth Sahib the eternal Guru: no person would succeed him, he instructed that the Granth Sahib be revered as the Guru, and after him the book became the living Guru for eternity. Accounts differ on when he made the declaration; it is placed between the founding of the Khalsa in 1699 and 1708. After compiling the final version, he arranged the first *Akhand Path*, the unbroken reading of the whole scripture, in which five readers read it to him while he stood in one place throughout.

In the nineteenth century a *granth*, a sacred book, of the tenth Padshah lay on a *takhtposh*, a wooden platform, at the Shahid Ganj *darbar*, or shrine, and another *granth* was kept there too. The Guru is also the author of the book known as the Dasant Granth, which the ascetics called the Nanghe Sadhus came to worship in place of the Guru Granth Sahib, refusing to acknowledge its supremacy as the eternal Guru.

The warrior was a poet too. In his *Vichitr Natak*, a portion of the Daswan Padshah ka Granth, he told how the Sodhis replaced the Bedis. The tale names Sodhi Rai, the Bedis at Kashi and the king of Madar Des, and in it the Bedis vowed to return the compliment in Kaliyuga, the last of the four ages of the world, when their descendant Nanak would raise the Sodhis to a prime position in the world.

## War and Loss

Guru Gobind Singh was a warrior who challenged the mighty Mughal Empire and set up a Sikh army. On Lohri, the Punjabi winter festival, the Sikhs under his command defeated a large Mughal army in a battle fought at Muktsar, in India, and he founded the Nihang order as a fighting body of the Khalsa.

He had four sons, among them Jujhar Singh and Fateh Singh, and he saw all of them die at the hands of the Mughals in his own lifetime, in 1705; accounts of their deaths differ. A warning of Amar Das is said to refer to the martyrdom of these grandsons of Tegh Bahadur.

Guru Gobind Singh died in 1708. Accounts of his death differ; it is said that he was assassinated by a Pathan, or Pashtun, horse trader. In one religious and historical reading, he and his father are cast together as victims of Aurangzeb.

## How the Guru Is Remembered

On his birthday his devotees pay tribute to him by enacting scenes of war exercises. Sports have always been an essential feature of the day, traditionally war games, with horse riding, swordsmanship, archery, spearing and the use of the stick, because the Guru was a warrior himself. When the birthday was celebrated at Nankana Sahib in January 2011, the songs and recitations were dedicated to his bravery, with an emphasis on the valour of the Singh, and all the recitations of that night to the Guru and the significance of the Khalsa. The birthday falls only a few days before Lohri. As one writer on Pakistan's religious minorities has observed, the Guru's birthday and Lohri "had no historical significance to particular shrines on this side of the border".

His image recurs elsewhere. On the banner at Janamasthan he is a young, good looking man in a silk gown and several pearl necklaces, with a turban like a tiara adorned with jewels, an eagle resting on his right hand and a quiver full of arrows on his shoulder. The dome at Jhaman shows him in battle, and again with his sons Jujhar Singh and Fateh Singh. Pictures of him hang on the wall of Rajesh's gurdwara at Manora, and two in the *kirtan* hall, the hall of devotional singing, at Panja Sahib, one of them showing him collecting money for *langar*, the free communal kitchen.

## Sukkur and Sindh

The history of Sukkur and of Sindh is the setting of the gurdwara rather than its own story. Sukkur stands at one corner of the triangle formed by Rohri, Sukkur and Shikarpur, and within the city, on an island in the Indus, lies Sadhu Bela, a *tirtha*, or Hindu place of pilgrimage. In the janamsakhis a journey runs from Multan to Sukkur, and from there south along the Indus.

Sukkur lay on the road of the armies that pursued Dara. News reached them that Dara, having passed Bhakkar, had halted at Sukkur on the twenty fifth of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic year. Shaikh Mir, Diler Khan and Qubad Khan crossed towards Sukkur; because of the thick jungle, the crowding of thorny trees and the hard stages of the road, many beasts perished and the baggage did not arrive, and on the sixth of Safar, the second month, they reached Sukkur. Shaikh Mir stayed there a day, and the *zamindars*, the landholders, told him that twenty five *kos*, an old measure of distance, from Sukkur a road branches off towards Kandahar. Saf Shikan Khan made an appointment to the *faujdari*, the military command, of Sukkur.

At the time of Nadir Shah's invasion of Hindustan and his sack of Delhi, Upper Sindh formed part of the *subah*, or province, of Multan, and its "Moghulee", or Mughal, portion, Sukkur, Bukkar and Shikarpur, was then annexed to the Durani kingdom. Towards the second half of the eighteenth century Sukkur rose, with Karachi, Hyderabad and Shikarpur, to be one of the four large towns of modern Sindh, displacing older towns, among them Tatta, Nasarpur, Rohri, Sehwan and Kandiaro. Unlike Sehwan, where no communal violence had ever been registered, Sukkur saw such violence following the Manzilgah riots. Between December 1939 and February 1940 the city was the scene of the Sukkur riots, whose first victim was Bhagat Kanwar Ram.

Guru Nanak himself came to Sindh. He visited Uch Sharif on his way there, towards the end of his travels, after he had already visited the East, South, North and West, and the temple at Clifton has been identified as the temple he visited on his tour of Sindh. In one summary of the many religions that had flourished in Sindh, such as Buddhism, Jainism and Hinduism, two others were said to have become dominant more recently: Sikhism and Sufism. Colonial rule brought a renewed religiosity among the Sindhis, whether Muslim, Sikh or Hindu, performed in the *darbar*, a word used by Sikhs, Muslims and Hindus alike. Sindh's figures are missing from the first census, of 1872; in one count of the province, Sindh had 1,718,688 Muslims, 393,092 Hindus and 5,034 Christians, while 86,663 persons were put in a category titled "Other castes such as Sikhs, Parsis, Jews, etc."

Among the Lohanas and related mercantile groups two main cults were followed, the Nanakpanth, the path of Nanak, and the Daryapanth, the path of the river. In the nineteenth century the Nanakpanth was probably the dominant religious path among the Hindus of Sindh. In Sindh many Nanakpanthis belonged to a subgroup known as the Udasis, an order of ascetics. As the religious life of Sindh took new shape, several important Nanakpanthi *darbars* were created and developed throughout the province. Some had been created in the late eighteenth century, and in the second half of the nineteenth century there was a renaissance of them, with many new *darbars* built all over Sindh. Because the Nanakpanth was so widespread, the Hindu Sufis of Sindh, Hindus who followed the Sufi path, were very familiar with Sikh terminology. Before Partition the temples devoted to Jhulelal in Sindh were built with a dome, as were some Sikh *samadhis*, or memorial shrines.

There is no settled view of whether Sindh's followers of Nanak are to be counted as Sikhs. Many Lohanas in Sindh follow the teachings of Nanak, which somewhat obscured their religious affiliation for the colonial officers, and in the census of 1881 the Lohanas of Shikarpur and Hyderabad were counted as Sikhs, while ten years later, in that of 1891, they were classified as Hindus. Many middle and upper class Hindus in Sindh follow the Nanak *panth*, or sect, and it is common to cover one's head before walking into a *tikana*, the temple containing the Guru Granth Sahib. The Nanak Panthis belong to South Punjab and Sindh, and they are found in very large numbers in the province of Sindh; in their temples portraits of Guru Nanak hang alongside Hindu deities. They do not believe in the Khalsa. The communities who refused the Khalsa and called themselves followers of Guru Nanak still exist in Sindh and in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; baptised Sikhs look down upon them, and at Manora they were seen merging into the larger groups of Sikhs.

## Legacy

Guru Gobind Singh is seen as having completed Nanak's mission. He codified Nanak's teachings and founded the Khalsa, completing the legacy that Guru Hargobind had begun, and by the time of the tenth Guru the movement had taken an institutional form, codified by the formation of the Khalsa. He concluded that both Hinduism and Islam were flawed religious traditions, and that any follower of Nanak who refused to obey the commandments of the later Gurus was not a Sikh.

The Khalsa he founded came to define Sikh identity in law: the Gurdwara Act of 1925 defined that identity, identifying it with the Khalsa of Guru Gobind Singh. He founded the Damdami Taksal, a Sikh religious organisation, to impart religious education. In 1746, twelve years before the death of Bulleh Shah, the son of Zakaria Khan carried out the general massacre of the Sikhs at Shaheed Ganj in Lahore and perpetuated the resistance begun under the Guru. There is a view that Ranjit was a true follower of Guru Gobind Singh, and Bhindranwale passionately claimed that the new generation of Sikhs did not respect the Sikh way of life as taught by the Guru.

Name: Gurdwara Dera Sahib
Events: Martyrdom anniversary of Guru Arjan Dev (Jeth, May-June)
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Dera Sahib, known more fully as Gurdwara Dera Sahib *Patshahi Panjvin*, "of the Fifth Guruship", stands in Lahore, just beyond the walls of the old city, and commemorates the place associated with the martyrdom in 1606 of Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth of the Sikh Gurus and the first to lay down his life for the faith. A *gurdwara*, a Sikh house of worship, it stands amid the great Mughal and Sikh monuments of Lahore, close by the Lahore Fort, the Badshahi Mosque, the Hazuri Bagh and the *samadhi*, the memorial tomb, of Maharaja Ranjit Singh. For Sikhs it is a place of profound solemnity, marking an event that transformed the character and history of their community, and pilgrims come to it above all on the anniversary of the Guru's martyrdom.

## Guru Arjan Dev

Guru Arjan was born in 1563, the son of the fourth Guru, Ram Das, and grandson of the third, Amar Das. He led the Sikhs as Guru from 1581 until his death in 1606; accounts of the year of his death are not unanimous, but 1606 is the year generally given. He presided over the Sikh *Panth*, the community of the faith, at a moment of remarkable growth and consolidation, and under his guidance Sikhism flourished as an organised community with its own scripture, its own centre and a widening body of devotees.

His succession was a contest with his elder brother, Prithi Chand. Sikh tradition finds the root of the conflict in a journey Arjan made to Lahore and in the machinations of Prithi Chand, who hid the letters Arjan wrote from Lahore to their father. When Arjan produced two letters that had been withheld, hidden in Prithi Chand's robe, Prithi Chand was deeply ashamed. Guru Ram Das disowned him and appointed his younger son, Arjan, as the next Guru. It is told that Ram Das, on the advice of the one who from the beginning had seated each Guru on the *gaddi*, the seat of the Guru, with his own hand, asked Arjan for a fourth *pauri*, a stanza, so that the name of the four *pauris* should be remembered until the Day of Judgement, and that when Arjan composed it at once, Ram Das seated him on the *gaddi* to stand in his own place. His fame spread within a short time.

بھاگ ہویا گر سنت ملایا …
جن نانک داس تمہارے جی

*The opening and closing words of the pauri that Guru Arjan composed when Guru Ram Das seated him on the gaddi.*

Prithi Chand then approached the Mughal authorities to get his share of the property, and so began the troubled relation between the Mughals and the Sikhs. He bore his brother enmity to the utmost degree and slandered him before the Emperor Jahangir, complaining through the emperor's *diwan*, a minister who was himself an enemy of the Guru, while Nawab Wazir Khan defended Arjan as a man of God. Arjan admonished his brother again and again, and still the harassment went on. Once Prithi Chand came against Amritsar with some Afghans, intending to kill the Guru, who hid in a village a few *kos*, an old measure of distance, from Amritsar; the Afghans died on the road. Prithi Chand petitioned the court with the support of Chandu Shah, and an officer, a *mir*, was sent to arrest the Guru, but near Ambala he was killed by four servants he had dismissed. The rumour spread that this had happened through the Guru's blessing; Chandu was rebuked, and the Guru was held blameless.

## The Scripture and the Community

Guru Arjan completed the Amrit Sar, the tank of nectar that his father had begun at Ramdaspur, and the central shrine at Amritsar, the Harmandir Sahib, later known as the Golden Temple, was raised there. He began the tradition of the *daswandh*, by which Sikhs gave a tenth of their earnings to the cause of the Guru, collected through the Masands, the Guru's deputies. In 1594 he founded Kartarpur, near Jalandhar, on land granted during the reign of the third Mughal emperor, Jalal-ud-din Muhammad Akbar.

The act for which he is most often remembered is the compilation of the scripture. In 1604, at Amritsar, he completed the *Adi Granth*, the first authoritative scripture of the Sikhs, also known as the Granth Sahib or the Guru Granth Sahib. He gathered into it the hymns of the Gurus before him, Guru Nanak's among them, together with those of Hindu and Muslim saints, including the poems of the fourteen *bhaktas*, devotional poets, who came before Guru Nanak. More than a hundred *slokas*, verses, ascribed to Baba Farid Ganj-i Shakar are in it: Guru Nanak had collected Baba Farid's poetry at Pak Pattan, and Guru Arjan later included it in the Granth Sahib. He installed the volume in the Harmandir Sahib with Baba Buddha as its first custodian.

He sent one of his followers, Bhai Bannu, to Lahore to bind the *Adi Granth*. After the compilation, at Prithi Chand's prompting, he was summoned to answer for its alleged content against Muslims and Hindus, and he sent Bhai Gurdas, who cleared up the misunderstanding. The *Adi Granth* played a large part in the growth of a separate Sikh identity, and among the reasons for its making, it is said, was the rumour that Meherban, the son of Prithi Chand, was compiling a scripture of his own. Guru Arjan himself has the greatest number of hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib.

It is said, too, that the Sufi poet Shah Hussein travelled to Amritsar to have his poetry included in the Granth Sahib then being compiled, and offered a *kafi*, a Sufi lyric, for inclusion.

Among Guru Arjan's verses are letters written in verse to Guru Ram Das, a part of his *gurbani*, the sacred verse of the Gurus. One opens with a line of longing for the *darshan*, the sight, of the Guru:

میرا من لوچے گورو درشن تائین

*A line of longing for the sight of the Guru.*

Another carries this line, in praise of the Guru's face:

تیرا مکھ سہاوا جی

*A line in praise of the Guru's face.*

His followers are remembered at shrines of their own. A gurdwara at Mandi Mangat was the house of Bhai Bannu, a devotee of Guru Arjan, and another shrine is that of Sahari Mal, a disciple of Guru Arjan.

## The Martyrdom of 1606

That very flourishing drew the suspicion of the Mughal state. The Emperor Jahangir, the fourth Mughal emperor, records in his memoir, the *Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri*, his displeasure at the Guru's rising influence and at the many who were drawn to him, and complains further that Arjan had given his blessing to the rebellious prince Khusrau, Jahangir's own son, then in flight through the Punjab. The emperor counted the blessing as treason. Accounts of where the prince and the Guru met differ. On these grounds the Guru was summoned to Lahore, where he came with five of his Sikhs, Bhai Jetha among them, and a heavy fine was imposed on him, with punishment if he failed to pay; accounts of the penalty differ.

Sikh tradition holds that the Guru refused to pay or to alter a word of the sacred scripture, and that, at the instigation of the Lahore financier Chandu Shah, he was subjected to days of torture: seated, it is recounted, upon a heated iron plate while burning sand was poured over him, and made to endure scalding water. Accounts of the torments, and of where he was held and for how long, differ; the torture is most often said to have lasted five days. One of his Sikhs, it is told, recited aloud the Guru's own hymns, his *bani*, while he was held. Bearing these torments with serene equanimity, and declining every inducement to convert, Guru Arjan died in 1606. Before his death he appointed his son, Hargobind, as the sixth Guru.

Accounts differ over who bore the chief responsibility for his death, and over Chandu Shah's name and office. Chandu's enmity is traced to a refused marriage: he had wished to marry his daughter to Guru Arjan's son, the match was declined after Sikhs wrote against it, and Arjan married his son to the daughters of two Sikhs. Prithi Chand is remembered as Chandu's ally.

Tradition holds that the Guru's end came in the River Ravi, which then flowed beside the fort, and that his body was never recovered; accounts of the manner of his death differ. It is believed that he lost his life at the place where the gurdwara stands. His *shaheedi*, or martyrdom, is traditionally commemorated in the month of Jeth, in late May or early June. He was the first Sikh Guru to be martyred, and his death is reckoned a watershed in Sikh history.

It is told that Guru Hargobind later told Jahangir that Chandu held Guru Arjan's *mala*, his rosary. Chandu, it is said, was in the end killed by a man of Lahore whom he had used in tormenting the Guru.

## The Gurdwara

Sikh tradition records that the Guru's son and successor, Guru Hargobind, raised a small memorial at the site of the martyrdom in the years that followed, to mark the Guru's *samadhi*; accounts of the first memorial differ. That small structure was still there in 2011. It was under Maharaja Ranjit Singh, in the early nineteenth century, that the present *gurdwara* was first erected, embellished in the manner of Sikh sacred architecture, with a gilded dome that answers, across the Hazuri Bagh, the domes of the Badshahi Mosque, and the Sikh community extended it in the early years of the twentieth century. Its nearness to Ranjit Singh's own *samadhi* binds it into the great ensemble of monuments in this quarter of Lahore. Within, the *Guru Granth Sahib*, the scripture that Guru Arjan himself first compiled, is enshrined and reverently read, and the shrine is a living house of worship.

In the nineteenth century Guru Arjan's *samadh* stood beyond the Roshnai Gate, between the gate and the royal fort. In the 1880s a *samadh* of Guru Arjan stood outside the city opposite the Roshnai Gate, with the wall of the fort to its east and the wall of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's *samadh* to its west. Its position fits Dera Sahib, but a great well inside its enclosure could point instead to Lahore's other shrine of the Guru, Gurdwara Baoli Sahib, and whether it was this shrine has not been settled.

That *samadh* had been a small building at first, and the grand building was made in Ranjit Singh's time. Its enclosure was of fired brick and lime, with a parapet. Two of its doors were kept shut, and all who came and went passed through the great eastern door. To the south, within the four walls, stood the grand domed *samadh*, and to its north a hall of three bays, in the middle bay of which the Granth Sahib was kept with full reverence. In one corner outside the hall was the great well, of fired brick, its stair running from north to south down to the water, where a slab of red stone was set so that a man standing on it could draw water. In another corner stood four *samadhs* of a man's height, one of them that of the mother of Lachhmi Sarkar, wife of Maharaja Ranjit Singh. On the north were rooms built for the Sikhs' rest, and on the south a building plastered with lime, where a stone mortar was sunk in the ground and a thick wooden pestle kept beside it for pounding *bhang*, a preparation of hemp, which the Sikhs ground and drank there.

After the Partition of 1947 the gurdwara came under the control of the Pakistan government through the Evacuee Trust Property Board, the ETPB, which maintains it and regularly carries out renovation work. In 1996 rooms were built in the complex for pilgrims from India and other parts of Pakistan, and the new hostel was named after the Sufi Mian Mir.

In 2011, facing the fort, the gurdwara was a small yellow building with a golden dome, protected by a thick yellow wall, with street vendors at the base of the wall and the Badshahi Mosque beside it. In the garden beside it, where the Sikh ruler of the Punjab, Maharaja Ranjit Singh, used to meet his subjects, stood a Mughal *baradari*, a pavilion with twelve pillars. A giant gateway leading from the garden into the yellow building was permanently locked.

Inside, beyond a last security check, the inner structure was the same yellow as the wall, and a couple of rooms at the entrance had been taken over by the security officials. The *Nishan Sahib*, the Sikh flag, stood at the edge of the courtyard on a circular platform about five feet from the ground. The heart of the shrine was a small room with windows on all sides, protected by iron bars, and at its centre a small bulge covered by a velvet cloth: the *samadhi* of Guru Arjan. A small door from the *samadhi* led to the Langar Hall, the hall of the *langar*, the free communal kitchen, which was divided into two sections, with its mats laid in four lines.

## Devotion and Pilgrimage

The shrine remains a solemn and much visited station for the Sikh pilgrims who come to Lahore, above all on the anniversary of the Guru's martyrdom in the month of Jeth. On 6 June 2011 about three hundred pilgrims from India had come to Lahore for the commemoration, and several hundred more from other parts of Pakistan. The Indians were to stay for three days, after which some would return home while others would go on to the sacred shrines of Nankana Sahib and Hassan Abdal. Most of the pilgrims were Sikhs bearing the five Ks, the five articles of the Sikh faith, with a few clean shaven Nanak Panthi Sikhs, followers of Guru Nanak's path, from South Punjab and Sindh. The lawn became a temporary camp for pilgrims without rooms, mostly Pathan Sikh families from Nankana Sahib, Hassan Abdal, Peshawar and the Tribal Areas, while the Indian pilgrims and other important guests had rooms.

The courtyard was tented against the intense heat of June and carpeted, the congregation facing the *granthi*, the reader of the scripture, and the recitation was carried through a small speaker. Men prayed to the *Khanda*, the Sikh emblem, on the *Nishan Sahib*, touched its base and kissed their hands, or touched their eyes to its platform. In the *samadhi* room, which could hold no more than five people, there were about twenty, and women recited from pocket Granths. At the conclusion of the *Akhand Path*, the unbroken reading of the whole scripture, came the *bhog*, the community prayer, and the whole congregation prostrated itself before the Granth Sahib as the living Guru. Sikh boys served cold milk, juice and freshly cut watermelons, and the *langar* was prepared by volunteers and employees, most of them, it seemed, Nanak Panthis of low caste from southern Punjab.

For all its renown, the approach to the shrine was closed. The place was deserted: the only road to it was cordoned off by the police behind a barricade fortified with barbed wire, and only people carrying special cards made for them by the ETPB could pass. Many local tourists returned disappointed. On ordinary days hundreds of local visitors peeked in, and the security men's answer was: "If you are a Muslim, you are not allowed." Male and female police searched the pilgrims, and bags passed through an X ray machine.

Members of Pakistan's own Sikh community were at the shrine that year. Kartar Singh Kartar was staying at the gurdwara for his education, given free accommodation and food at the shrine, and joked that he was a *langur*, a kind of monkey; he hoped to do a doctorate in the Punjabi language. Dr Manoj Singh, thirty two, the first MBBS doctor, holding the basic medical degree, from the Pakistani Sikh community, was serving at the Ganga Ram Hospital. Premjeet Singh, twenty five, the first Pakistani Sikh to be commissioned into the Pakistan Rangers, had been allotted a room because of his social standing, and shared it with five other members of his family.

## Legends

For devotees the Guru's end was more than a death. Legend has it that he was lifted alive into the sky by God, and in Sikh belief, when he went into the waters of the Ravi and did not come out, he had performed a miracle and passed on to the other world.

The Sufi Mian Mir has his own place in the story. In Sikh tradition Mian Mir asked the Guru's leave to bury his oppressors alive, and the Guru refused. The friendship between Mian Mir and Guru Arjan is the subject of several folk tales.

## The Setting

The Roshnai Gate, one of the thirteen gateways into the ancient walled city of Lahore, lies between the Alamgiri Gate of the fort and the Badshahi Mosque. Lamps were lit all along its passageway, hence its name, the gate of lights. Behind it lies the Heera Mandi bazaar, and the area is famous too for the food street that runs parallel to the wall of the Badshahi Mosque.

The river beside which the Guru died has moved: the Ravi, which flowed next to the fort, has changed its course, moving a few kilometres away. The city's Sikhs had thinned too, and by 2011 it had become rare to meet a Sikh in a city that was once ruled by a Sikh and was the seat of their political strength. Lahore holds more of the Gurus' memory than this shrine. Guru Ram Das was born in the city; Guru Arjan spent a lot of time in Lahore, and so did Guru Hargobind.

## Legacy

The martyrdom of Guru Arjan altered the course of Sikh history. He is remembered as the last of the Gurus who focused solely on spiritual matters, and his death marks the beginning of a long conflict between the Mughal authorities and the Sikh Gurus. His son, Guru Hargobind, on assuming the Guruship, is remembered as having girded himself with two swords, symbolising *miri* and *piri*, temporal and spiritual authority, and as having built the Akal Takht at Amritsar, so arming and organising the community for its own defence. After the death of the fifth Guru the Sikhs dropped their pacifist policy and took on the martial spirit for which they became famous. The martyrdom gave the community a cohesive motivation; it has been called the Karbala of Sikh history, and it is held to have hastened the development of the Khalsa, the order of initiated Sikhs.

For Sikhs, Gurdwara Dera Sahib stands not only as the memorial of a death but as the birthplace of an idea: that faith may be defended, and that the willing acceptance of martyrdom is itself a form of victory.

Guru Arjan is regarded as the first martyr of Sikhism, and a long list of martyrs followed him. His memory reaches far beyond Lahore: Operation Blue Star was launched on a day when thousands of Sikhs from all over the Punjab had gathered to commemorate it, and its victims became the latest entry in that list. Tegh Bahadur was the first Guru after Guru Arjan to compose hymns. Guru Arjan's name is among those painted after Guru Nanak's picture on the dome at Jhaman.

Name: Gurdwara Guru Ram Das Ji
Events: Guru Ram Das birth anniversary
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Janam Asthan Guru Ram Das stands in the Chuna Mandi quarter of the Walled City of Lahore, on the site traditionally revered as the birthplace and childhood home of Guru Ram Das (1534 to 1581), the fourth of the ten Sikh Gurus and the founder of the city of Amritsar. A gurdwara is a Sikh house of worship, and *Janam Asthan* means the place of birth. The shrine lies along the old *Shahi Guzargah*, the royal road that ran from the Delhi Gate to the Lahore Fort, near the Fort itself and the Begum Shahi Mosque, and it joins Lahore's several great gurdwaras in binding the city to the early history of the Sikh faith.

The Guru's childhood home is said to have survived here until the era of the Sikh Empire, and the gurdwara was raised on the spot by Maharaja Ranjit Singh. By the 1880s it was a stately building made on the pattern of the Darbar of Amritsar. Sikhs showed the blessed house the utmost reverence, and Hindus high and low also came to it and held the place extremely pure.

## The Guru

Ram Das was born in the Chuna Mandi bazaar of Lahore in 1534, into a family of modest means, and in his boyhood he was known as Bhai Jetha. His birth is placed in the month of Kartik. His father was Har Das, and the family, residents of Lahore, were Sodhi Khatris, a caste that has been called an ancient caste of kings. The house of his mother and father stood on this spot. Accounts of his boyhood differ, but this is revered as the place where he was both born and brought up. Orphaned young, he was raised by his grandmother.

He came under the influence of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, who belonged to the Khatri Bhalla caste, and served him with great devotion and humility. Jetha followed him to Khadur, where he looked after the *langar*, the free communal kitchen, at the Guru's *darbar*, his court, and later to Goindwal. He is remembered as having served in the *langar* for twelve years.

Amar Das's wife, it is said, recommended the young Jetha as a husband for their younger daughter, Bibi Bhani, and the Guru was relieved to learn that he was a Sodhi Khatri. The marriage took place at Goindwal. Jetha's own family complained of his servile attitude towards his in-laws.

Amar Das put his two sons-in-law and his two sons through a few tests, and chose his son-in-law Jetha as his successor. All the Sikhs accepted the choice except Amar Das's eldest son. At his death Amar Das seated his son-in-law in his place, although he had children of his own. Ram Das was Guru from 1574 until his death in 1581, and for those seven years he was the object of his disciples' prostration. He is named among the later Gurus whose stewardship Baba Budha witnessed.

With him the Guruship came to the Sodhi family. He was the first Sodhi Guru, and the office remained within the Sodhi family until Guru Gobind Singh, by whose time it was understood that it would pass only within the Sodhi caste. After Ram Das, it has been said, the succession became a family affair, in which the son of the Guru was preferred over others.

## Amritsar and the Succession

As the fourth Guru, Ram Das is remembered above all as the founder of the settlement that grew into Amritsar. He laid the foundation of Ramdaspur, which in time became Amritsar. The land is said to have been a huge tract that the Mughal emperor Akbar granted to Bibi Bhani, the daughter of Amar Das and the wife of Ram Das, when the emperor met Guru Amar Das. There Ram Das first dug the sacred pool, the *Amrit Sarovar*, the pool of nectar from which the city takes its name, and he is known for starting the construction of the Harmandir Sahib.

To pay for the building of the pool he introduced the system of the *masands*, deputies whom he appointed in different regions to spread the Guru's message and collect offerings, and under him the revenue of the Guru's seat began to increase. He also composed the *Lavan*, the four hymns that form the heart of the Sikh marriage rite and are sung at every *Anand Karaj*, the Sikh wedding ceremony, to this day, and his verses hold a cherished place in the *Guru Granth Sahib*, the Sikh scripture.

That the founder of Amritsar was himself born in Lahore gives this shrine its particular resonance, joining the two cities most closely associated with the early Gurus.

His own succession divided his sons. Accounts differ on how many sons Ram Das had, but two of them, Prithi Chand and the younger Arjan, came to quarrel over an immense property, essentially the whole city of Ramdaspur and the area around it. Ram Das made Arjan his heir and successor in place of Prithi Chand, to Prithi Chand's anger, and passing him over began a conflict that was to last for several generations.

Lahore has its part in the story. It is told that Ram Das sent Arjan to Lahore for a wedding, and that Ram Das, on discovering Prithi Chand's deception, called Arjan back and appointed him Guru; Sikh tradition traces the quarrel between the brothers to Arjan's trip to Lahore. Prithi Chand's rival shrine would lie on the route from Lahore to Amritsar; near Lahore, the Bedian road is the old route to Amritsar.

## The Gurdwara

The Guru's childhood home is said to have survived on this spot until the era of the Sikh Empire. Accounts differ over when the gurdwara was built and at whose wish. Tradition relates that Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the ruler of the Sikh state at Lahore, was asked to raise a fitting shrine here by his wife, Maharani Datar Kaur, during the celebrations that attended the birth of their son Kharak Singh in 1801. The Maharaja agreed and acquired the surrounding plots, the houses of Mohalla Saudagran that adjoined the spot. The gurdwara he built still stands, much altered.

Its place within the dense fabric of the old city, close to the Fort and the imperial mosque of the Mughals, speaks to the layered history of Lahore, where the monuments of Mughal, Sikh and later ages stand shoulder to shoulder.

In the 1880s the gurdwara stood in the southern lane of a bazaar. A lofty brick gateway opened on the bazaar, with a stair in the *deorhi*, the entrance hall. Within lay an upper courtyard, with a well in its north west corner and a *bel*, the wood apple tree. A standard, that is a flag, had been raised in the courtyard, and on the east stood a stepped *jharokha*, a projecting balcony window, of ornamented brick.

The building itself was made on the pattern of the Darbar of Amritsar. It had four doors on its four sides, and though there was no dome at its centre, it had four *shah-nashins*, raised alcoves, each of two storeys.

## Devotion and Festivals

In the 1880s an elaborate floor covering lay spread in the gurdwara, and the Granth Sahib was kept there with the greatest reverence. Sikhs came in numbers, and the Granth was read twice daily before large gatherings. There was singing, and not only by Sikhs: *qawwals*, singers of *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, delighted the people with monotheist *kafis*, short mystical lyrics.

A larger assembly came round every eighth day. In the third watch a great gathering of men and women took place, a selection from the Granths of the Gurus was read, and *shabads*, hymns, imbued with the oneness of God were sung; the gathering was held to be worth seeing. Once, in the days of Holi, the Hindu spring festival, the Singh Sabha held a great assembly here, lit up the whole temple and the bazaar, and sang *shabads* all night.

In the 1880s the gurdwara's *pujari*, its priest, was Jeet Singh, and the trusted agent of the circle was a man named Kanhiya Lal.

## Partition and After

The Partition of 1947 fell heavily upon the Sikh shrines of Lahore. On the eve of Partition, Tara Singh, a prominent Sikh leader of the time, drew his *kirpan*, the sword that Sikhs carry, on the stairs of the Punjab Assembly in Lahore and declared that the time to take revenge for the Gurus had come. Amid the communal violence that swept the city, some eighteen Sikhs are reported to have been killed within the premises of this gurdwara, one of many such tragedies that emptied the western Punjab of its Sikh population almost overnight.

In the decades that followed, the shrine, like the other historic gurdwaras of Pakistan, passed into the care of the Evacuee Trust Property Board. Across Pakistani Punjab, hundreds of temples and gurdwaras were taken over by refugees and turned into households, and some were taken over and destroyed by the migrants. It is now rare to meet a Sikh in Lahore, a city once ruled by a Sikh and the seat of the Sikhs' political strength.

In recent years the gurdwara has been reopened to worship and to pilgrimage, and the birthday of Guru Ram Das draws Sikh visitors to the narrow lanes of Chuna Mandi to honour the Guru at the place of his birth. Its careful upkeep forms part of the wider, if uneven, effort to preserve and restore Pakistan's Sikh heritage.

## The Setting

Lahore drew the Gurus before Ram Das and after him. Tradition tells that Guru Nanak came to the city when Daulat Khan Lodhi governed it, and that Duni Chand, the *amil*, the revenue collector, of Lahore, became his disciple and gave away his seven lakh rupees; Nanak and Mardana also reached Lahore on their way home. Guru Arjan spent a great deal of time in the city; summoned to Lahore by the emperor Jahangir, he was assassinated there and his remains interred. Guru Hargobind, too, spent a great deal of time in Lahore. Later in the line, Guru Har Rai reached Lahore with his forces and met Dara Shikoh there after the prince's defeat by Aurangzeb, and left Dara's camp at Lahore as others had slipped away.

In Aurangzeb's time Lahore was a great city and a mighty metropolis, with mosques beyond counting in every lane and bazaar. The gates of its walled city, the Delhi Gate among them, are most often counted as twelve. The Roshani Gate, one of the gateways that lead into the walled city, is between the Alamgiri Gate and the Royal Mosque.

The poet Bulleh Shah, who died in 1758, lived through a time when the Punjab was being persistently rent by petty chiefs and marauders. The full bitterness of his line 'Punjab has gone to the dogs', it has been said, comes through only against that backdrop:

*Now hell has opened its bogs. / Punjab has gone to the dogs. / This hell is the nethermost hell.* (translated by Taufiq Rafat)

Another of his lyrics says:

*The door of doom and torment has opened, and Panjab is in a bad state.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

A verse in a third lyric has been taken as an allusion to the Sikhs, whose guerrilla horsemen ultimately destroyed Mughal authority in the Punjab.

Ranjit Singh, who ruled the Punjab for forty years, came to Lahore in 1799 and was greeted with enthusiasm by a population sick of the lawlessness of that time. He was crowned ruler of the Punjab in 1801. Across the Punjab he spent large amounts of money on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras, and attached vast tracts of land to them so that their revenues could support their functioning. After his death the throne of the Punjab passed to his son, Maharaja Kharak Singh, whose birth tradition ties to the founding of this gurdwara. The Sikh state ended with Dalip Singh, who left Lahore.

Sikh building in Lahore, it has been observed, draws inspiration from both Hindu and Muslim architecture, as the Sikh religion picks up from both Hinduism and Islam. The Sikhs made smaller the domes that were first part of Muslim buildings, and Sikh shrines carry depictions of the Sikh Gurus and, in older buildings, sometimes of Hindu deities.

## Legacy

For the Sikh community, Gurdwara Janam Asthan Guru Ram Das is doubly precious. It marks the earthly beginning of the Guru who gave Sikhism its holiest city and its wedding liturgy, and it stands as a reminder that Lahore, for so long a great centre of Sikh power and devotion, was also his cradle. Amid the crowded bazaars of the Walled City, the shrine keeps alive the memory of a boy born here in 1534 whose life would reshape the faith and give the world Amritsar.

The Guru's image appears elsewhere too. His name stands among the figures in the frescoes of the dome at Jhaman, and in the nineteenth century he was pictured among the Gurus in the niche of a *samadh*, a memorial shrine.

Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Khoohi Bhai Lalo, also called Bhai Lalo di Khooi, stands in the old town of Eminabad and marks the home and the narrow well, the *khooi*, of Bhai Lalo, the honest carpenter with whom, tradition holds, Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith, lodged when he came to the town in the early sixteenth century. The site is inseparable from one of the most famous of all the *sakhis*, the stories of the Guru's life: the story of Malik Bhago's feast and of the milk and the blood. It is part of Pakistan's Sikh heritage and is visited by pilgrims, usually in the same round as the nearby Chakki Sahib and Rori Sahib shrines.

Bhai Lalo is traditionally said to have been born in 1452 into a family of carpenters at Saidpur, the old town held to be Eminabad. He became one of the most beloved of the Guru's early companions, and his house grew into a *dharamsala*, a gathering place for the local followers of Guru Nanak. The story of the milk and the blood, in which, as tradition tells it, the Guru preferred the labouring carpenter's plain bread to a rich official's feast, has ever since stood at the heart of the Sikh ethic of *kirat karni*, of earning one's bread by honest labour and sharing it with others.

## The Guru

Guru Nanak's dates are most often given as 1469 to 1539. He is counted the first Guru of the Sikhs and is believed to be the founder of Sikhism. His father was Kalyan Chand Das Bedi, called Mehta Kalu. He spent a major portion of his life in what is today Pakistan: he was born there, and he eventually settled in a small village that is now on the Pakistani side of the border. In Aurangzeb's reign his descendants were still living at his house on the bank of the Ravi, twelve *kos*, an old measure of distance, from Batala.

Before his travels the Guru worked at Sultanpur. In the *janamsakhis*, the cycles of tales told of the first Guru's life, he moved there, some 60 kilometres from Talwandi, as keeper of Nawab Daulat Khan's store, bathing in the Bein and gathering people in the evenings to hear his hymns. Vanishing for a week in the stream, the janamsakhis tell, he came back to say: "There is only one God. There is no Hindu, no Mussalman." It is widely believed that it was at Sultanpur that his religious life began. In the same telling he set out on his travels dressed in a strange garb, an approximate combination of what the holy men of Hinduism and of Islam would wear.

Accounts of how many journeys he made differ, but his *udasis*, the long journeys of his travelling years, are most often counted as four, and they lasted more than twenty years. He travelled mostly on foot, and with his companion Mardana he would cover thousands of kilometres. He preferred to stay on the outskirts of villages, and whenever he visited an area he would visit its religious shrines, Muslim, Hindu and of any other denomination.

He offended both Hindus and Muslims by stating that there was no Hindu or Muslim, and his advice to his two companions was that "if one is a Muslim then one should be a good Muslim and if one is a Hindu then one should be a good Hindu". He associated with people of the lower castes, calling them people of God, and he criticised high caste landlords and government officials as exploiters. He lived as a householder, and he taught that all men and women were equal, irrespective of caste, creed, wealth, social standing and gender, and that a good life rested on honest labour, compassion, selfless service and prayer. Nanak himself is held to have abhorred the association of miracles with religious personalities, yet the stories of his life are full of them. In one of those stories he tells Karori, who calls his cure a miracle, that "there is no such thing as a miracle".

On his deathbed the Guru appointed not his son but his most loyal student as his spiritual successor: Lehna, to whom at the hour of death he gave the title of Guru Angad, or Guru Angad Dev. His son Lakhmi Das, it was said, was a worthy son, but spiritual fortune was not his.

## Bhai Lalo

Bhai Lalo, the shrine's second figure, is the one who gives it its name. He was a carpenter of the *Getaura* caste, though accounts of his caste differ. In the janamsakhi telling he tells Nanak that people call him Lalo and that he is a carpenter. In the same telling he works on a daily wage for Ramdev, the master carpenter, and cannot afford to miss a single day's work. The stories draw his poverty in a few objects: a single oil lamp, a loosely strung string bed or *charpoy*, a single thick *bajre ki roti* of millet, and a single small onion.

In the janamsakhi telling the Guru came to Saidpur twice. The first time was early in the first of his journeys, when he came from Sultanpur by way of Talwandi. The second was at the end of the fourth, when he came home by Iran, Kabul, Peshawar, Kandahar, Hasan Abdal, Tilla Balnath and Katasraj to Saidpur, and went on to Kartarpur; on that journey, the stories tell, he took a south eastern route to the Punjab about the time of Babur's third incursion into India.

The janamsakhis tell that on the first visit Lalo warned Nanak that by staying with him he risked being cast out of his own *biradari*, his kinship group. Nanak answered, it is told, that "in God's eyes a man's worth is never measured in terms of his caste or social status or his wealth". In the same telling Lalo sings a *bhajan*, a devotional song, of Kabir as he sweeps, and Nanak asks him to lead "one of Bhagat Kabir's hymns". At Lalo's house, the story goes on, Nanak himself sings and the villagers gather, and the hymn he sings opens with the words of the creed, *Ik Onkar Satnam*, there is only one God. Lalo, it is told, marvels at the prescience the Guru displays.

## Malik Bhago's Feast

Malik Bhago, tradition holds, was a wealthy official of Eminabad who held a great feast, and he was affronted when the Guru preferred the plain fare of the labouring carpenter to his own rich table. Summoned to explain himself, Guru Nanak is remembered to have taken Bhai Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and Malik Bhago's fine bread in the other and pressed them. From the honest man's bread, the story goes, there flowed milk, and from the oppressor's, blood. It was a sign, the Guru is said to have explained, that Lalo's food was earned by the sweat of honest toil, while Bhago's was wrung from the exploitation of the poor.

In the janamsakhis Malik Bhago, humbled, came to realise the Guru's spiritual depth. The Guru's teaching that there was no Hindu and no Muslim, it is told, was questioned at three courts, and one of them was the court of Malik Bhago in Eminabad.

## The Gurdwara

Bhai Lalo's house, where tradition holds that Guru Nanak lodged, was made into a gurdwara, a Sikh house of worship, remembered as Bhai Lalu Di Khoi, and the well from which the Guru is said to have drunk is still preserved within it.

After the Partition of 1947 a refugee family of Muslim migrants occupied the building and lived inside it until 1989; accounts of its care after Partition differ. In 1989 Sardar Surjit Singh Panesar, a Sikh, bought the property with funds raised by the *Sangat*, the Sikh congregation, abroad, and restored it, and it was opened for worship. At the restoration the well was covered over with a platform.

One visitor came to the gurdwara through the town. Old men in a market guided him and his companion into an alley, where there was a lock at the entrance of the gurdwara, the site of the house of Bhai Lalo. Far from being a worn down place, it was in good shape, counted among the most popular Sikh shrines in Pakistan and visited by hundreds of devotees of Nanak. The lock was not a chance of the day. The gurdwara was kept locked at all times, and the keys were probably with members of the Sikh community at the nearby Gurdwara Rori Sahib.

## Devotion and Pilgrimage

The gurdwara is a place of pilgrimage. At pilgrimage time several Sikhs came to pay tribute to the memory of Guru Nanak and Bhai Lalo, and pilgrims usually visit it in the same round as the nearby Chakki Sahib and Rori Sahib shrines. Sikhs from abroad came to Pakistan for festivals such as Baisakhi and the birthday of Guru Nanak, which were attended by thousands of Indian pilgrims.

In Aurangzeb's reign the followers of Baba Nanak, as the Guru was also called, counted service to the traveller, to whoever comes and goes, as the highest worship. Whoever arrived at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name they treated as a brother and a friend and served, even a stranger, a thief, a highwayman or an evildoer. The sum of their worship was the reading of their master's verses, which they sang with song and melody. The tradition of *langar*, the free communal kitchen, is believed to have begun with Guru Nanak.

## The Guru's Verse

The poem most closely bound to Bhai Lalo is the Guru's *Babur Bani*, a long poem that Nanak wrote at the time the Mughal Babur attacked the Punjab, destroying the cities of Eminabad and Lahore on the way. In it Nanak lays the blame of Babur's wrath at God's feet, and again and again the poem addresses Lalo by name:

ਵੇ ਲਾਲੋ

*O Lalo*

Accounts of the year of Babur's invasion differ; one of its lines, in English translation, gives the poem's own reckoning:

ਆਵਨਿ ਅਠਤਰੈ …

*Coming in seventy-eight (1521 C.E)*

The Guru composed verses in Hindi on the truth of God, setting out divine unity. His *bani*, devotional verses of supplication, entreaty, humility and reverence, was sung by Mardana, who drew people into the net of faith. Lines from his hymns, in English translation, give a sense of the poetry. His *aarti*, the hymn sung as lamps are waved in worship, begins:

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ
ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ …

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps*

On the oneness of God he sang:

ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥
ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One*

And again:

*God is One, / The Path is One*

His poem on the sacred thread, the *janeu*, runs:

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ
ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ …

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment*

Of washing he sang:

ਭਰੀਐ ਹਥੁ ਪੈਰੁ ਤਨੁ ਦੇਹ ॥
ਪਾਣੀ ਧੋਤੈ ਉਤਰਸੁ ਖੇਹ ॥

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white*

The verse is sung beyond the gurdwaras too. The singer Abida Parvin has said: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak." In Sindh, Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the *banis* of Shri Guru Nanak and the *kalams*, the poems, of the Sufis.

## Eminabad and Saidpur

Eminabad is held to be the old Saidpur, renamed by Babur when he took over the city, though accounts of how the town came by its name differ. The town suffered when Babur came, for he destroyed the cities of Eminabad and Lahore. Coming back from eastern India, the Guru found the Punjab plunged into a number of political crises: Babur, after two minor raids, invaded the Punjab a third time, reaching as far as Sialkot.

The janamsakhis record a meeting between Nanak and Babur at Saidpur, in which Babur asks for a blessing to conquer India and Nanak rebukes him. The encounter was also taken to mark the beginning of the antagonism between the Mughals and the Sikhs, and Babur, the great grandfather of the emperor Jahangir, is remembered as having imprisoned Guru Nanak.

The cone like spires of ancient Hindu temples rose among the houses of Eminabad, in contrast to the Muslim architecture that had come to dominate the town. It was once an important trading centre on the Grand Trunk Road, which connected with Lahore and then Delhi; the highway has since moved south, and Gujranwala, not far away, has replaced Eminabad as a trading centre. One temple, abandoned in 1947, still looked sturdy, though its paint had worn off and a corrosive layer had formed on it. After the creation of Pakistan such temples were taken over by migrants from across the border. The same visitor looked for signs of attack on them after the destruction of the Babri mosque in 1992 and found none, and much of the town's historical architecture had been preserved.

Gujranwala lies in the heart of the Punjab, 75 kilometres from the provincial capital. Maharaja Ranjit Singh started from a small fief around it, and he allotted Baba Sahib Singh Bedi land around the cities of Gujranwala and Lahore.

## Legacy

Gurdwara Khoohi Bhai Lalo keeps the memory of a carpenter's house in which, as the stories tell it, the founder of the Sikh faith chose honest bread over a rich man's table. Lalo's name lives on, too, in the Guru's own lament for Babur's invasion, which turns again and again to "O Lalo".

Without the family that kept it, Ram Thamman, another shrine in the province, would also have been taken over by refugees and converted into a household, like the hundreds of temples and gurdwaras all over Pakistani Punjab, and across the country several gurdwaras and temples were taken over and destroyed by migrants. Yet at several sites all over the country where Nanak stayed or is said to have performed miracles, the gurdwaras built there later by his devotees still stand tall.

Muslims have claimed the Guru too. Many Muslims acquainted with the teachings of Guru Nanak are devoted to him and visit his shrine; to one Muslim painter, Guru Nanak is like a Muslim Sufi saint, and a Muslim storyteller at Gurdwara Sachkand called him "a true devotee of God. He was a rightly guided soul." A Muslim tradition holds that Guru Nanak was born by the blessing of Baba Naulakh Hazari; the Sikhs do not accept it. Baba Farid, it is said, became an inspiration for Guru Nanak when Nanak visited his shrine on his travels, and Farid's texts are revered among the Sikhs, for he is held to have influenced the founder of their religion. A twentieth century Chishti Sabiri shaykh counted Guru Nanak, with Krishna, Rama, Sita and Lachman, among the spiritual luminaries outside Islam who believed in the one true God and had a "Divine connection", *nisbat*. At the shrine of the goddess Hinglaj, the engraved footsteps of Guru Nanak are found.
