Founded/Opened: Built c.1740s (Diwan Kaura Mal), renovated under Ranjit Singh (early 19th c.)
Events: Sikh pilgrimage, especially Guru Nanak's Gurpurab
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Sri Mal Ji Sahib stands in Nankana Sahib, near the railway station and close to Gurdwara Kiara Sahib, and commemorates one of the miracles told of Guru Nanak Dev Ji's childhood. Nankana Sahib is the old Talwandi, the town in which Guru Nanak, the first Guru of the Sikhs, was born, and the gurdwara is one of the several there that mark events from his childhood. Pilgrims come to it on the great anniversaries.

Its name comes from the *mal*, a shady tree also called *van* or *jal*. The gurdwara remembers a *sakhi*, a story from the Guru's life, in which the young Nanak once lay asleep beneath such a tree while a great cobra shaded his face from the sun. A second gurdwara of the same name stands at Kanganpur in Kasur District; it is a different site.

## The Legend of the Cobra

The story belongs to Nanak's boyhood at Talwandi. Tradition tells that the young Nanak, tending his father's cattle, lay asleep beneath the *mal* tree in the heat of the day. The local landlord, Rai Bular, riding through his fields with his attendants, is said to have come upon the sleeping child and seen that a great cobra had spread its hood over Nanak's face to shade him from the sun. As the men approached, the story goes on, the cobra withdrew quietly. Accounts of how the wonder unfolded differ.

This wonder, told together with the miracle of the untouched crop at Kiara Sahib nearby, is said to have convinced Rai Bular of the boy's spiritual greatness, so that he became a devoted follower of Guru Nanak and later granted him half of his estate.

## The Gurdwara

A gurdwara was first built on the spot by Diwan Kaura Mall, and it was later renovated in the time of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, sovereign of the Punjab. It is larger and more ornate than Kiara Sahib. A central dome crowns it, with domed kiosks at the corners and porches along the hall, and its interior is faced with old ceramic tiles, each some four inches square and each depicting a cobra in memory of the miracle.

The gurdwara stands near the railway station, about five hundred metres from Gurdwara Janam Asthan, the shrine of the Guru's birthplace. Kiara Sahib is close by, and the two form the eastern cluster of the Nankana Sahib shrines, furthest from the Janam Asthan.

As sovereign of the Punjab, Ranjit Singh spent large sums on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras, and he attached vast tracts of land to them so that the revenues from the lands could support their running. After the British took over the Punjab, and amid sectarian divisions among the Sikhs, a large number of important Sikh gurdwaras came to be administered by Hindu *mahants*, heads of religious houses.

Accounts of how the town's gurdwaras fared after Partition differ, but they are most often said to have fallen into a bad state, with no Sikh left in Nankana Sahib. Giani Pratap, who came with a pilgrimage party from India in the 1960s, decided to stay and look after them, and it was the first time since Partition that anyone had taken the initiative to care for the gurdwaras of Nankana Sahib. Most of the town's gurdwaras were kept locked all year round and opened only at the time of the festival, with security guards employed at the entrance to all of them.

## The Guru

Accounts of his birth differ in their details, but Guru Nanak is generally held to have been born at Talwandi in 1469. The *janamsakhis* are the cycles of tales told of the life of the first Guru of the Sikhs, the earliest known of which dates from 1658, nearly 120 years after his death. In the janamsakhi telling, his father was Kalyan Chand Das Bedi, or Mehta Kalu as he was affectionately called, accountant to the Bhatti family under Rai Bular, and his mother was Mata Tripta. The Bhatti family, in that telling, was that of Rai Bhoe and his son Rai Bular; the head of the Bedi family, Shiv Ram, was accountant to Rai Bhoe, and his son Kalyan Chand Das Bedi succeeded him in that office. Nanak belonged to the Bedi caste.

Stories cluster around his birth. Tradition tells that Mata Tripta had no child for a long time after her marriage, and that she would regularly visit an ancient Hindu temple on top of a mound not far from Rai Bhoi di Talwandi to pray for a child; accounts of how his birth came about differ. The village astrologer, Pandit Hardyal, is said to have foretold greatness for the child. Even in childhood, it is said, signs of inner vision and of wonders beyond the ordinary appeared in him. At school, the janamsakhis tell, the boy showed a brilliance never before seen in any child in Talwandi.

At thirteen, in the janamsakhi telling, he refused the sacred thread, the *janeu*, in his father's courtyard, saying that "it is our actions and our actions alone" that give a man his position among men. At sixteen, the janamsakhis go on, he herded cattle, and he became well acquainted with a dervish, Sayyad Hussain, and gained an intimate knowledge of the Sufi line of thought; accounts of the dervish's name differ. Talwandi lay in the path of numerous mendicants, holy men and *sadhus*, the Hindu ascetics, who camped in a grove of trees on the outskirts of the village. It is believed that in the years between the episode of the *Sacha Sauda*, the "true bargain", and his move to Sultanpur, a period of six to seven years, the young Nanak began to frequent the old mound of Talwandi, and that he spent a lot of time there in conversation with the yogis, *sadhus* and dervishes who passed through the town.

From Talwandi, in the janamsakhi telling, Nanak moved to Sultanpur, around 60 kilometres away, as keeper of Nawab Daulat Khan's *modikhana*, or store, bathing in the Bein rivulet and holding evening gatherings at which his hymns were heard. It is widely believed that his religious life began at Sultanpur. The janamsakhis tell that he vanished into the stream for a week and was found on its bank saying: "There is only one God. There is no Hindu, no Mussalman." That saying was questioned at the court of Sultanpur, at Malik Bhago's court in Eminabad, and by friends and family at Rai Bhoi di Talwandi itself.

He married Sulakhini, daughter of Mul Chand and Chando Rani of the town of Batala, on 24 September 1487, though accounts of the marriage differ. They had two sons, Sri Chand, born on 8 September 1494, and Lakhmi Das, born on 12 February 1497.

Guru Nanak spent a major portion of his life in what is today Pakistan: he was born there, first preached travelling through the region, and eventually settled in a small village now on the Pakistani side of the border. He set out on his journeys from Talwandi with Mardana, a singer, and came back to it between them. The journeys, the *udasis*, took him far: east all the way to Bengal, south to the island of Sri Lanka, north to Kashmir, Nepal and Tibet, and west to Mecca, mostly on foot, over about twenty four years, before he returned to settle at Kartarpur. Accounts of how many journeys he made differ, but they are most often counted as four. About 1520 he returned from eastern India to find the Punjab plunged into a number of significant political crises. He preferred to stay on the outskirts of villages, and whenever he came to an area he would visit its religious shrines, Muslim, Hindu and of any other denomination. Crowds upon crowds came from every land to become his disciples, and Mardana sang his verses and drew people into the snare of devotion.

In the janamsakhi telling, Nanak and Mardana came home to Talwandi in 1506, after the first journey; his mother, Mata Tripta, felt great joy, and Mehta Kalu was a little in awe of his son. On a later return, after Pak Pattan, the janamsakhis tell, he found that Talwandi was no longer an obscure little village but had become a place of pilgrimage, and he sat by Rai Bular, who was sick and failing fast. Kartarpur in its turn became a town of pilgrims like Talwandi and Sultanpur. On his road home from Chuhrkhana, it is told, Nanak crossed a vast jungle that lay then between Nankana and Chuhrkhana.

He passed over his sons when he chose his successor. It was said that Lakhmi Das was a worthy son but that spiritual fortune was not his lot, and on his deathbed the Guru appointed not a son but his most loyal student as his spiritual successor: a man of the Khatri caste named Lehna, to whom he gave the title of Guru Angad. He asked Angad Dev to move to Khadur, away from Kartarpur, to avoid the ire of his sons. His eldest son, Sri Chand, ignored by his father when it was time to appoint the next Guru, is believed to have founded a sect of his own, the Udasis, who follow his tradition. Guru Nanak died on 22 September 1539, though accounts of the date differ.

He lived as a householder, with a wife and sons, and he taught that all men and women were equal, irrespective of caste, creed, wealth, social standing and gender, and that a good life rested on honest labour, compassion, selfless service and prayer. Born into a Hindu household and educated in a Muslim milieu, he was neither a practising Muslim nor a Hindu. He offended both Hindus and Muslims by saying that there was no Hindu or Muslim, and his advice to Bhai Bala and Bhai Mardana was that "if one is a Muslim then one should be a good Muslim and if one is a Hindu then one should be a good Hindu". He associated with people of the lower castes, calling them people of God, and criticised high caste landlords and government officials as exploiters. He was a *fakir*, a poor wandering mystic, or a *jogi*, an ascetic, who spent his entire lifetime in a few clothes.

Nanak himself is held to have abhorred the association of miracles with religious personalities, yet the stories of his life are full of them. Legend tells that at Mecca the Kaaba miraculously turned towards his feet. It is told, too, that a trader who told Nanak that his mules carried "Just some mud" found his sugar and *gur*, raw cane sugar, turned to mud until he repented.

## Devotion and Festivals

The great anniversaries bring pilgrims to Gurdwara Mal Ji Sahib. Guru Nanak's birthday is kept at Nankana Sahib every November, in the festival called Guru Nanak Jayanti or Gurpurab. Official estimates put the pilgrims who come to Nankana Sahib for it at ten to fifteen thousand every year; in 2011, by media reports, only three thousand came. That year the festival began on 8 November and ended on the 10th. Police stood at every entrance to the city, no car was let in, and devotees walked barefoot.

Trains brought pilgrims from Delhi, Gujarat and Amritsar across the border at Wagah, where representatives of the ETPB and the PSGPC received them and a *langar*, the free communal kitchen, was arranged; the tradition of the *langar* is believed to have begun with Guru Nanak. The pilgrims stayed three days at Nankana. There were three days of *Akhand Path*, the unbroken reading of the Sikh scripture, and the *Nagar Kirtan*, the procession singing hymns through the town, followed the closing *bhog*, the rite that ends the reading, on the last day; then the pilgrims went on to other cities. Richer pilgrims from Britain, America and Canada came by chartered plane, and travel companies promised them "all" the gurdwaras in Pakistan. For those few days the whole city looked like a little India. Pilgrim tourists came to Nankana Sahib and to Hassan Abdal, and Jeeta Singh of Manora held a small festival of his own every November, when the festival of Guru Nanak was celebrated at Nankana Sahib.

In Aurangzeb's reign it was said that most of the disciples and devotees of Baba Nanak, as the Guru was also called, were men of spiritual states, whose word was accepted, given to austerities, and whose prayers were answered. The sum of their worship was the reading of their master's verses, which they sang to melody. Many had put away worldly ties and lived at one with their friends and without war with their enemies, and their faith in their leader was seldom found among others. Their master's name was always on their tongues; they counted service to those who came and went, the traveller and the guest, as the greatest worship; and whoever arrived at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name they treated as a brother and a friend and served, even a stranger, a thief, a highwayman or an evildoer.

In the same reign the Udasis, devotees of Baba Nanak, were counted as a fourth class among the dervishes of Hind, India; they worshipped in their master's way, and their worship, too, was the singing of his verses. Near Sambhal lay Nanak Mata, a place where Baba Nanak's disciples and devotees thronged to pray.

## The Guru's Verse

Guru Nanak's sermon was his *bani*, devotional verse of supplication, entreaty, humility and reverence. He composed verses in the Hindi tongue on the truth of God, setting out the unity of God in clear words and shining metaphors, and poets such as Kabir and Nanak used the *doha*, a couplet whose two verses rhyme, to write their mystical poetry. Nanak brought into his verse several words that were not part of the Punjabi of his time.

Among his poems is one on the sacred thread, the *janeu* that the boy refused at Talwandi:

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ
ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ …

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment*

His *aarti*, a hymn of worship with lamps, begins:

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ
ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ …

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps*

He sings of the oneness of God:

ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥
ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One*

*God is One, / The Path is One*

Another verse speaks of washing:

ਭਰੀਐ ਹਥੁ ਪੈਰੁ ਤਨੁ ਦੇਹ ॥
ਪਾਣੀ ਧੋਤੈ ਉਤਰਸੁ ਖੇਹ ॥

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white*

In one modern retelling of his life, Nanak sings to innkeepers who meant to rob him and Mardana:

ਬਗਾ ਬਗੇ ਕਪੜੇ ਤੀਰਥ ਮੰਝਿ ਵਸੰਨਿੑ ॥

*The herons in their white feathers dwell in the sacred shrines of pilgrimage*

In the *Babur Bani* Nanak lays the blame of Babur's wrath at God's feet, and one line dates the invaders' coming:

ਆਵਨਿ ਅਠਤਰੈ …

*Coming in seventy-eight (1521 C.E)*

His verse is gathered in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, which holds the spiritual poetry of the Sikh Gurus, Guru Nanak among them, and of other spiritual teachers such as Bhagat Kabir, Baba Farid and Bhai Mardana. The poems of the later Gurus are recorded not in their own names but in that of Guru Nanak. His *bani* was compiled as part of the Adi Granth by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, in 1604.

The verse is sung beyond the gurdwaras too. The singer Abida Parvin counted Guru Nanak among the poets she sang, with Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast and Baba Farid, and in Sindh Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the *banis* of Shri Guru Nanak and the *kalams*, the poems, of the Sufis.

## Nankana Sahib

Nankana Sahib, the old Talwandi, lies about forty miles southwest of Lahore, in what is now Pakistan, and 180 kilometres from Kartarpur by way of Lahore. Originally called Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, the town was renamed Nankana Sahib in honour of Guru Nanak, who was born there. Because he spent his early years here, there are several gurdwaras in the city, marking events from his childhood, and pilgrims visit all of them; accounts of their number differ, from six to seven. Nankana is held to be one of the holiest cities in the world for the Sikhs, for the founder of their religion was born here.

Tradition tells that Talwandi was destroyed thirteen times and thirteen times, like the fabled phoenix, rose again from its ashes, for it lay between the Ravi and the Chenab, in the path of the armies that had set their eyes on Delhi. Its last rebirth, the tradition goes on, took place under the supervision of Rai Bhoe, a Bhatti Rajput who had converted to Islam.

An old mound rests behind Gurdwara Janam Asthan, away from the hub of the new settlement. It is held to be an archaeological mound: the settlement there was destroyed, after which Rai Bhoi di Talwandi was built within a boundary wall, and Nanak was born in the new town. The climb up the mound was steep, with no proper path, to a top at least twenty metres from the ground, covered with shrubs of *karir*, a thorny desert bush, with shards of broken pottery underfoot.

The city had a population of over a million. One main road ran through it, the buildings were old and the road had potholes, and most of the buildings were from the late British or the early Pakistan era. From the roof of a building in the city the small white domes of the gurdwaras could be seen among the minarets of the mosques, with the railway station and the remains of a few Hindu temples, cone like structures rising from houses abandoned at the time of Partition. During the Musharraf era, from 2001 to 2008, newly built roads and other government facilities came to the city, and in 2005 Nankana Sahib was separated from Sheikhupura and made a district of its own, with the city as its headquarters. Sikhs abroad asked for an international hotel and for visa free "holy city" status, with no progress.

Guru Nanak was celebrated all over Nankana Sahib. There were a Guru Nanak High School, a Guru Nanak grocery store and a Guru Nanak cloth shop, all run by Sikhs, while the town's Muslims generally refrained from honouring Guru Nanak in this way. Most of the Muslims of Nankana Sahib came from across the border after Partition. Some shopkeepers kept separate utensils for Muslims and for everyone else, and one restaurant owner refused Sikh customers, complaining: "We become prisoners within our own city." Not all traders felt so, since the pilgrims brought business.

## The Sikhs of Nankana Sahib

Giani Pratap housed the family of Kartar, a Sikh of the town, for a short time inside one of the gurdwaras in his care, and made Kartar's father a *sewaadar*, a worker, there. Most of the community were not natives of the city but recent migrants from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where there is a considerable Sikh population. Families arrived after the wars of 1965 and 1971 and after the demolition of the Babri Mosque in 1992, and the community grew; accounts of its size differ, but it was most often put at about two hundred households, with Jatha Singh as its leader for several years.

Most of the newcomers were housed within the gurdwaras, in rooms generally reserved for pilgrims, and the influx gave a confidence boost to the Sikhs, who until then had been dominated by the Muslim majority. Many Sikh families practised *hikmat*, the traditional medicine, and young men moved to Lahore, Faisalabad and Gujranwala for trade. Guru Nanak High School was the only school in the country where the Granth Sahib was taught to Sikh children. The caretakers of Gurdwara Rori Sahib at Eminabad, Pathan Sikhs, moved there from Nankana Sahib. Several people at Nankana Sahib felt that the PSGPC was not representative of the Sikh community in Pakistan.

The town's festivals grew with the community. Lohri and Guru Gobind Singh's birthday had only begun to be kept a couple of years before, made possible by the migration from the tribal areas; earlier there had been only a prayer at one of the town's gurdwaras. On Guru Gobind Singh's birthday in January 2011 the community held a cricket tournament on the ground of Guru Nanak Government College, with teams called Khalsa XI, Nankana XI and Singh XI. For the Sikh New Year, on 14 March 2011, *qawwals*, singers of Sufi devotional music, were invited from Faisalabad to sing first to Baba Farid; it was the first time since Partition that Muslim *qawwals* had been invited to perform at Nankana Sahib.

The festival has also seen violence. In November 1985, on Guru Nanak's birthday, a year after Operation Blue Star, thousands of Sikh pilgrims had come to Nankana from all over the world. At that time the SGPC in Amritsar still managed the Pakistani gurdwaras through the Indian High Commission. During a speech calling for a separate Sikh state, the gate of one of the town's gurdwaras was closed, and Counsellor B. Jain and First Secretary K. K. Khanna were attacked and barely escaped alive. The religious festivals at Nankana and in other cities of Pakistan went back to being religious festivals.

## Legacy

With Kiara Sahib, Gurdwara Mal Ji Sahib stands among the shrines that turn the town of Guru Nanak's birth into a map of his early life. Across Pakistan there are several sites where Nanak stayed or is said to have performed miracles, and gurdwaras built there later by devotees still stand.

In Aurangzeb's reign Baba Nanak was called the leader of the caravan on the roads of truth and the bearer of the torch of the mystic way. His seat passed on through his successors: Guru Har Rai was called the holder of Baba Nanak's seat, his *sajjada nashin*, one who sits on the prayer carpet. In the same reign the place of Baba Nanak lay twelve *kos*, an old measure of distance, from Batala, on the bank of the Ravi, and his descendants lived there.

Muslims have claimed him too. Many Muslims acquainted with his teachings were devoted to him and visited his shrine; Nadeem, a Muslim painter, said that Guru Nanak is like a Muslim Sufi saint, and a Muslim storyteller at Gurdwara Sachkand called him "a true devotee of God. He was a rightly guided soul." Baba Farid, it is said, became an inspiration for Guru Nanak when Nanak visited his shrine on his travels. Nanak is held to have been a spiritual follower of Baba Farid, and to have travelled to Pak Pattan to collect the saint's poetry from his descendants. Farid's verses are revered among the Sikhs, for he is held to have influenced the founder of their religion, and at one of the shrines of Guru Nanak at Nankana Sahib a picture of Baba Farid accompanied the picture of the Guru. A twentieth century shaykh of the Chishti Sabiri Sufi order counted Guru Nanak, with Krishna, Rama, Sita and Lachman, among the spiritual luminaries outside Islam who believed in the one true God and had a "Divine connection", *nisbat*.

His followers are many, in the Punjab and beyond. Nanak Panthi Hindus in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab and Sindh keep a picture of Guru Nanak in their temples beside the pictures of Hindu deities. Many Lohanas in Sindh follow the teachings of Nanak, and the Nanakpanth among the Hindus of Sindh may have been brought from the Punjab by the Aroras in the eighteenth century. At the shrine of the goddess Hinglaj, the engraved footsteps of Guru Nanak connect that temple to the Sikh and Nanak *panth*, or sect, traditions.

The gurdwara keeps a story of Nanak the son: a child herding in his father's fields at Talwandi, asleep in the heat of the day and shaded by a cobra.

- Haroon Khalid, *In Search of Shiva: A Study of Folk Religious Practices in Pakistan* (New Delhi: Rupa Publications India, first impression 2015).
- Harish Dhillon, *Janamsakhis: Ageless Stories, Timeless Values* (Hay House India, 2015; paperback 2020).

Name: Gurdwara Panja Sahib
Events: Vaisakhi (principal jatha pilgrimage); Saka Panja Sahib commemoration
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Panja Sahib lies in the small town of Hasan Abdal, in the Attock District of Pakistan's Punjab, some fifty kilometres north west of Rawalpindi. It is among the most revered of Sikh shrines and one of the most important in the country, celebrated above all for the great boulder it enshrines, on which, devout tradition holds, the open right hand of Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism, is miraculously imprinted. The shrine takes its name from this relic: *panja* means "the palm" or "the open hand". Set beside pools fed by springs, whose clear water flows over the marked rock, Panja Sahib is at once a place of miracle, a memorial of the Guru's travels through the north west, and the scene of a famous act of self sacrifice in 1922.

The *gurdwara*, the Sikh house of worship, has mountains on one side and the whole town of Hasan Abdal on the other, and from the mountain of Wali Kandhari, the Muslim holy man of its legend, it can be seen in the plain below. A few pilgrims come all year round to pay their respects at the shrine associated with the founder of the Sikh religion, and at the festival of Baisakhi in April they come in their thousands.

## The Guru's Visit

Guru Nanak was born in 1469 in what is today Nankana Sahib, and he died at Kartarpur in 1539. For more than twenty years he travelled on the long journeys known as his *udasis*, mostly on foot, east to Bengal, south to Sri Lanka, north to Kashmir, Nepal and Tibet, and west to Mecca; accounts of how many journeys he made differ, but they are most often counted as four. He preferred to stay on the outskirts of villages, and whenever he came to an area he would visit its religious shrines, Muslim, Hindu and of any other denomination.

The legend of the hand is told in more than one form, and accounts of when the Guru came differ. Tradition sets it on one of his *udasis* in the early sixteenth century, often dated to around 1521, when he was travelling with his devoted Muslim minstrel, Bhai Mardana. Weary and thirsty, the story goes, the Guru and his companion halted at the foot of a hill near Hasan Abdal. On its summit lived a Muslim *pir*, or holy man, remembered as Wali Kandhari, his name recalling an origin in Kandahar, who controlled the only spring in the vicinity.

Tradition tells that Mardana, parched, was sent up the hill to ask for water and was rebuffed; twice more he climbed, and twice more the *pir* refused, taunting the pair. Then, it is said, Guru Nanak touched a stone below, and a fresh spring welled up at the foot of the hill, even as the water at the summit ran dry. Enraged, Wali Kandhari is said to have hurled a great boulder down upon the Guru. Nanak, the story continues, raised his open hand and stopped the falling rock, which yielded to his palm as if it were soft wax and kept the imprint of his *panja*. Humbled by the miracle, the *pir* is remembered as having bowed before the Guru.

The tale's message, that spiritual grace outmatches worldly pride and that mercy answers arrogance, has made it one of the best loved episodes of Sikh sacred lore, and its image has travelled far from Hasan Abdal. In the gurdwara at Manora in Karachi there was a poster of Gurdwara Panja Sahib, and another of Nanak stopping with his hand a rock hurled at him from the top of a mountain where the Muslim saint was.

Other legends tell of Nanak and Muslim Sufis: of Hamza Ghous, who threatened to destroy Sialkot and whose people Nanak saved, and of Mian Mitha of Pasrur, a Sufi who became Nanak's devotee. Yet Nanak himself is remembered as one who abhorred the association of miracles with religious personalities, and in one story he tells Karori, who calls his cure a miracle, that "there is no such thing as a miracle".

## The Gurdwara

A deep imprint resembling a right hand is shown on the rock, over which spring water continually flows, and pilgrims come to touch and reverence it. The place is said to have been named Panja Sahib by Hari Singh Nalwa, the renowned general of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's Sikh Empire, who is credited with raising the first gurdwara here in the early nineteenth century; accounts of who built it differ. The shrine that grew up around the relic includes prayer halls and a *sarovar*, or sacred tank, fed by the springs, whose waters gather into pools where devotees bathe. The *Guru Granth Sahib*, the Sikh scripture, is installed within, and the customary *langar*, the free communal kitchen, is served. The setting, with its clear water, its shade trees and the hill rising behind, is known for its serenity.

In 2011 the main shrine was a grey building crowned with three white and yellow domes, with colourful cloths tied to the railing around it, and buildings of two storeys on all four sides held rooms for the pilgrims. Its façade was pink, and an iron gate closed off the inside. There were four entrances into the main shrine, one from each side, taken to symbolise the openness of the religion. Within, glass patterns recently put up by the Government of Pakistan in its renovation covered the fading frescoes; a wooden palanquin stood in the centre, a young Pathan Sikh read the Guru Granth Sahib, and pilgrims rested.

The sacred pool, said to have been created after the miracle of Nanak, lies in the shadow of the main shrine; accounts of its age differ. In 2011 its water was turquoise, and white marble stairs carrying the names of donors from Canada and the United States led down into it. Water still gushed into the pool through a stream that flowed into the complex from under protective walls recently raised by the Government of Pakistan, and newly built stairs led down to the stream, which came out behind the residential quarters and then flowed out of the complex.

The rock faces the main shrine from inside the pool. It is a grey stone, partly under water, in a small niche whose protective arch is made of ivory, with a black mark in the middle that looks like a handprint. There is a window on each side, through which women offer their devotion, and a marble plaque beside it describes its significance in Gurmukhi, the script of the Sikh scriptures.

Behind the main shrine stands the *kirtan* hall, the hall for the singing of hymns. In 2011 statues of two Sikh soldiers, dressed in yellow clothes and blue turbans and holding spears, stood guard at its entrances; the stage carried a picture of the gurdwara itself in the centre and one of Guru Gobind Singh at the top left, and behind the reader hung a picture of Guru Gobind Singh collecting money for *langar*. A staircase led underground to two spacious corridors where pilgrims without rooms lived. Behind the residential quarters stood the Langar Hall, newly built, of two storeys, and an alley ended in an open space surrounded by more buildings for the pilgrims, with a garden covered by tents to give makeshift rooms.

## The Saka of 1922

To the memory of the Guru's miracle, Panja Sahib later added the memory of martyrdom. Under British rule, amid sectarian divisions among the Sikh communities, a large number of important Sikh gurdwaras in the province had come to be administered by Hindu *mahants*, the heads of religious establishments.

On 30 October 1922, at the height of the Gurdwara Reform Movement, a train carrying Sikh prisoners was to pass through Hasan Abdal railway station. They had been arrested during the *morcha*, or non-violent agitation, at Guru ka Bagh near Amritsar. The local *sangat*, the congregation, wished to serve *langar* to the captives, but were told that the train would not stop. Refusing to let their brethren pass unfed, Bhai Pratap Singh and Bhai Karam Singh, leading the congregation, lay down on the rails, and others followed. The driver braked hard, but not before the engine had struck the foremost of them.

Bhai Karam Singh, a man of about thirty, and Bhai Pratap Singh, some twenty four years old, died of their injuries and were hailed as martyrs. The episode, remembered as the *Saka* Panja Sahib, the martyrdom at Panja Sahib, entered Sikh memory as a supreme example of devotion to the duty of feeding and serving others, and until the Partition of 1947 an annual fair was held at the shrine in the martyrs' honour.

The tradition of *langar* is believed to have begun with Guru Nanak. In Aurangzeb's time the followers of Baba Nanak, as the Guru was also called, counted the service of the traveller, of all who come and go, as the highest worship: whoever arrived at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name was treated as a brother and a friend and served, even a stranger, a thief or a highwayman.

## Baisakhi at Hasan Abdal

Baisakhi, when Sikh pilgrims gather to commemorate the formation of the Khalsa, the order of initiated Sikhs, is the shrine's great festival. As a boy named Amir put it, Sikhs come from India and other parts of the world to Hasan Abdal for Baisakhi, and they also visit the gurdwara at Mandi Mangat.

In 2011 pilgrims spent the 13th, 14th and 15th of April at Hasan Abdal, and most then went on to the other holy Sikh shrines. For those three days and nights the streets were cordoned off, no Muslim was allowed to venture near the gurdwara, and the local schools closed, their classrooms turned into hostels for the pilgrims. The market filled with thousands of turbaned Sikhs. By local media reports about seven thousand pilgrims came for the festival that year, about two thousand from India and the rest from within Pakistan, and more than two hundred people stood in the line at the entrance.

Not all of them came from across the border. Many were Pathan Sikhs, fair skinned and blue eyed, from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the tribal areas; others were clean shaven Hindus from different regions of the country. Some walked the tar road without shoes as an expression of extreme respect.

Entry was guarded, and a police officer checked everyone's security card. Until the year before, a turban or head cover had been enough, and those who looked more Muslim were turned away only if they were Muslim; in 2011 the security was intensified, and everyone needed a card from the Special Branch. Until recently Muslims had been allowed to pay their respects at the shrine of Baba Guru Nanak, but no longer. A television crew that threatened to broadcast its treatment was let through. By tradition anyone may enter a gurdwara, but the practice no longer existed in Pakistan.

Inside, *kirtan* in Punjabi, to the harmonium and the *tabla*, a pair of hand drums, carried across the complex. It usually includes verses from the Guru Granth Sahib, a tradition that goes back to Nanak's Muslim devotee, Bhai Mardana, and listeners offered notes and coins to the musicians. At the Granth devotees waved a fly whisk, a tradition that comes from Bhai Bala, the Hindu devotee of Guru Nanak, and the final chapters were read, marking the conclusion of the *Akhand Path*, the unbroken reading of the whole scripture. Paintings popular in Sikh hagiography show a serene Nanak listening to the songs of Bhai Mardana, who holds a *rubab*, a plucked string instrument, while Bhai Bala stands behind them holding a fly whisk.

At the pool men stood praying in the water, an old man swam, and children hung back on the stairs. Volunteers passed buckets of pool water to wash the white marble floor of the courtyard, a sacred duty called *sewa*, voluntary service, and cooked and served at the Langar Hall. Devotees queued for the *darshan*, the sight, of the stone, placed a hand on the mark while pouring water over it, and some kissed it.

At one Baisakhi a pilgrim in his sixties, in a saffron headscarf, put his hand on the mark and found that his hand too fitted Nanak's. "Miracle!" he said, and he laid a ten rupee note on the rock, kissed it, poured water from the pool over it and cleaned it. Devotees queued behind him, hands reached out from the windows on either side of the rock, and women placed money on top of it.

Some kept watch over the water. In 2011 Surjeet Singh, a Pathan Sikh of thirty five from Peshawar whose family came from a village in the Khyber Agency, chased boys out of the pool, "This is no place to play!", as his way of performing *sewa*. His shirt read "Never forget 1984", with the image of Sant Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale.

The procession with hymns, the *Nagar Kirtan*, had been drawn in. Until a few years before it had marched around the town of Hasan Abdal as local Muslims looked on; in 2011, because of the growing threat from Islamic extremists, it remained within the protected confines of the gurdwara. "I have always wanted to come to Pakistan. This is the land of Guru Nanak," said Avtar Kaur, fifty five, from Amritsar, but "here I have heard that the procession will not be allowed to leave the premises of this Gurdwara. That is sad."

Foreign pilgrims were usually given rooms, while Pakistanis settled wherever there was space. In the underground corridors older Indian pilgrims recalled the Khalistan days of insurgency, Khalistan being the name of a proposed separate Sikh state: Harvinder Singh, sixty five, whose shop in Lajpat Nagar in Delhi had been burnt, Jasdeep Singh, fifty four, and Virinder Kaur, fifty five, from a village in Amritsar District. Sikh boys served *doodh-soda*, milk with soda, at a stall, and volunteers guarded the crowded Langar Hall. Maninder Singh, a photographer of forty four from Amritsar, said, "I actually belong to Pakistan": his parents came from a village in Gujrat and from Shah Alamgir, and on his visit for Guru Nanak's festival the year before he had taken a brick from his mother's ancestral house.

The festival was also a market. A T-shirt reading "Never forget 1984" sold well at a stall behind the main shrine, kept by a boy from the south of the country, and a woman in a sari bargained over its price before confessing, "I don't understand this currency." On sale were CDs of *Sikh Gurdwaras in Pakistan*, a documentary sanctioned by the government, a poster of all the functioning gurdwaras of Pakistan, and Ravinder Singh's latest collection of *kirtan*. From behind an iron gate a man threw *nimko*, a savoury snack, into the crowd. Vendors sold head covers with Khalsa symbols, plates for *aarti*, the worship with lamps, and posters of Hindu deities and Sikh Gurus. Most of them were Pakistanis who travelled all over the country through the year attending Hindu and Sikh festivals. One of them, Vishal Chand, said, "I belong to the city of Multan but I live in Quetta"; almost all his goods came from India, brought by friends and relatives on pilgrimage.

## The Guru's Verse

The worship at Panja Sahib is sung, and its *kirtan* usually includes verses from the Guru Granth Sahib. Nanak's *bani*, his devotional verses of supplication, entreaty, humility and reverence, was compiled as part of the Adi Granth by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, in 1604. The Guru composed verses in Hindi on the truth of God and on divine unity, and a singer named Mardana sang his verses and drew people into the snare of devotion. In Aurangzeb's time the worship of his followers centred on reading their master's verses, which they recited with song and melody.

His *aarti*, the hymn sung as lamps are waved in worship, begins:

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ
ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ …

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps*

On the oneness of God he sang:

ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥
ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One*

And again:

*God is One, / The Path is One*

His poem on the sacred thread, the *janeu*, runs:

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ
ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ …

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment*

Of washing he sang:

ਭਰੀਐ ਹਥੁ ਪੈਰੁ ਤਨੁ ਦੇਹ ॥
ਪਾਣੀ ਧੋਤੈ ਉਤਰਸੁ ਖੇਹ ॥

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white*

And in another song:

ਬਗਾ ਬਗੇ ਕਪੜੇ ਤੀਰਥ ਮੰਝਿ ਵਸੰਨਿੑ ॥

*The herons in their white feathers dwell in the sacred shrines of pilgrimage*

The *Babur Bani* is a long poem that Nanak wrote at the time the Mughal Babur attacked the Punjab, destroying the cities of Eminabad and Lahore on the way, and one of its lines runs 'Coming in seventy-eight (1521 C.E)'.

The Guru's verse is sung outside the gurdwaras too. The singer Abida Parvin has said: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak." In Sindh, Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the *banis* of Shri Guru Nanak and the *kalams*, the poems, of the Sufis.

## The Setting

Hasan Abdal was a historic town that had kept its character, with narrow, curving streets and wooden balconies, set on hillocks. A few Hindu temples survived, used as makeshift houses or in some cases as wandering grounds for stray animals. Facing the gurdwara stood the remains of a Mughal garden in a dilapidated state, a garden mentioned in the *Ain-i-Akbari*, written by Abu-Fazl in the reign of Akbar, the third Mughal emperor.

In 2011 the town was home to about fifty to sixty Sikh families, who had moved there in the few years before from the tribal areas because of the rise of insurgency there, while the rest of the town was Muslim. Most of them spoke only Pashto, and they were mostly confined within the boundaries of the gurdwara, protected by police officials, tall walls and barbed wire on all sides. Sikh families from the tribal areas had moved to Peshawar, Hasan Abdal and Nankana Sahib and started living at gurdwaras.

Wali Kandhari's own shrine stands on the mountain above the gurdwara. It is a separate Muslim shrine, and at Baisakhi, when thousands descend upon the gurdwara, several of the pilgrims travel up to it as well.

A Mughal emperor returning from Kashmir, with his retinue, his servants and his elephants, made his halt at Hasan Abdal. Two of his intimates who died on that road, Mir Fathullah Shirazi and, before him, Hakim Abu'l-Fath Gilani, were buried there. The royal standards rested at Hasan Abdal for some time, and a garden was laid out before the court left for Kabul.

## Legacy

Since 1947 Panja Sahib has lain within Pakistan, cared for by the Evacuee Trust Property Board and the Pakistan Sikh Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee, and it remains one of the principal destinations of the Sikh *jathas*, the bands of pilgrims who travel from India and the diaspora on the great anniversaries, above all the Baisakhi festival, when the shrine draws large and joyful congregations. Baisakhi at Hasan Abdal was among the few religious events kept alive by the foreign pilgrims after Partition.

There are several sites all over Pakistan where Nanak stayed or is said to have performed miracles, and the gurdwaras built there later by his devotees still stand tall. Another impression of the Guru's body is shown at the shrine of the goddess Hinglaj, where the engraved footsteps of Guru Nanak connect that temple to the Sikh and Nanak *panth*, or sect, traditions.

Devotion to the Guru reaches beyond the Sikhs. Many Muslims acquainted with his teachings are devoted to him too, and Nadeem, a Muslim painter, said that "Guru Nanak is like a Muslim Sufi Saint". A Chishti Sabiri Sufi master of the twentieth century described Guru Nanak, with Krishna, Rama, Sita and Lachman, among the spiritual luminaries outside Islam, as a believer in the one true God and a religious leader with a divine connection, *nisbat*. Baba Farid's writings are revered among the Sikhs, for he is held to have influenced the founder of their religion.

Uniting a miracle of the founder Guru with a modern tale of sacrifice, and a marked rock with living springs, Gurdwara Panja Sahib holds an honoured and enduring place among the sacred sites of the Sikh faith.

Name: Gurdwara Panjvi Chati Patshahi
Founded/Opened: Commemorates Guru Hargobind's 1613 visit; Guru Arjan Dev's association with the site is traditional and undated
Events: Occasional pilgrimage; historically a Gur Mela
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Panjvin and Chhevin Patshahi, the gurdwara "of the Fifth and Sixth Kingships", stands in Nankana Sahib, the town of Guru Nanak's birth, near Gurdwara Tambu Sahib on the road leading to the central shrine of Janam Asthan. Unlike most of the town's shrines, which commemorate the boyhood of Guru Nanak Dev Ji, the founder of the Sikh faith, this gurdwara honours two of his successors: the fifth Guru, Arjan Dev, and the sixth Guru, Hargobind, whose visits to the birthplace of the founder are remembered here. It is a reminder that Nankana Sahib drew not only the devotion of later pilgrims but the presence of the living Gurus themselves.

Guru Arjan, who gathered the Sikh scripture, was the first martyr of the faith; his son, Guru Hargobind, was the first Guru to wear two swords, one for temporal and one for spiritual power.

## The Gurdwara

The gurdwara marks the tradition that both Guru Arjan Dev and Guru Hargobind came to the town of Guru Nanak's birth. Guru Hargobind, revered as the master of *miri* and *piri*, the union of temporal and spiritual authority, is remembered to have visited Nankana Sahib in the month of *Har* in the year 1670 of the Samvat reckoning, corresponding to 1613, while returning from a journey to Kashmir. In memory of his stay his followers are said to have established a *Gur Mela*, a fair, at the very spot where he had rested, and in time the site came to honour the fifth Guru as well. Accounts of the Gurus' visits differ in their details.

Within the enclosure there are two shrines, standing together within a common boundary wall: that of Guru Arjan Dev, built plainly and without a dome, and that of Guru Hargobind, surmounted by a dome. Their modest architecture gives visible form to the succession of the Gurus. As in the other shrines of Nankana Sahib, the *Guru Granth Sahib*, the Sikh scripture, is installed within; it rests on a *Thara Sahib*, a raised platform, with a fly whisk. The gurdwara has a *Nishan Sahib*, the Sikh flag on its tall pole, and a single storey block of rooms set aside for pilgrims.

The shrines form one of the quieter corners of Nankana Sahib, less frequented than the great shrine of Janam Asthan but valued by pilgrims who make the full round of the town's sacred sites. Their place beside Tambu Sahib sets them within the compact eastern cluster of the town's gurdwaras, and the site is cared for by the bodies charged with Sikh heritage in Pakistan.

The gurdwara also keeps a relic. A small room above the shrine is itself regarded as sacred, and in it stands a glass showcase holding a piece of a Waan tree. It is told that Guru Arjan and his son Guru Hargobind, coming on pilgrimage to Nankana Sahib, left their horses outside the city, tied to that tree at this spot, and walked about seven hundred metres on foot to Janam Asthan as a mark of respect. In this telling the gurdwara stands where the Gurus dismounted, at the edge of the town, so that they might enter the birthplace of the founder on foot.

## Devotion and Festivals

Pilgrims who come here prostrate themselves, go round clockwise and fan the scripture, and devotees touch the glass of the showcase that holds the piece of the Waan tree, for blessings. On one visit an old Sikh wrote his name on the platform of the *Nishan Sahib*.

Most of the gurdwaras of Nankana Sahib were kept locked all year round and opened only at the time of the festival, with security guards at the entrance to all of them. The festival is the birthday of Guru Nanak, Guru Nanak Jayanti or *Gurpurab*, celebrated in the last days of November. Official estimates put the people who come to Nankana Sahib for it at ten to fifteen thousand every year, though in 2011 only three thousand were reported to be attending.

Pilgrims from India came by train across the border at Wagah and waited at Nankana for three days. There were three days of *Akhand Path*, the unbroken reading of the scripture; on the final day the *bhog*, the rite that closes the reading, was followed by the *Nagar Kirtan*, the procession singing hymns through the town, and then the pilgrims went on to other cities. For those few days the entire city looked like a little India.

## The Fifth Guru

Guru Arjan was the fifth Sikh Guru and the son of the fourth, Guru Ram Das, who appointed him as the next Guru. He was born in 1563 and was Guru from 1581 until his death in 1606, a span of twenty five years.

His succession was contested. Guru Ram Das chose his younger son, and Arjan's elder brother, Prithi Chand, is said to have hidden the letters Arjan sent from Lahore to their father. Ram Das then disowned Prithi Chand and, a few days later, appointed Arjan as the next Guru. Sikh tradition finds the root of the conflict in Arjan's journey to Lahore and the machinations of Prithi Chand, who went on to approach the Mughal authorities for his share of the property; and so, it has been said, began the troubled relation between the Mughals and the Sikhs.

Guru Arjan built and gathered. He is credited with completing the Amrit Sar, the tank of nectar that his father had begun at Ramdaspur, after which the Harmandir Sahib was built there. He introduced the *daswandh*, the giving of a tenth of one's earnings to the cause of the Guru, collected through the *Masands*, the Guru's appointed collectors, a tradition that he began. In 1594 he founded Kartarpur, near Jalandhar in India, on land granted in the reign of Akbar, the third Mughal emperor.

He was the gatherer of the scripture. Guru Arjan began the compilation of the Guru Granth Sahib, and in 1604 he compiled the *bani*, the sacred compositions, of Guru Nanak as part of the Adi Granth. Into the scripture he gathered the writings of all the earlier Sikh Gurus and of other saints who were not Sikhs. Among them was the poetry of the Muslim saint Baba Farid, which Guru Nanak had collected at Pak Pattan. He himself has the greatest number of hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib. He sent one of his followers, Bhai Bannu, to Lahore to bind the Adi Granth. When it was complete the Guru was summoned over its alleged anti-Muslim and anti-Hindu content, and he sent Bhai Gurdas, who cleared up the misunderstanding. The Adi Granth played a significant part in the growth of a separate Sikh identity.

A meeting with an emperor is also remembered. The emperor crossed the Beas and came to where the Guru, the successor of Baba Nanak, had halted. He was pleased by the meeting, and by hearing from the Guru's own tongue the Hindi verses that Baba Nanak had composed on the knowledge of God, and the Guru, counting the visit an honour, presented a fitting offering. The Guru then pleaded for the peasants: while the imperial armies were quartered in the Punjab grain had been dear and the assessment had been raised, and now the peasants could not meet the demand. At his petition the high revenue officers were ordered to lighten the assessment on the peasants, and the revenue collectors to deal with them accordingly.

His followers are remembered elsewhere in the Punjab. A gurdwara at Mandi Mangat is held to have been the house of Bhai Bannu, and another shrine is that of Sahari Mal, also a disciple of Guru Arjan. The friendship between Mian Mir and Guru Arjan is the subject of several folk tales.

## The Martyrdom of Guru Arjan

Guru Arjan was the first martyr of the Sikh faith. He was summoned to Lahore by Jahangir, the fourth Mughal emperor, over his alleged support for the rebellion of Prince Khusrau, the emperor's eldest son; he appointed Hargobind as the sixth Guru, and in 1606 he was put to death. Khusrau, it is told, had stopped at the Guru's *langar*, the free communal kitchen, and sought his blessing for victory, and the mark of blessing was counted treason by the emperor. In his memoirs Jahangir wrote of "a Hindu named Arjan" at Goindwal on the river Beas, where the rebel prince "happened to halt", and of how Arjan made "a finger-mark in saffron which the Indians call Qashga". He called the Guru "this insignificant fellow", handed his property to Murtaza Khan, and ordered that he be dealt with under the penal laws of the Yasa, the Mongol code of law, and put to death. Accounts of why he died differ, but his death is most often tied to Khusrau's revolt.

For five days the Guru was tortured. In the walled city of Lahore, near the Rang Mahal, there is a place with a well, and it is believed that Arjan was kept in a room next to it, in what was the *haveli*, the mansion, of the Mughal Diwan of Lahore, and that there he was immersed in a cauldron. Sikh belief tells the end as a miracle: on the fifth day the Guru took a dip in the waters of the Ravi and did not emerge, and so passed into the other world. Mian Mir, the tradition continues, asked the Guru's leave to bury his oppressors alive, and the Guru refused. Accounts of his end differ. Guru Arjan's son raised a small structure at the spot of his *samadhi*, a memorial shrine. Both Guru Arjan and his son Guru Hargobind spent a lot of time in Lahore, the city where Guru Arjan died.

His martyrdom marks a turning point in the story of the Sikhs. It has been called "the Karbala of Sikh history" and a low point in Sikh history; Arjan, it has been said, was crushed in the fight between the Mughal "elephants". His death is held to have given the Sikh community a cohesive motivation and to have precipitated the development of the Khalsa, the order of initiated Sikhs. He was the last of the Gurus who focused solely on spiritual matters. Operation Blue Star was launched on a day when thousands of Sikhs from all over the Punjab had gathered to commemorate his death anniversary.

## The Sixth Guru

Guru Hargobind, Guru Arjan's son and successor, was Guru from 1606 to 1644. Known as the "soldier-saint", he is most often held to have begun the militarisation of the Sikh community after his father's death, though accounts differ over when it began. He was the first Guru to wear two swords, one representing temporal power and the other spiritual power.

On 24 July 1606 he gave *darshan*, an audience at which his followers beheld their Guru. He came dressed as a royal, in a saffron gown and the close fitting trousers called *churidar* pyjama, with an aigrette, a necklace and two swords, and he refused to take up the religious symbols of Guruhood. His words are remembered as: "My rosary shall be the sword belt and on my turban, I shall wear the emblem of royalty". This is *miri* and *piri*: one sword for temporal power, the other for spiritual prowess.

He kept a court. A saffron flag faced the Akal Takht, the Eternal Throne; there was a large drum, and he kept a hawk as a pet. He had fifty two bodyguards and a force of *Sant Sipahi*, saint soldiers, five hundred to begin with, who were not paid a salary but were exempt from paying the required tribute. Through his *Masands* devotees were told to offer arms and horses, and the offering of weapons at the Guru's court, a practice he began, was later reinforced by Guru Gobind Singh. To administer the community he created the *Sangat*, the congregation of followers, which was then put under a *Masand*. He reared horses and encouraged his followers to keep arms in their defence.

His relations with the Mughals turned more than once. Jahangir imprisoned him in Gwalior, and later the relationship grew cordial. Under Shahjahan three battles were fought, at Amritsar, Lahira and Kartarpur, and all of them were won by the Sikhs, after which he decided to settle at Kartarpur. Kiratpur, on the Sutlej, was also a place where he and Guru Har Rai lived.

He chose his grandson to follow him. His eldest son, Baba Gurditta, died in his lifetime, and he appointed Har Rai, Baba Gurditta's younger son, who thus sat in his grandfather's place. Following his grandfather's tradition, Har Rai too kept horses and a force of twenty two hundred fighters. The sword passed to Hargobind's younger son, Guru Tegh Bahadur, and then to Guru Gobind Singh.

Opinion on him is divided. Critics call his militarism a departure from the teachings of the early Gurus, and he was the first Guru not to compose a single hymn; Tegh Bahadur was the first Guru since Guru Arjan to compose hymns. Hargobind remains one of the most controversial of the Sikh Gurus, and he laid the foundations of the contemporary face of Sikhism.

Another story of the sixth Guru, told of a different shrine, also turns on a horse. In the village of Amar Sadhu, now inside the DHA in Lahore, a gurdwara built in honour of the memory of Guru Hargobind is known as Gurdwara Bibi Kaulan. Bibi Kaulan, it is told, was a maid bonded to a Muslim trader of Mozang; hearing that the Guru was encamped nearby, she begged him to rescue her, and he took her with him on his horse. They rested at that spot for a while before they went on to Amritsar.

## Nankana Sahib

Nankana Sahib was once the village of Talwandi, about forty miles south west of Lahore. Originally called Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, it was renamed Nankana Sahib in honour of Guru Nanak, the first Sikh Guru, who was born there in 1469. His early years there account for the several gurdwaras of the city, which is considered one of the holiest cities in the world for the Sikhs.

Tradition tells that Talwandi lay between the rivers Ravi and Chenab, directly in the path of the armies that had set their eyes on Delhi, and that thirteen times the village was destroyed and thirteen times, like the fabled phoenix, it rose again from its ashes. Its last rebirth, the story goes, took place under Rai Bhoi, who had converted to Islam, and by the end of Guru Nanak's life Talwandi was no longer an obscure little village but had become a place of pilgrimage. Behind Gurdwara Janam Asthan rises an old mound; the settlement there, it is said, was destroyed, after which Rai Bhoi di Talwandi was built within a boundary wall.

The modern town has one main road running through it, and most of its buildings are from the late British or the early Pakistan era. From a rooftop can be seen the minarets of mosques, the small white domes of the gurdwaras, the remains of a few Hindu temples, and the railway station. In 2005 Nankana Sahib was separated from Sheikhupura and made a district of its own, with the city as its headquarters.

After Partition the town's gurdwaras stood empty. As Kartar remembered it: "There was no Sikh left here after partition. Our Gurdwaras became barren and were in a bad state." Giani Pratap, seeing the dilapidated condition of the shrines, decided to stay and look after these holy buildings. In the early twenty first century most of the town's Sikhs were not natives of the city but recent migrants from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where there is a considerable Sikh population, and most of the newcomers were housed within the gurdwaras, in rooms generally reserved for pilgrims. The community numbered about two hundred households.

The town's pilgrimages have also known violence. In November 1985, on Guru Nanak's birthday and a year after Operation Blue Star, thousands of Sikh pilgrims had come to Nankana from all over the world. During a speech for a separate Sikh state at one of the town's gurdwaras, its gate was closed, and Counsellor B. Jain and First Secretary K. K. Khanna were attacked and barely escaped alive. The religious festivals at Nankana and other cities of Pakistan have since gone back to being religious festivals.

## Legacy

Since 1947 the gurdwara, like its neighbours, has come to life chiefly when pilgrim *jathas*, bands of pilgrims, arrive for the great anniversaries. Its dedication to the fifth and sixth Gurus lends the sacred geography of Nankana Sahib a fuller shape: the town is not only the cradle of Guru Nanak but a place touched by the later Gurus who carried his message forward, Arjan Dev, the compiler of the scripture and the first martyr of the faith, and Hargobind, who first girded the sword of temporal power. In honouring their visits, Gurdwara Panjvin and Chhevin Patshahi joins the beginning of the Sikh story to its unfolding.

The gurdwara keeps that succession in a single object: a piece of the tree to which, it is told, father and son tied their horses before they walked, on foot and as a mark of respect, into the birthplace of the first Guru. It is a shrine in Nanak's town to the Guru who gathered the scripture and the Guru who first bore the sword.

Name: Gurdwara Patshahi Chhevin (Hadiara), Lahore
Location: Hadiara village, Lahore District, Punjab, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: c. 1620 (visit of Guru Hargobind); present structure later
Events: Historically an annual Maghi fair
Description:
Gurdwara Patshahi Chhevin at Hadiara, a village of the Lahore District lying off the Lahore–Ghawindi (formerly Lahore–Patti) road near the Bambawali–Ravi–Bedian (BRB) canal, commemorates a visit by Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru (*Chhevin Patshahi*). By tradition the Guru — *Miri–Piri da Malik*, "master of the temporal and the spiritual" — came to Hadiara with a body of Sikhs around 1620 and stayed overnight to bless the local *sangat*. Before Partition the gurdwara held a large annual fair at *Maghi*, and in the days of the Sikh Empire it is said to have been endowed with some hundred acres of land; it was administered by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee until 1947. After Partition the shrine fell empty and was for a time occupied by refugees; during the 1965 war soldiers of the Indian Army's Sikh Regiment, reaching the border village, are reported to have repaired its shell-damaged dome and raised a *Nishan Sahib* upon it. The building, the tallest in Hadiara, survives with notable interior murals depicting episodes of Sikh history, including the Battle of Kartarpur of 1635. It should not be confused with the Gurdwara Chhevin Patshahi at Chitti Gatti near Mansehra (a separate entry in this dataset), which commemorates the same Guru at a different place. This account is corroborated by Iqbal Qaiser's on-the-ground survey of Sikh shrines in Pakistan, which independently confirms Guru Hargobind's visit "in recognition of the affection of the Sikh Sangat," describes the gurdwara as "the tallest building of the village," and records that by the time of his survey it was occupied specifically by refugees from Amritsar.
