Name: Gurdwara Patti Sahib
Events: Guru Nanak Gurpurab
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Patti Sahib, also known as Gurdwara Maulvi Patti, stands in Nankana Sahib, the town in Pakistan where Guru Nanak Dev Ji, the founder of the Sikh faith, was born. It lies midway between Gurdwara Janam Asthan, the central shrine that marks his birthplace, and Gurdwara Bal Lila, on the road that runs from the town centre towards the railway station, though accounts of its exact distance from the Janam Asthan differ. The gurdwara commemorates the place remembered in Sikh tradition as the village school to which the child Nanak was sent to learn, and where, the *sakhis*, the stories of the Guru's life, tell, he astonished his teacher with the depth of his understanding.

Its name comes from the *patti*, the wooden writing tablet on which the children of the Punjab once learned their letters. Pilgrims come to it on the great anniversaries of the Guru, and Sikh families have made their homes in its rooms, though accounts of who lives there differ.

## The Guru's First Lessons

In the Punjab of the fifteenth century, a *patti* was the smooth wooden board on which a pupil, with a reed pen and ink made at home, practised the letters of the alphabet under the eye of a teacher. Tradition relates that Nanak was taken as a young boy to the village schoolmaster to be taught in this way. The story tells that, rather than merely copying his letters, the child composed and recited an acrostic on the alphabet, a poem in which each verse begins with the next letter in turn, and set out in it deep truths about God and the soul. So amazed was his teacher, the story goes on, that the master confessed the boy had nothing more to learn from him.

Tradition holds that this composition is the *Patti Likhi*, set in *Rag Asa*, one of the musical modes of the hymns, and recorded in the *Guru Granth Sahib*, the Sikh scripture, under Guru Nanak's name. It is to this acrostic that the gurdwara's name ultimately refers, and it is told that it was the first poem Nanak wrote, and that he wrote it here.

The *sakhis* add further episodes of the Guru's early education: his study of Punjabi and of accounts, of Sanskrit with a Hindu *pandit*, or scholar, and of Persian with a Muslim *maulvi*, or religious teacher, named in some tellings Qutbuddin. Accounts of his teachers and of what he was taught differ, but through all these episodes the theme is the same: the learning of the schools was surpassed by the inward wisdom already present in the child. The gurdwara's other name, Maulvi Patti, keeps the memory of this Muslim teacher, and of a schooling that crossed the community lines of the age. At school, the janamsakhis, the cycles of tales told of the Guru's life, relate, the boy showed a brilliance never before seen in any child in Talwandi.

Nanak was born into a Hindu household and educated in a Muslim milieu, and he was neither a practising Muslim nor a Hindu. In his time all literate Punjabis, Hindus and Muslims alike, are held to have been conversant with the Persian poets Attar, Rumi and Sa'di. The alphabet poem was a form that the Muslim poets of the Punjab knew too: in the plains of Sind and the Punjab, the Muslim poets of the countryside wrote instructive Golden Alphabets to instil love for the Prophet into the souls of the villagers.

## The Guru

Guru Nanak was born at Talwandi, the village later called Nankana Sahib, in 1469; accounts of the exact day differ. In the janamsakhi telling his father was Kalyan Chand Das Bedi, or Mehta Kalu as he was affectionately called, accountant to the Bhatti family under Rai Bular, and the village astrologer, Pandit Hardyal, foretold the child's greatness. Nanak belonged to the Bedi caste. In his childhood, it is said, signs of spiritual unveiling, of wonders and of marvels beyond the ordinary appeared in him.

At thirteen, the janamsakhis tell, the boy refused the sacred thread, the *janeu*, in his father's courtyard, saying that "it is our actions and our actions alone" that give a man his position among men. At sixteen, in the same stories, he herded cattle, and he became well acquainted with the dervish Sayyad Hussain and gained an intimate knowledge of the Sufi line of thought; accounts of the dervish's name differ. Talwandi lay in the path of numerous mendicants, holy men and *sadhus*, as Hindu ascetics are called, who camped in a grove of trees on the outskirts of the village. It is believed that in the six or seven years between the episode of the *Sacha Sauda*, the "true bargain", and his move to Sultanpur, the young Nanak began to frequent the abandoned mound on the outskirts of the town.

From Talwandi Nanak went to Sultanpur, around 60 kilometres away, as keeper of the stores of Nawab Daulat Khan. He married Sulakhini, daughter of Mul Chand and Chando Rani of the town of Batala, on 24 September 1487, though accounts of the marriage differ, and his sons were Sri Chand, born on 8 September 1494, and Lakhmi Das, born on 12 February 1497. At Sultanpur, the janamsakhis tell, he vanished in the stream for a week and came out saying, "There is only one God. There is no Hindu, no Mussalman."

Accounts of how many journeys he made differ, but his *udasis*, his long journeys, lasted more than twenty years and took him, mostly on foot, east to Bengal, south to Sri Lanka, north to Kashmir, Nepal and Tibet, and west to Mecca. Whenever he came to an area he would visit its religious shrines, Muslim, Hindu and of any other denomination, and people are said to have come from every land to become his disciples, whole multitudes from the far parts of the realm.

Lakhmi Das, it was said, was a worthy son, but spiritual fortune was not his lot, and the Guru passed him over. On his deathbed he appointed not his son but his most loyal student as his spiritual successor, a Khatri named Lehna, to whom he gave the title of Guru Angad. Guru Nanak died on 22 September 1539, though accounts of his death differ.

He lived as a householder, and he taught that all men and women were equal, irrespective of caste, creed, wealth, social standing and gender. The tradition of the *langar*, the communal free kitchen, is believed to have begun with him, and in Aurangzeb's reign his followers counted the service of those who come and go, the traveller, as the highest worship.

## The Gurdwara

The shrine that grew up on the site of the remembered schoolhouse is a substantial building. Set on the road between Janam Asthan and Bal Lila, it forms a natural station on the circuit that pilgrims follow among the places of the Guru's childhood, and its sanctum houses the *Guru Granth Sahib*, before which the visiting faithful make their devotions. It is counted among the well kept shrines of the town, maintained by the authorities charged with the care of Sikh heritage in Pakistan, though accounts of its care differ.

On the night of Lohri in January 2011, an arch led in to a yellow building of two storeys with a white dome, raised on a platform, and a *Nishan Sahib*, the Sikh flagstaff, stood with candles, lamps and incense. The rooms of the gurdwara had been taken over by local Sikhs, among them the family of Kartar, a Sikh of the town.

## A Refuge and a School

As at the other shrines of Nankana Sahib, the community of worshippers departed for India at Partition in 1947. Kartar remembered that no Sikh was left in the town after Partition, and that the gurdwaras of the town became barren and fell into a bad state. In the 1960s Giani Pratap, an Indian citizen, came to Nankana Sahib with a party of pilgrims, and on seeing the dilapidated condition of the shrines he decided to stay and look after these holy buildings. He housed Kartar's family for a time inside one of the town's gurdwaras and made Kartar's father a *sewaadar*, a worker, there. Giani Pratap died in Lahore.

The Sikhs of Nankana Sahib were not natives of the city but recent migrants from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where there is a considerable Sikh population. Families came following the alienation after the wars of 1965 and 1971 as well as the demolition of the Babri Mosque in 1992, and most of the newcomers were housed within the gurdwaras, in rooms generally reserved for pilgrims. Their arrival gave a confidence boost to the Sikhs, who until then had been dominated by the Muslim majority. Some of the young men spoke Urdu with a Pashto accent, and not all the Sikhs of the town could speak Urdu or Punjabi. Kartar called Punjabi "the language of Baba Guru Nanak".

In the early days of this migration, after the wars of 1965 and 1971, many Sikh families from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the Tribal Areas found refuge in Gurdwara Patti Sahib. There Giani Pratap began to teach the young Sikh children the Gurmukhi alphabet, the script of the Sikh scriptures, and the Guru Granth Sahib. So the house remembered for the boy's first lessons became a schoolroom again, where the children of refugee families learnt the script of the Guru's hymns. Jasdeep, a young Pathan Sikh, lived at the gurdwara and had been educated there in Sikh precepts.

Teaching in the Guru's script and scripture went on elsewhere in the town too. Madan Singh, a businessman of Nankana Sahib and a former head of the Pakistan Sikh Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee, ran Guru Nanak High School, the only school in the country where the Granth Sahib was taught to Sikh children.

## Devotion and Festivals

Pilgrim *jathas*, bands of pilgrims, come to Patti Sahib on the great anniversaries, above all the *Gurpurab* of Guru Nanak's birth, when the town fills with visitors from India and the Sikh diaspora.

The gurdwara has also been the scene of a festival of the Punjab. On the night of Lohri in January 2011 the second Lohri fire of the town was lit in its courtyard, where Kartar lived. Kartar broke a wooden window into the pile, oil was poured over it and lit, children added branches, and *kheer*, a rice pudding, was served in steel cups and bowls. Afterwards the older boys went round the homes of the community for more *kheer*. Muslims in the shops and on motorbikes watched the procession through the town with burning curiosity.

Lohri, like Vaisakhi or Basant, is an ancient festival of the Punjab that commemorates the change of season. It is kept on the 13th of January, generally the last night of the month of Poh, and traditionally it means a village bonfire, dry fruit and folk songs; the children collect the wood, and *kheer* is left to cool overnight. After the creation of Pakistan this indigenous festival of the Punjab died down, and the Sikh and Hindu minorities of central Punjab also stopped the celebration. Kartar said that Lohri and Guru Gobind Singh's birthday had only begun to be kept in the last couple of years, made possible by the growth of the Sikh population through migration from the tribal areas; earlier there had been only a prayer. The Lohri of 2011 at Nankana Sahib was an attempt to revive this cultural tradition of the Punjab, carried by a group of Pathan men living in the Punjab.

The great day of the town is the *Gurpurab*. Because Nanak spent his early years in the city there are several gurdwaras in it, and the pilgrims visit all of them; the posters of travel companies promised pilgrims "all" the gurdwaras of Pakistan. Official estimates put the pilgrims who come to Nankana Sahib for the festival at ten to fifteen thousand every year; in 2011, when the festival ran from 8 to 10 November, media reports counted only three thousand. Pilgrims from India crossed at Wagah, where representatives of the Evacuee Trust Property Board and the Pakistan Sikh Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee received them and a *langar* was laid on, and they stayed three days at Nankana. Three days of *Akhand Path*, the unbroken reading of the scripture, ended in the *bhog*, the closing rite, followed by the *Nagar Kirtan*, the procession with hymns. Richer pilgrims from Britain, America and Canada came by chartered plane and hired buses, devotees walked barefoot, and for those few days the whole city looked like a little India.

## Legends

Many wonders are told of the Guru. Legend tells that Nanak once travelled to Mecca and performed the Hajj, and that he slept with his feet towards the Kaaba and was rebuked; he turned his feet, the story goes, and as he did so the Kaaba miraculously turned towards his feet. It is believed, too, that a trader who told Nanak that his mules carried "Just some mud" found his sugar and *gur*, raw cane sugar, turned to mud, and that when he repented they became sugar and *gur* once again. Other legends tell of Nanak humbling a Muslim Sufi at Sialkot and at Pasrur.

A Muslim tradition, which Sikhs do not accept, holds that Guru Nanak was born by the blessing of Baba Naulakh Hazari.

Nanak himself is held to have abhorred the association of miracles with religious personalities, yet the stories of his life are full of them. In one story he tells Karori, who calls his cure a miracle, that "there is no such thing as a miracle". The story told at Patti Sahib is of another kind: its marvel is a poem.

## The Guru's Verse

Guru Nanak's sermon was his *bani*, devotional verses of supplication, entreaty, humility and reverence. His *bani* was compiled as part of the Adi Granth by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, in 1604. The Guru Granth Sahib carries also the poetry of other spiritual teachers such as Bhagat Kabir, Baba Farid and Bhai Mardana, and the poems of the later Gurus are recorded not in their own names but in that of Guru Nanak.

He composed verses in Hindi on the truth of God, setting out the unity of the divine, and a singer named Mardana sang his verses. He brought into his poetry several words that were not part of the Punjabi of his time, and poets such as Kabir and Nanak used the *doha*, an old popular Prakrit and Hindi metre in which the two verses of a couplet rhyme, to write their mystical poetry. In Aurangzeb's reign the worship of his followers was the reading of their master's verses, which they recited in song and melody.

Lines from his hymns, in English translation, give a sense of the poetry. His poem on the sacred thread, the *janeu* that the stories say he refused as a boy at Talwandi, begins:

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ
ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ …

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment*

On the oneness of God he sang:

ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥
ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One*

And again:

*God is One, / The Path is One*

His *aarti*, the hymn sung as lamps are waved in worship, begins:

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ
ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ …

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps*

Of washing he sang:

ਭਰੀਐ ਹਥੁ ਪੈਰੁ ਤਨੁ ਦੇਹ ॥
ਪਾਣੀ ਧੋਤੈ ਉਤਰਸੁ ਖੇਹ ॥

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white*

The verses are sung beyond the gurdwaras too. The singer Abida Parvin has said: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak." In Sindh, Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the *banis* of Shri Guru Nanak and the *kalams*, the poems, of the Sufis.

## Nankana Sahib

Talwandi, the village later known as Nankana Sahib, lies about forty miles south west of Lahore, in what is now Pakistan. It lay between the rivers Ravi and Chenab, directly in the path of the armies that had set their eyes on Delhi. It is told that the village was destroyed thirteen times and thirteen times rose again from its ashes, like the fabled phoenix, and that its last rebuilding was overseen by Rai Bhoe, a Bhatti Rajput who had become a Muslim. Originally called Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, the town was renamed Nankana Sahib in honour of Guru Nanak. It is held to be one of the holiest cities in the world for the Sikhs, because the founder of their religion was born there, and it has several gurdwaras, most of them associated with incidents from his life, though accounts of their number differ.

One main road ran through the entire city, and most of the buildings were from the late British or the early Pakistan era. From a rooftop one could see the minarets of mosques, the small white domes of the gurdwaras, the remains of a few Hindu temples and the railway station. In 2005 Nankana Sahib was separated from Sheikhupura and made an independent district, with the city as its headquarters. Guru Nanak was celebrated all over the town: there were a Guru Nanak High School, a Guru Nanak grocery store and a Guru Nanak cloth shop, all run by Sikhs. The Sikh community was most often put at about two hundred households, though accounts of its size differ, and Jatha Singh was its leader for several years. Most of the Muslims of Nankana Sahib had migrated from the other side of the border after Partition, and their attitudes are said to have been shaped by those experiences.

## Legacy

Patti Sahib keeps the memory of the schoolboy who taught his teacher, whose first verses, in Sikh tradition, were a meditation on the letters of the alphabet turned towards the divine. Among the shrines of Nankana Sahib it takes its place in the line that marks, step by step, the unfolding of the Guru's early life, and it carries a particular meaning for a faith that has prized both learning and the transcendence of mere learning. That a Muslim *maulvi* is remembered among the boy's teachers ties the site to the plural religious world of the medieval Punjab from which Sikhism arose.

The building that remembers the Guru's first lessons sheltered Pathan Sikh families who came to Nankana Sahib after the wars of 1965 and 1971, and there Giani Pratap taught their children the Gurmukhi alphabet and the Guru Granth Sahib. In January 2011 its courtyard held one of the town's Lohri fires, part of the attempt to revive that tradition of the Punjab.

Devotion to the Guru reaches beyond the Sikhs. Nanak is held to have been a spiritual follower of Baba Farid, and to have travelled to Pak Pattan, where he met the spiritual descendants of Baba Farid and collected the saint's poetry. Farid's texts are revered among the Sikhs, for he is held to have influenced the founder of their religion. A twentieth century Chishti Sabiri shaykh described Guru Nanak, with Krishna, Rama, Sita and Lachman, among the spiritual luminaries outside Islam, as a believer in the one true God and a religious leader with a "Divine connection", *nisbat*.

Nanak Panthis, Hindus who believe in the teachings of Guru Nanak but not in the Khalsa, the order of initiated Sikhs, keep portraits of Guru Nanak in their temples in Sindh and southern Punjab, along with Krishna, Kali Mata and other Hindu deities, and many Lohanas in Sindh follow the teachings of Nanak. In Sindh there is a growing similarity between the iconography of Guru Nanak and that of Jhulelal. In the Hinglaj valley there are the engraved footsteps of Guru Nanak. For Nadeem, a Muslim painter, Guru Nanak is like a Muslim Sufi saint.

Name: Gurdwara Pehli Patshahi (Jind Pir), Sukkur
Location: Near the Sukkur–Rohri (Lansdowne/Ayub) railway bridge, Sukkur, Sindh, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: Traditionally linked to Guru Nanak's third udasi (early 16th century)
Events: Gurpurabs; daily prakash of the Guru Granth Sahib
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Pehli Patshahi, popularly called Jind Pir, stands on the Sukkur side of the great bridge that carries the Lahore to Karachi railway across the Indus between Sukkur and Rohri. By tradition it marks a spot graced by Guru Nanak, the first Guru, or *Pehli Patshahi*, during his third *udasi*, or journey, through Sindh, and it was from here, the tradition holds, that he crossed to the river islet later famous as Sadh Belo. The gurdwara is a characteristic monument of Sindh's syncretic Nanakpanthi tradition, the tradition of the followers of the path of Nanak, and it is distinct both from the island temple of Sadh Belo and from the other Sikh sites of Sukkur and Rohri. Much of its detailed history survives only in oral and community tradition.

## The Gurdwara

Its first custodian is said to have been an Udasi *sadhu*, a Hindu ascetic, of the Jhulelal devotion. The shrine passed into the keeping of the Nanakpanthi community of Sindh, Hindus and Sikhs together, who honour Guru Nanak without a firm confessional boundary; accounts differ on whether Sindh's followers of Nanak are to be counted as Sikhs.

Within, the *Guru Granth Sahib*, the Sikh scripture, is installed and its *prakash*, the ceremonial opening of the scripture, is performed, while images are also venerated. A lamp said to have been kindled by the Guru himself is kept burning day and night, and pilgrims bow before it.

The name Zinda Pir, or Jinda Pir, also belongs to an older shrine by the river at Sukkur, where Hindus and Muslims worshipped together until the late nineteenth century. At that time the Hindu congregation abandoned their claim and set up a shrine of their own to Jinda Pir on the Sukkur bank. Whether that shrine and this gurdwara are the same structure, two structures sharing one name, or otherwise related remains an open question.

## The Guru

Guru Nanak, the first Guru, is believed to be the founder of Sikhism. He was born in 1469 in a city now called Nankana Sahib, in Pakistan. His father was Kalyan Chand Das Bedi, affectionately called Mehta Kalu, accountant to the Bhatti family under Rai Bular. He was born into a Hindu household and educated in a Muslim milieu, yet he is held to have been neither a practising Muslim nor a Hindu. He died on 22 September 1539; accounts of the dates of his life differ.

In the janamsakhis, the cycles of tales told of the first Guru's life, at the age of thirteen he refused the sacred thread, holding that it is a man's actions alone that give him his position. In the same tellings he became well acquainted with the dervish Sayyad Hussain and gained an intimate knowledge of the Sufi line of thought.

The janamsakhis tell, too, that Nanak moved to Sultanpur, around 60 kilometres from Talwandi, as keeper of Nawab Daulat Khan's store. There he bathed in the Bein rivulet and in the evenings gathered people to hear his hymns. He vanished into the stream for a week, the story goes, and came out with the words: "There is only one God. There is no Hindu, no Mussalman." It is widely believed that it was in Sultanpur that the religious life of Nanak began. When he set out, the janamsakhis say, he was dressed in a strange garb, an approximate combination of what the holy men of Hinduism and of Islam would wear.

He married Sulakhini, daughter of Mul Chand and Chando Rani of the town of Batala, on 24 September 1487, though accounts of the marriage differ, and they had two sons, Sri Chand, born on 8 September 1494, and Lakhmi Das, born on 12 February 1497. In Aurangzeb's reign his descendants lived at the place of Baba Nanak, as the Guru was also called, twelve *kos*, an old measure of distance, from Batala on the bank of the Ravi.

Accounts of how many journeys he made differ, but they lasted more than twenty years. Mostly on foot, he went east all the way to Bengal, south to the island of Sri Lanka, north to Kashmir, Nepal and Tibet, and west to Mecca, and he returned to settle at Kartarpur. He preferred to stay on the outskirts of villages, and whenever he visited an area he would visit its religious shrines, Muslim, Hindu and of any other denomination. People came in their multitudes from every land and became his disciples, and a minstrel named Mardana sang his verses and drew people into the snare of devotion.

The gurdwara's tradition sets his passage through Sindh on his third *udasi*; accounts of which journey brought him to Sukkur differ. Sikh tradition also records that he came to the village of Kolachi and visited the temple of a sea god, for which he had to take a boat to an island neighbouring Kolachi. The temple at Clifton has been identified as the temple that Nanak visited on his tour of Sindh.

On his deathbed he appointed not his son but his most loyal student as his spiritual successor. This was Lahna, a Khatri, whom he gave the title Guru Angad and who is remembered as Guru Angad Dev.

The gurdwara's first custodian is said to have been an Udasi, and the Udasis follow the tradition of Sri Chand, the eldest son of Guru Nanak, who was not recognised as Guru by the mainstream Sikh community. The Udasi sect is believed to have been founded by him, and the sect called Nanghe Sadhu also derives its origin from him. In Aurangzeb's reign the Udasis were counted as a fourth class among the dervishes of Hind: devotees of Baba Nanak who worshipped the Creator in the way of their master.

## Legends

At Mecca, tradition tells, he slept with his feet towards the Kaaba; accounts of what followed differ. At Haridwar, the janamsakhis tell, he faced west and threw water to reach "my newly ploughed fields there", mocking a ritual.

At the Kumbh Mela, in the same tellings, he taught that "it is our souls, the real sinners, that we must wash and not our bodies". In Baghdad, the janamsakhis go on, he sang the *azaan*, the Muslim call to prayer, until his hearers knelt to pray.

Nanak himself is held to have abhorred the association of miracles with religious personalities, yet the stories of his life are full of them. In one, when Karori called his cure a miracle, the Guru answered that "there is no such thing as a miracle".

A Muslim tradition, which Sikhs do not accept, holds that Guru Nanak was born by the blessing of Baba Naulakha Hazari.

## The Guru's Verse

Baba Nanak composed verses in Hindi on the truth of God, and in them he set out the unity of God. The word *bani* itself means devotional verses such as those of Guru Nanak: verses of supplication, entreaty, humility and reverence. Like Kabir, he used the *doha*, an old popular Prakrit and Hindi metre in which a couplet is put together where the two verses rhyme, for his mystical poetry.

Lines from his hymns, in English translation, give a sense of the poetry. His *aarti*, the hymn of the ritual of lamps, has these lines:

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ
ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ …

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps*

On the oneness of God he sang:

ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥
ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One*

And again:

*God is One, / The Path is One*

On the sacred thread he refused:

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ
ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ …

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment*

On cleansing:

ਭਰੀਐ ਹਥੁ ਪੈਰੁ ਤਨੁ ਦੇਹ ॥
ਪਾਣੀ ਧੋਤੈ ਉਤਰਸੁ ਖੇਹ ॥

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white*

And in another hymn:

ਬਗਾ ਬਗੇ ਕਪੜੇ ਤੀਰਥ ਮੰਝਿ ਵਸੰਨਿੑ ॥

*The herons in their white feathers dwell in the sacred shrines of pilgrimage*

The singer Abida Parvin has said: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak." Among the Hindu Sufis of Sindh, Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the *banis* of Shri Guru Nanak and the *kalams*, the poems, of the Sufis.

## The Followers of Nanak in Sindh

In Aurangzeb's reign the sum of the worship of Baba Nanak's followers was the reading of their master's verses, which they recited in song and melody. Their master's name was always on their tongue, and they counted the service of travellers, of those who come and go, as the greatest worship. Whoever arrived at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name was treated as a brother and a friend and served, even a stranger, a thief, a highwayman or an evildoer. The tradition of *langar*, the communal free kitchen, is believed to have begun with Guru Nanak.

In nineteenth century Sindh the Nanakpanth, the path of Nanak, was probably the dominant religious path among the Hindu Sindhis. In Sindh many Nanakpanthis belonged to a subgroup known as the Udasis. Some of their *darbars*, as shrines are called in Sindh by Sikhs, Muslims and Hindus alike, had been created in the late eighteenth century, and in the second half of the nineteenth century there was a renaissance of the Nanakpanthi *darbars*, with many new ones built all over Sindh. Because the Nanakpanth was so widespread, the Hindu Sufis of Sindh were very familiar with Sikh terminology.

Among the Lohanas and related mercantile groups two main cults were followed, the Nanakpanth and the Daryapanth. The Daryapanth, in all probability the older of the two, is based on the deification of the Indus River and was run by a priestly caste, the Thakurs. The Thakurs were the priests of Jhulelal; they were settled in different cities of Sindh, and from 1947 onwards they migrated to India. Jhulelal was already worshipped by some of the Hindus of Sindh, but the Hindus of Sindh were for the most part Nanakpanthis. Offerings to the Indus are still made in the wider region of Sindh.

In colonial Sindh an attempt was made to create a centralised path devoted to Jhulelal, then known as Amar Lal or Udero Lal, with an attempt to impose a specific script, the Khudawadi, and a meeting organised by several Hindu *panchayats*, or councils, of Sindh at Udero Lal. There was a growing similarity between the iconography of Guru Nanak and that of Jhulelal. Before Partition, temples devoted to Jhulelal in Sindh were built with a dome, as were some Sikh *samadhis*, or memorial shrines.

Many upper caste Hindus in Sindh, especially from the Lohana community, refer to Nanak and his teachings, and many Hindus of the middle and upper classes in Sindh are followers of the Nanak *panth*, or sect. It is common to cover one's head before walking into a *tikana*, the temple containing the Guru Granth Sahib. Inside the temples of the Nanak Panthis in Sindh and Southern Punjab hang portraits of Guru Nanak, along with Krishna, Kali Mata and other Hindu deities. Guru Nanak is mostly depicted in saffron coloured clothes.

The Guru's image also hung in the *darbars* of the Hindu Sufis of Sindh. On the wall of Rochaldas, one of them, hung pictures of Guru Nanak, Qutub Ali Shah, Sai Baba, Ramachandra and Krishna. Among the Hindu Sufis of Sindh, a *jai*, a formula of praise, named among the gods Guru Nanak, Jhulelal and Mast Qalandar.

The Nanak Panthis belong to South Punjab and Sindh, and they are found in very large numbers in the province of Sindh. The communities who refused the Khalsa, the order of initiated Sikhs, and called themselves followers of Guru Nanak still live in Sindh and in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; baptised Sikhs look down upon them, and at Manora they were seen merging into the larger groups of Sikhs.

After Partition the *darbars* that the Hindus left behind in Sindh were most of the time preserved, with different arrangements for their management, often with *gaddi nashins*, the heads of the shrines, or followers in India paying the keepers; and despite the shifting diplomatic relations between Pakistan and India, it was always possible to travel across the border.

## The Setting

Sukkur stands at one corner of the triangle formed by Rohri, Sukkur and Shikarpur. In the Indus at Sukkur lies the island of Sadh Belo, a *tirtha*, or Hindu place of pilgrimage, which the gurdwara's tradition links to the Guru's crossing. Between December 1939 and February 1940 the city was the scene of the Sukkur riots, whose first victim was Bhagat Kanwar Ram.

Sukkur lay on the road of the armies that pursued Dara Shikoh. News reached them that Dara, having passed Bhakkar, had halted at Sukkur on the twenty fifth of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic year. Shaikh Mir, Diler Khan and Qubad Khan crossed towards Sukkur; because of the thick jungle, the crowding of thorny trees and the hard stages of the road, many beasts perished and the baggage did not arrive, and on the sixth of Safar, the second month, they reached Sukkur. Shaikh Mir stayed there a day, and the *zamindars*, the landholders, told him that twenty five *kos* from Sukkur a road branches off towards Kandahar.

Across the river, Rohri was the home of Hindu and Muslim mystics. Bedil, a Sufi born in Rohri who died in 1872, was a writer in five languages. Rochaldas, the Hindu Sufi, was born in Rohri in 1879, seven years after Bedil's death, and it is told that he once found himself wandering high in the sky above the port on the Indus at Rohri. Janullah of Rohri, a Suhrawardi mystic, was a Persian poet of Sind in the second half of the eighteenth century. Sain Vasan Shah, the singer of Guru Nanak's *banis*, has a *darbar* in Ulhasnagar and another in Rohri, on the bank of the Indus. The singer Alan Faqir is reported to have sung in his youth on the buses and trains between Rohri and Sehwan Sharif, and he also sang at the *dargahs*, the shrines, of Sind.

## Legacy

Guru Nanak is remembered as a teacher who crossed the line between Hindu and Muslim, and a shrine kept by Hindus and Sikhs together, where the Granth and images are honoured side by side, belongs to that memory. It is said that, asked which religion to adopt, he told his Hindu and Muslim companions to be true Muslims or honest Hindus: "That would be Nanak's religion."

Devotion to him reaches beyond the Sikhs. Many Muslims acquainted with the teachings of Guru Nanak are devoted to him too and visit his shrine, and to one Muslim painter, "Guru Nanak is like a Muslim Sufi Saint". Baba Farid, the Muslim Sufi saint who wrote devotional poetry in Punjabi, is said to have become an inspiration for Guru Nanak when Nanak visited his shrine on his travels, and Farid's texts are revered among the Sikhs, for he is held to have influenced the founder of their religion.

A twentieth century shaykh of the Chishti Sabiri order described, in certain lectures, Krishna, Rama, Sita, Lachman and Guru Nanak as believers in the one true God and religious leaders with a "Divine connection", *nisbat*. For the Hindu Sufis of Sindh, the message of the Sufis can also be found through Guru Nanak, Mirabai and Kabir, as well as in the poetry of other *sants*, the poet saints. At the temple of the goddess Hinglaj, the engraved footsteps of Guru Nanak are shown, and they connect Hinglaj to the Sikh and Nanak *panth* traditions.

Name: Gurdwara Rori Sahib
Events: Guru Nanak Gurpurab; jatha pilgrimage
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Rori Sahib stands at Eminabad, the old town near Gujranwala in the Punjab that was once known as Saidpur. A *gurdwara* is a Sikh house of worship, and this one marks the earthly travels of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith, remembering two figures: the Guru and his companion Bhai Mardana, the Muslim minstrel who travelled with him. Its name comes from the Punjabi word *rori*, the gravel, pebbles and coarse grit of the ground, for tradition holds that it was here, on a bed of pebbles, that the Guru rested during his sojourn in the town; accounts of how the place came by its name differ.

The gurdwara belongs to a wider constellation of sacred sites clustered around Eminabad, each preserving the memory of an episode from Guru Nanak's life, and together they make the town one of the most important centres of Sikh pilgrimage in present day Pakistan. It is a different place from another Gurdwara Rori Sahib, at Jhaman near the border of Lahore and Kasur.

## The Guru

Guru Nanak's dates are most often given as 1469 to 1539. He spent a major portion of his life in what is today Pakistan: he was born there, and he eventually settled in a small village that is now on the Pakistani side of the border. Accounts of how many journeys he made differ, but his *udasis*, the long journeys of his travelling years, are most often counted as four, and they lasted more than twenty years. He travelled mostly on foot. He preferred to stay on the outskirts of villages, and whenever he visited an area he would visit its religious shrines, Muslim, Hindu and of any other denomination.

He offended both Hindus and Muslims by stating that there was no Hindu or Muslim. In the *janamsakhis*, the cycles of tales told of his life, he is said to have declared, after vanishing for a week in the stream at Sultanpur, "There is only one God. There is no Hindu, no Mussalman." His advice to his two companions was that "if one is a Muslim then one should be a good Muslim and if one is a Hindu then one should be a good Hindu".

He associated with people of the lower castes, calling them people of God, and he criticised high caste landlords and government officials as exploiters. He lived as a householder, and he taught that a good life rested on honest labour, compassion, selfless service and prayer. Nanak himself is held to have abhorred the association of miracles with religious personalities, yet the stories of his life are full of them.

## The Guru at Eminabad

Eminabad holds a cherished place in the janamsakhis. In their telling the Guru came to Saidpur early, on the first of his journeys, from Sultanpur by way of Talwandi, and he passed through it again on the way home from the fourth, coming by Hasan Abdal, Tilla Balnath and Katasraj to Saidpur and going on to Kartarpur.

Popular memory often links this shrine with the story of the Guru lodging with Bhai Lalo, a low caste carpenter of honest livelihood, in preference to the lavish hospitality of the wealthy official Malik Bhago, though local tradition ties the episode most specifically to the nearby Gurdwara Khuhi Bhai Lalo. In the best loved telling, the Guru is said to have squeezed the simple bread of Bhai Lalo's honest labour in one hand and the rich food of Malik Bhago in the other, so that milk flowed from the first and blood from the second. In the devotion of the Panth, the Sikh community, it is a parable of the difference between righteous earnings and wealth wrung from others. Whether recounted as history or as a story that teaches, the episode fixed Eminabad in Sikh memory as a place where Guru Nanak honoured the dignity of honest work.

In the janamsakhis, Mardana has his own part in the story. At first, it is told, he refused Lalo's millet *roti*, the flat bread, and ate it only when Nanak called it *prasad*, food made holy by being offered; later it was Mardana who carried Lalo's *roti* to Bhago's house. The Guru's teaching that there was no Hindu and no Muslim is said to have been questioned at the court of Nawab Daulat Khan Lodhi at Sultanpur, at the court of Malik Bhago in Eminabad, and at Rai Bhoi di Talwandi.

The town is also associated with the turbulence of Babur's invasion. Babur, after two minor raids, invaded the Punjab a third time, reaching as far as Sialkot. Tradition holds that Guru Nanak witnessed the sack of Saidpur by the Mughal armies around 1520 or 1521, an experience that many hold inspired the anguished hymns known as the *Babur Bani*, in which the Guru lamented the suffering visited upon the innocent. It is told that the Guru and Mardana were taken captive at Saidpur.

The janamsakhis record a meeting between Nanak and Babur at Saidpur, in which Babur asks for a blessing to conquer India and Nanak rebukes him. The encounter was also taken to mark the beginning of the antagonism between the Mughals and the Sikhs.

## The Gurdwara

To Rori Sahib itself attaches the memory of the Guru seated in meditation upon the rough pebbled ground, and it is this humble scene of devotion, the Guru at prayer, indifferent to comfort, that the shrine was raised to preserve.

The gurdwara that survives today owes its grandeur to the era of the Sikh Empire: it was built during the reign of Maharaja Ranjit Singh (1801 to 1839), whose patronage adorned so many of the sites connected with the Gurus, though accounts of its date and its form differ. The central building is an imposing structure of finely cut brickwork rising through several storeys, crowned by a large central dome, the *gumbad*, flanked by smaller domed pavilions, the *chhatris*, in the manner characteristic of Sikh sacred architecture. A room at the rear, roofed with an especially graceful ribbed white lotus dome and ringed by a verandah for walking round the shrine, is said to enclose the very patch of pebbled earth on which the Guru rested.

The gateway was the work of Bhai Ram Singh, Principal of the Mayo School of Arts in Lahore, who designed the Indian gallery in Buckingham Palace. Ram Singh came from a family of carpenters, and he created the effect of woodcutting from the use of bricks. Over the doorway a verse from the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, was carved with an artistic effect of bricks.

The path to the gateway ran between empty grounds, and a few police officials lazed on a *charpoy*, a woven string bed. Visitors took off their shoes at the portal. Beside the gateway was a small courtyard with several rooms, where a few Pathan Sikh children were playing. The gurdwara's caretakers were Pathan Sikhs who had moved there from Nankana Sahib. In the ground beside the gurdwara stood a further structure, also part of the gurdwara, with buffaloes wallowing in the pools around it.

Like most Sikh shrines in the western Punjab, Rori Sahib was left on the Pakistani side of the border when the subcontinent was divided in 1947, and its congregation departed in the great and grievous migration of that year. The building is reported to have been damaged by fire in the disorder that followed Partition, and for decades it stood largely neglected; accounts of its state in those years differ. A bazaar for the sale of buffaloes used to be set up on the gurdwara's premises.

In more recent years, with the easing of pilgrimage across the border and the growing attention paid to Sikh heritage in Pakistan, the shrine has again received visitors, Sikh *jathas*, or pilgrim parties, travelling from India and from the worldwide diaspora, and efforts have been made towards its care and conservation. Security officials came to be posted there at all times, and Sikh pilgrims came every year.

## Bhai Mardana

The gurdwara's second figure is the Guru's companion. *Bhai*, brother, is a title given to Mardana for the exalted status he holds in the Sikh religion, and Mardana was his real name. He was a minstrel and a favourite friend of the Guru's, and he joined Nanak at Sultanpur, where the Guru worked in the commissariat of Daulat Khan; soon afterwards Nanak left Sultanpur, with Mardana beside him. Bhai Bala and Bhai Mardana, a Hindu and a Muslim, were both companions of Nanak.

Mardana was counted among the intimates of Baba Nanak, as the Guru was also called, and he sang the Guru's verses in song and melody and so drew people into the net of devotion. His own poetry is in the Guru Granth Sahib, which contains the poetry of several saints who were not Sikhs, among them Baba Farid, Bhai Mardana and Bhagat Kabir.

In the janamsakhis, Mardana, who played the *rubab*, a traditional stringed instrument, set out with Nanak on his travels. He went with him east all the way to Assam, to Haridwar and Prayag, to Lahore, Sialkot and Multan, to Mecca, Medina and Baghdad, and to Tilla Balnath and Katasraj. The stories give him a perpetual hunger, feet perpetually suffering from sores, and a homesickness that sometimes overcame him, so that he would often sob into his pillow. In one of them, turned away from house to house in an inhospitable village, he asks why two villages received opposite blessings. In the same stories, his parents settled at Kartarpur, and he and Nanak spent a lifetime on the road.

Stories of Mardana are told at other shrines too. At Ghavindi it is told that Mardana, told not to beg, came back hungry from a family celebrating the birth of a son; the child died, by an act of God, and the family sought Nanak's forgiveness. The shrine there had two plinths meant to represent the seats of Guru Nanak and Bhai Mardana, Nanak's higher than Mardana's. In the legend of Panja Sahib, Mardana climbs three times to Wali Qandhari for water. At Kanganpur, old shop paintings bore text that confirmed they were of Guru Nanak and Bhai Mardana.

Mardana died before the Guru. Accounts of where he died differ, and no grave marks the spot where he was buried.

## Devotion and Verse

The tradition of *kirtan*, the devotional singing of hymns, comes from Bhai Mardana. Ever since his time, his descendants as well as other Muslim *kirtan* performers performed at Sikh gurdwaras, a tradition that was disrupted at Partition. In the janamsakhis Mardana would take up his *rubab* and provide an accompaniment for the divinely inspired verses that Nanak sang, and the Guru's call to him was "Mardana, Bani aaye hai", "I have inspiration for a Bani". At a tomb in Baghdad, the stories tell, Mardana tuned his *rubab* and struck up the accompaniment to his master's singing. Sikh hagiography has a favourite scene, shown in several paintings: a serene Nanak listening to the songs of Bhai Mardana, who holds a *rubab*, while Bhai Bala stands behind them holding a fly whisk.

In Aurangzeb's time the sum of the worship of Baba Nanak's followers was the recitation of their master's verses, which they sang in song and melody. They counted service to the traveller, to those who come and go, as the highest worship, and whoever arrived at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name they treated as a brother and a friend and served, even a stranger, a thief, a highwayman or an evildoer. The tradition of *langar*, the communal free kitchen, is believed to have begun with Guru Nanak.

The Guru composed verses in Hindi on the truth of God, setting out divine unity. His *bani*, devotional verses of supplication, entreaty, humility and reverence, is sung outside the gurdwaras too. The singer Abida Parvin has said: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak." In Sindh, Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the *banis* of Shri Guru Nanak and the *kalams*, the poems, of the Sufis.

The poem most closely tied to Eminabad is the *Babur Bani*, a long poem that Nanak wrote at the time the Mughal Babur attacked the Punjab, destroying the cities of Eminabad and Lahore on the way. In it Nanak lays the blame of Babur's wrath at God's feet. One of its lines dates the invaders' coming:

ਆਵਨਿ ਅਠਤਰੈ …

*Coming in seventy-eight (1521 C.E)*

Lines from the Guru's other hymns, in English translation, give a sense of the poetry that, in the tradition, was sung to Mardana's *rubab*. His *aarti*, the hymn sung as lamps are waved in worship, begins:

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ
ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ …

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps*

On the oneness of God he sang:

ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥
ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One*

And again:

*God is One, / The Path is One*

His poem on the sacred thread, the *janeu*, runs:

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ
ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ …

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment*

Of washing he sang:

ਭਰੀਐ ਹਥੁ ਪੈਰੁ ਤਨੁ ਦੇਹ ॥
ਪਾਣੀ ਧੋਤੈ ਉਤਰਸੁ ਖੇਹ ॥

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white*

And in another song:

ਬਗਾ ਬਗੇ ਕਪੜੇ ਤੀਰਥ ਮੰਝਿ ਵਸੰਨਿੑ ॥

*The herons in their white feathers dwell in the sacred shrines of pilgrimage*

## The Setting

When Babur took the city of Saidpur, he renamed it Eminabad, though accounts of the renaming differ. The cone like spires of ancient Hindu temples rose among its houses, in contrast to the monolithic Muslim architecture that dominated the town, and its dusty roads and worn houses showed that it had lost its economic strength. Once it was an important trading centre on the Grand Trunk Road, which connected with Lahore and then Delhi; the highway has since moved south, and Gujranwala, not far away, has replaced Eminabad as a trading centre.

One temple, abandoned in 1947, still looked sturdy. Temples such as these had been taken over by migrants from across the border after the creation of Pakistan, and after the destruction of the Babri mosque in 1992 no signs of attack on them were to be found. Much of the town's historical architecture had still been preserved.

## Legacy

Gurdwara Rori Sahib endures as a quiet monument to the earliest chapter of the Sikh story, when Guru Nanak walked the roads of the Punjab teaching the oneness of God and the equality of all people. Its very name, a shrine of pebbles, carries the lesson of the tradition it commemorates: that holiness is found not in comfort or wealth but in humility and honest devotion. For the Sikhs of the world it remains a treasured link to their founder, and for the town of Eminabad it is the enduring sign of a visitor whose memory has outlasted empires.

It is also a shrine of the friendship between the Guru and his Muslim minstrel. Across Pakistan there are several sites where Nanak stayed or is said to have performed miracles, and the gurdwaras built there later by his devotees still stand tall. After the division of the Punjab, several other gurdwaras and temples were taken over and destroyed by migrants.

Devotion to the Guru reaches beyond the Sikhs. Many Muslims acquainted with his teachings are devoted to him too and visit his shrine, and to one Muslim painter, "Guru Nanak is like a Muslim Sufi Saint". A Muslim tradition, which the Sikhs do not accept, holds that Guru Nanak was born by the blessing of Baba Naulakh Hazari. Baba Farid is said to have become an inspiration for Guru Nanak when the Guru visited his shrine on his travels, and Farid's texts are revered among the Sikhs, for he is held to have influenced the founder of their religion. A Chishti Sabiri shaykh of the twentieth century counted Guru Nanak, with Krishna, Rama, Sita and Lachman, among the spiritual luminaries outside Islam who believed in the one true God and had a "Divine connection", *nisbat*. At the shrine of the goddess Hinglaj, the engraved footsteps of Guru Nanak are found.

Description:
## Overview

Shikarpur's only functioning Sikh gurdwara today is known locally as Gurdwara Sach Khand Sahib, sometimes rendered Gurdwara Sachkhand Hazoor Sahib — a modest, comparatively recent building serving the small Nanakpanthi Sikh community of this historic Sindhi trading city. It should not be confused with the much larger and more famous "Sach Khand" gurdwara of the Punjab, near Farooqabad/Chuharkana, which commemorates Guru Nanak's celebrated sugar-miracle with Bhai Mardana — a wholly different site, wrongly linked to Shikarpur in some casual accounts.

## Rebuilding After Partition

Like almost every gurdwara in Sindh, whatever pre-Partition Sikh place of worship once stood in Shikarpur was lost when the city's substantial Sikh and Hindu populations departed for India in 1947; its exact location and fate went unrecorded. The present gurdwara is a recent structure, built only within the last decade or so by the city's much-reduced Sikh community, and registered with the Evacuee Trust Property Board as a functional gurdwara on a plot of just over 3,000 square feet.

## Congregation and Practice

Shikarpur's resident Khalsa Sikh population numbers only a handful of families; the wider congregation drawing on the gurdwara is composed mainly of Nanakpanthi Sehajdhari Sikhs — Sindhi Hindus devoted to Guru Nanak who have long formed part of the region's syncretic religious landscape, and who learn Gurmukhi in order to read the Guru Granth Sahib. The Guru Granth Sahib is given daily *Prakash* (ceremonial opening) at the gurdwara, and a round-the-clock *langar* is maintained — a continuation of the communal-kitchen tradition central to Sikh gurdwaras everywhere. As of the mid-2010s the gurdwara's president and principal *sewadar*/granthi was Vikash Singh Khalsa, a Nanakpanthi convert to the Khalsa; under his leadership the gurdwara took part in a March 2017 meeting at Kandhkot that established the All Sindh Balochistan Gurdwara Management Committee, linking Shikarpur into the wider network of Sindh's surviving Sikh institutions.

## A Possible Second Site

Some sources also describe a separate or possibly older Shikarpur site called Gurdwara Sri Guru Nanak Sahib — locally rendered "Puj Udasian Samadha Ashram" — featuring a red-painted wooden *baradari*, the samadhs of past Udasi ascetics, and a banyan tree linked to a Guru Nanak legend. Whether this represents the same building as Sach Khand Sahib under an older name, an adjoining shrine within the same compound, or a genuinely separate site nearby is not clearly resolved in the available sources, and the question is noted here rather than resolved.

Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Sacha Sauda stands at Farooqabad, the town formerly called Chuharkana, in the Sheikhupura district of the Punjab. A *gurdwara* is a Sikh house of worship, and this one commemorates one of the best loved stories of Guru Nanak's youth, the *sacha sauda* or "true bargain", in which the young Nanak spent the money his father had given him for trade on feeding hungry holy men. Sikhs tell the story to children and elders alike as the seed of their faith's social teaching, and the shrine that marks its setting is a cherished stop on the pilgrim road through Pakistani Punjab.

The gurdwara stands on an ancient mound, in a walled courtyard with a few trees under which, it is said, Nanak discoursed with the leader of the yogis. After Partition its congregation departed; it has since been renovated with the support of the Sikh congregation of the United Kingdom and opened to organised parties of Sikh pilgrims.

## The True Bargain

The story is told in more than one way, but its heart is the same. Tradition tells that when Nanak was, by the usual reckoning, about eighteen years old, his father, Mehta Kalu, entrusted him with a sum of money, remembered as twenty rupees, and sent him to the nearby market town of Chuharkana to strike a profitable deal, so that he might learn the trade of a merchant and settle to a worldly living. Nanak set out from the town that is now Nankana Sahib with his lifelong companion, Bhai Mardana.

On the road, outside Chuharkana, he came upon a company of holy men who had gone without food. Moved by their need, he spent the whole of his father's money on food for them, holding that no trade could be more honest or more profitable than the relief of the hungry. When he returned empty handed, the story goes, his father reproached him for squandering the money, and Nanak answered that he had made the truest bargain of all, a *sacha sauda*, for he had spent it in the service of God's creatures. The episode is counted among the most important events of Nanak's early life.

In the *janamsakhis*, the cycles of tales told of the Guru's life, the story is told at length. There the boy buys food in Chuharkana from the biggest wholesale grocer, enough to feed fifty starving holy men, with vegetables, fruit and firewood; he hires two cooks and two porters and feeds the holy men at a grove of trees. "Any dilution of my bargain will be a dilution of the truth", he says, and feeding them is "a truly selfless service". At home his father calls him a failure, but Rai Bular, under whom Mehta Kalu served as accountant, takes the boy's part: he has used the money to feed a whole band of famished holy men, a bargain "true in the eyes of God".

In the devotion of the Panth, the Sikh community, the episode is read as the first flowering of the principle that would become central to Sikhism: *langar*, the free communal kitchen where all are fed without distinction of caste or creed, and *seva*, selfless service as an act of worship. It is believed that the tradition of *langar* began with Guru Nanak, when he fed the poor holy men at Chuharkana.

## The Gurdwara

Long afterwards, Sikhs raised a gurdwara at the place associated with the story, built to commemorate the event, and it grew into a popular place of pilgrimage, drawing devotees from across the Punjab and beyond. It is one of the gurdwaras that commemorate the story, and it is held to stand at the spot where the Guru fed the holy men. With the Partition of 1947 the shrine passed into Pakistan, and its congregation departed.

When the historian Iqbal Qaiser first saw the gurdwara, in 1993, while researching his book, buffaloes were tied in the courtyard, and drug addicts and gamblers had occupied the rest of the space. A local man, whom Qaiser remembered only as Shah, tried to keep the place sacred and was beaten by the addicts and gamblers. Qaiser and his companion, Ilyas Ghuman, took him to hospital and filed a police report, and the matter reached a few national newspapers. The Department of Auqaf, the government department of religious endowments, then came and appointed Shah the official guard of the place.

The gurdwara was then renovated with the support of the Sikh *sangat*, or congregation, of the United Kingdom. The renovation is dated to 1993 and 1994, though accounts of its timing differ, and Qaiser himself has said that he played a major part in it. The renovation of this and a number of other gurdwaras was fiercely debated, and once the work on the gurdwara was done, a new road had to be made to connect it with Nankana Sahib. Built for Sikh pilgrims, the road takes only about twenty minutes; before it, pilgrims had to travel to Sheikhupura and then head on towards Chuharkana.

The gurdwara stands a little distance from the main road, within a protective wall topped with barbed wire. Through a portal lies a marbled courtyard with a white gurdwara at its centre. Beside it, within a small boundary, grow a few *waan* trees, the last remnants of the jungle that once grew here, and gurdwara, courtyard and trees stand on an ancient mound, the highest point in and around the town. It is said that it was under these trees that Nanak discoursed with the leader of the yogis.

A Muslim storyteller at Gurdwara Sachkand, another gurdwara of the town, said that the yogis Nanak fed had been meditating "on top of a mound. The mound is where the big gurdwara stands". He called Nanak "a true devotee of God", a rightly guided soul, and said that this had come down from his elders, who used to live with the Sikhs before Pakistan was made.

On one visit, made in the monsoon season during the month of Ramzan, the gurdwara was a splendid structure, recently renovated, but entry was not easy. Two security men sat inside the gate, with a policeman beside them, his gun resting on his shoulder; they were new, Qaiser said, and did not know him, and a boy at the gate would not let the visitors in until the guard had telephoned the caretaker, Boota Singh. Qaiser had always come before with a *jatha*, a group of Sikhs, and Boota Singh showed the visitors round. He was about forty years old, dressed in a green shalwar kameez with a green turban, and extremely shy; he came with his youngest son, a boy of about ten, and he had worked at the gurdwara for twelve years.

Inside was a wooden palanquin in which the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, was placed, with a couple of swords before it. Behind the gurdwara was a new *sukhasan*, the chamber where the scripture is laid to rest at night, carpeted and panelled in wood, with an air conditioner, switched off for want of electricity, and a carved wooden bed. Asked whether the bed had been made in Amritsar, Boota Singh answered: "It was made in Nankana Sahib."

## Devotion and Pilgrimage

The gurdwara has been opened, under arrangement with the Government of Pakistan and the Evacuee Trust Property Board, to organised parties of Sikh pilgrims, especially on the great anniversaries of Guru Nanak's life. It is one of the major shrines visited by the pilgrims who come to Nankana Sahib and Hassan Abdal.

On that visit in Ramzan, before the Guru Granth Sahib, Qaiser placed a ten rupee note, walked round the palanquin and fanned the scripture with a whisk, and his fellow visitor did the same. Leaving the *sukhasan*, Boota Singh walked out backwards, so that his back never faced the Guru Granth Sahib, and the visitors did likewise.

In Aurangzeb's time the followers of Baba Nanak, as the Guru was also called, counted the service of all who come and go as the greatest worship, and whoever arrived at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name they treated as a brother and a friend and served, even a stranger, a thief or a highwayman.

## Farooqabad

Farooqabad is still a *mandi*, a market town. Its old name was Chuharkana, and it lies about 45 kilometres from Nankana Sahib in a straight line. The new name, it is said, comes from the 1980s. In the Zia era, when elections in the eighties were held without parties, a resident of the town, Farooq Dogar, was elected to the National Assembly. He supported the military dictator and was killed over a personal feud, and the town was renamed Farooqabad in his honour. The first part of the old name, *chuhr*, a Sanskrit word meaning to lead, is explained as the two bangles worn at the start and the end of a set of regular bangles.

Across the Punjab, Maharaja Ranjit Singh, who became its sovereign at the end of the eighteenth century, spent large sums on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras, and attached vast tracts of land to them so that their revenues could support their functioning.

## Guru Nanak

The dates of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh religion, are most often given as 1469 to 1539. In the janamsakhi telling, his father was Kalyan Chand Das Bedi, or Mehta Kalu as he was affectionately called, accountant to the Bhatti family under Rai Bular. At thirteen the boy refused the sacred thread, the *janeu*, the beginning of a lifelong crusade against the performing of empty rites and rituals; at sixteen he herded cattle, and he became well acquainted with the dervish Sayyad Hussain and gained an intimate knowledge of the Sufi line of thought. After the true bargain he moved to Sultanpur as keeper of the stores of Nawab Daulat Khan. It is also said that under pressure from his family he became a trader and farmer.

He brought a message of peace and harmony to the believers of Islam and Hinduism, and taught that all men and women were equal, irrespective of caste, creed, wealth, social standing and gender, and that a good life rested on honest labour, compassion, selfless service and prayer. He associated with people of the lower castes, calling them people of God.

He is held to have disavowed the miraculous and to have abhorred the association of miracles with religious personalities; yet, as one writer has put it, "his biography is nothing but a story of his miracles". In Aurangzeb's time it was held that signs of unveiling, of miracles and of wonders beyond the ordinary had appeared from him in his childhood.

Accounts of how many journeys he made differ, but his *udasis*, the long journeys of his travelling years, are most often counted as four, and they lasted more than twenty years. He travelled mostly on foot, and whenever he visited an area he would visit its religious shrines, Muslim, Hindu and of any other denomination.

Trade runs through another of his legends too: a trader, it is said, told Nanak that his mules carried "Just some mud"; his sugar and *gur*, or jaggery, had turned into mud, and when he repented, the mud became sugar and gur once again.

## The Guru's Verse

His *bani*, devotional verses of supplication, entreaty, humility and reverence, was compiled as part of the Adi Granth, the first compilation of the Sikh scripture, by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, in 1604. He composed verses in Hindi on the truth of God, setting out divine unity, and in Aurangzeb's time the worship of his followers centred on reading their master's verses, which they recited in song and melody. A minstrel named Mardana sang the Guru's verses and drew people into the snare of devotion.

Lines from his hymns, in English translation, give a sense of his poetry. On the oneness of God he sang:

ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥
ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One*

And again:

*God is One, / The Path is One*

His *aarti*, the hymn sung as lamps are waved in worship, begins in one translation:

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ …

*The sky the salver, the sun and moon the lamps …*

and in another:

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps*

His poem on the sacred thread runs:

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ
ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ …

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment*

Of washing he sang:

ਭਰੀਐ ਹਥੁ ਪੈਰੁ ਤਨੁ ਦੇਹ ॥
ਪਾਣੀ ਧੋਤੈ ਉਤਰਸੁ ਖੇਹ ॥

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white*

Other hymns of his open *O my merchant friend*, *As a beggar goes a-begging …*, *Launch ye the boat of austere contemplation …* and *His goodness cannot be priced or traded …*.

His verse is sung outside the gurdwaras too. The singer Abida Parvin has said: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak." In Sindh, Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the *banis* of Shri Guru Nanak and the *kalams*, the poems, of the Sufis, and Guru Nanak has been called "the greatest poet of the Bhakti", the path of loving devotion.

## Legacy

Gurdwara Sacha Sauda enshrines a story that is, in miniature, the whole ethic of Sikhism: that true profit lies in generosity, and that the service of the needy is the service of the divine. From the boy's true bargain the tradition traces the institution of *langar*, which to this day feeds millions in gurdwaras around the world without charge or condition. For Sikh pilgrims travelling in Pakistan, the shrine is a living link to the compassion of their founder; for the wider tradition, it is the place where a lesson in kindness became the cornerstone of a faith.

The gurdwaras built later by devotees at the places where Nanak stayed or is said to have performed miracles still stand tall, though after Partition several gurdwaras and temples were taken over and destroyed by migrants.

Muslims, too, have claimed the Guru. Many Muslims acquainted with his teachings are devoted to him and visit his shrine. He is held to have been a spiritual follower of Baba Farid: he travelled to Pakpattan and collected the saint's poetry, and Baba Farid became an inspiration for him when he visited Farid's shrine on his travels. Farid's texts are revered among the Sikhs because, it is said, he influenced the founder of their religion. A Chishti Sabiri shaykh of the twentieth century counted Guru Nanak, with Krishna, Rama, Sita and Lachman, among the spiritual luminaries outside Islam who believed in the one true God and had a "Divine connection", *nisbat*. At the shrine of the goddess Hinglaj, engraved footsteps are held to be Guru Nanak's.

Name: Gurdwara Sahib Saidpur (Guru Nanak Dev Ji)
Location: Saidpur Village, Margalla Hills, Islamabad Capital Territory, Pakistan
Sufi Saint: Guru Nanak (gurdwara-school dedicated to his teachings)
Events: Preserved as a heritage site; no regular events
Description:
The Sikh gurdwara at Saidpur Village stands at the foot of the Margalla Hills on the northern edge of Islamabad, within the historic multi-faith village that also preserves a Hindu temple complex (the Ram Kund mandirs). Saidpur is an old settlement — traditionally traced to the early sixteenth century and named after Sultan Said Khan, a chief of the Pothohar region — that served in Mughal times as a garden resort watered by its perennial springs, and that long sheltered a mingled population of Hindus, Sikhs, and Muslims. The gurdwara was built by the Sikh community in the early twentieth century and is remembered as having housed a school dedicated to the teachings of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith. It remained active until the Partition of 1947, after which, the Sikh congregation having departed, the building was repurposed — for a time as a girls' school — before being closed in the mid-2000s when Saidpur was developed as a cultural-heritage and tourist village by the Capital Development Authority. Standing beside the temples and close to an old mosque, the disused gurdwara is today valued chiefly as a monument to the religious plurality of pre-Partition Saidpur, a small but eloquent survival of the shared life of the Pothohar. This is the Saidpur Village of Islamabad's Margalla Hills — confirmed against the sheet's coordinates, which match this dataset's separate Ram Mandir, Saidpur entry — and is not to be confused with the historical Saidpur that is an alternate name for Eminabad in Gujranwala District, a distinct place described in other Sikh-shrine literature. Press coverage describes the gurdwara's construction only as "probably" twentieth-century, without a firmer date, and notes its bright yellow domes standing beside the temple complex, with the attached schoolroom serving as a base for teaching the philosophy of Guru Nanak.

Name: Gurdwara Shaheed Bhai Taru Singh
Events: Martyrdom commemoration (1 July)
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Shaheed Bhai Taru Singh, in the Naulakha bazaar quarter of the walled city of Lahore, marks one of the most harrowing and revered episodes in Sikh history: the martyrdom of *Bhai Taru Singh* (c. 1720–1745), the young cultivator who chose to have the skin of his scalp cut away rather than his sacred, uncut hair. His story stands at the heart of the eighteenth-century Sikh memory of persecution and steadfast faith, and the shrine that bears his name is a place of deep veneration for Sikhs across the world.

## The Life and Martyrdom of Bhai Taru Singh

Bhai Taru Singh was born around 1720 into a Sikh family of modest means and raised, after his father's early death, by his widowed mother alongside his sister, Bibi Tar Kaur. He took up farming at the village of Poola in the Kasur district of the Lahore region, growing crops and living simply. These were bitter years for the Sikhs of the Punjab: under the Mughal governor *Zakariya Khan*, a price was placed on Sikh heads and the community was driven into the forests and wastes, sustained by sympathisers in the villages. Bhai Taru Singh was one such sympathiser, quietly giving a share of his harvest to feed the Sikh bands who lived as fugitives.

He was denounced to the authorities — by tradition, betrayed by an informer — and arrested together with, in some accounts, his sister. Brought before Zakariya Khan at Lahore, he was offered the customary choice: embrace Islam, of which the outward sign would be the cutting of his *kesh* (the unshorn hair kept by observant Sikhs), or die. Bhai Taru Singh refused to cut his hair or renounce his faith. In an act of calculated cruelty, the governor is said to have ordered that his scalp be sliced from his skull with a blade, so that his hair could never be shorn nor grow again. This is believed to have taken place in the summer of 1745.

Sikh tradition relates that the martyr did not die at once, and that Zakariya Khan was soon afflicted by a torment of his own — an inability to pass water — that no physician could relieve. It was said he would find no ease until struck with the shoe of the man he had wronged; when Bhai Taru Singh's shoes were brought and struck against the governor's head, Zakariya Khan died in agony. Bhai Taru Singh, having outlived his persecutor, is said to have given up his life of his own will on 1 July 1745. His fortitude made him one of the great *shaheeds* (martyrs) of the Sikh Panth, remembered daily in the *Ardas*, the Sikh prayer that honours those who suffered for their faith.

## The Shrine

The gurdwara at Naulakha marks the place associated with his martyrdom, in the vicinity of the celebrated *Shahidganj* — the "treasury of martyrs" — where, through the eighteenth century, many Sikhs were put to death. The site has long been a focus of devotion and, in the colonial period, of legal and communal contest over its custody. Today the shrine preserves the memory of Bhai Taru Singh's sacrifice, and Sikh pilgrims visiting Lahore make their way to it to pay homage.

## Legacy

The martyrdom of Bhai Taru Singh has become one of the defining stories of Sikh identity — a parable of the *kesh* held dearer than life itself, and of faith unbroken by torture. His image, the young farmer whose scalp was taken rather than his principles, is invoked in sermon, art, and remembrance wherever Sikhs gather. The gurdwara in Lahore, standing on the soil where he suffered, is both a memorial to one man's courage and a monument to the endurance of a community through its darkest years.
