Name: Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj Singh Singhnian
Sufi Saint: Sikh women & children martyrs (18th century, Mir Mannu era)
Events: Martyrdom commemoration; pilgrim visits
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj Singh Singhnian, in the Naulakha Bazaar quarter of Lahore, outside Delhi Gate, is among the most solemn of Sikh memorials in Pakistan. Its name, from *Shahid Ganj*, "treasury of martyrs", and *Singhnian*, "of the Sikh women", commemorates the many Sikhs, above all the women and children, who were tortured and killed here during the great persecutions of the mid eighteenth century. It stands within the cluster of martyrdom sites at Naulakha, close to the shrine of Bhai Taru Singh, that together mark one of the darkest chapters of Sikh history, and Sikh pilgrims to Lahore come here to pay homage.

The gurdwara, a Sikh place of worship, is also known simply as Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj, and its history is contested as well as sacred. Its building was claimed as a mosque, and the question was fought out in a court battle lasting generations, from British rule into Pakistan's, before the present gurdwara was completed in 2004.

## The Martyrs

After the struggles between the Mughals and the Afghans in the 1740s, Muin-ul-Mulk, the governor of Lahore from 1748, known to the Sikhs as Mir Mannu, set himself to the extermination of the Sikh community. In his time a general order went out to seize and kill the Sikhs; it was given, it is said, because their numbers had grown. Mobile columns hunted the Sikhs who had taken refuge in the forests and wastes, and captives were brought in numbers to Lahore. The men, refusing conversion, were put to death. The women and children were consigned to a prison where they were set to grinding heavy quotas of grain by hand, starved and brutalised.

Sikh tradition preserves the memory of mothers made to watch the killing of their children, and of their steadfast refusal to abandon their faith in exchange for their lives. Traditional accounts speak of enormous numbers of dead. Such figures cannot be verified and are best understood as expressions of collective memory, but the historical reality of a sustained and savage persecution under Mir Mannu is well attested.

It is the constancy of the women, the *Singhnis*, that gives this gurdwara its name and its particular sanctity. In the retelling that every Sikh child learns, the women endured imprisonment, forced labour and the murder of their infants without renouncing the *Khalsa*, the community of initiated Sikhs, and their courage transformed a place of suffering into a place of honour.

The historian Iqbal Qaiser, who was asked to supervise the rebuilding of the gurdwara, tells of men, women and children slaughtered here and thrown into a well on the governor's orders, and of a room built to hold prisoners before their execution. When the gurdwara was being rebuilt, skeletons of children and adults would emerge from the ground, and he identified them as the Sikhs killed on Mir Mannu's orders.

## The Gurdwara

The site came to be venerated as a *shahid ganj*, a treasury of martyrs. Accounts of how the gurdwara began differ. In its own tradition, a gurdwara was raised here after the consolidation of Sikh power in the later eighteenth century, to enshrine the memory of the martyrs. In the nineteenth century a large building stood here, a *samadh* of the Sikhs, a memorial raised because Sikhs had been put to death on that spot, and the *samadh* was given the name Shahid Ganj.

The gurdwara lies outside Delhi Gate, in the area known as Naulakha Bazaar, where Prince Dara Shikoh is said to have had his Naulakha palace. In the nineteenth century the Shahid Ganj quarter also held the tomb of Mir Mannu himself. In the 1870s a tomb in Mohalla Sadhwan, the mass grave of Muslim martyrs of the Ghaznavid period, also bore the name Shahid Ganj; it may or may not be the same place as the Sikh Shahid Ganj at Naulakha.

Today the gurdwara is maintained under the Evacuee Trust Property Board, the state body that administers the properties of communities displaced at Partition, and pilgrims visit it alongside the neighbouring shrine of Bhai Taru Singh. It is austere, less an architectural showpiece than a site of remembrance.

## Devotion

At the gurdwara the recitation of the *Guru Granth Sahib*, the Sikh scripture, and the *ardas*, the formal prayer of the Sikhs, keep alive the names and the example of those who died. In the nineteenth century, too, the scripture was read at Shahid Ganj, and formerly, in the Maharaja's time, the place had been a source of open bounty to all.

More widely, when Maharaja Ranjit Singh became the sovereign of the Punjab at the end of the eighteenth century, he spent large amounts of money on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras, and attached vast tracts of land to them, so that the revenues from the lands could support their functioning.

## The Dispute

In the colonial period and after it, the Naulakha martyrdom sites became focal points of Sikh commemoration and, at times, of communal contest over ownership. Here, in the telling of Iqbal Qaiser, the quarrel goes back to a small mosque that stood on a vacant plot, from which the *qazi*, the judge under Islamic law, would announce punishment to criminals. "The mosque was small and was never used as a place of worship", he says. Under Maharaja Ranjit Singh, he goes on, the Sikhs "placed the Guru Granth Sahib inside it, converting it into a gurdwara. The Muslims could not do anything then". In the nineteenth century, too, the Sikhs used one of two mosques that stood near a *sarai*, a travellers' inn, outside Delhi Gate.

Under British rule, Qaiser relates, the Muslims applied to the courts for the building's return. The Lahore High Court asked for a living witness who had seen it used as a mosque, found none, and decided in favour of the Sikhs, who then razed the building. Rioting between Muslims and Sikhs followed, which Qaiser lays at the door of the British policy of divide and rule. Muhammad Ali Jinnah and Allama Iqbal, he says, became involved, and he has seen a photograph of Jinnah addressing a crowd at the Badshahi Mosque at the time of the riot. In the end, in his words, "the gurdwara remained a gurdwara".

After Partition, with the creation of the Auqaf Department, the government department of religious endowments, the question came back to the Lahore High Court, which ruled around 1957 or 1958 that the building would remain a gurdwara. In the late 1980s petitioners sought a review once again. The judge said he would convert the site if they could produce even one person who had prayed at the mosque, and none was produced.

In about 1994 or 1995 the Kar Sewa Committee of England sought permission to renovate the gurdwara, and the government agreed. Avtar Singh Panghedha asked Qaiser to supervise the construction, and, Qaiser says, "all the money, the contracts ... went through me". When the newspapers reported the work, in his words, "the Muslims tried once again to create an issue". The opposition was turned, as he tells it, by an ironsmith named Rana, who persuaded the local traders that the gurdwara would attract foreign pilgrims. The traders of Naulakha Bazaar became stakeholders in the project, and the gurdwara was at last completed in 2004.

## The Setting

Ahmad Shah Abdali, the Afghan, made his first assault on Lahore in 1748. Jani Khan, with his brother Mir Mannu, defeated Ahmad Shah, who went back to Kabul, and after his going Mir Mannu ran the Punjab in his own way. In one modern reading of the governor's war, Mir Mannu was constantly pestered by the Sikh insurgent groups called *misls*, which had sprung up all over the Punjab; they did not control much land, but because of their politics against the status quo the lower rungs of society supported and protected them. In this reading he cast the battle between the state and the insurgents as a war between Muslims and Sikhs, even though there were several Muslims in the Sikh groups and many soldiers who were not Muslims in his own army.

Ahmad Shah had agreed terms under which the governor was to pay him an annual tax for the right of governing the Punjab. Before Ahmad Shah could reach Lahore, "the prize possession of Punjab", Mir Mannu met him at a place near the city of Gujrat. On a later raid, in 1751, the Afghan bypassed the governor and laid siege to the city: "For months the citizens were trapped within the walls of their city". After Mir Mannu's death, wherever a Sikh found the chance, he set himself up as a ruler. The upheaval left its mark on the Muslim scholars of the province too: Ghulam Murtaza Qasuri, worn down by the Sikh disorders in the Punjab, migrated to Peshawar.

One modern writer, looking at these years from the side of the Punjab's peasantry, wrote that "Marauding Sikh bands formed themselves into robber baronies and imposed their own system of extortion on the Punjab farmer", and that Abdali's treatment of the Punjab weakened the government in Lahore and delivered the various *doabs*, the lands between its rivers, into the hands of the Sikh confederacy. In the same writer's words, "As Bulleh Shah lay dying in 1758 at the age of 78, the rape of the Punjab was proceeding apace."

The poet himself left verses on the state of the province that his translators read as a witness to the times. One *kafi*, a Sufi devotional lyric, speaks of 'The twelfth century' that 'has come with gaping mouth', the twelfth century of the Hijri era, the Islamic calendar, which answers to the eighteenth century of the Common Era. It goes on:

*"The door of doom and torment has opened, and Panjab is in a bad state. It has been struck by fear of the pit of hell."* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

In another translation:

*"Now hell has opened its bogs. / Punjab has gone to the dogs. / This hell is the nethermost hell." … "This century cramps our style."* (translated by Taufiq Rafat)

As that translator explained, "The full bitterness of Bulleh Shah's 'Punjab has gone to the dogs' will only come through against this backdrop", a Punjab "being persistently rent by petty chiefs and marauders". Another of the poet's verses is taken to be an allusion to the Sikhs, "whose guerilla horsemen ultimately destroyed the Mughal authority in Panjab".

## Legacy

In Sikh historical consciousness the martyrdoms at Lahore under Mir Mannu occupy a place beside the sacrifices of the Gurus themselves, the founding teachers of the Sikh faith, and they are invoked daily in the *ardas*, which recalls "the Singhs and Singhnis who gave their heads but did not surrender their faith". Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj Singh Singhnian is the physical anchor of that memory in the city where it happened. For the study of the Punjab in the eighteenth century it testifies to the ferocity of the state's campaign against the early *Khalsa*; for the Sikh community it remains sacred ground.

The rebuilding had consequences beyond Naulakha. Afterwards "the Government of Pakistan woke up to the potential of Sikh pilgrimage tourism" and invited the Sikh community abroad "to invest in the renovation of any Sikh gurdwara in the country". The long quarrel also became a byword: at Sachkand, "a situation similar to Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj" was named as the outcome to be feared.

Description:
## Overview

The Gurdwara Singh Sabha in Quetta is the principal Sikh place of worship in the capital of Balochistan, serving a small community whose roots in the province run deep. Restored to the Sikhs only in 2020 after more than seven decades of other use, the *gurdwara* has become an emblem both of the long Sikh presence in Balochistan and of the community's patient struggle to recover its sacred places. It takes its name from the *Singh Sabha*, the reformist movement that shaped modern Sikh congregational life across the subcontinent.

## Sikhs in Balochistan

Sikhs have lived in Balochistan for a very long time — by some accounts for around three centuries — settling as traders and shopkeepers in Quetta and the towns of the province. Their numbers were once substantial: the census of 1941 recorded some twelve thousand Sikhs in the Baluchistan Agency, a little over one per cent of the population, with the largest concentration in the Quetta–Pishin district. The community's long roots were violently disrupted at the Partition of 1947, when, like the local Hindus, the Sikhs were attacked and largely forced to flee eastward, and their properties and places of worship passed into the charge of the Evacuee Trust Property Board. A tradition of the city, attached to the nearby Gurdwara Tilganji Sahib, even holds that Guru Nanak himself passed through Quetta during his travels, though such associations are matters of devotional memory rather than documented history.

## From Gurdwara to Girls' School

The Gurdwara Singh Sabha is said to be around two centuries old, dating to the early nineteenth century. After the departure of the Sikhs in 1947, the building was put to secular use, serving for decades as a government girls' high school run under the auspices of the All Pakistan Women's Association. For the Sikhs who remained or who later returned to Quetta, the *gurdwara* stood as a visible reminder of a heritage from which they had been separated, and its recovery became a long-cherished aim of the community.

## Restoration in 2020

After more than seventy years, the building was at last restored to the Sikh community in 2020, an event widely reported and warmly welcomed as the fulfilment of a decades-long wait. The return of the *gurdwara* allowed the *sangat*, the congregation, once more to install the *Guru Granth Sahib* and to hold worship in a historic house of the Gurus in the heart of Quetta. The restoration was seen as part of a broader, if halting, effort to return and rehabilitate Sikh and Hindu shrines across Pakistan.

## Legacy

For the roughly two thousand Sikh families of Balochistan, the Gurdwara Singh Sabha is more than a building: it is the recovered centre of their communal and religious life in the province, and a symbol of continuity across the rupture of Partition. Its restoration has affirmed the place of the Sikhs in the story of Quetta and offered a measure of hope to a minority community intent on preserving its faith and its heritage in the land where it has so long belonged.

## Bibliography

- *Dawn*, "73 years on, gurdwara restored to Sikhs in Quetta" (2020) and "A gurdwara worth the seven-decade wait".
- *Bolan Voice*, "Historical background of the Sikh community in Balochistan province".
- World Gurudwaras, entry on Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha, Quetta.
- Wikipedia, "Sikhism in Pakistan" (with cited sources).

Name: Gurdwara Sri Kiara Sahib
Events: Guru Nanak Gurpurab
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Sri Kiara Sahib stands amid the fields on the eastern side of Nankana Sahib, the town in the Punjab that was the birthplace of Guru Nanak Dev Ji, founder of the Sikh faith. Its name comes from the Punjabi *kiara*, a field or plot of cultivated ground, for the gurdwara marks the field where one of the best loved miracles of Guru Nanak's boyhood is said to have taken place. Set a little apart from the great shrines at the centre of the town, Kiara Sahib belongs to the landscape of sites in and around Nankana Sahib that together preserve the memory of the Guru's early years, and pilgrims come to it on the great anniversaries.

## The Miracle of the Field

The tradition of Kiara Sahib belongs to the cycle of *sakhis*, the accounts of Guru Nanak's life, that centre on his childhood at what was then the village of Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, later renamed Nankana Sahib in his honour. As a boy, the stories tell, Nanak was set to tend the family's cattle, and he would let the animals graze while he sat absorbed in meditation, heedless of the world about him. On one such day, it is said, the buffaloes strayed into a neighbour's standing crop, and the aggrieved peasant hurried to Rai Bular Bhatti, the local landlord, to complain that young Nanak's herd had ruined his field.

When the field was inspected, the story goes on, the crop was found whole and unharmed, as though nothing had touched it. The onlookers, it is told, took this for a miracle, and the plot was thereafter revered as *Kiara Sahib*, "the honoured field". Accounts of the episode differ in their details. For the Sikh tradition it is one of a series of signs by which Rai Bular, a Muslim landlord, came to recognise the extraordinary nature of the child in his village, and it is remembered less as a marvel of crops than as an early disclosure of the Guru's sanctity and of the divine favour that rested upon him.

Other signs are told of his childhood. In his childhood, it is said, signs of spiritual unveiling and of wonders beyond the ordinary course of things became manifest in him. The janamsakhis tell that the village astrologer, Pandit Hardyal, foretold the child's greatness, and that at school the boy showed a brilliance never before seen in any child in Talwandi.

In the janamsakhi telling, the landlord of the story belonged to the family that had rebuilt the village: Talwandi's last rebuilding took place under the supervision of Rai Bhoe, a Bhatti Rajput who had converted to Islam, and Rai Bhoe's son was Rai Bular. In the same telling, Shiv Ram, head of a Bedi family, was accountant to Rai Bhoe, and he was succeeded by his son Kalyan Chand Das Bedi, or Mehta Kalu as he was affectionately called, the Guru's father, who kept the accounts of the Bhatti family under Rai Bular.

The same stories return to the family in the Guru's later life. When Nanak came back to Talwandi with Mardana from the first of his journeys, they tell, Nanak spent time every day with Rai Bhoe, who looked upon him as his Guru, and Mehta Kalu was a little in awe of his son. On a later return, after Pak Pattan, they go on, Talwandi was no longer an obscure little village but had become a place of pilgrimage, and Nanak sat by Rai Bular, who was sick and dying.

## The Gurdwara

A shrine was raised in later times to mark the sacred field, and the present building is associated with the great works of gurdwara construction carried out in the decades before Partition. It was reconstructed in the years leading up to 1947 by Sant Gurmukh Singh, known by the epithet *Sevavale*, "the one devoted to service", for his lifelong labour of building and restoring Sikh shrines. The gurdwara is a square, domed sanctum set upon a raised plinth, with a verandah running round it for the circling of the shrine, in the characteristic idiom of Punjabi gurdwara architecture, and it stands amid open ground that still recalls the farming setting of the miracle.

Nankana Sahib has several gurdwaras marking events from the Guru's childhood. Of those associated with Guru Nanak, Kiara Sahib and Malji Sahib are the furthest from Gurdwara Janamsthan, the shrine of his birthplace. Across the Punjab, Maharaja Ranjit Singh, who became sovereign of the province at the end of the eighteenth century, spent large sums on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras, and he attached vast tracts of land to them so that the revenues from the land could support their running.

Since the Partition of 1947, when the Sikh population of west Punjab migrated to India, Kiara Sahib, like the other shrines of Nankana Sahib, has stood in a land with few resident worshippers, cared for by the bodies responsible for Sikh heritage in Pakistan, though accounts of the care of the town's gurdwaras in the years after Partition differ. Kartar, who spoke of the town's gurdwaras as his own, remembered those years: "There was no Sikh left here after partition. Our Gurdwaras became barren and were in a bad state." Giani Pratap, Kartar recalled, came with a pilgrimage party from India sometime in the 1960s, and when he saw the dilapidated condition of the shrines he decided to stay and look after these holy buildings. Most of the town's gurdwaras were kept locked all year round and opened only at the time of the festival, and security guards were employed at the entrance to all of them.

## Devotion and Festivals

Kiara Sahib is visited chiefly by pilgrims who cross the border on the great anniversaries. On the *Gurpurab* marking Guru Nanak's birth, and on other occasions when *jathas*, bands of pilgrims, travel to Nankana Sahib, the gurdwara receives the devotions of the faithful who come to walk the ground of the Guru's childhood. Because Nanak spent his early years in the town, it has several gurdwaras, and the pilgrims visit all of them.

The festival of the Guru's birthday, Guru Nanak Jayanti or Gurpurab, is kept at Nankana Sahib every November. Official estimates put the pilgrims who come for it at ten to fifteen thousand every year; in 2011, by media reports, only three thousand came, and that year the festival ran from the 8th to the 10th of November. Police stood at all the entrances to the city, no car was permitted inside, and devotees walked barefoot. For those few days the entire city looked like a little India.

The pilgrims from India came by train from Delhi, Gujarat and Amritsar and crossed at Wagah, where representatives of the Evacuee Trust Property Board and the Pakistan Sikh Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee received them and a *langar*, the free communal kitchen, was laid on. They stayed three days at Nankana. Three days of *Akhand Path*, the unbroken reading of the Sikh scripture, ended in the *bhog*, the rite that closes the reading, and the *Nagar Kirtan*, the procession singing hymns through the town, followed on the final day; then the pilgrims went on to other cities. Richer pilgrims from Britain, America and Canada came by chartered plane and hired buses, and travel companies' posters promised them "all" the gurdwaras in Pakistan.

Pilgrims from abroad kept the festival alive. Guru Nanak's birthday at Nankana Sahib was among the events that foreign pilgrims kept up after Partition, and Sikhs from abroad came to Pakistan for festivals such as Baisakhi and the birthday of Guru Nanak, which were attended by thousands of Indian pilgrims. Pilgrim tourists came to Nankana Sahib and to Hassan Abdal, and at Manora in Karachi, Jeeta Singh held a small festival of his own every November, when the festival of Guru Nanak was celebrated at Nankana Sahib.

The Sikhs who lived in the town were mostly newcomers: not natives of the city but recent migrants from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where there is a considerable Sikh population. Most of them were housed within the gurdwaras, in rooms generally reserved for pilgrims. The community numbered about two hundred households, and Jatha Singh had been its leader for several years.

## Nankana Sahib

Tradition tells that Talwandi lay between the rivers Ravi and Chenab, directly in the path of the armies that had set their eyes on Delhi, and that thirteen times the village was destroyed and thirteen times, like the fabled phoenix, it rose again from its ashes. It lay too, the same tradition tells, in the path of numerous mendicants, holy men and *sadhus*, as Hindu ascetics are called, who camped in a grove of trees on the outskirts of the village. Originally called Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, the town was renamed Nankana Sahib in honour of the first Sikh Guru, who was born there. It lies about forty miles south west of Lahore.

An old mound rests behind Gurdwara Janamsthan, away from the hub of the new settlement. It is held to be an archaeological mound: the settlement there was destroyed, after which Rai Bhoi di Talwandi was built within a boundary wall. The climb was steep, with no proper path, to a top at least twenty metres from the ground, covered with shrubs of *karir*, a thorny desert bush, with shards of broken pottery and other mud utensils underfoot. The young Nanak, it is said, used to spend a lot of time there in conversation with the yogis, *sadhus* and dervishes who passed through Talwandi. On his road back from Chuhrkhana, it is told, he crossed a vast jungle that lay then between Nankana and Chuhrkhana.

The modern town had one main road running through it; the buildings were old, most of them from the late British or the early Pakistan era, and the road had potholes. From a roof the minarets of mosques could be seen, with the small white domes of the gurdwaras and the remains of a few Hindu temples, cone like structures rising from houses abandoned at the time of Partition. In 2005 Nankana Sahib was separated from Sheikhupura and made a district of its own, with the city as its headquarters. It is considered one of the holiest cities in the world for the Sikhs, for the founder of their religion was born there.

Guru Nanak was celebrated all over the town, with a Guru Nanak High School, a Guru Nanak grocery store and a Guru Nanak cloth shop, all run by Sikhs. The regard for Nanak found among the Muslims at Gurdwara Sachkand was not found among the Muslims of Nankana Sahib: most of them, it is said, had migrated from the other side of the border after Partition, and their attitudes had been shaped by those experiences. At one of the shrines of Guru Nanak at Nankana Sahib, a picture of Baba Farid accompanied the picture of the Guru.

## The Guru

The gurdwara exists for the sake of Guru Nanak. The *janamsakhis*, the cycles of tales told of the life of the first Guru of the Sikhs, were written by his devotees after his death, and the earliest known of them dates from 1658, nearly 120 years after he died. Accounts of his birth differ in their details, but he is generally held to have been born at Talwandi in 1469, and he lived there in his grandfather's house. Tradition tells that his mother, Mata Tripta, would regularly visit an ancient Hindu temple on top of a mound not far from Rai Bhoi di Talwandi to pray for a child; accounts of how his birth came about differ.

In the janamsakhi telling, at thirteen Nanak refused the sacred thread, the *janeu*, in his father's courtyard, saying that "it is our actions and our actions alone" that give a man his position. At sixteen, the janamsakhis go on, he herded cattle, and he became well acquainted with the dervish Sayyad Hussain and gained an intimate knowledge of the Sufi line of thought. Legend tells that when he turned eighteen his father asked him to take up a trade and gave him twenty rupees, and that Nanak left the town with Bhai Mardana; so begins the story of the *Sacha Sauda*, the true bargain.

From Talwandi, in the janamsakhi telling, Nanak went to Sultanpur, around 60 kilometres away, as keeper of Nawab Daulat Khan's stores, and there, it is told, he vanished into the stream for a week and came out saying, "There is only one God. There is no Hindu, no Mussalman." He married Sulakhini, daughter of Mul Chand and Chando Rani of the town of Batala, on 24 September 1487, though accounts of the marriage differ, and they had two sons, Sri Chand, born on 8 September 1494, and Lakhmi Das, born on 12 February 1497.

Accounts of how many journeys he made differ, but his *udasis*, the Guru's journeys, are most often counted as four. In the tellings of his life they lasted more than twenty years and took him, mostly on foot, east to Bengal, south to Sri Lanka, north to Kashmir, Nepal and Tibet, and west to Mecca. Whenever he visited an area, it is said, he would visit its religious shrines, Muslim, Hindu and of any other denomination. When at last he settled at Kartarpur, the story goes, he sent to Talwandi for his family.

People are said to have come in multitudes from every land to become disciples of Baba Nanak, as the Guru was also known. In Aurangzeb's reign the place of Baba Nanak lay twelve *kos*, an old measure of distance, from Batala, on the bank of the Ravi, and his descendants lived there. Lakhmi Das, it was said, was a worthy son, but on his deathbed the Guru appointed not a son but his most loyal student as his spiritual successor: a Khatri named Lehna, to whom he gave the title of Guru Angad. His eldest son, Sri Chand, was not recognised as Guru by the mainstream Sikh community, and the Udasis follow his tradition. Guru Nanak died on 22 September 1539, though accounts of the date differ.

In Aurangzeb's reign his followers counted service of the traveller, of all who come and go, as the highest worship, and whoever arrived at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name was treated as a brother and a friend and served, even a stranger, a thief or a highwayman. It is believed that the tradition of the *langar* began with Guru Nanak. He lived as a householder, and he associated with people of the lower castes, calling them people of God. It is said that when his Hindu and Muslim companions asked him which religion to adopt, he told them to be true Muslims or honest Hindus: "That would be Nanak's religion."

He is tied to the Sufis too. Nanak is held to have been a spiritual follower of Baba Farid, and to have travelled to Pak Pattan, where he met the saint's spiritual descendants and collected his poetry. Farid's texts are revered among the Sikhs, for he is held to have influenced the founder of their religion. A Chishti Sabiri shaykh of the twentieth century described Guru Nanak, with Krishna, Rama, Sita and Lachman, as a believer in the one true God and a religious leader with a "Divine connection", *nisbat*.

Devotion to him reaches beyond the Sikhs. Nanak Panthis, Hindus who believe in the teachings of Guru Nanak but not in the Khalsa, the order of initiated Sikhs, keep portraits of Guru Nanak in their temples in Sindh and southern Punjab, along with Krishna, Kali Mata and other Hindu deities, and many Lohanas in Sindh follow his teachings; in Sindh, too, the iconography of Guru Nanak and that of Jhulelal have grown more and more alike. Many Muslims acquainted with his teachings are devoted to him too and visit his shrine. In the valley of the goddess Hinglaj, engraved footsteps held to be Guru Nanak's connect that temple to the Sikh and Nanak *panth*, or sect, traditions.

The field of Kiara Sahib is one miracle among many told of the Guru. Legend tells that Nanak once travelled to Mecca, where he performed the Hajj, and slept with his feet towards the Kaaba; rebuked, he turned his feet, and as he did so the Kaaba miraculously turned towards them. It is told, too, that a trader who told Nanak that his mules carried "Just some mud" found his sugar and *gur*, raw cane sugar, turned to mud, and that when he repented his mud became sugar and *gur* once again. Other legends tell of Nanak humbling a Muslim Sufi at Sialkot and at Pasrur. Yet Nanak himself is held to have abhorred the association of miracles with religious personalities, and in one story he tells Karori, who calls his cure a miracle, that "there is no such thing as a miracle".

## The Guru's Verse

The Guru's *bani*, his devotional verse, was compiled as part of the Adi Granth by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, in 1604. He composed verses in Hindi on the truth of God and on divine unity, and a singer named Mardana sang his verses and drew people into the snare of devotion. In Aurangzeb's reign the whole of his followers' worship was the reading of their master's verses, which they recited with song and melody. Like Kabir, Nanak used the *doha*, a rhyming couplet in an old Prakrit and Hindi metre, for his mystical poetry, and he brought into his verse several words that were not part of the Punjabi of his time. In the *Babur Bani* he lays the blame of Babur's wrath at God's feet.

Lines from his hymns, in English translation, give a sense of the poetry. His *aarti*, the hymn sung as lamps are waved in worship, begins:

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ
ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ …

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps*

On the oneness of God he sang:

ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥
ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One*

And again:

*God is One, / The Path is One*

His poem on the sacred thread runs:

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ
ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ …

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment*

Of washing he sang:

ਭਰੀਐ ਹਥੁ ਪੈਰੁ ਤਨੁ ਦੇਹ ॥
ਪਾਣੀ ਧੋਤੈ ਉਤਰਸੁ ਖੇਹ ॥

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white*

In one modern retelling of his life, Nanak sings to innkeepers who meant to rob him:

ਬਗਾ ਬਗੇ ਕਪੜੇ ਤੀਰਥ ਮੰਝਿ ਵਸੰਨਿੑ ॥

*The herons in their white feathers dwell in the sacred shrines of pilgrimage*

His verse is sung beyond the gurdwaras too. The singer Abida Parvin has said: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak." In Sindh, Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the *banis* of Shri Guru Nanak and the *kalams*, the poems, of the Sufis.

## Legacy

Kiara Sahib is one of the cluster of gurdwaras that make Nankana Sahib the holiest town of the Sikh world after Amritsar, each marking a remembered moment of the Guru's early life: his birth, his schooling, his play, and the miracles of his boyhood. The field of the untouched crop speaks to a theme dear to Sikh devotion: that the greatness of Guru Nanak was manifest from his earliest years, and that even a landlord of another faith was moved to acknowledge it. For the pilgrim, to stand at Kiara Sahib is to enter the pastoral world of the *sakhis*, where a boy lost in the remembrance of God let his cattle wander, and the very fields, it is told, bore witness to his sanctity.

Guru Nanak was born in the city now called Nankana Sahib and died in a small village called Kartarpur, both in present day Pakistan, and the gurdwaras built there later by his devotees still stand tall.

Name: Gurdwara Sri Tilganji Sahib
Events: Daily worship; Sikh anniversaries
Description:
Gurdwara Sri Tilganji Sahib stands on Masjid Road in the heart of Quetta, the capital of Balochistan. By Sikh tradition the site marks a visit by Guru Nanak, the first Guru, during one of his great journeys, or udasis: it is said that the Guru honoured the assembled sangat by distributing til — sesame seeds — as parshad, the sanctified offering, and that from this the shrine took its name, Tilganji deriving from til (sesame) and ganj (treasury or store). The gurdwara is a substantial domed building whose main gateway is said to resemble that of a mosque; within its precincts, in a pattern common to many gurdwaras in Pakistan after 1947, a government school — the Government Sandeman School — has long functioned, occupying land belonging to the shrine. Quetta was almost entirely destroyed in the catastrophic earthquake of 1935, so that the present fabric of the building, like much of the city, is unlikely to be of great antiquity, even if the sanctity of the site is older. The gurdwara is one of the principal Sikh shrines of the city and is to be distinguished from the Gurdwara Singh Sabha of Quetta, recorded separately in this dataset. Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey of Sikh shrines in Pakistan records that, in addition to the Sandeman School already functioning within the shrine's precincts, a new government school building had by then been constructed on vacant land belonging to the gurdwara, and that the Sangat of Quetta had filed suit in the lower courts seeking to recover possession of the property.

## Bibliography
- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Lahore: Punjabi History Board, 1998), p. 134.

Name: Gurdwara Tambo Sahib
Events: Guru Nanak Gurpurab
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Tambu Sahib, also written Tambo Sahib, stands in Nankana Sahib, a short distance east of Janam Asthan, the central shrine that marks the birthplace of Guru Nanak Dev Ji, founder of the Sikh faith. Its name comes from the Punjabi *tambu*, a tent, for the gurdwara grew up around a great *van* tree whose spreading, low hanging branches formed a natural canopy, a living tent, beneath which the young Nanak is remembered to have taken shelter. It is one of the cluster of shrines in and around the holy town that preserve, site by site, the episodes of the Guru's boyhood, and pilgrims tie pieces of cloth to the tree's branches as a supplication.

## The True Bargain

The tradition of Tambu Sahib is bound up with one of the most beloved of the *sakhis*, the stories of Guru Nanak's life: the *sacha sauda*, or "true bargain". Legend tells that when Nanak turned eighteen, his father, Mehta Kalu, anxious that his contemplative son should learn a trade, gave him twenty rupees and sent him to the market town of Chuharkana to buy goods and turn a profit, and that Nanak set out with Bhai Mardana. On the way, it is told, he met a company of hungry holy men, and judging that no bargain could be truer than the feeding of the poor and the servants of God, he spent the whole sum on food for them and turned for home empty handed but content.

Fearing his father's anger, the boy is said to have stopped short of the village and sat down beneath the great *van* tree, whose branches enclosed him like a tent, and there, the story goes, he stayed until his family found him and brought him home. The road back from Chuharkana to Nankana Sahib, then still known as Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, ran, it is told, across a vast jungle that lay at that time between the two. The tree stood outside the town. It is an ancient tree, spread out like a tent, and it still stands, held sacred by Sikh devotees.

The gurdwara raised on the spot preserves the memory of that refuge, and it is one of two gurdwaras that commemorate the episode. Another legend of Nankana Sahib, often confused with this one, tells of a tree's shadow that stood still while all others moved; it belongs to the nearby Gurdwara Mal Ji Sahib, not to this site.

## The Gurdwara

A shrine was established beside the tree during the period of Sikh rule in the Punjab, about a furlong east of Janam Asthan, and its architecture echoes that of the other gurdwaras of Nankana Sahib: a domed sanctum set within a square hall, decorated in the idiom of Sikh sacred building, though plainer in some of its detailing than its neighbours. It is a small building, yellow and of a single storey, with a white dome on top. It lies between Janam Asthan and the gurdwaras of Kiara Sahib and Mal Ji Sahib, close to Mal Ji Sahib and to the gurdwara of the fifth and sixth Gurus, so that the pilgrim moving among them traces a compact circuit of the Guru's early life.

The tree is protected by a boundary fence with a single gate, and shoes come off before entering. Behind the tree stands the gurdwara, with a board bearing its name, and the saffron *Nishan Sahib*, the Sikh flag on its tall pole, rises in the courtyard. Within the sanctum the *Guru Granth Sahib*, the Sikh scripture, is installed. Inside stands the *Thara Sahib*, a wooden pavilion that holds the scripture, and two swords lie there in sheaths of blue velvet.

The grounds are large. The area belonging to Tambu Sahib is the second largest in the town, big enough to host an international cricket match, making the gurdwara the town's second most popular destination after Janam Asthan. A tall wall with barbed wire ran round it on all sides, with one gate from the main market and a board by the road in English and in the Punjabi scripts Shahmukhi and Gurmukhi; a second, blue gate was kept permanently locked for security reasons. Vast land lay vacant on both sides of the shrine and was used for farming, with a tractor and a single storey building used by farmers.

Behind the gurdwara stand large hostels, used by Sikh pilgrims at the time of the largest Sikh festival in Pakistan, the birthday of Guru Nanak, celebrated every November. By the entrance stood a newly built residential hall of three storeys, with two larger residential buildings raised from devotees' donations and a Langar Hall of a single storey, which houses the *langar*, the free communal kitchen. Hostel blocks were built here with donations from pilgrims coming from Britain, Canada and America, and a large amount was given by Kar Seva, a non-profit organisation based in England; a yellow board on the Langar Hall read: "This newly constructed building has been made by Kar Seva". Next to the Langar Hall stood Shaheed Hall, a building of five storeys, recently completed and also built from Kar Seva's donations, whose roof was closed to pilgrims. The Government of Pakistan planned to build a Guru Nanak University near the complex, a persistent demand of the Sikh community abroad.

Like the other shrines of the town, the site is maintained by the authorities responsible for Sikh heritage in Pakistan. The gurdwara's vast property was allotted to it in the nineteenth century by Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the Sikh ruler who became sovereign of the Punjab at the end of the eighteenth century; across the province he spent large sums on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras and attached vast tracts of land to them, so that the revenues from the land could support their running.

That property was in the charge of Jatha Singh, who had appointed himself the gurdwara's caretaker. He received millions of rupees in donations from Sikhs living in the countries of the first world, to be spent on the betterment of the gurdwara and of the Sikh community of Nankana Sahib, which he had led for several years. He kept a room in one of the hostels, and on one visit he was found arbitrating between two feuding Muslim families, while his guests were served *langar* of vegetables and lentils.

One historical event began within the gurdwara's grounds. On 20 February 1921 unarmed Sikhs from other districts gathered at Tambu Sahib, accused the *mahant*, and after a short prayer resolved to walk to Janam Asthan. Behind the gathering lay the state of the Punjab's gurdwaras: as a result of sectarian divisions among the Sikh communities and the British takeover of the Punjab, a large number of important Sikh gurdwaras were being administered by Hindu *mahants*, heads of religious establishments.

## Devotion and Festivals

The tree is the heart of the devotion, and pilgrims tie pieces of cloth onto its branches as a supplication. In January 2011 the town's Sikhs kept Lohri at the gurdwara. Lohri, like Vaisakhi or Basant, is an ancient festival of the Punjab that marks the change of season, celebrated on the 13th of January. Kartar Singh Kartar tore a saffron cloth from inside the gurdwara, and each person tied a piece of it to the tree; his Muslim friends tied cloth too. Tying a cloth on the branches of this sacred tree, Kartar said, makes wishes come true, and at Guru Nanak's birthday people tie their cloths over one another's. Candles were lit at the base of the *Nishan Sahib*.

The prayer that followed was for Sikhs only, with the other three doors closed. Kartar prostrated himself before the *Thara Sahib* and offered a ten rupee note; the highest note among the offerings was one of fifty, and the donations were to be used for the renovation of the gurdwara. The room filled to about fifty people, as many men as women. A *Granthi*, a reader of the scripture, in his mid sixties read for half an hour; then came a community prayer with *Waheguru*, the Sikh name for God, and *Prasad*, the consecrated offering, of naan and a sweet made in *desi ghee*, clarified butter. Candles were held up in a circle around the *arti*, which carries lit incense, and people placed a hand on top of the fire and rubbed it on their faces. From there the procession went on to Janam Asthan.

Such celebrations, Kartar explained, were new: Lohri and Guru Gobind Singh's birthday had begun only in the last couple of years, made possible by the increase in the Sikh population through migration from the tribal areas, and earlier there had been only a prayer at the gurdwara. As one writer observed, it was ironical that a Punjabi tradition shunned by the Punjab was being revived by a group of Pathan men living in the Punjab.

At the birthday of Guru Nanak, known as Guru Nanak Jayanti or *Gurpurab*, the gurdwara fills. Official estimates put the people who come to Nankana Sahib for the festival at ten to fifteen thousand every year; in 2011, by media reports, only three thousand came, and that year it ran from the 8th to the 10th of November. Most of the town's gurdwaras were kept locked all year round, to be opened only at the time of the festival, and security guards were employed at the entrance to all of them. Tambu Sahib housed most of the pilgrims from the developed countries, and Shaheed Hall was their first choice, though as their numbers fell it came to house many Indian pilgrims. Security was lax compared with Janam Asthan: there were metal detectors and a few guards, but it was fairly easy to walk in unnoticed. Food was served around the clock.

In the parking area stood a book stall of the Dyal Singh Memorial Trust, a trust from before Partition based in Lahore, where Iqbal Qaiser, then fifty eight, sold his *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan*; this was the only time in the year his book sold, he said, somewhere between twenty and thirty copies. Police stood on the roofs of the Langar Hall and the residential buildings. Arshad Malik, a constable of thirty five with eighteen years in the police, on a duty of twelve hours since eight in the morning, said that the entire police force of the town had been deployed at the gurdwaras for the three days. He would not eat from the *langar*: "We are Muslims. We don't eat with the Sikhs or Hindus."

## Nankana Sahib

Nankana Sahib was once the village of Talwandi, about forty miles south west of Lahore. Originally called Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, it was renamed Nankana Sahib in honour of Guru Nanak, the first Sikh Guru, who was born there, and his early years there account for several of the town's gurdwaras. It is considered one of the holiest cities in the world for the Sikhs.

Tradition tells that Talwandi lay between the rivers Ravi and Chenab, directly in the path of the armies that had set their eyes on Delhi, and that thirteen times the village was destroyed and thirteen times, like the fabled phoenix, it rose again from its ashes; its last rebirth, the story goes, took place under Rai Bhoi, who had converted to Islam. It lay too, the same tradition tells, in the path of numerous mendicants, *sadhus*, or Hindu ascetics, and holy men, who camped in a grove of trees on the outskirts of the village.

Behind Janam Asthan rises an old mound. The settlement there, it is said, was destroyed, after which Rai Bhoi di Talwandi was built within a boundary wall. It is believed that in the six or seven years between the *sacha sauda* and his move to Sultanpur, Nanak began to frequent this place, talking with the yogis, *sadhus* and dervishes who passed through.

After Partition the town's gurdwaras stood empty. As Kartar remembered it: "There was no Sikh left here after partition. Our Gurdwaras became barren and were in a bad state." Giani Pratap, seeing the dilapidated condition of the shrines, decided to stay and look after these holy buildings. In the early twenty first century the town's Sikh houses grew in about ten years from only about thirty or forty to about two hundred. Most of these Sikhs were not natives of the city but recent migrants from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where there is a considerable Sikh population, and most of the newcomers were housed within the gurdwaras, in rooms generally reserved for pilgrims.

## The Guru

The gurdwara exists for the sake of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh religion. His story is kept in the *janamsakhis*, the cycles of tales told of the life of the first Guru of the Sikhs. Accounts of his birth differ in their details, but he is generally held to have been born at Talwandi in 1469. His father was Kalyan Chand Das Bedi, or Mehta Kalu as he was affectionately called, who in the janamsakhi telling kept the accounts of the Bhatti family under Rai Bular. In his childhood, it is said, signs of spiritual unveiling, of miracles and of wonders beyond the ordinary became manifest in him.

In the janamsakhi telling, at thirteen Nanak refused the sacred thread, the *janeu*. At sixteen, the telling goes on, he herded cattle, and he became well acquainted with the dervish Sayyad Hussain and gained an intimate knowledge of the Sufi line of thought. After the *sacha sauda*, it is told, he moved to Sultanpur, around 60 kilometres from Talwandi, as keeper of Nawab Daulat Khan's stores. Guru Nanak died on 22 September 1539, though accounts of the date differ.

He brought a message of peace and harmony to the followers of Islam and of Hinduism, religions hostile to each other, and taught that all men and women were equal, irrespective of caste, creed, wealth, social standing and gender, and that a good life rested on honest labour, compassion, selfless service and prayer. In Aurangzeb's reign his followers counted the service of those who come and go as the greatest worship, and whoever arrived at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name was treated as a brother and a friend and served, even a stranger, a thief or a highwayman. It is believed that the tradition of the *langar* began with Guru Nanak. He is held to have disavowed the miraculous and to have abhorred the association of miracles with religious figures; yet, as one writer has put it, "his biography is nothing but a story of his miracles".

He is tied to the Sufis too, and devotion to him reaches beyond the Sikhs. Many Muslims acquainted with his teachings are devoted to him and visit his shrine. Guru Nanak is held to have been a spiritual follower of Baba Farid, and Farid's texts are revered among the Sikhs because, it is said, he influenced the founder of their religion. At one of the shrines of Guru Nanak at Nankana Sahib, a picture of Baba Farid accompanies the picture of the Guru. A Chishti Sabiri shaykh of the twentieth century described Guru Nanak, with Krishna, Rama, Sita and Lachman, as a believer in the one true God and a religious leader with a "Divine connection", *nisbat*. At the shrine of the goddess Hinglaj there are engraved footsteps held to be Guru Nanak's.

## The Guru's Verse

The Guru's *bani*, his devotional verses of supplication, entreaty, humility and reverence, was compiled as part of the Adi Granth by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, in 1604. He composed verses in Hindi on the truth of God and on divine unity, and a minstrel named Mardana sang the Guru's verses and drew people into the snare of devotion. In Aurangzeb's reign the worship of his followers centred on reading their master's verses, which they recited in song and melody. Among his poems, fitting for a gurdwara that remembers a bargain, is one that opens "O my merchant friend".

Lines from his hymns, in English translation, give a sense of the poetry. His hymn of praise, the *aarti*, begins:

ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ
ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ …

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps*

On the oneness of God he sang:

ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥
ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ਭਾਈ ਏਕੋ ਹੈ ॥

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One*

And again:

*God is One, / The Path is One*

His poem on the sacred thread runs:

ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ
ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ …

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment*

Of washing he sang:

ਭਰੀਐ ਹਥੁ ਪੈਰੁ ਤਨੁ ਦੇਹ ॥
ਪਾਣੀ ਧੋਤੈ ਉਤਰਸੁ ਖੇਹ ॥

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white*

His verse is sung beyond the gurdwaras too. The singer Abida Parvin has said: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak." In Sindh, Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the *banis* of Shri Guru Nanak and the *kalams*, the poems, of the Sufis.

## Legacy

Since Partition in 1947 Tambu Sahib, with the other shrines of the town, has been visited chiefly by pilgrim *jathas*, bands of pilgrims, who travel from India and the diaspora for the great anniversaries, above all the *Gurpurab* of Guru Nanak's birth, when the town fills with the faithful. The tent tree of Tambu Sahib carries a lesson dear to the Sikh conscience, that the truest use of wealth is the service of others, the principle of *sacha sauda*; and the site endures as a gentle monument to the boy who thought the feeding of the hungry the best of all bargains.

Tambu Sahib is thus two things at once: a sacred tree that pilgrims and townspeople, Sikh and Muslim, hang with cloth, and, with its grounds the second largest in the town, the second most popular destination after Janam Asthan, where the pilgrims of the Sikh diaspora sleep and the halls their donations built now stand.

Name: Guru Gurpat Mandir (DB-80 Sirey Ghat)
Location: DB-80 Sirey Ghat, Hyderabad, Sindh, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: 1931 (present darbar building); Baba Gurpat Sahib active in Hyderabad c. 1830-1877
Events: Community worship; langar-adjacent hospitality
Description:
## Overview

On a plot known as DB-80 in the Sirey Ghat quarter of Hyderabad, Sindh, stands the Guru Gurpat Mandir, also called the Darbar of Baba Gurpat Sahib. It is a *darbar*, or shrine, of the Nanakpanthis, who follow the Nanakpanth, the path of Guru Nanak, and it is registered with Pakistan's Evacuee Trust Property Board as a functional *mandir*, or temple. It is built around a Sant, a holy man, revered as a descendant of Guru Nanak in the twelfth generation, in the Jagiasi lineage. Unlike many of the small shrines of Sants in upper and central Sindh, of which little is known, the darbar keeps an unusually detailed memory of its founder's life and of its own founding, preserved by the trust that cares for it today.

## The Sant

The darbar's tradition holds that Gurpat Sahib was born in the Punjab into the Jagiasi lineage of Nanakpanthi Sants, the spiritual descendants of Guru Nanak through the Udasi line of Baba Sri Chand, and that he travelled to Sindh in the early nineteenth century. He is said to have settled first at Khairpur, in the reign of the Talpur ruler Mir Murad Ali Khan, carrying letters of introduction and support from the Sikh court of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, and to have moved on to Hyderabad around 1830.

He is said to have brought relics with him and enshrined them, including hair said to be from Baba Sri Chand, a rupee of the Nanak Shahi era, and a ring attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru of the Sikhs. These objects are still spoken of at the darbar today. In the course of his ministry he is credited with founding several Jagiasi *tikanas*, or seats, beyond Hyderabad, among them at Khairpur, Halani and Kandyaro. He died in 1877, at the age of about seventy.

## The Darbar

By the community's reckoning, the present building at DB-80, Sirey Ghat dates from the year 1988 of the Vikram Samvat, a Hindu calendar era, which is 1931 in the Gregorian calendar. It stands on a plot of some 595 square yards. Today it is kept as a registered charitable trust, and its trusteeship in former times is remembered under Bao Santokdas.

Besides its hall of worship, the darbar today runs a modest vegetarian eatery and has space where pilgrims can stay, and the names of its donors are inscribed on tiles. In this it carries on a hospitality akin to the *langar*, the free communal kitchen, that has long been associated with the shrines of Nanakpanthi and Sikh Sants across Sindh.

The Guru Gurpat Mandir belongs to a wider constellation of small Jagiasi and Nanakpanthi shrines scattered across the belt of Sindh between Dadu and Hyderabad. The same milieu produced the darbars of Sant Baba Bhagat Ram, Bhai Sant Thawan Das and Gurdas Ram, all of them likewise registered with the Evacuee Trust Property Board. With a named founder, a dated building and a preserved lineage, it is one of the better documented sites in this cluster, though little of its history can be traced beyond the memory of its own community.

## The Path of Nanak in Sindh

In nineteenth century Sindh the Nanakpanth was probably the dominant religious path among the Hindu Sindhis. The Lohanas and related mercantile groups followed two main cults, the Nanakpanth and the Daryapanth, which is based on the deification of the Indus River, and in Sindh many Nanakpanthis belonged to a subgroup known as the Udasis. Guru Nanak himself, tradition holds, visited Uch Sharif on his way to Sindh, towards the end of his travels.

There is no settled view of whether the followers of Nanak in Sindh are Hindus or Sikhs. Many Lohanas in Sindh follow the teachings of Nanak, which somewhat obscured their religious affiliation for the colonial officers: in the census of 1881 the Lohanas of Shikarpur and Hyderabad were counted as Sikhs, and ten years later, in that of 1891, as Hindus. As an outcome of the Singh Sabha, a movement of Sikh reform, the Sindhi Nanakpanthis were not included in the Sikh community, and they identified themselves as a Hindu religious sect. The communities who refused the Khalsa, the order of initiated Sikhs, and called themselves followers of Guru Nanak still exist in Sindh and in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Baptised Sikhs look down upon them, and at Manora they were seen merging into the larger groups of Sikhs.

The Nanak Panthis, as they are also called, belong to the south of the Punjab and to Sindh, where their temples hold portraits of Guru Nanak alongside Hindu deities, and they are found in very large numbers in Sindh. Today many middle and upper class Hindus in Sindh are followers of the Nanak *panth*, and it is common to cover one's head before walking into a *tikana*, the temple that holds the Guru Granth Sahib, the holy book.

With the spread of the Nanakpanth in Sindh, the Hindu Sufis, Hindus who followed the Sufi path, were very familiar with Sikh terminology, and in Sindh neither the Sufis nor the Nanakpanthis had a central organisation ruling an encompassing body of followers. The Sufi poets Shah Abdul Latif and Sachal have been described as late participants in the Bhakti movement, the movement of loving devotion to God, which had a major impact in Sindh through the spread of Guru Nanak's teaching.

## The Darbars of Sindh

The word by which this site is also known has a history of its own in the province. In Sindh the Persian word mostly used was *darbar*, a term used by Sikhs, Muslims and Hindus alike, and the *darbar* was the sacred territory in which the Sufi culture was at work. British colonisation, it has been argued, brought a renewal of religious life, tied to the spread of a composite middle class and marked by the emergence of the *darbars*, which spread a *darbar* culture.

The Nanakpanthi *darbars* belong to that story. Some had been founded in the late eighteenth century, but the second half of the nineteenth saw a renaissance of the Nanakpanthi *darbars*, and the religious recomposition that Sindh went through in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries showed itself in the building of many new Nanakpanthi *darbars* all over the province.

After Partition the *darbars* of Sindh were for the most part preserved, with different arrangements for their management, often with Indian *gaddi nashins*, the holders of the seat, or followers paying the keepers; and despite the changing diplomatic relations between Pakistan and India, it was always possible to travel across the border. The *darbars* that the migrants founded in India are not centred on tombs, unlike those of Sindh. In the early twenty first century government funding was seen in a wave of restorations of temples across Sindh.

## Hyderabad

Hyderabad was the Talpur capital, the capital of independent Sindh before the British conquest. One Hindu holy man of the city, Dalpat Sufi, founded an *astano*, a place of residence for a renunciant, on the Sipahimalani Lane. He is said to have attracted many followers, Muslims and Hindus, and the Talpur mirs, the rulers of Sindh, are said to have looked after it. After his death it became a centre of pilgrimage under his successor, Keshavram Sipahimalani, and was known as Guru Sehwani's place. Dalpat Sufi seems to have stayed in a place in Hyderabad that can be called a *darbar*. The Sipahimalanis were a well known family of Amils, the Hindu scribal class, of Hyderabad.

Several Hindu Sufis came from the city. Hiranand Advani was born in Hyderabad in a family of Khudabadi Amils, and Molchand Kripalani was born there in 1887 in a Krishnaite family, devoted to Krishna. Mulchand studied up to class 6 at the Hiranand Academy in Hyderabad, and in 1901, aged 22, Rochaldas married and settled in the city to enrol as a student at its medical college. The Amils of Hyderabad played a part in the spread of the Sufi culture, although the devotional centres of Sindh may have shifted north after the British conquest. Annie Besant, known in Sindh as Basanti Devi, delivered a number of lectures in Hyderabad, where her speech was about the Hindu religion, and a printing house founded in Hyderabad was named Blavatsky Printing.

The city has its Sufi shrines. Tando Jahaniyya in Hyderabad was one of three Sufi traditions among the Hindu Sufis. Qutub Ali Shah was a famous Sufi from Hyderabad, and his *dargah*, his shrine, is in Jahaniyya, a neighbourhood of the city; its *sajjada nashin*, the hereditary custodian, came from Pakistan twice, in 1957 and in 1980, to perform the *dastarbandi*, the ceremony of tying the turban, for two Hindu Sufis. One community of musicians takes as its *pir*, its spiritual guide, Qutb Din Darya, whose shrine is called Tando Jahana and stands in the Civil Lines at Hyderabad. Shah Abdul Latif was born in Hala, near present day Hyderabad, and Jhok is not far from the city.

Hyderabad is a centre of Sindhi devotional music on the air. The singer Taj Mastani left Sehwan for the city because it is a large urban centre, and there she could earn a living from the radio. In places such as Hyderabad and Faisalabad local recording companies have helped women musicians earn a living by recording their Sufi lyrics with music, and at Radio Pakistan Hyderabad its director, Sikander Baloch, and its music director, Naseer Mirza, said that they no longer had to go to the *melas*, the fairs, at the Sufi shrines to hunt for talent. The city has two *gharanas*, schools of classical music, the Indore *gharana* and the Gawalior *gharana*, and the singer Zeena Bai is buried in the Hyderabad graveyard where all the great musicians of the city are buried. The Institute of Sindhology in Hyderabad is a source for the documentation of Sindhi Sufi music.

The city is also a place of Sindhi publishing. The Shah Waliullah Academy in Hyderabad, under the presidency of Maulana Ghulam Mustafa Qasimi, has published a number of Waliullah's works and studies of him. The Sindhi Adabi Board of Hyderabad published five volumes between 1960 and 1962, and Lilaram Watanmal's biography of Shah Abdul Latif was published in Hyderabad in 1889. From the 1960s the Sindhi newspaper *Daily Ibrat*, published in Hyderabad, reported the *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of a saint's death, at Sehwan in great detail.

Pilgrims from Hyderabad travel to the temple of the goddess Hinglaj at *mīlād-al-nabī*, the Prophet's birthday, and *ʿāśūrah*, the tenth of Muharram, and at *ʿīd*, the Muslim festival, and in *muḥarram*. On 28 March 2014 a temple in Hyderabad was attacked. A railway line once connected Hyderabad to Barmer and Jodhpur.

## Sindh

In 1843, with the Talpurs in power, the Baluchis stood at the top of the society of Sindh. Muslims were divided between Sunnis and Shiites; the Sunnis were in the majority, but the sovereigns, the Talpurs, were themselves Shiites. Among the Hindus, the Lohanas made up half of the total Hindu population and were divided into Amils and Bhaibands, and the *panchayat*, the community council, prevailed among the Hindus of Sindh. Under Talpur rule, from 1783 to 1843, the Amils almost monopolised the office of *kardar*, the local revenue officer. The *hurr*, the disciples of the Pir Pagaro, gathered first to support Ahmad Brelwi's struggle against the Sikhs, from 1829 to 1831, and later actively joined in the struggle against the British. After 1857 many Kayasht, a caste of Hindu scribes, migrated to work in the princely states, the Khairpur emirate in Sindh among them.

The Sindhi language continued to flourish after the British occupation in 1843. Sindh had always been proud of its mystical heritage: it is told that when Nadir Shah invaded in 1739, the minister Diwan Gidumal gave him the most precious treasure Sindh had to offer, some of the dust of its saints. British policy, especially in the Punjab and Sindh, was to treat the hereditary saints in essentially the same way as landlords and tribal leaders were treated. The integration of Sufism into the religious life of the Hindu Sindhis has been dated to the nineteenth century, its main actors being the Amils, the literary class. In the religious life of Sindh, the devotional relationship of a follower with a spiritual master prevailed over affiliation to an institutional religion.

By early November 1947, 246,000 Hindus had already left Sindh by sea, air or rail, and by 1 January 1948 nearly 500,000 people were estimated to have sought refuge in India; estimates of how many left in all differ, from around a million to 800,000 or fewer. The departure of the Hindu elite and the influx of Muslim refugees from India, the Muhajirs, dramatically altered the local demography. K. R. Malkani, a Sindhi in exile, was a Hindu who left Hyderabad after Partition and settled in New Delhi. After Partition, too, Molchand worried that it was difficult for the Hindu Sindhi Sufis to visit the Sufi places of Sindh, now in Pakistan. The common notion that the religions of Sindh lived in harmony has been called a nationalist utopian ideal: communal violence in Sindh never reached the level of the Punjab's, but it was not absent, though the Sufi culture, it has been argued, still pervades Sindhi society.

Although a large majority of its Hindus have migrated to India since 1947, Sindh is the province of Pakistan with the most significant Hindu population, home to the majority of Pakistan's Hindus. The majority of the Hindu community lives in Sindh and the south of the Punjab, with a proportionate representation of the lower and the upper castes. Pakistan's Hindus are put at between 6 and 10 million, an estimate that varies widely; in Sindh they number several millions, most of them belonging to the scheduled castes, and by the census of 1998 the Hindus were the country's largest minority. It is often claimed that there was no caste system in Sindh. Sindh may have had a social fabric of its own, which colonial rule renewed, but the claim is contested: it is bound up with Sindhi nationalist discourse, which Dalit organisations, speaking for the castes once held untouchable, oppose. In the early twenty first century the formula *Sab ka malik ek hai*, all have one master, was very popular among the Hindus of Sindh.

Under the emperor Aurangzeb, the Mughal province of Thatta ran in length from Bhakkar to Kach Makran. Its greatest river was the Indus, by which merchants from Multan and Bhakkar shipped their goods to Thatta, and most of its traffic went by boat.

Alan Faqir recited a line of song that he read as a statement about Sindh:

*Punnu is not in the Kec / Sind is not the amir*

Its second half means that Sindh is not in the position of leadership, or amirship. Of his land he said that it has been looted, plundered and assaulted, and yet it goes on: it has not died, it will not die, it has existed for centuries and it shall exist; Sindhri, the name the poetic traditions give to Sindh, is beaten, and yet Sindhri goes on.
