Name: Langer Makhdoom
Events: Annual urs (16-18 March); Friday gatherings at the tomb
Description:
## Overview

Langar Makhdoom is a village of Chiniot District in the Punjab that takes its name from the Sufi saint to whom its shrine is dedicated, Makhdoom Burhan-ud-din, remembered locally as Hazrat Langar Makhdoom. His shrine is a modest but venerable one of the medieval centuries, traditionally dated to the thirteenth century, and it belongs to the great movement of Sufi settlement that carried Islam into the Punjab countryside. The village's very name keeps the memory of the *langar*, the free communal kitchen that has always stood at the heart of the Sufi hospice, and the shrine remains a focus of local devotion, with gatherings at the tomb on Fridays and the saint's yearly festival in spring.

The village, on the river Chenab, is also remembered as a seat of Sufi teaching: the house of another master, Makhdum Abdul Karim, whose name it once carried as well.

## The Saint

Tradition holds that Makhdoom Burhan-ud-din lived and taught in this corner of the Chiniot region, and that he died in 1245. In his humility, it is said, he asked to be buried in the simple mud dwelling that had been his home, and his grave is said to lie in a burial ground near the village of Changranwala, in the Lalian area of the district. He is not the Burhan al-Din Gharib who lived a century later and far from the Punjab, moving to Daulatabad in 1329, dying in 1337 and lying buried at Khuldabad in the northern Deccan.

In the devotion of the region he belongs to the first generation of Muslim holy men who made their homes among the villages of the central Punjab in the thirteenth century, and his traditional dates place him firmly within that formative era. It was the age of the great Chishti master Farid al-Din Ganj-i-Shakar of nearby Pakpattan, Baba Farid, whose ancestors had come from Kabul and settled in the Punjab in the middle of the twelfth century. In that age, it is held, the teaching and example of the Sufis, rather than the sword of conquerors, drew much of the rural population of the Punjab towards Islam, though there is no settled view of how far Baba Farid himself converted anyone, or of how quickly, and how consciously, the change came. A number of Punjabi tribes still claim to have been converted by Baba Farid, and most of the Jat and Rajput groups that became Muslim in the medieval period credit either him or his contemporary, Baha' al-Haqq Zakariya.

In the invocation that opens his *Hir and Ranjha*, the poet Waris Shah praised Farid, whom he calls Shakarganj, for making his home at Pakpattan:

*"When Shakarganj made his abode at Pakpattan, the Punjab was delivered of all its troubles."* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

## The Shrine and Its Devotion

A mosque bearing the saint's name, the Masjid Burhan-ud-din, stands in his memory. By tradition his devotees gather at his tomb every Friday, the day of congregational prayer, to offer the *fatiha*, the opening chapter of the Qur'an, and to seek the saint's intercession.

His *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of a saint's death, kept in Sufi practice as a joyful "wedding" of the soul with the divine, is observed each spring, traditionally from the sixteenth to the eighteenth of March, and it draws the surrounding countryside to the village.

The name that the saint and his village share is itself telling. Langar Makhdoom means the *langar* of the Makhdoom, a title of honour for a Sufi master. The *langar*, the kitchen where food is cooked and served freely to all who come, whatever their rank or creed, is one of the most characteristic institutions of the Sufi lodge in South Asia, an enactment in daily bread of the ideals of hospitality, charity and the equality of all before God. That the saint should be remembered by this name suggests the reputation for open-handed generosity that clung to his hospice, and it links his memory to the tradition of feeding the poor that Sufi shrines across the Punjab and Sindh keep alive to this day.

## A House of Teaching

The village has another Makhdum in its history. It was the home of Hazrat Makhdum Abdul Karim, remembered as a perfect gnostic, one who knows God, and its name was once written with his, as Langar Makhdum Abdul Karim Sahib.

Shaikh Muhammad Ismail became Abdul Karim's pupil at the age of five, and it was from this master, his enlightened *pir*, or spiritual guide, that he received the *khirqa* of *khilafat*, the cloak by which a master makes a disciple his deputy, in the *Suhrawardiyya*, the Sufi order founded by Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi. In the fourteenth century that order spread from Uch to Gujarat, the Punjab and Kashmir.

Mian Wadda's mother moved with him to Langar Makhdoom, and there he studied with Makhdum Abdul Karim, his *murshid*, or spiritual master. He was first given a task; it is told that a miracle brought that service to an end, and afterwards he was set to study and to cooking for the household. Later, it is said, he was seen carrying the milk vessels and told that he had become a perfect *wali*, a friend of God. It is not settled whether Mian Wadda and Shaikh Muhammad Ismail are one man.

In Mian Wadda's chain of masters, two generations above Abdul Karim, stands a Hazrat Makhdum Burhan al-Din, who bears the saint's name. Nor is it settled whether he is the saint of the shrine.

## The Setting

The village stands on the river Chenab, which in the folk culture of the Punjab is known as the river of love, a river that calls to mind Sohni and Mahiwal and the Takht Hazara of Ranjha.

The town of Chiniot appears in the wars of the Langah sultans of Multan. Sultan Husain, son of Qutb al-Din, took Chiniot from Malik Manjhi Khokhar, the agent of Sayyid Khan. When the army of Barbak Shah was beaten, it fled as far as the town of Chiniot, and Sultan Husain's agent at Chiniot was seized after the battle and sent to the house of nothingness, that is, put to death.

Chiniot is known for its woodwork, and a fine example of it was the *haveli*, or great mansion, of Omar Hayat, completed in 1935. To those who lived in it, it was a cursed house, which claimed the life first of the father, then of the son, and then of his mother; the mother and the son are buried in its main hall. After Partition the haveli fell into disrepair and its top two floors crashed down. More recently the government of Pakistan took it over and renovated it to serve as a museum and a library.

## Legacy

Langar Makhdoom is not among the grand shrines of the Punjab. Yet in this it is representative of a whole class of country shrines whose collective importance is very great: the resting places of the humble Sufi teachers who, village by village, wove Islam into the fabric of Punjabi rural life. Islam took root much more readily in the Punjab, as in Bengal, than in upper India, and in the Punjab and Sind the shrines of great Sufis drew pastoral clans that were not yet farmers, and not Muslim, into their ritual, social, economic and political orbits. The successors of Baba Farid, like those of other shrines in the Punjab, still write *taʿwidh*, written amulets, for ordinary people, a practice that has not changed from the thirteenth century to the present.

The shrine's endurance across some eight centuries of tradition, its Friday gatherings and its spring *ʿurs*, testify to the tenacity of local devotion and to the way a single holy man's memory can give a village its name and its identity. The village is remembered, too, as a seat of teaching: the house of Makhdum Abdul Karim, where Mian Wadda served and studied, and from whom Shaikh Muhammad Ismail received his *khilafat* in the Suhrawardiyya.

## Bibliography

- Kanhaiya Lal Hindi, *Tarikh-e Lahore* (1884 original).

Name: Loh Temple (Lava Temple)
Location: Lahore Fort (near Alamgiri Gate), Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Sufi Saint: Lava (Luv), son of Rama and Sita
Events: Recently restored and reopened to visitors; no congregational worship
Description:
## Overview

Wedged into the narrow space between the western wall of Lahore Fort and the eastern wall of Hazuri Bagh, close to the Alamgiri Gate, stands one of Lahore's most storied yet architecturally modest religious survivals: the Loh, or Lava, Temple. According to Hindu tradition, Lahore takes its name from Lava, also rendered Luv, a twin son of Lord Rama and Sita in the *Ramayana*, the Hindu epic of Rama. Lava is said to have founded the city, known in Sanskrit as Lavapuri, the "City of Lava", while his brother Kusha is traditionally credited with founding nearby Kasur.

Despite this ancient legendary association, the surviving building is not itself ancient: historians date it to the early nineteenth century, likely built during or shortly after Maharaja Ranjit Singh's conquest of Lahore Fort in 1799. It is thus a commemorative shrine of the Sikh period to an ancient legend. Long neglected, the temple was restored between 2024 and 2026 and reopened to the public on 27 January 2026, although it does not currently host regular congregational worship.

## Lava, Son of Rama

The temple's whole meaning rests on a founding legend. In the tradition the temple keeps, Lava, or Luv, is a twin son of Lord Rama and Sita and the founder of Lahore, which bore the Sanskrit name Lavapuri, the "City of Lava"; his twin brother Kusha, or Kush, is credited with founding Kasur. The twins, the story goes, were born to Sita at the *ashram*, or hermitage, of Valmiki, after she had been banished by Rama. Lahore and Kasur are said to be named after them.

The brothers have a second place in Lahore's living Hindu memory. A portico painting at Neela Gumbad, in Lahore, shows Valmiki teaching his two pupils, Luv and Kush, beside the River Parsuni, the old name of the Ravi, which flows next to Lahore.

By the reign of Aurangzeb, the founding of Lahore, an ancient city on the banks of the Ravi, was attributed to Lo, son of Raja Ram Chand. In the nineteenth century the founder of the city was named Lohu, a son of Raja Ramchandar. Not every account of the city's name agrees, and the name has also been derived in other ways; the tradition the temple embodies is that of Lava.

The name of Lava also travels far beyond Lahore. Among Sindhis a story of the origins of a caste is told in which Rama's son, called Lava, gave his name to the Lohana community, the name Lohana ultimately developing from his.

## The Temple

The surviving temple is a modest building. It is a simple hexagonal brick structure of interconnected chambers around an inner sanctum, historically topped by a dome that has since been lost. It contains no surviving Ramayana carvings or frescoes, consistent with its comparatively late construction. The Walled City of Lahore Authority, which now manages the site, calls it "the temple of Raja Loh", a cluster of interconnected chambers open to the sky, housing a memorial shrine.

There is a belief that the original temple here was built by Luv himself. Accounts of the age of the present building differ; historians date it to the early nineteenth century, likely during or shortly after Ranjit Singh's conquest of Lahore Fort in 1799.

The uncertainty is old. Visiting in 2018, a journalist found the temple, not yet restored, littered with an empty water bottle and marked by graffiti. Neither of the two historians she consulted could say who built it, when, what it once housed, or whether it was ever used for worship at all, questions about which, she concluded, "we can only speculate".

The temple is not to be confused with another building of the Fort that bore the name of a *mandir*, or temple. Ranjit Singh renamed the Fort's Moti Masjid, the Pearl Mosque, the Moti Mandir and kept the treasury of the state there, and in the 1880s the British government kept the treasury of the Punjab in the same building.

For much of the twentieth century the temple stood neglected and largely inaccessible within the Fort precincts. Between 2024 and 2026 it underwent careful restoration by the Walled City of Lahore Authority in partnership with the Aga Khan Cultural Service, Pakistan, funded by the United States Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation, alongside related monuments of the Sikh period nearby. It reopened to the public on 27 January 2026. It does not currently host regular congregational worship in the manner of Lahore's active *mandirs*.

## The Setting

Lahore fell into ruin over long ages, so that little trace of it was left, and the seat of government of the region passed to Sialkot. After Sultan Mahmud's conquest, Malik Ayaz rebuilt the city and built a *pakka*, or solidly built, fort. Akbar built a strong fort, a city wall and a palace, and Jahangir raised the lofty building that still stood in Aurangzeb's reign. In the 1870s the Fort held twenty-nine relics, kept in a separate building.

The Fort was also the scene of a small literary moment at court. On Akbar's second visit to Kashmir, in the thirty-seventh year of his reign, which set out from Lahore in the rains, the emperor, at the crossing of the Ravi below the Fort of Lahore, asked about whom this verse had been written:

کلاه خسروی و تاج شاہی
بہر گل کی رسد حاشا و کلا

The Fort was besieged more than once. In Shihab al-Din Ghuri's fifth campaign, Khusraw Malik, unable to hold out, shut himself up in the Fort of Lahore. In Akbar's reign Muhammad Hakim Mirza besieged the Fort for twenty-two days while Raja Bhagwant Das, governor (*subadar*) of Lahore, held it firm. Under Jahangir, the governor Dilawar Khan strengthened the Fort against the rebel prince Khusrau, and however hard the prince tried, the Fort did not fall to him. In the Sikh period the killers of Maharaja Sher Singh met their end after the siege of the Fort of Lahore and a great battle. In the nineteenth century a building facing the throne on the south side of the Fort, in which a grave had been built, was called by common people the Nigar Khana, the picture house.

The temple's likely date ties it to Ranjit Singh's taking of Lahore in 1799. When Lahna Singh, then ruling the city, began destroying the monuments of former kings, the elders of the city invited Ranjit Singh to come to Lahore and take possession of it, and in 1799 he was greeted enthusiastically by a population sick of the lawlessness of that time.

The Alamgiri Gate, beside which the temple stands, takes its name from the imperial title of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, and the domes of the Badshahi Masjid face it. Between the Alamgiri Gate and the Royal Mosque is the Roshani Gate, one of the thirteen gateways that lead into the ancient walled city, once reserved for the prince and the princess, who would go from the Fort to the city through it. The gate also carries Sikh memory: Guru Arjan's torture took place outside the Alamgiri Gate. The Ravi, which once flowed next to the Fort, has changed its course, moving a few kilometres away, and the Fort, once an emblem of power and wealth, is now a tourist destination, where visitors can tour even the private chambers of the Emperor Jahangir.

The temple's quiet sits within a harder history of Lahore's Hindu places. After 6 December 1992, Sitla Mandir at Shah Alami, the Jain Mandir at Anarkali and Bhadra Kali Mandir at Thokar Niaz Baig, all in Lahore, were among the prominent temples attacked, and functional temples such as Krishna Mandir on the Ravi Road and Valmiki Mandir at Neela Gumbad were burned down. The Valmiki temple at Neela Gumbad serves a small community of Balmiki Hindus in Lahore, numbering only a few hundred, most of whom are Christians on record.

## Legacy

The Loh Temple's reopening on 27 January 2026 drew renewed attention in both Pakistani and Indian media to a rare, tangible link between Lahore's Hindu mythological heritage and its physical urban fabric. The Walled City of Lahore Authority frames the restoration as part of a wider effort to show the Fort's heritage across cultures, its Sikh and Hindu temples, Mughal mosques and buildings of the British period standing alongside one another.

The legend the temple commemorates is older and wider than the building. Across three centuries of writing on Lahore, in Persian, in Urdu and in English, the city's founder appears again and again as Rama's son, under the names Lo, Lohu, Luv and Lava. The small hexagonal building by the Alamgiri Gate is where that story is given a place in stone.

Name: Mausoleum of Waris Shah
Location: Jandiala Sher Khan, Sheikhupura District, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: Annual urs; Heer recitation and qawwali
Description:
## Overview

At Jandiala Sher Khan, in the Sheikhupura district of the Punjab, stands the mausoleum of Waris Shah, who lived from about 1722 to about 1798: the Sufi poet who gave the Punjab its national epic. His *Heer*, the great verse romance of Heer and Ranjha, completed in 1766, is at once the supreme achievement of Punjabi poetry and a profound Sufi allegory of the soul's love for God, and it has been sung, wept over and quoted across the Punjab for two and a half centuries. His tomb is honoured both as the shrine of a saint and as the resting place of the poet whom Punjabis revere as the "Shakespeare of the Punjabi language", and it draws the devout and the lovers of Punjabi letters alike.

The romance he told has been elaborated in more than a hundred versions, in Punjabi, Urdu, Sindhi and Persian, and it was Waris Shah who gave it its final form. By the early 2000s, whenever the legend of Heer and Ranjha was mentioned, it was mainly his text that was meant.

## The Poet Saint

Waris Shah was born around 1722 into a Sayyid family, descendants of the Prophet Muhammad, at Jandiala Sher Khan; accounts of his dates differ. He received a thorough religious and literary education, studying at Kasur, and like other Sufi poets he was well read in Persian and Arabic literature. He belonged in spirit to the Chishti Sufi tradition, the order prominent in South Asia, and traced his discipleship to the line of the saint Makhdoom of Kasur, though accounts of his allegiance and of his teacher differ. Bulleh Shah was his older contemporary, who also took up the tale of Heer and Ranjha in Punjabi, and the two are said to have studied religion together under the same teacher.

Little of his life is recorded with certainty, and much is woven from legend. Tradition holds that the poem grew out of, and transcended, an unfulfilled love of his own. One line of the poem calls on a woman directly:

*Bhag Bhari, help me to meet my Ranjha.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

The line has been read as addressed to the woman with whom the poet fell in love, though Bhag Bhari need not have been her real name.

He lived through the anarchic eighteenth century, between the collapse of Mughal power and the rise of the Sikhs, and his poem bears witness to the disorder of his age. Its Epilogue describes the troubles of the latter half of that century, which marked the decline of the Mughal Empire in India and was a period of great confusion and disturbance. The Punjab had often been the battleground of invading forces from the North, and the invader rides through the poem's similes: "as if armies from Kandahar had swept over the Punjab", and "today the Punjab has fallen into the hands of Kandaharis". The second line is probably a reference to the invasion of Ahmad Shah Abdali, whose capital was Kandahar and who, in 1748, began a series of invasions of India through the Punjab.

In the Epilogue he turns to Kasur, the town where he had studied:

*Of all the wretched Punjab I am most concerned for Kasur. I am concerned for my faith and conscience even as Moses was frightened on Holy Sinai.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

When the poem was done, he writes, "Having finished the story I presented it to my master for his acceptance." In his own voice he claims the help of Shakarganj, Baba Farid of Pakpattan: "With the aid of Shakarganj", he writes, "I have conferred this benefit on the world". He died around 1798 and was buried at his native Jandiala Sher Khan.

## Heer

Waris Shah's fame rests on a single work of genius. Taking up the old Punjabi love legend of Heer, daughter of the Sials, and Ranjha, the herdsman who becomes a *jogi*, a wandering ascetic, for her sake, he retold it in some hundreds of stanzas of matchless Punjabi verse. He completed it in 1766, a year he gives in the poem as 1180 of the Hijri calendar; accounts of the date differ. There is no settled view of where he wrote it, though tradition holds that he composed it while living at a village called Malka Hans, in a small chamber beside a mosque. In his own words, "When love came to me I felt a desire to write this story in verse."

On its surface it is a tragic romance; beneath, it is a Sufi allegory in which the human lover's longing is the soul's longing for God, and the pain of separation the very engine of the spiritual path. Its opening lines set love at the foundation of the world:

اوّل حمد خُدا دا ورد کیجے،
عشق کیتا سُو جگ دا مُول میاں

*First, let us utter the praise of God, who made love the very origin of the world.*

The poet tells how the poem came to be written. Near its opening he records a request:

*My friends came to me and said, 'Write for us afresh the forgotten story of the Love of Hir.' So we have written it right cunningly and plucked a new rose in the Garden of Poetry.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

At the end he reports the task done: "By the Grace of God I have fulfilled the request of my dear friends." The poem's devotional frame is an invocation of Baba Farid of Pakpattan, and one line of it runs:

*When Shakarganj made his abode at Pakpattan, the Punjab was delivered of all its troubles.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

In the Invocation he also speaks of Mohiuddin Abdul Qadir Gilani, founder of the Qadiri order of Sufis, as one who can score out even the writing of the Pen of Destiny. In the Punjab countryside it was a popular belief that Pirs, Fakirs and Jogis could by the force of their piety "make the Moving Finger of Destiny cancel what it has written".

The story was old when Waris Shah took it up. The legend of Heer and Ranjha existed for a long time before him and was probably sung in the folk traditions for several centuries. It is set in the world of the Jat pastoral tribes of western Punjab, and his is the version that tells the whole story of how Ranjha leaves his family home in search of Heer. When he rewrote it in the eighteenth century the legend became his, and today it is also called Waris Shah's Heer.

Heer belonged to the family of the powerful Sial Jats of Jhang, landowners of the Punjab. The Jats of the Punjab were *zamindars*, landowners, known for practising widow marriage, and the Sial tribe was one of the few tribes in the Punjab that allowed women to inherit property under customary law. The Kheras, a powerful clan of landowners, have their place in the tale too. In his telling the Five Pirs, five saints, intervene miraculously on Ranjha's behalf.

He wrote in the *bait*, the stanza of four lines adopted in Punjabi Sufi poetry, the form Sultan Bahu also used in his *Abiat*. In the talk of his women he uses *nī*, an intimate term of the feminine gender with which women in Punjabi address one another.

Along the way the poem becomes an encyclopaedia of Punjabi life in the eighteenth century, its trades and customs, its proverbs, its landscape and its faith, so that to know *Heer* is to know the Punjab. Its world is the village of the old Punjab, where Ranjha was a well known caste of the Jats, and the poem's dawn at the mosque was how a morning began in a Punjab village. Spinning parties, *tarinjan* or *bhora*, were a famous institution of the village, and a spinning wheel, the *charkha*, used to be the inseparable companion of every woman, old or young, in the rural Punjab. Old houses in the countryside had a big courtyard with living rooms and bedrooms round it, and brothers living with their parents as a joint family was quite common. Sawan and Bhadon were the two rainy months of the year; the Gujars, a famous tribe, kept animals and sold their milk; and the *turrah*, the tuft of the turban, was beloved of the rural aristocracy.

Judging by their names, some of Heer's girl friends are Hindus, and in the village of the old Punjab the community as a whole was regarded as one social unit irrespective of caste or creed. It was by no means unusual for a Muslim family to depend on Hindu Brahmans for fixing a marriage. The arrival of Heer's *baarat*, the bridegroom's wedding procession, is told in a line of the poem that runs "Jevein log nigahein te raatan thaman dhol marde te rang lawande ne". After the *mangni*, or betrothal, a girl did not see her fiancé until marriage, and a traditional Punjab marriage kept the symbolism of marriage by capture. Brides wore coloured garments, while white clothes, by tradition, were worn by widows, particularly among the Hindus; the *arsi* was one of a bride's favourite ornaments, and *dandasa* was the equivalent of lipstick in the rural Punjab. *Gur*, raw sugar, was well known as a ceremonial offering in the countryside, and jugglers with their bears were a familiar sight.

A vow of thanksgiving in the poem reads:

*Oh poet Waris Shah! If I hear that my lover is returning, I will offer sweet cakes and light my lamps with rich butter for oil.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

Lighting lamps in a mosque, even with ordinary oil, was a well known way of expressing gratitude to God for His favours, and Punjabi mothers promised to light lamps in mosques when they prayed for their children.

## The Poet in His Poem

The poet writes himself into his story. Like most Persian and Urdu poets who wrote verse romances, he makes a personal appearance whenever it pleases him, and even enters into conversation with his characters. He breaks in as a named commentator: "Quoth the poet: 'This is not a boat but a marriage procession.'" He comments, "See what a net of deceit Hir, the Jat girl, has spread". Other asides follow: "Ask Waris the poet, he knows this well."; "Waris, if you trust in God, he will give you your portion of the good things of this world."; and, of the *qazis*, the judges of Islamic law, "Qazis have no fear of God and eat the bread of iniquity". Two more of his asides:

*(Poet Waris: 'None can withstand when eyes fight eyes in the tourney of love.')* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

*Waris, I shall be called the Hir of Ranjha in Heaven, in the assembly of Fatima, the daughter of the Holy Prophet.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

His name even enters a curse: "May the curse of the Poet Waris Shah fall upon you, Hir, for you have robbed us of our dear brother-in-law." And Luddan the ferryman speaks of him: "Even the son of a Pir like Waris", he declares, "we will not take into our boat for nothing".

The poet makes large claims for his work, and repeats them:

*Poets, you should determine the worth of any poem. I have let my horse loose in the arena. Other poets have wasted their efforts in writing on petty themes. I have composed a grand poem.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

Only the poet's poetry, he writes, remains in everlasting remembrance, "for no one has written such a beautiful Hir". Of himself and the Kheras he says: "There are none so fortunate as the Kheras, no one so full of sin as the Poet Waris and there is no spell like that of his poetry." He tells himself, "Waris Shah, your name will be famous, if God be kind.", and he adds at the close that "Waris Shah has shed the light of his genius over all the faithful in the world." Beside the boast stands the penitent:

*I have no capital of good works. Of what can I be proud? I have no hope without Thy grace. I am only a poor sinner. Without the favour of the Prophet I am helpless.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

He closes asking pardon, "God, overlook the fault of poor Waris Shah", and "If I have let fall a word in ignorance may God forgive me."

It is the poet himself who declares that the poem has an inner sense:

*Oh wise man, you should note that there is a secret under the guise of my words. I have written this Hir with care and meditation… I have planted a flower to give a sweet savour.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

At its close he says, "I have written it as a parable.", and of its readers: "The story of true lovers is like the scent of a rose in a garden. He who reads it with love in his heart will be able to separate the true from the false." Of himself he writes, "Waris Shah is anxious to see God's face even as Hir longed for her lover."

He used the story as a vehicle for mystical thought and interspersed it with mystical explanations. Since the tale was known to everybody, he has his heroes recite short verses, which are commonly interpreted in a mystical sense. The spiritual reading of the tale is traced to the poet Shah Hussain, whose theme was subsequently taken up by Bulleh Shah and Waris Shah.

An allegorical key to the romance, twenty two lines long, carries the mystical interpretation given by Waris Shah. In it, "Our soul is the tragic heroine" Heer, and the key goes on:

*Our body is the lover Ranjha, / Our spiritual preceptor is the Yogi Balmath,*

Further down the key reads:

*The secret chamber is the grave, / Saida Khera is the angel of death.*

*Reason is the flute / that to us the music of Divine wisdom conveys.*

His signature line runs:

*Warith Shah says: Those alone cross over / who have silently prayed to the Lord, / and ever devotedly recited His glorious Name.*

One of the characteristics of Sindhi and Punjabi poetry is that the longing soul is always depicted as a woman, and the tragic heroines of the folk tales of both provinces, Heer, Sassui, Sohni and many others, represent the human soul in search of the beloved.

## The Shrine and the Song

Waris Shah's mausoleum at Jandiala Sher Khan is a place of pilgrimage for the devout and of homage for the lovers of Punjabi letters, and it has been developed over the years into a dignified complex befitting the poet's stature. Devotees recite the *Fatiha*, the opening chapter of the Quran recited as a prayer, and seek blessing; singers come to perform *Heer* and *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis; and the *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, gathers crowds who honour the poet saint with music and remembrance. The shrine stands as a monument not only to a holy man but to the Punjabi language itself.

The poem was made to be heard. Waris Shah composed it as an epic poem to be sung to music in public, and he is said to have recited it with great emotion among the people who shared his speech in the Punjab. He names three kinds of people who will carry it on, those who copy it, those who recite it and those who read it: "May he who reads or copies my poor efforts derive pleasure", he writes, and:

*May God pardon him who copies these words and give his bounty to those who recite it. May its readers enjoy the book.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

The tale was sung in the Punjab before him. In Aurangzeb's reign the people of the Punjab composed wonderful verses and designs on the love of Heer and Ranjha and sang them.

A historian of Lahore called the tale the story that was on the tongue of good and bad, small and great, rich and poor in the land of the Punjab. By the 1970s a visitor who stayed in a Punjabi village would certainly find somebody to sing the old romance of Heer and Ranjha in the classical form given it by Waris Shah, and a Punjabi would be deeply touched when the story was sung. By the early 1980s his verse was sung, time and again, wherever Punjabis met. For centuries the tale has been sung and dramatised.

Generations of Punjabis have known long passages of *Heer* by heart, and its verses are sung by professional singers of *Heer* in a distinctive traditional style. The poem is invoked in joy and in grief alike, most famously by the modern poet Amrita Pritam, who at the Partition cried out to Waris Shah himself to rise and witness the suffering of the Punjab.

By the early 2000s there was substantial recorded material of his *Heer*, on audiocassettes and videos, sung in the folk traditions, and many renowned folk artists of the Punjab had sung it, among them Reshma, Zahida Parvin, Nazir Begum, Sabiha Khanum, Tufail Niazi and Iqbal Bahu. Heer's lament as she is carried off in her palanquin is traditionally sung at almost every Punjabi wedding at the time of the bride's departure to her husband's home.

The song is not welcome everywhere. In many villages, it has been said, the recitation of Waris Shah's *Heer* is not allowed, for people believe that if the sounds of the verses fall on the ears of young girls, they too will elope like Heer. At another shrine, that of Sahari Mal, a young man put on Waris Shah's *Heer* on his mobile phone while a group of men was playing cards in a corner.

## The Setting

Rani Jindan was first sent to the fort of Sheikhupura, and then to the fort of Chunar Garh. The Ghazi Pir is buried at the foot of the hillock near Shah Kot in the Sheikhupura district, and the people of five districts, Sheikhupura among them, congregated annually at his shrine. Before the new road, Sikh pilgrims had to travel to Sheikhupura and then head towards Chuhrkhana.

## Legacy

Waris Shah occupies a place in Punjabi culture that few poets hold in any language: his *Heer* is the canonical classic of the tongue, memorised, sung and quoted by millions, and revered as scripture is revered. Through it he wove together the Sufi vision of divine love, the folk romance of the Punjab and the living speech of its people, and he made a single poem into a mirror of a whole civilisation.

The closing section of one of Bulleh Shah's lyrics is hardly intelligible without close familiarity with the story as *Heer* tells it. Punjabi poets and their eager audiences poured into Heer and Ranjha the same erotic emotion that was invested in Radha and Krishna in regions closer to the Ganges, and the story of Heer and Ranjha became a favourite Sufi device for conveying the value of erotic passion in spiritual life.

He is counted with Baba Farid and Bulleh Shah among those who spread the message of peace and brought several religious communities together instead of shedding blood. Yet the poetry of Baba Farid, Guru Nanak, Shah Hussain, Waris Shah and Bulleh Shah is also what the educated elite of the Punjab ends up disowning, and even ridiculing. His tomb at Jandiala Sher Khan keeps the memory of the saint who was also the supreme poet of the Punjab.

## Bibliography

- Waris Shah, *Heer* (1766; verse quoted in standard published wording).
- General established histories of Punjabi literature.
- Waris Shah, *The Adventures of Hir and Ranjha*, recounted in Panjabi by Waris Shah and translated into English by Charles Frederick Usborne (1874–1919), with a later unnamed annotator's numbered notes (2004 edition).
- Bullhe Shah; Christopher Shackle (tr.), *Sufi Lyrics* (Murty Classical Library of India, Volume 1; Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 2015; new edition 2021).
- Taufiq Rafat (tr.), *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, with an introduction by Khaled Ahmad (Lahore: Vanguard Publications Ltd., 1982).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Pain and Grace: A Study of Two Mystical Writers of Eighteenth-Century Muslim India* (1976 (1997 edition)).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *As Through a Veil: Mystical Poetry in Islam* (New York: Columbia University Press, 1982; Lectures on the History of Religions, New Series 12).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* (Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina Press, 1975; 35th Anniversary Edition, with a new Foreword by Carl W. Ernst, 2011).

Name: Mazar of Bulleh Shah
Location: Mazar of Bulleh Shah, Kasur, Punjab
Events: Annual urs; kafi singing through the night
Description:
## Overview

The shrine of Hazrat Bulleh Shah stands in the heart of Kasur, south of Lahore, over the grave of Sayyid Abdullah Shah Qadiri, the towering Punjabi Sufi poet whose *kafis*, short sung lyrics, are among the most loved verses ever composed in the language. Heir to the tradition of Shah Hussain and forerunner of Waris Shah, Bulleh Shah wrote verse that scorned the hypocrisy of the learned, dissolved the boundaries of caste and creed, and sang of a love for God that overturns the self. Pilgrims and lovers of his poetry come to his tomb alike, and his songs are sung there by the shrine's own *qawwals*, the singers of Sufi devotional music, as they are by folk singers and pop musicians across South Asia.

By the 1870s the tomb was a place of pilgrimage for the people, and his Punjabi verses and *kafis* on *tauhid*, the oneness of God, were sung by *qawwals* in the gatherings of the *faqirs*, the wandering Sufis. Still more than his tomb, his poetry is a living presence, and Kasur itself is known above all as the place where he lies.

## The Saint

Bulleh Shah was born around 1680 into a respected family of Sayyids, descendants of the Prophet Muhammad. His given name was Abdullah Shah: Bullha is the familiar form of Abdullah, and Bulleh Shah the honorific form proper to a Sayyid, the name by which he is known. He is generally said to have been born at Uch Gilanian, the city of saints in Bahawalpur, though neither the year nor the place of his birth is known for certain, and the family is said to descend from Abdul Qadir Gilani, the founder of the Qadiri order of Sufis.

His father, Sayyid Darvesh Sakhi Muhammad, was a learned and pious man, an imam and a teacher. Accounts of the family's moves differ, but most say that it settled in the Kasur region of the Punjab when the boy was six, and there he received a strictly orthodox religious training. His first teacher was his father, and he became well educated in Arabic and Persian and in the religious sciences. At Kasur he is most often said to have studied under Hafiz Ghulam Murtaza, a scholar for whose learning the town was famed, and tradition holds that this teacher trained two rebellious pupils, Bulleh Shah and the poet Waris Shah.

He might have become a scholar of the orthodox kind, but he was drawn instead to the burning inward path. Having finished with the outward sciences, he longed for the inward ones, which cannot be had without a perfect guide, and he gave himself to the search for one. Accounts differ over how he found his master. It is told that, asleep under a tree, he saw Sayyid Abd al-Hakim, his ancestor five generations back, seated on a throne that flew through the air. The throne came down and the elder asked who he was, and he answered that he was a Sayyid. When they met, the elder asked for water and was given milk; he drank a little of the bowl and returned the rest, and when the young man drank it he was carried out of himself and his breast was filled with light. On parting, the elder said that he had held something in trust for him and had that day handed it over, assigned him ten rupees a day, and ordered him to seek a *murshid*, a perfect spiritual guide.

His father gladly gave him leave to go to Shah Inayat Qadiri, and gave him some rupees and a *dastar*, a turban, to present to the master. Shah Inayat was a Sufi master of Lahore of the Qadiri and Shattari line, and an Arain, of a caste of gardeners and cultivators, rather than a Sayyid of high birth. Bulleh Shah was initiated at his hand in Lahore, taking *bai'at*, the oath by which a disciple pledges himself to his *pir*, his spiritual guide, and was afterwards given the robe of a *khalifa*, a deputy who carries on the master's line. Accounts of his own order differ; he is most often counted a Qadiri, a follower of the order of his master.

That a proud Sayyid should bow to a master of humbler caste scandalised his relations, and the tension became one of the great themes of his verse and of the stories told of his life. In one poem his sisters and his brothers' wives reproach him: "stop clinging to the Arain's skirt. Why have you brought disgrace on the family of the Prophet and the descendants of Ali?" He answers them:

*May anyone who calls us a Sayyid suffer the punishments of hell. / Swings are set up in paradise for anyone who calls us an Arain.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

In another translation of the same scene, the women of the household tell him that "it's a sin to condemn the prophet's kin", and he replies:

*Does sanctity deserve such scorn? / It's God's carelessness where one is born. … / My caste? I've none. I'm just a man.* (translated by Taufiq Rafat)

Elsewhere he asks: "What ecstatic being is here who is so drenched in oneness for caste he has no care?" Love, not lineage, he defiantly proclaimed, was the only nobility. From Shah Inayat he received the word, the *kalma*, of his Sufi teaching. After a time in his master's service he settled on the bank of the Chenab, given to worship and spiritual exertion, and then made his home at Kasur once more, teaching, instructing and preaching. He had a great love of *sama*, the Sufi practice of listening to music, knew the art of music well and was a poet too. Aware of the Qadiri custom of *sama* and devotional dance, he took up the *sarangi*, the stringed instrument associated with the wandering dervish, and began to sing and dance. He loved his master with a rapturous love, and "love" was the word he used for what he felt towards his teacher. By the 1870s he was remembered as Shah Inayat's *khalifa*, living in the small town of Kasur, with *sama* and *wajd*, ecstasy, his practice day and night, and marvels often coming from him unbidden. Bulleh Shah remained unmarried and left no direct descendants.

His times were violent. He lived through the turbulent decades of the Mughal decline, a time of great social upheaval in the Punjab, when the authority of the declining Mughal empire was challenged by armed Sikh rebellion and by local notables, and they were hard times for the Qadiri order. When the last great Mughal ruler, Aurangzeb, died in 1707, Bulleh Shah was 27 years old. Sikh bands under Banda Bairagi, who lived from 1670 to 1716, laid waste the whole province except Lahore and Kasur, and he lived to see the second and third invasions of the Punjab by Ahmad Shah Abdali, in 1748 and 1752. When plunder became routine in the Punjab, he had no choice of factions, and he died, it is said, a disenchanted man. Like Shah Abdul Latif in Sind and Shah Waliullah, Mir Dard and Mazhar Janjanan in Delhi, he was a witness of an epoch of great political disasters, and like these mystics he found peace in the inner world of love and surrender, singing his mystical songs to console himself and his friends.

These unsettled conditions are only occasionally reflected in his poetry, whose main focus is his spiritual guide. He never directly criticised the rulers, though he appears to have been deeply bruised by the upheavals in the Punjab. One *kafi* speaks of the century itself, the twelfth of the Hijri era, which corresponds to the eighteenth century of the Common Era:

*The twelfth century has come with gaping mouth. / The door of doom and torment has opened, and Panjab is in a bad state. / It has been struck by fear of the pit of hell.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

He died at Kasur. Accounts of the year of his death differ; the year his tomb keeps is 1171 of the Hijri calendar, which corresponds to 1757 or 1758. The tomb gives it in a Persian chronogram, a phrase or verse whose letters, read as numbers, yield the date. Tradition holds that the orthodox at first refused him burial in the common graveyard, so fierce had been his attacks on their hypocrisy, and that his body lay out in the sun while the mullahs disputed his right to be buried there.

## The Poetry

Bulleh Shah's fame rests on his *kafis*, short sung Punjabi lyrics of astonishing directness and power. The *kafi* is the primary genre of Sufi poetry in Punjabi. It is designed for singing in *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, and also lends itself to solo singing by devotees and professional performers. Its final verse is regularly marked by the poet's signature, his own name. In his *kafis* he mocks the empty learning of the mullah and the pandit, tramples the divisions of Hindu and Muslim, high and low, and insists that the seeker must lose the self entirely in the Beloved.

His most famous *kafi* asks the question at the heart of all mysticism, who am I, and answers by refusing every label of religion and identity:

بُلھیا! کی جاݨاں میں کوݨ
نہ میں مومن وِچ مسیتاں، نہ میں وِچ کُفر دِیاں ریتاں

*Bulleh! What do I know of who I am? / I am not the believer in the mosque, nor am I in the ways of unbelief.*

The poem has attained the status of a proverb. Its speaker is "neither an Arab nor from Lahore, nor an Indian from the city of Nagaur". The earliest heterodox tradition he took in was that of the Persian mystic poet Rumi, who lived from 1207 to 1273, and this *kafi* is often said to be modelled on Rumi's great Persian ghazal that begins: "What can I do, oh Muslims, for I do not know myself. I am not a Christian nor a Jew, not a Zoroastrian nor a Muslim."

The refusal of labels comes again and again:

*I am not a Hindu, nor a Muslim. I have forsaken pride and become unsullied. / I am not a Sunni, nor a Shia. I have adopted the path of peace toward all.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

"Bullha is not a Shia or a Sunni, neither a learned scholar nor a magician or philosopher." He sets aside, too, the ranks of caste and the rules of purity:

*I am not twice-born, nor am I thrice-born. / I do not recognize pure and impure.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

Elsewhere he turns on dry scholarship with a cry that has become proverbial, insisting that a single letter of love outweighs a library of knowledge:

عِلموں بس کریں او یار

*Enough of learning, my friend / Only one letter 'A' is all you need* (translated by Naveed Alam)

The same quarrel with the schoolroom runs through his portraits of himself. In one poem he is the pupil who cannot get past *alif*, the first letter of the alphabet:

*The mullah taught me the lesson, but I could not get beyond alif. / I suffered a beating with his slippers* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

It is said of him, as of the Turkish folk poet Yunus Emre and of Shah Abdul Latif, that he was illiterate and knew only the *alif*. He calls himself a *faqir*: "Bullhe Shah is a fakir of the lord; he disturbs those who are awake", and "Bullhe Shah is a poor fakir; he has departed, proclaiming to the sound of the drum". He takes up the image of the mystic as a dog before God: "Dogs are awake at night, dogs are superior to you".

His verse fuses the imagery of Punjabi village life, the spinning wheel, the beloved's lane and the tale of Heer and Ranjha, with the boldest mystical claims, and this union of the homely and the sublime has kept it alive on the tongues of the Punjab for nearly three centuries. He wrote in traditional forms, among them the *siharfi*, or Golden Alphabet, a poem whose verses run through the letters of the alphabet, and the *baramah*, which follows the lovers' feelings through the twelve months. He used the whole mystical vocabulary and imagery inherited from classical times, but joined it to the rural imagery of his homeland, so that it could be understood by every villager and ploughman and sung by the large crowds who would flock to the shrines of the saints. Like all the folk poets, he defended the unity of Being, the doctrine of Ibn Arabi.

The spinning wheel, the *charkha*, is the basic metaphor of the poems. The life of a rural woman was permanently linked to it, since whatever she spun would become part of her dowry, and the monologue he built on it is "unsurpassed in Indian poetry in its sustained anatomy of a physical object". The spinning theme in the Sindhi poetry of Shah Abdul Latif has been compared with his. The romance of Heer and Ranjha, which Shah Hussain had already read as a spiritual tale, served him, as it served his own younger contemporary Hashim Shah of Amritsar and Waris Shah, for mystical meditation.

Much of the poetry is spoken in a woman's voice: "I, Bullha, am the slave girl of the lord"; "Ranjha is a yogi and I am his yogini"; "I'm just a sweepress". His *kafis* on Hindu themes are written in Hindi, the characteristic language of the yogis, and one *kafi* is a ghazal in fairly standard Urdu. With the Sindhi poet Sachal Sarmast, he is one of the poets who so frequently invoked the ecstatic cry *anā 'l-ḥaqq*, "I am the Truth". Besides being the leading poet of Punjabi Sufism, he also composed a number of Persian prose treatises.

He is the poet most often quoted in Punjabi conversation, the call of his own name, Bullha, fitting easily into common speech; so easily that people often pass off lines of their own as his by adding his name. The line "Bullhya, hor wi neenva ho", for one, is a popular fabrication, and there have been attempts to put verses of the Bektashis, a Turkish Sufi order, into Punjabi and declare them to be his. "Teray Ishq nachaya" is among the most popular of his *kafis* today. One *kafi* is known above all by the second verse of its refrain, ending in the syllables *thaia thaia*, which teachers of dancing use to mark the rhythm of the steps.

There is no settled count of the poems that are truly his. His lyrics, like those of the other Sufi poets of the Punjab, were never kept by an organised community of the faithful, and most were written down and gathered into printed collections only in the late nineteenth century, among them one printed at Lahore in 1889 and another at Kasur in 1896. Faqir Muhammad Faqir's edition of his poems, published at Lahore in 1960, holds 156 *kafis*, besides *siharfis*, *baramahs* and other verse.

## The Shrine

Bulleh Shah's *mazar*, the tomb of a saint, stands in the heart of Kasur. Once, by tradition, a grave the orthodox had shunned, it is today a revered shrine, and in an age that has rediscovered him it has become a place of pilgrimage not only for the pious but for musicians, students and admirers of Punjabi letters. The way to it ran through extremely narrow streets, where large carriages drawn by horses, the *tangas*, passed. The tomb bears a Persian chronogram that gives the year of his death.

By the early 1980s the tomb stood in a concrete courtyard, where the afternoon sun beat down on the barefoot votaries, as if exacting penance from them for a distant injustice to the poet. The cemetery where, by tradition, he had been refused burial was mostly in ruins, encroached upon by a fast growing town. The tomb and the area around it were the only place there free of refuse, and the privileged of the city paid handsomely to be buried near the man they had once rejected; their graves carried stone canopies adorned with mosaic paintings of the sort seen on the back of trucks. The poet lay inside the dilapidated building of his tomb, its stone filigree work broken. Inside, the Auqaf Department, the department of religious endowments, had allowed banners of Urdu verse by the local poets of Kasur to festoon the walls, and a local grandee had given a framed couplet in which his name appeared more prominently than the verse; Bulleh Shah's own poetry was conspicuously absent. The poet lay under layers of tinsel and flowers, and cats slept leaning against his grave on the cool floor.

By the early 2000s, like most shrines, the tomb stood at the centre of a brick courtyard covered with a concrete canopy. The crypt was covered with green and red sheets decorated with gold tinsel, which devotees bring as offerings. Several small tombs surrounded the main tomb within the same compound, where female and male relatives of the poet are buried, and devotees lit candles at them and offered the *fatiha*, the opening chapter of the Quran recited as a prayer. The street outside was colourfully lined with shops selling marigolds, rose petals, candles and *divas*, small earthenware lamps filled with mustard oil and fitted with a cotton wick, which are lit at the shrine. The shops also sold incense sticks, prayer beads and bangles plated with silver and inscribed with verses of the Quran, which devotees take to the shrine or home as souvenirs, and sweets that devotees buy as *tabarruk*, *nazar* or *niaz*, food for distribution in the shrine. Today the shrine has a radically modernised appearance.

## Music and Devotion

The shrine keeps the familiar devotional life of a Punjabi *darbar*, a saint's shrine: the recitation of the *fatiha*, *qawwali*, and the offering of vows. It draws its greatest crowds at the annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, when his *kafis* are sung through the night. It is also one of the shrines where *qawwali* is sung every night, and it is said to be a shrine of the *jamali*, or aesthetic, mystics, Sufis who were poets and wrote narratives that could be sung to music, some of them musicians themselves.

The shrine has its own *qawwals*. They have included Muhammad Bakhsh and his paternal uncle Karam Bakhsh, with a young man said to be a nephew and two other musicians, playing a harmonium, a *dholak*, a drum shaped like a barrel and played on both sides, and a pair of tambourines. In their own words: "We sing here twice a day. We sing in the morning from eight to ten, and then throughout the evening." They say they inherited the songs orally from their ancestors, who had been *qawwals* at the shrine for the last three centuries. "The saint will not let us leave this shrine," Muhammad Bakhsh has said, "and even if we do go away to other shrines to sing for the urs, we always return here." They say too that they came with Bulleh Shah's family from Uch Sharif, that they sing his poetry to his own melodies, and that they are the guardians of his oral poetry, some of which has not yet found its way into the written texts.

The women of their family do not sing at the shrine. "Our women have never sung at the shrine," they say; perhaps a century ago their women would go to the Sayyid households on special invitation and sing Baba Bulleh Shah's poetry for the Sayyid women, singing only among women. The *qawwals* sing the poet's Punjabi verse in the Punjabi *ang*, or style, in which they create the female myths of his lyrics.

On one spring evening, two days before the start of the fasting month of Ramazan, they sang the entire evening, until after the evening prayers. All together, including the musicians, there were fifty women and men in the shrine. They sang six compositions on the female voice, all in Punjabi: one was about the Prophet Muhammad, and the other five, which the musicians said were Bulleh Shah's own, were narratives of the stages of his spiritual growth as a mystic and of his relationship with his master, Shah Inayat. Outside the *ʿurs*, a performance of *qawwali* need not follow a strict ritual pattern, and the routines may differ from shrine to shrine. Women who had been praying or lighting candles and incense sticks at the tomb joined the gathering to listen. Men made a small circle in front of the musicians and began to dance in rhythm with the music, and later some *hijras*, eunuchs, joined them, with *ghungru*, small bells, tied to their ankles. The *hijras* are probably linked to the shrine by tradition, through the story of his years among the dancing girls.

By the early 1980s, too, a hoarse group of *qawwals* was constantly singing his rebuking lines, "Tamba chook-chook mandi javain", while the votaries, their feet burning, ran toward the shade of the graves of the city's rich, whose gaudy presence lent the lines an edge.

His songs travel far beyond Kasur. Sufi poetry by poets from outside Sindh, his among them, has sometimes played a liturgical role in Sindhi devotional performances: at one *versi*, a gathering for a death anniversary, in 2012, most of the songs were in Sindhi, but there was also a composition of Bulleh Shah and another of Mirabai. In an anthology compiled in 1959 he is one of the very few Sufis included who are not Sindhi, and he is quoted in a Siraiki anthology too. Ghulam Ali's *dandiya* group, dancers who perform with sticks, has played at Bulleh Shah's shrine as at Data Darbar and Baba Farid Shakar Ganj's, all famous Muslim shrines.

The singer Abida Parvin counts him among the poets she sings, with Shah Hussain, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sachal Sarmast, Baba Farid and Guru Nanak, and at a concert in Islamabad she blended his Punjabi into a text of Sultan Bahu, closing on a line that means "O gentle Bulle, God is found only by those who are true and noble of heart". Pop musicians and ensembles playing electronic instruments sing his poetry; young musicians draw on it for their lyrics; and his mystical poetry, like Khusrau's, is sung at weddings in Pakistan. His verse also reaches listeners today through well known Sikh and Muslim singers and through the popular selections issued by Indian and Pakistani publishers.

## Legends

Wonders gather around his life. It is said that when he came to Shah Inayat, the master set a price on his initiation, a condition of four items of five hundred rupees each. Another story tells of a young man in despair who sat on the bank of the Ravi, resolved to drown himself. A masked horseman rode up and asked him to hold his horse and guard his things while he bathed, and handed over four things, as many as the items of that price: a purse of five hundred rupees, a pair of gold bangles, his clothes and the horse. Then he went into the river and never came out. When the young man went into the city, people cried out that the clothes and the horse were Shah Inayat's, and Shah Inayat smiled on seeing him.

It is also told that, when Bulleh Shah was a boy, the owner of a field found him asleep with a cobra shading him with its hood. The owner reported the boy dead; his father came with some men, the snake vanished and the boy sat up, and the field proved greener than before. Jiwan Khan then made over the whole field to the boy's father as an offering.

The most popular tale of all tells how he once fell out of favour with his master, allegedly for being too outspoken in his criticisms of formal Islam, and was dismissed from his company. Accounts of the quarrel and of how long it lasted differ, but most tell that Bulleh Shah went away to learn music and dance and came back to win his master over. Knowing Shah Inayat's fondness for music and dancing, he is said to have taken lessons with a dancing girl, then reappeared in Lahore one day dressed as a dancing girl himself, and danced and sang in front of Shah Inayat, who was won over by his performance and took him back into his favour. At the shrine the *qawwals* sing of his reconciliation with his master: in their song Bulleh Shah portrays himself as a dancing girl who tells how she won back her beloved through dance, so that it is the disciple who is the dancing girl. It was the first of the narratives they sang on that spring evening before Ramazan.

His poems lament a separation from his master:

*With the departure of Inayat Qadiri, / my story has again become difficult* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

And they sing the return through dance:

*Bullha, let us go and sit at the gate of Shah Inayat, who made me dress in green and red. / When I started dancing, I found my way to him* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

"Bullha, the lord has made me dance, and the sound is very loud," he sings; "I have stripped off my blanket and dance, making him hurl astonished looks at me"; and "Bullha, it is indeed a strange thing for a woman to start dancing with her veil on." A reproach is heard too: "Satan makes her dance in the courtyard. Talk to her and make her stop." The image of Bulleh Shah dancing is a popular one in modern pictures of him. The *qawwals* of the shrine also keep several legends of how he defied the ways of his family and community to remain Shah Inayat's disciple, though he was a Sayyid himself.

Another story tells of a flight. His father worked as imam of the mosque in the village of Pandoke, and after his father's death the *chaudhris*, the headmen of the village, asked Bulleh Shah to take his place, but he refused. Threatened with a beating, he fled the village, heading towards Kasur, and took refuge in a *gurdwara*, a Sikh place of worship, in the village of Daftu, saying: "I am in the house of God. Let's see who can take me from here." The Sikhs refused to put him out, and in the end, after long discussions, he was allowed to go on to Kasur.

## Kasur

Kasur lies south of Lahore and has been called its twin city. Tradition links the two towns from their beginnings: Lahore and Kasur are said to be named after Luv and Kush. One of the sons of Ram Chand is said to have founded Kasur, and it is also told that Kushu founded Kashur, the town now known as Kasur, before he took the throne, the *gaddi*, at Ajodhya. The father of Baba Farid, too, moved to Kasur. The town has known war: at one time Sikhs gathered at Kasur, many were killed, and the town was badly damaged. Kasur also holds the graves of another family altogether, in a different burial ground from Bulleh Shah's: a Kasur lineage of Naqshbandi Mujaddidi scholars from Sindh, who died in the Hijri years 1202, 1270 and 1295.

In Bulleh Shah's verse, Takht Hazara, Multan and Prem Nagar are idylls, but Kasur, the city where he lived and sang, is a kind of inferno. Two of his *dohras*, or couplets, refer directly to the city after the rise of the Pathans, to the chaos of moral and political values in it and to the suffering this visited upon the common man. It is also the town of an absent beloved:

*You are gone, friend, far away beyond my reach. / Many a day Kasur has missed your smile.* (translated by Taufiq Rafat)

In his verse the whole province, too, is lost, at a time when the Punjab was being persistently rent by petty chiefs and marauders:

*Now hell has opened its bogs. / Punjab has gone to the dogs. / This hell is the nethermost hell.* (translated by Taufiq Rafat)

Waris Shah, whom tradition makes his fellow pupil, turned to the same town in the epilogue to his own *Hir*, the romance of Heer and Ranjha, a poem he dates to the year 1180 of the Hijri calendar:

*Of all the wretched Punjab I am most concerned for Kasur.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

## Legacy

Bulleh Shah is, with Shah Hussain, Sultan Bahu and Waris Shah, one of the pillars of classical Punjabi poetry, and perhaps the most beloved of them all. He is one of the most celebrated Sufis of the Punjab, and his personality looms large in its poetry of the eighteenth century. He is considered the greatest of the Punjabi mystical poets and the greatest master of the mystical Sufi lyric in Punjabi, and his poetry was so highly esteemed that he was called the Rumi of the Punjab. With him Punjabi mystical folk poetry reached its peak, in exactly the same period as Shah Abdul Latif, and his highly ecstatic songs have been set beside those of the Sindhi poet Sachal Sarmast. His use of the spoken language of the people has helped to ensure his continuing popularity across religious boundaries and modern national frontiers, and his more familiar, outspoken style stands in contrast to the more elusive manner of Shah Abdul Latif.

His insistence that love is higher than law, that the divisions of religion and caste are veils over a single truth, and that the self must be annihilated in God has made him a voice of tolerance and of the ordinary human heart. He is counted with Baba Farid and Waris Shah among those who spread the message of peace and brought several religious communities together instead of shedding blood. His social critique, though vividly expressed, is only a small part of his poetry.

His reputation has been made and remade. In the twentieth century he was read as an exponent of universal spiritual truths owing as much to Vedanta as to Sufism, as an authentic spokesman of the Punjabi folk tradition, as a social revolutionary, or simply as a Romantic poet before his time. Yet he is also among the Punjabi poets whom the educated elite of the Punjab has disowned, and even ridiculed. His *kafis* are sung today from village shrines to concert stages, and his shrine at Kasur remains a fixed point of Punjabi devotion, the resting place of the rebel saint who taught the Punjab to sing its way to God.

Name: Mithankot (Kot Mithan)
Events: Annual urs; kafi singing; qawwali; langar
Description:
## Overview

At Kot Mithan, also called Mithankot, in the Rajanpur district on the edge of the Cholistan desert, lies the shrine of Khwaja Ghulam Farid (1845 to 1901). He is honoured as the supreme poet of the Seraiki language and one of the last great masters of the classical Sufi *kafi*, the short mystical lyric. A Chishti saint of the Kot Mithan line, he poured the mysticism of *wahdat al-wujud*, the unity of being, into verses sung in the sweet Seraiki of the southern Punjab and steeped in the landscape of the Rohi, the great desert he loved. His shrine is the spiritual centre of the Seraiki belt, and his *kafis* are sung across it to this day.

He was one of the great Chishti masters of the nineteenth century, and a popular Seraiki poet of its last decades. His verse has passed into the repertoire of singers such as Abida Parvin and of the qawwals, and into the devotions of the Sindhi Hindu Sufis. His discourses survive in Persian, compiled between 1893 and 1901 and translated into Urdu in 1979.

## The Saint

Ghulam Farid, also known as Khwaja Farid, was born at Chachran, near Kot Mithan, in 1845, though accounts of the year differ. He came of a Sayyid Koreja family of the Chishti Sufi tradition. Sayyids are descendants of the Prophet Muhammad, and the Chishti order of Sufis, or Muslim mystics, founded by Moinuddin Chishti, is prominent in South Asia. His father and, after him, his elder brother were the *sajjada nashins*, the spiritual guides, of their line, and on his brother's death Ghulam Farid succeeded to the seat.

Learned in Arabic and Persian and in the religious sciences, he was nonetheless a poet and mystic to the core. He is famous for the years he spent in the wilderness of the Rohi, the Cholistan desert, whose dunes, herders and camel caravans fill his poetry with a local beauty. He lived in the time of the Nawabs, the rulers, of Bahawalpur, and in matters of the spirit he was their critic; he is remembered for counselling the ruler in the interest of the people.

He also took disciples. Among them was Khwaja Hasan Nizami, whose brother made him a *murid*, a pledged disciple, of Ghulam Farid at the age of sixteen.

Ghulam Farid died in 1901 at Chachran and was buried at Kot Mithan. He is not to be confused with a namesake, Maulvi Ghulam Farid Lahori, who died in 1216 AH and is buried in the Miani graveyard at Lahore, a century earlier and in another city.

## The Poetry

Khwaja Ghulam Farid's fame rests on his *Diwan*, the collected volume of his Seraiki *kafis*. These are hundreds of short mystical lyrics, cast, like those of Shah Hussain and Bulleh Shah before him, largely in the longing voice of a woman for her absent beloved, in which the Beloved is God and the desert of Rohi the very landscape of the soul. His verse unites the boldest metaphysics of the unity of being with the sweetest folk idiom of the southern Punjab, and its refrains are known by heart across the Seraiki country. A further theme of his work is the combination of spiritual exercise and interior pilgrimage; pilgrimage, with its sacred geography, is itself a subject of his poetry.

The *kafi* as a form, a stanzaic poem built on folk themes and techniques, was easy to understand and to memorise. It served as the ideal means of spreading mystical teaching among people who could not read and depended on knowledge passed on by word of mouth, and in the early twenty first century most Punjabis and Sindhis were still more likely to have heard a *kafi* than read one.

The woman who speaks in his *kafis* mourns her separation from her beloved, who has gone to a distant land. Her voice is borrowed from the romance of the Punjab: Ghulam Farid also takes up the voice of Hir, a tragic heroine of its folk tales, to speak of *ishq-e haqiqi*, the ultimate spiritual union, through the imagery of *ishq-e majazi*, earthly love. The figure belongs to the mystical poetry of the region at large. In Sindh as in the Punjab, and rarely elsewhere in the Muslim world, the longing soul is represented in the form of a woman, and the tragic heroines of the Sindhi and Punjabi folk tales, Hir, Sassui, Sohni and many others, stand for the human soul in search of the beloved.

Most famous of all is his declaration that the Beloved is everything, the only reality:

میڈا عشق وی توں، میڈا یار وی توں

*You are my love, and You are my beloved; You alone are all.*

His *kafis* are sung to this day by the folk singers and qawwals of the Seraiki belt, and he is honoured as the poet who gave that language its highest literary and spiritual expression.

One of his lyrics takes up the lovers Layla and Majnun. The singer Abida Parvin sang this song of a black Layla at her Open University concert, attributing the poetry to Ghulam Farid. In the song, when people asked Majnun about his black Layla, he answered with an example from the Quran: if the pages of the Quran can be white while the ink is black, what is so wrong in his loving a woman of colour? It is the poet himself who asks the question on Majnun's behalf, and in one of the lyric's lines he names himself: *Ākhe Ghulām Farīd-ā O jeh nāl dil aṛ pave O gorī hove yā kālī*.

## The Discourses

Beside the poetry stands a book of his conversations. His discourses, or *malfuzat*, were compiled in Persian between 1893 and 1901 as *Maqabis al-majalis*, The Lessons of the Spiritual Assemblies, a work also known as *Isharat-i Faridi*. Christopher Shackle rendered them into English as *The Teachings of Khwaja Farid* (Multan, 1978), and in 1979 Captain Wahid Bakhsh Siyal translated them into Urdu.

The translator was a twentieth century shaykh, and his introduction became a work in its own right. In his long Urdu introduction he gave more than a third of 225 pages to explaining and defending *samaʿ*, spiritual listening, the Sufi session of music, and one chapter of the work is called *Zauq-i samaʿ*, The Taste of Samaʿ.

Through their translator the discourses kept a living Chishti readership. The will of Wahid Bakhsh's master, Shahidullah Faridi, says that Wahid Bakhsh had begun a circle of *zikr*, the remembrance of God, and spiritual guidance in Bahawalpur, and that he should spread the *silsila*, the Sufi chain of teaching, in that place only. In effect, it has been said, his master marked out the southern Punjab as Wahid Bakhsh's own spiritual domain.

## The Shrine and Its Devotion

Khwaja Ghulam Farid's shrine at Kot Mithan is the chief centre of pilgrimage of the Seraiki region. It is kept by his descendants and draws devotees throughout the year for prayer, blessing and the singing of his verse. The annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, gathers great crowds for days of *kafi* singing, *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, and *langar*, the free communal kitchen. The town of Kot Mithan is known above all as the resting place of the poet, and his memory is inseparable from the cultural identity of the Seraiki people. A book of his verse, *Kalam-e Khwaja Ghulam Farid*, has been advertised as the work of Khwaja Ghulam Farid of Kot Mithan Sharif, a style that adds to the town's name *Sharif*, noble, the honorific given to holy places.

His verse is sung far beyond the town. Abida Parvin's repertoire includes him, and he is among the spirits invoked at the outset of performances of Sufi poetry. Her improvised performance at Islamabad drew on Shah Abdul Latif's poetry and on Ghulam Farid's texts, and two items on the programme of that concert were his, both in Seraiki. His name also stands in the full title of a recording, *A Tribute to Great Mystics*. Surraiya Multanikar, a Seraiki singer of Sufi poetry, and of his in particular, has said that she is specially blessed by her *pir*, her spiritual guide, a Gilani Syed, and that because of his prayer there is much *sur*, melody, in her voice.

He is also among the poets of the qawwals' repertoire, as is Mehr Ali Shah. His verse has crossed into the devotions of another community too. Among the Sindhi Hindu Sufis, Sufi poetry by poets who were not Sindhis sometimes played a liturgical role in their performances, and Ghulam Farid is quoted there, as are Bulleh Shah and Shah Bahu; Seraiki is a language in which many Sindhis also composed poetry.

## The Setting

Kot Mithan was a place of learning a century before Ghulam Farid. In the *qasba*, the small town, of Kot Mithan, Qazi Muhammad Aqil kept a *madrasa*, a religious school, and there, in his early days, Khwaja Sulaiman Taunsvi studied with him and acquired the outward sciences. The teacher is identified as Khwaja Muhammad Aqil, of the Faruqi family, whose father was Muhammad Sharif; he died on 14 Rajab 1229 AH. Sulaiman Taunsvi, who was born in 1184 AH and died in 1267 AH, was the saint through whom the Chishti Nizami Fakhri line spread most widely in the Punjab. On his mission to Lahore and Bahawalpur of 1832 to 1833, Captain C. M. Wade made a voyage from Lodiana to Mithankot by the river Satlaj.

Seraiki, the language of Ghulam Farid's verse, is spoken mainly in the southern Punjab, with Multan as its capital, and also in northern Sindh; in the Middle Ages the southern Punjab was a part of Sindh. On the road south through Bahawalpur the boundary between Sindh and Punjab becomes a blur and the cultures of the two merge, and Seraiki has been called an amalgamation of the two languages: the Seraiki of Multan is closer to Punjabi, while further south it is more like Sindhi. Seraiki forms the transition to Punjabi, and so the imagery of all three linguistic areas, Sindhi, Seraiki and Punjabi, is very closely related. The legend of Sohni is sung in Sufi poetry in all the regions of Sindh and in the Seraiki speaking area of the Punjab.

## Legacy

For Seraiki, Khwaja Ghulam Farid is what Bhittai is to Sindhi and Bulleh Shah to Punjabi: the poet who raised his mother tongue to the summit of mystical expression and made of its desert landscape an image of the soul's love for God. His *kafis* remain among the most cherished poetry of the southern Punjab, and his shrine at Kot Mithan endures as the spiritual and cultural heart of the Seraiki belt.

His work has been carried into print and into English largely from Multan. Besides *The Teachings of Khwaja Farid*, Christopher Shackle translated *Fifty Poems of Khawaja Farid* (Multan, 1983). Multan editions of his work also include *Kalām-e Farid*, edited by Kefi Jampuri, *Naghmā-e Sehrā*, translated by Kashafi Multani, and M. Abdul Wasi's *Divān-e Farid Ma Dhorājāt*.

Description:
Mohra Sharif is a celebrated *khanqah* — a Sufi lodge and spiritual centre — set in a small village in the Murree hills of the Punjab, some distance above Islamabad and Rawalpindi. It is the home of the *Naqshbandi Mujaddidi Qasimiya* order, and takes its name (the "holy village") from its sanctity. The centre was established by *Khwaja Muhammad Qasim Sadiq*, born about 1846 (1263 AH), whose forebears are said to have migrated from Iran and settled in the Rawalpindi district. According to the traditions of the order, he journeyed on foot to the shrine of his spiritual guide, *Khwaja Nizamuddin Aulia* of Kahiyan Sharif in the Neelam Valley of Kashmir, and there received *khilafat* with the instruction to settle at Mohra Sharif. He is said to have undertaken a *chilla* — a forty-day retreat of unbroken devotion — and the stone slab on which he sat throughout is preserved at the shrine as a relic (*tabarruk*). On his death the spiritual seat passed to his son Khwaja Pir Muhammad Zahid Khan, remembered as the first *sajjada nashin* (custodian) of Mohra Sharif, and thence down a line of successors. The khanqah remains an active centre of Naqshbandi devotion, drawing pilgrims especially at its annual *urs*, and is counted among the important Sufi shrines of the northern Punjab.

The khanqah's own historical account names the specific line of succession only broadly gestured at above: Khwaja Pir Muhammad Zahid Khan, the founder's third son and first *sajjada nashin*, is recorded as having died on 9 December 1993; he was followed by Hazrat Khawaja Pir Badshah Sahib, who died on 13 August 2008; and then by Pir Auliya Badshah Farooq Sahib as the third *Sajjada Nasheen*. In January 2026, the German Ambassador to Pakistan, Ina Lepel, visited the khanqah — described in press coverage as a "200-year-old Sufi centre" — and met with its custodian, named in that report as Pir Mujtaba Farooq Gull; a second report of the same visit notes that she spent considerable time at the khanqah's attached madrassa, observing classes and discussing curriculum with students.
