Name: Nagarparkar Jain Temples (Nagarparkar Cultural Landscape)
Location: Karoonjhar Mountains region, Nagarparkar, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: None - abandoned; heritage visitation
Description:
## Overview

Scattered across the pink-granite folds of the *Karoonjhar* mountains and the plains around Nagarparkar, in the far south-east of Sindh, stand the abandoned Jain temples that give this remote corner of Pakistan its most celebrated monuments. Built between roughly the twelfth and fifteenth centuries by a prosperous local Jain community, the temples — grouped by the Government of Pakistan under the title *Nagarparkar Cultural Landscape* — were placed on UNESCO's tentative list of World Heritage Sites in 2016. Though the dataset files them, for convenience, among Hindu temples, they belong properly to the *Śvetāmbara* Jain tradition, and together they represent one of the high points of Jain architectural achievement in the subcontinent.

## The Jain Community and the Port of Parinagar

Nagarparkar lies in a zone of transition, where the salt-flats and marshes of the Rann of Kutch give way to stabilised sand dunes and the ancient granite of the Karoonjhar hills. For several centuries this was a flourishing centre of Jainism. The Jains of the region were maritime merchants and financiers who served as advisers to the Rajput chiefs, the Delhi Sultans and the Mughals, and who dominated the trade of the area through the nearby port of *Parinagar*, believed by tradition to have been founded many centuries before the common era. The wealth generated by this commerce was poured into pious building, and the hills around Nagarparkar became a place of pilgrimage known as *Sardhara*, where Jain ascetics established themselves and where temple after temple rose in honour of the *Tirthankaras*.

## The Temples and their Architecture

The surviving monuments are dispersed across several locations — among them the temple in Nagarparkar town itself, the cluster at *Bhodesar*, the shrines at *Viravah* near the old site of Parinagar, and, most famously, the *Gori* temple between Islamkot and Nagarparkar. They are built in the *Māru-Gurjara* idiom of western India, distinguished by finely carved stone, richly ornamented ceilings, clustered subsidiary shrines and stepped tanks. The Gori temple, dated to 1375–76, is especially prized: its interior frescoes are held to be the oldest surviving Jain wall-paintings in the northern part of the subcontinent. So powerful was the local architectural language that even the fifteenth-century mosque at Bhodesar was raised in a style visibly indebted to the temples around it — an eloquent testament to the shared craft traditions of the region.

## Decline and Abandonment

The prosperity that raised the temples proved impermanent. As silt carried by the Indus gradually filled the Rann of Kutch, the Arabian Sea retreated from the centres of Jain commerce, and the trade on which the community depended withered. A large-scale movement of the Jain population away from the area took place in the nineteenth century, and those who remained departed at the Partition of British India in 1947. The temples were left empty, their sanctuaries silent, and over time they passed into the care of the state as protected monuments and popular heritage sites rather than as living places of worship.

## Significance Today

The Nagarparkar temples endure as among the most important pre-Islamic monuments in Pakistan and as the principal surviving witnesses to the once-thriving Jain civilisation of the lower Indus. They draw travellers, scholars and heritage enthusiasts to a landscape of striking beauty, where the rose-coloured Karoonjhar hills frame the carved stone of the shrines. Their inclusion on the UNESCO tentative list has focused attention on the need for their conservation, even as quarrying and neglect threaten parts of the wider landscape. For the study of religion in the region they are invaluable: a reminder that the sacred geography of Sindh has embraced Jain, Hindu and Muslim devotion alike, and that this arid frontier was once a centre of learning, art and pilgrimage.

## Bibliography

- UNESCO World Heritage Centre, tentative list entry, "Nagarparkar Cultural Landscape" (2016).
- Endowment Fund Trust for Preservation of the Heritage of Sindh, documentation on the Nagarparkar temples.
- *The Friday Times*, "Jain Legacy of Nagarparkar" (2019).
- Wikipedia, "Nagarparkar Jain temples" and "Nagarparkar" (with cited sources).
- Ahmad Nabi Khan, *Islamic Architecture of Pakistan* (for the Bhodesar mosque and regional context).

Name: Panj Tirath
Events: Historically Kartik bathing; not currently observed
Description:
## Overview

Panj Tirath — the "five bathing places" — is one of the most ancient sacred sites of Peshawar, a Hindu pilgrimage complex whose name records the five pools of water that lay at its heart. Set in the Hashtnagri quarter of the old city, it belongs to a stratum of the region's religious history far older than the Islamic and Sikh monuments that surround it, reaching back through the Hindu and Buddhist antiquity of the Peshawar valley. Long neglected and much reduced, it was declared a protected national heritage site in 2019, an acknowledgement of a sanctity that local memory traces to the age of legend.

## Antiquity and Legend

The site takes its name and its holiness from its five *tirthas*, the pools in which pilgrims bathed. Local tradition, recorded by Munshi Gopal Das in his *Tareekh-e-Peshawar* of 1874 and repeated by the Hindu community, connects Panj Tirath with the five sons of *Pandu* — the *Pandava* heroes of the *Mahabharata* — and holds that the site was hallowed by their presence, so that its origins are woven into the great epic geography of the subcontinent. Alongside this Hindu memory runs a Buddhist one: the celebrated archaeologists Sir Alexander Cunningham and Alfred Foucher identified Panj Tirath and its environs with places associated in ancient accounts with the Buddha, including the relic of his begging-bowl, which was long kept at Peshawar (the ancient *Purushapura*). The site thus stands at the confluence of the two great faiths that shaped the valley before Islam, and its sanctity is best understood as very old and layered, rather than fixed to any single founder.

## History

Like so many of the region's shrines, Panj Tirath passed through cycles of destruction and revival. It is recorded to have been damaged during the turbulence of the Durrani period in the eighteenth century, around 1747, and then rebuilt by the Hindus of Peshawar in 1834, in the years of Sikh ascendancy in the north-west, when worship was restored at the pools. Through the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries it remained an active centre of pilgrimage, its waters visited especially during the month of *Kartik* — the season, falling between late October and late November, when bathing at sacred *tirthas* carries particular merit in the Hindu calendar.

## Decline and Protection

The Partition of 1947 and the departure of most of Peshawar's Hindu population left Panj Tirath without a resident community to maintain it, and in the decades that followed the site was encroached upon and largely built over: much of its ground was absorbed into a public park, and its structures — two temples and a gateway among them — fell into dilapidation, some pressed into use as storerooms. In January 2019 the Directorate of Archaeology, acting under the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Antiquities Act of 2016, declared Panj Tirath a protected national heritage site, a step welcomed by heritage advocates and the Hindu community alike, though the physical fabric of the complex remains fragile and in urgent need of conservation.

## Legacy

Panj Tirath is a witness to the deep and plural past of Peshawar — a city that has been in turn a Buddhist metropolis, a Hindu centre, a Mughal and Durrani stronghold, and a Sikh and British garrison. Its five pools, and the memory of the Pandavas and the Buddha that clings to them, connect the modern city to an antiquity measured in millennia. That the site survives at all, and now enjoys a measure of legal protection, offers some hope for the preservation of a heritage that belongs not to one community but to the long history of the region as a whole.

## Bibliography

- Munshi Gopal Das, *Tareekh-e-Peshawar* (1874), for the tradition linking the site to the sons of Pandu.
- A. Cunningham, *The Ancient Geography of India*, and A. Foucher's studies, on the Buddhist associations of Peshawar (*Purushapura*).
- Reporting in *The Friday Times* and *Dawn* on the 2019 heritage listing and the condition of Panj Tirath.
- Directorate of Archaeology, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, notifications under the KP Antiquities Act 2016.

Name: Parnami Mandir
Events: Historically an annual mela in Chaitra; not currently observed
Description:
## Overview

At Malka Hans, a historic village of the Pakpattan district in southern Punjab, stands the crumbling but still imposing *Parnami* (or *Pranami*) temple, one of the most significant surviving monuments of a distinctive Hindu devotional tradition in Pakistan. Once a central *ashram* of the Pranami faith west of the present border, the multi-storeyed building enshrined the *samadhi* of a revered teacher remembered locally as *Dya Ram*, and it drew large gatherings of devotees before the Partition of 1947. Today it survives chiefly as a heritage landmark in a village otherwise famous for its association with the Punjabi poet Waris Shah, who is said to have composed his celebrated *Heer* in a nearby mosque.

## The Pranami Tradition

The Pranami *sampradaya* — also called *Dhami* or *Nijananda* — is a Vaishnava tradition within Hinduism centred on the worship of *Krishna*. It emerged in western India in the seventeenth century from the teachings of the *bhakti* saint Devchandra Maharaj and, above all, of his foremost disciple Mehraj Thakur, better known as *Mahamati Prannath*, from whose name the tradition takes its own. Its adherents "bow" (*pranam*) in devotion — hence the name Pranami — and its teaching, gathered in a scripture called the *Tartam Sagar*, is notable for a strongly monotheistic emphasis and for language that sought common ground between Hindu and Islamic conceptions of the divine. The tradition spread across northern and western India and into Sindh and the Punjab, establishing temples and *dhams* that became centres of pilgrimage; the movement is also remembered for its historical links to the ruler Chhatrasal of Bundelkhand.

## The Temple at Malka Hans

Local accounts describe the Malka Hans temple as a tall building of several storeys, richly conceived, whose main chamber housed the *samadhi* of Dya Ram, honoured as the teacher associated with the establishment of the shrine. Precisely who Dya Ram was, and exactly when the temple was raised, are matters on which the surviving evidence is thin: heritage writers variously place its construction two centuries or more ago, while the Pranami tradition to which it belongs reaches back to the seventeenth century, and these datings should be treated with caution rather than as false precision. What is consistently reported is that the site functioned as an important Pranami centre, that a large annual *mela* was held here in the spring month of *Chaitra*, and that several further *samadhis* stand on the outskirts of the village, marking it as a place of sustained religious activity. The temple's height and prominence made it a notable feature of the local landscape.

## Decline and the Present Day

With the Partition of 1947 the Hindu population of this part of the Punjab migrated to India, and the temple, deprived of its congregation, fell silent. In the decades since it has suffered the familiar fate of abandoned sacred buildings — weathering, encroachment and the slow accumulation of decay — even as its scale continues to impress visitors. It has attracted the attention of heritage enthusiasts, photographers and journalists who document Pakistan's vanishing Hindu monuments, and it features in accounts of Malka Hans alongside the village's literary associations. Whether the structure will be conserved remains uncertain, and its condition has been a recurring subject of concern.

## Legacy

The Parnami temple of Malka Hans is a reminder that the religious map of the Punjab was once far more varied than it now appears, embracing not only the major Hindu, Muslim and Sikh traditions but also smaller reforming movements such as the Pranami faith, with its ecumenical cast and its Krishna-centred devotion. As one of the few tangible remains of that tradition on the Pakistani side of the border, the temple has a value for the history of religion in the region that far exceeds its present ruinous state, and it stands as a quiet monument to a community and a devotional world that have almost entirely passed from the local scene.

## Bibliography

- Wikipedia, "Pranami" (Pranami Sampradaya) and "Mahamati Prannath", with cited sources.
- Documentation of the Malka Hans temple by heritage writers on Pakistan's Hindu monuments (e.g. the *lahOre and mOre* and Ali Usman Baig field accounts).
- Haroon Khalid, writings on the folk and minority religious heritage of the Pakistani Punjab.
- General literature on the *bhakti* movements of western India and their spread into Sindh and the Punjab.

Name: Prahladpuri Temple
Location: Fort of Multan (near Shrine of Bahauddin Zakariya), Multan, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: None - destroyed 1992
Description:
## Overview

The Prahladpuri Temple stood on a raised platform at the southern tip of the great fort of Multan, immediately beside the shrine of the Sufi saint Bahauddin Zakariya, so that Multan's Hindu and Muslim sacred pasts meet on the same commanding mound. It was dedicated to *Narasimha*, the incarnation of the god Vishnu as half man and half lion, and named for *Prahlada*, the prince who was Vishnu's devotee. It was among the most storied Hindu temples of the Indus plain, and popular tradition remembers it as a place from which the spring festival of *Holi* took its origin. Today the temple survives only as a ruin.

Known also as the temple of Prahlad Bhagat, Prahlad the devotee, it was one of the most important Hindu temples of Multan, a city that tradition makes the very setting of Prahlada's story. Its destruction in 1992 severed a line of worship that legend traced back to the beginnings of the world's ages.

## The Legend of Prahlada

The temple belongs to the cycle of the *Narasimha* legend, one of the best known stories of Vaishnava devotion, the worship of Vishnu, and a myth canonised in the *Bhagavata Purana*, a Hindu scripture devoted to Vishnu. As the story is told, the *asura*, or demon, king Hiranyakashipu had won a boon that made him all but invincible, and he demanded to be worshipped as a god. His own son, Prahlada, remained steadfastly devoted to Vishnu. Enraged, the king sought to destroy the boy, whose faith was at last vindicated when Vishnu burst forth from a pillar in the royal court in the form of Narasimha, half man and half lion. Narasimha slew the tyrant at a threshold that was neither inside nor out, at a twilight that was neither day nor night, and so got round every term of the boon.

Local tradition holds that it was Prahlada himself who raised the temple at Multan in thanksgiving, enshrining an image of Narasimha on the spot, though accounts of its founding differ. Hiranyakashipu, the tyrant of the story, is believed to have ruled the city of Multan thousands of years ago.

Bound to this is the tradition that connects Multan with the origins of *Holi*. Holika, the demoness sister of Hiranyakashipu, sought to burn the child Prahlada, but she herself was consumed while he emerged unharmed. Her bonfire is remembered in the spring festival of colour and fire, and the temple at Multan was long held to be the very stage of that deliverance. Whatever weight one gives these legends as history, they made Prahladpuri a site of unusual resonance in the sacred geography of the subcontinent.

## The Temple

It is held that the mound came to be considered holy because of the temple, and that it then became a popular spiritual site with mystics and saints. Among the Muslim mystics it drew was Bahauddin Zakariya, whose shrine came to stand next to the temple. In the days of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith, Multan was one of the biggest cities of the Punjab, known for the shrines of Muslim saints and for its Jain and Hindu temples, a sacred space for people of every religious denomination.

For centuries the temple was a living centre of worship, repaired and rebuilt through the changing fortunes of Multan's turbulent history. During the siege of Multan in 1848, in the campaigns that came before the British annexation of the Punjab, a shell struck a powder magazine inside the fort, and the explosion that followed is said to have carried away the temple's roof. In the aftermath the East India Company held the fort directly for some years, before restoring the shrines to their communities around 1852. The building suffered again in 1881, when it was set alight amid communal violence, and once more Multan's Hindu community renovated it.

## Destruction and After

The temple's end came in December 1992. On the 6th of December that year the Babri Masjid at Ayodhya in India was demolished, and in the wave of reprisals that followed across Pakistan a mob attacked and destroyed the Prahladpuri Temple and its adjoining *dharamshala*, the rest house for pilgrims, reducing the historic structure to rubble. Accounts differ over whether worship there had continued after Partition, and over how much of the building still stands. Hindus who were well known in the cities of the Punjab had to hide for several months after the demolition at Ayodhya.

Parvati Devi, a classically trained professional singer of Multan who is also a social activist, lived through those days. She recalls that a mob which had destroyed the Valmiki temple near her house wanted to burn her alive; afterwards she took up a Muslim name, Shaila Bibi, and stopped appearing on radio and television.

The site of the temple is held by the Evacuee Trust Property Board, the state body that administers the properties of communities displaced at Partition, though accounts differ over which government body has charge of it. Proposals for its restoration have been discussed from time to time, but no full rebuilding has been achieved. The order of the two holy places on the mound has reversed: in the early twenty first century the temple lay in obscurity under the shadow of the massive shrine beside it.

Parvati Devi recalls that in 2006 and 2008 the authorities of Bahauddin Zakariya's shrine extended it into the premises of the historical Prahlad Temple, building first a place for ablutions and then a hall for the *langar*, the free communal kitchen. The matter reached the courts. Usman Chaudary, president of the RAS Society, the Organisation for Religious and Sexual Minorities, filed a petition in the High Court, and the court passed a stay order against any further construction on the premises of the temple. The society has petitioned that the temple be handed back to the Hindu community of the city. The demand of Multan's Hindus, in Parvati Devi's words, is that the temple "be restored and given to the Hindus of the city who are its real owners".

## Holi in Multan

In the early twenty first century the festival that tradition ties to this temple was kept in Multan, though not at the temple itself: the celebrations were held in a Hindu locality and in front of the city's press club. The Hindus who kept it had lived in Multan since before it became a part of Pakistan, and the thirty odd women who burned the Holika were by then the only link that the city had with that story. The locality, next to the railway station, was one of several areas where the city's Hindus lived. The community numbered little more than a thousand and had no centralised celebration; the settlement had about a hundred houses, only about ten to twelve of them belonging to Hindu families. Multan had several historical temples from the days before Partition; by then all of them had become ruins, and the community had turned other spaces into makeshift temples.

The public festival had lapsed and then returned. As recently as 2010, festivals including Holi were not celebrated in the city. That year Usman Chaudary organised a token celebration of Holi in front of the Multan Press Club, and by the early 2010s Holi, though on a small scale, was celebrated every year in Multan and regularly featured in the local media. Usman has been alleged to be an Indian agent, and more than once he and his friends have been physically attacked.

## The Setting

Multan, the city in which the temple stood, lies where three rivers merge before the Indus, and it was a commercial hub for trade at home and abroad, including trade with Persia, Central Asia and the Arab world. In the time of the *Mahabharata*, the Sanskrit epic, it was the capital of the Tuganta kingdom, and legend has Alexander struck by an arrow there. For the next thousand years Multan was ruled by Hindu and Buddhist kings. A Chinese traveller visited it in 641, and it has been called the city of gold; its Suraj temple, the temple of the sun, was claimed to be by far the biggest temple in the subcontinent.

In 711 the Arabs conquered Sind and the provinces to its north up to Multan, and in time Multan became a dependency of the Fatimids of Egypt. In the eleventh century Mahmud of Ghazni damaged the Suraj temple and destroyed its giant idol, and by the middle of that century Sufism had reached the country around Multan. In 1175 Mu‘izzu'd-Din Muhammad bin Sam seized the city. In time the town became studded with mosques as it had once been with Hindu temples. By the time Guru Nanak came to Multan it was famous as a major centre of Sufi learning and philosophy, and in the reign of Aurangzeb it was counted one of the ancient cities, with a fort of brick, and many saints lay at rest in that blessed city.

The wars of the nineteenth century touched the whole city. Hafiz Muhammad Jamal, a successor of Nur Muhammad, is said to have taken part in resistance to Sikh attacks on Multan before his death in 1811. When Ranjit Singh conquered Multan, with Kharak Singh sent against the city, Nawab Muzaffar Khan was killed, and others of his family were captured with their households and came to Lahore. Diwan Mulraj, son of Sawan Mal, governor of Multan, raised a disturbance in the city and had its new governor killed, together with two sahibs, men of rank. The troubles spread from Multan through Hazara and four hard battles, until the whole country passed into English rule.

Multan enters the poetry of the region too, though never this temple. In one *kafi*, a Sufi devotional lyric, by Madho Lal Hussein, the city is named as the place where one item of a bride's trousseau was bought:

*The dress / someone carried across the snows / all the way from Kashmir. The dress / someone brought from Gujarat… The dress bought in Multan* (translated by Naveed Alam)

For the poets of Pakistan's own languages, Mecca and Medina are inside the heart, and for those who wrote in Sindhi and Punjabi, so is Multan.

## Legacy

The ruins of Prahladpuri remain among the most poignant of Pakistan's lost Hindu monuments, a fragment of the deep Hindu antiquity of Multan, a city whose very name has long been bound to a famed sun temple and whose fort mound has borne temples and shrines in almost unbroken succession for millennia. That the remains of the Narasimha temple and the tomb of a great Muslim saint share the same eminence is itself a lesson in the layered religious history of the Indus valley.

For the Hindu communities of Pakistan, and for pilgrims and scholars abroad, Prahladpuri endures as a place of memory: a temple whose legend gave the subcontinent one of its most joyous festivals, and whose fate marks one of the harder chapters of the region's recent past. Its claim on memory runs both ways. Multan goes on unaware of its ancient past and of its tie to the story of Hiranyakashipu and Prahlad Bhagat, while its Hindus ask that the temple be given back to them.

- Colonial-era accounts of the 1848 Siege of Multan and *Multan District Gazetteer* notices of the fort and its shrines.
- Studies of the *Narasimha* and *Holika*–Prahlada legend cycle in Vaishnava tradition.
- Reports on the 1992 destruction of Hindu temples in Pakistan and the status of Evacuee Trust properties.

- Harish Dhillon, *Janamsakhis: Ageless Stories, Timeless Values* (Hay House India, 2015; paperback 2020).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* (Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina Press, 1975; 35th Anniversary Edition, with a new Foreword by Carl W. Ernst, 2011).

Name: Purana Bhalwal
Events: Annual urs; qawwali; langar
Description:
## Overview

At Purana Bhalwal, the old settlement that gives its name to the modern town of Bhalwal in Sargodha District, stands the shrine of Hazrat Shah Sulaiman Nuri, a Sufi of the sixteenth century who belonged to the *Qadiriyya*, the Sufi order founded by ʿAbd al-Qadir Gilani. Locally he is remembered with the affectionate title *Sakhi Badshah*, 'the generous king'. His *dargah*, the shrine complex of a Sufi saint, is the spiritual heart of an otherwise unassuming corner of central Punjab, drawing devotees from the surrounding villages of the Chaj Doab, the fertile tract between the Jhelum and the Chenab.

Shah Sulaiman is remembered for a life of devotion, teaching and open-handed hospitality, and for his place in the spiritual line from which the Naushahi order of the Punjab began. Devotees gather at his tomb, above all for his *urs*, the yearly commemoration of his death.

## The Saint

His devotees remember Shah Sulaiman as a scholar and an ascetic trained in the *Qadiri* path. His father is remembered as Shaikh Abdullah, known as Mian Mangu, or simply Mangu, and is said to have lived in the village of Bhalwal. Accounts of the family's caste differ. Besides Nuri, the saint is also known as Shah Sulaiman Qadri.

At the shrine his spiritual guide, or *pir*, is remembered as Shah Maroof Khushabi of the nearby town of Khushab. It is related that this teacher, recognising his disciple's attainment, directed him to settle at Purana Bhalwal and to make it the centre of his teaching and service. There Shah Sulaiman is said to have spent the rest of his life in devotion, in instruction and in feeding travellers and the poor, and it is from this open-handed hospitality that his title *Sakhi Badshah* is popularly derived.

It is said that he listened to *sama*, the spiritual listening of the Sufi music session, and that in *wajd*, the ecstasy of the mystic, he would fall so senseless that he reached the condition of death. Thousands are said to have entered his *bai'at*, the pledge by which a disciple is initiated by his *pir*, and to have reached high degrees, and his whole life was spent in guiding students.

Tradition gives him a remarkably long life, from the early sixteenth century until 1604. Accounts of the year of his death differ; the year the shrine keeps is 1604, which falls in the Hijri year 1012. He is said to have died at a great age on the night of the 27th of Ramadan, one of the most sacred nights of the Muslim calendar, a detail that has only deepened the reverence in which he is held.

## Master and Disciple

Of the Qadiri order in the Punjab, the first master to arrive is held to have been Hazrat Sayyid Muhammad Ghaus Uchchi Jili Gilani, whose ancestors had left Baghdad in the time of Hulagu Khan. He came by way of Khurasan to Multan and settled at Uch, which he entered in 887 AH.

Shah Sulaiman stands at a turning in the history of the Sufi orders of the Punjab. The shrine remembers Shah Maroof Khushabi as his *pir*; his spiritual line is most often traced from Shah Maruf Chishti, a master who held authority to initiate disciples in both the Qadiri and the Chishti orders, and Shah Sulaiman is counted his *khalifa*, a spiritual deputy of his master. Shah Maruf is said to have marked Sulaiman out while he was still a child.

From Shah Sulaiman the line passed to Haji Muhammad Naushah Ganj Bakhsh, also known as Shaikh Haji Muhammad Qadri, who was brought to him by Mulla Karim al-Din. With Naushah Ganj Bakhsh the Naushahi way began, and in the 1870s its *faqirs*, or mystics, in the Punjab were counted in the thousands. The same line, from Maruf Chishti through Shah Sulaiman Nuri to Naushah Ganj Bakhsh, appears in the *shajra*, or spiritual pedigree, of one Bhage Shah.

## The Shrine and Its Devotion

The shrine at Purana Bhalwal follows the familiar pattern of the Punjab's smaller Sufi *dargahs*. A whitewashed tomb chamber shelters the grave, within a courtyard where devotees gather to offer the *Fatiha*, the opening chapter of the Qur'an, to tie threads of intention and to distribute food.

The saint's *urs* marks the anniversary of his death, understood in Sufi thought as the soul's union with the Divine, and it is the principal event of the devotional year. Then *qawwals*, the singers of *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, perform, and *langar*, the free communal meal, is served to all who come.

The gathering draws on the devotional traditions of the Punjab. *Qawwali* has two principal regions, Uttar Pradesh and the Punjab, and Punjabi tunes tend to be organised rhythmically by stress, with the drum stressing the beats of the metre more strongly than in Uttar Pradesh. The Punjab, like Sind, has also produced hymns in praise of the great masters of the mystical orders, especially ʿAbd al-Qadir Gilani, in imagery that anyone in the village could easily understand.

For the cultivators of the district the saint remains a figure of intercession and blessing, invoked at times of illness, harvest and family need, in the manner characteristic of the living shrine culture of rural Punjab. The shrine remains in active use today, cared for by the descendants and devotees of the saint and, like many such sites, under the general oversight of the provincial Auqaf administration, the government department of religious endowments.

## The Setting

Bhalwal grew as an agricultural market town under the canal colonies of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. As the newer town expanded around the railway, the shrine anchored the older village of Purana, or 'old', Bhalwal.

Across the province, the British linked the five rivers of the Punjab with one another by canals, turning jungle into farmland. Thousands of new villages, called *chaks*, were founded, and farming families from all over the Punjab were invited to settle in them. The land's former inhabitants had been mainly nomads who could not prove that they owned it, and it was taken from them and allotted to the newcomers.

Before the canals, under the Mughals, the *suba*, or province, of Lahore was divided into five *doabs*, the tracts between its rivers. Its wells were each worked by a wheel of 360 pieces of wood carrying more than a hundred small pots and turned by a pair of oxen, while the *kharif* and *rabi* harvests, of autumn and of spring, and the cheapness of grain depended on the rain.

## Legacy

Shah Sulaiman Nuri belongs to the dense network of Qadiri and Chishti saints whose shrines dot the Chaj and Rechna Doabs, forming a sacred geography that shaped the religious life of the Punjab long before modern boundaries were drawn. He never won the fame of a Data Ganj Bakhsh or a Baba Farid beyond his own region, but his *dargah* shows how Sufi devotion took root at the local level, giving small communities their own centre of blessing and continuity. In the history of the orders he is remembered as the link between Shah Maruf Chishti and Naushah Ganj Bakhsh, with whom the Naushahi way began.

In 1875 a book on the saints of the Punjab gave Shah Sulaiman a notice of his own. The book closes with chronograms for its own completion, verses whose letters give a year. One of them, by Mufti Ghulam Safdar Lahori, whom the book names as the author's son, sets out its scope, the saints of the Punjab:

جو خدا کے دوست تھے پنجاب میں
حال ان کا اس سے ہوتا ہے عیان

*A chronogram couplet on the book's scope, the saints of Punjab; the closing chronograms read 1292 AH.*

Location: Hazarkhwani (Ring Road), Peshawar, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
Events: Annual urs with mushaira (poetic assembly); rabab recitals
Description:
## Overview

At Hazarkhwani, on the edge of Peshawar, stands the mausoleum of Rahman Baba, the poet Abdur Rahman Mohmand. He is the most beloved poet of the Pashto language and the great mystic voice of the Pashtuns, and his shrine is the spiritual and literary heart of the Pashto speaking world, a traditional gathering place of poets and singers.

For three centuries his *Diwan*, the collected volume of his verse, has been the book most cherished after the Qur'an in countless Pashtun homes. Its verses of love, humility and the vanity of the world are quoted as proverbs and sung by musicians from Peshawar to Kandahar.

## The Poet and Saint

Abdur Rahman, lovingly called Rahman Baba, was born around 1653 near Peshawar, into the Mohmand tribe of the Pashtuns. He lived in the reign of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. Little of his outward life is documented: he was no courtier, and he left no chronicle of himself. He is remembered as a man of humble means and retiring temperament, a dervish who shunned the powerful and lived in poverty and prayer, and legend has it that he led a life of withdrawal and seclusion.

His verse reveals a soul of deep devotion in the way of the Sufis, the mystics of Islam: gentle, unassuming and wholly turned towards God. He belonged to the broad Sufi current of his time and place, and he is counted a mystic of the Chishti order, a Sufi order prominent in South Asia. Another remarkable poet of the same order, Khwaja Muhammad Bangash, also tried to express mystical teachings in Pashto.

By tradition Rahman Baba performed the Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca. He died around 1711, though accounts of the year differ, and he was buried at Hazarkhwani, where his shrine arose.

## The Poetry

Rahman Baba's fame rests entirely on his *Diwan*, a body of Pashto verse of unmatched sweetness and moral depth. His great themes are the love of God, the transience of the world, humility, tolerance and the dignity of the poor. Again and again he preaches that one should return kindness for cruelty and sow good rather than harm. One of his most quoted teachings runs, in sense: "Sow flowers, that your garden may bloom about you; the thorns you plant will wound your own feet."

His poetry is at once popular and profound, simple enough for the unlettered to carry in memory and deep enough to nourish the mystic, and it has done more than any other book to shape the moral imagination of the Pashtuns. His verses are sung to the *rabab*, a plucked string instrument, and recited in gatherings, and his name is spoken with an affection given to no other Pashto poet. His poetry also reflects a sadness and an ascetic feeling not often found among the mystical poets of his period. His verse has reached readers abroad in selections, among them Jens Enevoldsen's *Selections from Rahman Baba*, published in 1977.

## The Shrine

Rahman Baba's mausoleum at Hazarkhwani has long been a centre of pilgrimage and of Pashto literary life. Poets and singers gather there, and an annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, is held in his honour with music and *mushaira*, a poetic assembly, alongside the rites of devotion.

In March 2009 the shrine was severely damaged by a bombing, an attack on the tolerant, musical devotion it represents, though accounts of the attack differ. It was afterwards rebuilt, and pilgrims and lovers of his poetry returned. It remains the great shrine of the Pashto speaking world.

## The Setting

Peshawar is an old city; in earlier writings its name also appears as Parshawar and Farshawar. In the reign of Aurangzeb, the district of Peshawar had grapes, peaches and melons like those of Turan in Central Asia; heat, cold, seasons and rain like those of Hindustan; rice better than Bengal's; and crops and grain in plenty. The district was then the home of the Mohmand Afghans and others, and it was into the Mohmand tribe that Rahman Baba was born.

Three roads led from Peshawar to Kabul in that age. One went by Nikshab, hard and long. Another joined the highway at Jalalabad, with narrow defiles, little water and Afghan raids. The third went by Ali Masjid and the Khyber Pass; it was easier than the others and was used by armies and caravans.

The city's religious past goes back long before the poet. From the eleventh century the Nath yogis, an order of ascetics devoted to yoga, began to spread throughout northern India, and from their centre at Peshawar they moved to all parts of Central Asia and Iran, at the same time influencing both the Sufis and the *qalandars*, the wandering dervishes.

## Legacy

Rahman Baba stands to Pashto as Bhittai stands to Sindhi and Bulleh Shah to Punjabi: he is the poet who gave his people's language its deepest and most beloved voice, and he is usually regarded as the best mystical poet in Pashto. For three centuries his gospel of love, humility, tolerance and the emptiness of worldly pride has been a moral compass for the Pashtuns, and his *Diwan* a household treasure. His shrine at Peshawar, rebuilt after violence, endures as the hearth of Pashto poetry and the resting place of a saint whose verse still teaches a gentler way.

Name: Ram Mandir, Saidpur (Ram Kund Mandir)
Location: Saidpur Village, Margalla Hills, Islamabad Capital Territory, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: 16th century (traditionally attributed to Raja Man Singh I)
Events: Heritage/tourist site; regular worship discontinued
Description:
## Overview

The Ram Mandir, also known as the Ram Kund Mandir, stands in the historic village of Saidpur, set in a fold of the Margalla Hills on the northern edge of Islamabad. It is a Hindu temple dedicated to Lord Rama, traditionally dated to the sixteenth century and attributed by some to Raja Man Singh I, the Rajput general of the Mughal emperor Akbar. Its sanctity is bound to the belief that Rama passed through this country during his exile. No longer a place of regular worship, the building is now a protected monument and a popular destination for visitors to Islamabad.

Rama himself, the divine hero of the *Ramayana*, the epic of his life, is honoured far beyond Saidpur: in the festivals of the Hindu year, on the pilgrimage to the goddess Hinglaj, and in the verse of Sufi poets, the mystics of Islam, who took up Ram as a name of God.

## The Temple

Tradition holds that Rama, with Sita and Lakshmana, passed through this country during the years of exile told in the *Ramayana*. The natural springs of the village, fed by the hill streams, were revered as sacred pools, and four of them are traditionally named for Rama, Sita, Lakshmana and Hanuman. Local memory also ties the site to the adjoining Ram Kund pond, where an annual fair once drew Hindus from across the district.

Before Partition, Saidpur was a place of notable interfaith coexistence, home to Muslims, Hindus and Sikhs together. Its skyline held a mosque, this Hindu temple and, from the early twentieth century, a Sikh *gurdwara*, a place of worship of the Sikh faith.

After 1947 the temple ceased to function as a place of worship, and for a time it was used as a girls' school. In the 2000s the Capital Development Authority restored Saidpur as a heritage and arts village, conserving the temple's fabric while its idols were removed and its images painted over. In 2006 it had the temple, by then vacated, formally cleared and preserved as a tourist attraction. Since then, visitors have documented restaurants operating within the complex and serving meat dishes, a practice Hindu commentators have criticised as an affront to the site's sanctity.

The building survives as a protected monument and a popular destination for visitors to Islamabad. The local Hindu community, however, has not been permitted to resume regular rituals there, a matter on which Hindu representatives continue to appeal. In 2020 regular Hindu worship there was still barred.

## Rama and the Ramayana

Rama, to whom the temple is dedicated, is revered by Hindus as the seventh incarnation of the god Vishnu and as the divine hero of the *Ramayana*, who killed the demon king Ravana. Ram is also a Hindu name of God. Vishnu has been adored in the form of two of his ten incarnations, Rama and Krishna, and devotion has been paid to Rama and to his consort Sita.

In the epic, Sita, the wife of Rama, was the daughter of Raja Janak, and she is held to be the perfect woman. Ravana, the demon king of Lanka with ten heads, abducted her, and her rescue is the main theme of the epic. Rama's brother Lakshmana, also called Lachhman, shared his exile, and Lanka came under attack by Rama and Lakshmana. Hanuman, a follower of Rama, played a central role in the battle between Rama and Ravana. Rama banished Sita, sending her into *banwas*, exile from the land, and at the *ashram*, the hermitage, of Valmiki she bore his twin sons, Luv and Kush.

In the nineteenth century Rama's story was also told as the history of a royal line. As Raja Ramchandar he was the son of Dasrath, whose sons also included Bharat and Lachhman, Ramchandar's own full brother. Ramchandar was the eye and lamp of the Suraj Bansi, the solar line of kings, and in the belief of the Hindus he was an *avatar*, an incarnation of the divine, in the Treta age, one of the four ages of the world in Hindu reckoning. His tale ran through the *ban bas*, the exile in the forest, the story of Ravan and the bridge from the Deccan, and after him the rule remained among his descendants for a full five hundred years. By the reckoning of English historians, the first of his line lived two thousand or two thousand two hundred years before the Christian era, and Ramchandar twelve hundred years before it.

In the reign of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, a Persian translation of the *Ramayana* from the Sanskrit, containing the life of Sri Ram Chand, was counted among the famous books. In the same period the founding of Lahore was attributed to Lav, the son of a Raja Ram Chand.

Images of Rama are found elsewhere too. At a temple at Manora, tiles of Ram and Sita have had their faces wiped clean, and depictions of Ram and Sita are among the faded frescoes of the *samadhi*, the memorial, of Ranjit Singh. The demolition of the Babri Mosque was justified by the claim that the mosque had been built on the site of a Hindu temple, the birth site of Ram.

## Festivals of Rama

Rama's victory over Ravana is celebrated every year at the Hindu festival of Dussehra, when Ravana's effigy is ceremonially burnt. In one telling of Navratri, the festival of nine nights, Sita prayed for nine nights while Ravana and Rama fought. On the tenth day the goddess heard her plea, and Rama was able to kill Ravana and win the war; the burning at Dussehra, on the tenth day, is a remembrance of that victory.

It is said, too, that when Rama set out with his army for Lanka, he worshipped a little tree called the *cheonkul*, which stood near his capital of Ayodhya. At the festival of Dussehra a procession of more than seventy thousand people was once seen attending their prince to worship the tree.

Ram Navami celebrates the birth of Ram, a popular deity. Streets are lit, the entire community takes part, and Hindus have been celebrating it for centuries. It has been argued that the Muslim festival of Eid Milad-Un-Nabi, the birthday of the Prophet, was originally inspired by it.

## Rama on the Road to Hinglaj

No figure was ever as present in the representations of the traditional pilgrimage to the goddess Hinglaj as Rama. Its legend tells of Rama's *brahm hatyā*, the sin of killing a Brahmin, and of the pilgrimage he was sentenced to make. At the pass of Ungakhera Bherum Luk he was defeated by the goddess's army, and he fought a battle of twelve years. A condition was set that he come as a simple pilgrim from Ram Bagh; the goddess made a promise to those of his men who were excluded; Hanuman, Lakshmana and Sita worked miracles of water; and Rama carved a sun and a moon on the mountain opposite the temple of the goddess Hinglaj.

Rama's ninety six Brahmins, it is said, accepted Hinglaj as their clan goddess. According to legend, the Saraswat Brahmins had their *ṭīkā*, the mark on the forehead, from Rama: in need of a priest, and unable to find one in Balochistan, he simply applied a *ṭīkā* to the forehead of a *mlecch*, a barbarian. Lalu Jasraj is remembered as the *aguā*, the guide who led the way, of Rama's party.

Along the route he has his places of *pūjā*, or worship: the resting place of Rama, *rām jharoku* in Sindhi, and Khari Nadi, where people bathe in the ocean and worship Rama in the Rama *pūjā*. Of the journey of Rama and his entourage, part myth and part history, much has now been destroyed by the growth of Karachi.

## Rama in Sufi Poetry and Thought

Rama's name and story also run through Sufi poetry, where Ram can stand as a name of God. The Sufi poet Bulleh Shah appeals to him:

*When I realized this, I appealed to Ram: you and I are one, there is no one else in this house in the city of love* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

Elsewhere the lyrics speak of the *tilak*, the mark Hindus wear on the forehead:

*Sometimes you utter appeals to Ram, sometimes you put the tilak on your forehead.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

The epic enters his lyrics too. One line says to its addressee, 'you had Lanka plundered by Ram', and a passage recalls Kumbhakaran, Ravan and Lachhman:

*When Kumbhakaran goes back the way he came, the mystery of Lanka is created. Now that Ravan the ten-headed is destroyed and Lachhman remains, the unstruck music sounds.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

One such reference in the lyrics describes a reversal of the arrival of Kumbhakaran to assist his brother Ravan, when Ravan's capital of Lanka was under attack by Ram and Lachhman. In a poem of two lines headed NAMES, Bulleh Shah also sets the name Ram beside the name Allah, in an argument about the names given to God.

Waris Shah's romance of Hir and Ranjha invokes the epic in a single question:

*Did not a woman kill Ravana?* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

Later in the poem the epic returns as an analogy in a court of law, "This swindler took her away as Ravan ran away with Sita", a reference meant, it is explained, to curry favour with the Raja, who is a Hindu.

The Sufi poet Madho Lal Hussein uses Ram, with Sain, Rab and Maula, in place of Allah, and he uses it often. In his *kafis*, short mystical lyrics, it is the name to be recited and sung:

*Time to invoke, girl, let's rise and praise Ram* (translated by Naveed Alam)

*What's the joy of life / without the constant evocation of Ram?* (translated by Naveed Alam)

Other lines run "Praise Ram, I pranced all the way to the groom", "Sometimes rise and recite Ram in the morning", "You lose if you don't sing of Ram" and "Come, girl, let's praise Ram". One *kafi* addresses him directly, *The whole world begs your favours, O Ram*, and so does its Variation: *You are the great giver, O Rama*.

Mai Dhadli's Urdu song, sung at a dwelling of *fakirs*, wandering Sufis, in Sehwan, runs:

*Muhammad in one place, Ali in another, and yet elsewhere, Qalandar is Ram.* (translated by Omar Kasmani)

The memory of the saint there is said to span "Muhammad, Ali, or Ram".

Rama has his place in Sufi thought and Hindu devotion at large. The story of Rama and Sita has been read as one in which Ravana and Hanuman figure as two poles of mystical knowledge. Pitambar Pir has been identified with the Hindu god Rama, and Kabir's 'Nirguna Rama', Rama without attributes, has been set against Ram Chandar. Some held that Ram and Rahim, the Merciful, a Muslim name of God, were the same Being, and Rama was among the traditional names by which Hindus and Muslims invoked God, with Allah, Khuda, Sahib and Hari. In the usage of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith, Hari and Rama are names for a single formless God, not the deities of cult sites.

Among the Sufis, Sachal mentions Hindu gods such as Ram, Hanuman, Sita and especially Krishna, and he also refers to an episode of the *Ramayana*, Ram's return to Ayodhya. Qutub Ali Shah names Lakshmana and Sita, Ram and Krishna, and the *jogis*, the ascetics, are said to be fascinated by Rama. In certain lectures the Sufi *shaykh*, or master, Zauqi Shah described Krishna, Rama, Sita, Lakshmana and Guru Nanak as believers in the one true God and religious leaders with a Divine connection, or *nisbat*.

## The Setting

Saidpur lies on the northern edge of Islamabad, Pakistan's capital city. Rawalpindi is the twin city of Islamabad, and on Islamabad's outskirts stand the village of Nurpur Shahan and the shrine of Barri Imam.

In the heart of the Margalla Hills, where the federal capital lies, stands the Dharmarajika of Taxila: a *stupa*, a Buddhist relic mound, around which are the remains of a monastery and giant sculptures of Lord Buddha and Bodhisattva, the Buddha to be, dating back to the third century BCE. It is believed to have been built by the great Mauryan emperor Ashoka. A bodhi tree, the tree sacred to Buddhists, is said to grow in Islamabad, and another near Jhelum.

Name: Ramapir Temple, Tando Allahyar
Location: Tando Allahyar, Tando Allahyar District, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Ramapir Mela (1 Bhadva, three days)
Description:
## Overview

The Ramapir Temple at Tando Allahyar, in Sindh, is a Hindu shrine dedicated to *Ramdev Pir*, also called Ramapir or Baba Ramdev, a saint of Rajasthan venerated across western India and Sindh as a worker of miracles and a champion of the poor and of those of low caste. The temple is the focus of the annual *Ramapir Mela*, which is widely reckoned the second largest Hindu pilgrimage in Pakistan after the *yatra*, the pilgrimage journey, to Hinglaj. It is celebrated above all for the way its devotion reaches across the boundaries of community, drawing Muslims as well as Hindus into its festival.

## Ramdev Pir

Tradition remembers Ramdev Pir as a ruler and saint of medieval Rajasthan, held by his devotees to have been an incarnation of Krishna, who used his powers to defend the humble and to dissolve the barriers of caste. Accounts of when he lived differ; tradition places him in the fifteenth century, and he is said to have taken *samadhi*, the final meditation in which a holy man leaves the world, in the year 1459. His principal shrine stands at Ramdevra, also called Runicha, in the Jaisalmer region of Rajasthan, though the temple at Tando Allahyar has also been called his main temple.

His cult spread widely among both Hindus and the Muslim communities of the desert borderlands, so that he is honoured as a *pir*, the title of a Sufi spiritual guide, as readily as a Hindu saint. In Sindh he is still known as Rama Pir, and he is also the object of widespread worship in Gujarat and Rajasthan. Among the untouchable castes of Sindh, who venerated the goddess Devi as well as heroes raised to the rank of gods, he was one of the most popular of these deified heroes, alongside Pithoro Pir, Pabuji and Guga Pir.

He is very present among the untouchable castes, yet he is also venerated by the *Nathpanthis*, the followers of the Nath tradition of yogis, in Gujarat. Pithoro Pir, another of these heroes, is most often associated with figures of salvation, and of these Ramdev Pir is the most venerated. Most of the Meghwars who venerate Pithoro Pir also venerate Ramdev Pir, though the reverse is less sure. The images of the two saints seem to share a common model of holiness, founded on renunciation.

In Sindh today he is also honoured within the temples dedicated to the gods worshipped across India. In Karachi, for example, a painting of Ramdev Pir stands in the temple of Lakhshmi Narayan, and the city's Narayanpur neighbourhood has a Ram Pir temple of its own, a different place from the temple at Tando Allahyar.

## The Temple

The temple's legend tells that a devotee carried an earthen lamp from the original shrine at Ramdevra, some four hundred and sixty kilometres to the north east, across what is now the frontier between India and Pakistan, and enshrined its flame here, founding the temple in his master's honour. The building itself dates from the British colonial period, and is traditionally placed in the middle of the nineteenth century, around 1859.

Beyond the days of its fair, the temple serves the settled Hindu population of Tando Allahyar and the surrounding district, a community with deep roots in the agrarian society of lower Sindh. The cult of Ramdev Pir, with its emphasis on the dignity of the poor and the irrelevance of caste before the divine, has long held a special appeal for communities at the margins, and the temple remains a place where that message is renewed in song and ritual. Many of Pakistan's Hindus, especially in the rural areas, follow either the teachings of local Sufi *pirs* or those of Ramdev Pir.

## The Ramapir Mela

The temple's fame rests chiefly upon its great fair, or *mela*. Held on the first day of the month of *Bhadva*, which falls in August or September, the Ramapir Mela is a pilgrimage of three days that draws thousands of the faithful from across Sindh and beyond. Its rites unfold in a rhythm of flags hoisted at dawn, barefoot processions, the singing of *bhajans*, or devotional songs, offerings of coconuts and lengths of cloth, and the communal *langar*, the free kitchen that feeds all comers without distinction.

What most strikes observers of the mela is its shared character. Hindu ritual predominates: the *aarti*, the waving of lamps before the deity, the offerings and the devotional song. Yet the festival's appeal has never been confined to a single community. Muslim devotees, too, come to the shrine, offering *chadars*, the embroidered sheets laid upon the tombs of Sufi saints, and joining the processions. It is a fusion of Hindu temple worship and the idiom of the Sufi *dargah*, the shrine of a Sufi saint, that is characteristic of the folk religion of Sindh. In a country where the Hindu minority is small and often anxious, the Ramapir Mela stands out as a rare and vivid expression of a devotional culture that both faiths can share.

## The Setting

Sindh is home to the majority of Pakistan's Hindus, whose number is put at between 6 and 10 million, an estimate that varies widely. Despite mass migration, the Hindus of Sindh still number several millions. Over 90 per cent of Pakistan's Hindus belong to underprivileged Hindu tribes or subcastes, such as the Meghwar, the Bhil and the Kohli, who often work as manual labourers for the powerful landowning elite of Sindh. Since Partition the majority of the Hindus of Sindh have belonged to the low castes. Some name them Dalits, the people of the castes once held untouchable, and some even claim they are not Hindu; among the Hindus there is a debate over whether the term "Dalit" is relevant. The Sufi legacy is still alive among the Dalits of Sindh. Most of the country's remaining non-Muslims are Hindus living in southern Punjab, inner Sindh and Baluchistan.

Several of these communities look east, across the present border, towards the Rajasthan of Ramdev Pir's own legend. Contrary to popular belief, there were many untouchables in Sindh, among them the Bhils or Kohlis and the Meghwars, who are mostly settled around Umerkot, and many of them are thought to have migrated from Gujarat or Rajasthan between 1843 and 1872. The Kohlis are the indigenous peasant communities of Sindh, sometimes migratory, and together with the Bhils they are the native inhabitants of the lands that run on from Sindh into Rajasthan. There is evidence of roving minstrels in that region, and the Manganhar are its hereditary professional musicians.

Sindh offers common ground to Hindu and Muslim devotion. As early as 1851 it was observed that the worship of the intercessors, the saints who plead for the faithful, was the common religious idiom of Hindus and Muslims. In Sindh a number of sacred figures have a dual identity, Muslim and Hindu: the Muslim side is always tied to Sufism, while the Hindu side usually belongs to the Nathpanth. Hindus of Sindh have come to the Sufi mausoleums since the nineteenth century, and the large majority used to visit the Sufi shrines; this does not make them Sufis, but for them the Sufis are part of their religious legacy. Sindh's geography, at once isolated and a buffer zone, has made it host to many unorthodox forms of Hinduism and Islam. Hindu participation in the Muslim mystical orders has been more visible in Sindh than in the Punjab, and Hindu writers wrote mystical poems in the imagery of the Muslims. The south of Pakistan, Sindh above all, offers a whole range of places of salvation, visited by different religious communities and joined in a network of pilgrimage routes.

That shared devotion has not meant a history without strain. The Hindus of Pakistan, Sindh included, are said to be more and more under threat from the country's radical Muslims, and after the demolition of the Babri Mosque on 6 December 1992 Hindu communities in Sindh and Quetta were attacked. In the early twenty first century, government funding for minority places of worship brought a wave of restorations, and many temples across Sindh were renovated, coinciding with changes in the political landscape.

## Legacy

The Ramapir Temple at Tando Allahyar is at once a major centre of Hindu pilgrimage in Pakistan and a living emblem of Sindh's syncretic religious temperament. In the flame said to have been carried from Ramdevra, in the pilgrims who walk barefoot to its doors, and in the Muslim chadars laid alongside Hindu offerings, it preserves a vision of shared sanctity that has become increasingly precious. Second only to Hinglaj among the Hindu pilgrimages of the country, it testifies to the endurance of the faith and to the older, more porous boundaries of devotion in the Indus lands.

## Bibliography

- Dominique-Sila Khan, *Conversions and Shifting Identities: Ramdev Pir and the Ismailis in Rajasthan* (Manohar).
- Michel Boivin, studies of the shared religious culture and shrines of Sindh.
- Contemporary press coverage of the annual Ramapir Mela (Dawn, The Express Tribune).
- Reports of the Pakistan Hindu Council on the temples and festivals of Sindh.
- Regional gazetteer material on the cult of Ramdev Pir and Ramdevra.
- Michel Boivin, *The Hindu Sufis of South Asia: Partition, Shrine Culture and the Sindhis in India* (London and New York: I.B. Tauris / Bloomsbury Publishing Plc, first published 2019).
- Jürgen Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi: Identity, Change, and Solidification at a Hindu Temple in Pakistan* (New York: Oxford University Press, 2018; print line 2017).
- Shemeem Burney Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual* (Austin: University of Texas Press, 2002).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* (Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina Press, 1975; 35th Anniversary Edition, 2011).
- Haroon Khalid, *A White Trail: A journey into the heart of Pakistan's religious minorities* (westland ltd, 2013; first e-book edition).

Name: Ranmal Sharif
Events: Annual urs; qawwali and naat; langar
Description:
## Overview

At Ranmal Sharif, near Phalia in the Mandi Bahauddin region of the Punjab, stands the shrine of Hazrat Syed Muhammad Noushah Ganj Bakhsh (1552 to 1654), the founder of the Naushahia branch of the Qadiri Sufi order. A saint of long life and wide influence, he established a spiritual line that spread across the Punjab and beyond and endures to this day. His *darbar*, or shrine, is the mother shrine of that order and remains an important centre of pilgrimage; its yearly *ʿurs*, the commemoration of the saint's death, draws great crowds.

Noushah Ganj Bakhsh is remembered both as a saint of powerful blessing and as the organiser of an enduring order. He lived through a full century of the Mughal age, and in the 1870s the *faqirs*, or Sufi mystics, of his path in the Punjab numbered in the thousands.

## The Saint

Muhammad Noushah was born in 1552. He is honoured as *Ganj Bakhsh*, 'the bestower of treasure', and as *Noushah*, 'the bridegroom', and he is also known as Haji Muhammad. He is remembered as a *wali*, a friend of God, from his birth. It is said that states of *jazb* and *sukr*, the rapture of a soul drawn towards God and spiritual intoxication, of love and longing, dominated him, and that he had no equal in asceticism, in piety and in *karamat*, the miraculous deeds of a saint.

His father, Haji Ala al-Din, was himself a great elder, who performed the Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, seven times and, it is said, was honoured with a vision of the Prophet. His mother, Bibi Jiwani, was also a great worshipper and ascetic. He had a brother, Shaikh Ismail. A story is told, too, of the marriage of his daughter, at which the bride's side demanded a hundred rupees of *lagan*, customary wedding dues, after the custom of the Muslims of the Punjab.

By the age of seventeen he had completed the outward sciences. Then he renounced the world and gave himself to *zikr*, the remembrance of God, in a reed bed of the Sandal Bar or the Gondal Bar, for accounts differ over which. His parents would not leave him there. When he came away, Mulla Karim al-Din brought him to Shah Sulaiman Qadri, at whose hands he took *bai'at*, the oath by which a disciple pledges himself to a *pir*, a spiritual guide, and within a few years he had reached completion on the path. He became Shah Sulaiman's *khalifa*, his spiritual deputy.

He took the Sufi path in the Qadiri order, the order founded by Abd al-Qadir Gilani, and, attaining a high spiritual station, founded his own branch of it, the *Naushahia*, also called the Naushahia Qadiria, which he spread with great energy across the Punjab. Over his long life he guided a vast body of disciples and built a network of successors.

Accounts of the year of his death differ, as do accounts of where he lies. The year his shrine keeps is 1654, when he died full of years, and he rests at Ranmal Sharif, which became the seat of his line. A Persian chronogram, a verse whose letters, counted as numbers, give a year, marks his passing; its last line carries the phrase *pir-e fayyaz*, 'the bountiful pir'.

حضرت حاجی محمد پیر نوشہ گنج بخش
آنکہ شد مشہور در اہل جہاں اجلال او
کرد چوں آخر عروج از فرش بر عرش بریں
پیر فیاض است ہم اہل سخاوت سال او

## His Disciples

Two of his *khalifas* were renowned: Abdul Rahman, called Pak Rahman, and Pir Muhammad Sachyar. Pak Rahman was his great *khalifa*, and it is said that his master showed him a favour shown to no one else. In the 1870s Pak Rahman's own radiant tomb was a place of pilgrimage.

One chain of succession runs from Noushah Ganj Bakhsh to Pir Muhammad Sachyar, from him to Shah Farid Lahori, and on through Muhammad Siddiq and Rahman Shah to Fazl Shah. In the 1870s most of the disciples of this line were in the city of Lahore, and the line received material support from the Sikh state through Raja Dina Nath. The spiritual pedigree of Shah Kamaita, too, leads back to Noushah Ganj Bakhsh.

Four of his disciples were *majzubs*, men absorbed in divine love, and each of them bore the name Naushahi: Shaikh Mittha, Sayyid Shah Abdullah, Nanu and Hafiz Tahir. Absorption so mastered Shaikh Mittha, it is said, that he wandered the wilderness and spoke with beasts and birds, and whoever he turned his attention upon became a *majzub* too.

Nanu's real name was Namak, but among the people he became known as Nanu. Hearing that on the Day of Judgement all men save the Prophet would be beardless, he bought tweezers and plucked out every hair of his beard and moustache. After his master's death he left for the wilderness and gave up living among people, and there highway robbers killed him. He is buried in a village of the Gujrat district.

## The Shrine and Its Devotion

The shrine at Ranmal Sharif is kept by the saint's descendants and successors and is a busy centre of pilgrimage. It maintains the customary devotions: prayer, *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, and *naat*, poetry in praise of the Prophet, together with *langar*, the free communal kitchen. Its annual *ʿurs* draws great crowds of the order's followers and of the wider devout. The Naushahia remain active across the Punjab and among the Punjabi diaspora, so that the shrine stands at the head of a living and widespread spiritual family.

In the 1870s it was said that everyone in the Naushahi order was a person of ecstasy and *sama*, spiritual listening, the Sufi session of music, and of longing, relish and intoxication. Most intoxicated of all at *sama* were the *faqirs* of the line of Pak Rahman. They would not cool until a rope was put round their feet and they were hung upside down, and so they danced for an hour or two; failing that, they were dragged along the ground, and the rope was not untied until they came to themselves. In the nineteenth century, too, the Naushahi followers had their *qawwali* and their *hal*, the state of ecstasy.

## Legends

His miracles, it is said, have no end, and the order's chronicle, the *Tazkira-e Naushahi*, sets them out in detail. Wonders are told of his birth. His father, it is said, set out three months into his mother's pregnancy, saying that the child would be a champion of the faith, and came back from the journey to Mecca when the boy was four. Hazrat Shah Sulaiman, the *qutb* of the age, the axis of the saints in his time, foretold the birth and counselled the family.

Tradition also tells of his youth. He grew up strong and fought in many battles. In the wilderness he fasted without a break and was fed each night with milk, and while studying at a village near Nowshera he learned the whole Quran by heart in a single night.

Two more of his wonders are told through his disciples. Sayyid Shah Abdullah, a *mansabdar*, an officer holding rank, at the court of the emperor Alamgir, came to Noushah Ganj Bakhsh when the saint lay ill, with one day left before his death. The saint accepted his *bai'at* and gave him leave for *zikr* and spiritual practice. But Shah Abdullah insisted on becoming a *majzub*. To remain detached amid attachments, the saint answered, is the work of men; becoming a *majzub* is easy. He gave way only when Shah Abdullah invoked God between them. Left with no choice, the saint gave him a shirt he had worn for some days and told him to put it on, and as soon as Shah Abdullah wore it, it is said, the angelic realm was disclosed to him.

Hafiz Tahir had left Islam and joined a party of Hindu *faqirs*, or ascetics. One day the party passed the saint's house, and he ordered wheat to be given to every one of them. All received it except Hafiz Tahir, for the grain had run out. Then the saint called the stranger by name, telling Hafiz Tahir to come to him, for his share was with the saint. He ordered his servant to take off the man's shirt and break the sacred thread at his neck, and Hafiz Tahir became a Muslim anew; with a single look, it is said, the saint brought him to God.

## Writings and Chronicles

The saint was also a poet. His Urdu and Punjabi verse was selected and edited by Sayyid Sharafat Naushahi as *Ganj-e Sharif* and published at Lahore in 1975.

The Naushahia line has its own written history, in works that include the *Risala al-Ijaz* of Mirza Ahmad Beg Lahori (1107 AH), on the lives of the shaikhs of the Naushahia line, which also carries Razi al-Din Qazi Ganjahi's *Risala Tuhfa-e Razwiya*; Sadaqat Muhammad Mah Ganjahi's *Thawaqib al-Manaqib* (1126 AH); the *Tazkira-e Naushahi* (1146 AH); the *Sahaif-e Qudsiya* of Pir Kamal, son of Shaikh Usman Lahori, and Imam Bakhsh Barqandazi Jalandhari's *Mirat al-Ghafuri*, both of 1186 AH; Muhammad Ashraf Manjri's *Kanz al-Rahmat* (1220 AH), printed at Lahore in 1330 AH; Ghulam Muhi al-Din Faqir Lahori's *Tashrif al-Fuqara*; and Sayyid Sharafat Naushahi's own *Sharif al-Tawarikh*, three volumes of seven thousand pages kept in manuscript by its author.

The *Tazkira-e Naushahi* was composed by Hafiz Sayyid Muhammad Hayat Rabbani Naushahi Sahnpalvi, who died in 1173 AH. It began as an annotated copy of the *Risala al-Ijaz* with additions, and it holds only the affairs of the Naushahia elders; four of its manuscripts are in Sayyid Sharafat Naushahi's library and two in the Punjab University Library. Other works of the order include Umar Bakhsh Rasulnagri's *Manaqibat-e Naushahi*, Ghulam Qadir Naushahi's *Bayaz-e Qadri*, Gul Muhammad Naushahi's *Lataif-e Gul Shahi* and the *Kitab al-Fawaid*, the last three among the family's manuscripts. In modern times most of the order's manuscripts have been kept in a private Naushahi library at Sahanpal, in Gujrat.

## The Setting

Phalia, the town near the shrine, has a story of its own. It is said that the town was named after Bucephalus, the legendary horse of Alexander, so that Phalus became Phalia, and that the horse's grave is there. The story has been disputed, on the grounds that the horse was buried near Jalalpur, on the other bank of the river, where his grave was swept away by a flood only a few months later; that coins of the Indo-Greek era found on the *pahari*, the old mound of Phalia, gave birth to the rumour; and that the version became popular in the colonial era, when British officers roamed all over the country collecting oral history.

In the early twenty first century the old mound held a government office and a school. An old shopkeeper reported that the department had sold it for nine *crore* rupees, a *crore* being ten million, and that a shiny new shopping plaza would stand there.

## Legacy

Syed Muhammad Noushah Ganj Bakhsh is remembered as the founder of the Naushahia Qadiri order, one of the enduring Sufi lines of the Punjab, a saint whose long life and organising genius planted a spiritual family that has lasted nearly four centuries. His shrine at Ranmal Sharif remains its living heart and a major centre of Qadiri devotion in the region.

His spiritual line also reached Lahore. In the 1880s the spiritual pedigree of Jawahar Shah, keeper of a tomb outside the city's Mochi Gate, passed through Alahi Shah, Gami Shah and Pak Rahman up to Noushah Ganj Bakhsh. Jawahar Shah rebuilt that tomb and made its mosque *pakka*, of fired brick, and he became its *sajjada nashin*, the custodian who sits on the prayer carpet of the saint buried there; a hall, a small room and a well for the comfort of the *faqirs* stood within its enclosure.
