Name: Sadh Belo (Sadh Belo Island Temple)
Location: Sadh Belo Island, near Sukkur/Rohri, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Annual festival (boat pilgrimage to the island)
Description:
## Overview

Sadh Belo is a temple complex on a wooded island in the River Indus, between the twin cities of Sukkur and Rohri in Sindh. One of the most important living centres of Hindu worship in the province, it belongs to the *Udasi* tradition, the ascetic order that traces its lineage to Sri Chand, elder son of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith, and so it stands where Hindu and Sikh devotion meet. Pilgrims reach it by boat across the river, and its annual festival gathers Hindus from across Sindh and beyond.

The complex spreads across two connected islets, with temples, shrines, *samadhis*, the memorial tombs of holy men, gardens, a communal kitchen and living quarters. It was founded in the early nineteenth century amid the palms and greenery that give the island its name.

## Baba Bankhandi and the Island

The founding of Sadh Belo is attributed to the *Udasi* saint Baba Bankhandi Maharaj, born Balchand Sharma, whose origins are variously traced to Kero Khetar near Delhi or to Nepal. As a young spiritual seeker, still in his teens, he is said to have arrived in 1823 in Sukkur, then a flourishing trading hub of the subcontinent. Drawn to the tranquil, forested island in the Indus, he settled there and made it a place of meditation and worship, and it came to be known as *Sadhu Belo*, "the woods of the sage". Under Baba Bankhandi and the line of *gaddi nashin*, the spiritual successors who followed him, the island grew into a substantial religious establishment.

Baba Bankhandi is credited with establishing places of worship dedicated to Hindu deities including Annapurna, Hanuman, Ganesh and Shiv Shankar, while also providing for the *Guru Granth Sahib*, the scripture of the Sikhs, and the *Bhagavad Gita*, a Hindu scripture, to be venerated side by side, an expression of the inclusive *Udasi* spirit.

Much of the architecture seen today, the principal temple among it, was raised somewhat later. The main shrine is generally dated to the closing years of the nineteenth century, when it was built under the eighth successor in the line, Sant Harnam Das, and it was further embellished in the decades that followed.

The temple is also counted among the works of princely patrons. The amirs, or rulers, of Khairpur were themselves staunch Shia Muslims, and in the nineteenth century they built beautiful *imambaras*, halls for the Shia rites of mourning. That did not prevent them from being generous patrons of religious buildings of every kind, and the famous *Udasi* temple at Sadh Belo was created thanks to a gift of land.

The principal island, Sadh Belo itself, holds the temples, verandahs and a kitchen in the manner of a *langar*, the free communal kitchen, which fed pilgrims and residents. The adjoining island, sometimes called Deen Belo, holds *samadhis*, a park and the Rishi Nol *mandir*, or temple. Reached by boat across the Indus, the complex offered pilgrims a sacred world complete in itself in the midst of the river, its white temples and shaded courtyards standing out against the surrounding waters.

## The Udasis and the Path of Nanak

The character of Sadh Belo flows from its roots in the *Udasipanth*, the *Udasi* path. This religious and ascetic movement grew from the teachings of Sri Chand, the elder son of Guru Nanak, and blended devotional streams in a way that resists neat sectarian classification, honouring Sikh scripture and Hindu deities alike and cultivating a tradition of renunciation, pilgrimage and hospitality. Sadh Belo became one of the foremost seats of *Udasi* religious life in Sindh.

The temple belongs to a wider world of devotion in the province. In Sindh many Nanakpanthis, followers of the Nanakpanth or "the path of Nanak", belonged to a subgroup known as the *Udasis*, and in the nineteenth century the Nanakpanth was probably the dominant religious path among Hindu Sindhis. Among the Lohanas, a trading community, and related mercantile groups, two main cults were followed, the Nanakpanth and the Daryapanth, the path of the river.

In the colonial period the religious life of the province was recast, and several important Nanakpanthi *darbars*, or shrines, were created and developed throughout Sindh. Some had been created in the late eighteenth century, but the second half of the nineteenth century saw a renaissance of the Nanakpanthi *darbars*. The word *darbar* itself was used by Sikhs, Muslims and Hindus alike.

Many Lohanas in Sindh follow the teachings of Nanak, which somewhat obscured their religious affiliation in the eyes of colonial officers: in the census of 1881 Lohanas from Shikarpur and Hyderabad were counted as Sikhs, while ten years later, in the census of 1891, they were classified as Hindus. In the wake of the Singh Sabha, a movement of Sikh reform, the Sindhi Nanakpanthis were not included in the Sikh community, and they identified themselves as a Hindu religious sect, although the *Udasis* of Sindh have also been described as a heterodox Sikh tradition.

Today many middle and upper class Hindus in Sindh follow the path of Nanak, and it is common to cover one's head before walking into a *tikana*, as Sindhi calls the temple containing the *Guru Granth Sahib*. The Nanakpanthi temples of Sindh and southern Punjab hold portraits of Guru Nanak alongside Hindu deities, and these communities are found in very large numbers in Sindh. The communities who refused the Khalsa, the order of initiated Sikhs, and called themselves followers of Guru Nanak still exist in Sindh and in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and baptised Sikhs look down upon them.

## Worship and Festivals

The island remains the focus of an annual festival that gathers Hindus from across Sindh and beyond. Boats ferry the pilgrims to the island for days of worship, music and communal meals, and its kitchen has long fed pilgrims and residents alike.

The river crossing was the pilgrims' way to the island in the colonial period too. At the time of the riots at Sukkur, the local Hindus opposed the rehabilitation of a site in the harbour on the Indus, because it was from that harbour that pilgrims reached the sacred site of Sadh Belo.

The temple's hospitality also reached a pilgrim bound for the goddess Hinglaj. On his way, the pilgrim, Shastri, went to Sadh Belo, which he was told was a *tirtha*, a Hindu place of pilgrimage, on an island in the Indus in the city of Sukkur. There the *mahant*, the superior of the monastery, its abbot, grew very fond of Shastri and gave him supplies and advice for his pilgrimage. The advice was practical. The abbot told him to carry plenty of onions in case drinking water ran short, for the juice of an onion would help stave off nausea and dizziness as well as provide liquid.

## Partition and After

The Partition of 1947 dispersed much of Sindh's Hindu population. By early November 1947, 246,000 Hindus had already left Sindh by sea, air or rail, and by 1 January 1948 nearly 500,000 people were estimated to have sought refuge in India; many Hindu Sindhis began to leave especially after the Karachi riots of January 1948.

Partition put the future of Sindh's many shrines in doubt, yet Sadh Belo endured as one of the most significant functioning Hindu sites in Pakistan. It has continued to be maintained by its custodians and to draw devotees, and its survival has made it a cherished anchor for the Hindu community of the region. Accounts differ over what Partition meant for Sadh Belo, but on its island it is counted a rare instance of continuity across that rupture.

Across Sindh, the *darbars* left behind were most of the time preserved under different arrangements for their management, often with *gaddi nashins* or followers in India paying keepers, and despite the fluctuating diplomatic relations between Pakistan and India it was always possible to travel across the border. Sindh is home to the majority of Pakistan's Hindus, and in the early twenty first century government funding for the places of minority communities could be seen in a wave of restorations of temples across the province.

## The Setting

Sukkur, Rohri and Shikarpur form a triangle of northern Sindh rich in sanctuaries. On both sides of the Indus there are remarkable ones such as Khwaja Khizr, on an island, Sadh Belo, on another island, and the *dargah*, the Sufi shrine complex, of Sachal Sarmast.

Between December 1939 and February 1940 there were riots at Sukkur, and they also occurred beyond the city, in Rohri and in other parts of Sindh such as Lakki. In Sehwan, unlike other cities of northern Sindh such as Sukkur after the Manzilgah riots, no communal violence had ever been registered.

Rohri was the birthplace of the Sufi Rochaldas, born there in 1879 to a family remembered as modest, and of the poet Bedil, also a Sufi, who died in 1872, a prolific writer in five languages. Janullah of Rohri, a mystic of the Suhrawardi order of Sufis, was one of the outstanding Persian poets of Sindh in the second half of the eighteenth century. The singer Alan Faqir is said to have sung on the buses and trains between Rohri and Sehwan Sharif in his youth.

In the *Janamsakhis*, the traditional stories of Guru Nanak's life, the Guru comes from Multan to Sukkur, and from there turns southwards along the Indus. Sukkur also appears in Mughal history. In the pursuit of Dara Shikoh, news reached the pursuing armies that Dara, having passed Bhakkar, had halted at Sukkur on the 25th of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic year. The Mughal commanders who crossed towards Sukkur lost many beasts to the thickness of the jungle, the press of thorny trees and the hard stages of the road; the baggage did not come up, and on the 6th of Safar, the second month of the Islamic year, they reached Sukkur. Shaikh Mir stayed a day at Sukkur, where the *zamindars*, the landholders, told him that a road branches off towards Qandahar twenty five *kos*, an old measure of distance, from Sukkur, and a *faujdar*, a military governor, was appointed for Sukkur.

## Legacy

Sadh Belo stands as a testament to Sindh's plural religious heritage and to the enduring vitality of the *Udasi* tradition on the banks of the Indus. A place of active pilgrimage and a monument to the syncretic devotion of Baba Bankhandi and his successors, the island temple remains one of the most beloved sacred sites of Hindu Sindh, its shrines rising from the river much as they have for two centuries.

Its name now stands in two places. Among the Sindhi *darbars* of India is a Sadh Belo in Mumbai, in Maharashtra, which was transferred from Sukkur, though in the Mumbai Sadh Belo it is difficult to see any architectural continuity with the Sadh Belo on its island in the Indus.

Name: Sain Vali Vilayat Rai Darbar, Kambar
Location: Shivalo mohalla, Kambar (Qambar) town, Qambar–Shahdadkot District, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Commemoration of Sain Vali Vilayat Rai; Nanakpanthi worship
Description:
The darbar of Sain Vali Vilayat Rai stands in the *Shivalo* quarter of Kambar (Qambar), the headquarters town of the Qambar–Shahdadkot District of upper Sindh, and is described by the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro as the largest Nanakpanthi *darbar* in the district. Its founder, Vali Vilayat Rai, was born in 1825 into a prosperous Hindu family of Old Hala; his father, Pratab Rai, had served as a *munshi* (secretary) to the Talpur Mirs of Hyderabad. Vali Vilayat Rai settled first at Larkana and later moved to Kambar, where he chose the then-unpopulated Shivalo locality — remembered as a resort of *yogis*, *sants* and *sadhus* drawn from Kambar, Shahdadkot, Larkana and the surrounding towns — and there established his darbar, raising a great hall in which the *Guru Granth Sahib* was installed. Like the wider body of Sindhi Nanakpanthis, his followers venerate the Hindu deities together with Baba Guru Nanak, his son Baba Sri Chand, and the other Sikh Gurus, so that the darbar belongs at once to Hindu and to Sikh devotional worlds; it is entered here under "Hindu Temple" as the closest of the dataset's three categories, following the convention used for the other Sindhi *sant* darbars in this collection. The darbar and the *samadhi* (memorial shrine) of Vali Vilayat Rai remain at Kambar, and the lineage retains a devotional following, though — as with most Sindhi Hindu shrines — much of the community associated with it now lives in India. The saint is counted among a constellation of nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century Nanakpanthi masters of the Larkana country, among them Swami Dharmdas of Larkana and Bhai Waliram of Digano Mahesar.

According to a hagiographic account recorded by the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, Vali Vilayat Rai's turn to spiritual life followed his time as a *tapedar* (village accountant) under British rule: irregularities found in his accounts led to imprisonment, during which he is said to have received a vision of Guru Nanak revealing his own previous incarnation as a yogi; thereafter he is remembered as making an annual pilgrimage to the Sufi shrines of Rohri, Sehwan, and Jhok. The present darbar building, a three-storey structure with ornately carved doors and windows in a colonial idiom, is believed to have been erected in 1887. Leadership passed after his death to Sain Jiwat Singh, who ran a free dispensary for the poor of Kambar until his own death in 1899, and then to Jiwat Singh's chief disciple, Vishandas; a branch of the darbar was later established at Kandivali, Bombay (now Mumbai), in 1960, reflecting the wider migration of Sindhi Hindus after Partition.

Name: Sakhi Sarwar
Location: Sakhi Sarwar, Dera Ghazi Khan, Punjab
Events: Annual urs and pilgrimage; seasonal banner processions
Description:
## Overview

In the town of Sakhi Sarwar, also called Nigaha, at the foot of the Sulaiman range in the Dera Ghazi Khan district, stands the shrine of Sultan Sakhi Sarwar, a saint of the twelfth century honoured across an extraordinary breadth of communities. He is known by the loving title *Lakhdata*, "the giver of hundreds of thousands", for his boundless generosity. For centuries his cult was one of the most widespread in the western Punjab, drawing not only Muslims but Hindus and Sikhs, and his shrine at Nigaha remains a major place of pilgrimage in the southwest of the province.

Tradition holds that the saint pitched his tent at the foot of the mountain, where Nigaha now stands, and was martyred there; his tomb stands on the same spot. It has drawn pilgrims for centuries. In the reign of the emperor Aurangzeb the road to it from Multan was crowded with them, and the devotion has continued even after the shrine was bombed in 2011.

## The Saint

His name was Sayyid Ahmad Sultan, and he is called Sakhi Sarwar, "the Generous Chief". A Sayyid is a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad. He lived in the twelfth century, and tradition places his origins in the region of Multan and Shahkot; his life is wrapped in legend more than in documented history. He is counted among the ancient *mashaikh*, the Sufi masters, and the great *awliya*, the friends of God, of the Multan region, and he is remembered as a saint of miraculous power and open-handed charity.

His father was Sayyid Zain al-Abidin, and a genealogy traces the family back to Ali: Sayyid Ahmad was the son of Sayyid Zain al-Abidin, son of Sayyid Umar, son of Sayyid Abd al-Latif, son of Sayyid Baha al-Din, son of Sayyid Ghiyas al-Din, son of Sayyid Baha al-Din, son of Sayyid Salah al-Din, son of Sayyid Zain al-Abidin, son of Sayyid Isa, son of Sayyid Salih, son of Sayyid Abd al-Ghani, son of Sayyid Jalil, son of Sayyid Khair al-Din, son of Sayyid Zia al-Din, son of Sayyid Daud, son of Sayyid Abd al-Jalil Rumi, son of Sayyid Ismail, son of Imam Jafar Sadiq, son of Imam Muhammad Baqir, son of Imam Zain al-Abidin, son of Imam Husain, son of Ali.

Zain al-Abidin came from Arabia to Hind, as India was called, because of some dissension, and settled at a village in the Multan area. He was devout and ascetic and kept vigil through the night, and the headman of the village, Pira, gave him his daughter, Bibi Ayesha, in marriage. The headman is also said to have become his *murid*, his pledged disciple, and to have built a mosque. From Bibi Ayesha the saint was born, a *wali*, a friend of God, it is said, from his birth. There were two wives in his father's household, one of them the saint's mother, and the saint had a brother, Sayyid Abd al-Ghani. Zain al-Abidin lies with Sayyid Mahmud and Sayyid Sohrab in the burial place of his family, a place of pilgrimage for the people.

In his early youth, it is said, he mastered the *nafs-e ammara*, the commanding self, by hard austerities and by devotions beyond what can be borne, and the lamp of mystic knowledge lit the chamber of his inner being. After his father's death his fame spread, and people came to him in droves. His maternal cousins, with whom he owned half the village, grew jealous and tormented him, and he left.

Accounts of his masters differ. He is said to have gone to Baghdad and there to have received inward grace in the service of the Ghaus al-Azam, a title meaning the greatest helper; of Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi, called the Shaikh al-Shuyukh, the master of masters; and of Shaikh Maudud Chishti. He returned to Hind perfected. He is also said to have received the blessing of *wilayat*, sainthood, from Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan, and his family is counted as belonging to both the Chishti and the Suhrawardi Sufi orders. Back in the Punjab he lived for a while at Dhaunkal, and then returned to his village.

He married, though accounts of his marriage differ, and his wife is most often named Bibi Bai. He had a young son, but accounts differ over the boy's name, Siraj al-Din or Sayyid Raj.

## The Martyrdom

Warned of a plot against him, the saint left the village in secret with his brother Abd al-Ghani, his wife and his young son. At the foot of the mountain, in the very midst of a waterless wilderness, he pitched his tent, at the place where Nigaha now stands and where his tomb is. Tradition holds that by the blessing of his step God made a spring flow there out of the desert, and in the 1870s the spring was still there.

There he was martyred, in 577 AH by the Islamic calendar. Accounts differ over who killed him: some tell of his jealous kinsmen, who learned that he had gone, gathered a great company and rode after him; others of a fight with the Khokhars that broke out by chance, in which he and his brother were martyred. His wife and young son died too, with him or after him, and accounts of their deaths differ. The saint and his family were buried at the foot of the hills, and the tomb became known as the tomb of the martyr.

His memory was also set in verse. A Persian chronogram, a verse whose letters, read as numbers, yield a date, names him Sayyid, Sarwar and Sakhi Ahmad:

سید و سرور و سخی احمد
بود در ملک سروری والی
رفت چوں از جہاں بخلد بریں
شد زمین از وجود او خالی
سال تاریخ وصل آں سرور
گفت سرور کہ سرور عالی

The words that carry its date are its last two, *sarwar-e ali*. A second chronogram, written for his death, joins the names Sarwar and Sakhi Ahmad with the title *Sultan-e Alam*.

## The Shrine

The shrine complex, set in the hills, comprises the saint's tomb together with a mosque and associated buildings. The *darbar*, as the shrine is called, remains the defining landmark of its town. The tomb lies forty *kos*, the old measure of road distance, west of Multan, at the foot of the hills of Baluchistan.

In the reign of Aurangzeb the tomb was kept by the descendants of three men, one blind, one a leper and one impotent, who, it is said, had taken up attendance at the tomb and been cured. Devotees also tell of Shaikh Garha, who held the saint's horse while he prayed, and who brought people from the village of Kotli to sweep the *khanqah*, the lodge where a Sufi's disciples gather.

The hills of Baluchistan, at whose foot the tomb stands, were the Baloch borderland of the old *suba*, or province, of Multan. In the time of the Langahs, Sultan Husain Langah granted the country from Karorkot to Mankot in *jagir*, a grant of land and its revenue, to Malik Sohrab and other Baloch who had come to him from Kech Makran. In the reign of the emperor Akbar, Raja Todar Mal, the chief *diwan*, or minister of revenue, confirmed that country to the Baloch and set it as a strong outpost and barrier between Khurasan and Hindustan.

## Devotion and Pilgrimage

His devotees, the *Sultanias* or *Sarwarias*, carried his banners in seasonal pilgrimages, and until modern times his following crossed the boundaries of religion, with Hindus and Sikhs of the Punjab honouring him alongside Muslims; the Sikh tradition itself preserves references to the *Sakhi Sarwar* pilgrims. This shared devotion made him one of the great examples of the composite religious culture of the old Punjab. Devotees come to seek blessing, to fulfil vows and to honour the *Lakhdata*, and the annual pilgrimage and the *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, are great occasions of music, offering and celebration in the regional manner.

In the reign of Aurangzeb multitudes came from every region and corner of the world, gave *nazrs*, votive offerings, and asked for their wishes, which, it was said, were granted. The crowds were greatest at the beginning of winter, and the whole road from Multan to the tomb was full of people, a crowd beyond what writing could set down. The tomb is said to have become a place of pilgrimage after the healing of a Qandahar merchant's camel. In the same reign a place twelve *kos* from Sialkot, associated with Sultan Sarwar, was always a place of pilgrimage too: in summer people came to it from every region and offered *nazrs*, and for two months there was a great throng.

In the nineteenth century a caravan of the black blanket, its people in black caps, stopped in Lahore and went on towards a place some *kos* from Multan. When his pilgrims set out, they halted for a night at the sarai west of Jahangir's tomb in Lahore, and there were ten days of great festivity. It was said that in every village a house of the saint had been built.

Lahore also had a *chauki* of Sakhi Sarwar, a building in his name. In the nineteenth century it stood south of the sarai of Muhammad Shafi in the Anarkali Sadr Bazaar: a building shaped like a *kotha*, or house, with niches for lamps and a wooden door that had once been white and had turned black. It was not his tomb, nor any true place of his retreat. It had been built in his name, it was said, out of worldly desire, and it belonged to six men.

In the early twenty first century his shrine was one of a few Muslim places in Pakistan where Baisakhi, the spring harvest festival of the Punjab, was still celebrated, despite its being considered a non-Muslim celebration. Like other major shrines, it has been touched by the violence of recent years. On 3 April 2011 a suicide bombing at the shrine struck a procession of its pilgrims, and around fifty people were killed. Yet the devotion has continued.

## Legends

Devotees tell a long cycle of his miracles, set in his village and in Multan. In the village, it is said, goats were brought back to life by divine power, and a goat was given as an offering of thanks, while the villagers said that these were sorcerers. When the land was divided he answered that it did not matter, for it was their right, and the wheat he held in trust as a *faqir*, a mystic vowed to spiritual poverty, thrived. He killed a lion, and gave the heap away in the way of God to the *lagis*, the village servants who received a customary share of the harvest.

At Multan, the story goes on, the ruler saw an army and found a man with a shade over him. Sealed vessels that had been left empty were filled by the grace of God, and there was food of paradise. The saint's brothers were jailed, and he was dismissed with a splendid robe of honour. He said that all the prisoners in the jail were his brothers, so all were freed and the *nazr* was shared. *Faqirs* came asking for *iftar*, the meal that breaks a fast. The robe was cut into rags, and the horse was eaten, and by divine power the horse rose up alive and whole. His father, Zain al-Abidin, refused such a king, and the whole city was in uproar. The ruler offered a princess in marriage. Then all the *awliya* and *aqtab*, the saints and the poles of sainthood, came to the gate of Multan; in a contest of archery a khan missed the mark and a holy man hit it, and the *milni*, the meeting of the two families at a wedding, followed.

Devotees tell, too, of his martyrdom. A rider on the plumed mare killed a number of the enemy and was martyred, and the saint, at prayer while Shaikh Garha held his horse, destroyed their army. Then he turned to an old man, told him that he was his killer, and bade him come and martyr him, and he ordered Shaikh Garha and the *mukabbir*, who repeats aloud at prayer the call of God's greatness, to bury him. His widow, Bibi Bai, refused to marry again, and the grave opened and took her; her son Sayyid Raj, six months old, was swallowed after her.

## Legacy

Sultan Sakhi Sarwar is remembered as one of the most widely venerated saints of the old western Punjab, the open-handed *Lakhdata* whose cult, crossing the lines of Muslim, Hindu and Sikh, embodied the shared sacred world of the region before the divisions of modern times. After his death his shrine became the centre of a devotional cult of remarkable reach and endurance. In the reign of Aurangzeb crowds filled the road from Multan to his tomb; in the nineteenth century his pilgrims halted in Lahore and a house of the saint stood in every village; and in the early twenty first century Baisakhi was still kept at his shrine. His shrine at Nigaha endures as a major centre of pilgrimage and as a monument to that older, composite devotion.

Name: Samadhi of Maharaja Ranjit Singh
Location: Hazuri Bagh (near Lahore Fort), Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: Death anniversary commemoration (27 June); Vaisakhi pilgrimage season
Description:
## Overview

Immediately beside Lahore Fort and the Badshahi Mosque, on the spot where, by most accounts, his body was cremated, stands the samadhi, or memorial shrine, of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, one of the grandest funerary monuments of the Sikh Empire. Ranjit Singh, the "Lion of Punjab", founded the Sikh Empire and ruled it from 1801 until his death on 27 June 1839. Though formally a samadhi rather than a constituted gurdwara, a Sikh house of worship, the site has long been a living place of Sikh devotion, and it remains an active place of pilgrimage. The Evacuee Trust Property Board administers it as one of the most visited symbols of Sikh heritage remaining in Pakistan.

## The Maharaja

Ranjit Singh's family is traced back to one Kalu, and it kept shops in salt and tobacco. One of the family became the *chela*, or disciple, of a Sikh and stopped shaving, and Budh Singh took the *pahul*, the Sikh rite of initiation, at Amritsar; he rode a piebald mare and died in 1716. The line then divided: from Naudh Singh began Ranjit Singh's family, and from another branch the family of the Sandhanwalias. Naudh Singh was shot in 1742.

Charat Singh, an ancestor of the Maharaja, built a fort in the village of Gujranwala, became *sardar*, or chief, fought towards Jammu, and died. In those years Khwaja Abid, the Mughal *subadar*, or governor, of Lahore, attacked Charat Singh's fort, and victory fell to the Sikhs. Mahan Singh, Ranjit Singh's father, succeeded as a boy of ten, and he was the first to seize the collection of relics kept at Rasulnagar. Ranjit Singh was born in 1780. As a boy he had smallpox, and the illness cost him one eye.

After Mahan Singh's death, in the year 1211 of the Islamic calendar, when Shah Zaman Durrani came from Kabul, Ranjit Singh in fear sent his best goods and the relics of Rasulnagar from Gujranwala to his mother-in-law, Sada Kaur, at the fort of Makerian. He later pressed for them more than once and was refused, and under stronger pressure she moved them to the fort of Chunda. At last, when he had seized all her property, she gave them to his son Sher Singh, her grandson, who kept them by him until the day he was murdered; from him the collection passed through Hira Singh and Jawahar Singh to Lahore Fort under the English. By Ranjit Singh's order Faqir Nur al-Din was appointed to subdue Chatti, and the Faqir family then bought a second collection for themselves.

Starting from a small fief around Gujranwala, Ranjit Singh won Lahore at the end of the eighteenth century; accounts of how and in which year the city came to him differ. When he took it, Qazi Nizam-ud-Din was the city's *qazi*, or judge. In 1801 he was crowned Ruler of Punjab by Sahib Singh Bedi, a descendant of Guru Nanak.

He fought at Gujrat and elsewhere, took Kangra, and conquered Multan in 1818, when Nawab Muzaffar Khan was killed, and then the fort of Khyber; Jammu he granted to Gulab Singh and Suchet Singh. In 1802 he employed Akali Phula Singh, a Nihang, a member of an armed Sikh order, to capture the city of Amritsar, and Phula Singh brought two to three thousand Nihangs into the army of the state. He captured the Pathan regions of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the tribal areas, as a result of which several people converted to Sikhism. Besides the Punjab, Kashmir, the Derajat and other lands were in his possession, and his empire reached from the tribal areas to Kashmir, to Multan in the south and to the River Sutlej. His infantry, not less than seventy thousand strong, drew its pay through Bakhshi Bhagat Ram, and he came to terms with the British. He ruled in the Punjab for forty years, the first Punjabi to rule a land that for more than a thousand years had been ruled by Afghans, Mughals and others who were not Punjabis.

Among the great men of his court was Jamadar Khushal Singh, who received *havelis*, or mansions, and gardens in Lahore and Amritsar, and Dina Nath built a large temple to Shiva in Lahore. Faqir Aziz al-Din held the offices of prime minister and foreign minister, and his family went on living in their ancestral house inside the walled city of Lahore. The Faqir family were known in Lahore as the family of the Faqir sahibs and the *hakims*, the physicians. Among his generals were the Muslims Mohammad Sultan, Elahi Baksh and Ghaus Mohammad Khan. Hira Singh was the Maharaja's favourite, and while the Maharaja lived five rupees were put under Hira Singh's head every night.

The courtesan Moran held such favour with him that he never disobeyed her word. Coin was struck in her name, and the Moranshahi rupee was current throughout the Punjab; he built the village of Moranwala and the Moranwali mosque. Moran held her own court of justice and her own *darbar*, or audience, separately, and her word brought about the ruin of Mehr Muhkam and the destruction of Nawan Kot. He married Gul Begum with the *phere*, the rounds of the wedding rite, and the procession went from Lahore to Amritsar. In Lahore he built a mosque in a *mohalla*, or quarter, called Gul Begum, in memory of his Muslim wife, and another Muslim wife of his, Jind Kaur, ordered the construction of a library at Data Darbar.

## The Maharaja and Lahore

Under him Lahore began to be peopled again. Though none of its ruined outer quarters was resettled, the city within the walls was well peopled once more in the years of his rule, his courtiers laid out large gardens on the outer ruins, and until his death the city grew more populous day by day. He kept the city wall in constant, daily repair, had a deep ditch of masonry dug on all four sides, and put at each gate a bridge and a second solid gate, so that no enemy could ever take the city; he also ordered the deserted quarters resettled. One Nura, who fed his wheat on milk, won access to the court and an appointment to the digging of the ditch. Inside the Khizri Gate the Maharaja kept two lions in cages, for which the guards of the gate answered; the cages went under the British, but the name Shiran Wala Darwaza, the Gate of the Lions, stuck.

In the fort he renamed the Moti Masjid, the Pearl Mosque, as the Moti Mandir, the Pearl Temple, and kept the treasury of the state there, and in the 1880s the English government still kept the treasury of the Punjab province in it. He also restored the Shalamar garden.

He was a patron of shrines and holy men in and around Lahore. It was said of the *majzub* Subah Shah, one spiritually intoxicated and absorbed in divine love, that the outward king was the Maharaja; all the pillars of the state, with the Maharaja, held Subah Shah in regard, and Subah Shah prayed for him. The Maharaja and his successors down to Duleep Singh came every Saturday and gave *nazr*, offerings, and the *sajjada nishin*, the head of the shrine, received four or five thousand rupees each Saturday. Data Darbar received a yearly sum and some sweets, and the shrine of Mauj Darya a monthly allowance; he granted a well at the site of Ghore Shah; at the site of Mani Singh a *sadabart*, a standing distribution of food to the poor, of twenty five rupees a day ran under him; he visited Bhai Sahib Singh time and again; and he remained a heartfelt devotee of Syed Ali Shah all his life.

He also set up a *dera*, or camp, of four hundred *granthis*, readers of the Sikh scripture, with five standards, a *nagara*, or great kettledrum, and five hundred men with *qawwals*, singers of *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis. The samadhi at Shahid Ganj was completed in his reign, and he gave a fund and a *jagir*, a grant of land revenue, to the Baoli Sahib. When he became sovereign of the Punjab he spent large amounts of money on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras, attaching vast tracts of land to them so that their revenues could fund them. In his time Baba Sahib Singh Bedi was allotted vast tracts of land around Gujranwala and Lahore, on which he founded Bedian. The gurdwara of Panja Sahib was extended under him, and its frescoes were part of the original complex he built; he first erected the present structure of Dera Sahib and raised the present gurdwara at Mandi Mangat; and in his time the village of Maraka was repopulated a few kilometres from the ruins of the old one.

He also took from older monuments. In his time red, black and marble stones were torn down all around Lahore. At the tomb of the Emperor Jahangir the railings of marble, amber and red stone, worth lakhs of rupees, a lakh being a hundred thousand, were taken to the Darbar Sahib at Amritsar and set in the Ram Bagh; he had the lattices of the minarets pulled out, and the *jagirs* of the tomb's *mujawirs*, its attendants, were confiscated, leaving only the garden. The marble slabs and lattices of Mian Mir's tomb went to a *baradari*, a pavilion of twelve openings, at Amritsar, and the marble of the Sawan-Bhadon *baradaris* of the Shalamar garden was set in the Ram Bagh at Amritsar. The tomb and mosque of Shaikh Ashraf were demolished on his orders, and he had the stone pulled out of the tomb of Pir Hadi Rahnuma, on the road from Anarkali to Mian Mir, which had once been a building of stone. He had all the marble, worth lakhs of rupees, taken off the graves of Zakariya Khan; mosques were used as powder magazines; the mosque and tomb of Shah Sharaf were demolished for the glacis of the Bhati Gate, after which the coffin was reburied and, by his order, a small masonry platform was built over it; and Mohalla Saudagran was expropriated for the gurdwara of Guru Ram Das.

Beyond Lahore, in 1810 he seized the extensive holdings of the shrine at Pakpattan and allowed its *diwan*, the head of the shrine, and his retainers only a thousand rupees a year for their maintenance, drawn from the town duties of Pakpattan, with a fourth share of four small villages nearby. In his time the Sikhs took over the mosque at Shaheed Ganj, placed the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, inside it and made it a gurdwara, and the Muslims could do nothing then. It is said that the Badshahi Mosque was used as a stable for horses.

He was a devotee of Lahore's *majzubs*. He had complete faith in the majzub Mastan Shah Lahori and would give him thousands of rupees, which the majzub would not take; once he seated Mastan Shah on his own elephant to bring him to the fort, and the majzub jumped off. He was the devoted follower of Mai Bhagi Lahori, a *majzuba*, a woman absorbed in divine love, and though she abused him he would not leave her. He first offered her five hundred rupees as *nazr*, and she struck him with bricks more than once; the appointment of a Hindu pandit to a *diwani* post, in the civil administration of his court, was credited to her word. She refused Dhian Singh and Suchet Singh but came with Kharak Singh and stayed eleven days, a building at Kot Saeed was put up for ten thousand rupees, and her fame spread because the ruler was her devotee.

A story is told of him at the tomb of Mian Mir. He came to strip the tomb, it is said, but his horse Laili bolted, and he fell and was hurt; now, he said, he had been punished for his disrespect. In the story he gave five hundred rupees as an offering, ordered the tomb whitewashed, and remained a devotee of the saint and respectful of its *mujawirs*.

## His Death and His Heirs

Ranjit Singh died on 27 June 1839. Ill and near his end, it is told, he sent for the majzub Taj Shah Lahori and asked him for his health, and the *faqir*, the poor wandering mystic, answered that death is for everyone, as the Maharaja's father and the faqir's own father had died, and that sandalwood should be brought to burn him. Hearing this, the story goes on, the Maharaja lost hope, and as Taj Shah left the fort he gave up his life. Tradition holds, too, that on that very day the faqir foretold the ruin of the Sikh kingdom: it would last nine more years, and then the Firangis, the Europeans, would be masters of the Punjab. Taj Shah himself died in the year 1261 of the Islamic calendar.

At the Maharaja's death the buildings of the Baoli Sahib were still going up, and they were left unfinished. His son, Maharaja Kharak Singh, sat after him on the throne of the government of the Punjab. After the Maharaja's death the city did suffer slight blows at the hands of the Sikh army itself.

After the deaths of Kharak Singh and Nau Nihal Singh, Rani Chand Kaur became mistress of the kingdom, set on the throne by the Sandhanwalias, close kin of hers and of the Maharaja, and Raja Dhian Singh withdrew in anger to Jammu. Dhian Singh told Sher Singh that, God willing, he would soon be ruler of the Punjab. Sher Singh came to the throne and was murdered, and his killers were destroyed after a siege of Lahore Fort and a great battle. Raja Hira Singh, minister to Duleep Singh, fled on the pretext of a hunt on the day he was killed; the Sikhs pursued and killed him and made Jawahar Singh minister, and the heads of Raja Hira Singh and Pandit Jalla were hung from a gutter spout.

A treaty was made in 1846, with a Resident at Lahore, and in 1849 the British annexed the Punjab. In December 1849 Duleep Singh, the last Maharaja of the Punjab, left Lahore, and a *qitʿa*, a short poem, was written on his departure. When he had been exiled and English rule was complete, the troops left the Badshahi Mosque.

## The Samadhi

Construction of the samadhi began in the month after the Maharaja's death, under his son Kharak Singh, and it was largely completed by 1848 under his youngest son, Duleep Singh; the British funded the final repairs after their annexation of the Punjab in 1849.

The building brings together Sikh, Hindu and Islamic styles. Gilded, fluted domes and cupolas rise above doorways of red sandstone carved with images of Ganesha, of Devi, the Goddess, and of Brahma, though accounts of which deities they show differ. At the heart of the monument, beneath a marble pavilion inlaid with *pietra dura*, a work of cut and fitted coloured stones, a marble urn shaped like a lotus holds the Maharaja's ashes; accounts of how his remains are marked differ. The frescoes that survive inside were painted between 1839 and 1849.

Around the Maharaja's urn, smaller urns commemorate the four queens and seven attendants who died on his funeral pyre by the custom of *sati*, the death of a widow on her husband's funeral pyre, a custom that came from the ancient Rajput tradition; accounts of who they were differ. With them stand the two smallest memorials, those of two pigeons, which, it is told, came flying at the burning of the body, fell into the pyre and were burned with the Maharaja.

As it stood in the nineteenth century, the samadhi was entered from the east. The gateway was of two storeys, with red stone and floral work above, and shopkeepers kept shops in the cells of the first storey of the eastern wall. Five steps of red stone led up to the doorway, which was framed in red stone. Inside the east gate were a room facing south, a stair facing north and an upper door framed in red stone, and the courtyard was floored with lime. South of the gate lay a *dalan*, a hall open on one side, of five arches, its ceiling of painted and coloured lime plaster, with two rooms, in one of which the income of the place was collected.

The samadhi chamber stood on a grand platform about five feet high, faced with marble to the east and north and with brick to the south and west, and hollow beneath like a cellar; a door on the west led to a cool chamber below. Above a course of marble rose the building itself, of brick in white plaster. Each of its four sides had three doors framed in marble, the middle one large and the two beside it small; only the middle door on the east was kept open, with a large slab of black stone before it. Within was a roofed hall, at its centre a grand marble *baradari* with a *ghulam-gardish*, a covered gallery, running round all four sides, and at the centre of the baradari a marble pavilion whose columns were marble but whose dome was of brick. Over the baradari rose two domes, one below and one above; the floor was of marble, and the ceiling of the great dome was set with mirrors and elaborate gilding.

The gallery was divided into eight bays, four at the corners and four on the sides, with floors and walls of brick but glass work on the ceilings, the four corner ceilings gilded and the four side ones white. A stair of red stone in the south west corner rose to the second storey, which had two balconies on each side, each of three doors, with a latticed bay of three openings between them, railings of red stone in the lattices of the balconies and of marble within the openings. A brick stair from the same corner led to a large roofed terrace with small domes along the parapets and four at the corners, and at the centre of each wall a domed, elongated sitting place of eight doors. Above the great dome stood another lofty baradari, all of brick, with three doors to each side, crowned by a round dome bearing a gilded finial, with four small gilded domes at its corners. Four corner towers carried *kalas*, finials in the form of a pot.

Images of Hindu deities had their place in the samadhi. Inside stood a marble image of Devi Mai, the Mother Goddess, and in a southern niche a marble image of Hanuman. In the 1880s a marble image of the Devi stood with great reverence in one of the chambers of the gate range, her throne and canopy all of marble and the Devi mounted on a marble lion. Rani Jindan, mother of Maharaja Duleep Singh, had kept it in the fort, and when she was exiled she sent it to the samadhi; a separate *pujari*, or priest, was appointed for it. In the dalan stood a movable marble baradari, one that could be carried wherever one wished, holding an image of a *devi*, or goddess, a bull and a marble lion.

In the nineteenth century the whole place had a keeper, who managed the samadhi, with a servant attending there on his behalf. Today the Evacuee Trust Property Board administers the site.

The grand marble baradari at the centre first stood on eight marble columns, which cracked after a few years under the weight of the dome, and the building came near to collapse. Seeing its state, the authorities ordered the Executive Engineer of the Buildings Division at Lahore, Kanhaiya Lal, to secure it; he added eight brick columns to the eight, making sixteen, and bound the cracked ones with very strong iron rings.

Adjoining Ranjit Singh's samadhi, smaller ones honour his son Kharak Singh and his grandson Nau Nihal Singh; their joint building stands to its west, on the western edge of the same platform that lies beneath it. The Maharaja's wives have samadhis of their own, as separate monuments, among them the samadhi of Rani Nakain and Rani Chand Kaur.

In 2011 the samadhi was a white building, adorned with detailed frescoes and other artwork, standing on top of another single storey building painted yellow, in a courtyard with rooms for the pilgrims on its sides. Two loudspeakers had been placed on top of the samadhi, facing the ground, opposite the mosque and the city. In the hall the pavilion stood at the centre on a raised platform, its pillars of white marble. On ordinary days a portrait of the Maharaja, dressed in a white robe and with a long white beard, was placed at the pavilion beside that of his youngest son, Duleep Singh, the last Maharaja of the Punjab; on the anniversary that year the portraits had been removed. The dome was decorated with coloured glass, green, orange and red, in geometric patterns; niches held frescoes; and the walls of the balconies showed scenes of the court and religious drawings from Hindu mythology, among them Krishna, Ganesha, Ram and Sita. The paintings had faded, some had disappeared altogether, and visitors had noted down their names and numbers on them, disfiguring them.

The art historian Dr Nadhra Shahbaz Naeem Khan uncovered guardian figures beneath the whitewash on the building's eastern facade, but later coats of whitewash have covered and lost this decoration again.

## Devotion and Pilgrimage

For decades after it was built, the Guru Granth Sahib was installed and read in the samadhi, and today the samadhi remains an active place of pilgrimage, especially around the anniversary of Ranjit Singh's death and in the spring season of Vaisakhi, the harvest festival of the Punjab, when Sikh visitors, delegations from India among them, gather to pay homage.

In June 2011 the anniversary of his death was marked with an *Akhand Path*, an unbroken reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, held in honour of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, also known as Sher-e-Punjab, the Lion of Punjab. About a hundred and fifty people, all men, were in the hall for its conclusion. It fell twelve days after the commemoration of Guru Arjan's death anniversary in the same complex; the earlier pilgrims had left, and a new set had arrived from India. A police official sat on top of the samadhi with his gun in front of him. After the ceremony *langar*, the free communal kitchen, was served in two rows, with dal, rice, rotis and water, and tea boiled with sugar and ginger, which is highly popular in East Punjab.

Among the pilgrims was Amanpreet Singh, 35, a trader from Ludhiana, on his first visit to Pakistan: "The Maharaja was a great leader ... There was no crime". Jaswant Singh, 54, and a friend had come for the first time from the city of Qadian in East Punjab.

## The Setting

The samadhi stands outside the Roshnai Gate, against the city wall and wall to wall with the Badshahi Mosque, and its wall lies to the west of the samadhi of Guru Arjan. The Roshnai Gate, one of the thirteen gateways into the ancient walled city of Lahore, lies between the Alamgiri Gate and the Badshahi Mosque. Lamps were lit all along its passageway, hence its name, the gate of lights, and it was once reserved for the prince and the princess, who would go from the fort to the city through it. Behind it lies the Heera Mandi bazaar, which in 2011 was still one of the largest markets for traditional instruments in the city.

In the middle of these monuments lies the Hazuri Bagh, a small open ground, with a single storey pavilion set symmetrically at the centre of the garden and four lanes leading towards it. Ranjit Singh laid out the garden and held his *darbar* on the *shah-nashin*, the raised royal seat, of its baradari. The pavilion is said to have been built from part of an older tomb, though accounts differ over whose.

## Legacy

Beyond its place in Sikh devotion, the monument is listed by the Punjab Directorate General of Archaeology among the province's protected religious monuments of the Sikh period. The ruler it commemorates was at once the man under whom Lahore revived, a patron of Muslim shrines, and the man who carried the marble of Mughal tombs to Amritsar. He is remembered, too, through the faqirs he could not buy: the majzub who refused his thousands, the majzuba who abused him and whom he would not leave, and the faqir who, it is told, bade him send for sandalwood.

In 2011 his memory was kept on his anniversary by pilgrims from across the border, with the *Akhand Path* read in his honour and the *langar* served afterwards. For the city that the Maharaja once ruled, as one visitor wrote, "he is an alien, his memory kept alive not by people of the land he once ruled but by people from the other side of the border"; it had become rare to meet a Sikh in Lahore, a city once ruled by a Sikh and the seat of Sikh political strength.

Name: Sant Baba Asudaram Darbar (Panno Aqil)
Location: Panno Aqil (Pano Akil), Sukkur District, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Annual death anniversary (Anant Chaturdashi); continuous sadavrat
Description: The Darbar of Sant Baba Asudaram at Panno Aqil (Pano Akil), a town of the Sukkur District some forty kilometres north of Sukkur city, is among the surviving *sant* shrines of the Sindhi Hindu (Nanakpanthi) tradition. Asudaram (1895–1960), remembered by the honorific *Sakhi Baba*, "the generous master," was born on 3 April 1895 in the village of Jatoin near Panno Aqil, the son of Bhai Ludhrodmal and Chaini Bai. As a boy he came under the influence of Sant Shiromani Satramdas of Raharki (whose *Devri Sahib* is a separate entry in this dataset), and he later served at the Raharki *darbar* under the martyr-saint Bhagat Kanwar Ram (also recorded separately here), who is said to have given him the name *Shiv Swaroop*. On his Guru's instruction he returned to Panno Aqil in 1940 and there established his own *Darbar Sahib*. Around it grew a network of social works for which he became renowned — schools (*pathshalas*), a dispensary, and homes for the elderly and destitute — sustained by a *sadavrat* said to serve food and sweet water around the clock without distinction of caste or creed. He died on 4 September 1960, on the day of *Anant Chaturdashi*, and was succeeded by his son Sai Chanduram, whose activity later shifted to Lucknow in India. The darbar at Panno Aqil endures as the principal shrine of his lineage in Pakistan.

Name: Sant Baba Bhagat Ram Darbar Mandir
Events: Not documented
Description:
## Overview

The Sant Baba Bhagat Ram Darbar Mandir stands in the Shahi Bazar of Dadu, a district town on the right bank of the Indus in central Sindh. It is one of a number of functioning Hindu shrines in the province administered under the *Evacuee Trust Property Board*, and it belongs to a characteristically Sindhi form of religious site — the *darbar mandir*, in which the seat or memorial of a locally revered *sant* is joined to a temple of ordinary image-worship. Named for the saint Bhagat Ram, the shrine serves the Hindu families who remain in Dadu and preserves a strand of the region's devotional heritage. It should be noted at the outset that this is a modest local site on which scholarly documentation is sparse, and much of what follows is offered with due caution.

## Sant Baba Bhagat Ram and the Daduvansi Tradition

Local tradition associates the shrine with a *sant* named Bhagat Ram, remembered as one of a line of Hindu holy men active in and around Dadu, sometimes described as belonging to a *Daduvansi* lineage — literally the "line" or descendants of a saintly founder. Writers on the town's history mention such figures, among them a Dayo Ram Daduvansi said to have lived in the nineteenth century (dates variously given as 1836–1906), and it has even been suggested, though this is no more than a local hypothesis, that the name of the town of Dadu is itself connected to this saintly line. The historical detail behind these names is thin, and the biography, dates and teachings of Bhagat Ram himself are not securely recorded in accessible sources; the safest statement is that he was a locally venerated holy man whose memory the shrine keeps alive. Such *sant* devotion in Sindh characteristically drew on a blend of Vaishnava *bhakti*, Nanak-panthi and *Udasi* currents, in which the veneration of a living or departed teacher sat comfortably alongside the worship of images.

## The Darbar Mandir

The designation *darbar mandir* points to the dual character of the site. The *darbar* is the "court" or seat of the saint — often a *gaddi*, *samadhi* or memorial *takht* — before which devotees pay their respects, while the *mandir* houses the images and observances of temple worship. This pattern, in which a personal cult of a holy man is embedded within a temple, is widespread in the Sindhi Hindu landscape and reflects the province's distinctive religious culture, shaped by centuries of coexistence with Sufi Islam and by the shared idiom of saint-veneration. The shrine's location in the Shahi Bazar, the old commercial spine of Dadu, is typical of such urban community temples, which grew up amid the shops and homes of Hindu traders.

## Community and Custodianship

The Partition of 1947 and subsequent migrations greatly reduced the Hindu population of central Sindh, and shrines such as this passed, in the main, into the custody of the Evacuee Trust Property Board, the body that administers the religious properties of those who left. Where a resident community remained, sites like the Sant Baba Bhagat Ram Darbar Mandir continued in worship, sustained by local families and by the wider networks of Sindhi Hindu devotion that persist in the province. The shrine's survival, and its continued identification with a named local saint, make it a small but genuine witness to the endurance of Hindu religious life in the towns of the Indus valley.

## Bibliography

- *Sindh Courier*, "Dadu: Exploring the Historical Background".
- Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, writings on the Hindu shrines and saint-cults of Sindh (e.g. "Sindh: A Place of Sadhus, Sanyasis, Sants, Udasis, Bairagis and Sufis").
- Evacuee Trust Property Board listings of functioning temples in Sindh.
- Wikipedia, "Hinduism in Sindh" and "Dadu, Sindh", with cited sources.

Name: Sant Bhagat Kanwar Ram Temple (Chak)
Events: Annual commemoration (2 November)
Description:
This temple at Chak, a town in Shikarpur district, is dedicated to the memory of Bhagat Kanwar Ram (1885–1939), one of the best-loved Sindhi Hindu saint-singers of the twentieth century. Born in the village of Jarwar in the Sukkur region, he became renowned for his rendition of the *Sur Prabhati*, sung in the early morning; the gramophone company HMV is said to have preserved a number of his devotional songs on record, spreading his fame across Sindh. Revered by Hindus and Muslims alike as a figure of piety and communal harmony, he was assassinated at Ruk railway station in the Sukkur area in November 1939 and is remembered as a martyr. The temple at Chak was raised in his name after his death and was rebuilt in 2006; its main hall holds canopies bearing images of Bhagat Kanwar Ram and of Sant Satram Das, the saint of the *Sacho Satram* tradition with whom his memory is closely linked. In a syncretic touch characteristic of Sindhi devotion, the *Guru Granth Sahib* is also installed within, so that the darbar is honoured by Hindu and Sikh worshippers together. Every year on 2 November his followers gather to mark the anniversary of his martyrdom, both at this shrine and at Ruk station where he was killed.

The temple stands specifically in the Lakhi Ghulam Shah taluka of Shikarpur district, roughly 24 km east of Lakhi Ghulam Shah town. Kanwar Ram — born 13 April 1885 at Tarachand's house in Jarwar, then part of Mirpur Mathelo tehsil, and a disciple of Sant Satram Das (1866-1910) — was also remembered for singing the verses of Sufi poets including Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, Sachal Sarmast, Sami, and Kabir alongside his own devotional compositions. The Chak temple was first managed by Ladak Mal and his family and, following its 2006 rebuilding, has been maintained by Bal Chand Esrani, Tara Chand Thawani, and Prakash Lal Devani. A separate commemoration, distinct from both the Chak temple and the Ruk station gathering, has also been held at the Institute of Sindhology in Hyderabad, where in 2008 the university's vice-chancellor marked Kanwar Ram's 69th death anniversary by announcing a dedicated Bhagat Kanwar Ram Memorial Corner.

Name: Sant Satram Dham, Raharki (Sacho Satram / Devri Sahib)
Location: Raharki (Raherki Sahib), Daharki Taluka, Ghotki District, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Annual birth-anniversary celebrations (October)
Description:
The town of Raharki (Raherki Sahib) in Ghotki district, in upper Sindh close to the Punjab border, is home to the *Sant Satram Dham* — also known as *Devri Sahib*, and, after the devotional movement it anchors, as *Sacho Satram* — reckoned among the largest and most frequented Hindu shrines in present-day Pakistan. It marks the birthplace of *Satguru* Swami Sai Satramdas Sahib, the revered Sindhi saint born here, according to the tradition, on 25 October 1866. He gave his life to spiritual teaching in the syncretic Sindhi devotional mould, preaching love, humility and service to the destitute, and drawing followers from across Sindh who came to him for blessing and healing; the tradition records that he "left the mortal body" on 25 January 1910. After his passing the *Devri* (shrine) at Raharki grew into the principal seat of his lineage, whose devotees revere a holy text recited at the shrine known as the *Dhuni Sahib*. Today thousands of pilgrims — Sindhi Hindus from Pakistan, India and the diaspora — gather at Raharki, especially each October to mark the saint's birth anniversary, and the site is locally described as one of the biggest temples in the country. A succession of *sants* has continued to lead the community, and the darbar sustains traditions of communal hospitality and worship; the town itself is noted as one where Muslims and Hindus have long lived together. His memory is closely linked with that of Bhagat Kanwar Ram (also recorded in this dataset), with whom the *Sacho Satram* tradition is associated.

According to *Dawn*'s 2012 reporting, the darbar forms a sprawling, multi-acre complex a few kilometres from the Bharchundi Sharif shrine, with an enormous pilgrim hostel under construction and a causeway, funded by the federal government, easing access to the site; caretakers there described a mid-April festival marking the death anniversary of Bhagat Kanwar Ram that draws tens of thousands of visitors, including from Dubai and India. A satellite Sant Satram Dham was separately established in Shikarpur town on 9 October 2000, its own displays acknowledging the Raharki complex as the "principal" *Devri Sahib*. In September 2019 the temple — also referred to in press coverage as the SSD Dham Mandir — was attacked during communal unrest in Ghotki; government and civil-society delegations investigating the violence met community leaders on-site and concluded the attack had been planned the night before, and PPP chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari visited the ransacked temple in its aftermath.

Name: Sevapanthi Darbar (Bhai Gurdas), Gandava
Location: Heart of Gandava (Gandawah) town, Jhal Magsi District, Balochistan, Pakistan
Sufi Saint: Bhai Gurdas (Sevapanthi tradition); veneration of Guru Nanak
Events: No regular events documented
Description:
In the heart of Gandava — the old headquarters town of the Jhal Magsi District on the Kachhi (Kach Gandava) plain of Balochistan — stands a *darbar* of the *Sevapanthi* tradition, the order of devotees descended from Bhai Gurdas, the disciple of Guru Gobind Singh who is said to have carried the Nanakpanthi teaching into Sindh and Balochistan in the eighteenth century. According to the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, who has surveyed the Hindu and Sikh heritage of the region, the Gandava darbar was founded by one of Bhai Gurdas's disciples; the *Sevapanthis* (also written Sewapanthis, "those of the path of service") established such darbars and *dharamshalas* in many towns of Sindh and Balochistan, joining the veneration of Guru Nanak to a discipline of charitable hospitality. The Gandava darbar is celebrated above all for its woodwork: an intricately carved wooden frame decorating the main façade depicts Baba Guru Nanak flanked by his companions Bhai Bala and Bhai Mardana, together with the Hindu deities Ganesha (*Ganpati*) and Krishna — a vivid emblem of the syncretic Nanakpanthi devotion in which Sikh and Hindu figures share a single sacred idiom. The carving belongs to the same tradition of craftsmanship that produced the famed woodwork of the Khatwari Darbar at Shikarpur (a separate entry in this dataset), and the wider district is noted for such carvings of Krishna, Ganpati and Guru Nanak with his minstrel companions. Filed here under "Sikh Gurdwara" as the closest of the dataset's three categories, the darbar is more precisely a Nanakpanthi–Sevapanthi shrine of the kind once common among the Hindu mercantile communities of the Sindh–Balochistan borderland. Its exact date of foundation is not securely recorded, and — like many such darbars whose congregations dispersed after 1947 — the details of its present custody and use are uncertain, though the building and its carved façade were reported still standing when documented in recent years. Kalhoro's account also gives Bhai Gurdas's personal history: born Bhai Kanya Lal, he is remembered as a Khalsa saint who received the blessing of Guru Gobind Singh himself before carrying that teaching into the towns of Sindh and Balochistan. Independent confirmation that Gandava possesses a Hindu temple comes from a 2019 Dawn survey of the town's heritage sites, which lists "a Hindu temple" alongside the tombs of Syed Noor Shah Hussaini and Mian Saleh among the settlement's notable structures — though this piece does not itself identify the temple with the Sevapanthi darbar described above, so it stands as corroboration only that such a building exists in the town, not as confirmation of the specific Bhai Gurdas attribution.

## Bibliography

- Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, "The Magnificent Khatwari Darbar in Shikarpur," *Youlin Magazine*, 6 June 2024.
- Sheikh Javed Ali Sindhi, "Heritage: A Refuge and Fort for Ancient Armies," *Dawn*, 22 December 2019.
qa_note: This entry's Sevapanthi/Bhai Gurdas attribution for the Gandava darbar rests on a single author (Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro) writing across two publications — "Gurus in Shikarpur," The Friday Times, 12 January 2018, and "The Magnificent Khatwari Darbar in Shikarpur," Youlin Magazine, 6 June 2024 — and has not been independently corroborated by a second, unrelated source; an independent Dawn piece (Sheikh Javed Ali Sindhi, "Heritage: A Refuge and Fort for Ancient Armies," 22 December 2019) confirms only that a Hindu temple exists in Gandava, without naming or identifying it as this darbar. Per the research verdict this addition is treated as PARTIAL rather than STRONG: it rests on this single author's reporting and has not yet been corroborated by an independent source specific to the Sevapanthi/Bhai Gurdas identification. Three related conflicts remain unresolved: (1) a companion research file for the sibling entry Khatwari Darbar, Shikarpur, records the same author's later account that "Some believed Bhai Gurdas first preached in Gandava, Balochistan, before Shikarpur," raising an unresolved question of priority between the Gandava and Shikarpur darbars; (2) it is unclear whether the "Sevapanthi darbar" described here (Kalhoro, 2018) and the "Khatwari Darbar of Gandava" (Kalhoro, 2024) are one and the same building — both accounts point to the same town, author, and wood-carving description, but neither source states this explicitly; (3) Wikipedia's uncitable "Sikhism in Sindh" article attaches the Khatwari tradition's founding water-carrier legend to Bhai Kanhaiya, the historical founder of the Sewapanthi sect, while Kalhoro's articles attach the same story to "Bhai Gurdas (alias Kanhiya/Kanya Lal)" — whether these are the same figure is not resolved by any source fetched. None of these conflicts are resolved here, per this archive's standing practice of reporting contradictions rather than silently choosing a side.

Name: Shah Noorani Shrine (Syed Bilawal Shah Noorani)
Location: Lahoot Lamakan valley, Khuzdar District, Balochistan, Pakistan
Events: Annual urs; evening dhamal; qawwali and langar
Description:
## Overview

Deep in the mountains of the Khuzdar district of Balochistan, in the remote valley of Lahut Lamakan, stands the shrine of Shah Noorani, also called Syed Bilawal Shah Noorani. It is one of the most venerated and most inaccessible Sufi shrines in Pakistan. Set amid a landscape long held sacred and reached by a hard journey through the hills, it draws pilgrims from across Sindh and Balochistan, who come in great numbers for its *dhamal*, the ecstatic trance dance of its pilgrims, and its blessing, undeterred by its remoteness.

## The Saint and the Sacred Valley

Shah Noorani is remembered as a Sufi saint of the medieval centuries who settled in the wild valley of Lahut Lamakan. The valley's very name, *la-hut la-makan*, "the placeless place of the divine", marks it as a landscape of ancient sanctity, associated in legend with the mystic quest and revered across religious traditions. The saint's life is known more through devotion and legend than through documented history, but his sanctity is held in the highest regard, and his shrine has for centuries been a goal of arduous pilgrimage.

The setting, with its mountains, caves and springs held holy, gives the shrine an aura unlike any other. The valley bears fascinating similarities to the valley of the goddess Hinglaj: both are small oases with natural springs and caves, set in confined valleys.

The valley's holiness is thought to be older than the saint and wider than Islam. It has been suggested that Lahut was once an important place of Hindu worship, which would be in keeping with the history of other Hindu sites in the area that became Sufi centres over time.

Other saints, too, are tied to the valley. Lahut, in the Khuzdar district, is counted among the places where Shah Abdul Latif wandered. A saint called Lal is remembered as having stopped at Lahut Lamakan on a journey that also took him to Makran, Panjgur and Pasni in Balochistan and to Naing, Lake Manchhar and Sehwan in Sindh. These memories belong to the valley and to those saints, not to Shah Noorani or his shrine.

## The Shrine

The heart of the site is a cave, the cave of Shah Noorani, who is said to have lived in this valley. Inside it lies a curiously shaped stone that is said to be the image of Ali's camel. It has also been claimed that, before the place became associated with the Sufi saint, this stone was worshipped as a *śiva liṅga*, an emblem of the god Shiva, and the shape of the stone would support that idea. Cave and stone together carry the memory of more than one faith.

## Devotion and Pilgrimage

Despite its remoteness, Shah Noorani's shrine is a place of intense devotion. It is famous above all for its *dhamal*, driven by the drum and performed by crowds of pilgrims, and for the *langar*, the free communal kitchen of a shrine, and the *qawwali*, Sufi devotional music, that mark its gatherings. Pilgrims undertake the difficult journey to seek healing, to fulfil vows and to share in the charged atmosphere of the sacred valley.

Lahut lies on a pilgrimage route that runs from Sehwan in Sindh, where Lal Shahbaz is the starting point of the pilgrimage to the valley. Many fakirs, wandering Sufis, proceed to Lahut when the annual fair of Sehwan, which lasts three days, comes to its close. One woman's journey from Sehwan may have ended at Lahut, and her husband, searching for her, wondered whether she would trace her way back to Sehwan or follow other fakirs on to shrines in Karachi.

The route once ran further, to the Makran Coast and the abode of the goddess Hinglaj, "Nani Hinglaj", but today this path seems to have been widely forgotten. A trace of it survives at the end of an Urdu book named after the valley, *Lāhūṭ lā Makān*, which describes the way from Lahut to Hinglaj. In 2010 a Punjabi pilgrim at Lahut who had come from Sehwan Sharif confirmed that the stretch from Sehwan was still frequented, but said that the longer path to Hinglaj was no longer used because of the dangerous political situation in the area.

The journey itself has changed. Before the attack of November 2016, Lahut, like Hinglaj, saw a new wave of interest, mainly because a newly constructed road leading to the shrine had made the journey through the mountainous area easier.

## The Attack of 2016

The shrine's fame and its throngs also made it a target. In November 2016, during the evening *dhamal*, a suicide bombing struck the shrine. It killed more than fifty people and injured many worshippers, one of the deadliest attacks on a Pakistani shrine.

The terrible blast curbed the growing influx of visitors and created a volatile situation for the shrines of Balochistan. Yet, as at other shrines struck by such violence, the devotion of the pilgrims endured, and the shrine continued to draw them.

## The Setting

The history and devotional life of Balochistan in general frame the shrine's world. In 710 Muhammad bin Qasim al-Saqafi began his advance through Makran and Balochistan, and he conquered Sindh between 711 and 712. After that conquest a long line of Sufi mystics came to the region through Balochistan, Makran, Multan and Sindh itself. Proper names such as Ghauth Bakhsh, "gift of the help", in Sindh and Balochistan point to the popularity there of the saint Gilani.

The mystical lore of Sindh, Balochistan and the coastal belt of Iran shares myths, melodies and linguistic codes, and the *Mast Qalandar* *dhun*, a devotional melody, is said to be sung all along the Rajasthan, Sindh, Balochistan and Iran continuum. Families often bring women who are emotionally disturbed to take part in the *dhamal*, which devotees hold to have healing powers; in Balochistan such healing ceremonies are called *guāṭi*. The *mugarmān* drum is held sacred by the Sidi communities of Sindh, Balochistan, Rajasthan and Gujarat, who use it in their shrines and for their rituals.

Balochistan shares its poetry and legend with Sindh. The story of Sassi is told in the lands of Sindh and Balochistan, the hill slopes of Balochistan belong to the geography of Sindh's folk tales, and the poetry of the two lands has certain elements in common. The poetry of the Baluchis was wholly oral, sung by professional minstrels called Doms or Dombs at the gatherings of the clans.

The province is hard to reach for pilgrims from India, who must obtain an additional visa to travel to Balochistan, a province that has been in a state of latent insurgency since the establishment of Pakistan.

## Legacy

Shah Noorani stands among the great shrines of Balochistan and lower Sindh: a saint of the sacred mountain valley of Lahut Lamakan whose shrine, for all its remoteness, remains a powerful centre of ecstatic devotion. Its *dhamal*, its legends and its holy landscape make it one of the most singular pilgrimage places in Pakistan, and its endurance after the tragedy of 2016 is a testament to the tenacity of popular faith.

The valley is a station on a long road of devotion: a goal for the fakirs who leave Sehwan when its fair is over, once a stage on the way to the goddess of Hinglaj, and a place whose cave and stone carry the memory of more than one faith.

Events: Annual urs
Description:
## Overview

A shrine locally known as Darbar Hazrat Shah Yousuf stands in the Shah Yousaf locality of Shahpur tehsil, Sargodha District, Punjab — a modest, little-documented Sufi shrine that should not be confused with the far more famous shrine of Shah Yusuf Gardezi in Multan, a twelfth-century saint of an entirely different lineage and city, some 150 kilometres to the south. The Shahpur shrine is officially recognised in its own right: it appears on the notified-shrines list maintained by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department under its Sargodha zone, alongside other local dargahs of the district.

## A Locally Rooted, Thinly Documented Figure

Beyond its official listing, and the place-name it has given to its own locality — a government secondary school in the area is registered as "GHS Shah Yousaf, Shahpur" — almost nothing about the saint's life, lineage, or era survives in accessible written sources. The fifteenth-century founding date sometimes attached to the site could not be corroborated in gazetteers or published local histories and should be treated as provisional pending a district gazetteer or Auqaf departmental record. Notably, the neighbouring town of Shahpur itself is documented to take its own name from a different, later Sufi figure — Syed Shams Shah Shirazi, said to have arrived around 1606 and to have converted the formerly Hindu-majority settlement then known as Rampur — so the naming of this shrine rests on local memory rather than a firm documentary trail distinct from that town history.

## Distinguishing from Shah Yusuf Gardezi

Because the honorific "Shah Yousuf/Yusuf" recurs among Punjabi Sufi figures, this Shahpur shrine is easily conflated with the much larger, better-documented shrine of Shah Yusuf Gardezi in Multan, a twelfth-century saint of the Gardezi Sayyid lineage. The two are unrelated: different centuries, different cities, and no source treats them as the same figure. This entry describes only the local Shahpur site.

## Present State

Practically nothing has been published on the shrine's current physical form, custodianship, or the rites practised there. What can be said with confidence is that it remains an active, Auqaf-administered site of local pilgrimage in the Sargodha countryside.

Name: Shahwala Teja Singh Mandir
Events: Maha Shivratri
Description:
## Overview

The Shivala (or Shawala) Teja Singh Temple stands in the Dharowal quarter of the old city of Sialkot, in the Punjab, a historic Hindu temple dedicated to *Shiva* whose soaring shikhara long dominated the surrounding rooftops. Named for Teja Singh, who is remembered as its builder or patron, the temple is counted among the oldest surviving Hindu shrines of the Pakistani Punjab, and its recent restoration and reopening — after more than seven decades of closure — made it a symbol of the fragile revival of Hindu heritage in the region.

## Antiquity and Tradition

Heritage accounts hold the site to be very ancient; some traditions reckon it nine hundred to a thousand years old, which would place its origins among the oldest Hindu places of worship in this part of the Punjab. Such figures should be treated with caution, for they rest largely on local memory and devotional tradition rather than firm documentary record; what is clear is that the temple served for centuries as a living centre of worship for the Hindu community of Sialkot, a city that before 1947 possessed a substantial Hindu and Sikh population. Dedicated to Shiva, it would have drawn its greatest crowds at *Maha Shivratri*, the night sacred to the god.

## Architecture

The temple is built in the characteristic north Indian *nagara* idiom, its sanctum crowned by a tall, curvilinear tower rising in tiers above the shrine — a form designed to be seen from afar and to mark the sacred centre against the skyline of the crowded old city. For much of the twentieth century, standing sealed and neglected, it survived as one of the most conspicuous relics of Sialkot's pre-Partition religious landscape, its weathered tower a landmark even in disuse.

## Closure, Damage, and Restoration

Like most Hindu temples in the western Punjab, the Shivala Teja Singh Temple was abandoned at the Partition of 1947, when Sialkot's Hindus departed for India, and it was thereafter sealed. In 1992 it suffered further damage during the unrest that followed the demolition of the Babri Masjid in India, when a number of temples across Pakistan were attacked. For decades it stood shuttered and decaying, and by the 2010s Hindu leaders were publicly urging the authorities to arrest its ruin.

The turn came at the end of the decade. Under the Evacuee Trust Property Board, and with the help of the Lahore-based Sir Ganga Ram Heritage Foundation, the temple was renovated, and in 2019 it was formally reopened and handed over for the use of pilgrims — the first time in some seventy-two years that Hindu worship was again possible there. The reopening was widely reported as a gesture towards Pakistan's religious minorities and towards the preservation of the country's diverse heritage.

## Legacy

The Shivala Teja Singh Temple endures as one of the most evocative Hindu monuments of the Pakistani Punjab: a shrine of great, if imprecisely known, antiquity, damaged by the passions of the twentieth century and partly restored in the twenty-first. Its reopening did not conjure back the vanished Hindu community of Sialkot, but it returned to that community's descendants and to the wider public a place of worship and a piece of the city's layered past. As both a functioning temple and a heritage site, it stands as a reminder of the plural religious life that once flourished in Sialkot.

## Bibliography

- Reeta Grewal and others on the urban and religious history of the colonial and pre-colonial Punjab.
- Reports of the Evacuee Trust Property Board (Pakistan) and the Sir Ganga Ram Heritage Foundation on temple conservation.
- Contemporary press coverage of the 2019 restoration (Dawn, The Express Tribune, and international agencies).
- Prakash Tandon, *Punjabi Century* (for the texture of Hindu life in pre-Partition Punjab).
- George Michell, *The Hindu Temple: An Introduction to Its Meaning and Forms* (on the *nagara* tradition).
