- Habib University Ethnography Lab, field documentation of the Shree Ratneshwar Mahadev Temple.
- Wikipedia, "Shree Ratneshwar Mahadev Temple, Karachi" and "Jehangir Kothari Parade" (with cited sources).
- Reema Abbasi, *Historic Temples in Pakistan: A Call to Conscience* (Niyogi Books).

Name: Shri Laxmi Narayan Mandir (Native Jetty Bridge)
Location: Under Native Jetty Bridge, Karachi, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Ganesh Chaturthi; Holi; Raksha Bandhan; asthi visarjan rites
Description:
## Overview

The Shri Laxmi Narayan Mandir is a Hindu temple in Karachi, remarkable for where it stands: beneath the Native Jetty Bridge, on the banks of the Chinna Creek, it is the only temple in the city set directly upon the tidal waters that open onto the Arabian Sea. Reputed to be some two hundred years old, it is dedicated to Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune, and Narayan, the preserving god Vishnu, and it is among the oldest continually operating temples of Karachi. It is cherished above all for the seaside rites that its unique location makes possible.

## Devotion by the Sea

The pairing of Lakshmi and Narayan is one of the most beloved in the Hindu tradition, expressing the union of prosperity and divine sustenance. Lakshmi is the spouse of Lord Vishnu, and on the wall of one Valmiki temple she was pictured resting on a lotus flower. In Saidpur, where every shop kept idols, Lakshmi was the most popular of them.

At Karachi the temple's devotion has been shaped by its place at the water's edge. Overlooking the creek where it meets the sea, the shrine is a favoured site for the rituals that require flowing or tidal water, most importantly *asthi visarjan*, the immersion of the ashes of the dead, by which Hindus commit the remains of the departed to sacred waters. For a community far from the great *ghats*, the stepped landings, of India's rivers and from its coastal *tirthas*, or places of pilgrimage, the temple on the Chinna Creek has offered an irreplaceable link to the wider ritual geography of the faith. Within the sanctuary, alongside the principal images, devotees also honour *Hanuman*, the monkey god, and *Sai Baba* of Shirdi.

The temple's setting is at once its glory and its vulnerability. Tucked beneath the approaches of the Native Jetty Bridge, it looks out across the water, and the sea has long lapped close to its precincts. Its festivals mark the turning of the devotional year: *Ganesh Chaturthi*, the birthday of Ganesha, is celebrated here, together with the spring festival of *Holi* and *Raksha Bandhan*, the observance of the bond between brothers and sisters. On these days the modest shrine fills with the Hindu families of Karachi, for whom it is a place of gathering as much as of worship.

## A Painting of Ramdeo Pir

In a Karachi temple of Lakshmi Narayan, taken to be this one, stands a painting of Ramdeo Pir, one of the deified heroes whom the Hindus of Sindh shared with their Muslim neighbours. In Sindh the most popular of these heroes were Rama Pir, also called Ramdeo or Ramdev, Pithoro Pir, Pabuji and Guga Pir. Ramdeo Pir is still known in Sindh as Rama Pir, and in Sindh he is today integrated into the temples dedicated to the divinities worshipped throughout India; the painting in Karachi is an instance of that. The case of Pithoro Pir shows the variety of the negotiations between Sufism, the mystical path of Islam, and Hinduism in Sindh.

Such figures belong to a wider pattern. In Sindh a number of sacred figures have a dual religious identity, Muslim and Hindu: the Muslim identity is always related to Sufism, while the Hindu side usually belongs to the Nathpanth, the path of the Nath yogis. The Hindus of Sindh are related to Sufism in three ways. The most common is a Sufi tomb visited by both Muslims and Hindus; also relatively common is a saint with a double identity, Muslim and Hindu; and there is the Sufi *darbar*, or shrine, managed by Hindus. The large majority of the Hindus used to visit the Sufi shrines. That does not make them Sufis, but it does mean that for them the Sufis are a part of their religious legacy.

The Muslim Sufis of Sindh were mostly attracted by the Vishnuite school of Hinduism, the tradition devoted to Vishnu. Among the Hindus themselves, the worship of Krishna had already developed among the Amils in Sindh in the late nineteenth century, and the Vallabhachari sect was accepted by some members of the Amil community. A number of Sufis of nineteenth century Sindh, among them Sachal, Qutub Ali Shah and Bedil, included Krishna in their Sufi poetry, and although Sindh was Muslim dominated, Krishnaite *bhakti*, loving devotion to Krishna, was influential among the *wujudi* Sufis, those who held to the unity of being. Wall paintings of Krishna in Hindu temples could mean that there was a kind of Krishnaite revival among the Sindhi Hindus in the nineteenth century.

The Hindu share in the Muslim orders is more visible in Sindh than in the Punjab. Hindu writers wrote mystical poems in which they used the imagery of the Muslims, and they composed poems in honour of the Prophet.

## Under Threat

The very features that make the temple precious have placed it in jeopardy. The development of the port and the construction that has crowded the shoreline near the site have threatened both its access to the seawater essential for its rituals and the integrity of the structure itself. In September 2012, after a petition brought by the local Hindu community, the Sindh High Court issued an order restraining the Karachi Port Trust from demolishing the temple. The episode drew wide attention to the fragility of the city's surviving Hindu heritage and to the community's determination to defend it.

In the early twenty first century, government funding for the places of minority communities brought a wave of temple restorations across Sindh, coinciding with changes in the political landscape. Yet Karachi has also been a city of violence against Hindus, and the Hindus of Pakistan, Sindh included, have come more and more under the threat of the country's radical Muslims. After the demolition of the Babri Mosque in December 1992, Hindu communities in Sindh and Quetta were attacked.

## Karachi

Among the old temples of Karachi is one at Ram Bagh, an area now called Aram Bagh, an added letter that, it has been said, neutralises its religious sense. The temple had a painted Krishna with his maidens under its roof and a peacock guarding the entrance. It was much more elaborately decorated, and its community much larger, than in Lahore. An old man there gave its age as a hundred and fifty years; an officer did not know exactly how old it was, but said that it was old and had existed before Partition. Like the temple at Clifton, it is thought to have been a Hindu temple already in the time of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith, and the Clifton temple has been identified as the temple that Nanak visited on his tour of Sindh.

A temple within the Port Grand complex had a newly built mosque for tourists right on top of it. There were separate entrances for women and for men, food was being prepared, probably as an offering from a rich Hindu, and rooms were set aside for different deities. A mural showed a male deity, Jhule Lal, sitting on top of a giant fish. Stairs led down into water blackened by industrial waste; there were fishermen's boats, and pigeons were fed with rice.

At the time of Partition, Karachi was a minor port city; migrants from India made it the largest city of Pakistan. Its port was a modest structure, a minor tower with a clock placed within it, a symbol of colonial rule. The city's Hindu fisherfolk lived here before Kolachi became Karachi, and they are now the only connection between the city and the old village of Kolachi. Legend explains the name: an old woman known as Mai Kolachi, whose son was killed by a fish, is said to have torn the fish apart and retrieved him, and so the place came to be known as Kolachi. It is told, too, that on the quay of Karachi port a disciple about to sail to Iraq saw his master's face in the water.

In colonial Karachi, Sir Charles Napier, the conqueror and first governor of Sindh, built a Masonic lodge in 1843, and the Theosophical Society was founded in the city in 1896 by Dhunjishaw, Jamshed Nusserwanji and Dayaram Jethmal. A printing press was brought to Karachi in the 1850s, but for Sufism the main event was the printing in 1866 of the *Shah jo Risalo*.

Karachi has also been a supplier of Hindu worship elsewhere in Pakistan. Boys from Bahawalnagar bought an idol of the goddess Durga there; a vendor's idols were brought from Karachi, where a reasonable number of Hindus still live, or from India through illegal channels; and pilgrims came from as far as Karachi for *Navratri*, the festival of nine nights. The city is the seat of the Nagnath and Jagnath *akhāṛās*, houses of Hindu ascetics, the staging city for pilgrims from India, the home of the Devipujak-Vagri community, and the start of the road to the goddess Hinglaj, a route of about 240 kilometres from Narayanpur. The growth of Karachi swallowed the old pilgrim road: as the areas where the early stops lay were built over, all but a few of the resting places disappeared completely.

In the late twentieth century Karachi, with Hyderabad in India, was one of two important urban centres of Sufism where members of the Qawwal Bachche lineage actively maintained their special heritage of *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis. In the early twenty first century the teaching shaykh of one Sufi order, Siraj 'Ali Muhammad, led weekly *halqa*, communal sessions of *zikr*, the remembrance of God, on Thursday evenings in Karachi. A Sidi congregation is held in April at Manghopir in Karachi, and at Mango Pir, near Karachi, a miracle of alligators is said to have happened.

## Sindh and Its Hindus

Under the emperor Aurangzeb, the greatest river of the Mughal province of Thatta was the Sind, down which the merchants of Multan and Bhakkar shipped their goods to Thatta. The salt sea was the province's southern bound, and its life turned on boats, which carried most of its traffic and were reckoned, small and great, at forty thousand. Its diet rested on rice, curds and fish.

The Lohanas, the trading caste that formed the great body of the Hindus of Sindh, and related mercantile groups followed two main cults, the Nanakpanth, the path of Nanak, and the Daryapanth. The Daryapanth, in all probability the older of the two, is based on the deification of the Indus River, and it was served by a priestly caste, the Thakurs. The Thakurs were the priests of Jhulelal; they were settled in different cities of Sindh, and from 1947 onwards they migrated to India. In the nineteenth century the Nanakpanth was probably the dominant religious path among the Hindu Sindhis. With the growth of new trading centres in Sindh, Karachi above all, the Lohanas invested in land, and by the end of the nineteenth century they had become powerful landowners, known locally as *zamindars*. It is often claimed that Sindh had no caste system, but there were many untouchables in Sindh.

In 1941 the Hindus made up about 21 per cent of the population of Sindh. By early November 1947, 246,000 Hindus had already left Sindh by sea, air or rail, and the Hindu Sindhis started leaving especially after the Karachi riots of January 1948; estimates of how many left in all differ, from around a million to 800,000 or fewer. Accounts differ, too, over whether Sindh was free of communal strife; its communal violence never reached the level of the Punjab's, but it was not absent. In the narrative of the Hindu Sufi Rochaldas, the violence that spread through Sindh was not perpetrated by the Muslim Sindhis but by the Muhajirs, the Muslim refugees from India, who wanted to take over the houses of the Hindus, at least in Karachi. The departure of the Hindu elite and the arrival of the Muhajirs dramatically altered the local demography. After 1947 the *darbars* of Sindh were for the most part preserved, with different arrangements for their management.

Although a large majority of its Hindus migrated to India from 1947 onwards, Sindh is still the province of Pakistan with the most significant Hindu population and home to the majority of Pakistan's Hindus. By the census of 1998 the Hindus were the largest minority in the country. The majority of them are based in Sindh and southern Punjab. Pakistan's Hindus are put at between 6 and 10 million, an estimate that varies widely; over 90 per cent of them belong to underprivileged tribes and subcastes, and in Sindh, where they number several million, the majority belong to the scheduled castes. Many middle and upper class Hindus in Sindh are followers of the Nanak *panth*, the path of Nanak, and in the early twenty first century the formula *Sab ka malik ek hai*, all have one master, was very popular among the Hindus of Sindh.

The singer Alan Faqir spoke of the province, which the poetic tradition calls Sindhri, as a land that had been looted, plundered and assaulted and yet goes on: it has not died, it will not die, it has existed for centuries and it shall exist; Sindhri is beaten, and yet Sindhri goes on. Among the lines he recited was this:

*Punnu is not in the Kec / Sind is not the amir*

Its second half means that Sindh is not in the position of leadership, or amirship. It is one of Alan Faqir's own political readings of the tales of women.

## Legacy

The Shri Laxmi Narayan Mandir endures as a small but singular monument: a living temple that has kept its place on the Karachi waterfront through two centuries of change, and that continues to serve the ritual needs of a community whose presence in the city long predates the creation of Pakistan. Its survival, secured in part through the courts, stands as a testament to the resilience of Karachi's Hindus and to the enduring importance of the sea in their devotional life. It is also taken to be the Karachi temple of Lakshmi Narayan where a painting of Ramdeo Pir, one of the deified heroes of Sindh, bears witness to the shared religious culture of the province.

Name: Shri Panchmukhi Hanuman Mandir (Karachi)
Location: Soldier Bazaar, Karachi East, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Hanuman Jayanti; Holi; Diwali
Description:
## Overview

The Shri Panchmukhi Hanuman Mandir, in the Soldier Bazaar quarter of Karachi, is one of the most ancient Hindu temples in Pakistan. It is famed for its *panchmukhi*, or five faced, image of the monkey god Hanuman, which devotees hold to be *svayambhu*: manifested of itself, not made by human hands. Believed by tradition to be many centuries old, the temple was declared a protected site of national heritage under the Sindh Cultural Heritage (Preservation) Act of 1994, and it remains a busy centre of worship for Karachi's Hindu community.

## The Five Faced Image

Hanuman, one of the most loved deities of popular Hinduism, is the devoted servant of Rama, the hero of the Sanskrit epic, the *Ramayana*. Here he is venerated in his rare *Panchamukha* form, with five faces. In classical iconography the five faces represent Hanuman himself together with *Narasimha*, half man and half lion, *Garuda*, the eagle, *Varaha*, the boar, and *Hayagriva*, the form with the head of a horse; each face is turned to a direction, and each embodies a divine power.

What sets the Karachi image apart, in the belief of its devotees, is that it is a "natural" statue, carved by no sculptor but revealed from the earth, and the faithful hold that this makes it unique among shrines of Hanuman. Pilgrims come to offer worship before it, and the temple is especially thronged at *Hanuman Jayanti*, the deity's birth anniversary, as well as at *Holi*, the spring festival of colours, and *Diwali*, the festival of lamps.

## Tradition and Renewal

The temple's origins are wreathed in legend. Devotional tradition holds that Rama himself passed this way during his years of exile, and that long afterwards the image of Hanuman was uncovered at the spot, whereupon a shrine was built to house it. The site is popularly said to be at least fifteen hundred years old, and some accounts reach back further still. Such datings belong to tradition, but they express the deep sense of sanctity and age that the temple carries for its worshippers.

In modern times the temple has passed through periods of difficulty, including the loss of part of its land, but it has also seen renewal. A programme of renovation was undertaken in 2012, supported by donations from local Hindus. In 2019, during construction and restoration work, a number of further images and artefacts were unearthed, reported to include several statues of Hanuman together with other sacred figures. The discovery drew the interest of archaeologists and museum authorities and renewed public attention to the temple's long history. These finds, and the temple's protected status, have strengthened its standing as a heritage site of national importance.

## Hanuman in Legend and Verse

In two legends set beyond Karachi, Hanuman makes water flow. On the pilgrim road that starts from Karachi and leads to the goddess Hinglaj Devi, the Bahur River is said to have been created by Hanuman's attempt to get water for Sita, Rama's wife. Further along the same road, in the Hinglaj valley, pilgrims have even put a small statue of Hanuman at a *parav*, a halting place whose dedication is contested. Another legend holds that the Ram Thamman pool was first dug by Hanuman, who created the ancient pool digging with a shovel only two and a half times.

His image appears elsewhere too. In the nineteenth century a marble image of Hanuman stood in the southern niche of the *samadh*, the memorial shrine, of Ranjit Singh, the Sikh ruler of the Punjab, and at Chandrat he was among the pictures on the walls, beside Ganesh, the elephant headed god. In the early twenty first century, on the wall of a Valmiki temple, he was painted carrying an entire mountain on his hand while flying back to Lanka, the kingdom of Ravana.

Hanuman's name also lives in the poetry of the Sufis, the Muslim mystics. The Sufi poet Bulleh Shah recalls Hanuman's part in the epic of Rama:

*When Ravan the ten-headed abducted poor Sita, Hanuman burned Lanka. Ravan was completely humiliated, and finally you killed him* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

In one modern reading of Bulleh Shah's poems, Ravana and Hanuman figure in the story of Rama and Sita as two poles of mystical knowledge. In the folk verse of one Muslim poet, in which all categories collapse, paired opposites become one and the same: Hallaj and his judge, Shams-i Tabriz and the molla, and Abu Hanifa and Hanuman; there is no longer Turk, Hindu or Peshawari. Sachal and Qutub Ali Shah, counted among the Sufis of nineteenth century Sindh, brought Krishna into their poetry and named Hanuman's circle as well: Sachal mentions Hindu gods such as Rama, Hanuman, Sita and especially Krishna, and Qutub Ali Shah gives the names of Laxman, Rama's brother, and Sita, Rama and Krishna.

## Karachi

Karachi, the temple's city, was once the village of Kolachi. A legend explains the name: an old woman known as Mai Kolachi, whose son was killed by a fish, tore the fish apart and retrieved him, and the place came to be known as Kolachi. The city's Hindu fisherfolk lived here before Kolachi became Karachi, and in the early twenty first century they were the only connection between the city and the old village.

In the late nineteenth century Karachi grew as a new emporium of Sindh. Sir Charles Napier, the conqueror and first governor of Sindh, had built a Masonic lodge there in 1843; a printing press was brought to the city in the 1850s, and the Theosophical Society was founded there in 1896. At the time of Partition Karachi was a minor port city, which migrants from India made the largest city of Pakistan.

The city has other Hindu temples. The area of Ram Bagh is now called Aram Bagh, an added letter that, it has been said, neutralises the name's religious sense. In the early twenty first century its temple had a painted Krishna with his maidens under its roof and a peacock guarding the entrance, and most of the quarters behind it held Hindu households. It was much more elaborately decorated, and its community much larger, than in Lahore, and an officer there said that it existed before Partition. It has been suggested that, along with the temple at Clifton, it was a historical Hindu temple in the time of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith, and the Clifton temple has been identified as the temple which Nanak visited on his tour of Sindh. At Port Grand a newly constructed mosque for tourists had been built on top of another temple, whose rooms were reserved for different deities and whose mural showed Jhule Lal, a male deity sitting on top of a giant fish.

Karachi is the start of the pilgrim road to the goddess Hinglaj Devi, whose temple at Hinglaj lies about two hundred and fifty kilometres from the city. Karachi is the staging city for pilgrims from India, the seat of the Nagnath and Jagnath *akharas*, Hindu religious establishments, and the home of the Devipujak-Vagri community. The ongoing growth of Karachi and the urbanisation of the areas where the early stops lay caused all but a few of the resting places on the road to disappear. In the early twenty first century the city, where a reasonable number of Hindus still lived, also supplied images of the gods to Hindus elsewhere in Pakistan: boys from Bahawalnagar bought an idol of Durga, the warrior goddess, from Karachi, and a vendor's idols had been brought from Karachi or, through illegal channels, from India. The city has also known violence against Hindus.

Karachi is a city of Sufis too. It has been counted, with Hyderabad in India, as one of two important urban centres of Sufism, where the Qawwal Bachche, a lineage of singers of *qawwali*, Sufi devotional music, keep their heritage. In the early twenty first century a teaching shaykh of the Chishti Sufi order led weekly *halqa*, communal sessions of *zikr*, the remembrance of God, on Thursday evenings in the city, and after the annual fair at Sehwan, *fakirs*, wandering Sufis, followed other fakirs and proceeded to shrines in Karachi. A congregation of Sidis, a community of African descent, gathered at Manghopir, near Karachi.

## Sindh and Its Hindus

In 711 Muslim navies conquered and occupied the densely populated Hindu and Buddhist society of Sindh. In the centuries after the mass conversions to Islam, Hindus visited Muslim shrines and made votive offerings, and in 1940 it was observed that most of the musicians in Sindh had been Hindus and not Muslims. The stories of the Sufi poet Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit have been held to be all Hindu in origin. The Hindu traders of Sindh undertook long sea voyages to places such as Aden, Gujarat and Lanka; their wives made offerings to the water deity for their husbands' safe return, and the Hindu festival of lamps, celebrated in the autumn, marked the beginning of the trading season.

The *Risalo*, Shah Abdul Latif's collected poetry, carries a prayer for the province itself. Its rain song, the Sarang, catalogues the places the rains reach, among them Umarkot, of which the verse says "Some have passed over Umarkot and have made the ground green". It closes by asking God to make Sindh flourish forever, and that final invocation is one of the most often quoted verses of the *Risalo*:

*Dear friend and sweet beloved, make the whole world prosperous* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

In 1941 Hindus made up about 21 per cent of the population of Sindh. By early November 1947, 246,000 Hindus had already left Sindh by sea, air or rail, and the Hindu Sindhis started leaving especially after the Karachi riots in January 1948. Accounts of how many left in all differ, but the number is most often put at around a million. The narrative of Rochaldas alludes to violence spread through Sindh that was not perpetrated by the Muslim Sindhis but by the Mohajirs, Muslim migrants from India, who clearly wanted to take over the houses of the Hindus, at least in Karachi. The departure of the Hindu elite and the influx of Muslim refugees from India dramatically altered the province's demography. Accounts differ over how peaceful Sindh was between the faiths, but communal violence did occur there, even if it never reached the level of violence in the Punjab.

Sindh is the province of Pakistan with the most significant Hindu population, home to the majority of Pakistan's Hindus, and by the census of 1998 the Hindus were the largest minority in the country. Their number in Pakistan is put at between 6 and 10 million, though estimates vary widely, and most of them belong to underprivileged tribes and castes. Ramdeo Pir, a saint known in Sindh as Rama Pir, is "today integrated into the temples dedicated to the pan-Indian divinities". After the demolition of the Babri Mosque in December 1992, Hindu communities in Sindh and Quetta were attacked. In the early twenty first century, government funding for the places of minority communities was seen in a wave of restorations of temples across Sindh, renovations that coincided with changes in the political landscape.

## Legacy

The Shri Panchmukhi Hanuman Mandir holds a singular place among the Hindu shrines of Pakistan: a temple whose central image is held to be born of itself, whose traditions reach back to the age of the *Ramayana*, and whose soil has yielded up sacred figures buried for generations. For the Hindus of Karachi it is a cherished house of worship and a point of continuity with a distant past; for the wider heritage of the city it is a monument that binds legend, devotion and archaeology into a single enduring landmark.

Name: Shri Swaminarayan Mandir, Karachi
Location: M. A. Jinnah Road, Karachi, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Janmashtami; Holi; Diwali
Description:
## Overview

The Shri Swaminarayan Mandir, rising behind its long frontage on M. A. Jinnah Road in the heart of Karachi, is the principal Hindu temple of Pakistan's largest city and the only surviving temple of the *Swaminarayan Sampradaya* — the devotional tradition founded in early nineteenth-century Gujarat — in the country. Spread across a walled compound of some thirty-two thousand square yards, it has for well over a century been both a place of worship and a refuge, and its story is woven into the history of Karachi itself.

## The Swaminarayan Tradition

The Swaminarayan movement takes its name from *Swaminarayan* (Sahajanand Swami, 1781–1830), the reformer and teacher who gathered a large following across Gujarat and Kutch and preached a disciplined, devotional Hinduism centred on the worship of Narayana, ethical conduct, and service. His followers spread with the trading networks of the Gujarati mercantile castes, and it was these communities — the *Lohana* and *Bhatia* merchants of Kutch and Kathiawar who had settled in the port of Karachi — who raised the temple to serve their spiritual needs. The temple is generally held to have been established around the middle of the nineteenth century, in the decades after Karachi passed under British rule and grew rapidly as a commercial port.

## The Temple and Its Life

Within its spacious precincts the mandir houses shrines to Swaminarayan and the deities of the tradition, together with halls, lodgings, and open courtyards that can accommodate large gatherings. It has long been the focal point of Hindu festival life in Karachi, most notably at *Janmashtami*, the celebration of Krishna's birth, and *Holi* and *Diwali*, when the compound fills with worshippers. The temple's ample grounds have also served secular and civic purposes over the years, hosting community functions and, at times, providing shelter in the crowded life of the city.

## Partition and the Refuge of 1947

The most poignant chapter in the temple's history came with the Partition of the subcontinent in 1947. As communal violence convulsed the region and hundreds of thousands of Hindus and Sikhs sought to leave the newly created Pakistan, the spacious compound of the Swaminarayan Mandir became a transit camp for refugees awaiting passage by ship from Karachi's port to India. Tradition records that *Muhammad Ali Jinnah*, the founder of Pakistan, visited the temple during this period and is said to have offered reassurance to those sheltering there. The episode is remembered as a moment when the great temple stood as a place of sanctuary amid the upheaval that reshaped the subcontinent.

## Legacy

Today the Shri Swaminarayan Mandir remains an active and well-attended temple, serving Karachi's Hindu minority and standing as one of the most visible symbols of the community's long presence in the city. Its survival — as the last Swaminarayan temple in Pakistan and one of the country's largest functioning Hindu shrines — makes it a landmark of both religious devotion and shared history, a reminder that the great port of Karachi has always been home to many faiths.

## Bibliography

- Williams, Raymond Brady. *An Introduction to Swaminarayan Hinduism*. Cambridge University Press.
- Markovits, Claude. *The Global World of Indian Merchants, 1750–1947*. Cambridge University Press.

- Contemporary press reporting (Dawn, The Express Tribune) on Karachi's Hindu heritage and festivals.
- Studies of Partition migration through the port of Karachi.

Name: Shri Varun Dev Mandir
Location: Manora Island (Manora Beach), Karachi, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: None - derelict; conservation appeals ongoing
Description:
## Overview

On the low, wind-scoured island of *Manora*, guarding the mouth of Karachi harbour, stands the Shri Varun Dev Mandir — a temple dedicated to *Varuna*, the ancient Vedic lord of the waters and the sea. It is believed to be the only temple to Varuna in Pakistan, and its weathered stonework, set almost within reach of the waves, makes it one of the most atmospheric and least-known of the country's Hindu shrines. For the Hindus of Sindh, and especially for seafaring and mercantile communities, it has long been a place to honour the deity who rules the ocean on which their fortunes depended.

## Varuna, Lord of the Waters

In the oldest stratum of Hindu tradition, Varuna is among the most exalted of the gods — guardian of cosmic order (*rita*), sovereign of the celestial ocean, and in later devotion the presiding deity of the seas, rivers, and rain. In the religious life of coastal and riverine Sindh, reverence for the water-god blended with the veneration of *Jhulelal*, the beloved Sindhi Hindu deity likewise associated with the waters of the Indus, so that the temple at Manora belongs to a distinctly Sindhi tradition of devotion to the divine in its aquatic form.

## History and Antiquity

The precise age of the temple is uncertain, and tradition claims for it a very great antiquity, with some accounts holding the site sacred for many centuries. According to one local tradition, Manora Island was purchased in earlier times by a wealthy sailor — remembered as *Bhojomal Nenshi Bhatia* — whose family is said to have commissioned a temple upon it. The structure that survives today is generally dated to the early twentieth century, with records pointing to construction or major rebuilding around 1917–18 and further embellishment, including its tilework, in the years around 1937–40. It is prudent to treat the temple's more ancient origins as traditional rather than documented, while its present fabric belongs to the last century or so.

## Decline and Preservation

For many decades the temple stood neglected and exposed to the elements. The salt-laden sea winds of Manora have eaten into its masonry and eroded the fine carvings that once adorned its walls, and by the early twenty-first century it had fallen into a dilapidated condition. Its plight has drawn the attention of heritage advocates and of Hindu community organisations in Pakistan, and there have been calls and efforts to conserve and restore the shrine as an important relic of Sindh's religious and architectural heritage.

## Legacy

The Shri Varun Dev Mandir is a rare and poignant survival — a temple to the god of the ocean standing on an island at the edge of the sea, its stones slowly yielding to the salt air that is itself the element of the deity it honours. As the only known temple of Varuna in Pakistan, and as a monument to the maritime and mercantile Hindu communities of old Karachi and Sindh, it holds a singular place among the sacred sites of the country, and its preservation is a matter of concern to all who value that shared heritage.

## Bibliography

- Cousens, Henry. *The Antiquities of Sindh, with Historical Outline*. Archaeological Survey of India.
- Boivin, Michel. *Historical Dictionary of the Sufi Culture of Sindh* and related studies on Sindhi religion.
- Contemporary press reporting (Dawn, Youlin Magazine, The Express Tribune) on Manora and its temple.
- Studies of the cult of Jhulelal and water-veneration among Sindhi Hindus.
- Heritage documentation of Manora Island and Karachi's endangered monuments.

Name: Shrine at Odero Lal (Udero Lal Teerath Asthan)
Location: Odero Lal Village (near Tando Adam), Matiari District, Sindh, Pakistan
Sufi Saint: Sheikh Tahir (also revered as Udero Lal/Jhulelal)
Events: Cheti Chand; shared Hindu and Muslim observance year-round
Description:
## Overview

The shrine at Odero Lal, also spelt Udero Lal, stands in the village of the same name near Tando Adam in Sindh. It is a single sanctuary revered and used in common by Hindus and Muslims, where a Hindu temple and a Muslim tomb stand together under one roof and are tended by caretakers of both faiths. To the Sindhi Hindus its saint is Jhulelal, an incarnation of Varuna, the ancient deity of the waters; to the Muslims he is a holy man called Sheikh Tahir, or, in a name both communities honour, *Zinda Pir*, "the living saint". The shrine is one of the great living symbols of the shared religious culture of Sindh, and of the reverence, common to both traditions there, for the waters of the Indus.

The sanctuary is known as the darbar of Udero Lal, a *darbar* being a saint's shrine. It is the main shrine devoted to Jhulelal and the chief centre of the Daryapanth, the cult of the river Indus. The sanctuary is vast and dates back to the seventeenth century, and it is the best example in Sindh of a sacred place whose saint has a double identity, Muslim and Hindu.

## The Legend of Jhulelal

The story that gives the shrine its meaning is set in a time of persecution, and it is told in more than one way. In the telling of Sindhi Hindu tradition, a tyrannical ruler remembered as Mirkh Shah of Thatta commanded the Hindus of Sindh to abandon their faith and accept Islam. In their fear the Hindus gathered on the banks of the Indus and prayed to Varuna, the lord of the river, for deliverance, and the god answered that he would be born among them as a child, at Nasarpur, to save them.

The saviour so promised is Jhulelal, whose birth the Sindhi Hindus still celebrate at *Cheti Chand*, the festival that marks the Sindhi new year and is kept as his birthday. In the devotion of Sindh he is the protector of his people and the spirit of the river itself, and Udero Lal is honoured as the centre of his cult. Tradition also gives the story an ending at the shrine: Jhulelal is said to have disappeared into a well within the darbar of Udero Lal.

## Jhulelal and Sheikh Tahir

The saint of the shrine carries many names, and accounts of who he was differ. The Hindus worship Jhulelal as an *avatar*, an incarnation, of the Vedic god Varuna, the god of the Indus. He is probably a modern form of that ancient god, and history mentions him only briefly. The Indus itself was worshipped under the name Udero Lal, pictured as an incarnation of Varuna, and the figure is also known as Amar Lal, Darya Shah and Darya Nath. The name Udero Lal has also been given to a different saint at a different place: Shah Lal Baz, the Qalandar, or wandering dervish, of Sehwan.

The Muslims know him as Sheikh Tahir. Muslim tradition at the shrine holds that the saint buried here was born a Hindu named Udero Lal and embraced Islam, becoming known as Sheikh Tahir. Some identify him with *Khwaja Khizr*, the deathless guide associated in Islamic lore with the waters, and in Sindh it is Udero Lal who is most often merged with Khizr. Muslims venerate him as a Sufi, a Muslim mystic, who may have belonged to the Suhrawardi order, founded by Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi. A Sufi lineage built for him at an unknown date makes him a disciple of Bahauddin Zakariyya.

Sheikh Tahir is also remembered as a mystic. More visibly in Sindh than in the Punjab, Hindus shared in the Muslim Sufi orders, and some saints were claimed by both communities; the most famous case is Sheikh Tahir, who is venerated by members of both. He was one of the most ardent defenders of the unity of being, *wahdat al-wujud*, the metaphysical doctrine of Ibn Arabi. There is no settled date for his life: he is placed in the sixteenth or the seventeenth century.

Strange legends are told of his ecstatic states. It is said that he saw God even in a camel, and started running after it.

## The Sanctuary

The sanctuary lies about 50 kilometres north of Hyderabad. There are several temples dedicated to Udero Lal, but the village that bears his name is the main centre of his cult. Before Partition the temples devoted to Jhulelal in Sindh were built with a dome, as were some Sikh *samadhis*, memorial shrines, and the darbar of Udero Lal has many domes. Within it is the well into which Jhulelal is said to have disappeared.

A legend accounts for the shrine's double character. When Hindus and Muslims disputed over the saint, it is said, a voice came from the heavens commanding that the shrine be made acceptable to both, one part a temple and the other a *dargah*, a Sufi shrine, for the saint belonged to all.

The plan of the sanctuary answers to its two communities. It is a single sanctuary, but each community worships the saint under its own name and in its own chapel: the Hindus venerate Udero Lal in one chapel, and the Muslims worship Sheikh Tahir in another. Hindus perform *puja*, worship with offerings, and *aarti*, the waving of lamps before the deity, while Muslims offer their prayers at the tomb. A perpetually burning lamp and the veneration of the nearby Indus are shared by both.

The care of the shrine is divided between the two communities, with a *gaddi nashin*, the holder of the seat, for the Hindus and a *sajjada nashin*, the custodian who sits on the saint's prayer carpet, for the Muslims. The annual fair is held separately. The two groups interact very little, and disputes arise regularly. The crossing runs one way: Hindus visit Sheikh Tahir's tomb, but Muslims do not go to the space devoted to Jhulelal.

## Devotion and Festivals

As the main centre of the Daryapanth, the darbar belongs to a cult followed among the Lohanas and related mercantile groups. The Daryapanth is based on the deification of the Indus. It was managed by a priestly caste, the Thakurs, and most of its rituals were related to the changes in the level of the Indus through the year. Among these groups two main cults were followed, the Nanakpanth, the path of Guru Nanak, and the Daryapanth, which is probably the older of the two.

The Thakurs were the priests of Jhulelal. In Sindh they were settled in different cities, and from 1947 onwards they migrated to India. In Sehwan they ran Jhulelal's temple in the northwestern part of the town.

In the colonial period the darbar was a meeting place for the Hindu community of Sindh. In the last decade of the nineteenth century several Hindu *panchayats*, community councils, of Sindh held a meeting at Udero Lal, in the main darbar devoted to Jhulelal. This was the time of an attempt, in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, to create a centralised path devoted to Jhulelal, then known as Amar Lal or Udero Lal.

At the annual fair of April 2016 a huge poster in the darbar showed Shah Abd al-Latif and Jhulelal together, with the epigram *Sab ka malik ek hai*, meaning that all have one master. The formula had for some years been very popular among the Hindus of Sindh.

Devotion to Jhulelal has its own words and songs. An inscription reads *Jhulelal bera par*, "May Jhulelal safely guide our nave", and the devotional songs to Jhulelal are called *panjro*. One devotional book opens with Guru Nanak and Jhulelal, here named Darya Shah, with Zinda Pir in the caption of his image, and its last four pages are filled with *panjro*. The images of Guru Nanak and Jhulelal have also grown more and more alike.

## The Setting

The shrine's double devotion belongs to a wider pattern in Sindh, where the Hindus are bound to Sufism through three kinds of sacred place: a Sufi tomb visited by both Muslims and Hindus, as at Bhit Shah; a saint with a double identity, Muslim and Hindu, as at Udero Lal; and a Sufi darbar managed by the Hindus, as at Pithoro Pir. A number of sacred figures in Sindh have such a dual identity. Their Muslim side is always related to Sufism, while their Hindu side usually belongs to the Nathpanth, the path of the Nath yogis. As early as 1851 it was observed that the worship of the intercessors is the common religious idiom of Hindus and Muslims.

The river had its own place in this common religion. In Sindh the cult of Khwaja Khizr was linked with the worship of the Indus and supported by Muslim and Hindu alike, and Khizr was called Zinda Pir. Under the name of Khwaja Khizr this saint has always held great power in Sindh, and in popular belief he became identified with the spirit of the waters and with the deity of the river Indus. The Daryapanthis of Sindh believed in the sanctity of the river god, the god of the waters, a belief that touched Hindu and Muslim alike. Hindus visited Muslim shrines and made votive offerings there, and offerings to the Indus are still made in the wider region of Sindh.

The name of Jhulelal reaches beyond this shrine. Jhule Lal, now a chant directed at a saint, was once a call to the river deity of the Indus worshipped by the Hindu Daryapanthis, and in the figure of Lal the Quranic river saint Khizr meets an Indic fish god. A pilgrim train, the Jhule Lal Express, carried the name. At Port Grand a temple mural shows a male deity seated on top of a giant fish, with water beneath: Jhule Lal, the famous Hindu deity also revered in certain Muslim traditions.

## Legacy

The shrine at Odero Lal has endured as a symbol of tolerance and common humanity, a place of shared reverence for a single saint and a single sacred river. In a subcontinent whose modern history has too often been marked by communal division, Udero Lal stands as testimony to an older and more generous pattern of coexistence. It continues to draw pilgrims of both faiths, Sindhi Hindus above all, for whom it is a spiritual homeland, and Muslims who honour the *Zinda Pir*. Its festivals, and especially the celebration of Cheti Chand, keep alive a devotion that has bound the peoples of Sindh together for centuries.

After Partition the cult of Jhulelal travelled with the Sindhi Hindus to India. There Jhulelal became the *isht devta*, the community god, of the Hindu Sindhis, the Sindhi god of India above all others and the embodiment of Sindhi culture in India. Before Partition, when most Hindus of Sindh were Nanakpanthis, followers of the path of Guru Nanak, he was already worshipped by some groups among them. The turn to his worship has been seen as a kind of soft Hinduisation of the Sindhi legacy in India, and as his exaltation spread, room for the Sufi legacy among the Hindu Sindhis shrank. The tradition of Jhulelal reaches from Udero Lal in Sindh to Ulhasnagar in Maharashtra, where a temple of Jhulelal was recently built by Thakurs from Sehwan.

Name: Shrine of Abdullah Shah Ghazi
Events: Annual urs; Thursday-evening qawwali and dhamal
Description:
## Overview

On a low hill in Clifton, overlooking the Arabian Sea in the heart of Karachi, stands the shrine of Hazrat Abdullah Shah Ghazi, the patron saint of the city. Tradition places him in the eighth century and holds him to be a descendant of the Prophet through the line of Imam Hasan. For the people of Karachi he is the guardian of the city, believed to shield it from storm and calamity, and his *darbar*, or shrine, crowned by a green dome, is among the most visited and most beloved sacred places in Pakistan's largest metropolis, a ceaseless resort of pilgrims of every kind.

## The Saint

The historical record of Abdullah Shah Ghazi is thin and wrapped in legend, but the tradition is strong and old. No year of his birth or death has come down, and no teacher and no order of the Sufis, the Muslim mystics, are remembered for him. He is held to be a Sayyid, one of the family of the Prophet Muhammad, by the usual account a descendant of Imam Hasan, who came to Sindh in the early Islamic centuries. Tradition sets his coming in the eighth century, the age when Islam was first spreading in the region through Muhammad bin Qasim and after.

Tradition holds that he came as a merchant, as a preacher and as a warrior, a *ghazi*. He is said to have settled by the sea near what became Karachi and to have died there, and some traditions hold that he was martyred.

## The Shrine

His grave on the Clifton hill became a place of blessing, and over the centuries it grew into the great shrine that now bears his name. As one writer on the folk religion of Pakistan put it, this is "the most famous shrine in the city".

Like other great shrines, it has been a target of violence, and it is counted among the Sufi shrines of Pakistan that have come under attack. In 2010 it was struck by a suicide bombing; the attack came on 6 October and killed eight people. The devotion of Karachi has never faltered, and the shrine, since rebuilt and expanded with its landmark green dome, remains thronged.

## Devotion and Festivals

Abdullah Shah Ghazi is woven into the very identity of Karachi. It is widely believed that his presence protects the coastal city from cyclones and disaster, and that the sea has never brought ruin upon Karachi because the saint keeps watch over it from his hill.

His shrine draws people from right across the city in great and constant numbers, rich and poor, of every sect and background. They come to recite the Fatiha, the opening chapter of the Quran, to tie vows, to distribute food, and to share in the *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, and the *dhamal*, the vigorous ritual dance performed at Sufi shrines in Punjab and Sindh. *Qawwali* and *dhamal* fill its evenings, above all on Thursdays and at the *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death.

On one occasion a news anchor who styled himself a vigilante entered the shrine and secretly filmed people consuming hashish, then began harassing the caretaker for allowing such a practice. Under pressure, in front of the camera, the caretaker gave an apologetic response and promised to monitor the situation better in the future.

## The Setting

Muhammad bin Qasim, in whose age tradition sets the saint's coming, began his advance through Makran and Baluchistan in 710, and conquered Sindh between 711 and 712. The early Arab conquerors settled their families in large numbers in the various towns of Sindh, though in that early period Sindh is not known to have seen the spread of Sufism found further north and west. The Sufi mystical traditions came to the subcontinent through Sindh, and after the conquest a long line of Sufi mystics came to the region through Baluchistan, Makran, Multan and Sindh itself.

A large part of Clifton is built on reclaimed land. Of the city's name, it is said that the area was once known as the area of Mai Kolachi, after an old woman known by that name whose son was killed by a fish; she tore the fish apart and retrieved him, and the city came to be known as Kolachi. At the time of Partition Karachi was a minor port city, and migrants from India made it the largest city of Pakistan.

Karachi is one of two important urban centres of Sufism, the other being Hyderabad in India; in both, members of the same lineage of qawwali musicians, the Qawwal Bachche, actively maintain their special qawwali heritage. The city's shrines are also a stage in the round of the *fakirs*, wandering Sufis: after the annual fair of Sehwan, which lasts three days, fakirs follow other fakirs and go on to shrines in Karachi.

## Legacy

Abdullah Shah Ghazi is the spiritual guardian of Karachi: a saint whom tradition places in the earliest Islamic centuries, whose shrine on the Clifton hill has become the sacred heart of a modern megacity of many millions. In him a coastal metropolis of migrants and strangers finds a common patron and a place of refuge, and his *darbar* remains one of the most vibrant centres of popular devotion in Pakistan.

Name: Shrine of Abul Faiz Qalander Ali Suharwardi
Events: Annual urs (11-12 Rabi al-Awwal); weekly Sunday milad; daily langar
Description:
## Overview

On the Multan Road at Hanjarwal, on the south-western edge of Lahore, stands the shrine of Hazrat Abul Faiz Qalandar Ali Gilani Suhrawardi — a rare instance of a great Sufi shrine that belongs not to the distant past but to living memory. Abul Faiz Qalandar (died 1958) was at once a scholar, orator, author, and spiritual master: a distinguished pupil of the celebrated Ala Hazrat Ahmad Raza Khan of Bareilly, an heir to the Qadiri-Gilani and Suhrawardi orders, and the guide of thousands of disciples in twentieth-century Punjab. His darbar, kept by his own descendants beside the Jamia Masjid Suhrawardia, is a busy centre of devotion and learning, and it shows how the ancient traditions of Sufi Lahore continued to put out new life into the modern age. To understand the shrine is to follow the life of a man who joined the learning of the seminary to the ecstasy of the *qalandar*.

## The Life of the Saint

Abul Faiz Qalandar was born into a learned Gilani sayyid family of the Sialkot district in the last decades of the nineteenth century — by one careful account on Monday, 18 November 1885, at Kotli Loharan, and by another — the account kept by the shrine's own custodians — on 4 January 1895. Devotional tradition holds that his birth was foretold: a saint is said to have brought his grandfather, Jamal-ud-Din Gilani, the glad tidings that a grandson would be born in his house who should be named Abul Faiz Qalandar, and who would win great fame, serve the faith, and reach a lofty spiritual station — and so the grandfather named him. His father, Rasool Bakhsh Gilani, was himself a man of much learning, but the boy was able to keep him only some eight years before his father died; from him he had his first schooling, and thereafter he set out into the world of knowledge alone, often withdrawing for many days at a time into the wilderness.

In 1910 he came to Lahore, and for four years pursued the religious sciences at the Madrasa Shah Al-Maali. There, and in the years that followed, he mastered both the outward learning of the scholar and the inward knowledge of the mystic, until — in the phrase his devotees use — “his knowledge began to speak.” At the Jamia Shah Al-Maali he served as imam and preacher (khatib) and taught the memorisation and recitation of the Qur’an, and it was from this base of sober learning that he grew into one of the notable Sufi masters of his age. He died on 9 September 1958, and was buried at Hanjarwal, where his shrine now stands.

## Teachers and the Chain of Transmission

Abul Faiz Qalandar’s spiritual formation passed through the hands of several of the greatest figures of the age. He presented himself before Ala Hazrat Ahmad Raza Khan of Bareilly — the towering scholar of the Barelvi tradition — and, deeply impressed, took the oath of allegiance (bai‘at) at his hand, becoming counted among his special pupils; he would later write a commentary on the famous *Qasida Ghausiya*. He also received knowledge from Pir Mian Sher Muhammad of Sharaqpur, and drew great light from Hazrat Pir Meher Ali Shah of Golra Sharif. It was Meher Ali Shah, tradition says, who told him that his true portion lay in the Suhrawardi order, with Hazrat Ghulam Muhammad Suhrawardi, and bade him take allegiance there — which he did.

His lineage was thus doubly rich: his family descent as a Gilani sayyid is traced, through some twenty-three links, to Shaikh Abd al-Qadir Jilani of Baghdad, and his Sufi allegiance, through some nineteen links, to Shaikh Shihab al-Din Umar Suhrawardi, the great systematiser of the Suhrawardi way. Though he carried both the Gilani-Qadiri and the Suhrawardi inheritances, it was the Gilani-Suhrawardi path that he made his own. A cherished story tells that his master Ghulam Muhammad Suhrawardi once summoned him and said that his own murshid, Baba Jango Pir Shah Suhrawardi, had appeared to him in a dream, foretelling the coming of a young man who should be cared for, “for his manifestation will come about through my name.” Returning to Lahore, Abul Faiz kept his first spiritual retreat (chilla) at the shrine of Shaikh Hassan, known as Sohteli Suhrawardi; and when at last he met his master again, Ghulam Muhammad Suhrawardi told him, “You have made me happy; go, I am pleased with you.” To the end, Abul Faiz would say that whatever he was, he was fulfilling the word of Baba Jango Pir Suhrawardi — as though, he said, the saint were working within him.

## The Scholar and Author

Unusually among the qalandars, Abul Faiz was first and foremost a man of the pen. A recognised scholar of the Ahl-e-Sunnat tradition and a pupil of Ala Hazrat, he is listed among the notable disciples of Ahmad Raza Khan in the biographical compendia of the school, and he devoted much of his life to writing. His books — among them *Jamal-e-Rasool* (“The Beauty of the Messenger”), *Jamal-e-Ilahi* (“The Divine Beauty”), his commentary on the *Qasida Ghausiya*, and many other treatises, tracts, and poems — are steeped in the love of God and of the Prophet, and are still read with esteem. *Jamal-e-Rasool*, dedicated directly to the Prophet and composed in the memory of his own murshid, is a scholarly work saturated in *ishq-e-Rasool*, the passionate love of the Messenger that lay at the heart of his devotion, and he was known too for his devotional verse (naat) in the Prophet’s praise. In an age of religious controversy he wielded both the sermon and the book, and his learning was regarded by his followers as itself a kind of miracle.

## Teaching and Reform

Abul Faiz Qalandar is remembered above all as a reformer of souls — a master of *islah*, the correction of character — whose method was gentleness and example rather than censure. In a gathering, reproving those quick to condemn the faults of others, he is said to have taught: “Keep your own shirt clean and do not point at another’s dirty shirt; seeing your clean shirt, the man with the soiled one will mend himself of his own accord.” And again: “The time you would spend reforming others, spend it on reforming yourself.” He held that his knowledge was a trust to be spent in the service of others — “this is my duty, that I benefit people through what I know” — and his door was famously open: he used to say that whoever came to it never went away empty-handed, and that God does not turn away the prayer of one who comes to this threshold. It was for this union of learning, humility, and generosity that the great scholars of his day sought his company and, having met him, came to love him.

## Miracles

As with every saint, a body of miracle-stories (karamat) gathered about him, and they are still told at the shrine. Once, standing in the mosque as the rain began, he stretched his blessed hands out into it and, wetting them, remarked that he would be no true friend of God who could not number the drops that fall upon the earth. On a journey by train with his students, all the travellers stepped down at the end with their clothes soiled and their faces streaked with grime — all, that is, but the saint, whose face alone was clean; and when they asked how, he answered, “The dirt is subject to us; we are not subject to the dirt.” His students marvelled, too, that in writing his books he would cite other works of the scholars and the saints though those books were nowhere at hand; asked how this could be, he explained that when he began to write, all those books opened themselves before him. He was believed to know the outward and the inward alike, and to answer the need of those who came to him before ever they voiced it.

## A Life in a Changing Country

Abul Faiz Qalandar’s life ran through the last decades of British India and the birth of Pakistan, and he did not stand apart from the affairs of his people. He is remembered as having played a part in the politics of the age and in the Pakistan Movement, and, at the time of the First World War, as having roused a spirit of courage and steadfastness among the people. He belonged to that long line of Indian Sufis — reaching back to Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan, whose Suhrawardi order he inherited — who joined the inward path to an active concern for the community, and he laboured, as his followers put it, day and night for the faith through the middle of the twentieth century.

## The Suhrawardi Way

The order into which Abul Faiz Qalandar was ultimately drawn is one of the oldest and most influential in Islam. The Suhrawardiyya takes its name from Abu Najib al-Suhrawardi and, above all, from his nephew Shaikh Shihab al-Din Umar al-Suhrawardi of Baghdad, whose manual *‘Awarif al-Ma‘arif* became one of the classic guides of the Sufi path. In contrast to some of the more antinomian and ecstatic movements, the Suhrawardi way was known for its sobriety, its insistence on the outward law and on refined manners (*adab*), and its readiness to engage with rulers and society for the good of the community — a temper well suited to a scholar-saint. The order was carried into the Indian subcontinent in the thirteenth century, most famously by Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan, whose great shrine remains one of the anchors of Sufism in Pakistan, and it put down deep roots across the Punjab and Sindh. In taking allegiance in this line, Abul Faiz Qalandar joined a chain of transmission seven centuries deep — even as he bore, in his Gilani descent, the blood and the blessing of the Qadiri order of Abd al-Qadir Jilani. His life thus gathered up two of the great rivers of Islamic spirituality, the Qadiri and the Suhrawardi, and carried them into twentieth-century Lahore.

## The Shrine

Abul Faiz Qalandar died on 9 September 1958, and his resting place at Hanjarwal Mor, on the Multan Road in Lahore, was raised into a shrine that his family has tended ever since. It stands within a wider sacred ground — beside the Hanjarwal graveyard and the shrine of Baba Pir Hanjar Wali Sarkar, where other holy men of the region also lie. Around the tomb has grown a small religious complex that reflects the saint’s own character as a scholar-Sufi: the Jamia Masjid Suhrawardia, where the five daily prayers are offered in congregation, together with a Madrasa Suhrawardia and a library at which students still read. Buried alongside the saint are his four sons; of one of them, Ejaz Ahmad Gilani Suhrawardi, who had gone into the film world, it is remembered that his father, disowning that path in his lifetime, said he could do no more for him than pray for his hereafter — yet at his death he too was laid to rest here. The shrine is not a government-managed darbar but private property, held and maintained by the Gilani-Suhrawardi family.

## The Living Lineage

What most distinguishes this shrine is that the spiritual line it commemorates is unbroken and still living. After Abul Faiz Qalandar, the seat (gaddi) passed to his successor Miraj-ud-Din Gilani Suhrawardi, who guided and initiated many disciples and who is buried beside his master; after him to Rasool Shah Gilani Suhrawardi, likewise buried at the shrine; and it is now held by the latter’s son, Shahid Rasool Shah Gilani Suhrawardi, who oversees the darbar and continues to accept the allegiance of new disciples. Pilgrims come not only to honour a saint of the past but to enter a living chain of guidance — to take *bai‘at* at the hand of the present successor and to be counted, as tens of thousands before them have been, among the disciples of the Suhrawardi way as it has been kept at Hanjarwal.

## Devotion and Events

The shrine draws a steady daily stream of visitors — up to some two thousand on an ordinary day — who come to recite the Fatiha, to seek the saint’s intercession (waseela), and to lay their needs before God at a threshold famed for never sending anyone away empty. Every Sunday the darbar holds gatherings and *milad* assemblies in honour of the Prophet, well attended, at which disciples also present themselves to the living successor. The great occasion of the year is the annual urs, held on the 11th and 12th of Rabi-ul-Awwal, when the shrine fills with as many as two hundred thousand devotees for days of qawwali and *dhol*, *langar* (the free distribution of food), the ceremonial washing (*ghusl*) of the tomb and the changing of its cloth (*chadar*). The adjoining mosque, madrasa, and library mean that the life of the shrine is one of learning and prayer as much as of festival, in keeping with the character of the scholar-saint it honours.

## Legacy

Abul Faiz Qalandar Ali Gilani Suhrawardi stands as a bridge between the classical world of the Punjabi Sufi orders and the modern age. In him the disciplined learning of Ala Hazrat’s school met the ecstatic freedom of the qalandar and the ordered devotion of the Suhrawardi silsila; he wrote and preached and reformed, and gathered thousands into a chain of guidance that his descendants carry still. His shrine at Hanjarwal — mosque, madrasa, library, and tomb together — is at once a place of pilgrimage, a seat of a living Sufi order, and a reminder that the sacred history of Lahore did not close with the great saints of the past but continued into the century just gone.

## Bibliography

- Sayyid Abul Faiz Qalandar Ali Suhrawardi, *Jamal-e-Rasool* (Lahore: Oriental Publications) — the saint’s own devotional work in praise of the Prophet.
- Professor Dilawar Khan, *Talzeem-e-Ala Hazrat: Hazrat Abul Faiz kī ‘Ilmī Khidmāt kā Mutāla‘a* — a study of the saint’s scholarship as a pupil of Ahmad Raza Khan.
- *Darbar Abul Faiz Qalandari Gilani Soharwardi* — Urdu account of the shrine and lineage.
- Shrines Project field survey, Darbar Abul Faiz Qalandari responses (surveyor: Saifullah), 2026.

Name: Shrine of Akhund Darweza Baba
Events: Pilgrimage to the tomb; visited year-round
Description:
The shrine of Akhund Darweza Baba lies in the Hazarkhwani area of Peshawar, a short way south of the Ganj gate of the old walled city, where the saint was buried in the historic Hazarkhwani graveyard. *Akhund Darweza* (traditionally 1533-1638) was one of the most influential religious figures of the Pashtun country in the age of the Mughals — a Sufi and a formidable scholar of the outward religious sciences, a poet in both Pashto and Persian, and a disciple of *Sayyid Ali Tirmizi*, the saint known as *Pir Baba* of Buner (himself honoured at a shrine in this collection). He is best remembered for his learned and combative opposition to the *Roshani* movement of Bayazid Ansari (Pir Roshan), against whose teachings he wrote and preached, and for his religious works, among them the *Makhzan al-Islam* and the *Tazkirat al-Abrar wa'l-Ashrar*, which remain landmarks of early Pashto and Indo-Persian religious literature. He died in the reign of Shah Jahan and was laid to rest at Peshawar, where his tomb became, and remains, a place of pilgrimage for those who seek his blessing. The shrine is a characteristic Peshawar *ziyarat*, its custodianship and its customs handed down over the centuries, and it stands as a memorial to a saint who shaped the religious identity of the Pashtuns as both teacher and defender of orthodox belief. Its situation in the crowded graveyards east of the old city ties it to the deep Islamic heritage of Peshawar, the ancient meeting-place of Central Asia and the subcontinent.

A separate compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints, Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, independently corroborates both the shrine's location — giving it as Hazarkhwani, Peshawar, matching this entry — and the saint's discipleship: it names him a *khalifa* (successor) of "Mir Syed Ali," i.e. Syed Ali Ghawwas Tirmizi, the saint venerated as Pir Baba of Buner elsewhere in this archive, confirming the teacher-student relationship already recorded above from the other side at that entry. The tazkira gives a year of death, but its digits are illegible in the OCR scan and are not reproduced here.

Name: Shrine of Akhund Panju Baba
Location: Akbarpura, Nowshera District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
Sufi Saint: Hazrat Syed Abdul Wahab (Akhund Panju Baba)
Events: Annual urs; large gatherings of devotees
Description:
## Overview

The shrine of Akhund Panju Baba stands at Akbarpura, a town in Nowshera District of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, in the historic Peshawar valley. It honours *Hazrat Syed Abdul Wahab*, known to all as *Akhund Panju Baba*, a Sufi and preacher remembered as one of the great teachers of Islam in the Pashtun country during the reign of the Mughal emperor Akbar (1556-1605). Tradition holds that many were guided to Islam through him, and that his circle of disciples included some of the most notable saints of the region — among them, it is said, *Bahadur Baba*, the father of the celebrated *Kaka Sahib* of Nowshera, so that Akhund Panju Baba stands near the head of a whole genealogy of Pashtun Sufi teachers. His tomb at Akbarpura, together with the historic mosque associated with him — a Mughal-era foundation reckoned to be some four centuries old — forms a shrine complex attended by thousands of devotees, who gather especially at the annual *urs* to seek his blessing. Set amid the fields and orchards of the Nowshera plain, the shrine is a characteristic example of the Sufi *ziyarat* of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the memory of the early preacher-saints remains woven into the devotional life of the surrounding villages. Its enduring draw testifies to the reverence in which Akhund Panju Baba is held as a founder of the region's Islamic learning and as the spiritual ancestor of a line of saints whose shrines dot the valley.

## A Second Source, a Different Locality

A general compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints separately records an "Akhund Panju Baba" whose shrine it places at Misri Pura, in Peshawar Sadar — a different named locality from Akbarpura, Nowshera District, where this entry's other sourcing places the shrine. That compendium gives a specific origin for the name: it states that opponents mockingly nicknamed him "Panju" ("five") for his insistence on preaching the five pillars of Islam, and that the name stuck. It does not give his birth name, and does not mention Bahadur Baba or Kaka Sahib. Whether this is the same saint remembered with a variant locality tradition, or a distinct Pashtun preacher who happened to share the same by-name — "Akhund [X] Baba" is a common honorific pattern in the region — is not resolvable from these two sources alone, and is reported here rather than silently merged.

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, vol. 2 (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.
