Name: Shrine of Baba Shah Chiragh
Location: The Mall (near Lahore High Court), Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: No confirmed annual urs date documented
Description:
## Overview

The shrine of Baba Shah Chiragh stands beside the Lahore High Court on The Mall, in the shadow of the colonial Aiwan-e-Auqaf building that now bears its name. It is the tomb of Sayyid Abdul Razzaq, a Sufi, or Muslim mystic, of the Qadiri lineage, who was known as Shah Chiragh, from *chiragh*, a lamp, and who lived in the reign of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan and died in 1657. Raised by order of the emperor Aurangzeb, the tomb holds eight graves of his family, his own among them, and it survives as a piece of Mughal Lahore among the government buildings of the modern city.

His family were Gilani Sayyids, descendants of the Prophet, who traced their line to Sheikh Abdul Qadir Gilani of Baghdad, the founder of the Qadiri order, and who came to Lahore from Uch, in what is now Bahawalpur. A mosque was later added beside the tomb under Zakariya Khan, the Mughal viceroy of Lahore. Under British rule the mosque became a government office and the precinct was absorbed into the Aiwan-e-Auqaf complex, and since 1973 the shrine has been in the care of the Auqaf Department, the government's department of religious endowments.

## The Saint

Shah Chiragh is remembered as one of the shaikhs of the Qadiri order, a man of worship and discipline, of abstinence and piety, learned in the outward sciences. His real name was Sayyid Abdul Razzaq, son of Sayyid Abdul Wahab Gilani, and Shah Chiragh was his title. Abdul Razzaq and Shah Chiragh are most often taken to be one man, though accounts differ, and Lahore has known other men of both names.

His family's line ran back from his father, Sayyid Abdul Wahab, through Sayyid Abdul Qadir Thalith, Muhammad Ghaus Bala Pir, Zain al-Abidin and Sayyid Abdul Qadir Sani to Sayyid Muhammad Ghaus Uchi Halabi Gilani. Accounts of his descent differ in detail, but the grandfather most often named is Sayyid Abdul Qadir Thalith. Muhammad Ghaus Uchi was the first of the Qadiri line to come to the Punjab. His ancestors had left Baghdad in the time of Hulagu Khan, and he came by way of Khurasan to Multan and settled at Uch, which he is said to have entered in 887 AH, a year of the Islamic calendar.

Like Shah Chiragh, his grandfather Abdul Qadir Thalith lies in a tomb around Lahore; both men descended from Abdul Qadir Sani, a son of Muhammad Ghaus Uchi. The family's road to Lahore ran in two stages. Its elders came from Uch, in the territory of Bahawalpur State, first to a *qasba*, a small town, in the Montgomery district, and from there they came to live in Lahore.

His name has its own story. On the day he was born, it is said, his father declared that a lamp had been born into their house, by which the whole family would be lit, and so he was named Shah Chiragh. Accounts differ over who gave him the name.

He loved travel, and journeyed through many lands for the sake of experience; he also went on pilgrimage to the Haramain Sharifain, the two holy cities of Mecca and Medina. The emperor Shah Jahan was wholly devoted to him, and tried hard to give one of his daughters in marriage to him or to his son, Sayyid Mustafa. The offer was not accepted.

Shah Dargahi Qadri, a man given to visions and miracles, to sincerity and purity, to abstinence and discipline, is remembered as the *murid*, the pledged disciple, of a Hazrat Shah Chiragh Gilani Lahori, though it is not settled that this master was the saint of the Mall. Shah Dargahi's own grave lies beside that of Shah Ismail Muhaddith, with a well whose cure became a standing ritual of Lahore.

Accounts of the date of his death differ, but he is most often said to have died on the twenty second of Dhu al-Qa'da, the eleventh month of the Islamic year, in 1068 AH. He was buried in Lahore. A chronogram on his death, a verse whose letters, read as numbers, give a year, is attributed to Mufti Ghulam Sarwar, the author of a *tazkira*, a book of the lives of the saints. It ends with this line:

گفت سرور میر شمس العارفین

*The line names its poet, Sarwar, and calls the saint Mir Shams al-Arifin, the sun of those who know God.*

## The Shrine

The tomb stands in Lahore, adjoining the High Court. The ground was once the quarter of Langar Khan Baloch, a *murid* of the family, and that is why the tomb was built there; in the nineteenth century the area was known as Mohalla Langar Khan. By the 1880s the tomb was counted among the Muslim buildings outside the city.

It was built by order of the emperor Aurangzeb, Alamgir. Of limestone, on a square plan and in a restrained Mughal style, it has its door facing south, a roof of brick and a grand dome above. Its façades carry niches with cusped arches and panelled cartouches, and inside, traces of floral fresco decoration remain. In the nineteenth century the tomb had a wooden door with a lattice, and an inscription of the *kalima*, the profession of faith, could be seen there.

Inside lie eight graves, Shah Chiragh's own and those of his family, so that the tomb is a family shrine across generations rather than the resting place of one man. Accounts differ over which of his kin lie with him; one of the graves is that of a *sahibzada*, a saint's son, named Zain al-Abidin. In the nineteenth century there was also a walled enclosure, a *chardiwari*, holding graves, with a well, trees and a broken floor, and its ground, it seems, had once been a small garden.

The mosque beside the tomb was added in 1716, under the patronage of Zakariya Khan, the Mughal viceroy of Lahore, in the reign of Muhammad Shah Rangeela. Khan Bahadur Zakariya Khan ordered it built because his mother was a *murida*, a woman disciple, of this family. She had willed that her grave should be here and that a mosque should be built from her jewellery. In the nineteenth century the mosque had five domes and four cells, and the grave of the Nawab's mother lay under a tree.

Under British rule the mosque was made a *kothi*, a residence, where Deputy Commissioners among others lived, and then the government's Accountant's office was set up there; it still housed that office in the 1880s. By then the mosque stood in an enclosure of its own, apart from the tomb's. The complex had been split in two by colonial occupation, the mosque taken into government use as an office and the tomb left in the hands of the Gilani Sayyids, the saint's own lineage.

In the 1880s this part of Lahore was also remembered as the quarter of Sayyid Chiragh Shah Gilani, where Gilani Sayyids lived, east of the quarter of Mauj Darya Bukhari. The quarter had been settled as a *jagir*, a grant of land, and was later laid waste by plunderers, and the Chief Court building had begun to go up where it stood. Sayyid Chiragh Shah's tomb and his *pakka* mosque, solidly built of fired brick, still stood, the mosque in government possession and the tomb held by his descendants.

In the nineteenth century the shrine had a *sajjada nashin*, the custodian who sits on the saint's prayer carpet. There was also a broken enclosure where a *faqir*, a Sufi of spiritual poverty, lived. In the time of the Sikhs, before British rule, the mosque and the rest of the shrine had held land, but by then little of it was left.

In the late nineteenth century the precinct around the tomb was absorbed into the grand Indo-Saracenic complex of the Aiwan-e-Auqaf, built by the British administration between 1875 and 1880. That complex today houses the offices and library of the Auqaf Department, the same body that has administered the shrine since 1973.

## Devotion and Festivals

In the nineteenth century the tombs of Shah Chiragh and of his grandfather Abdul Qadir Thalith were places of pilgrimage for the people. Under Muslim rule the family had stood very high, and because its lineage joined that of Piran-e-Pir Muhi-ud-Din, the pir of pirs, people held its members in great respect.

By the 1880s a *mela*, a fair, was held here every year on the seventeenth of Rabi-us-Sani, the fourth month of the Islamic year, and great crowds gathered for it. In the nineteenth century a faqir had for a long time held the *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, taken its income and served as *khadim*, the attendant of the tomb. Every Thursday, too, music sounded at the tomb of Hazrat Shah Chiragh.

## Other Men of the Name

Several other men called Chiragh or Abd al-Razzaq, in Lahore and beyond, are remembered separately from the saint of the Mall. Sayyid Abd al-Razzaq of Mohalla Dola Wari was a *khalifa*, a spiritual deputy, of Mauj Darya Bukhari, and the first to settle in that quarter, which flourished after him. His *pakka* tomb stood in a lane of a bazaar, with a *pakka* mosque inside its enclosure. Under Ranjit Singh iron shot was made in the mosque courtyard, and the British emptied both buildings. When the cantonment left Anarkali, the meat contractor Munshi Najm al-Din took the mosque and tomb from the government, repaired the mosque and opened it again, and a grave was made in the tomb.

Others of the name were also linked with Mauj Darya. One Sayyid Abd al-Razzaq, after Mauj Darya's death, worshipped by night at his tomb and rested by day in a cell where his own tomb later stood, and he was buried in that cell as he had willed. His tomb was built by subscription, with a large mosque beside it from what was left over, and when an order later threatened to seize the building unless it was put in order within two months, merchants raised money for it. Shah Abd al-Razzaq Makki, a *murid* of Mauj Darya, died in 1084 AH and lies in Anarkali bazaar; he bore the saint's personal name and lived in the same part of Lahore, but he had a different master and died in a different year.

Other Chiraghs include a Chiragh Shah whose *mazar*, a saint's tomb, is outside the Roshnai Gate, the successor of a Sayyid Ali Gilani; a Shah Chiragh of Delhi; Hazrat Shah Chiragh Sahib Qadiri Sultanpuri, who looked on Nur Husain with the utmost kindness; and Sayyid Chiragh Shah Hakim, living in the 1880s, who had *murids* in the Chishti and Qadiri orders. Remembered separately, too, are Shaikh Abd al-Razzaq Makki of the Nila Gumbad, and the Sayyid Abd al-Razzaq who was a son and *murid* of Hazrat Ghaus al-Azam and stands in the spiritual chain of Mian Mir.

## The Setting

The patron of the mosque, Nawab Zakariya Khan Bahadur, was among the governors and rulers of the Punjab, with Shahnawaz Khan and others, who lived in Mughalpura. He also built another mosque in Lahore, west of the *mazar* of Madho Lal Hussain. A tile inscription on its north *mihrab*, the niche that marks the direction of prayer, dates that building to the reign of Muhammad Shah and carries this verse:

زبدۂ بارگاہ او نواب
زکریا خان صوبہ پنجاب

*The verse names its builder, Nawab Zakariya Khan, governor of the Punjab.*

In the 1880s the Chief Court, whose building was rising on the old quarter of Sayyid Chiragh Shah Gilani, was the court that gave the final decision in civil and criminal cases. Appeals from the commissionerships of the Punjab came before it, and capital sentences needed its sanction.

Today Mall Road is one of the busiest boulevards in the city, and the Lahore High Court, which combines European and Eastern architectural techniques, stands close to the Panorama Market. The shrine of Mauj Darya Bukhari stands nearby, and his grave is said to lie inside Shah Chiragh's mausoleum complex.

## Legacy

Though it lacks the international renown of some of Lahore's other Sufi sites, the shrine is formally catalogued as a protected heritage monument by the Punjab Directorate General of Archaeology. Its distinctive Mughal fabric, set incongruously amid the bureaucratic buildings of modern Lahore, makes it a quietly significant survival from the city's religious landscape of the seventeenth century.

Aurangzeb, it has been said, gave importance to some Qadiri Sufis who were mindful of the *sharia*, the religious law, and Shah Chiragh, whose tomb the emperor had built, was one of them. Raised by that emperor's order over a saint whom Shah Jahan had revered, the tomb has seen its mosque become a residence and a government office and its precinct absorbed into a complex built by the British administration, and its keeping has passed from the saint's own lineage to the Auqaf Department.

Name: Shrine of Baba Shah Kamal
Location: Muslim Town / Samanabad (near Ichhra), Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: Annual urs; weekly Thursday devotional gathering
Description:
## Overview

The tomb of Hazrat Baba Shah Kamal lies in Muslim Town, near Ichhra in Lahore, within an old graveyard that still bears his name and lends it to the housing scheme around it. Shah Kamal is remembered above all as the elder brother of the celebrated Sufi, or Muslim mystic, Baba Shah Jamal, whose shrine stands nearby. Local devotees gather at his tomb every Thursday evening for drumming and devotional music, and once a year for his *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death.

Far less is known of Shah Kamal than of his famous brother. He is remembered as a devout Sayyid, given to spiritual rapture and famed for his wonders, who settled with his brother at Ichhra and was buried in a domed tomb raised by the disciples of his family. That tomb has outlived the fall of its own enclosure wall, and the city that once lay three miles away now surrounds it. It now stands within a complex of mosque and graveyard, catalogued as a monument of the historic period, in a graveyard still used for burials.

## The Saint

Much of what is remembered of Shah Kamal is bound up with his brother. The two were the sons of Syed Ahmad Shah, and the shrine traces the family's descent from Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari of Uch Sharif. Accounts of the family's ancestry differ in detail, but Shah Kamal is remembered as a Sayyid, a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad. Their father himself instructed both his sons in Islamic theology, and the two brothers afterwards settled together in the Ichhra area of Lahore. In the nineteenth century the two brothers were known as a pair, the one Shah Jamal and the other Shah Kamal.

By the late nineteenth century Shah Kamal was remembered as a devout man, given to *jazb*, the rapture of a soul drawn towards God. There is no settled view of his order, but he is most often counted a Suhrawardi, a follower of the Sufi order founded by Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi, and he is said to have come of a Suhrawardi family. Local devotion honours him with the double title Qadiri Suhrawardi, which joins to the Suhrawardi name that of the Qadiri order, founded by Abd al-Qadir Gilani, and so suggests an affiliation with the same overlapping Sufi orders associated with his brother's shrine nearby. No master of his own and no chain of spiritual descent are remembered for him.

He is not to be confused with the other saints who shared his name. Shah Kamal of Kaithal, a Qadiri master in the spiritual line of the Mujaddid, the renewer of the faith, is remembered quite separately from the brother of Shah Jamal, and so are Kamal Bukhari, called Pir Jahaniyan, a Sayyid Kamal, and Sayyid Kamal Shah Chishti, outside the Kashmiri Gate. Nor is he the Sayyid Kamil Shah Lahori of the village of Babu Sabu, whose name is Kamil, not Kamal.

Accounts of his dates differ, and no year of his death is settled. His life is generally placed in the age of the Mughal emperors, between the late sixteenth and the seventeenth century, much the same years as his brother's. He was buried here, close to the brother with whom he had settled at Ichhra.

## The Shrine

The tomb stands within the historic Shah Kamal graveyard, which is still in active use as a burial ground. In the nineteenth century it lay outside the city, near the villages of Ichhra and Rawan, three miles south of Lahore, right beside Shah Jamal's *khanqah*, the lodge where a Sufi's disciples gather.

In the nineteenth century a high wall enclosed the tomb, though part of it had fallen. Within it rose an octagonal platform and an octagonal dome. There had once been four doors, but three had been closed, leaving only the southern door open. The grave itself was finished in lime plaster and was broken in places, and a *kikar*, a thorny acacia, grew to the north of it. For a long time a man named Nihal, known as Nihal Shah, had swept the tomb and lit its lamps.

In the 1880s it was a grand tomb of *pakka*, or fired, brick, standing on an octagonal platform of the same solid brickwork, with its octagonal dome at the centre. Inside, a second platform of fired brick carried Shah Kamal's grave, itself solidly built. There were four doors, one on each side, three of them closed and only the southern one open. The tomb had been raised not by a ruler or a state but by the *murids*, the pledged disciples, of the saint's family.

The place had once been much frequented. By the 1880s its enclosure wall, which had been very high and solidly built, had fallen, but the tomb itself still stood, though it was in need of repair. In a city where building after building was pulled down, its survival was put down to its distance from Lahore: had it stood among the city's buildings, it too would have been pulled down.

Today the shrine forms part of a complex of mosque and graveyard at Karnalpura, Muslim Town, Combo Colony, Lahore. It belongs to the Auqaf Department, the Punjab government's department of religious endowments, which lists it in its Lahore Zone as the "Darbar & Jamia Masjid Hazrat Shah Kamal", the shrine and congregational mosque of Hazrat Shah Kamal. The Punjab Department of Archaeology and Museums formally catalogues it as a monument of the historic period. It is counted among the historic monuments of Mughal Lahore, and its condition is rated "Satisfactory".

## Devotion and Festivals

The tomb continues to draw local devotees. Every Thursday evening they gather for drumming on the *dhol*, a large barrel drum, and for *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, echoing in more modest form the famous *dhamal*, ecstatic devotional dancing to the beat of the drum, for which Shah Jamal's shrine is known.

Once a year an *ʿurs* is held in his honour, drawing pilgrims from the surrounding neighbourhoods. By the late nineteenth century he was famous for his *karamat*, the miraculous deeds and spiritual gifts of a saint, and for his marvels, though little is told of what they were.

## The Setting

Where the tomb once stood among villages three miles south of Lahore, it now lies within the city, in Muslim Town near Ichhra, with his brother's shrine close by and a housing scheme named after his graveyard all around it. In Lahore today the city's Qalandars, wandering dervishes, are still associated with its great Qadiri saints, among them Shah Jamal, Shah Hussayn and Miyan Mir.

A legend of the founding of the towns round about is tied to Rawan, the village beside which the tomb stands. The tale is told in more than one way; in the version tied to this place, it is said that Raja Ram Chand had three sons: one built Lahore, a second settled another town, and the third founded Rawan. The story ends with the pious formula "God knows best". It is a legend of the place rather than of the saint.

## Legacy

Together with his brother's shrine, the tomb of Shah Kamal helps anchor the religious identity of this part of Lahore as a historic centre of Sufi devotion. It reflects a wider pattern in the city, where whole neighbourhoods have taken their names and character from the saints buried within them, and the graveyard that holds his tomb still lends his name to the housing scheme around it. Raised by the disciples of his family rather than by any ruler, it has outlasted the fall of its own enclosure wall. In the nineteenth century only its southern door stood open, and for a long time a single keeper swept it and lit its lamps. Today it stands within a complex of mosque and graveyard in the care of the Auqaf Department, still visited on Thursday evenings and at its yearly *ʿurs*.

Name: Shrine of Bahauddin Zakariya
Events: Annual urs; qawwali; daily langar
Description:
## Overview

In the old city of Multan, the "City of Saints", stands the shrine of Hazrat Bahauddin Zakariya, the saint who planted the Suhrawardi order of Sufis, or Muslim mystics, in the soil of the subcontinent and made Multan one of the first great centres of Islamic mysticism in South Asia. A contemporary and friend of Baba Farid of Pakpattan, and like him a shaper of the spiritual map of the Punjab, he founded a *khanqah*, a Sufi lodge, at Multan whose influence reached across the region for centuries. His tomb, raised in the thirteenth century, is among the oldest and most revered Muslim shrines in Pakistan, and pilgrims come to it throughout the year.

He lived from around 1170 to 1267. He is considered the patron saint of Multan, and his shrine, which stands beside a Hindu temple, became the symbol of the Muslim city. In Punjabi poetry he is counted among the Five Pirs, five great saints who are believed together to possess special powers, and his tomb is a major centre of pilgrimage. His disciples and descendants, among them the Persian poet Fakhr-ud-Din Iraqi and his grandson Shah Rukn-e-Alam, carried the order he brought to Multan across Sindh and the Punjab.

## The Saint

Bahauddin Zakariya was born around 1170 at Kot Karor, near Multan; accounts of the year of his birth differ. He is said to have been born on a Friday morning, the twenty seventh of Ramazan, the month of fasting. He came of a Qureshi family of Arab descent that had settled in the region. His grandfather, Kamal al-Din Ali Shah Qureshi, a dervish by nature and an honoured member of the Quraish, the tribe of the Prophet, left Mecca and lived in Khwarazm, and from Khwarazm he came to Multan, then a centre of the Islamic sciences and arts, where he settled for good and many became his devotees. Accounts of the family's descent within the Quraish differ, but Bahauddin is held to have been a Hashimi, of the clan of Hashim, the Prophet's own clan.

His father was Shaikh Wajih al-Din Muhammad, son of Kamal al-Din, and his mother was Bibi Fatima. Her father is most often named Maulana Husam al-Din Tirmizi, who had left his homeland of Tirmiz when the Tatar plundering began and lived at Kot Karor. It is told that the child was born a *wali*, a friend of God, and that as an infant he would stop suckling to listen whenever his father recited the Quran. His father died when he was twelve. As a boy he memorised the Quran, and as a schoolboy, it is said, he claimed to remember the primordial covenant: he remembered, he said, all that had happened from the moment God said *Am I not your Lord?* until that day.

He came to be known by many names and titles. His *kunya*, the name of honour formed with Abu, "father of", was Abu Muhammad. He was called Shaikh al-Shuyukh, the Shaikh of Shaikhs, Makhdum al-Alam, the Master of the World, and Bahauddin Zakariya Qureshi Multani; he bears the title Baha al-Haq, and in Bulleh Shah's verse he is invoked as Bahaval Haq. Among the titles heaped on him are peerless *pir*, or spiritual guide, and treasury of generosity, and he is counted among the greatest of the *awliya*, the friends of God.

After his father's death he set out in search of learning. Accounts of his route differ, but he is said to have spent seven years at his studies in Khurasan and then to have gone to Bukhara, where he completed his learning and became famous as Bahauddin Farishta, "the angel". From there he went to the Hejaz. At Medina, where he stayed five years, he studied *hadith*, the sayings of the Prophet, with Shaikh Kamal al-Din Muhammad Yamani, one of the great scholars of *hadith*, and obtained an *ijazat-nama*, a written licence to teach. On his travels he met the dervishes of Khurasan, Bukhara, Mecca, Medina and Bait al-Muqaddas, Jerusalem.

At last he came to Baghdad, and there he took *bai'at*, the oath by which a disciple pledges himself to a master, from Shaikh Shihab-ud-Din Abu Hafs Umar al-Suhrawardi, the great systematiser of the Suhrawardi order and author of the *‘Awarif al-Ma‘arif*. Under him he completed his training with remarkable speed. Within eighteen days, it is said, he received the *khirqa*, the patched cloak of the Sufi, as the mark of his *khilafat*, his authority to guide others, and he was sent to Multan with leave to carry the order to India.

The chain of masters that ran to him began with Junaid of Baghdad, the chief of the Sufi company, and passed, among others, through Mamshad Alu Dinawari, Ahmad Aswad Dinawari, Abu Abdullah Khafif, Abu al-Qasim Gurgani, Abu Bakr Nassaj, Shaikh Ahmad Ghazali, the brother of Imam Muhammad Ghazali, Ziya al-Din Abu al-Najib Suhrawardi and Wajih al-Din Suhrawardi to Shihab-ud-Din Umar Suhrawardi, and from him to Bahauddin Zakariya.

On the road to Multan, it is told, he met a learned *qalandar*, a wandering dervish, Sayyid Abd al-Quddus of Mosul, who had put on the qalandars' dress at the grave of Sayyid Jamal al-Din Mujarrad; Bahauddin had the qalandar's garment taken off him and brought him from *jazb*, the rapture of a soul drawn towards God, to *suluk*, the ordered journey of the Sufi path. Shaikh Jalal al-Din Tabrizi travelled with him as far as Nishapur, where the two parted; accounts of why they parted differ.

Coming from Baghdad to Multan, he took up permanent residence there; many became his disciples, and he became the foremost Suhrawardi shaykh of the subcontinent. The dervishes already in the city, the story goes, did not want him there and sent him a cup filled with milk, to say that there was no room for another in the city. He laid a flower on the milk and sent the cup back, meaning that his place in the city would be as a flower is on milk; and, the story ends, they were astonished and became his devotees.

He was on good terms with Sultan Shams al-Din Iltutmish and supported him against Sultan Qabacha, and under Iltutmish he became *Shaikh al-Islam*, the chief religious dignitary; accounts of how the office came to him differ.

At Delhi he sat in judgement at a trial. When a complaint against Shaikh Jalal al-Din Tabrizi reached Sultan Iltutmish, the Sultan summoned the notables and the *mashaikh*, the Sufi masters, to Delhi; more than two hundred *awliya* came, and after the Friday prayer all assembled in the Masjid Minar. The Sultan let the accuser name the arbitrator, and the accuser chose Bahauddin, counting on the old estrangement, for he believed that the two saints had fallen out at Nishapur. But when the accused entered and all rose in his honour, Bahauddin lifted Shaikh Jalal's shoes in his own hands and declared that he was bound to make the dust of Shaikh Jalal's feet the kohl of his eyes, because for seven years Shaikh Jalal had stayed in the service of his own *pir*. The Sultan said that since the arbitrator had shown such honour the matter was decided, and Bahauddin then questioned the woman in the case, who confessed the whole plot. Such an assembly, a *mahzar*, was a gathering of *ulama*, the scholars of religion, and of Sufis, called to decide an important dispute.

## Life at Multan

His *khanqah* at Multan drew people of every rank. The kings of the time and people high and low alike entered his *bai'at*, thousands of attendants were present at his court, and through him, it is said, hundreds of thousands benefited from the Suhrawardi way. He also had a *madrasa*, a school, in Multan, where the children of the local Nawab and other important officials were taught; it was an elite school of its era.

Unlike the Chishtis, who embraced absolute poverty and kept their distance from the courts, he represented the Suhrawardi temper. He engaged openly with rulers and mixed freely with the ruling classes, as his own master, Abu Hafs Umar Suhrawardi, had served the caliph an-Nasir, and his association with the rulers in Delhi raised him to importance. He accepted endowments and gifts and managed considerable resources. He was a landlord of means, agriculture and trade were carried on at his house on a large scale, and his *khanqah* prospered on gifts from merchants and trade guilds: many merchants traded outside India, were largely independent of the government, and could not be prevented from giving. Outward and inward wealth were his portion: he was himself extremely rich, and his own *pir* had vast wealth too. He looked after the needs of his family and never failed to keep a supply of grain in his house.

He used his wealth in charity and hospitality on a grand scale, though accounts differ over how freely his table and his company were open to all. He was a lively host who followed to the letter the Quranic injunction to eat of what is pure and act righteously, and he greatly honoured the *ulama*, the great *mashaikh* and his guests. He gave thanks in every condition, was very charitable and unconcerned with the world, and lived with simplicity and contentment, eating very little, but strong food. He completed one reading of the Quran every night, and forbearance and patience, ardour and longing, rapture and absorption were his marked qualities. In his early life he fasted much, but in his last years he did not fast daily.

His house had its rules. He did not encourage his disciples to perform *sajda*, prostration, before him; they greeted him with *as-salam alaikum*, "Peace be with you", and he expected them to finish their obligatory religious duties first and to greet him afterwards. In his lifetime he insisted that Sufis join one order only, though from the fourteenth century Sufis were often initiated into both the Chishti and the Suhrawardi orders.

He disliked the *qalandars* intensely and never encouraged their unwelcome visits. Mongol domination of Central Asia and Iran made it easier for bands of Qalandars and Jawaliqis to travel from Turkey and Egypt to India, and those passing through Multan often came into conflict with him, though the generosity of Baba Farid made up for such experiences. Yet he made exceptions. Fakhr-ud-Din Iraqi went on living as a wandering dervish even after his initiation by him, and Lal Shahbaz he adopted as his disciple.

His wealth was enough to make him the target of accusations by other Sufis. Hamid ad-Din Suwali Nagauri, seeking the attitude of the Suhrawardi order towards wealth, carried on an extensive correspondence with him on the question of poverty and wealth. The first letter set out the difficulty: by the teaching of the Shaikhs, the Quran and the *hadith*, the property of this world is an obstacle to union with God, yet it was heard that some of the Shaikhs of the age enjoyed a handsome share of it and at the same time performed miracles. The letter was addressed to Bahauddin, and it left the wealthy Shaikhs unnamed. Hamid ad-Din was left unsatisfied, and in a second letter he wrote that the answer had come to him instead from God.

The two men met at Delhi during the *mahzar* on the charges against Jalal al-Din Tabrizi. In defence of his wealth Bahauddin said: "Although wealth is a serpent, someone who has learnt the incantation to overcome the venom, need not have any fear from the serpent." Pressed further, he answered: "Your achievement as a dervish is not endowed by such beauty and elegance as to be immune from the evil eye, but our achievements as dervishes are endowed with such great beauty as to gain no harm even if the whole of the world's blackness were applied to its face." It is told that in the end he was left without a reply. The quarrel outlived the letters. One of his sons, annoyed by the controversy over the wealth of the Suhrawardis, visited Ajmer, and finding that Hamid ad-Din did not attend the Friday congregational prayers, used this as a pretext to attack him, and gained some support from a group of *ulama* who demanded that Hamid ad-Din fulfil his religious duties.

His own sayings on wealth were remembered: however much worldly wealth there is, it is still little; the company of a snake harms the one who does not know its charm; in his view worldly wealth has no reality; and for *faqirs*, those who have embraced poverty, its absence and its presence are the same, with no grief at its going and no joy at its coming.

Accounts of his attitude to music and poetry differ, but *qawwals*, singers of Sufi devotional music, performed in his gatherings. A *qawwal* named Abdullah, who came from Turkey, enlivened his assemblies. Another, Abu Bakr, who came from Multan to visit Nizam ad-Din's teacher, recalled how he had been reciting in *samaʿ*, the Sufi session of spiritual listening to music, before Shaikh Baha ad-Din, and reached the line "The snake of desire has stung my heart"; he could not recall the second half of the couplet, but the Shaikh did. He went on to praise the Shaikh's hospice, where devotion to God was such that even the slave girls recited the names of God while grinding grain, though his words made no lasting impression on the heart of the young Nizam ad-Din.

Among his contemporaries, Baba Farid of Pakpattan was his great friend. The two were together for a time, and Farid profited from his company. Bahauddin once wrote that between them there was a play of love, and Farid replied that between them there was love, and no play. The two men, separated by only a few hundred miles, stood for two styles of life, and the difference of method between the Suhrawardi and the Chishti, the two poles of early Indian Sufism, is often illustrated by their cordial contrast. In the same period Bahauddin and Muin al-Din Chishti were both preaching divine love and union. Their spheres had a frontier: Baba Farid, it is told, once said to a traveller that the land from his own town to a certain village was in his charge, and that beyond a certain reservoir the land was in the charge of Shaikh Bahauddin Zakariya.

The Chishti Khwaja Qutb al-Din Bakhtiyar Kaki, coming from Baghdad through Khurasan, reached Multan and formed a friendship with him there, before going on to Delhi in the reign of Iltutmish. Bahauddin was also a great admirer of the weaver Shaikh Ahmad Naharwani.

One book of his survives, the *Kitab al-Awrad*, the Book of Litanies; Maulana Ali bin Ahmad Ghori, a *murid*, or disciple, of Shah Rukn-e-Alam, wrote a commentary on it, the *Kanz al-Ibad fi Sharh al-Awrad*. His sayings were gathered in the *Khulasat al-Arifin* and in a *Malfuzat*, a record of his discourses. Among the sayings remembered from him is a definition of renunciation: *zuhd*, asceticism, is three things, and whoever lacks them is no ascetic: to know the truth of the world and let it go; to serve the Lord and keep to his *adab*, the courtesy due to him; and to long for and seek the hereafter. Safety, he said, lies in little food, the soul's safety in leaving people, and the faith's safety in the prayer of the Best of Creation, the Prophet.

He was a poet too, and wrote a famous *manqabat*, a poem in praise of a saint, in honour of Ghaus al-Azam Shaikh Abd al-Qadir Jilani, with the refrain *Muhyi al-Din Jilani*. One couplet opens with a plea to the Shah of Jilan for help:

مدد یا شاہ جیلانی بریں افتادہ حیرانی

The poem closes on a couplet that carries his own name, calling Baha al-Din Multani a stone of the threshold of Jilani.

He died at Multan in 1267, full of years and honour; accounts of the year of his death differ. The day of his death was the seventh of Safar, the second month of the Islamic year. He is said to have reached the age of a hundred and to have died on reading a sealed letter. He was buried at Multan.

## Disciples and Successors

Bahauddin Zakariya's lasting achievement was to root the Suhrawardi way in the subcontinent. From his khanqah at Multan the order spread through Sindh and the Punjab, carried by his disciples and descendants. It was marked by strict adherence to the Sharia, the religious law, by sober devotion and learning, and by an active engagement with society and state, a pattern that made Multan a hub of both spiritual authority and worldly influence and shaped the religious life of the western Punjab and Sindh for centuries. Less austere in its practices than the early Chishti order, the Suhrawardi order sent its members throughout the country and gained disciples even in eastern Bengal. Shihab-ud-Din Suhrawardi had other disciples, but the continuous history of the Suhrawardi order in India can be traced only through the *khalifas* of Bahauddin Zakariya, the deputies he appointed.

He had many famous disciples. Besides his son, he had five eminent *khalifas*: Sayyid Jalal al-Din Surkh Bukhari; Sayyid Usman, known as Lal Shahbaz; Shaikh Hasan Afghan; Shaikh Fakhr al-Din Ibrahim Iraqi; and Sayyid Sadr al-Din Ahmad, known as Sayyid Husain.

Sayyid Jalal al-Din Surkh Bukhari, also called Jalal Surkh, "the Red", came to Multan and became his *murid*. He received the *khirqa* of *khilafat* from him and, by his *pir*'s order, took up residence at Uch. Bahauddin's own *khirqa* was worn by Makhdum Jahaniyan, who received it from his father, Sayyid Ahmad Kabir.

Hasan Afghan could neither read nor write, yet the Shaikh was proud of him and used to say that if God asked him what he had brought from the world, he would present Hasan as a gift. By the Suhrawardi tradition, Lal Shahbaz Qalandar of Sehwan was initiated by him at Multan; accounts of the relations between the two men differ.

Fakhr-ud-Din Ibrahim, known as Iraqi, one of the leading Persian mystical poets, came to Multan with a party of wandering *qalandars*, who stayed with the Shaikh. When the party broke up in a storm, Iraqi returned to the Shaikh's *khanqah* and began living in a cell the Shaikh had assigned him as a spiritual retreat. He attached himself to Bahauddin at Multan, lived in his circle for nearly twenty five years, and dedicated *qasidas*, odes, to him.

His fellow disciples were shocked to learn that a *ghazal*, a love lyric, of his was being sung in the local taverns to the accompaniment of the harp and zither, and they complained to the Shaikh, but the Shaikh ruled for Iraqi. He declared Iraqi's training complete, ordered him to give up retirement and meditation, gave him his own *khirqa* to wear and later gave him his daughter in marriage; before he died, he appointed him his *khalifa*. Soon after his master's death Iraqi left Multan for Konya, where he met Sadruddin Qonawi and perhaps Jalaluddin Rumi, and he lived in Konya for some years. Iraqi wrote verse for his master, naming him the guide of men:

*If thou shouldst ask of the world 'Who is the guide of men?' / Thou wilt hear from heaven no other answer than 'Zakariyya'.*

His name reaches into Sindh and into devotions beyond Sufism. Pithoro Pir is held to have been a Muslim Sufi initiated by Bahauddin Zakariya, and Udero Lal, too, is called his disciple.

Spiritual chains ran back to him. He stands at the head of the chains of Shah Jamal and of Shah Daula, of eight and of thirteen steps, of the *silsila*, the spiritual lineage, of Mian Wada, also of thirteen steps, and of a Suhrawardi chain of nine steps from the Lahore scholar Shaikh Hamid Qari Suhrawardi, whose last links run through Husam al-Din Muttaqi and Shaikh Sadr al-Din to Shaikh Bahauddin. From him, too, came the gift of *wilayat*, sainthood, to Sakhi Sarwar.

## Family and Descendants

He had seven sons: Shaikh Sadr al-Din Arif, Shaikh Burhan al-Din, Shaikh Ziya al-Din, Shaikh Ala al-Din, Shaikh Shihab al-Din, Shaikh Qudwat al-Din and Shaikh Shams al-Din. A daughter of his married Fakhr-ud-Din Iraqi. Unlike the sons of most of the early Chishti saints, his sons followed in his path, and in the Suhrawardi order succession became, generally, hereditary. On his death his estate was divided.

His son Shaikh Sadr al-Din, known as Arif, "the Gnostic", was his *murid*, his *khalifa* and his successor as *sajjada nashin*, the hereditary custodian who sits on the saint's prayer carpet. He took *bai'at* from his father and received from him the *khirqa* of *khilafat*. When his share of the estate came to him, he gave it all to the *fuqara*, the poor. His reasoning began from this: his father had mastered the world, and so the presence of wealth and gold could do his father no harm. Sadr al-Din died in the year 709 of the Hijri calendar.

Sadr al-Din's wife, Bibi Rasti, was a disciple of her father-in-law in her own right, and through her the Suhrawardi *nisbat*, the spiritual bond of the order, reached many women. She died in the year 695 of the Hijri calendar.

It is told that Bahauddin foresaw the greatness of his grandson Rukn al-Din before the child was born: rising to his feet for his pregnant daughter-in-law, he said that the honour was for the child in her womb, who would be the lamp of the family and the candle of the line. He supervised the boy's education and upbringing. At the age of four Rukn al-Din put on his grandfather's turban, and although his father objected strongly, Bahauddin approved and told Sadr al-Din not to forbid the child. When Rukn al-Din succeeded his father, he wore the same turban. He is remembered as Shah Rukn-e-Alam, another saint of Multan, the grandson and successor of Bahauddin Zakariya.

His descendants appear across the history of Multan and Lahore. When the province of Multan was left without a ruler, its people raised Shaikh Yusuf Qureshi, one of his descendants, to rule them. Shaikh Yusuf struck coin and had the *khutba*, the Friday sermon, read in his own name, and he ruled for two years before the Langahs seized him. He escaped to Sultan Bahlul Lodi at Delhi, who married his own daughter to Shaikh Yusuf's son, Shaikh Abdullah, and at Shaikh Yusuf's urging Bahlul's army was then sent against Multan. Sultan Firuz Shah, on reaching his capital, gave Shaikh Sadr al-Din, another of the saint's descendants, the title of *Shaikh al-Islam* and a place near himself.

One descendant, Shah Rahmatullah Qureshi, came from Multan to Lahore, and by the 1870s his family lived in Lahore and in the village of Dholanwal on the *nazr*, the offerings, of their disciples; one of them was Bahadur Shah. Shaikh Hamza Dharsawi was also of his descendants. The family of the Lahore mufti Shaikh Kamal-ud-Din Qureshi was held to descend from him as well: the mufti's father, Shaikh Makhdum, had been summoned from Multan under Muhammad Tughlaq and appointed to the office of *ifta*, the giving of legal rulings. The nineteenth century mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori claimed the same descent for his own family of muftis, whose first elder, Makhdum Mufti Shaikh Muhammad Qureshi, known as Mian Kalan, came from Multan and settled in Lahore.

## The Shrine

Bahauddin Zakariya lies at Multan, in the old fort area of the city. His mausoleum, built in the thirteenth century, is one of the earliest monuments of Islamic architecture in the subcontinent: a square tomb chamber surmounted by a hemispherical dome, much rebuilt after damage over the centuries, among other times in the siege of Multan in 1848. In Aurangzeb's reign the resting place lay inside the fort, and over the tomb, where divine lights were held to be made manifest, a lofty dome of brick and lime had been raised.

It remains a working shrine and the seat of his descendants, the Qureshi *makhdooms* of Multan, who have been among the most prominent religious and political families of the region.

The shrine stands beside the temple of Prahlad Bhagat, a Hindu temple of Multan, and is one of the most popular Muslim shrines. The saint, one of the Muslim mystics drawn to the holy mound, came and settled next to the temple, and his shrine came to be situated beside it; religious traditions once moved freely between the two shrines. The singer and activist Parvati Devi said that the shrine authorities built on the premises of the Prahlad Temple, in 2006 and 2008, first a place for ablutions and then a *langar* hall for devotees visiting the shrine, and that a stay order of the High Court followed on a petition by Usman Chaudary.

The tomb has had its keepers and its petitioners. When the Khan-e Khanan reached Multan, he presented himself at the saint's khanqah and gave two hundred rupees as an offering; it was accepted, and then returned the next morning because of a dream that had come to the *sajjada nashin*. It is told, too, that Maulana Hussam al-Din, while at Multan, was returning one day from the tomb when he conceived the wish to ask for a plot of ground for his own grave, and that Sadr al-Din Arif knew of it by *kashf*, inner unveiling, and told him that it was not difficult for him to give a place for a grave, nor did he object, but the Prophet had chosen a place at Badaun for him, and there he would be buried.

The khanqah's prosperity ended with the execution of Shaikh Hud and the seizure of the khanqah's property. Shaikh Hud's war cry, it was alleged, had been the ill treatment of the saint's descendants by the Sultan. The Suhrawardi order began to flourish in other regions, while Multan became a shadow of its former glory.

## Devotion and Festivals

Pilgrims come throughout the year to recite the *Fatiha*, the opening chapter of the Quran, to seek blessing and to honour the saint, and the shrine keeps the round of daily prayer, of *qawwali*, Sufi devotional music, and of the *langar*, the free communal kitchen, that marks the great shrines, or *darbars*, rising to its height at the annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death. Thousands of devotees visited the shrine every day. In the 1970s the love poems of Fakhr-ud-Din Iraqi were still being sung by Pakistani musicians at the door of his master's tomb.

The tomb drew travelling saints, and an emperor came to it to ask for help. Shaikh Jamali, on a journey that ran from the Haramain, the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, to Egypt, Baghdad and other lands as far as Khurasan, presented himself at the tomb in Multan. One saint, it is told, spent the night of Eid at the tomb in the remembrance of God. When the imperial camp lay near Multan in the pursuit of Dara Shikoh, the emperor went on the ninth of Muharram to visit the tomb, and there sought the help of the saint's spiritual power and the outpouring of his lights.

His image travels beyond Multan. At Uch Sharif posters of him are sold in the market at the Gilani shrine, and a banner at Jalaludin's shrine shows him dressed like a rich man, with pearls around his neck and a fancy gown. At Uch he is also named as one of three saints said to have meditated in the rooms of a mosque.

## Legends

By Aurangzeb's reign many wondrous and astonishing stories of the saint were on the tongues of small and great alike. One tells how he received his robe in a dream. He saw a house of light, with the Prophet present and his own *pir* standing respectfully, and many *khirqas* hanging on a rope; he was summoned, his hand was taken, and the Prophet told Umar to clothe Shaikh Bahauddin Ghaus al-Alam, the Helper of the World, in this *khirqa*. In the morning, the story goes on, his *pir* called him, and he found the house exactly as it had been in the dream. The same *khirqa* was taken down and put on him by hand, and the *pir* disclaimed any authority of his own: all these *khirqas*, he said, were the Prophet's, he himself was only an intermediary, and without the Prophet's leave he could clothe no one in them.

It is told, too, that when Jalal al-Din Surkh Bukhari came to Multan and pined for the weather of Bukhara, the saint knew it by *kashf*. He sent a *khadim*, a servant, to the mosque with orders to roll up the prayer rows and sweep the courtyard; a cloud appeared, heavy rain fell, and hailstones, and outside the mosque, the story goes, there was neither rain nor hail. At the midday prayer he came smiling and asked the Sayyid whether the hail of Multan was better or the snow of Bukhara, and the Sayyid answered that in that case the hail of Multan was a hundred times better. The same day, the story ends, he conferred on the Sayyid the *khirqa* of *khilafat*.

Khwaja Kamal al-Din Masud Shirazi, another story runs, was caught in a storm at sea and called on him, and the saint appeared on the ship, where all the passengers saw him plainly; he gave them tidings of safety, and the ship reached Aden safely. The passengers gave a third of their goods to Khwaja Kamal al-Din as an offering and a thanksgiving, and he sent all of it, with half of his own jewels, to Multan by his nephew, who on arriving, it is said, recognised the saint at once, in the very dress in which he had seen him on the ship. The saint, the story ends, distributed the goods and the jewels to the people within thirty days.

In Sindh he is remembered for a miraculous birth. In most tellings of the legend, one Madan asked for his intercession to obtain a son when the saint was touring in Sindh. Bahauddin offered him a small end, a *pithu*, of a dried date, and at the moment Madan's wife tasted the blessed piece she became pregnant. The son they had was named Pithoro, after the end of the date, and in the legend Pithoro became the disciple of Bahauddin.

The stories of Guru Nanak's life tell that he met the saint at Multan, though Bahauddin belonged to the thirteenth century, before Nanak's time; Nanak did enjoy the company of Sufis in that town.

## Poetry

The Punjabi poets remembered him too. Bulleh Shah often refers with reverence to Multan as a holy city and to Bahauddin Zakariya, and in a lyric that may be a later addition to his verse, Hir calls Ranjha to the tomb:

*Come, Ranjha, let us go to Multan, to pay homage to the great saint Bahaval Haq. Let us gain our desire immediately. My heart longs for the lord* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

Bulleh Shah's lyrics also invoke the Five Pirs, five great saints who are believed collectively to possess special powers: the legendary Khwaja Khizr, Farid Shakarganj of Pakpattan, Baha ud Din Zakariya of Multan, Jalal ud Din Makhdum Jahaniyan of Uch and Lal Shahbaz Qalandar of Sehwan. The Pirs guard the beloved:

*The Five Pirs protect my beloved, they search for him among people* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

And they are propitiated:

*I belong to the yogi, after propitiating the Five Pirs.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

Waris Shah's romance of Hir and Ranjha also brings the Five Pirs to Ranjha, among them Zakaria, saint of Multan, and among their gifts to Ranjha his is a thick blanket.

## The Setting

In 711 the Arabs conquered Sind and the provinces to the north of it up to Multan. Multan had become a dependency of the Fatimids of Egypt, by the middle of the eleventh century Sufism had penetrated the lands around it, and in 1175 Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad bin Sam seized the city. During the twelfth century many Sufi scholars made Multan their base, and conversion to Islam gained momentum in the early thirteenth century.

By the time Guru Nanak came to Multan, the city was famous as a major centre of Sufi learning and philosophy. It was then one of the biggest cities of the Punjab, known for the shrines of Muslim saints and for its Jain and Hindu temples, a sacred space for people of all religious denominations. In Aurangzeb's reign it was counted one of the ancient cities, with a fort of brick; people of every kind lived there, and the goods of every land were bought and sold; its winter was mild, its summer excessively hot, and it had little rain; and many *awliya* rested in that blessed city.

Under Sultan Balban, when Prince Muhammad Sultan governed Multan, Amir Khusrau and Amir Hasan were in the prince's service there, and the prince twice sent to Shiraz for Sa'di, wishing to build a khanqah for him at Multan and endow it with villages; Sa'di could not come because of his age. An older sanctity is remembered too: the tyrant Hiranyakashipu is believed to have ruled the city of Multan thousands of years ago. For the Sindhi and Punjabi poets, Multan, like Mecca and Medina, was inside the heart, and in Bulleh Shah's eyes Takht Hazara, the birthplace of Ranjha, held the same standing as Multan, the seat of the Suhrawardi school of mysticism.

## Legacy

Bahauddin Zakariya stands beside Baba Farid as one of the two founding fathers of Punjabi Sufism, the Suhrawardi to Farid's Chishti, and his khanqah made Multan a wellspring of the tradition. Through his descendants and disciples, and through the later saints of Multan who trace to his line, his influence runs through the whole later history of Sufism in the western subcontinent. His shrine anchors Multan's ancient identity as the "City of Saints", and his memory endures as that of the master who first gave the Suhrawardi order an Indian home.

Of the Jat and Rajput groups that became Muslim in the medieval period, the vast majority claim to have been converted either by Baba Farid or by him. He is named, with Fariduddin Ganjshakr and Jalaluddin Surkhposh Bukhari, among a quartet of mystics, the *chahar-yar* or "four friends"; the shrines of these three are spread across southern Punjab, and Chothanbi, a site between Lal-bagh and Sehwan that pilgrims visit, is believed to be the place where the four friends met.

Name: Shrine of Bibi Pak Daman
Events: Annual urs; Thursday-night gathering; Muharram observances (peak attendance)
Description:
## Overview

The shrine of Bibi Pak Daman, "the pure, chaste ladies", stands in the heart of old Lahore, a short way from Empress Road and the old Qila Gujjar Singh. It is one of the oldest and most venerated sacred sites in the city, and among the busiest, drawing many thousands of pilgrims every day and immense crowds through Muharram, the month in which the martyrs of Karbala are mourned. Within its enclosures lie the graves of six holy women, remembered for their piety and for the miracle by which they are said to have chosen death over dishonour, together with the grave of their maidservant. For centuries the *darbar*, or shrine, has been a place of prayer, vows and refuge, cherished above all by women, and Sunni and Shia Muslims alike revere it.

Most pilgrims honour the Bibis as women of the Prophet Muhammad's own household who came to Lahore after the tragedy of Karbala, and tradition holds that when they were threatened the earth itself opened to receive them. Their shrine is one of the rare great shrines of the subcontinent whose sanctity is that of women.

## The Bibis

Accounts differ over who the six women were, and over when and from what country they came to Lahore. The question has been argued over by scholars for generations, and the debate is itself part of the shrine's history. The older and by far the more popular tradition, held by most pilgrims and reflected in the shrine's traditional founding date of about 63 AH, in the first century of Islam, makes them women of the household of the Prophet, the Ahl al-Bayt, the People of the House. In the nineteenth century it was the common tradition on people's tongues. A second tradition, advanced by the shrine's own custodial family and by a line of scholars, makes them the daughters of a saint of Lahore, Sayyid Ahmad Tokhta Tirmidhi, and the shrine holds meaning in both.

In the popular tradition the chief of the six was Sayyida Ruqayya bint Ali, a daughter of Hazrat Ali, the Prophet's son in law, sister of Hazrat Abbas the standard bearer, and wife of Muslim ibn Aqeel. With her were kinswomen and companions of the Prophet's house, among them women remembered as Bibi Hoor and Bibi Noor of the line of Abi Talib, six in all, together with a faithful camel driver named Basheer. Because of this the shrine is a memorial to the family of the Prophet, a place of especially intense devotion for Shia Muslims and for all who love the Ahl al-Bayt, and its whole atmosphere turns towards the remembrance of Karbala.

Both traditions know the six by the same names, each with the title Bibi, lady: Bibi Haj, Bibi Taj, Bibi Noor, Bibi Hoor, Bibi Gauhar and Bibi Shahbaz. Both share, too, the heart of the story: six women of extraordinary holiness, their choice of death over dishonour, and the miracle by which the earth is said to have received them. Divided over history, the traditions are united in reverence. As the shrine's own keepers say, asking forgiveness for any error in what they tell, no book survives from the holy women themselves, and all that is told of them has come down through later scholars and saints.

The Bibis are counted among the women who brought Islam to the subcontinent, and among the female mystics of Islam beside Rabia al-Adawiyya, the great woman mystic of its early centuries. Tradition remembers them as learned in reading and interpreting the Quran and versed in the *hadith*, the sayings of the Prophet, and holds that once they reached Lahore they set about spreading the faith. They are said to have founded assemblies of *zikr*, the remembrance of God, for the recitation of the Quran, to have guided the lives of ordinary people, and to have held mystical assemblies with male Sufi scholars, drawing those men into spreading Islam among the ordinary people of the Punjab who were not Muslims. They spoke to the scholars and to their audiences from behind the veil. Their teaching, in which mysticism had its place, awakened their hearers' interest in the discussion of Islam, and many people are said to have come to Islam through the blessing of their footsteps.

Devotional tradition also tells of an astrologer who boasted that he could read the hidden and the unseen. The elder Bibi had food prepared for the poor and for travellers, and sent him a dish in which fine food lay concealed beneath a plain covering of dry *khichri*, rice cooked with lentils. The astrologer scorned the humble rice, and when he learned what lay beneath it he was humbled, for a man who claimed knowledge of the unseen had not seen the feast under the *khichri*. He became a disciple. Such stories express what the shrine has always meant to ordinary people: a place of hospitality, of humility and of quiet wonder.

## The Journey from Karbala

In the popular telling, the story begins in the aftermath of Karbala, where in 61 AH Imam Hussain, the grandson of the Prophet, was martyred with his companions. The women's ordeal had begun even before that day. Sayyida Ruqayya's husband, Muslim ibn Aqeel, was the cousin and emissary whom Imam Hussain had sent ahead to the city of Kufa, and he was betrayed and martyred there together with his young sons. After the martyrdom of Hussain himself and his companions on the plain of Karbala, the surviving members of the Prophet's household were taken captive and for a year suffered the cruelty of the court of the caliph Yazid, a captivity so harsh, tradition holds, that the very sanctities of Islam were trampled. Hazrat Zain al-Abideen, Hussain's son and the surviving Imam, is said to have charged Sayyida Ruqayya to depart with a few of the women, so that the faith and the lineage of the Prophet's house might be carried to safety and continue.

She set out with her companions and, it is told, with the camel driver Basheer. He had served in Yazid's own palace and had once spoken harshly to the holy women, but he was bound to them by a hidden love, and he was trusted precisely because their destination was to be kept from strangers. They journeyed east across the length of the Muslim world until they reached the land of Hind, as the subcontinent was then known. At Lahore a Hindu raja, named in local tradition as Mahabrand Bhatti, held sway, and scarcely a Muslim was to be found. It is said that the women halted on a mound with no settlement around it, and that the raja's people were thrown into disorder, saying that descendants of the Prophet had come from Arabia. Tradition also preserves the women's lament in their own voice: first the parting from their brothers and the calamity of Karbala, then a strange land where no one understood even their speech, where they were poor travellers, wronged and homeless, beyond all help.

As the women arrived, wonders are said to have followed: the idols of the temples toppled and their lamps went dark. The raja, disturbed, sent his son, remembered as Raja Kumar Bikrama Sahay, with soldiers to discover who these strangers were. When the prince came before the women he was overwhelmed by a radiant light and fell senseless. On recovering he heard from their own lips the tale of Karbala, and he was so moved that he embraced Islam, took a new name, remembered as Abdullah Shah Khaki or Shaikh Jamal, and stayed among them as their servant. Tradition also remembers four *hafiz*, men who had memorised the whole Quran, who stayed behind with the women: Abu al-Fath, Abu al-Fazl, Abu al-Makarim and Sad Allah.

When the enraged raja came with an army to seize the women, they lifted their hands in prayer, begging God to spare them exposure to strangers. The earth opened and drew them into itself, closing again and leaving only the edges of their veils above the ground, and over these their graves were later raised. Their maidservant, Bibi Halima, is said to have been taken into the earth with her mistresses. From this guarding of their honour to the last comes the name by which the women are known, Pak Daman, "the pure of hem".

The tradition is steeped in the devotion of Karbala. On the frontispiece of one of its major histories stands the old Persian line of the lovers of the martyrs, a verse of devotion to the martyrs of the House of the Prophet:

خوشا آنان کہ در خاک و خون غلطیدند

*Blessed are those who rolled in dust and blood.*

## The Shrine

The graves lie within enclosed courtyards. Tradition places the six Bibis in two adjoining walled enclosures, Bibi Haj, Bibi Taj and Bibi Noor in the first and Bibi Hoor, Bibi Gauhar and Bibi Shahbaz in the second, their tombs built up in lime and plaster. Counted among them is the grave of their maidservant, Bibi Halima, remembered affectionately as Bibi Tanoori. The shrine has been rebuilt many times over the centuries, and its most recent major renovation was carried out in 2024.

In the nineteenth century the oldest parts of the fabric were attributed to Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni, who brought Lahore under Muslim rule in the early eleventh century. For four hundred years after the Bibis, it was said, Hindu rajas had ruled; then Mahmud built a wall of fired brick and *dalans*, halls open along one side, and a *dalan* with five doors, repaired from time to time, was attributed to the Ghaznavid sultans of his line. In the reign of the Mughal emperor Akbar many buildings were raised and the graveyard was laid out. Successive rulers attached endowments of land, or *waqf*, to the shrine, and its old land was continued under every ruler.

In that century the grave of one of the Bibis lay on a raised platform of white marble within a *pinjra*, a lattice screen, always covered with a *ghilaf*, a cloth cover for a grave, and its white plaster was attributed to the Ghaznavid sultans. To the south a lower, broken platform held two more graves, and to its west lay two maidservants whose names are not known. A *van* tree spread over the Bibis' tomb. The shrine's mosque, first built by Baba Khaki, had been rebuilt some years earlier, and a house with a *dalan* of three arches had been built for one of the *mujawirs*, the shrine's hereditary attendants.

In the 1880s these tombs, known together as the Mazars of Bibi Pak Daman, were famous among the city's Muslim shrines as the most ancient and blessed. The site, which was also called a *khanqah*, a Sufi lodge, was then counted among the Muslim sites outside the city, two miles from Lahore. A visitor entered from the west, followed a passage like a lane to a second gate, and turned north to the graves. They lay in three enclosures: an outer one holding the graves of the Bibis' maidservants and a domed mosque of *pakka*, or fired, brick; a large second enclosure with the graves of three of the Bibis; and a third holding the graves of Bibi Hoor, Bibi Gauhar and Bibi Shahbaz. Every enclosure was finely built in lime plaster. Many buildings had belonged to this graveyard, and many had fallen for want of care.

Holy men and others of later centuries sought burial in the women's company. Within the complex, in a corner of one of the enclosures, stands a domed masonry tomb of the eleventh century of the Hijra, about 1600 CE, in which lies Sayyid Jalaluddin Haider Bukhari, son of Safi al-Din Bukhari and brother of Shah Mauj Darya Bukhari, of the celebrated Bukhari sayyids of Uch. He died in 1016 AH and was buried by the wall of the Bibis' sanctum, and his tomb was built in 1017 AH. In the nineteenth century its door opened inside the shrine's *khanqah*, and people called it the tomb of the Bibis' teacher.

Others lie in the graveyard of the Bibis too: Khwaja Ayyub Qureshi Lahori, and Mufti Ghulam Muhammad, who died in 1274 AH, the son of Mufti Rahimullah Qureshi Lahori and the father of Mufti Ghulam Sarwar, a nineteenth century historian of Lahore's saints; a chronogram, *Khurshid-e Din-e Muhammad*, the sun of Muhammad's faith, honours him. Syed Mahmud II was buried beside the tomb of the Bibis, and in the nineteenth century the goldsmiths' graveyard lay next to the graveyard of the Bibis. In the 1880s the tomb of Shah Rahmatullah Qureshi stood to the north of the Bibis' *khanqah*.

The shrine stands within a wider sacred neighbourhood, and in 1974 it lay in the settlement of the Bibis Pakdamanan at Muhammad Nagar. Other holy figures are associated with the place, among them Hazrat Ali Rangrez and Hazrat Alif Shah, who is said to have come with the Bibis themselves at the time of their arrival.

The nearby quarter of Chilla Bibiyan holds the tomb of Sayyid Ahmad Tokhta Tirmidhi, the saint whom the second tradition makes the father of the six. He died in 602 AH, 1205 CE, near the beginning of the reign of Sultan Qutb al-Din Aibak, and his title *Murshid-e Punjab*, the guide of the Punjab, is a chronogram of that year, a phrase whose letters, counted as numbers, give the date. A large tomb once stood over his grave, but it collapsed after its marble was taken down under Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the Sikh ruler of the Punjab, and the graveyard around it was cleared for a *haveli*, a great mansion. By the 1880s the grave, solidly built, stood inside a stable, that of Hazrat Ghulam Muhi al-Din, where people came to visit it, and it is now enclosed within the property of a later custodial family. A Persian chronogram, or *tarikh*, preserved in his memory hails him in verse:

سیّد احمد، شہِ برنا و پیر
پیرِ ہادی، میرِ عالی جاہ

*Sayyid Ahmad, king of the young and the old; a guiding master, a lord of lofty station.*

## Keepers of the Shrine

The shrine's hereditary caretakers, the *mujawirs*, are traditionally held to descend from the convert prince, Abdullah Shah Khaki or Shaikh Jamal, who is said to have built the first shrine over the women's graves and to have served it for the rest of his life. He is said to have refused to return to his old faith and to have sat as the attendant of the women's tomb. It is told that at the tomb it was revealed to him that his marriage to a Hindu's daughter was lawful, and the land to the east and south of the *khanqah* was given to his descendants.

In the modern era the shrine has been taken into the charge of the Punjab Auqaf Department, the provincial government's department of religious endowments, which administers it as a shrine under Sunni management. Given the scale of the crowds, government security and the Punjab Police are kept on site at all times.

The question of who the Bibis were carries a sectarian dimension that persists to this day. Because the popular tradition makes the shrine a memorial of the Prophet's martyred family, it is a focus of intense Shia devotion, and the shrine gives its own devotional identity simply as Syed and Shia, while its formal administration and much of its custodial lineage are Sunni. Old disputes have gathered around this difference, over whether the graves are those of Sayyida Ruqayya and the Ahl al-Bayt or of a Punjabi saint's daughters, and over who may claim the shrine. Yet in practice Bibi Pak Daman is revered by Sunni and Shia alike, and the two devotions meet, without merging, in the same courtyards.

Its visitors are not only Muslims. In the early twenty first century Prem Gupta, a Hindu activist from Lahore, then forty years old, and head of the Hindu Sudhar Sabha, whose family lived near the shrine, visited it often, a habit one writer saw as part of "the religious syncretism that was once part of this land but is now vanishing".

## Devotion and Festivals

Bibi Pak Daman is a living centre of devotion, alive around the clock. Pilgrims come to recite the Fatiha, the opening chapter of the Quran, to tie vows, or *mannat*, and to seek the Bibis' intercession, or *waseela*, for healing, for children and for relief from every kind of hardship. Many recount cures received here after physicians had given up hope, and tell of the impossible made possible through the women's grace.

Women in particular find in the *darbar* a sanctuary, a place of comfort and of dignity, and in the affection of the city it is above all a women's shrine. For generations the mothers of Lahore have brought the Bibis their deepest hopes and fears, praying for children, for good marriages, for the safety of daughters, for healing and for protection from harm, and it is chiefly women who fill its courtyards, tie their threads of vow at its screens, and find in it a refuge that the world outside does not always offer them. In Pakistan, where the major mosques keep only a small space for women to pray on Fridays and at festivals such as Eid, and the neighbourhood mosques none, one scholar of women's devotion has concluded that "the important spheres of religious and spiritual participation for women are the Sufi shrines".

Every Thursday night the shrine fills for its largest weekly gathering, with *langar*, the free communal kitchen, *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufi shrines, *dhamal*, ecstatic devotional dancing to the beat of the drum, and prayer. A mosque attached to the shrine holds the five daily prayers.

The shrine's greatest season is Muharram, when the sorrow and devotion of Karbala are remembered; it was said in the nineteenth century that at Hussain's death the lament of Karbala rose in the Punjab too. Enormous crowds converge on the *darbar*, and many are said to walk barefoot in groups from their homes to reach it. On an ordinary day the shrine receives on the order of 8,000 to 12,000 visitors, some 250,000 in a month, and at the height of Muharram the numbers rise towards 1.2 million.

Music has a particular place here. Reshma, a renowned singer of Sufi poetry, said that she sang at the shrine whenever the Bibi summoned her, at any time of night or day, and both she and Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan counted themselves devotees of the shrine.

Lahore's own saints came here in devotion, and one tradition in particular is cited by devotees as proof of the shrine's great antiquity. It is said that when Data Ganj Bakhsh, the eleventh century saint Ali ibn Usman Hujwiri, author of the *Kashf al-Mahjub* and patron saint of Lahore, first came to the city, he would go every Thursday night to the graves of the Bibis and sit in attentive reverence at a respectful distance, out of *adab*, courtesy before their sanctity. He is remembered as a devotee of their shrines, where he offered prayers and spent considerable time in meditation.

That so great a saint should honour the shrine in this way is taken to show that the graves were already ancient and holy in his day, for the shrines are said to have stood long before he reached Lahore. He arrived in about 1035: Khattali, who had earlier ordered his disciple Shaikh Husain Zinjani to move to the Punjab, sent Hujwiri after him. The tradition binds the shrine to Data Darbar, the shrine of Data Ganj Bakhsh, the two standing together at the head of Lahore's sacred geography. Mian Mir, another of Lahore's saints, often went to the Bibis in devotion too.

## Legacy

However the question of who they were is answered, the meaning of the shrine is the same: it stands for purity, for courage, and for a refusal to bow before injustice at the cost of one's honour. In the nineteenth century even those who could not accept that the women had come from Arabia at the time of Karbala did not doubt that the place was most blessed. In a sacred landscape crowded with the tombs of male saints, Data Ganj Bakhsh, Mian Mir, Madho Lal Hussain and the rest, Bibi Pak Daman is something rare: a great shrine whose sanctity is that of women. The six Bibis are honoured not for conquest or office or learning alone, but for a purity and courage so absolute that they are said to have chosen to be swallowed by the earth rather than be seen by strangers. In this the *darbar* gives the women of the city a mirror of their own dignity, a place where female holiness stands at the very centre, and where the qualities most often asked of women, and most often unhonoured, are raised to the rank of the sacred.

That a shrine of such scale and antiquity should be dedicated to women is, in the religious geography of the subcontinent, almost without parallel. Across sectarian lines it stands as one of the clearest expressions in South Asian Islam of the veneration of female sanctity. By the 1880s all the people of Islam held the place blessed and served it with heart and soul, and amid the debates of scholars and the changing life of the city the *darbar* of Bibi Pak Daman endures as a place of refuge and of blessing, one of the deepest spiritual anchors of the old city.

Name: Shrine of Fariduddin Ganjshakar
Events: Annual urs (Muharram) with the opening of the Bahishti Darwaza; qawwali; langar
Description:
## Overview

At Pakpattan, on the old bank of the Sutlej in southern Punjab, stands the shrine of Hazrat Baba Fariduddin Mas‘ud Ganjshakar, known as Baba Farid, one of the founding saints of the Chishti order of Sufis, or Muslim mystics, in South Asia, and among the most beloved holy figures of the Punjab. A disciple and spiritual heir of Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki of Delhi and the master of the great Nizamuddin Auliya, he made the town then called Ajodhan into a centre of Sufi devotion so important that it came to be renamed Pakpattan, "the Holy Ferry". His tomb, perhaps the most famous shrine of its kind in the Punjab, remains one of the greatest places of pilgrimage in Pakistan, most of all when its *Bahishti Darwaza*, the Gate of Paradise, is opened at his *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death.

He was also a pioneer of Punjabi as a language of spiritual poetry, and verses attributed to him were later gathered into the Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, a mark of how far his memory reaches across the communities of the Punjab. He has been called Pakistan's most famous Sufi saint and the patron saint of Pakistan, and since the partition of India Pakpattan has stood as the unrivalled centre of a distinctly Pakistani Sufism. The shrine is the focal point of the town, which seems to have grown up entirely around it.

## The Saint

Baba Farid was born around 1173 at Kothewal, near Multan, the village known today as Tibba Haji Deen; accounts of the year of his birth differ. He came of a family of learned émigrés of Central Asian origin, who traced their descent to the Commander of the Faithful, Hazrat Umar ibn al-Khattab, and counted themselves of the house of Farrukh Shah, king of Kabul. His forebears left Kabul for the Punjab in the middle of the twelfth century, driven by the upheavals of the age, the destruction of Ghazna by Ala al-Din Husain of Ghur in 1150 and 1151 and the invasion of the Ghuzz six years later.

Accounts of the family's coming differ, but his grandfather is said to have come from Kabul. He is remembered as Qazi Shuaib, who came to Lahore with three sons and his goods, went on from Lahore to Kasur, and was made *qazi*, or judge, of Kothewal, a town in the Multan region between Maharan and Ajodhan, by the Ghaznavid sultan of the Punjab; there he settled. Farid's father is most often named Shaikh Jamal al-Din Sulaiman, and his mother Qursum Khatun, daughter of Mulla Wajih al-Din Khujandi. His father died while he was still a small child. He had an elder brother, Azz al-Din Mahmud, and a younger, Najib al-Din Mutawakkil, "the Trusting in God", and the three brothers were held to be unique in their age; he had a sister too, Hajira, famous by the title Jamila Khatun. Najib al-Din became his brother's disciple and *khalifa*, his deputy; the woman saint Bibi Fatima Sam used to call him her own brother, and he carried the family's messages between Hansi and Ajodhan. Farid's own given name was Masud, and the name Farid al-Din, it is said, was bestowed on him by Hazrat Farid al-Din Attar.

His mother was an exceedingly pious woman who prayed through long vigils at night, and while his father was a scholar, it was she who exerted the greater influence on the future saint and first set him on the path of prayer. She is counted among the women of their families who contributed to the spiritual formation of great Sufi leaders, and by the 1870s she was remembered as the gnostic of her age, a woman whose prayers were answered and whose every word came to pass.

He was taught at home, and he had memorised the Quran by the age of twelve. As a young man he went to Multan to study, reading the *Nafi*, a famous book of *fiqh*, Islamic law, with Maulana Minhaj al-Din Tirmizi, who taught in a mosque there, and acquiring the religious sciences. There, it is told, a chance meeting changed his life. Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki, the Chishti master of Delhi, came to Multan and entered the mosque in the Sarai Halwai quarter where the young man sat with his book. After the prayer the Khwaja asked what he was reading. The *Nafi*, came the answer; and when the Khwaja asked whether he knew that his benefit would come from this *Nafi*, the young man replied that his benefit would come from kissing the Khwaja's feet, and laid his head on them.

He asked to become the Khwaja's disciple, and in time he followed him to Delhi; accounts differ over where he took his pledge of initiation, at Multan or at Delhi, and over whether his master first sent him away to complete his studies at Qandahar. He is said to have travelled widely as well, to Iraq, Syria, Siwistan, Ghazni, Bukhara and Qandahar, and to have benefited from the company of many masters, among them Shaikh Shihab al-Din Umar Suhrawardi, Shaikh Baha al-Din Zakariya and Shaikh Farid al-Din Muhammad Attar Nishapuri.

In Delhi he lived in a small cell near his master's *jama'at-khana*, the hall where the master's disciples lived and gathered, and under guidance he gave himself to the severe austerities for which he became famous. When Khwaja Mu'in al-Din visited Delhi, he was so impressed by them that he took a special interest in the young disciple, foretold his later fame, and asked Khwaja Qutbuddin to join him in prayer for his disciple's future greatness. In renunciation and austerity, in knowledge and practice, in inner unveiling and in miracles, Farid was held to have outstripped everyone of the Chishti line, and he was wholly given to spiritual taste and longing, to love, to ecstasy and to *sama*, the Sufi practice of listening to music. His fast was perpetual; his days were given to instructing the people and his nights to worship.
