Name: Shrine of Hazrat Muhammad Ayub Shah Bukhari
Location: Gandawah (Gandava), Jhal Magsi District, Balochistan, Pakistan
Events: Annual urs
Description:
The shrine of Hazrat Muhammad Ayub Shah Bukhari is one of the principal Sufi dargahs of the Jhal Magsi district of Balochistan, situated at Gandawah (Gandava), the historic administrative town of the Kachhi plain. Its saint bore the *Bukhari* lineage, marking descent from the influential family of Sayyids who traced their origins to Bukhara and whose forebears — most famously Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari of Uch Sharif — spread the *Suhrawardi* devotional tradition across Sindh and the southern Punjab. The tomb is locally admired as one of the finest examples of shrine architecture in the district, and it stands among a cluster of Sufi graves in the Gandawah area that together form an important sacred landscape for the surrounding Baloch and Brahui communities. Devotees from across the district and beyond visit to seek blessing and intercession, and the saint's *urs* is observed as the chief event of the devotional year, drawing pilgrims, *qawwali* and the distribution of food. As with many shrines of interior Balochistan, the documented history of the saint is thin and his dates uncertain, so his biography is best treated as living tradition rather than established record; the *Bukhari* attribution and the shrine's standing as a regional pilgrimage centre are, however, well attested locally. It should not be confused with the separate and larger Dargah of Fateh Pur Sharif (Pir Rakhail Shah), also in the Jhal Magsi district. Independent confirmation of the tomb's standing among Gandava's principal monuments comes from a 2019 Dawn survey of the town's heritage, which names "the tombs of Ayub Shah Bukhari, Murad Kaleri, and Meeri of Khan-e-Qalat" together with the Jamia Mosque of Gandava among "the best examples of Islamic architecture in the area," though the article gives no further individual detail — no dates or architectural description — specific to this tomb.

Name: Shrine of Hazrat Shah Ali Akbar (Shah Ali Akbar Shamsi)
Events: Annual urs
Description:
The Shrine of Hazrat Shah Ali Akbar Shamsi stands in the historic neighbourhood of Suraj Miani in Multan, the celebrated "city of saints", and is counted among the oldest and most beautiful mausoleums of the city. Shah Ali Akbar is remembered as a descendant — by tradition of the eighth generation — of the great Sufi Shah Shams Sabzwari of Multan, and it is said that after the death of his father he settled permanently in the city. His tomb, built of brick in the octagonal, tiered form so characteristic of Multan, is often likened to a smaller version of the famous shrine of Shah Rukn-e-Alam, and it belongs to the classic tradition of Multani funerary architecture with its glazed tilework and tapering silhouette. According to inscriptions and local tradition, construction of the mausoleum began in 993 AH (about 1585 CE) and took some fifteen years to complete; it is said to have been raised by the saint's grandson, who is himself buried within the complex, and the work is attributed to the builders Ibrahim and Rajab, sons of the noted architect Musa Lahori. Despite its remarkable beauty and its importance to the architectural history of Multan, the shrine has often been described as one of the city's more neglected monuments. It remains a place of *ziyarat* and hosts an annual *urs* in the saint's honour. Also known by the alternate name Kabuli Mohallah, the shrine's compound is registered as a protected monument under the Antiquity Act of 1975 by the Directorate General of Archaeology, Punjab, whose own listing describes the building's brick construction as embellished with panels of glazed tiles, three arched panels on each side surmounted by a series of merlons set on bold moldings, its lower walls plastered in lime, and an interior decorated with panels of fresco painting — though the same listing notes this fresco work and lime plaster have been considerably damaged by the smoke of mustard-oil lamps and votive candles over the years. In 2019 the Punjab Archaeology Department proposed a Rs 30 million conservation and restoration project for the mausoleum, and by November of that year a related tender for a Rs 27.104 million project was opened for bids, though press reporting does not clarify whether this represents the same project re-costed or a later phase of the work.

Name: Shrine of Hazrat Shah Daula Daryai
Events: Annual three-day urs (Auqaf-administered); langar
Description:
## Overview

The shrine of Hazrat Shah Daula Daryai stands in the city of Gujrat, in the fertile plain between the Chenab and Jhelum rivers in the Punjab. It honours a Sufi saint of the Mughal period, remembered above all as a builder of bridges, wells and *sarais*, or rest houses, and as a benefactor of the poor, the traveller and the afflicted. His epithet *Daryai*, from *darya*, river, is traditionally explained by the works he built across the region's torrential streams. For nearly four centuries the *darbar*, as the shrine is called, has been a focus of popular devotion in central Punjab.

It is also the place around which one of South Asia's most persistent and troubling folk traditions grew up: that of the *chuhas*, or "Shah Daula's mice", children with microcephaly who were historically associated with the shrine.

## The Saint

Shah Daula lived in the Mughal period. His birth name is given as Qasim, and tradition places his birth around 1581. His ancestors are said to have been Afghans, though he is also claimed as a Sayyid, a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad.

Accounts of his early years differ, and so do the names given to his master. He is said to have travelled in his youth to the neighbourhood of Sialkot, where he became the disciple of a Suhrawardi *faqir*, a mystic of the Sufi order founded by Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi; his master is remembered as Shah Saidan Sarmast. He served at his master's *khanqah*, the lodge where a Sufi's disciples gather, with great devotion, spending, it is said, twelve years at his feet, and in time he was entrusted with its care.

Tradition tells that his master, as he lay dying, cast a glance full of grace on his disciple. Shah Daula's state was transformed: the chamber of his inner self was lit with the lights of gnosis, the knowledge of God, and the treasures of the unseen were revealed to him. He is said to have settled in Gujrat in the early seventeenth century, and he established his own *khanqah* there, at the place formerly known as Garhi Shah Daula.

There is no settled view of his order. His master is remembered as a Suhrawardi, but Shah Daula is also said to have been initiated into the Qadiri order, founded by Abd al-Qadir Gilani. His spiritual chain, or *silsila*, is traced back through a long line of masters, by way of Shaikh Sadr al-Din Rajan Qattal of Uch, to Shaikh Baha al-Din Multani, and he is said to have received the full measure of *faiz*, spiritual grace, from the Chishtis as well. By the 1870s he was counted among the famous saints of the Punjab: a man of lofty spiritual stations and of marvels, of *jazb*, ecstatic rapture, of *ishq*, love, of *zuhd*, renunciation of the world, and of *riyazat*, spiritual discipline, who united in himself both outward and inward gifts.

In his lifetime his household was like the court of a king, with thousands of servants, horses and palanquins waiting at his door, and a crowd of people in need was there at every hour. Multitudes came from every quarter to visit him and made abundant offerings in cash and in kind, and he gave his visitors and petitioners more than they had brought. His generosity, it was said, was such that a whole lifetime of the generosity of Hatim, the proverbial giver, would not come to a tenth of a tenth of it. He was popular with Hindus as well as Muslims, became famous for his miracles and received large gifts in kind, but he refused to accept grants of land.

He is also credited with *karamat*, the miraculous gifts of a saint, by which, it is said, he was able to check the killing of infant girls, then widespread in Jammu State.

He died at a great age in Gujrat, in 1675, though accounts of the year differ. His death is also marked by a chronogram, a phrase whose letters are read as numbers to give a date: *Khuda Dost*, Friend of God.

## The Builder of Bridges

What is most consistently remembered of Shah Daula is not doctrine but works of public benefit. He is credited with bridges over seasonal watercourses, among them, by tradition, a bridge over the Nala Dek, and with wells, mosques and rest houses along the routes of travel, at a time when such works eased both trade and pilgrimage across the Punjab. He is remembered too for his *langar*, the free communal kitchen, for his charity to the destitute, and for his care for animals and for people living with disabilities. His was a practical sanctity, honoured for the tangible relief of hardship.

When he settled in the *qasba*, the small town, of Gujrat, he built tanks, wells and mosques, and he bridged the Chenab, which came down from the hills and used to damage the town. He raised buildings and bridges in many places, above all a bridge on the highway over the river Deg, five *kos*, an old measure of distance, from Eminabad in the direction of Lahore. It was said to be so solidly built that no man of wealth could raise a building as strong, and it became a landmark: the Deg ran below Shah Daula's bridge, which stood on the highway.

Gujrat, it is said, had never been much of a place until Shah Daula settled there, and his coming made the town grow in people and prosperity. His works of public benefit and his religious buildings are said to have earned him the name *Daula*, wealth, and his bridges above all the second title, *Daryai*, one affiliated to water.

## The Shrine

His tomb, crowned by a dome and set beside a spacious mosque, dates in its essentials from the seventeenth century. It was substantially rebuilt in 1898 and has been repaired and extended since. In the reign of Aurangzeb the tomb was already a place of visitation for people of every class, and by the 1870s it was a place of pilgrimage for the people.

No land was attached to the shrine, so it had no regular income, and its holy men depended entirely on the alms and offerings of the followers. Since the middle of the twentieth century the shrine has been administered by the Punjab Auqaf, or Religious Affairs, Department, the government department of religious endowments. The takeover, it has been observed, could not wholly change the perceptions rooted deep in the minds of the rural people, or the authority of the shrine's administrator on the spot, the *mujawir*.

## Devotion and Festivals

The Auqaf Department now organises the shrine's annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, which lasts three days, with arrangements for *langar*, sanitation and security, and with gatherings devoted to the saint's life and teaching.

The shrine has a particular reputation for fertility, justice and punishment. The *dargah*, the shrine complex, is a female domain, at least in numbers, in contrast to the mosques, which are frequented by men; yet the power in shrines is usually held by men.

It was once the custom for parents who had sought a child through his intercession to leave the child, as soon as it was weaned, at Shah Daula's *khanqah* as an offering to him. After his death, devotees would vow either to present the child when it was born or to make an offering to the shrine. The exchange at the tomb has been likened to a bargain between the parents and the *mujawir*, much like the *mahr*, the bridewealth: the shrine's administrator declared the parents *jannati*, dwellers of paradise, and in return they left the child, the gift or *ni'mat*, as a trust, an *amanat*, at the shrine.

## The Chuhas of Shah Daula

*Chuhas*, a Punjabi word meaning mice or rats, is the name long given to children with microcephaly who were associated with the *darbar*. The tradition concerns vulnerable and disabled human beings, and it has often been sensationalised, so it must be approached with care.

Microcephaly is a medical condition in which the head and brain are abnormally small, typically accompanied by intellectual disability. It has recognised genetic and environmental causes and occurs in populations everywhere. At Gujrat, people with this condition came to be linked with the shrine through a folk belief, first described by an observer in January 1839 in the earliest printed notice of the *chuhas*: that childless women who prayed for offspring at the *darbar* would be granted a child, and that the first such child, by the legend, must be dedicated to the shrine and would be born with the characteristic small head. Such dedicated children were called *chuhas*, and they were often kept at the shrine or associated with it. Accounts differ over when the tradition took shape.

In the legend as colonial writers told it, Shah Daula, like other saints, could bring about the birth of a child for a couple who longed for one, but the first child born through his intercession would be a *chuha*. After his death, the legend went on, the miracle continued in a changed form: where a promised gift was withheld, the spirit of the offended saint worked on the parents so that the next child was born a *chuha*, and every child after it, until the original vow was fulfilled. These are the words of a legend, not a description of any person.

From the middle of the nineteenth century the children attracted European medical and ethnographic attention, and with it came the sensational speculation that their small heads were produced deliberately, by binding the skulls of infants or by fitting clamps or vessels to them. The claim has never been substantiated: no such instrument has ever been found, no such procedure has ever been witnessed, and medical authorities regard the deliberate production of microcephaly in this way as implausible without fatal injury.

The modern consensus is that the *chuhas* were, and are, people with naturally occurring microcephaly, whose condition was interpreted through local religious belief and who were drawn into the economy of the shrine. In some periods they were sent out as wandering beggars: after some initial training they were passed on to a *faqir* and made to beg in the name of Shah Daula. A band of faqirs made its living from these children and from the existence of an important shrine; it held no land, had no recognised right of succession to its leadership, and depended entirely on its earnings. Colonial writers also suspected the shrine's followers of trafficking in women. The folk belief that linked the condition to the saint's blessing or curse has no basis in fact.

Reform came in the twentieth century. When the Auqaf Department took control of the shrine, it forbade both the abandonment of such children to the *darbar* and the alleged deforming practices, and the number of *chuhas* associated with the site steadily declined. By the early twenty first century observers reported that only one or two remained. The episode endures chiefly as a cautionary study for historians of medicine, disability and popular religion, in which a genuine medical condition, human vulnerability, exploitation and folk piety became tragically entangled.

## The Shrine in Fiction

The shrine is also the setting of a work of Urdu fiction, Ahmad Nadim Qasimi's story 'Bain', or 'Dirge', which deals with the activities in and around the *dargah* of Shah Daula Daryai in Gujrat. The story does not refer directly to the cult of the *chuhas*, and the shrine it portrays is the story's own.

In the story the shrine has become an institution of justice, symbolised by the holy hand of Shah Daula, which rises from the grave to judge. The upper part of the holy grave opens and the *pir*, the spiritual master, stretches out his holy hand; the culprit, drawn to the shrine from wherever he is, lays his neck in it and dies on the spot. So nobody dares to neglect the orders of Sain Daule Shah, as the story calls the saint.

In the story, the shrine's *mujawir* rules through a dream. He demands that the girl Rano recite at the *dargah* for three days, which, he says, Shah Daula has ordered in a dream; otherwise, the villagers are warned, the saint will put them all to fire and ash.

The story's crisis comes at the *ʿurs*. Rano's coming of age and a proposal of marriage coincide with the anniversary of the saint's death, which marks his union with God, and during the *ʿurs* she falls victim to a corrupted society. The shrine's kitchen and its bath house become the scene of defiance: Rano flings the skirt her parents bring into the burning coals of the *langar*, and her father later throws the *mujawir*'s shroud into the coals of the fire that heats the water for the great ablution, the *ghusl*.

One scholar reads the story as showing that the shrine cult has become a falsehood void of any mysticism, an expression of corrupt political power, in which fear is the prime force that keeps the villagers and devotees loyal to the moral authority of the shrine.

## The Setting

Gujrat lies in the Chaj *doab*, the land between the Chenab and the Bihat. The town was settled under the emperor Akbar, when villages were taken out of the *pargana*, the revenue district, of Sialkot to make it a pargana of its own. Its founding is told this way: all this land had been part of Sialkot, under the sway of the Jats, and as the emperor was travelling from Lahore to Kashmir, a body of Gujars came to him after the crossing of the Chenab to complain of oppression by the Jats. The villages of their *zamindari*, their landholding, were separated off as a pargana, and a small fort and a town were founded. It is said that Gujrat became an important city under Akbar, having been a small village before, and that one of Akbar's wives is buried there.

In the reign of Aurangzeb the town was a market of the province, a resort of every kind of people and a gathering place for the goods of every land and the rare things of the age. Rare swords and *jamdhars*, a kind of dagger, were made there, and more *chikan* work, fine embroidery, was done there than in Sialkot; the district bred Iraqi horses, some worth up to ten thousand rupees.

The town also has its place in Mughal history. When the prince Khusrau rebelled and was turned back at the Chenab, he was seen at the ford at dawn, and Mir Abu al-Qasim Khan and the eunuch Hilal Khan, who were in the neighbourhood of Gujrat, seized him and carried him to the town.

Gujrat is one of several Punjab towns, with Gujranwala and Gujar Khan, named after the Gujars, a famous tribe of the old Punjab who keep animals and sell their milk, and who also farm on a large scale. The town has other saints too: a crow saint seems to have quite a following in this historic city, and when a blast struck in Sindh the city's major shrines were put on high alert.

The Chenab country around the town is the land of Punjabi romance. The tale of Sohni begins with a potter who lived in the Gujrat district of the Punjab, and Takht Hazara, the home of Ranjha's clan, lies in what is now the Gujrat District of Pakistan.

## Legacy

Shah Daula Daryai is remembered in the Punjab as a saint of works and mercy, whose bridges and wells served the living and whose shrine remains a busy centre of devotion in Gujrat. The disquieting tradition of the *chuhas* that attached itself to his name in later centuries belongs to the social history that grew up around the shrine rather than to the saint himself, and it is best understood today through medical fact and compassion for those who were affected. The *darbar* still draws pilgrims, feeds the poor at its *langar* and holds its annual *ʿurs* under the Auqaf Department.

In the reign of Aurangzeb he was remembered as the man who made Gujrat grow in people and prosperity, the builder of a famous bridge on the Lahore highway, and the saint whose tomb drew people of every class. By the 1870s he was counted a saint of the Punjab whose tomb was a place of pilgrimage and whose death was remembered in a chronogram. By the end of the twentieth century his shrine had a particular reputation for fertility, justice and punishment, and it had become the setting of one of Urdu fiction's critiques of shrine power.

A small literature has grown up around him: a *Karamat Nama*, or book of marvels, on his life by Mushtaq Ram Gujrati, dated 1132 AH in the Islamic calendar; a *Tazkira*, a biographical account, of Shah Daula Gujrati by M. S. Nasim, published in Lahore in 1970; and Sharif Kunjahi's life and teachings of the saint, *Hadrat Shâh Daulah Daryâ'î Gujrâtî: Hayât o ta'lîmât*, published in Lahore in 1985 by the Punjab Auqaf Department's imprint.

In 1875 a book on the saints of the Punjab gave him a notice of his own, under the name Shah Daula Daryai Gujrati. That book closes with a verse chronogram by Mufti Ghulam Safdar Lahori, which gives the year 1292 AH:

جو خدا کے دوست تھے پنجاب میں
حال ان کا اس سے ہوتا ہے عیان

*A chronogram on the book's own subject, the saints of the Punjab.*

Name: Shrine of Imam Ali-ul-Haq
Events: Annual urs; devotional music and langar
Description:
## Overview

The shrine of Hazrat Imam Ali-ul-Haq, known to the people of Sialkot simply and affectionately as Imam Sahib, stands in the heart of the old city of Sialkot in the Punjab, at the spot where the saint is traditionally believed to have died. He is venerated as a warrior saint and a *shahid*, a martyr, one of the missionary holy men whom local tradition credits with the coming of Islam to this corner of the upper Punjab. His *darbar*, or shrine, is among the most important devotional sites of the city, and devotees come to it throughout the year to pray and to seek his blessing.

He is a separate figure from the celebrated Bari Imam, Syed Abdul Latif Shah Kazmi, of Nurpur Shahan near Islamabad, with whom the similar honorific Imam sometimes causes confusion. The saint venerated at Sialkot belongs to the local history of that city, and already in the reign of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb his tomb was a place of visitation.

## The Saint

Accounts of Imam Ali-ul-Haq differ widely, and on when he lived they differ by some three or four centuries. The account more commonly repeated locally places him in the medieval period, often in the thirteenth or fourteenth century, and sometimes associates him with the reign of the Delhi sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq. His name is also written Ali al-Haq, and he is known too as Ali al-Haq Sialkoti, Ali al-Haq of Sialkot.

In the local telling he came as a preacher and a holy warrior, and is said to have brought a large part of the surrounding population to Islam, so turning Sialkot into a predominantly Muslim town. Accounts of his lineage and his companions differ, and some bring him from Arabia, but what they share is the memory of a holy man who came from afar, who is credited with bringing Islam to Sialkot, and who died a martyr on the spot now marked by his tomb.

Tradition holds that he was at last martyred by an unbeliever. Accounts of how he died differ; most tell that he fell in battle, and companions are remembered as having fallen with him.

## The Shrine

The *darbar* of Imam Sahib is not a single monumental tomb but a dense and atmospheric complex in the old city. Visitors describe it as a maze of narrow corridors and stairways opening onto several graves: by tradition those of unnamed companions who fell with the saint, together with the resting places of later *pirs*, or Sufi spiritual guides, and other holy men who chose to be buried in his shadow.

The tomb of the saint himself is approached through a mirrored gateway ornamented with Qur'anic inscriptions and geometric tilework, in the idiom of Punjabi shrine decoration, and the passages leading to it are often lined with prostrating and praying pilgrims.

In the reign of Aurangzeb his tomb, held to be a place where divine lights are made manifest, was visited by small and great alike. Today the shrine, like many of the province's major *darbars*, is administered under the auspices of the Punjab Auqaf Department, the government's department of religious endowments.

## Devotion and Festivals

As a martyr's shrine, the site carries the particular charisma that Punjabi popular religion attaches to the *shahid*, the martyr who is believed to be present and living, and whose intercession and *baraka*, the blessing that flows from a holy person, are sought by the faithful. Devotees come throughout the year to offer prayers, tie votive threads and seek blessings.

The shrine is the focus of an *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death. On such occasions the surrounding lanes fill with pilgrims, and the customary features of a Punjabi shrine festival accompany the gathering: devotional music, the recitation of poetry, and the distribution of *langar*, the food of the free communal kitchen.

Because Imam Sahib is regarded as the spiritual founder of Muslim Sialkot, his memory is woven into the civic and religious identity of the city itself, and local commemorations periodically recall his role in its history.

## The Setting

Sialkot lies in the Rachna *doab*, a tract of land between two rivers. It was a bustling city in the foothills of the Himalayas, famous for its silk, and an important post on the trade route between West Asia and Delhi. It is located right on the border, and historically it gave the Punjab a connection to Kashmir.

It is an ancient city. Its earliest recorded mention is found in ancient Greek texts going as far back as 322 BC, which call it Sagala, and in the reign of Aurangzeb it was counted a city of the ancients. It was once called Shalkot, a city held to be named in the *Mahabharata*, the Sanskrit epic, and it was also called Salkot. Legends of its founding differ; the founder most often named is Raja Salbahan, also called Salivahan, whose memorial was a fort of fired brick.

In legend the raja's son was Puran Bhagat. Tradition tells that Puran was thrown into a well, his hands and feet cut off; the well lay a little distance from the city and could still be seen in the nineteenth century, and devotees raised a temple around it, the most important temple in the ancient city of Sialkot. It is told, too, that when Puran came to Sialkot a dried up garden revived on his arrival.

In former times Sialkot was the seat of government of the Punjab, its habitation stretching two or three *kos*, an old measure of distance. In early times, when Lahore lay in ruins, it became the seat of government of the country, until Sultan Mahmud's conquest and Malik Ayaz's rebuilding of Lahore. The city became part of the Muslim Sultanate when Shahabuddin Muhammad Ghori captured the Punjab in 1192. Ghori also came to Sialkot after failing at Lahore in the year 580 AH, a year of the Islamic calendar; he repaired the city's old fort, whose foundation was ancient, and left his army there, and Khusraw Malik with the Khokhars besieged the fort for a time without success. Many Sufi missionaries settled in the region, making it predominantly Muslim and giving it a rich Sufi tradition.

The Mughal emperor Babur described Jat pastoralist groups in the Sialkot region. Under Akbar, Raja Man Singh, the *faujdar*, or military commander, of Jammu and the *jagirdar* of Sialkot, the holder of its land grant, repaired the fort and improved the city. In Jahangir's time Safdar Khan rebuilt the fort and its tower, and most later governors made repairs too.

In the reign of Aurangzeb Sialkot surpassed every other town of its *suba*, or province, in population, and it was a city of crafts. Its paper, of the kinds called Mansinghi, silk or *hariri*, and *khass-i Jahangiri*, was white and durable and was sent to other regions; its *karchikan* embroidery in silk and *kalabatun*, thread of gold or silver, went all over the world; and its *jamdhar* and *katari* daggers and its *barchhi* spears were well made. Gardens surrounded the city, among them the garden of Nazar Muhammad, and the buildings of the *qanungos*, the keepers of the land records, and of some others were most pleasing and delightful. A stream rising in the hills of Jammu flowed below the city. When it flooded in the rains, all the people of Sialkot, great and small, played in the water, naked but for a loincloth and carrying leather water skins, and anyone from the city who was far away remembered it with pleasure.

The city was also a seat of learning and a gathering place of scholars. Under Akbar, Maulana Kamal al-Din Husain left Kashmir, came to Sialkot in the year 971 AH and established teaching there. Under Shah Jahan, Maulvi Abd al-Hakim spread the sciences, wrote glosses and drew students to his *madrasa*, his religious school; his son Maulvi Abdullah ran the *madrasa* after him and was called the imam of his time. Sialkot was one of the centres of Islamic scholarship in the Mughal period, and Ahmad Sirhindi studied there.

Other holy men of the city are remembered too. Shah Daula's first master lived in Sialkot, and Shah Daula himself is said to have left the city after disputes with its people, moving after some years to Gujrat. Stories are also told of the *faqir*, or wandering mystic, Hamza Ghaus, whose curse was pronounced in the centre of the market square, and of the fear of him that gripped Sialkot.

In the early twenty first century Sialkot had become one of the most important cities in Pakistan. Its business community financed its own airport, which handles international flights, and the highway, and on the way into the city stood several factories and many mounds, probably archaeological ruins, converted into graveyards.

## Legacy

Imam Ali-ul-Haq occupies a place in Sialkot comparable to that of a patron saint: the figure to whom the city's Muslim character is popularly traced, and whose martyrdom sanctifies its very ground. That so little of his life is settled, not even the century in which he lived, has done nothing to diminish his standing in local devotion. This may indeed be characteristic of the earliest layer of Punjabi Muslim sacred history, in which the memory of the warrior saint who "opened" a region to Islam is preserved more in cult and story than in dated record.

That memory has long been written down. An account of his martyrdom, the *Waqa'i Sialkot* of Muhammad Muqim, is dated 1071 AH; it was edited by Dr Abdullah Chaghatai and published at Lahore in 1977. His shrine remains a living centre of pilgrimage and one of the defining landmarks of old Sialkot.

- District Gazetteer of Sialkot (Punjab Government gazetteer series), for the local history and topography of the city and its shrines.
- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, and comparable hagiographical compendia of the saints of Pakistan.
- General studies of the Islamisation of the Punjab and of warrior-saint (*ghazi*/*shahid*) cults in South Asian Islam.

- Sujan Rai Bhandari of Batala, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* (Persian; composed in regnal year 40 of Aurangzeb; 1918 Delhi lithograph edited by Zafar Hasan).
- Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* (dated 1867 for the original, the date unconfirmed).
- Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya* (Persian, composed 1292 AH / 1875 CE; read in an Urdu edition annotated by محمد اقبال مجددی and issued by تصوّف فاؤنڈیشن).

- Haroon Khalid, *Walking with Nanak* (2016).

Name: Shrine of Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari (Jalaluddin Bukhari)
Location: Uch Sharif, Bahawalpur District, Punjab, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: Rebuilt 1670 (site associated with saint d. c.1290)
Events: Annual urs; qawwali; langar
Description:
## Overview

At Uch Sharif, the ancient town near the confluence of the Chenab and the Sutlej in southern Punjab, lies the shrine of Sayyid Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari, the saint who made Uch one of the great centres of Sufism in the subcontinent. Known as Surkh-Posh, the Red-Robed, he came from Bukhara to settle at Uch, where he propagated the Suhrawardi order of Sufis, or Muslim mystics, and founded the celebrated family of the Bukhari sayyids, descendants of the Prophet Muhammad. Through his descendants, among them his grandson Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht, his line shaped the religious history of the region for centuries. His shrine anchors the remarkable cluster of tombs that has made Uch Sharif a place of pilgrimage and a treasury of Islamic architecture.

## The Saint

Sayyid Jalaluddin was born at Bukhara, in Central Asia, into a family of sayyids who traced their descent from the Prophet; accounts of the year of his birth differ, and the year the shrine keeps is 1192. His genealogy runs in ten links back to Imam Muhammad Taqi. Sayyid Ali Asghar, his seventh ancestor, had two sons, Sayyid Abd Allah and Sayyid Ismail, and from the descendants of Abd Allah came the family of the Bukhari sayyids, and from those of Ismail another family of sayyids. In Hindustan his standing rested on that lineage: all the sayyids, shaikhs, *amirs*, or nobles, and sultans treated him with deference because of the soundness of his descent.

He migrated southward in the age of the Mongol upheavals. In that age Mongol pressure drove waves of Turkish settlers into the subcontinent, many of whom settled for good in the cities of the Punjab, such as Lahore, Dipalpur and Multan, and Balban's garrisoning of those cities drew in thousands of refugees fleeing before the advancing Mongols, artisans, merchants, petty officials and the like. The Mongol invasions of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries devastated parts of the Punjab.

Accounts of his road from Bukhara differ, but he is remembered as coming first to Bhakkar in Sindh, where local jealousy forced him to move on, and as settling at last at Uch, which he made the base of his mission. There he remained until his death, preaching and guiding, and the family of the Bukhari sayyids that he founded there became one of the most influential religious lineages of the Punjab and Sindh.

He was a disciple of Shaikh Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan and one of his *khalifas*, the spiritual deputies a master authorises to guide others. He is remembered as a propagator of the Suhrawardi way, the Sufi order founded by Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi, connected to the great Multan line of his master. Bahauddin Zakariya died in 1263, and his tomb is in Multan city. The Qalandari and Jawaliqi dervishes, wandering ascetics who passed through Multan, often came into conflict with Bahauddin Zakariya in his lifetime.

He is remembered as Surkh-Posh, the Red-Robed, for the red garment he habitually wore, and he is also called simply Surkh, the Red. He is also known by the fuller name Sayyid Jalal al-Din Sher Shah, titled Mir Surkh Bukhari Uchi, *Uchi* meaning "of Uch".

Accounts of his sons differ, but he is most often said to have had three: Sayyid Ahmad Kabir, Sayyid Baha al-Din, and Sayyid Sadr al-Din, known as Muhammad Ghaus.

He died at Uch, full of years, on the nineteenth day of Jumada al-Awwal, the fifth month of the Islamic year, in 690 of the Hijri calendar, the year that corresponds to 1291; accounts of the year of his death differ. Most accounts place his grave at Uch, where he was buried and where his shrine stands.

## The Bukhari Line

Through Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh and his descendants, Uch Sharif became a spiritual capital of the southern Punjab, rivalling Multan as a seat of the Suhrawardi order and producing a succession of saints of the first rank. Chief among his descendants was his grandson and namesake, Sayyid Jalaluddin, known as Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht, one of the most revered Suhrawardi saints of the fourteenth century, his title Makhdoom Jahaniyan meaning one "whom all the inhabitants of the world serve". The grandson was born on 15 Sha'ban 707 AH, a date that fell on 9 February 1308, Sha'ban being the eighth month of the Islamic year, and he took his *bay'a*, the pledge of initiation into a Sufi order, in the Suhrawardi order from a son of the saint.

In the grandson's time Uch was, for a while, the centre of the Suhrawardi order, chiefly thanks to him. In his day the order spread from Uch to Gujarat, the Punjab and Kashmir, even extending its influence to the Delhi of Sultan Firuz Shah Tughluq. Makhdoom Jahaniyan is said to have written in almost every religious field. Uch, near Bahawalpur, was the base of the second period of the Suhrawardi order.

The line continued through generations of *sajjada-nashins*, the hereditary custodians of the saint's seat, who carried great religious and worldly authority. Among the saint's descendants were Sayyid Haji Abd al-Wahhab Bukhari Dehlvi, "of Delhi", and Mauj Darya Bukhari, who was the *sajjada-nashin* of his forefathers' *khanqah*, a *khanqah* being a Sufi lodge where disciples gather. Bibi Jawindi, whose tomb is among the tiled tombs of Uch, is said to have been the saint's great granddaughter, though accounts of who she was differ.

## The Shrine

The shrine of Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari is a working *darbar*, or saint's shrine, and the ancestral seat of the Bukhari sayyids. Standing amid the celebrated monuments of Uch Sharif, it is at once a place of living devotion and a link to the deep medieval history of Sufism in the subcontinent.

On one visit the group of shrines of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, which stood on a mound, was reached through the market, and the saint's shrine was also situated on that mound. It was protected by a thick wall with barbed wire on top, built shortly before to protect it from terrorist attacks. Almost all the visitors there, who numbered in the hundreds, were heading towards this shrine. An old banyan tree stood in the centre, and a banner depicted the saint with Bahauddin Zakariya, Baba Farid and Lal Shahbaz Qalandar; Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith, was not among them.

Next to the shrine, within the same compound, stood a mosque, itself a historical building. A *madrassa*, a school of religious learning, used to run at the shrine, and a board of the Archaeology Department recorded that Baha-ul-Halim taught there. In the market at the Gilani shrine a poster of the saint was on sale.

## Devotion and Festivals

The shrine is visited throughout the year by pilgrims who come to honour the founder of the line and to seek his blessing. It keeps the round of prayer, *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, and *langar*, the free communal kitchen, and its annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, draws devotees from across the region.

On one visit women, it seemed, were not allowed in, and looked on from the boundary. A man showed a visitor three rooms where, he said, Baba Farid, Bahauddin Zakariya and Lal Shahbaz Qalandar had meditated, put a green shawl with Quranic verses on it round the visitor's neck, and offered water; the visitor, expecting to be asked for a donation, walked off. People stood by the grave for blessings, another man waited with a green box, and devotees offered their donations to the saint.

## Guru Nanak and Uch

Sikh tradition holds that Guru Nanak was invited to Uch Sharif by the saint himself, when the two met at Kandahar on the way back from the Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca. Nanak is said to have made the visit on his way to Sindh, after he had settled down. The story is doubted, since the saint had lived in the thirteenth century.

Of Nanak's traces in the town, little was left. On one visit the well of Nanak lay hidden within a field, shielded by a grove of trees, abandoned, with juice tetrapaks and wrappers floating in its black water. Beside it was a grassy mound, which had been the Gurdwara of Nanak, a Sikh place of worship; nothing of it remained.

## The Setting

Uch Sharif is an ancient town built on a hill overlooking the confluence of the Sutlej and Chenab rivers, some seventy miles from Multan and about seventy kilometres from Bahawalpur. Its name, Uch, means high or great, and it has also been called Uch Miran. The town the saint and his descendants made holy is today a dense and evocative landscape of shrines and tombs, among them the exquisite tiled tombs of Bibi Jawindi and others, and it is counted among the most important heritage sites of Pakistan. In April 1996 a visitor spent a day wandering through the magnificent blue and white tiled mosques and desolate tombs of this ancient centre of learning, trade and pilgrimage.

Uch was famous for its Gilani and Bukhari saints, who came originally from Gilan and from Bukhara in Central Asia. Uch Gilanian, the city of saints in Bahawalpur, was where the family of the poet Bulleh Shah, who were sayyids, had settled, and where he was born, and Bulleh Shah's mentor, Inayat Shah, also belonged to Uch. Muhammad Bakhsh, of a hereditary family of *qawwals*, the singers of *qawwali*, at Kasur, once said, "We came with Bulle Shah's family from Uch Sharif, and we have learned his poetry from our ancestors, who have always sung here". In the early 2000s the landowning sayyids of Bahawalpur and Multan supported the shrines of their ancestors.

A legend of the town's founding tells of Shaikh Safiu'd-Din Kaziruni, who was ordered to mount a camel, travel in whatever direction the animal led him and remain where it finally halted. In the legend, the camel halted in the middle of a desert, and there the Shaikh founded a town later called Uch. Another legend of Uch tells of a contest in flight with a yogi, a Hindu ascetic, and all the stories of three generations of the Sufis of Uch tell of conflicts with Hindu yogis.

Uch was also a seat of the Gilani Qadiris, Sufis of the Qadiri order, which was founded by Abd al-Qadir Gilani. The first missionaries of the Qadiri order settled at Uch in the late fifteenth century, and from there the order spread into the subcontinent, where it soon gained a firm footing, and was carried as far as Indonesia and Malaysia. Shaikh Muhammad al-Husseini al-Jilani, a native of Turkey who travelled to Khurasan and then Multan before settling with his family in Uch, founded the first Qadiri *khanqah* there, and his son, Abd al-Qadir Jilani Thani, who died in 1533, is the famous Qadiri saint of Uch Sharif. In the nineteenth century some of Abd al-Qadir Sani's descendants held the *sajjada*, the seat of a saint's successor, at Uch, and the four sons of Hazrat Muhammad Ghaus lay at Uch Sharif beside the tomb of Shah Muhammad Ghaus. A Gilani forebear of Hazrat Pir Muhammad Shah came from Uch Sharif in the time of Akbar Shah, and the elders of the Faqir family lived at Uch Sharif Sayyidan and served the sayyids of Uch.

Uch lay on the roads of armies. The first campaign of the conqueror Shihab al-Din took it and left a deputy there, and his second came again to Multan and Uch and went on to Gujarat; Mirza Pir Muhammad crossed the Sind and took Uch and Multan; and on one march toward Jodhpur, Uch was a dependency of Multan. In Aurangzeb's reign the province of Thatta ran from the borders of Multan and Uch to Thatta and Kach Makran.

On one journey to Uch Sharif, the boundary between Sindh and Punjab became a blur on the road through Bahawalpur, where the cultures of the two provinces merge: some roadside hotels were called Punjab Hotel and others Sindh Hotel. The language there, Siraiki, is an amalgamation of the two languages, and the Siraiki spoken there was more like Sindhi, while in Multan it was closer to Punjabi. Siraiki is mainly spoken in the southern Punjab, with Multan as its capital, and in the Middle Ages this area was a part of Sindh.

The older city stood on a mound, with the massive *havelis*, or mansions, of the Gilanis and the Makhdooms. On the mound were graves covered arbitrarily with the blue and white Multani tiles that had been recovered from the historical shrines there. The river Sutlej, the lost river of Pakistan, used to flow here, before it was lost after the Indus Water Treaty was signed between India and Pakistan in 1960.

## Legacy

Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari holds a foundational place in the spiritual history of the Punjab and Sindh: the Bukhara-born saint who rooted the Suhrawardi way at Uch and fathered a dynasty of saints whose influence endured for centuries. Through his descendants, above all Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht, his line shaped the religion and society of the region, and through the shrines of Uch Sharif his memory is bound to one of the great sacred landscapes of Pakistan.

He has been called "the forefather of a long line of devout mystics and theologians". He is also counted as the third of three figures said to have met Lal at Chothanbi, and their shrines are spread across southern Punjab. In the nineteenth century the sayyids of Uch were famous for their authority in questions of descent: where a dispute over a man's descent arose and they accepted him as of sound descent, the matter was closed, and no one then dared say a word.

Name: Shrine of Lakhi Shah Saddar
Location: Laki (Lakhi), near Sehwan Sharif, Jamshoro, Sindh, Pakistan
Sufi Saint: Laki Shah Saddar (Syed Shah Sadaruddin Lakyari)
Events: Annual urs; ritual bathing in the Laki hot springs
Description:
## Overview

The Shrine of Lakhi Shah Saddar stands at Laki, a small settlement in the Kotri–Sehwan corridor of Jamshoro district in Sindh, tucked into the fold of the Lakhi range of hills that flank the western bank of the Indus as the river bends towards Sehwan Sharif. The dargah honours *Sayyid* Shah Sadaruddin, remembered by devotees as Lakhi Shah Saddar — the name is also written Laki Shah Sadar — a Sufi saint whose family, according to tradition, traced its descent from the Prophet's household through the *Imam* Ali ibn Abi Talib. The saint has lent his name to the surrounding locality and to the railway halt beside the tomb, and the shrine sits within one of the most storied stretches of Sindh's sacred geography: the same limestone hills that hold the celebrated hot springs of Laki, only a short distance from the great shrine of Lal Shahbaz Qalandar at Sehwan. Long carried in this dataset under the bare placeholder "Jamshoro District", the site is properly identified with this dargah, whose associated saint had always been recorded as Laki Shah Saddar.

## The Saint and His Lineage

Reliable biography of Lakhi Shah Saddar is thin, and much of what is remembered comes through devotional and local tradition rather than dated record; the account that follows is therefore given as it is preserved by his followers. He is held to have been a *Sayyid* of the Lakyari branch, and local accounts trace his ancestry to a forebear, Sayyid Ali Makki ibn Abbas Mousavi, said to have come originally from Samarra in Iraq. According to this tradition, that ancestor migrated to Sindh at the head of a company of more than a hundred followers and settled in the hill country of the lower Indus, where the family established itself and the settlement of Laki grew up around them. From this line came Shah Sadaruddin, who is venerated as a preacher and ascetic and around whose tomb the present dargah took shape. Precise dates for his life have not been securely established, and devotees emphasise his spiritual station and the miracles (*karamat*) attributed to him rather than a fixed chronology.

## The Shrine and Its Setting

What gives the shrine much of its distinctive character is its landscape. Laki lies among the Lakhi hills, a spur of the Kirthar system long famous for its thermal waters, and the sulphurous hot springs of Laki have drawn visitors seeking relief from skin ailments and other complaints for generations. Tradition binds these natural features to the saint: local accounts hold that some two miles west of the tomb, on a hilltop, lies the place where the saint kept a *chilla* — a forty-day retreat of prayer and seclusion — and pilgrims point there to marks revered, according to legend, as footprints associated with the *Imam* Ali. Such claims belong to the register of sacred legend rather than history, and are recounted here as part of the living devotion of the site. The tomb itself stands close to the Kotri–Sehwan railway line, and the modest halt beside it takes the saint's name, so that even the timetable of the old North Western Railway came to carry his memory. The proximity to Sehwan places the shrine on the well-worn pilgrim road to Lal Shahbaz Qalandar, and many who journey to the *qalandar*'s great *urs* have long paused at lesser shrines such as this along the way.

## Devotional Life and Legacy

Like most Sindhi dargahs, the shrine of Lakhi Shah Saddar is a place of continuous popular devotion rather than of formal institution. An annual *urs* marks the saint's death anniversary, gathering the faithful for prayer, recitation and the sharing of food in the manner customary at Sufi tombs across the province. The site belongs to the dense fabric of shrine culture that gives lower Sindh much of its religious texture — a countryside in which the tombs of *sayyids*, *faqirs* and *pirs* punctuate the hills and river plains, and in which pilgrimage, healing springs and the veneration of saints are woven together. The Lakhi springs and the dargah continue to attract both pilgrims and those drawn by the reputed medicinal waters, and the site is listed among the heritage places of Jamshoro district. That the shrine survived in the dataset only as an unnamed district entry is itself a reminder of how lightly documented many of Sindh's smaller yet locally cherished shrines remain, and how much of their history is preserved in oral and devotional memory rather than in the written record.

Name: Shrine of Makhdoom Abdul Rahim Girhori
Location: Girhor Sharif, near Pithoro, Umarkot, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Annual urs; visited by both Muslims and Hindus
Description:
## Overview

The shrine of Makhdoom Abdul Rahim Girhori stands at Girhor Sharif, a village some eight kilometres west of Pithoro in Umarkot district, in the semidesert borderlands of eastern Sindh. It honours a leading Naqshbandi mystic and scholar of eighteenth century Sindh, who lived from 1739 to 1778. He belonged to the Mangrio tribe and came to be known as *Girhori* after he settled at Girhor and established there his *khanqah*, the lodge where a Sufi's disciples gather. He is venerated as a *shaheed*, a martyr, and today his shrine is a place of pilgrimage frequented by both Muslims and Hindus, with an annual *urs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, held in his memory.

He is remembered as a scholar and an ascetic, a disciple of the celebrated Naqshbandi master Muhammad Zaman, a commentator on the Qur'an in Sindhi verse, and a saint who died attacking a Hindu shrine.

## The Saint

Abdul Rahim was among the foremost *khalifas*, or deputies, of Khwaja Muhammad Zaman of Luari Sharif, the celebrated *Sultan al-Aulia*, the king of the saints, of the Sindhi Naqshbandis, under whom he was trained. Muhammad Zaman had himself been a disciple of masters who included Mian Muhammad Thattawi. Accounts of Abdul Rahim's order are not unanimous, but he is most often counted a Naqshbandi, a follower of the Sufi order founded by Baha-ud-Din Naqshband, and he is remembered as an orthodox and militant one.

He was a younger contemporary of Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit, and like Mir Dard he was a Naqshbandi mystic. A verse by him expresses his admiration for Shah Abdul Latif, whom he may have met when still a child.

A learned man, Abdul Rahim Girhori is remembered for his religious scholarship and his ascetic life. Unlike the Naqshbandis of Thatta, he was little interested in legal problems. He was an energetic man: once, while attacking the "dry trees" of the school of Makhdum Muhammad Hashim, he even threw an inkstand at a scholar's head. He relied completely upon the Qur'an and tradition, and led a perfectly ascetic life, with long periods of fasting, made harder still because he used to take a purgative every third day.

He died in 1778. Accounts of his death differ in detail. Tradition holds that he fell in battle against a rival Hindu ascetic: he killed the ascetic and destroyed his *marhi*, or shrine, but was himself mortally wounded in the same encounter. That episode is remembered as the origin of his status as a *shaheed*.

## Writings and Teaching

He is said to have composed works in Sindhi, Arabic and Persian, and his principal compositions include *Sharh Abayat Sindhi*, *Fath-al-Fazal*, *Risala Gul Numa* and *Kalam Girhori*. He was a good writer, who commented in Arabic upon his master's Sindhi sayings and composed poetical commentaries on several suras, or chapters, of the Qur'an. Most of his books, however, were destroyed during the Afghan raids in Upper Sindh in 1781.

Perhaps the finest of them is his rhymed commentary on Surat al-Kauthar, the favourite theme of mystical veneration of the Prophet. It is an example of highly complicated *naʿtiyya* poetry, verse in praise of the Prophet, in the Sindhi language. Besides Ad-Duha and An-Najm, Surat al-Kauthar was always a favourite of poets who praised the Prophet, and Girhori's commentary takes up many earlier elements. In it God speaks, saying among other things:

*So much gift did I not give to anyone but you* (translated by Annemarie Schimmel)

The divine address runs on through Jesus, the Torah and Joseph, and closes with words to Ahmad, a name of the Prophet:

*A small quantity only of your love, O Ahmad, has reached Zulaikha … Hell is at your door supplicating like a beggar* (translated by Annemarie Schimmel)

His mystical teaching on the Prophet is in some ways reminiscent of Mir Dard's deep mystical love of the Prophet. Apparently following the statements of his master Muhammad Zaman, he understood the *haqiqa muhammadiyya*, the archetype of Muhammad, as a kind of mediator between the Divine and the human sphere. In this view of the Prophet, Girhori and Mir Dard stand together, and Shah Abdul Latif stands apart from them. His theoretical works describe Muhammad in exalted terms as the Perfect Man, who is like the dawn between the divine light and the darkness of human existence.

Other sayings and readings of his are remembered too. In one saying he called the perfect mystics Kapari, that is Yogis, a special group of Sanyasin, or Hindu renunciants, as Shah Abdul Latif often did. He quoted the Arabic saying *ad-dunya sihr*, "The world is magic". And he applied the words of the Qur'an at Sura 57:4, "And He is with you wherever you are", to the journey of Sassui, the heroine of a Sindhi folk tale, through the desert, something Shah Abdul Latif did not do.

## The Shrine and Its Setting

The shrine stands at Girhor Sharif, where he had settled and established his *khanqah*, and his tomb is honoured as that of a martyred saint. Today the shrine complex draws pilgrims of both faiths, and an annual *urs* commemorates him. The shrine has kept its local importance into recent times: in 2015 an armed attack on its custodian, Syed Asif Ali Shah, stirred sectarian unrest in the area.

Pithoro, the nearby town, is the seat of another saint's tomb. The tomb of Pithoro Pir lies in the hamlet of Pithoro, between Mirpur Khas and Umarkot, on the railway line which formerly connected Hyderabad, in Sindh, to Barmer and Jodhpur in Rajasthan; as at many other sanctuaries, the place bears the saint's name. The area of Umarkot was once a place of rough combat between two groups of Rajputs, the Somras and the Sodhas, and it stood at the centre of conflicts of local, regional and central interests. The chief of the Sodhas, Parmar Sodha, is said to have been established as king, or *rano*, at Umarkot, and in 1907 the Sodhas were described as worshippers of Shiva. Another important group, the Menghwar, counted among the untouchables, mostly settled around Umarkot.

The town has its place in other stories too. One group of pilgrims from a village near Umarkot walked around 600 kilometres to the goddess's temple at Hinglaj. In the legend of Mumal, Umarkot is the seat of the vizier Rano. And in Mughal history, under the name Amarkot, it is the fortress where the emperor's party halted after crossing the desert; its ruler received them with the duties of service, and Prince Muhammad Akbar was born there.

## His Times

The Naqshbandi order came to Sindh from the sixteenth century onwards, with the Tarkhans and the Arghuns, two Central Asian dynasties that ruled Sindh, and it has several important centres in the province. The Naqshbandis of Sindh followed the reforming enterprise led by Shah Waliullah in Delhi, and the majority of them are strongly opposed to music and to the singing of devotional songs. Apart from them, Sufism in Sindh is dominated by poetry expressing *wahdat-e wujud*, the unity of being. At the beginning of the eighteenth century a strong Naqshbandi influence changed the spiritual climate of southern Sindh to a certain extent: Makhdum Muhammad Hashim of Thatta and his relatives attacked the Sufis who defended the emotional side of religion, and this group helped to promote a more sober mystical piety. It was this Muhammad Hashim's school whose "dry trees" Girhori attacked.

His books were lost in the troubles that closed the Kalhoro period. The Kalhoros were overthrown by the former disciples of their saintly ancestor, Adam Shah Kalhoro, and the Talpurs, who thus came to power in 1781, ruled the country until it was conquered by the British in 1843. The Afghan raids in Upper Sindh in which most of Girhori's books were destroyed came in that same year, 1781.

## Legacy

His memory forms part of the wider Naqshbandi devotional network that the disciples of Khwaja Muhammad Zaman spread across Sindh in the eighteenth century. His verse was published in 1956 as *Kalam-i Girhori*, in an edition by Umar Muhammad Daudpota.

For all his militant zeal, it would be wrong to regard Girhori as a typical exponent of Sindhi Sufism. On the whole there was, in one writer's words, "a common basis of understanding, by Muslim and Hindu alike, of the mystical message of Islam", and a number of Hindus became devoted disciples of Muslim saints.
