Name: Shrine of Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht
Location: Uch Sharif, Bahawalpur District, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: Annual urs; qawwali; langar
Description:
## Overview

At Uch Sharif, in the southern Punjab, stands the shrine of Sayyid Jalaluddin Bukhari, who lived from 1308 to 1384 and is known by his honorifics *Makhdoom-i-Jahaniyan*, "the Master of the World", and *Jahangasht*, "the World Traveller". A grandson of Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari, he was among the most learned and widely revered saints of the Suhrawardi order of Sufis, or Muslim mystics, in fourteenth century India, a tireless traveller and preacher whose authority was sought by sultans and commoners alike. His shrine is one of the principal *darbars*, or saints' shrines, of Uch Sharif and a major centre of pilgrimage in the southern Punjab.

In his time Uch was, for a while, the centre of the Suhrawardi order, chiefly thanks to him: after the death of Shaikh Rukn al-Din the order had declined at Multan, and at Uch it was renewed. He was held in the highest esteem by the rulers of the Delhi Sultanate, particularly in the Tughluq age, brokered the peace between Sultan Firuz Shah and the Samma ruler of Thatta, and left a line of descendants and disciples whose branches reached into many regions of the subcontinent. His shrine stands in one of Pakistan's richest concentrations of sacred architecture, and it is kept by his descendants.

## The Saint

Jalaluddin was born at Uch on 15 Sha'ban 707 AH, in the Hijri or Islamic calendar, which fell on 9 February 1308. He came of the Husaini sayyids, the descendants of the Prophet through his grandson Husain, of a respected family of Bukhara, and he was born into the Bukhari sayyid family founded by his grandfather, Sayyid Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari, "Surkh-Posh" meaning the one clad in red. The grandfather was a disciple of Shaikh Baha al-Din Zakariya. He had three sons, Sayyid Ahmad Kabir, Sayyid Baha al-Din and Sayyid Muhammad, and his successor was his son Sayyid Ahmad Kabir. Accounts of the saint's father differ, but he is most often named as this Sayyid Ahmad Kabir, and Jalaluddin and his younger brother, Sayyid Sadr al-Din, known as Raju Qattal, were his sons.

Sayyid Ahmad Kabir, also called Ahmad Kabir al-Din, was himself a venerable Sufi. He attended Shaikh Jamal Khandan Ru, and his inward training was given by Shaikh Sadr al-Din Arif of Multan.

In full the saint was Sayyid Abu Abdullah Jalal al-Din Husain bin Ahmad Bukhari, *bin* meaning son of. His name was Sayyid Jalal al-Din Husain; Abu Abdullah was his *kunya*, a name of honour formed with *Abu*, "father of"; and his title was Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht, though some called him simply Makhdoom Jahaniyan. He was honoured, too, with a chain of titles of praise: the lamp of the family, the manifestation of the lights of the Lord, the dawning place of the epiphanies of the All Glorious, the unveiler of the mysteries of the Path, the guide on the ways of Reality, the master of guidance, and the leader of the *awtad*, the saints called the "pegs" of the world.

He began his schooling at Uch under the learned Qazi Baha al-Din, a *qazi* being a judge. After the *qazi*'s death he came from Uch to Multan to finish two textbooks of Islamic law, the *Hidaya* and the *Bazdawi*, under Shaikh Musa and Maulana Majd al-Din, and then he went to Medina and studied further.

Having received a formal religious education, he became his father's disciple. He took his first *bay'a*, the pledge of initiation, at his father's hand in the Suhrawardi order, the Sufi order founded by Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi, and from him received the *khirqa*, the patched cloak of the Sufi, as the mark of his *khilafat*, the authority to guide others. He then drew inward grace from his uncle, Sayyid Sadr al-Din, known as Muhammad Ghaus, and at Sadr al-Din's direction he became the disciple of Shaikh Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath of Multan, completed his training under him and received from him, too, the *khirqa* of *khilafat*. He is counted among the famous *khalifas*, or spiritual deputies, of Shah Rukn-e Alam, together with Maulana Zahir al-Din, Sultan Hamid al-Din Hakim, Shaikh Fakhr al-Din Iraqi and Shaikh Sama al-Din Dehlvi. Of Shaikh al-Arif at Multan he said that he taught every beginner and every advanced student without any distinction.

He wore other *khirqas* as well. He claimed the *khirqa* of his sayyid descent from Hazrat Ali, the robe that had come to Ali from the Prophet, and he wore the *khirqa* of Baha al-Din Zakariya, which he had received from his father. The *khirqa* is said to have come to him from many other masters besides, among them Shaikh Qawam al-Din, the *khalifa* of Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath, Qutb al-Din Munawwar, Imam Abdullah Yafi'i, Shaikh Ishaq Kazaruni, Shaikh Amin al-Din, Shaikh Hamid al-Din, Sayyid Ahmad Rifa'i, Shaikh Najm al-Din Kubra, Shaikh Nur al-Din and Hazrat Khizr, the immortal guide of seekers in Muslim tradition.

He made the Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, and at Mecca he stayed with the Shaikh al-Islam, the chief religious dignitary, Shaikh Afif al-Din Abdullah Matri, for outward and inward benefit. He spent six years in Medina and Mecca and returned home in 752 AH. At Medina, when he led the prayer in the Prophet's mosque in the imam's absence, he stood out of reverence one row behind the place where the Prophet used to stand.

He earned the name *Jahangasht* through his travels. He journeyed across the Muslim world, performed the Hajj many times and visited the great centres of learning and sanctity of his age, drawing grace from hundreds of guiding saints, though accounts differ over how often and how far he travelled. For most of the reign of Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq he seems to have lived abroad, while his *khanqah*, the Sufi lodge where disciples gather, was administered by his brother.

After his return he went to Delhi, where Shaikh Nasir al-Din Chiragh-i Dihli also initiated him into the Chishti order, a Sufi order prominent in South Asia, and gave him a further *khirqa* of *khilafat*. He is said to have taken *bay'a* and *khilafat* in fourteen *khanwadas*, or spiritual families, and the practice of initiation into more than one order seems to have been started in India by him. He was a Suhrawardi who also had close ties to the Chishti order.

He married, and of his sons, Sayyid Mahmud Nasir al-Din also lived at Uch and attracted disciples from Multan and neighbouring areas; he had a very large family and is believed to have died in 847 AH, 1443 to 1444. Another son was named Muhammad.

Makhdoom Jahaniyan died on 10 Zil-Hijja 785 AH, the day of Eid al-Adha, the Feast of the Sacrifice, which fell on 3 February 1384; accounts of the year of his death differ. Most accounts place his grave at Uch, where his shrine became a focus of devotion.

## The Sultans of Delhi

Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq appointed him Shaikh al-Islam and made him head of the Khanqah-i Muhammadi, a Sufi lodge at Siwistan, the town of Sehwan, to which several villages were attached. He accepted, and for a time he held the office over Siwistan and its dependencies and discharged it well, but he did not remain there long: he resigned at the order of Shaikh Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath.

Muhammad's successor, Sultan Firuz Shah Tughluq, was his devotee and obedient to him. In Firuz's reign the saint lived mainly at Uch and came several times to Delhi. One of his visits lasted from Sunday 8 Rabi II 781 AH, 24 July 1379, to Tuesday 17 Muharram 782 AH, 23 April 1380. The Sultan gave him a royal reception and went on visiting him in his *khanqah* throughout his stay, and so great was the saint's hold on him that all his recommendations were granted. From him, after his arrival from Uch, the Sultan learned to say the *chasht*, the morning prayer, and the *tahajjud*, the prayer of the night, and he derived many benefits from his company. The governors of Sind, too, sought his help.

He used that regard for others. When Sultan Firuz, advised by the *ulama*, the religious scholars, summoned Shaikh Sharaf al-Din from Bihar to account for his conduct, the order was cancelled at Makhdoom Jahaniyan's request, and it seems that his strong recommendations, which neither the Sultan nor the *ulama* could ignore, saved Shaikh Sharaf al-Din from the axe. The abolition by Sultan Firuz of about twenty eight taxes, laid largely on the towns of the empire, may be ascribed to his influence.

He is credited, too, with the peace of Thatta. Accounts of its year differ, placing it between 1362 and 1367, but when Sultan Firuz marched on Thatta with a large army, the Samma ruler, Jam Jauna bin Babinya, sought to arrange terms of peace through him. It was agreed at last that the Jam's son, Mani, should rule as a tributary of Sultan Firuz of Delhi, and the peace was generally hailed as a triumph for Makhdoom Jahaniyan.

It is told that Khan Jahan, the *wazir*, or chief minister, of Sultan Firuz, had imprisoned the son of a *muharrir*, a clerk. The saint went nineteen times to plead for him and was not received. The twentieth time Khan Jahan sent word asking whether the Sayyid had no shame. He answered, calling him dear one, that every time he came he earned merit, and that he wished to free the wronged man from Khan Jahan's hand so that Khan Jahan too might reach the rank of merit. Khan Jahan came to him bareheaded, with a rope round his neck, asked his pardon and became his *murid*, his disciple, and he released the clerk's son with a robe of honour and a horse. When he offered the saint a *nazrana*, a gift of homage, the saint gave it to the clerk's son.

At Delhi the Sultan and his nobles used to pay their respects to him. Shaikh Ahmad, though urged to become the saint's disciple, would not leave his own *pir*, his spiritual guide; and on a visit to Delhi Makhdoom Jahaniyan called on Ahmad-i Khattu and embraced him, telling him that he reminded him of his friend, Baba Ishaq.

## Teaching and Devotion

He strongly opposed the customs that had grown up around Shab-i Barat, the festival held in the evening of the middle of Sha'ban, the eighth month of the Muslim calendar, when fireworks were let off, graves were whitewashed and lighted lamps were placed on them. Muslims, he taught, should pray and give to the poor the money that would otherwise go on crackers and lamps; only in India, he added, was there such disregard of the holy law, for such innovations were not to be found in Ghazna, Khurasan or Arabia. He sternly disapproved of giving God such Hindi names as Thakur, "Lord", Dhani, "Rich", and Kartar, "Creator", and he advised the *a'imma*, the imams, not to accept any payment that came from illegal sources of revenue.

He urged dervishes, Sufis and *ulama* to visit rulers, officials and the rich in order to win help for the deprived, and he justified his own visits to Sultan Firuz on these grounds. Dervishes, however, should never allow such people to visit them at their *khanqahs*, and if it did happen, the time should be used well, in preaching on the meaning of the *Sharia*, the religious law. Royal stipends, he ruled, were *makruh*, disapproved, in the collections of *fatwas*, or legal rulings, but not invalid under the *Sharia*. He preferred to call his disciples *Akhi*, "brothers", an ideal he took both from the Akhi system of the craft guilds of Anatolia and from the Akhi and Futuwwa brotherhoods of the dervishes of Khurasan and Transoxiana. Beginners on the mystic path, he taught, should not concern themselves with trying to understand the *Wahdat al-Wujud*, the doctrine of the unity of being, for it was for experts only.

His teaching ranged over the *khirqa*, over patience, *sabr*, and the fear of God, *taqwa*, over the office of the shaikh, and over *shari'at*, *tariqat* and *haqiqat*, the law, the path and the Truth. Whenever he took a *murid*, he would say that he was only a *wakil*, an agent. He distinguished two kinds of *khirqa*: the *khirqa-yi tasawwuf*, the cloak of Sufism, is the robe of companionship, *suhbat*, while the *khirqa-yi tashabbuh*, the cloak of likeness, is the *khirqa* of blessing, *tabarruk*, for which companionship is not a condition. For being a shaikh he laid down three conditions, and without all three it was not valid: that he be learned in the sciences of *shari'at* and *haqiqat*; that the *ulama* of his age accept him and become his believing *murids*; and that he seek nothing but God Most High. His daily *wird*, the litany he recited, included the teaching that *Ya Hayy, Ya Qayyum*, "O Living One, O Sustainer", is the Greatest Name of God.

Five hundred *rak'ats*, the cycles of the ritual prayer, by day and night were his custom, and even in his last years he prayed a hundred; he could recite the Qur'an in all seven of its *qira'at*, or canonical readings; he performed much *dhikr*, the remembrance of God, aloud; and his dress was plain. Whether he listened to *sama'*, the Sufi practice of spiritual listening to music, is not settled. His humility reached to the turban: he prayed in a cap, saying that the turban is for men alone, and "I am not a man".

He is said to have written in almost every religious field, and his disciples gathered his teachings. At Delhi his disciple Abu Abdullah Ala al-Din Ali bin Sa'd bin Ashraf bin Ali al-Quraishi al-Husaini recorded his discourses in the *Khulasat al-Alfaz Jami al-Ulum*; the saint encouraged him in the work and explained points he could not understand. Another disciple, Makhdumzada Abdullah, compiled a summary of the discourses he gave on different occasions, the *Siraj al-Hidaya*. The *Khazinat al-Fawa'id al Jalalaliyya*, composed by Ahmad bin Ya'qub in 752 AH, 1351, and the *Khazinah-i Jalali* of Abu al-Fazl bin Ziya are compendiums of his teachings.

## Disciples and Descendants

His successor was his younger brother, Sayyid Sadr al-Din, who won fame under his nicknames, Raju and Qattal, "the Slayer", for his militant evangelism; his *sajjada*, the prayer carpet and seat of a saint's successor, passed to his brother and not to his son. Among his *khalifas* were Qazi Abd al-Malik, known as Shah Ajal, and his brother Raju Qattal, and the Suhrawardi line spread further through the sons and grandsons of both Makhdoom Jahaniyan and Raju Qattal.

In his time the order spread from Uch to Gujarat, the Punjab and Kashmir, and its influence reached even the Delhi of Sultan Firuz Shah. Shaikh Qiwam al-Din went to Uch to receive initiation from him in the Suhrawardi order, and a Shaikh Qawam al-Din, a famous elder of his time, is counted among his *murids* and *khalifas*. To Shaikh Rajgiri, a native of Daryabad in Awadh, he gave the title *Akhi*, and he gave him his *khirqa* when Akhi first settled at Kanauj. Kalpi became a centre of the order through the prestige of Shaikh Siraj Sukhta, a favourite imam of his; it is told that Qadir Shah, the ruler of Kalpi, sought Siraj Sukhta's protection, and that the shirt the Shaikh gave him to wear cured him. In Kashmir the Suhrawardi order was revived by Sayyid Muhammad Isfahani, a disciple of his, and Sayyid Jamal al-Din, a Sufi of his order, made a spectacular impact on the Sufis of Kashmir. Ashraf Jahangir Simnani came to Uch and drew on his spiritual grace and blessings.

Makhdoom Jahaniyan carried the prestige of the Bukhari sayyids of Uch to its height. He was one of the masters of the second period of the Suhrawardi order, and he was then based at Uch. A guide with a wide following, he strengthened the Suhrawardi presence across the Punjab and Sindh, and his descendants and disciples spread the *Jalali* Bukhari line far and wide, a lineage of sayyids who remained religiously and politically prominent for centuries. His grandson was Qutb Alam. He stands seventh among the ancestors of Mauj Darya of Lahore, with Jalal al-Din Surkh-Posh ninth, and he appears with Shaikh Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath of Multan in the spiritual chain of Mian Wada. Sain Qutb Shah was a Husaini Bukhari sayyid of his line, and Qutub Ali Shah was his descendant in direct line. Among the male ancestors of the modern saint Zauqi Shah, traced for thirty six generations back to the Prophet Muhammad, was Makhdoom Jahaniyan; after the fifteenth century that lineage fell into obscurity, until it suddenly reemerged into history during the British Raj.

The customs and ideas of the Qalandars, dervishes who wholly abandon legal norms and social conventions, and of the Nath yogis, an order of Hindu ascetics, had a considerable impact on the beliefs of a section of his followers. Unlike other Sufis they adopted Shi'ism, and like the Madari dervishes they went naked and sat before fires to warm themselves; their hair was unmatted, but they shaved their heads, beards, moustaches and eyebrows, and spent their time wandering from place to place. When they came into the order they offered all their goods to their preceptors, and in return they were given a cap and the spiritual tree of the order, worn on the head or hung round the neck. Of these Jalali saints, those who had achieved a certain standard of perfection would, it is said, like the Haidari dervishes, swallow snakes, calling them Ali's fish, and they called scorpions Ali's prawns. *Malang* dervishes too, wandering ascetics, and others called Dudae, naked from head to foot, were counted among his *murids* in every quarter, and they performed the *dhikr* aloud.

## The Shrine

The shrine of Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht is a busy *darbar* amid Uch Sharif's famous complex of tombs, and it is kept by his descendants. It stands close to the celebrated tiled tombs of Uch, among them that of Bibi Jawindi, who is held to be his descendant, though accounts of her relation to him differ.

By the 1870s his *roza*, his tomb, at Uch was a place of pilgrimage for the people. Pilgrims come throughout the year to seek the blessing of the Master of the World. The shrine keeps the customary devotions, prayer, *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, and *langar*, the free communal kitchen, and its annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, draws crowds from across the region.

In his lifetime Mir Sayyid Ali, the Hamadani sayyid, passed through Uch on his way to Kashmir and visited the saint's *khanqah* there; when Makhdoom Jahaniyan was told of the visit, he took little notice and remarked merely that *Hamadan*, "the All Knowing", was none but the Great Knower of the Invisible World, God Most High.

## Legends

Tradition tells how he came by the title Makhdoom Jahaniyan. On a night of Eid he kept vigil at the tomb of Baha al-Din Zakariya and then presented himself at the tombs of other saints; at each he asked for an *idi*, an Eid gift, and from each the title Makhdoom Jahaniyan was conferred on him.

The stories begin in his childhood. At seven, it is told, he was given dried dates from a tray set before Shaikh Jamal al-Din Khandan, and he ate them stones and all, explaining that there was blessing in the stones too, and that to throw them away would be disrespect. It was said of him that whenever he embraced anyone, he drew into himself at that moment whatever gift that person had.

Two *khirqas*, it is said, came to him in dreams, one from Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath and one from Nizam al-Din Auliya, and each was found on his head when he woke. At Medina, tradition holds, he greeted the Prophet's grave with peace, calling the Prophet his grandfather, and an answer came to him from the grave, returning the peace and calling him son.

One Ramadan, the month of fasting, it is told, he kept *i'tikaf*, a retreat of prayer, in the Jami Masjid, the congregational mosque, of Uch. Sumra, the governor of Uch, came into the mosque, where many people had gathered about the saint, and turned them all out. The saint asked Sumra whether he had gone mad, that he troubled the dervishes, and no sooner had he said it than Sumra went mad. His mother brought him and asked pardon, and the saint told her to bathe Sumra, clothe him, take him to the tomb of Hazrat Jamal al-Din Khandan, and then bring him back. She did so, and after Sumra had made his apology, through the saint's prayer he was entirely restored.

At Delhi, it is told, people distressed by drought asked for his prayer, and so much rain fell that, overwhelmed, they asked him to pray for it to stop; he prayed, and the rain stopped.

One story turns on a moment's distraction. His youngest son, a child of four, played near his prayer mat during the *chasht* prayer and drew his attention. Afterwards he told Sayyid Shams al-Din that it seemed hard to him that the boy would live, for in the very midst of the prayer his heart had inclined towards him; at the time of the noon prayer the boy fell into a fever, and that same night he died.

It is told, too, that a saint of Panipat reached Delhi by spiritual power in a single hour, found Makhdoom Jahaniyan in the throes of death, prayed for him and gave him some years of his own life, and returned to Panipat in a moment.

Tales of his journeys carry him further still. In them he made the rare and hazardous journey to China and Mongolia, converting the people he met on the way; he met yogis, all of whom in the end he converted to Islam; and he travelled through Ceylon, where Islam had failed to penetrate, and converted a yogi there too. All the stories of three generations of the Sufis of Uch tell of contests with Hindu yogis in feats of supernatural power, and they habitually end with the vanquished embracing Islam.

Conversions are ascribed to him. It is believed that the Sumirahs of lower Sindh, who were Isma'ilis, a branch of Shi'a Islam, adopted Sunni Islam under his influence, and a Jat chief of Sindh, afterwards named Abdullah, is said to have embraced Islam through a supernatural feat that he performed.

A story is told of his death bed. Nawahun, a Hindu who was the *darogha* of Uch, a revenue official entrusted with keeping accounts in Persian, visited him as he lay dying, and while praying for his recovery declared that the Sayyid was the seal of the saints, just as the Prophet Muhammad was the seal of the prophets. The saint held that these words amounted to a profession of faith. Nawahun was afterwards handed over to Sayyid Raju, and when he again refused to embrace Islam he was executed.

## The Setting

Uch Sharif is an ancient city some seventy miles from Multan, near Bahawalpur in the Punjab, built on a hill overlooking the confluence of the Sutlej and Chenab rivers. Its name means high or great. In April 1996 a visitor spent a day wandering through the magnificent blue and white tiled mosques and desolate tombs of this ancient centre of learning, trade and pilgrimage. Uch Gilanian, the city of saints in Bahawalpur, was where the family of the poet Bulleh Shah, who were sayyids, had settled, and where he was born. Muhammad Bakhsh, of a hereditary family of *qawwals*, the singers of *qawwali*, at Kasur, once said, "We came with Bulle Shah's family from Uch Sharif, and we have learned his poetry from our ancestors, who have always sung here". In the early 2000s the landowning sayyids of Bahawalpur and Multan supported the shrines of their ancestors.

A legend of the town's founding tells of Shaikh Safi al-Din Kaziruni, who was ordered to mount a camel, travel wherever the animal led him and remain where it finally halted. The camel halted in the middle of a desert, and there the Shaikh founded a town later called Uch. Another legend of Uch tells of a contest in flight with a yogi.

Uch was also a seat of the Gilani Qadiris, Sufis of the Qadiri order, which traces its descent to Shaikh Abd al-Qadir Jilani of Baghdad. The first missionaries of the Qadiri order settled at Uch in the late fifteenth century, and from there the order spread into the subcontinent, where it soon gained a firm footing, and was carried as far as Indonesia and Malaysia. Shaikh Muhammad al-Husseini al-Jilani, a native of Turkey who travelled to Khurasan and then Multan before settling with his family in Uch, founded the first Qadiri *khanqah* there, and his son, Abd al-Qadir Jilani Thani, who died in 1533, is the famous Qadiri saint of Uch Sharif. Four sons of Hazrat Muhammad Ghaus lie at Uch Sharif beside the tomb of Shah Muhammad Ghaus, and in the nineteenth century some of Abd al-Qadir Sani's descendants held the *sajjada* at Uch.

In the nineteenth century the sayyids of Uch were famous. Where a dispute over a man's descent arose and they accepted his lineage as sound, the matter was closed, and no one then dared say a word against it. The elders of the Faqir family lived at Uch Sharif Sayyidan and served the sayyids of Uch, and a Gilani forebear of Hazrat Pir Muhammad Shah came from Uch Sharif in the time of Akbar Shah.

Uch lay on the roads of armies. The first campaign of the conqueror Shihab al-Din took it and left a deputy there, and his second came again to Multan and Uch and went on to Gujarat; Mirza Pir Muhammad crossed the Sind and took Uch and Multan; and on one march toward Jodhpur, Uch was a dependency of Multan. In Aurangzeb's reign it was a *qasba*, a small town, and the province of Thatta ran from the borders of Multan and Uch to Thatta and Kach Makran.

On one journey to Uch Sharif, the boundary between Sindh and Punjab became a blur on the road through Bahawalpur, where the cultures of the two provinces merge: some roadside hotels were called Punjab Hotel and others Sindh Hotel, and the Siraiki, the language of the southern Punjab, spoken there was more like Sindhi, while in Multan it was closer to Punjabi. The older city stood on a mound, with the massive *havelis*, or mansions, of the Gilanis and the Makhdooms. The group of shrines of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries was reached through the market, and on the mound were graves covered arbitrarily with the blue and white Multani tiles that had been recovered from these historical shrines. The river Sutlej, the lost river of Pakistan, used to flow from here, before it was lost after the Indus Water Treaty was signed between India and Pakistan in 1960. Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith, is said to have visited the town on his way to Sindh, after he had settled down. Of his traces there, a well lay hidden within a field, shielded by a grove of trees, abandoned, with juice tetrapaks and wrappers floating in its black water, and beside it a grassy mound was said to have been the Gurdwara of Nanak, a Sikh place of worship.

## Legacy

Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht is remembered as one of the great Suhrawardi saints of medieval India, the learned and far travelled Master of the World whose authority spanned the Sultanate and whose lineage shaped the religious landscape of the Punjab and Sindh for generations. His memory is bound to that of his grandfather Surkh-Posh and to the whole flowering of sanctity that made Uch Sharif a spiritual capital of the south, and his shrine keeps alive the memory of the age when Uch, with Multan, was a beating heart of Sufism in the subcontinent.

In the poetry of the Punjab he is one of the Five Pirs, saints credited together with special powers and with miraculous intervention for Ranjha, the lover in the romance of Hir and Ranjha by Waris Shah. In the poem, "Sayyid Jalal of Bukhara, whom men also call Makhdum Jahanian" is among the holy men whose help Ranjha seeks; Ranjha "saw by their countenances that they were holy men and besought their help". His gift to Ranjha is a dagger, which the hero grasps in a later passage:

*and he grasped the dagger given him by Makhdum Jahanian* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

The poet Bulleh Shah, too, invoked the Five Pirs in his lyrics, a company in which Jalal ud Din Makhdum Jahaniyan of Uch is counted.

Name: Shrine of Makhdoom Nooh (Hala)
Events: Annual urs
Description:
## Overview

The Shrine of Makhdoom Nooh stands at Hala, a town some fifty six kilometres north east of Hyderabad in Sindh. It honours Makhdoom Lutufullah, universally known as Makhdoom Nooh and often as Makhdoom Sarwar Nooh, one of the most revered saints and scholars of the province. A Sufi, or Muslim mystic, of the Suhrawardi order, he is remembered as the founder of its *Sarwari* branch in Sindh, and above all as the first religious scholar of the region to render the Holy Quran into Persian. His shrine is the spiritual heart of Hala, drawing devotees throughout the year and at his annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death.

He is generally dated to the sixteenth century. He was first buried near his native village, close to Halakandi, but the shifting of the Indus twice compelled the removal of his remains, the second time, in 1777, to the site of new Hala, where his mausoleum now stands.

## The Saint

His real name is given as Lutufullah, and he is known by the title Makhdoom Nooh, *Makhdoom* being a title of honour meaning master; he is often called Makhdoom Sarwar Nooh as well, and by his town he is known as Makhdoom Nooh of Hala. Accounts of the century in which he lived differ, but he is generally dated to the sixteenth century. Tradition places his birth around 1500 to 1505 and his death about 1590, and he is said to have died at the age of 87.

He belonged to the Suhrawardi order, the Sufi order founded by Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi, and is honoured also with an Uwaisi spiritual lineage, a bond with a master never met in life. He is remembered as the founder of the *Sarwari* branch of the order in Sindh. Hala was a place where mystical leaders of the Suhrawardi order had settled, and among them his is the best known name.

His lasting fame rests above all on his scholarship: he is remembered as the first religious scholar of the region to render the Holy Quran into Persian. In his work the *dhikr*, the Sufi remembrance of God through repeated recitation, is itself called a high priced pearl.

## The Shrine

Makhdoom Nooh was first buried near his native village, close to Halakandi. The Indus, shifting its course, twice compelled the relocation of his remains: first to Mula Sanwani, about 1601, and again, in 1777, to the site of new Hala. Accounts differ over where his shrine stands, but it is at new Hala that his mausoleum now stands. The shrine is the spiritual heart of the town. It draws devotees throughout the year and hosts an annual *ʿurs* in the saint's memory.

## The Setting

Hala, in the Matiari District, is a town long associated with the *Makhdoom* line of saints, with Sufi devotional music and with the celebrated blue and white *Kashi* pottery of the region. It is also the birthplace of the great Sindhi poet and saint Shah Abdul Latif, who was born there in 1689 into a family of mystics who were Sayyids, descendants of the Prophet Muhammad. The blue and white tiles that cover his tomb at Bhit Shah are typical of Hala.

The town is the heart of a fertile agricultural belt, where Kolhi and Bhil women who are devotees at the shrine of Shah Abdul Latif can make a living working on the large feudal farms. The country about the town was not always safe: between Sehwan and old Hala, a people given to robbery were a danger to traders, so that the country could not be passed "without a strong guard".

An older name for the town appears in an account of the origins of the Hindu goddess Hinglaj, which holds that Hala was called Kohala in former times, and that the goddess was once the queen of the Kohala or Kohana area. It is a story of the town; it makes no link between the goddess and the shrine.

## Legacy

Makhdoom Nooh is remembered in Sindh as one of the most revered saints and scholars of the province: the founder of the *Sarwari* branch of the Suhrawardi order there, and the first religious scholar of the region to render the Holy Quran into Persian. He has been called "the great Suhrawardi leader of Sind". Twice moved by the shifting Indus, the second time to new Hala in 1777, his remains lie in a shrine that is still the spiritual heart of the town, visited throughout the year and at his annual *ʿurs*.

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, vol. 2 (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Pain and Grace: A Study of Two Mystical Writers of Eighteenth-Century Muslim India* (1976; 1997 edition).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* (Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina Press, 1975; 35th Anniversary Edition, 2011).
- Michel Boivin, *The Hindu Sufis of South Asia: Partition, Shrine Culture and the Sindhis in India* (London and New York: I.B. Tauris / Bloomsbury Publishing Plc, first published 2019).
- Shemeem Burney Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual* (Austin: University of Texas Press, 2002; Modern Middle East Series).
- Jürgen Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi: Identity, Change, and Solidification at a Hindu Temple in Pakistan* (New York: Oxford University Press, 2018; print line 2017).
- H. T. Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit: His Poetry, Life and Times — A Study of Literary, Social and Economic Conditions in Eighteenth Century Sind* (Lahore, Karachi and Dacca: Pakistan Branch, Oxford University Press; London: Oxford University Press; first published 1940, reprinted 1966).

Name: Shrine of Mauj Darya Bukhari
Location: Edward Road, Anarkali, Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Sufi Saint: Hazrat Meeran Muhammad Shah Bukhari ("Mauj Darya")
Events: Annual urs (17-19 Rabi al-Awwal); weekly Thursday milad; Mela Chiraagha
Description:
## Overview

On Edward Road, near the old Customs House in Anarkali, Lahore, stands the octagonal tomb of Hazrat Meeran Muhammad Shah Bukhari, popularly called Mauj Darya, the "Wave of the River". He was a saint of the Suhrawardi order and came of the Sadaat of Uch Sharif, the *sayyids*, or descendants of the Prophet, of that town, and in Lahore he is remembered above all as a spiritual confidant of the Mughal emperor Akbar. He died in 1604, and he lies in a small graveyard in the company of his family, his spiritual successors and the *gaddi nasheen*, the custodians who sit on the saint's seat.

The shrine is one of scores of Lahore shrines administered by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department, the Mehkama Auqaf, the department of religious endowments. It continues to draw a devoted following, with its gatherings of Thursday night and a yearly *ʿurs*, the commemoration of the saint's death, in the month of Rabi-ul-Awal.

## The Saint

He was born in 1533 in Uch Sharif, the son of Safi-ud-Din Bukhari of the Sadaat of that town. He was a descendant of Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari, whose name is given in more than one form, and his descent is traced through Syed Jalal-ud-Din Jahaniyan Jahangasht. His line runs from father to son: Miran Muhammad Shah was the son of Sayyid Safi al-Din, son of Sayyid Nizam al-Din, son of Sayyid Ilm al-Din the Second, son of Jalal al-Din, son of Sayyid Ilm al-Din the First, son of Sayyid Nasir al-Din, son of Sayyid Jalal al-Din Makhdoom Jahaniyan, whose own father was Sayyid Ahmad Kabir al-Din. Sanctity, nobility and the gift of miracles are held to have been his by inheritance.

He was an adherent of the Suhrawardi *silsila*, the spiritual lineage founded by Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan, and in his youth he became a *hafiz-e-Quran*, one who has memorised the whole Quran. At Uch he was famous for his renunciation, scrupulousness, piety and miracles, and there he held the seat of the *khanqah*, the Sufi lodge, of his forefathers. A Persian quatrain names him Hazrat Miran Muhammad Shah and calls him a Suhrawardi *pir*, a spiritual guide, in the line:

سہروردی پیر شیخ با صفا

*A line of the quatrain, which calls him a Suhrawardi pir.*

His name is met in several forms. He is called Miran Muhammad Shah, known as Sayyid Mauj Darya Bukhari Lahori; in full, Hazrat Miran Muhammad Shah Mauj Darya Suhrawardi Lahori; and Sayyid Miran Shah Bukhari, whom people also call Mauj Darya. Accounts of how he came by the name Mauj Darya differ. Popular tradition holds that he earned it by miraculously turning the River Ravi, which was prone to flooding, away from Lahore.

Above all he is remembered as a spiritual confidant of Akbar. The shrine's tradition relates that the emperor was foretold, through the saint's father, of a windstorm and a lit lamp that would mark the saint's presence at the fort of Chittor, and that when both signs appeared and the Rajput army surrendered, Akbar became his disciple. In the same tradition his prayer and intercession are credited with securing the fort's surrender to Akbar. After Akbar's campaign at Chittorgarh the saint came to Lahore at the emperor's request, and Akbar was his great devotee.

Legend credits him with giving away to the poor a substantial reward that Akbar granted him near Batala; accounts of the size and place of the grant differ. It is said that on the saint's arrival in Lahore the emperor gifted him the land on which he settled. He was the first to settle at the place where his tomb stands, coming there in Akbar's reign, and he founded a whole quarter of the city. His *darasgah*, the seat of learning in which he lies buried, is said still to hold land documents bearing Akbar's own signature, though accounts of where the documents were kept differ.

He lived mostly in Lahore, and there he kept alive the work of a *shaikh*, a spiritual master. He also kept a second household, where his second wife lived and where there were *havelis*, large houses, and he lived sometimes there and sometimes in Lahore. In Akbar's reign he was famous as a God-fearing man of sanctity and miracles, and he was counted an elder possessed of miracles, devout and ascetic. He is remembered, too, as a missionary presence who drew many Hindus and Sikhs to Islam.

Among his disciples was Shah Abdul Razzaq Makki, his *murid*, or pledged disciple. Abdul Razzaq Makki came to Lahore, took service with Akbar and then renounced the world, and from Mauj Darya, it is said, he received such grace that he became the *qutb*, the pole of the saints, of his age. Of Shaikh Abdul Razzaq Makki of the Nila Gumbad it is told that he reached such perfection that Mauj Darya himself honoured him. One of the saint's *khalifas*, the deputies who carry on a master's teaching, was a Sayyid Abd al-Razzaq of Dola Wari. A Sayyid Abdul Razzaq worshipped nightly at the saint's tomb, and his own tomb, it is said, was ordered in a dream.

He died in 1604; accounts of the year and day of his death differ. His son Sayyid Safi-ud-Din brought his body to Lahore, and in the nineteenth century people regarded as blessed the mosque where the body was washed.

By the 1870s his death had been set in a Persian chronogram, a verse whose letters, read as numbers, give a year. The year it gives, written twice within it, is 1014 of the Hijri, or Islamic, calendar, one of the differing accounts of the year of his death:

چوں محمد شاہ ملک عاقبت
در مقام قرب حقانی نشست
از حضور ۱۰۱۴ھ آمد عیان تاریخ او
نیز سرور گفت مرد حق پرست ۱۰۱۴ھ

*A chronogram on the death of Muhammad Shah*

## His Family

He married twice. His first wife, Syedna Bibi Fatima Sani, is remembered as "Bibi Killah" and popularly as Mai Fatima; accounts of her name differ. She was a daughter of Sayyid Abd al-Qadir the Third, son of Sayyid Abd al-Wahhab, son of Sayyid Muhammad Bala Pir Gilani. She died in the year 1016 of the Hijri calendar, and she rests in a separate shrine facing his own, near the historic Jain Mandir, though accounts of where she lies differ. She is remembered as a saint in her own right. She objected to his second marriage. A brother of the saint lies in a domed tomb of baked brick, built in the year 1017 of the Hijri calendar, in the corner of an enclosure at Bibi Pak Daman.

He is most often said to have had three sons, though accounts of their number and of their mothers differ. Sayyid Safi al-Din, named for his grandfather, and Sayyid Baha al-Din were born of his first wife, and Shah Shihab al-Din of the second; tradition tells that Shihab al-Din could take the form of a lion. By the 1870s Shihab al-Din's descendants lived at Tibala, where he had settled, and Safi al-Din's in Lahore; accounts of the town where Shihab al-Din's line settled differ.

It is told that Shihab al-Din was put to school at four years, four months and four days, by the custom of the law of Muhammad. He is said to have slapped his teacher and recited the whole Quran, and his father, greatly pleased, offered two *rakʿat*, cycles of prayer, in thanks.

The division in the household outlived the saint. When Shihab al-Din's body was brought for burial, Safi-ud-Din refused it a place in his father's tomb, saying that only those born of the chaste womb of the first wife might be buried there, and Shihab al-Din was buried elsewhere.

His *langar*, the free communal kitchen, has continued, devotees say, under his descendants to this day. In the 1880s his descendants in Lahore, Sayyid Husain Shah among them, traced their line to him through Safi-ud-Din. In the nineteenth century Sayyid Asghar Ali was among the Sayyids of sound descent in Lahore, and the descendants of the servants of his *langar* were still living.

## The Shrine

At the very spot where the tomb stands, his house stood, and a public *langar* ran there continually. Hundreds of the poor and destitute ate at his *langar*; accounts of how many *langars* he kept differ. Accounts of when the tomb was built differ too, but most hold that it was raised in his lifetime by order of Akbar.

Architecturally the tomb is unusual among Lahore's shrines for its octagonal plan, with a low dome, corner towers at each of its eight angles, and a mixture of recessed blind arches and plain panelled facades, a style thought to echo Multani funerary tradition.

In the 1880s the octagonal tomb stood on a platform of baked brick, with its door on the south. Over the door a niche carried, in a bold hand, a Persian inscription saying that the sacred tomb of the choicest of those who have attained, the exemplar of the gnostics, accepted at the court of the Creator, Miran Sayyid Muhammad Shah Mauj Darya Bukhari, may God illumine his resting place, was built in the reign of Akbar Badshah. There were verses on each of its eight sides. By the 1870s his lofty tomb was a place of pilgrimage for the people, and by the 1880s the *khanqah* was counted among the famous and well known places of Lahore. In the nineteenth century the building stood on a high mound, with its entrance on the south, a *dalan*, or open hall, and two small rooms where the trustees sat, four lattices of brick, and verses over the doors.

The saint lies in a small graveyard in the company of his family, his spiritual successors and *gaddi nasheen*, and his cook, Allahu Samad. In the 1880s the tomb itself held, beside the saint's own grave, the graves of his sons, Safi-ud-Din among them, and of others of his offspring. Outside the tomb, on a platform, lies a great-grandson of the saint, a son of Sayyid Abd al-Rahim, son of Safi-ud-Din, of whom too people said that he was a saint and a man of God. The small tomb of the servant Mian Murid was built by order of Akbar.

In the 1880s the enclosure held a mosque of baked brick, dwellings for the servants of the *khanqah*, a well and other buildings, all of baked brick. In the nineteenth century there stood an old mosque with the name of Abdur Rahman, an officer of the army, over its arch, along with a well, trees and *hujras*, small cells.

The shrine gained unwelcome national attention in 2018, when construction of the underground Anarkali station of the Orange Line Metro Train demolished its mosque, *langar khana* and courtyard, with tunnelling reported to pass close to the saint's grave in apparent violation of the rules for a heritage buffer zone. The episode became a flashpoint in Lahore's debates over balancing infrastructure development against the protection of religious heritage. Yet devotees hold that for all the government construction pressing around it, nothing has ever tarnished the shrine's beauty.

It is reported that the shrine's upkeep ran down a long line before the Auqaf Department took it on: from the emperor Akbar through the rulers who followed him and Maharaja Ranjit Singh, and through the saint's own descendants. In Maharaja Ranjit Singh's time forty rupees a month were received for the expenses of the *khanqah*; by the 1880s nothing at all was received. Among those who later held his seat as *sajjada nashin*, the head of the shrine, were Hazrat Shams Shah and Sayyid Hayat Shah.

## Devotion and Festivals

Daily devotion includes the recitation of the *Fatiha*, the opening chapter of the Quran, the lighting of *diyas*, small oil lamps, the making of vows, or *mannat*, and the presentation of *niyaz*, consecrated offerings. The gatherings of Thursday night, Jummay Raat, remain the busiest of the week.

The annual *ʿurs* is held on the 17th to the 19th of Rabi-ul-Awal, with a Mela Chiraagha, a festival of lights, the ceremonial washing, or *gusal*, of the tomb, the changing of its *chadar*, the sheet of cloth laid over the grave, and *langar* throughout. Some 2,200 to 2,500 visitors come on an ordinary day, and between 225,000 and 300,000 across the *ʿurs*. In the 1880s, too, an *ʿurs* was held at the shrine every year, and a great multitude gathered.

## Legends

His cook, Allahu Samad, is himself the subject of one of the shrine's most striking tales, in which the saint, to answer sceptics, had his cook sit unharmed in a burning cauldron.

Other wonders are recounted of him. A cauldron of rice that he blessed during a shortage is said to have fed the people for nearly seven days. He is said to have prayed over brackish irrigation water for local landowners, and it turned sweet; tellings differ over whose prayer it was. A tree planted in his lifetime, "the blessed tree", is said never to have needed cutting.

One story turns on a *ber* tree, the jujube, in the courtyard of his wife's house, while the saint was in the courtyard of the *khanqah*. Miran Muhammad Shah asked where she had got this bounty, and she answered that this wealth was her ancestral inheritance. A tree at her house could be seen from the *khanqah* of Hazrat Mauj Darya Bukhari. A miracle of a *chadar* is told there too, after which, it is said, the Bukhari and Gilani Sayyids no longer married one another.

It is also reported that books about him by Muslim, Hindu and Sikh authors alike are widely read.

## The Setting

The saint came to Lahore in Akbar's reign, when the emperor had turned to the settlement of Lahore from the start of his reign, built a city and a palace there, raised large buildings and stayed for a time. The quarter that the saint founded was known as Mohalla Mauj Darya. It stayed settled to the end of the Chughtai, or Mughal, sultanate, and it was ruined in the time of the Sikh plunder and the attacks of Ahmad Shah; part of its land went into the roads.

Anarkali, the market district in which the shrine stands, is named after the legendary lover of the Mughal emperor Jahangir, and over the years the area became the largest tyre market in the city.

## Bibliography

- Shrines Project field survey, Darbar Meera Mauj Darya Bukhari responses (surveyor: Saifullah), 2026.

- Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* (dated 1867 for the original, the date unconfirmed).
- Kanhaiya Lal Hindi, *Tarikh-e Lahore* (1884 original).
- Haroon Khalid, *A White Trail: A journey into the heart of Pakistan's religious minorities* (westland ltd, 2013; first e-book edition 2013).

Name: Shrine of Mian Mir
Events: Annual urs (7 February); Thursday-evening qawwali; daily langar
Description:
## Overview

In the Dharampura area of Lahore, once the garden suburb of Baghbanpura, stands the shrine of Hazrat Mian Mir, one of the greatest Sufi saints, or Muslim mystics, of the Mughal age and among the most beloved holy figures in the history of the city. A master of the Qadiri order, he was revered in his own lifetime by beggars and emperors alike for the fierceness of his asceticism, the depth of his learning and the breadth of a heart that welcomed Muslim, Sikh, Hindu and Christian without distinction. For nearly four centuries his tomb has drawn pilgrims seeking peace, healing and blessing, and because of his celebrated friendship with the Sikh Gurus it endures as one of Lahore's living symbols of interfaith reverence.

The tomb was raised by a Mughal prince for a dervish who, tradition holds, had forbidden any dome over his grave. Today it is a place of daily prayer, of *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, on Thursday evenings, and of free food for visitors, and each year its *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, fills its courtyards with hundreds of thousands of devotees.

## The Saint

His name was Mir Mohammad, and he bore the titles Mian Mir and Shah Mir; *Mian* is used in the local language as a mark of respect, in the sense of *sahib*. He was also often called Bala Pir, and he is not to be confused with Sayyid Muhammad Bala Pir Gilani, another man known by the same epithet.

Mian Mir was born in the sixteenth century at Sehwan, also called Sivastan, a town in Sindh between the cities of Thatta and Bhakkar. Accounts of the year differ; it is most often given as 1550. He came of a devout and learned family that traced its lineage to Umar al-Farooq, the second Caliph of Islam, and from that descent he is often given the epithet Farooqi. His father, Qazi Sain Ditta, son of Qazi Qalandar Faruqi, was a man of religious standing respected throughout Sindh, and his mother was Bibi Fatima, daughter of Qazi Qadan. He had four brothers, Mian Qazi, Qazi Usman, Qazi Tahir and Qazi Muhammad, and two sisters, Bibi Badi and Bibi Jamal Khatun, the second of whom was herself counted among the saints.

His father died when he was seven. At about the age of twelve, with the consent and blessing of his widowed mother, the boy left home in search of inner enlightenment, and for a time he wandered as a seeker. His mother is remembered among the saintly mothers who, like those of Shaikh Abdul Haqq Muhaddis Dehlavi and Khwaja Baqi Billah, played a part in making their sons great Sufis. He was drawn to the inward path and joined the Qadiri *silsila*, the spiritual lineage of the order that traces its descent to Shaikh Abd al-Qadir Jilani of Baghdad. Accounts of his initiation differ, but his master is remembered at the shrine as Shaikh Siyustani and is most often named Shaikh Khizr Sistani. From him Mian Mir received his training and, in time, the *khilafat*, the authority to guide others. His Qadiri line runs from Shaikh Khizr Sistani back through Sayyid Abdul Razzaq, called Qutb al-Afaq, to Abdul Razzaq's father, Abd al-Qadir Jilani himself.

At about the age of twenty five, with his master's permission, Mian Mir came to Lahore. He settled in the leafy neighbourhood of Baghbanpura, also called Khanpura, on the edge of the city beside the river Ravi, and there he remained for the rest of a very long life, passing his days and nights in devotion, teaching and the disciplined practice of the spiritual arts, until Lahore itself became inseparable from his name. In Lahore he studied the sciences of his day with Mawlana Saad Allah Lahori, who also taught Shah Husain, and with Akhund Nemat Allah. He is counted the founder of the Qadiri order in Lahore, where he represented it together with his sister, Bibi Jamal.

He was remembered as a worshipper and an ascetic, God fearing in the highest degree, devoted to God, a man who had left the world, and his contemporaries remembered him above all for the severity and the sincerity of his renunciation. In his *hujra*, the bare cell in which he lived, he spread nothing more than a piece of old sackcloth on the floor, and on that humble seat even the emperors of Hindustan did not hesitate to sit. He wore only coarse homespun *khaddar*, washed his own clothes with his own hands in the waters of the Ravi, and carried none of the outward marks of a Sufi master: no staff to lean on in his old age, and no patched cloak, or *khirqa*, to advertise his station. Once, when a devotee brought him a staff and he had walked a few steps leaning on it, he cast it away, saying, "He who has Allah for his support has no need of any artificial prop." When the wealthy pressed gifts of money and goods on him for his needs, he turned them away with the words "I stand in no need of these. I am not a beggar; I am rich, for my Provider looks after my needs", and told them to give their gifts to the poor and the needy. A dervish who begs from another beggar, he held, forfeits his trust in God.

He was a renowned adept of *habs-e-dam*, the disciplined regulation of the breath, a practice akin to the yogic *pranayama*, which he would carry through the night from the *Isha* prayer, the prayer of nightfall, until the light of dawn; it was a discipline he passed on to his own successor. He is said never to have slept at night, to have broken his fast only after a week, and at times, absorbed in God, to have gone a month without eating.

Though a man of deep and illumined learning who could expound the intricacies of the Qur'an and the Hadith, the sayings of the Prophet, to the astonishment of the scholars of his day, he neither wrote prose nor composed verse, and he showed no wish to keep letters or to set down his own words. When a dervish scatters his inner state on paper, he held, the secret entrusted to him by God is unveiled to those unworthy to keep it. Alone among the great figures of Punjabi Sufism, he left behind no *diwan*, no collection of poetry. Ordinarily he was not eager even for visitors: he would welcome a guest, raise his hands in prayer and blessing for him, and then gently ask him to return to his own affairs. Shy of courtly favour, he was extremely popular with people of all religions.

His teaching, as his disciples preserved it, was as demanding as his life. A human being, he taught, is made of three things, *nafs*, the ego, *dil*, the heart, and *rooh*, the soul, and the whole labour of the spiritual traveller is to bring these into balance: to submit to the *Sharia*, the religious law, to walk the path of *tariqat*, the Sufi way, in search of *marifat*, the inner knowledge of God, and so to reach *haqiqat*, the Truth. He counselled his followers to fix the heart on God alone and to empty it of the love of the world; to live plainly, eating little, speaking little and sleeping little; to meet honour and insult with the same evenness of soul; and to accept all weal and woe alike as a blessing from God. Above all he treated every human being, of whatever faith, as a creature of the one God. Nor did he flatter power: unmindful of royal displeasure, he would try to dissuade the emperor and his sons from any act he judged unjust or unethical. In an age of magnificence, he made poverty and truthfulness his splendour.

Of all his family, most is told of his sister, Bibi Jamal Khatun. She received her bond with the Qadiri order, her *nisbat*, from her full brother and from their mother, and in her renunciation she was called the Rabia of her time. The Mughal prince Dara Shikoh wrote her life in detail in both his books of the saints, the *Sakīnat al-Auliyā* and the *Safīnat al-Auliyā*, and she was one of the outstanding saints of the Qadiri order during its formative period in the Punjab. She was the mother of Hazrat Muhammad Sharif, the first *sajjada nashin*, the hereditary custodian who sits on the saint's prayer carpet. Accounts differ over the year of her death, which they place between 1000 and 1057 AH, and over where she lies; most place her grave in Lahore. By the 1870s it was counted within the enclosure of her brother's *khanqah*, the Sufi lodge; in 1974 the place lay between the Karachi railway line and the village of Miani Sahib.

By tradition Mian Mir lived some eighty eight years. In his final illness, worn by age and by the gout that had crippled his legs, he is said to have refused treatment, explaining that he did not wish to be dulled into unconsciousness: he wished to meet death fully aware, and to feel it come. He had spent some sixty years in the same small cell, and it was there that he passed away, at the time of the midday prayer on the seventh of Rabi al-Awwal, the third month of the Islamic year. He died in the reign of Shah Jahan, in 1635 (1045 AH), the year the Auqaf Department holds and most accounts give, though a few place his death in 1645.

## Disciples and the Mughal Court

For all his withdrawal from the world, Mian Mir's fame reached the very summit of the Mughal state. Lahore was then a seasonal capital, home of the Mughal court during its perennial rotation, and the emperor Jahangir sought the saint out. The two held a long interview, for which Mian Mir, notwithstanding his great age and weakness, took the trouble to come to the emperor; Jahangir, deeply moved, wrote to him both before and after their meeting, asking to see him again. Such visitors the saint received seated on his sackcloth, offered a prayer for them, and then dismissed with courtesy to their own concerns.

The emperor Shah Jahan, too, came into his presence several times. In one story of Shah Jahan and the saints of Lahore, Mian Mir refused an offering that Shah Bilawal, another of the city's elders, accepted; speaking to the emperor, Mian Mir likened the perfect *wali*, the friend of God, to a river, and Shah Jahan gave thanks for such perfect saints.

His deepest imprint on the age, however, came through his disciples, and the foremost of them was Mullah Shah Badakhshi. It is told that Mullah Shah came from Kashmir to Lahore, where his search did not succeed; on the road to Agra he learned Mian Mir's name from a stranger and regretted that he had not met him in Lahore, and he returned from Agra and presented himself before the saint. Then the master tried him. For three years Mian Mir showed him no regard. At last he asked where he lived, and when told that it was in a mosque, said that living in a mosque was not fitting; he asked what he ate, and when told that it was bread from the bazaar, said that bazaar bread ought not to be eaten. The disciple gave up both and began to starve, and only then did Mian Mir honour him with *bay'a*, the pledge of initiation, and give him the *khirqa*, the cloak, of *khilafat*.

Mian Mir called his disciple by a title of his own, Muhammad Shah. Once, asked for whom he had prayed, he answered that it was for Mullah Shah, through whom his way would shine; and of his disciple's *riyazat*, his spiritual austerities, he said that none of the masters of the past had performed the like. With his master's permission Mullah Shah spent the summers in Kashmir and the winters at Lahore in his service, and he carried on Mian Mir's nightly practice of the breath. He holds a distinguished rank among the elders of the Qadiri order, and he died in 1660.

Dara Shikoh, son of Shah Jahan and the crown prince famed for seeking the common ground between Islam and the mystical traditions of India, became Mian Mir's most ardent admirer. Accounts describe the bond in different ways, but the prince's own guide is most often named as Mullah Shah, who drew him into the Qadiri way and introduced him to the saint, and Mian Mir was his *dada murshid*, his guide's guide. When Dara Shikoh came to write of the Qadiri order, he set aside another lineage and acknowledged only the line that came down to Mian Mir and then to Mullah Shah. He devoted a whole book, the Persian *Sakīnat al-Auliyā*, "The Tranquillity of the Saints", to the saint, his circle and his wonders, of which it records thousands; it is a fine biography of Mian Mir and the Qadiri order in Lahore, and today one of the principal sources for his life.

In Persian verse the prince honoured him as the very pole of sainthood of his age: Mir Mohammad, he wrote, is the pathfinder for all the friends of God of this age, and while the Qadiri line endures it shall lead others, so long as the universe abides. That a prince of the empire should write so of a barefoot dervish in sackcloth is itself a measure of the awe that Mian Mir commanded.

Dara Shikoh gave his life to the search for the unity underlying Islam and the mystical traditions of India. He gathered the lives and sayings of the saints in his *Safīnat al-Auliyā* and *Sakīnat al-Auliyā*; he wrote the *Majma-ul-Bahrain*, "The Mingling of the Two Oceans", to show the deep harmony between Sufi and Indian metaphysics; he was a patron of Hindu mystics, the *sannyasis*; and he caused the Upanishads, the ancient philosophical scriptures of Hinduism, to be rendered into Persian, a labour that would one day carry Indian thought to Europe. His sister, the princess Jahanara, Shah Jahan's eldest and best loved daughter, was herself a disciple of Mullah Shah, who thought her worthy to be his successor, though this did not come to pass. She set down her own spiritual journey in the *Risala-i-Sahibiya*, one of the rare mystical works to come from the hand of a woman of the imperial house. Through these royal disciples the bare Qadiri cell beside the Ravi reached into the very centre of the empire, and for one brief generation the circle of Mian Mir and Mullah Shah became the spiritual heart of the Mughal court.

Yet the same nearness marked the circle for tragedy. When the throne passed, in blood, to the austere and orthodox Aurangzeb rather than to his mystically minded elder brother, Dara Shikoh was condemned as a heretic and put to death in 1659. The liberal and seeking spirit that Mian Mir and Mullah Shah had nourished was driven from the court, to survive thereafter not in palaces but at shrines such as Mian Mir's, where it had first been kindled.

The line itself ran on. Mullah Shah was Mian Mir's *khalifa*, his successor, and in Lahore the Qadiri chain passed from Mullah Shah to Shaikh Muhsin Shah, and from him to Shah Abd al-Rashid Lahori, and further down to Sayyid Bhawan Shah, reaching the year 1213 AH. Pir Burhan, who came from Bukhara in Akbar's time, received the grace of the Qadiri order, its *fayz*, from Mian Mir and Shah Bilawal, elders of Lahore. The chain of Shaikh Abdullah Shah Baloch joined Mian Mir through four intermediaries; the spiritual pedigree, or *shajra*, of one Mehr Shah ran back through Miran Shah Said to Mian Mir; and Shah Enayat was counted a successor to the Qadiri seat, or *gaddi*, of Mian Mir. The saint's disciples were thousands of people, among them a *faqir*, a mystic who has embraced poverty, named Abd al-Haqq.

Not every order honoured the line. A tradition of the Naushahi order tells of one Hafiz Tahir, who attended Mullah Shah, Mian Mir's *khalifa*, for some years in pursuit of inner knowledge but gained nothing there; he lost his faith, turned from Islam itself, put on the *zunnar*, the sacred thread, and went begging among Hindu *faqirs*, until Naushah restored him.

## A Friendship Across Faiths

The most famous tradition attached to Mian Mir binds his memory to the Sikh faith. He was a close friend of the fifth Sikh Guru, Arjan Dev, and of the sixth, Guru Hargobind, and the Qadiri school he founded in Lahore formed a close and sympathetic link with the Sikhs of that time. Sikh tradition has long held that it was Mian Mir whom Guru Arjan Dev invited to lay the foundation stone of the Harmandir Sahib, the Golden Temple at Amritsar, so that the holiest shrine of the Sikhs might be founded by the hand of a Muslim saint. The contemporary Persian chronicles do not mention the episode, and historians differ over it; but Mian Mir's cordial and brotherly relations with the fifth Guru are well attested, and the tradition is cherished across communities as an emblem of the friendship between Muslims and Sikhs in the Punjab. It continues to draw Sikh pilgrims to the saint's memory.

The friendship between Mian Mir and Guru Arjan Dev is also the subject of several folk tales, and the Sikh memory of the Gurus' ordeals tells of him too. When Guru Arjan Dev was tortured, it is said, his Muslim friend came to him, incensed, and asked whether he should destroy the Guru's oppressors; the Guru told him that he should not. It is believed, too, that Guru Hargobind was released after Mian Mir interceded on his behalf.

Not everyone looked on the saint kindly. The Naqshbandi Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi is said to have disliked him and, for that reason, to have spoken to the king against him. Mian Mir himself received Sikhs, Hindus and Christians with the same courtesy and reverence he showed his fellow Muslims, and treated them all as children of the one God.

## Legends

As with every great saint, a rich body of tales of *karamat*, the miraculous deeds of a saint, gathered around Mian Mir; his wonders were said to be beyond counting. They were told and retold well into the colonial era, when British collectors of Punjabi folklore took them down. One tells of a dove: a hunter's stone struck down a bird that had been sweetly praising God, and at Mian Mir's touch it revived and flew away unharmed; when the hunter aimed once more, the stone turned back and wounded his own hand, until, repenting and vowing never again to harm a winged creature, he was healed. Devotees tell, too, of a black snake that came to the saint as he sat by the Ravi, circled him three times and slipped quietly away; of a mute boy whom he taught to say "Bismillah", in the name of God, after which the child could speak; of a handkerchief he gave that healed the sick who used it in faith; and of food that appeared, in answer to his prayer, when there was nothing in the house to set before a guest.

Many such tales turn on his knowledge of hidden things and his power over sickness and death. A man came seeking his blessing for a journey to Khorasan; Mian Mir advised him not to go, for the way, he said, was closed, and so, unseen, it proved. Another came in anguish over a son who was choking and suffocating; the saint fell into a trance, called for a cup of water, breathed his recitation over it, and by it the child was relieved. To one visitor he said simply, "you may depart", and within a few days the man breathed his last. A disciple, Meerak Mohammad Lahori, told how, having taken up and chewed a discarded betel leaf from the saint's own mouth, he was carried into so deep an ecstasy that his breast seemed near to bursting with felicity. Stories such as these, more than any doctrine, bound ordinary people to the saint, and they still draw the troubled and the hopeful to his shrine.

A wonder is told of the tomb itself. When Shah Muhammad Ghaus came to Lahore in search of the truth, he spent his first night at the tomb of Mian Mir. In a dream the saint appeared to him and, with complete attention, bestowed on him a *shughl*, a spiritual exercise to practise. In the morning Shah Muhammad Ghaus went to Shaikh Hamid Lahori and asked him, too, for an exercise, and Shaikh Hamid laughed and said that the one Mian Mir had given him that night was enough.

Another wonder is told of his sister. There were some two *man* of wheat in the household, a *man* being a traditional measure of weight. Bibi Jamal Khatun put her hand into it, and for a year it fed the *faqirs*, the poor, the dervishes of the *khanqah* and its dependants every day, as though the two *man* had become several hundred. When the news reached Mian Mir, he said that the display of *karamat* is forbidden and that God is the giver of sustenance: what need was there to obtain grain in this way?

A saying of his concerns his attendant, or *khadim*, Mir Inayatullah, whose *murshid*, his spiritual guide, gave him the title Miskin Shah Amri, because no one knew where he got his food. When someone described his state to Mian Mir, the saint said that this Miskin is Amri: his food comes to him by the *amr*, the command, of God, and he has no need to earn it. Miskin Shah Amri's tomb lies on the west side of the Mian Mir cantonment.

A modern story, told in Bahawalpur by a senior *murid*, a pledged disciple, is set at the shrine too. Captain Wahid Bakhsh Sahab and Hazrat Shahidullah Sahab once went to visit the tomb, and a *majzub* there, one spiritually intoxicated and absorbed in divine love, asked Shahidullah where his hometown was. He answered, "My hometown is London"; the *majzub* laughed and said, "No, no. Your hometown is Medina!", and repeated it many times.

## The Shrine

Tradition records that when his disciples spoke of raising a fitting monument over his resting place, Mian Mir forbade any dome or mausoleum, and he is said to have spoken a Persian couplet on the vanity of such display:

صورتِ قبرم ز بعدِ مرگ ویرانہ خوشتر است
نیستی مانندِ من با خاک یکساں خوشتر است

*The face of my grave, after death, is better left in ruins; for one like me, to be as nothing, level with the dust, is better.*

Yet a mausoleum was raised at his resting place in the years that followed, during the lifetime of Dara Shikoh, who could not bear that his master should lie unmarked. When Shah Jahan entrusted the governorship of the Punjab to the prince, he raised many buildings, among the first of them a *chowk*, a public square, and the lofty tomb of Mian Mir, for which he gathered much stone and building material; he built the tomb and garden of his own guide, Mullah Shah, as well. He meant, too, to lay a road of red stone to the saint's tomb, so clean and pure that he could go and come barefoot every day to pay his respects, and on which none but the prince himself would travel. The plan was cut short when Alamgir Aurangzeb overcame his father and imprisoned him, and had his brother Dara Shikoh killed.

The war of succession also stopped the building work, and the building stood idle for some years; only on a petition to Alamgir was it taken up again and finished, though not to the finish Dara Shikoh had intended. The shrine's mosque shows the two reigns: its base, faced with stone, was laid in Dara Shikoh's time, and the rest was built under Alamgir. Tradition holds that Aurangzeb also drew on stone from the complex in raising the great Badshahi Mosque of Lahore.

The tomb grew into a dignified monument in the Mughal manner, its chambers finished in fine stone, and in the nineteenth century it was counted among the famous and splendid buildings of Lahore. Accounts differ over the stone it is built of; the shrine describes a mausoleum of red sandstone. In the nineteenth century a solid enclosure finished in lime plaster surrounded it, with arches in all four walls and its door on the south. The tomb stood on a grand square platform, or *chabutra*, nineteen by nineteen *zar'a*, an old measure of length, with a marble stair on the south and stone paving on top. Its door panel was of marble in a frame of red stone. Inside, a marble floor was inlaid with black stone, and three arches stood in the walls, with the door in the fourth, the southern one; the marble work of the interior was built in Dara Shikoh's time. Glass work in a vine pattern and a large mirror adorned the flanks of the northern arch and the ceiling of the dome. The grave stood on a marble platform a foot high, its *ta'wiz*, the raised marker over the grave, of marble and always covered with costly cloths, and the finial of the dome, the *kalas*, was of marble too. The glass work belonged to a later age: an Englishman in a merchant's service had it made, and had the outside whitewashed as well.

The shrine's offices were built into its fabric. On the west of the enclosure stood a grand hall, or *dalan*, as the seat of the *mujawirs*, the attendants of the tomb, and beside it a further building held the special seat of the *sajjada nashin*. There was no well within the walls, so a man named Nur Muhammad had one made over the course of fifty years, with a bathhouse beside it. Over the door of the tomb was set a chronogram, a verse whose letters, read as numbers, give a year, and from it the year of the saint's death is obtained.

By the 1870s his tomb in Lahore was a place of pilgrimage for God's creatures, and a Persian chronogram of four lines was written in the saint's honour. Its opening line praises Mian Mir with a play on his name, *Mir*:

میر دنیا و دیں میاں میر ست

Around the tomb, in time, gathered the graves of others who had loved him, so that the barefoot dervish who owned nothing and had asked for nothing came to rest at the centre of a small city of tombs, his wish overruled by the devotion of a prince. Dara Shikoh's wife, Nadira Begum, lies buried near the saint's mausoleum, and the shrine holds that the prince himself was laid to rest close to the saint. Mullah Shah's tomb lies outside Mian Mir's, and the grave of Khwaja Bihari adjoins the saint's tomb. Accomplished disciples of Mian Mir lie by the tomb, among them Haji Sulaiman and Shaikh Abu al-Khair, and so do keepers of the shrine, among them Hafiz Allah Yar and Sain Mir Shah. Beside the *khanqah* and tomb of Khwaja Bahar lies a burial ground of the kin of the late Muhammad Sharif, its graves of various dates, the names of those buried there unknown.

The locality itself bears the saint's name, as the *qasba*, the small town, or the *mauza*, the village, of Mian Mir, and his grave lies at Mian Mir near a railway station. Within the enclosure of Mullah Shah's tomb, whose garden Dara Shikoh also built, there came to stand a village bearing Mian Mir's name; in the nineteenth century *zamindars*, local landholders, lived in the garden, and the whole village was called Mian Mir.

The tomb passed through the turbulence of later ages. In Ranjit Singh's time red, black and marble stones were torn down around Lahore, and when the cantonments of his armies were built, the bricks of old tombs and houses were pulled out, so that thousands of old tombs, domes, mosques, gardens and *havelis*, the great mansions that were the memorials of the nobles of the past, were lost. Mian Mir's tomb did not escape: much of its valuable stone was carried off by the builders of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, who prized the material. Yet through every change of rule the shrine endured as a place of devotion.

Under British rule the tomb came under the care of the department of ancient monuments, and in 1985 it was formally declared a protected site by the Punjab Auqaf Department, the department of religious endowments, which administers it to this day together with the shrine's traditional *sajjada nashins*. Late in the twentieth century the shrine had fallen to pieces; it was then restored and, like Data Darbar, extended and renovated as a mosque with Friday congregational prayer. The mausoleum stands in the Dharampura (Hashimpura) area of Lahore, its dome and gateway a familiar landmark, with an attached mosque and open courtyards to receive the crowds who gather there. Successive generations have repaired and adorned it, so that the austere saint who wished only for a ruined and level grave is honoured, instead, by one of the enduring monuments of the city.

## Devotion and Festivals

The shrine of Mian Mir remains a living centre of popular piety. On ordinary days it draws on the order of one to three thousand visitors, who come to recite the *Fatiha*, the opening chapter of the Qur'an, to tie vows, and to seek the saint's intercession for healing, for children and for relief from hardship; many speak of the peace they feel within its walls and of prayers answered there. *Qawwali* is sung on Thursday evenings, the five daily prayers are held in the shrine's mosque, and *langar*, free food from the communal kitchen, is given out to visitors, sometimes twice a day.

The great occasion of the year is the *ʿurs*, held on 7 February, which marks the saint's union with the Divine; the courtyards then fill with hundreds of thousands of devotees for days of *qawwali*, prayer and communal feasting. Across the centuries, under Mughal, Sikh and British rule and in the Pakistan of today, the shrine has served as a shared space of devotion, a place where the boundaries of community grew soft.

In the nineteenth century five fairs, or *melas*, were held at the tomb each year: one yearly gathering, when the crowd stayed two days and two nights, and four in the rains, on the four Wednesdays of the month of *Sawan*, the month of the monsoon rains. A great fair was held there under the Sikhs too, but later the gathering grew more prosperous still, for the people of Lahore itself, of the Mian Mir cantonment and of the villages gathered in great numbers on the day of the fair, and the offerings brought in much income.

Pilgrims and seekers of many kinds have come to the tomb. The city's Qalandars, dervishes who wholly abandon legal norms and social conventions and even the distinctions of gender, are still associated with Mian Mir, as with Shah Husain and Shah Jamal, among the great Qadiri saints of Lahore.

## The Setting

Mian Mir's life wove him into the deeper Sufi history of Lahore. He is said to have kept a *chilla*, a retreat of forty days in seclusion, at the *khanqah* of Data Ganj Bakhsh, Ali Hujwiri, the eleventh century saint whose *Kashf al-Mahjub* is among the earliest Persian treatises on Sufism and whose shrine, Data Darbar, is the spiritual heart of the city. In going to sit in devotion at Data Sahib's threshold, Mian Mir joined his own sanctity to that of Lahore's patron saint, and later devotion has treasured the link as binding together the two greatest Sufi presences of the city. He was a contemporary, too, of Shah Abul Maali.

In the city itself, in Sadr Bazaar, Anarkali, a house known as Mian Mir's *chilla* stood in the nineteenth century beside a merchant's mansion and shops. Its rent went to *faqirs*; it had an arched way, an underground chamber, or *tah khana*, that was an old building, trees and a well. The saint's *sajjada nashin* held that Mian Mir had spent nights there and that the house had once been a garden, and Qazi Muhammad Afzal, called Fazl Gada, is said to have visited the saint at the place in Anarkali where his *chilla* stood.

The name Mian Mir runs through the map of Lahore. A road ran from Anarkali to Mian Mir, and the tomb of Sayyid Jan Muhammad Huzuri adjoins the Mian Mir road on its west. When the cantonment at Anarkali was given up, a new one was set in the plain of Mian Mir for the breadth of its land, with its own Sadr Bazaar of Mian Mir, great barracks, a church and countless *kothis*, or bungalows, costing lakhs, that is, hundreds of thousands. The city of Lahore had once reached as far as Hashimpura.

## Legacy

Mian Mir stands in memory as the very type of the Sufi ideal: a man who owned nothing and was sought by emperors; who wrote not a single verse and yet was praised in verse by a prince; who, rooted absolutely in his own faith, made his threshold a meeting place for people of every religion. His disciples shaped the spiritual life of the Mughal court, and the Qadiri line that grew from him ran on in Lahore through Mullah Shah and his successors. His friendship with the Sikh Gurus became a legend of tolerance that the Punjab still cherishes, and a hostel for pilgrims built at Dera Sahib in 1996 was named after him. The retreat he is said to have kept at Data Darbar bound him to the patron saint of Lahore, and his tomb remains one of the anchors of the city's sacred landscape. In honouring Mian Mir, Lahore remembers not only a saint of extraordinary austerity and learning, but a vision of holiness generous enough to hold an entire, plural world.
