Name: Shrine of Mian Umar Baba (Chamkani)
Events: Annual urs (first Wednesday and Thursday of Rajab); langar
Description:
The shrine of Mian Muhammad Umar Baba lies at Chamkani, a village on the eastern outskirts of Peshawar about seven kilometres from the old city. Mian Umar (traditionally 1671-1776) was a Sufi of the Naqshbandi order — a scholar, poet, social reformer, and historian who is counted, together with Akhund Darweza Baba and the warrior-poet Khushal Khan Khattak, among the great literary and spiritual figures of the Mughal-era Pashtun frontier. Said to have been born near Lahore and to have lived to a great age, he attracted disciples from every rank of society; tradition holds that even Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani), the founder of the Afghan kingdom, visited him and became his devotee. Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* gives a specific account of his death — in the month of Rajab, 1119 AH (approximately 1707-1708 CE) — and records his burial at the village of Chamkani, three miles from Peshawar, consistent with the shrine's location as given above; that date, however, falls roughly seven decades earlier than the 1776 death year given elsewhere in this entry, and the discrepancy is left unresolved here, with both figures reported rather than reconciled. His tomb at Chamkani grew into a shrine and khanqah that remains a place of resort for the surrounding population, drawing its largest crowds at the annual urs, held over the first Wednesday and Thursday of the Islamic month of Rajab, when devotees gather for sermons, collective dhikr, and na'at, and the langar (free kitchen) is served. Like a number of Sufi shrines in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the site was targeted in militant attacks during the years of insurgency in the region, but it endures as an active centre of devotion. It complements the nearby shrine of the saint's contemporary Akhund Darweza Baba, also recorded in this dataset.

Name: Shrine of Miran Hussain Zanjani (Zanjani Sahib)
Events: Annual urs (autumn)
Description:
## Overview

In Chah Miran, an old riverside locality of Lahore named in his honour, stands the tomb of Syed Miran Hussain Zanjani, one of the earliest Muslim missionary figures associated with the city. Unusually for a site of such age, the grave rests on a simple raised platform without a dome, within what was once a garden named for the saint. The shrine is maintained by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department, and local devotees still gather there every year for his *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death.

Zanjani is remembered as the elder of the two missionary saints credited with the early spread of Islam in Lahore, the other being the more widely celebrated Data Ganj Bakhsh, Ali Hujwiri. Tradition holds that Data Ganj Bakhsh reached the city to find Zanjani's funeral under way, the saint having died during the night. His modest tomb is one of Lahore's oldest surviving Islamic devotional sites, older by centuries than the grander shrines of the Mughal era for which the city is more widely known, and it remains the spiritual anchor of the neighbourhood that bears his name, on the historic bank of the River Ravi near the old walled city.

## The Saint

Syed Miran Hussain Zanjani, also remembered as Hazrat Shaikh Hussain Zanjani and as Shah Husain Zanjani, was a Hussaini Syed, a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad, and his family's descent is traced from Imam Musa Kazim through the Zanjan line. Tradition holds that he was born in 958 at Zanjan, in what is now Iran. He is counted among the ancient elders, the saints of old: a man of guidance, austerity, piety and nobility. His spiritual chain, or *silsila*, the line of masters through which a Sufi's teaching is handed down, is said to lead back to Junaid of Baghdad.

He came to Lahore, it is said, around 998, on the instruction of his spiritual master, Sheikh Abu al-Fazal Khatil, who ordered his disciple to move to the Punjab and later sent Ali Hujwiri after him. He is also said to have come together with another saint from Zanjan, Sayyid Yaqub Zanjani, known as Sadr Diwan, whose own grave is on Hospital Road in Lahore. Accounts differ over when and how Zanjani came, but he is remembered to have preached in the city for some thirty six years, converting large numbers of its people to Islam well before the Ghaznavid and later Mughal periods reshaped the religious landscape of the region, and to have spent his whole life guiding them.

The year of his death that the shrine keeps is 1042. He was buried alongside his brother, Hazrat Musa Hussain Zanjani, whose own shrine lies nearby. Accounts of his dates differ, and it has been argued that two men of the same name, an earlier and a later, have been run together; but the shrine and most accounts remember a single saint, the one whose funeral Data Ganj Bakhsh is said to have found under way when he reached Lahore.

## Legends

The best known story about Zanjani, and one of Lahore's early Sufi foundation stories, ties him to Ali Hujwiri, Data Ganj Bakhsh. Tradition holds that when Hujwiri's master ordered him to go to Lahore and preach, he objected that his senior brother in the path, Hussain Zanjani, a fellow disciple of the same master, was already there, and asked what need there was of him. His master repeated the order.

When Hujwiri reached Lahore, the story continues, he saw Zanjani's bier going past: the saint had died during the night, and in the morning his coffin was carried out for burial. Data Ganj Bakhsh joined the funeral and saw to the shrouding and the burial at Chah Miran. On seeing the bier, it is said, he understood how far his *murshid*, his spiritual guide, had seen. In the nineteenth century Zanjani's *karamat*, the miraculous deeds of a saint, were said to be famous by the thousand.

The founder of the Chishti order in India, Khwaja Muin al-Din Chishti, is also linked with Zanjani. When the Khwaja came to Lahore, it is said, he kept company with Zanjani, or else stayed near the tombs of Zanjani and Ali Hujwiri; accounts differ over whether he found the saint alive.

## The Shrine and Its Devotion

The tomb has a modest footprint that belies its historical significance: a grave on a simple raised platform, with no dome. Today it lies in Miran Husain Park, in Chah Miran, which by the 1970s was a suburb of Lahore.

In the nineteenth century the place was known as the *khanqah*, the Sufi lodge, of Hazrat Sayyid Husain Zanjani, on the south side of the village of Khoi Miran. The tomb had a brick enclosure taller than a man, with its entrance on the north. There were also a niche with wooden shutters, a second enclosure with a niche for a lamp, a *dalan*, or hall, of three arches, a few graves and a *kotha*, a small room, and a well with a Persian wheel, a wheel hung with a chain of pots that lifts the water.

By the 1880s the shrine was counted among those outside the walled city, a mile from Lahore to the east. The grave was built of brick, houses of *pakka*, or fired, brick had been put up for *faqirs*, wandering Sufis, to live in, and the Persian wheel at the well was in working order. The building was small, but the place was ancient, and the man buried there was counted among the earliest elders of Lahore.

In the nineteenth century the shrine was in the possession of Karam Ali Shah, the *gaddi nashin*, or holder of the seat, of the line of Sadr Diwan Sahib, the saint said to have come to Lahore with Zanjani, and only a few faqirs lived there. Today the shrine is formally recognised and maintained by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department, the provincial government's department of religious endowments.

Under Sikh rule a great *mela*, or fair, was held at the tomb every year. By the 1880s its liveliness had gradually gone, as attendance had also fallen at the shrine of Fateh Shah Mast once the Sikh state came to an end. An *ʿurs* was held at the grave once every year in the nineteenth century, and the yearly *ʿurs* still draws local devotees today.

## The Setting

In the Punjab at large, the annexation of the province by Mahmud of Ghazna and its incorporation into his empire prompted many Sufis to settle there, and in the eleventh century a number of mystics and scholars had settled in Lahore.

The title of the first to call Lahore to Islam has been given to another man, Shaikh Muhammad Ismail Muhaddith Lahori, a Bukhari sayyid who taught *hadith*, the reported sayings of the Prophet, and *tafsir*, the interpretation of the Quran, there, and through whom, it is said, the faith of Islam spread in the Punjab, though that account, and the year it gives for his death, have been disputed.

In the 1880s a second shrine, that of Faqir Sain Qutb Shah Qadri, lay to the east of the village of Khoi Miran. The shrine of Shah Gada Lahori had the same arrangement in those years: quarters of fired brick for faqirs and a working Persian wheel.

## Legacy

As one of the earliest known Sufi graves in the Lahore region, the shrine bears valuable witness to the gradual spread of Islam in the Punjab, carried by missionaries in the centuries before the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal empire. Already in the nineteenth century it was counted among the oldest in the city, and its saint was honoured as the first of a company of saints who came from abroad to the land of Hind, and as the master of masters.

His name has also travelled with the story of Data Ganj Bakhsh, whose arrival in Lahore is told through Zanjani's funeral, and with that of Khwaja Muin al-Din Chishti, who is said to have kept company with him or to have stayed near his tomb. Around the grave, the locality of Chah Miran is named in his honour.

Name: Shrine of Peer Makki
Location: Bhati Gate area (near Data Darbar), Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Sufi Saint: Hazrat Syed Azizuddin al-Hassani wal-Hussaini (Peer Makki)
Events: Annual urs (9-11 Rabi al-Awwal); Thursday-night gatherings; dhamal and qawwali
Description:
## Overview

The shrine of Peer Makki stands in the Bhati Gate quarter of Lahore's Walled City, close to the great shrine of Data Ganj Bakhsh. It honours Hazrat Syed Azizuddin, a scholar and mystic born in Baghdad, who is said to have spent twelve years in seclusion at Mecca, the years that gave him his title, Makki, before coming to Lahore in 575 AH, around 1178 CE, where he taught for some thirty six years. Devotional custom in Lahore holds that pilgrims should pay their respects at his tomb before going on to Data Darbar, and his yearly *ʿurs*, the commemoration of the saint's death, fills the quarter with devotees.

Like Data Darbar itself, the shrine is administered by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department, the Punjab government's department of religious endowments, and its tradition is Syed and Ahl-e-Sunnat, the Sunni way. Its complex includes an adjoining mosque, the Hazrat Pir Makki Masjid. Despite its nearness to one of Pakistan's most visited shrines, Peer Makki's own tomb receives markedly fewer pilgrims, which gives it a more intimate, contemplative atmosphere.

## The Saint

Hazrat Syed Azizuddin al-Hassani wal-Hussaini was born in Baghdad, the son of Hazrat Peer Syed Abdullah. He was a Syed, a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad, and came of a Hasani and Hussaini family of religious scholars that counted Junaid Baghdadi, Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal and Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani among its kin. His father was himself a saint and a scholar who taught in Baghdad, and the son had his first education from him, memorising the Qur'an and then learning the knowledge of the soul and of the sect, seated in the same row as everyone else in his father's circle.

Having taken the outward sciences as far as they went, he judged that he must go in search of the hidden knowledge. In 562 AH, at about the age of thirty, he left Baghdad for Mecca, and he spent twelve years there in ascetic seclusion; from those years came his popular title, Makki, "of Mecca". He heard the pleas of those who came to him and helped them, and kept his nights in the Haram, the sacred mosque, in the remembrance of God. It is said that he received the blessing of the Prophet many times, and that he came to know what was to come but did not show it.

Tradition holds that his coming was by divine instruction. While he was worshipping in the Haram, it is said, he received the Prophet's command to go to Hind, where the people had fallen into associating partners with God, and to bring them back to the Sunna, the Prophet's way, and to the oneness of God. He did not wish to leave the House of God, but the command was the command. He made his last Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, took some companions with him, and turned first to Baghdad, to tell his family and to say the Fatiha, the opening chapter of the Qur'an, at his father's grave.

Two roads led to India, one through the dry desert and one by sea. The journey was long and dangerous, with little to eat or drink, but he preached along the way, and people were moved enough to join his caravan. After nearly a year he reached India and gave thanks.

He came to Lahore in 575 AH, around 1178 CE, and settled in the mosque that today carries his name beside his shrine. There he led the prayers, taught the Qur'an and called people away from polytheism. For some thirty six years, it is said, he taught both the outward sciences of Islamic law and the inward path of the Junaidi Sufi lineage, which traces back to the classical Baghdad master Junayd.

Accounts of who he was and of the year of his death have not always agreed. The shrine remembers him as Hazrat Syed Azizuddin of Baghdad, and the year it keeps for his death, 612 AH or 1215 CE, is the one most accounts give.

## The Shrine

Kings, it is said, maintained the shrine after him and added to its beauty, and in 1958 the Auqaf Department took charge of it. The adjoining Hazrat Pir Makki Masjid is the mosque in which the saint is said to have settled on reaching Lahore.

Accounts differ on exactly where the tomb stands. In the nineteenth century it lay at the southeastern corner of a garden called the Committee Bagh. A brick wall higher than a man enclosed it, and within it the saint's grave, built of brick and mortar, stood on a platform. There were two masonry wells, a platform marking a mosque, and a *ghusl-khana*, a bathing room.

In that century the keeper of the tomb was a woman *faqir*, one who has taken the Sufi path of poverty, and she had two sons, Fateh Din and Karam Din. The shrine also held cultivated land, free of revenue for as long as the *khanqah*, the Sufi lodge, should stand.

## Devotion and Festivals

The custom of paying respects at Peer Makki's tomb before going on to Data Darbar honours him as a spiritual forerunner in the same sacred place. On an ordinary day some 3,500 to 4,000 pilgrims come to his tomb, and the gatherings on Thursday nights draw larger crowds. The narrow street and the Peer Makki Bazaar around it can make the shrine hard to reach.

His annual *ʿurs* is held from the 9th to the 11th of Rabi-ul-Awal. It fills the quarter with gatherings and *dhikr*, the remembrance of God, with drums and *dhamal*, ecstatic devotional dancing to the beat of the drum, and with *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis. The shrine is ritually bathed and offerings are given out, and the festival draws on the order of 400,000 to 500,000 devotees.

In the nineteenth century, too, an *ʿurs* was held at the tomb, and *halwa*, a sweet, and *kheer*, a rice pudding, were served, though fewer people came then than in earlier days.

## Legends

A well loved story tells how the saint foretold the end of Khusrau Malik's rule in Lahore. Khusrau Malik, said to be the last of the line of Mahmud of Ghazni and the son of King Khusrau, is remembered as given to pleasure and unjust, and Muhammad Shahab-ud-Din Ghori, who had already taken Multan and Sialkot, was advancing on the city. When Khusrau Malik came to ask how long his rule would last, the saint told him plainly that it would soon end, that what God has written must come, and that he should turn to God and deal justly with his people.

When Ghori laid siege to Lahore in 1178, the king and the people alike ran to the saint for his prayers. He told them to be patient and to repent: the danger would pass, he said, and return in six years. Ghori withdrew, and the saint's name went round the city. But the people soon returned to their old ways, and exactly six years later Ghori came again. Once more the saint promised a respite, and said it would be the last, and once more the army turned back; this time people called him a liar, saying that the old man only ever said such things and that Ghori had left out of fear.

When Ghori at last took Lahore, Khusrau Malik's men were killed or went over to him, and the king himself was taken prisoner and later killed. Ghori, it is said, came to the saint's door and told him that he had known he was there, and that everything he had said had been true.

Devotion binds Peer Makki to his great neighbour, and traditions of the bond between the two saints differ. The one told at the shrine itself holds that when Ali Hujwiri, Data Ganj Bakhsh, was ordered to migrate to Lahore, he objected that "Peer Makki is present there, who is enough for Lahore", only to arrive and find Peer Makki's funeral already under way. The story fits loosely with the dates, for Hujwiri's death is conventionally placed around 1072, a century before Peer Makki's own arrival, and it should be understood as devotional tradition rather than strict chronology. But it carries the shrine's essential teaching: that Lahore has never been without a saint of Allah.

## The Setting

Bhati Gate is one of the twelve gates of Lahore's walled city. Lahore's Makki Gate is named for another man. Properly the Zaki Gate, it takes its name from Pir Zaki, a gate guard of Mughal times who was martyred at the gate, and the form Makki is said to be a corruption of Zaki; Pir Zaki is a different man from Peer Makki.

In Hujwiri's day Lahore was the Indian capital of the Ghaznavids, the house of Mahmud of Ghazni. Hujwiri reached the city around 1035, while Sultan Mas'ud I, who reigned from 1031 to 1041, ruled in Ghazna. Hujwiri died in Lahore, and his shrine is still a popular place of pilgrimage there. When the Ghurids drove Khusrau Shah, son of Bahram Shah, from Ghazni, he took Lahore, made it his capital and governed the Punjab until his death in 555 AH. His son, Sultan Khusrau Malik, succeeded him, and his rule in Lahore lasted twenty eight years. The Ghurids seized Multan in 1175, when Mu'izzu'd-Din Muhammad bin Sam established firm control and Sunni rule over the southern part of the Punjab.

The Ghurid sultan Shahab-ud-Din Ghori campaigned against Lahore more than once. In his third campaign the fort was nearly taken after siege and battle, and Khusrau Malik sent his son with an elephant as tribute and made peace. In the fifth the sultan besieged Lahore again; Khusrau Malik shut himself in the fort, and the city could not be mastered. In the sixth Khusrau Malik submitted and was taken to Ghazni, and the sultan set his own deputy over Lahore. With that surrender the rule of the Ghaznavids came to an end and that of the Ghurid sultans in Hind began; the Ghurids, it is said, took the land by a thousand tricks and deceits. Accounts of the years of these campaigns differ.

## Legacy

Many writers, among them, it is said at the shrine, authors from the Hindu and Christian communities, have written books about the saint that are still read with interest today. A detailed article on him, under the heading "Pir Makki", the name by which Lahore knows him, has been written for the *Danishnama-e Shibh-e Qarra*, an encyclopaedia of the Subcontinent published in Tehran. The shrine has kept its name and its place beside Data Darbar, and the quarter around it, with Peer Makki Bazaar and Pir Makki Street, carries the title Makki that his years in Mecca are said to have given him.

Name: Shrine of Pir Baba (Syed Ali Tirmizi)
Location: Pacha Kalay, Buner District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: 16th century (saint died 1583 CE; shrine developed thereafter)
Events: Annual urs (24-26 Rajab)
Description:
The Shrine of Pir Baba at Pacha Kalay, in the mountainous Buner District of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, honours *Syed Ali Tirmizi* (c. 1502–1583), the Sufi saint universally known as *Pir Baba*, one of the most revered holy figures of the Pashtun lands. Of *Sayyid* descent, he was traditionally said to have been born at Tirmiz in Central Asia (in present-day Uzbekistan) — though some accounts instead give Fergana as his birthplace — and, according to tradition, came to the region in the train of the Mughal advance, settling at Pacha in Buner around the middle of the sixteenth century. From there his spiritual influence spread widely, and he is remembered as a supporter of the early Mughals — the emperor Humayun is said to have granted him lands in Kunar — and as an opponent of the heterodox teacher Bayazid Ansari, the "Pir Roshan." A separate compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints, Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, gives his fuller name as Syed Ali Ghawwas Tirmizi and names Akhund Darweza — the Peshawar-based Chishti saint venerated at the Shrine of Akhund Darweza Baba elsewhere in this archive — as his most renowned khalifa (successor). His green-domed mausoleum, which also holds the grave of his son Syed Habibullah, became the nucleus of a devotional complex; an adjoining mosque was raised in the twentieth century, between about 1938 and 1965, under the care of his descendants. The shrine draws great crowds of pilgrims, above all at the annual *urs* commemorating the saint, held from 24 to 26 of the Islamic month of Rajab. Its prominence made it a target during the militancy that afflicted the region: in December 2008 militants attacked the shrine, destroying religious inscriptions and hoardings, and in 2009 it was briefly closed when Taliban fighters seized control of Buner, before being reopened as security was restored. It remains among the most important Sufi shrines of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Name: Shrine of Pir Chhatal Shah Noorani
Location: Near Naulung (Moola gorge), Gandava area, Jhal Magsi District, Balochistan, Pakistan
Events: Visited year-round by Muslim and Hindu pilgrims; no fixed urs recorded
Description:
The shrine of *Pir* Chhatal Shah Noorani stands at a spring-fed oasis near the mouth of the Moola gorge, where the Moola River shears clear across the Kirthar range to reach the Kachhi plain at Gandava, in the Jhal Magsi district of Balochistan. The point where the river debouches from the hills is known as *Naulung* ("Nine Fords") or, among the highland Baloch, *Punjmunh* ("Five Mouths"); for thousands of years this was the most convenient passage between the Indus valley and the Kalat uplands. The site is celebrated for a small, clear pond, fed by a copious spring bursting from the rock, that teems with large *mahseer* fish. By long tradition the fish were the saint's pets and no one has ever eaten them; local lore holds that any fish caught and cooked would emerge again alive, a taboo that has in effect made the pond one of the oldest fish-conservation sanctuaries in the region. Chhatal Shah Noorani is remembered as a granter of wishes to whom Hindus and Muslims alike came to have their hearts' desires fulfilled. The tomb sits on a low knoll: in 1831 the traveller Charles Masson (James Lewis) recorded it as a conspicuous *gumbaz*, or domed building, that served as the usual halting-place for caravans crossing between Kalat and Kachhi, though the dome has since collapsed and the grave now stands within plain modern walls. In recent years improved access has turned the once-remote spot into a popular picnic destination. Salman Rashid, who first visited the site in 2003, described the pond as "teeming with mahseer fish, nearly 60 cm long," and recorded a keeper's own account of the saint's identity: asked who Chhatal Shah Noorani had been, the man replied simply, "Only Allah knows!" — adding only that he was "a granter of wishes" to Hindus and Muslims alike. The Jhal Magsi district government's own heritage listing independently confirms the shrine, naming it among the district's principal shrines and placing it "near Kotra."

Name: Shrine of Pir Lakha (Aab-e-Shifa), Jhal Magsi
Location: Near Kotra (Moola gorge area), Jhal Magsi District, Balochistan, Pakistan
Events: Year-round pilgrimage; ritual bathing in the hot springs
Description:
The shrine of Pir Lakha lies in the north-western uplands of the Jhal Magsi District of Balochistan, in the broken country near Kotra where the Moola river descends through its gorge — the same tract that holds the shrine of Pir Chhatal Shah Noorani (a separate entry in this dataset). District heritage listings count Pir Lakha among the principal shrines of Jhal Magsi, alongside the *dargahs* of Rakhyal Shah at Fatehpur and Muhammad Ayub Shah Bukhari at Gandava. Its particular fame rests less on a documented saintly biography — of which little is recorded — than on the hot springs beside it, known as *Aab-e-Shifa*, "the water of healing." Pilgrims travel from far-flung parts of Balochistan and Sindh to bathe in these thermal waters, which are believed to cure skin ailments and other afflictions, so that the site functions at once as a shrine and as a place of folk therapeutics. Like several shrines of the Kachhi–Gandava plain, it draws Muslim and Hindu visitors alike. Because the life of the eponymous *pir* is essentially undocumented in accessible sources, only the shrine's living role as a pilgrimage-and-healing centre can be stated with confidence. This listing is independently confirmed by the Jhal Magsi district government's own Culture & Heritage page, which names "Pir Lakha" both as a page heading and among the district's main shrines. That official listing, however, does not mention the Aab-e-Shifa hot springs at all; no citable source consulted for this entry corroborates the healing-spring claim that gives the site its popular name, which currently rests only on social-media and blog accounts.

Name: Shrine of Pir Mangho
Events: Annual urs; Sheedi Mela (drumming, dance, offerings to the crocodiles)
Description:
## Overview

Mangho Pir, on the northern outskirts of Karachi, is one of the most unusual and atmospheric shrines in Pakistan. It is famous for three things that meet nowhere else: a medieval Sufi saint, a pool of sacred crocodiles, and hot sulphur springs believed to heal. The *darbar*, or shrine, of Pir Mangho, Hazrat Haji Syed Sakhi Sultan, is a centre of pilgrimage of great antiquity. It is bound up with the culture of Karachi's Sheedi community, Afro-Pakistanis of East African descent, whose annual festival at the shrine is one of the city's most distinctive traditions.

## The Saint

The saint of Mangho Pir is remembered as a holy man of the medieval centuries who settled at this spot in the hills above Karachi. A *pir* is a Sufi spiritual guide, a master of the mystical path of Islam. Accounts differ over whom the shrine honours; it is known as the shrine of Pir Mangho, Hazrat Haji Syed Sakhi Sultan. The titles in that name carry meanings: *Hazrat* is a respectful title for a holy person, a *Haji* is one who has made the pilgrimage to Mecca, a *Syed* is a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad, and *Sakhi* means the generous one.

To one man, speaking of the big Sheedi gathering at the shrine, he was "the pir of the crocodiles".

## The Shrine

Below the tomb lies a pond inhabited by crocodiles. They are held sacred and cared for by the shrine's attendants, and the eldest and largest of them is honoured with the title *Mor Sahib*. Pilgrims make offerings of meat, for the crocodiles are believed to be under the saint's protection, and their favour is taken as a sign of blessing.

Nearby, hot sulphur springs rise from the earth. Bathing in their waters is believed to cure skin ailments and other diseases, so that the shrine is a place of healing as much as of prayer. The springs are a natural phenomenon, one of several thermal sites along the same anticline as Chandrakup, an anticline being an upward fold in the layers of rock.

The shrine stands in the hills above Karachi, in what is now the northern part of the city. Mangho Pir is also the name of the locality, which was home to a leper asylum.

## Devotion and Festivals

Mangho Pir holds a special place for the Sheedi community of Karachi, the descendants of Africans brought to the subcontinent over the centuries. The Sheedis regard the saint as their own and the shrine as a spiritual home. Their annual *Sheedi Mela*, the Sheedi fair, with its drumming, dance and offerings to the sacred crocodiles, is a vivid survival of African rooted culture in Pakistan and one of the most striking festivals of Karachi, binding the shrine to a living community and its heritage.

The festival falls in April. Sheedis come to it from all over, it is a large gathering, and it draws wide coverage in the press.

The shrine also keeps an annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death.

## Legends

Tradition weaves the crocodiles and the springs into the miracles of the saint himself.

The springs have a place in Hindu tradition too. In the narratives of the Kapri community, Lalu Jasraj is the founder of the Kapris, and the guide and staff bearer of Rama, the hero of the Ramayana, and of his entourage. It is said that Lalu Jasraj stayed at a hermitage near the hot springs, and that story has led to the suggestion that the shrine was once associated with him, an association that would tie the shrine to the Hindu pilgrimage to Hinglaj. This is a possibility, not an established fact, and how widely the Lalu Jasraj stories are told outside the Kapri community of Gujarat is open to question.

## The Setting

The Sheedis, also known as Sidi or Syedi in Sindh and Gujarat, were first brought from Africa as slaves to work in the subcontinent. They came to Sindh continuously through the ages, and in large numbers because of the slave trade, and in Sindh too they were set free when slavery was abolished. Though free, some of them are attached to the feudal households of Sindh, and their native language is Sindhi. The Sheedis of Sindh and Kacch claim descent from Hazrat Bilal, a companion of the Prophet Muhammad.

The drumming of the Sheedi festival has its context in the community's music and ritual. The Sheedi drum, the *mugarmān*, is held sacred by Sheedi communities in Sindh, Baluchistan, Rajasthan and Gujarat, who use it in their shrines and for their rituals. In Sindh the Sheedis and the Manganhar musicians perform the ceremonial singing of devotional narratives, and Sheedi women perform ritual music in the households of the province.

Karachi itself is one of two important urban centres of Sufism, with Hyderabad in India, where members of the Qawwal Bachche lineage keep up their own heritage of *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis. After the annual fair of three days at Sehwan, *fakirs*, wandering Sufi mystics, follow one another on to the shrines of Karachi. A legend tells how the city got its name: the area was known after an old woman, Mai Kolachi, whose son was killed by a fish; she tore the fish apart and retrieved him, and the place came to be known as Kolachi. At the time of Partition, the division of British India, Karachi was a minor port city, and migrants from India made it the largest city of Pakistan.

Karachi is also the starting point of the road to Hinglaj, the Hindu pilgrimage route of about 240 kilometres from Narayanpur. The growth of the city and the urbanisation of the areas where the early stops lay have caused all but a few of the pilgrims' resting places along it to disappear.

## Legacy

Pir Mangho is unlike any other shrine in Pakistan: a place where Sufi devotion, a pool of sacred crocodiles, healing sulphur springs and the African descended culture of the Sheedis come together. Ancient, strange and beloved, the *darbar* remains a centre of pilgrimage, healing and festival on the edge of the great city, and a monument to the many strands that weave through the popular religion of Sindh, among them, it has been suggested, a link to the Hindu pilgrimage to Hinglaj.

Name: Shrine of Pir Sher Muhammad
Events: Annual urs; naat and qawwali; daily langar
Description:
## Overview

At Sharaqpur Sharif, north-west of Lahore, stands the shrine of Hazrat Mian Pir Sher Muhammad Sharaqpuri (1865 to 1928), a widely revered Sufi master of the Qadiri and Chishti traditions and one of the notable saints of the Punjab in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Known for his piety, his learning and the great number of disciples he guided, Pir Sher Muhammad made Sharaqpur a centre of devotion and religious teaching. His darbar, or shrine, remains an important place of pilgrimage in central Punjab.

## The Saint

Mian Sher Muhammad was born in 1865 at Sharaqpur into a devout family, and from his youth he turned to the religious sciences and the Sufi path. Trained both in the outward learning of the seminary and in the inward discipline of the Sufi orders, he became a spiritual guide of great reputation. He united the lineages of two Sufi orders, the Qadiri, founded by ʿAbd al-Qadir Gilani, and the Chishti, and drew disciples from across the Punjab and beyond.

He was among the teachers whose light shaped the next generation of Punjabi Sufis. The saint Abul Faiz Qalandar Ali Suhrawardi of Lahore, for instance, is remembered as having received knowledge from him. Pir Sher Muhammad is remembered for a life of prayer, austerity and service, and for the reforming, sober devotion he taught. He died in 1928 and was buried at Sharaqpur.

## The Shrine

The shrine of Pir Sher Muhammad at Sharaqpur Sharif is a large complex kept by his successors, and a busy centre of pilgrimage. It maintains the five daily prayers, gatherings of *naat*, poetry in praise of the Prophet, and of *qawwali*, Sufi devotional music, and the free kitchen. Its annual *ʿurs*, the commemoration of the anniversary of the saint's death, draws great crowds of devotees who come to honour the saint and seek his blessing.

The town of Sharaqpur Sharif takes its very identity from the darbar, and the saint's line has continued as its custodians and as respected religious figures.

## The Setting

Sharaqpur is also the burial place of an earlier saint, Shaikh Muhammad Saeed Chishti Sabri Sharaqpuri, a Chishti Sabiri of the same town. He is not the saint of this shrine: he died in 1214 AH, by the Islamic calendar, and his death and Pir Sher Muhammad's fall more than a century apart.

Sharaqpur has its place in the history of books as well. A work called the *Khazina-e Marifat*, by Muhammad Ibrahim Qasuri, was printed there, and a manuscript of Lal Beg Lali's *Thamarat al-Quds*, a work dating from after 1017 AH, has been held at Sharaqpur in the possession of Maulana Nusrat Naushahi of Sharaqpur. Rani Jindan gave Bhai Budh Singh a *jagir*, a grant of land revenue, in the Sharaqpur area to feed travellers at the *samadhi*, the memorial, of Jawahar Singh.

In the Sikh period no printed book came into the Punjab from Hindustan, and scribes copied books by hand for sale. The British conquest of the Punjab in the 1840s laid new patterns of modernity over the literary culture of the Sufi tradition: Persian gave way to Urdu and English, and publishers in Lahore brought the older Sufi poetry into print. The lyrics of the Punjab's Sufi poets were for the most part collected in printed form only in the late nineteenth century. By the 1880s Lahore was the capital of the province of the Punjab, where the Lieutenant-Governor held his court.

In the Punjab after 1800 the literary heritage of Panjabi was rarely continued by Muslims, who turned to Urdu, though in the twentieth century a number of mystical treatises were written and published in Panjabi. British policy, especially in the Punjab and Sind, was to treat the hereditary saints in essentially the same way as landlords and tribal leaders were treated. In the countryside of Punjab and Sindh, in many cases, the local *pir*, the Sufi spiritual guide, represents the local landlord or is at least closely related to him.

In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries the British connected the five rivers of the Punjab with each other through canals, turning jungle land into agricultural land. Thousands of new villages were founded, and farming families from all over the Punjab were invited to settle. In the early twentieth century Muhammad Ilyas, founder of the Tableeghi Jamaat, worked in undivided rural Punjab, exhorting Muslims to "purify" their religious practices, which he argued were corrupted by the influence of the dominant Hindu culture.

## The Sufi Orders in the Punjab

Both of the orders in which Pir Sher Muhammad stood had spread in the Punjab before his time. The first of the Qadiri line to come to the Punjab was Hazrat Sayyid Muhammad Ghaus Uchi Jili Gilani, Sayyid Muhammad Ghaus of Uch. His ancestors had left Baghdad in the time of Hulagu Khan, and he came by way of Khurasan to Multan and settled at Uch. In the time of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith, the Qadiris had made the Punjab the main centre of their activities. Another Sufi way, the Naushahi, began with Hazrat Naushah Ganj Bakhsh, and by the 1870s its *faqirs*, wandering Sufis, numbered in the thousands in the Punjab.

The Chishti order spread in Hind and the Punjab from Khwaja Muin al-Din Hasan Sijzi, and it is usually considered one of the most powerful Sufi orders in Northern India and the Punjab. The Nizami Chishtis came to prominence in the eighteenth century, principally in Delhi, the Deccan and the Punjab, through masters who were related to local political leaders but in tension with them. The order's Nizami Fakhri branch spread in the Punjab chiefly through Khwaja Sulaiman Taunsvi, who consolidated the order by stressing learning through the establishment of institutions: the academy at Taunsa and other religious schools throughout the Punjab. In the nineteenth century the Nizami branch of Chishti Sufism expanded in the upper Punjab through his disciples.

The Muslim conquest of northern India carried the Persianate world to the Punjab, where Persian remained the dominant literary language of the ruling elite through the Mughal period and beyond, and a strong Sufi presence was quickly established there with the coming of figures of the main Sufi orders. As one historian has observed, "Islam took root much more readily in Bengal or the Punjab than in upper India".

## Devotion and Poetry in the Punjab

The qawwali tunes of the Punjab are distinguished from those of Uttar Pradesh by their rhythm, since they tend to be organised according to stress, and the name Qalandar continues to be intoned in the popular qawwali lyrics of the Punjab. *Dhammal* is the vigorous ritual dance performed at Sufi shrines in the Punjab and Sind. The writing of *taʿwidh*, amulets, for the people has not changed since the thirteenth century: the successors of Baba Farid and his assistants, in common with those of other shrines in the Punjab, continue to write *taʿwidh* for the masses. The Punjab and Sind have also produced hymns extolling the great masters of the mystical orders, particularly ʿAbd al-Qadir Gilani.

In 1292 AH Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori completed *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, a book on the saints of the Punjab, and his son, Mufti Ghulam Safdar Lahori, marked the year with a chronogram, a verse written to record a date, on the book's subject:

جو خدا کے دوست تھے پنجاب میں
حال ان کا اس سے ہوتا ہے عیان

The Punjabi poet Waris Shah opens his *Hir and Ranjha* with an invocation that praises Baba Farid of Pakpattan:

*When Shakarganj made his abode at Pakpattan, the Punjab was delivered of all its troubles.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

In the epilogue, where he dates his poem to 1180 Hijri, he laments the disorder of the country and turns to a single town:

*Of all the wretched Punjab I am most concerned for Kasur.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

The Sufi poet Bulleh Shah's verse speaks of the Punjab of the eighteenth century in the same troubled terms:

*The door of doom and torment has opened, and Panjab is in a bad state. It has been struck by fear of the pit of hell.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

Another of his poems runs:

*Now hell has opened its bogs. / Punjab has gone to the dogs. / This hell is the nethermost hell.* (translated by Taufiq Rafat)

## Legacy

Pir Sher Muhammad Sharaqpuri is remembered as one of the influential Sufi masters of modern Punjab, a guide of many thousands whose teaching joined the Qadiri and Chishti ways and whose disciples carried his influence onward. His shrine at Sharaqpur Sharif remains a centre of the devotion he inspired, and his memory endures among the notable saints of the Lahore region.

## Bibliography

- General established histories of the Qadiri-Chishti tradition in modern Punjab.
- Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya* (Persian, composed 1292 AH / 1875 CE; read in an Urdu edition annotated by محمد اقبال مجددی and issued by تصوّف فاؤنڈیشن).
- Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* (dated 1867 for the original, the date unconfirmed).
- Kanhaiya Lal Hindi, *Tarikh-e Lahore* (1884 original).

- Carl W. Ernst and Bruce B. Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love: Chishti Sufism in South Asia and Beyond* (2002).
- Michel Boivin, *The Hindu Sufis of South Asia: Partition, Shrine Culture and the Sindhis in India* (London and New York: I.B. Tauris / Bloomsbury Publishing Plc, first published 2019).

- Robert Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound: Politics and Piety in Twenty-First Century Pakistan* (2007).
- Pnina Werbner and Helene Basu (eds.), *Embodying Charisma: Modernity, Locality and the Performance of Emotion in Sufi Cults* (1998).

Name: Shrine of Qalandar Baba Auliya
Events: Annual urs
Description:
## Overview

In Karachi lies the shrine of Hazrat Qalandar Baba Auliya — Sayyid Muhammad Azeem Barkhiya (1898–1979) — a modern Sufi master and the founder of the Azeemia Sufi order. Unusual among the saints for the intellectual character of his teaching, Qalandar Baba Auliya sought to present the inner science of Sufism in a form intelligible to the modern mind, and through his order and his writings his influence has spread widely in Pakistan and abroad. His darbar is a contemporary shrine and the centre of a living Sufi movement.

## The Life of the Saint

Muhammad Azeem was born in 1898 at Khurja, in the United Provinces of British India, into a Sayyid family, and is known by the spiritual title *Qalandar Baba Auliya*. After the creation of Pakistan he settled in Karachi. He is remembered as a saint of deep contemplative attainment who devoted himself to expounding the inner realities of the Sufi path — the science of the soul, of thought, and of the unseen — and to guiding disciples. His best-known work, *Loh-o-Qalam* (“The Tablet and the Pen”), sets out his teaching on metaphysics and the workings of the mind and spirit, and is studied as a foundational text by his followers. He died in 1979 and was buried in Karachi, where his shrine arose.

## The Azeemia Order

Qalandar Baba Auliya’s lasting legacy is the Azeemia Sufi order, which he founded and which was carried on and spread by his foremost disciple, Khwaja Shamsuddin Azeemi. The order is distinctive for its emphasis on the systematic teaching of Sufi inner science — meditation, spiritual healing, and the understanding of consciousness — presented in a modern idiom, and it has established centres in Pakistan and among the diaspora. The shrine in Karachi is the spiritual centre of this living movement, a place of both devotion and study.

## Legacy

Qalandar Baba Auliya represents the continuation of the Sufi tradition into the twentieth century and its meeting with the modern world — a saint who framed the ancient inner science of the mystics for contemporary seekers, and founded an order that carries his teaching still. His shrine in Karachi is at once a place of pilgrimage and the heart of the Azeemia order he brought into being.

## Bibliography

- Qalandar Baba Auliya, *Loh-o-Qalam* — the saint's principal work.
- Established histories of the Azeemia Sufi order (and the writings of Khwaja Shamsuddin Azeemi).

Name: Shrine of Sachal Sarmast
Events: Annual urs; poetry, music and dhamal
Description:
## Overview

At Daraza, near Ranipur in the Khairpur district of northern Sindh, lies the shrine of Sachal Sarmast (1739 to 1826), "the Truthful, the Intoxicated One", one of the boldest and most beloved of the Sufi poets of Sindh. Where Shah Abdul Latif is the serene ocean of Sindhi mysticism, Sachal is its ecstatic fire: a poet of dazzling daring who sang the unity of being in seven languages, and who was called, for the reckless intensity of his verse, the *Second Mansur*, after Mansur al-Hallaj, martyred for crying "I am the Truth". His shrine at Daraza is a major centre of Sindhi devotion and music, and his poetry is sung across Sindh and among Sindhi Hindus in India.

Daraza lies not far from Khairpur, and its *dargah*, the Sufi shrine complex, is counted among the remarkable sanctuaries of the country around Rohri, Sukkur and Shikarpur. With Lal Shahbaz Qalandar at Sehwan Sharif and Tando Jahaniyya in Hyderabad, Daraza is one of the three main Sufi traditions of Sindh. As a Sufi poet Sachal has been placed second only to Shah Abdul Latif, and in the 1970s his melodies and words were still almost as popular as they had been a century and a half before.

## The Saint

Sachal Sarmast was born in 1739 at Daraza into a Sayyid family of the Farooqi line; Sayyids are descendants of the Prophet Muhammad. His given name was Abdul Wahab, which is also given in a longer form as Khwaja Salah al-Din Ḥafiẓ Abd al-Wahhab. He became known as *Sachal*, "the truthful", and *Sarmast*, "the intoxicated" or "the ecstatic". *Sachal* is a diminutive of *sach*, truth, and seems to allude to the word *Haqq*, the Truth, in Hallaj's saying *anā'l-ḥaqq*, "I am the Truth"; *Sarmast* marks him as an intoxicated Sufi, or Muslim mystic.

His father died when he was young, and he was raised and initiated by his uncle and spiritual guide, Khwaja Abdul Haq. A versatile mystic who led a solitary life, he spent almost all his years in his native Daraza, rarely travelling, absorbed in devotion and song.

The best remembered story of his childhood is his meeting with the great Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, and it is told as a legend. When the boy was about seven, it is said, Shah Abdul Latif came to pay homage to the local *murshid*, the spiritual guide, and on seeing Sachal exclaimed: "This God-gifted child will one day uncover those divine secrets which I have still kept concealed." The meeting is cherished as the passing of a torch from one master of Sindhi verse to the next. Sachal, Shah Abdul Latif's younger contemporary, took up his tradition and developed it.

He was also an admiring contemporary of the Punjabi poet Bulleh Shah of Kasur, and avowedly his follower, and he continued to send his disciples to Amritsar for homage. His own spiritual heir in verse was Bedil of Rohri.

Another legend tells of an attempt on his life: the swords, it is said, passed through his body as if it were water. He lived to a great age. Accounts of the year of his death differ; it is most often given as 1826.

## The Poetry

Sachal Sarmast poured out poetry in a remarkable range of tongues. Accounts of how many languages he wrote in differ, but he bears the title *Shair-e-Haft-Zaban*, the poet of seven languages: Sindhi and Seraiki above all, and also Urdu, Persian, Punjabi, Balochi and Arabic. He uttered whatever came into his heart with no thought for the consequences. His Persian and Urdu poetry is traditional and conventional in style, but in his mother tongue his feeling overpowers him. Like the poets before him, he relied on folk tales and made their heroines, Sohni among them, his own, though he did not elaborate these subjects as much as Shah Abdul Latif did.

His theme, sung with unrestrained ardour, was *wahdat al-wujud*, the unity of being, and the annihilation of the self in the divine reality. His verse breaks fearlessly through the forms of orthodoxy towards a naked declaration of union with the Beloved, and his ecstatic poetry surpassed all limits of expression. In Shah Abdul Latif's poetry, allusions and subtle images lead the understanding listener into the secrets of love, longing and union; in Sachal's poems the mysteries of the all embracing Unity are put openly before the listener.

It was this that won him the name of the *Second Mansur*, for like al-Hallaj he sang the identity of the lover and the Beloved without disguise. Shah Abdul Latif only covertly alludes to Hallaj's famous saying, *anā'l-ḥaqq*; Sachal, like Bulleh Shah, invoked it directly. His love for Hallaj was ardent, and Hallaj's name occurs hundreds of times in his verses. Hallaj's ideas lived on under the surface and broke out now and then in ecstatic utterance, in Sarmad, in Shah Abdul Latif and in Sachal, until Muhammad Iqbal brought them once more into a fascinating system.

Sachal has also been called the ʿAttar of Sindh, and the influence of ʿAttar's imagery is clearly visible in his poetry. He drew on the *hadith*, the sayings of the Prophet, inserting them into his poetry in various forms and with very outspoken preferences of his own, and in one of these sayings he found proof of his ecstatic experience of union with God and of God's all embracing Unity. He is among the heirs of the image of the Beloved who dwells within the heart. Why should one roam about the marketplaces to search for the friend, he asks: the friend is in the heart, and He whom heaven and earth cannot contain is the guest in the narrow hut of man's purified heart.

His verse often recalls the enthusiastic folk songs of the medieval Turkish mystics, such as Yunus Emre, who died in 1321; one could almost translate a Sindhi poem of his into Turkish and take it for an original verse by Yunus. With the Punjabi Bulleh Shah, he is the most typical voice of those poets who, in their highly ecstatic songs, identify themselves with everything created.

Krishna, the Hindu god, is important to the Sindhi Sufis, Muslim Sufis such as Sachal and Qutub Ali Shah among them, and Sachal, like Qutub Ali Shah and Bedil, brings Krishna into his Sufi poetry. He and Shah Abdul Latif have been called late participants in the Bhakti movement, the Hindu devotional movement that had a major impact in Sindh through the spread of Guru Nanak's teaching.

A line he repeats more than once sets the wine of Mansur against the *Kanz* and the *Quduri*, handbooks studied in the *madrasa*, the religious school:

*Intoxication came from the wine of this Mansur-dom, Kanz and Quduri became annihilated!*

Elsewhere he says the same of those who have tasted love:

*Those who have tasted a sip from the syrup of the ocean of love* … *They say goodbye to syntax, and don't look any more at grammar!*

His spiritual heir, Bedil of Rohri, took up the same theme:

*The ordinary men read Kanz Quduri, the lovers wisdom from God* (translated by Annemarie Schimmel)

Where Shah Abdul Latif is more careful and less outspoken in his allusions, Sachal loved to name, one by one, those killed by their overwhelming divine love. A Sindhi poem of his begins:

*Welcome, welcome You are-- / to which place will You bring me? / You will again cut off a head! / Giving a kick to Sarmad You have killed him,* (translated by Annemarie Schimmel)

The poem goes on that the Beloved brought Mansur to the gallows and cut off the head of Shaikh ʿAttar, and it closes: "Now You are asking the way here!" To these generally known Sufis, Sachal adds the names of martyred Indian religious heroes, such as Sarmad, the friend of Dara Shikoh, and he speaks too of Shah ʿInayat of Jhok. His litany of afflicted lovers counts among the slain Bulleh Shah, Jaʿfar, Sarmad, Mansur, Shaikh ʿAttar, Zakariya, Joseph, Shams, Sanʿan, Karmal and Bilawal, and Shah ʿInayat, the martyred mystic of Jhok. He also left a riddle on the self that opens "Perhaps I am".

He wrote a political poem as well. Its speaker has seen a boat in midstream whose expert oarsmen consider themselves the rulers of the ocean and think nothing of Sindh and India:

*They are a proud people and consider themselves rulers but they are nothing but plunderers. Whenever they get the chance they take the goods of others by force. Yet the local people put a lot of trust in them...*

His poems are sung by the *faqirs*, the mystics, of his shrine and by folk singers across Sindh, and their ecstatic boldness has made him a patron of all who prize love over law and truth over caution.

## The Shrine

Sachal Sarmast's shrine at Daraza is ornamented in the glazed blue tilework of Sindh. It is a busy centre of pilgrimage and, above all, of music: the singing of his poetry, often to the beat that stirs the *dhamal*, the ecstatic devotional dance, is central to its devotion, and the shrine keeps his memory as the ecstatic voice of Sindhi Sufism. On the main gate of the *dargah* is written the inscription *haqq mawjud*, "the Truth is present".

On a wall at Daraza hangs the "official" picture of Sachal. It is said to have been drawn by a Sikh follower of his. It shows him in majesty, in a pose that could recall the iconography of Guru Nanak, seated on a *gaddi*, the cushioned seat of a spiritual master, with a club in his right hand and a musical instrument in his left.

Daraza also holds the remains of Hindu Sufis. Nimano Faqir, a Hindu Sufi, was cremated, but his ashes were laid in a tomb in the *dargah* compound, near the tomb of Sachal Sarmast. A woman who died in 1963 was cremated, and her ashes were carried to Daraza, where they were buried in a grave close to Sachal Sarmast.

Daraza has its own line of masters, its *sajjada nashins*, the successors who sit on the saint's prayer carpet. For generations they have borne the honorific title *Sakhi*, the generous; the name is given to the Sufi masters of Daraza in general, but it designates Sachal Sarmast above all. Pir Khwaja Abd al-Haqq II (1915 to 1978) was the new *sajjada nashin* of Daraza when, in 1956, he made a visit to consecrate the spiritual authority of Nimano Faqir. Nimano Faqir's own master was a Sakhi Qabul Muhammad of Daraza, a *murshid* of Sachal's *dargah*, nicknamed Sakhi Darazi. In the early twenty first century the *sajjada nashin* of Daraza was Sakhi Qabul Muhammad Faruqi.

## Devotion and Festivals

The annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, draws great crowds from across Sindh for days of poetry, music and celebration in the exuberant Sindhi manner, alongside the rites of prayer and remembrance. The *ʿurs* falls on the 14th of Ramazan, and since it follows the Islamic calendar, its date changes every year in the Christian calendar and in the Hindu calendar, the Vikram Samvat. In the years before the late 1960s the Sindhi publications of the state regularly featured Sachal Sarmast, with Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai and Shah Inayat, and marked their annual fairs with special editions.

The singer Abida Parvin sings his verse. She is able to sing the poetry of Shah Abdul Latif and Sachal Sarmast in Sindhi, which her male counterparts among the *qawwals*, the singers of devotional Sufi music, cannot.

His following reached beyond Muslims. Daraza and Jhok were the two main Sufi traditions that were very popular among the Hindus, and Sachal had a large number of followers among the Hindu trade castes of northern Sindh. When they migrated in the wake of Partition, some of them carried their love for singing his poetry to India.

## Daraza Across the Border

In India those followers kept the name of Daraza. The Daraza school of Sufism still attracts many Hindu Sindhis there, and in Mumbai and Ulhasnagar they have organised Darazi *satsangs*, gatherings for devotional singing, to sing Sachal Sarmast's *kalam*, his poetry. Sachal is the model case of a Sindhi Sufi carried by a Hindu path without any formal tie to it, and his poetry is sung in all the Sufi *darbars*, the shrines, of India. Other Sufi poets too have claimed to be Darazi, among them a Hindu *faqir* who took the name into his own, Faqir Radhakrishin Lal Sahib Darazi, whose *Kalam* was printed at Ulhasnagar in 1986.

The spiritual masters of the Hindu Sufi lineages of India are still in Sindh. They are the *sajjada nashins* of Daraza, of Tando Jahaniya and of Jhok Sharif, and to each a great Sufi poet is attached: Sachal Sarmast, Qutub Ali Shah and Nasir Faqir.

Two *darbars* devoted to Sachal Sarmast stand in the same area of Ulhasnagar, Camp 5. At one of them, the Maqbul Manzil, only a weekly rite is held: every Thursday, from seven until nine in the evening, a Darazi *satsang* meets under the supervision of Soni Kataria. It opens with an *arti*, the Hindu rite of worship with lamps, which nothing distinguishes from the *arti* of any Hindu temple. Then the devotees sing Sachal's *kalam*, one playing the harmonium and another the *tablas*, the hand drums, with Soni as the leading singer; she knows the verses by heart. About twenty people attend. The *darbar* has passed down a family: Hari Ram took charge of it and of singing Sachal's poetry, and after him his daughter Soni led the *satsang* every Thursday evening.

The tie to Daraza is kept by its master in Sindh. The *sajjada nashin* of Daraza has paid three visits to the *darbar*, and it is he who gives the date of Sachal's *versi*, the yearly death anniversary: Soni calls him, or he calls her, by telephone, so that he can tell her its timing. In India Sachal's *versi* is celebrated on the 14th of Ramazan and Hari Ram's at the beginning of November, while at the Sachal Sain *darbar* the two *versis* celebrated are Sachal's and Pratap's.

In the Rohani Rah, whose name means the spiritual path, the core of worship is a *murti*, a statue, of Sachal Sarmast, carved after the official picture that hangs at Daraza; the only difference is that in the statue Sachal has a golden *tilak*, the sacred mark, on his forehead. Above the *murti* is Krishna as a flute player, without Radha, and higher still the *darbar* of Sachal Sarmast at Daraza. At the Radha Krishin Lal *darbar* it is the other way: at the core of the altar is a photograph of a master of Daraza, Sakhi Qabul Muhammad, instead of a representation of Sachal, though the whole set of pictures is dominated by an inscription in the Latin alphabet, "Sai Sachal". Asked why it was Sakhi and not Sachal, Soni answered that Sakhi is the one who looks most like Sachal.

His verse is the core of these gatherings' song. Their repertoire consists mainly of works by Sachal and Nimano, and *kalams* by Sindhi Sufis such as Sachal are still sung every day at Nimano Faqir's shrine. At the *versi* of Dadi Dhan in 2012, Sachal Sarmast was the most requested poet, followed by Rochaldas; the *versi* of Daulatram was kept with the chanting of Sufi songs by Sachal Sarmast, Shah Abdul Latif and Qutub Ali Shah; and Mira Rajani used to sing Sachal's poetry during the *satsang*. Hindu teachers drew on him as well: Mulchand quotes Sachal's poetry in his explanation of *om*, the sacred syllable, and Rochaldas quotes verses from Kabir, Bedil, Sachal and Ajiz.

In some places his presence has waned. Sachal stood at the origin of the Sakhi Kuthiyya, founded by Nimano Faqir in Baroda, later Vadodara. Its name means something like the abode of the generous, and it referred to the original *dargah* in Sindh and to its spiritual head. Yet in Vadodara Sachal has declined, and Nimano now stands at the forefront. In the Nimanal Sangam the reference to Sachal has even been suppressed, and the 2011 Vadodara edition of Nimano Faqir's verse leaves out Sachal's poetry, which had a large part in Nimano's original *kalam*, while keeping Guru Nanak's. Even so, Nimano Faqir's verses still embodied the very spirit of Sindhi Sufism, and especially that of the Darazi *silsila*, the Sufi lineage of Daraza.

## The Setting

Daraza lies in the Khairpur country of northern Sindh. After 1857 many Kayasht, a Hindu community of scribes, migrated to work in the princely states, among them the Khairpur emirate. The amirs of Khairpur were themselves staunch Shia Muslims, and in the nineteenth century they built beautiful *imambaras*, halls for the Shia rites of mourning, but that did not prevent them from being generous patrons of all religious buildings.

Seraiki, the northern dialect of Sindhi, is mostly spoken in northern Sindh, and especially among its Baluchi population. Many Sindhi Sufi poets, especially from northern Sindh, composed Sufi poetry in several languages, and many of the later ones, mainly those of Baloch origin, also used Seraiki. The Sufis to whom the Hindus of Sindh look mostly belong to Upper Sindh, where Seraiki is used for Sufi poetry besides Sindhi. In Sindh, Hallaj, the figure at the centre of Sachal's verse, is very popular, and many Sufi poets mention his name in their verses.

## Legacy

With Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, Sachal Sarmast is one of the two great poet saints of Sindh, the intoxicated counterpart to Bhittai's sublime serenity, and among the most fearless voices of *wahdat al-wujud* in all of South Asian Sufism. His multilingual verse, his ecstatic sincerity and his refusal of every veil between the soul and God have kept him beloved for two centuries, and his shrine at Daraza remains a living hearth of the Sindhi Sufi song he raised to such heights. As one scholar of Islamic mysticism put it, "none of the later mystical poets can match Sachal's intense glow; he is a vigorous poet, and the rhythms and energy, the intense yearning and love, give his verses an almost magical quality."

He has been named, with Shah Inayat and Shah Abdul Latif, among the three great Sufi teachers, and counted the second of the trinity of the Sindhi poets. In anthologies of Sindhi Sufi verse he stands at or near the head. One opens with Sachal Sarmast, with forty six extracts from his Sindhi poetry; in Vaswani's anthology of 1955 the Muslim Sufis begin with Shah Abdul Latif, followed by Rohal, Murad, Sachal and Bedil; and another book focuses on Shah Latif and Sachal.

A body of scholarship has grown around him. Jethmal Parsram wrote a book on him in 1922. A work titled *Sachal Sarmast*, under the name of an Agha Sufi, dates from 1933, and by 1940 a large edition of his poetry had appeared. One woman edited his Sindhi *kalam* in 1955, and was herself the author of a Sindhi *kalam* with the title *Haqq mawjud*, the same words that are written on the shrine's main gate. Abd al-Karim Sindilo published a glossary of his poetry, *Lughat-e Sachal*, at Khairpur in 1984, from the Sachal Chair of Shah Abdul Latif University; Ram Panjwani published a book on his poetry, *Sachal jyun kafiyun*; and in 2002 the Culture and Tourism Department of the Government of Sindh published a *Study of Mysticism in Darazi School of Sufi Thought* by Dr. Sakhi Qabool Muhammad Faruqi.

His verse has been printed in Sindhi, Seraiki and Persian. The Sindhi Adabi Board published a Sindhi *Risalo*, a collection of his poems, at Karachi in 1958, edited by Othman Ali Ansari, and a Seraiki *Kalam* edited by Maulwi Hakim Muhammad Sadiq Ranipuri at Karachi in 1959; a Persian *Diwan-i Ashikar*, edited by Makhdum Amir Ahmad, appeared at Lahore in 1957. Later editions include *Sachal jo risalo. Siraiki kalam*, edited by Mowlana Muhammad Sadiq Ranipuri and published at Kandiaro in 1997, and *Sachal Sarmast Jo Kalam*, from the Sindhi Akademy at Delhi in the same year.

Name: Shrine of Shah Abdul Karim Bulri
Location: Bulri Shah Karim, Tando Muhammad Khan District, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Annual urs
Description:
## Overview

The Shrine of Shah Abdul Karim stands at Bulri, in Tando Muhammad Khan district in southern Sindh, a town that bears his name as Bulri Shah Karim. It honours one of the earliest and most influential of the Sindhi Sufi poets, a mystic of simple, laborious life and a pioneer of devotional verse in Sindhi. He is remembered, too, as the forebear of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, the poet of Bhit, who is said to have overseen the building of the shrine about 1741. The *dargah*, the shrine complex of a Sufi saint, remains a vibrant place of devotion, and its annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, draws thousands of pilgrims.

Shah Abdul Karim was a noted spiritual teacher in his own right, and among the first to bring the folk romances of Sindh into mystical verse. His short verses in Sindhi were gathered by a disciple soon after his death; Shah Abdul Latif kept them always at hand and inserted some of their lines into his own poetry, and several of the later poet's images are already found in them.

## The Saint

Shah Abdul Karim, often called simply Shah Karim and also Sayid Abdul Karim, was born in 1536 into a Sayyid family of Matiari, a family descended from the Prophet Muhammad. He spent most of his life at Bulri, the place from which he takes his epithet. Before he settled and preached there, he was himself a *murid*, a disciple pledged to a Sufi master, of Makhdoom Nooh of Hala. Beyond that discipleship, no Sufi order and no chain of spiritual descent are remembered for him. He is remembered as a mystic of simple, laborious life and as a noted spiritual teacher in his own right. He died in 1623.

In the generations just before the birth of Shah Abdul Latif, the family went back to the neighbourhood of Matiari; how it had come to Bulri in the first place, and why it returned, is not known.

Above all, he is the forebear of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai. Accounts differ over how many generations separated the two, but by tradition Shah Abdul Latif was his descendant in the fourth generation. Shah Abdul Latif's father, Shah Habib, was himself a descendant of Shah Abdul Karim, one of the first noted poets in the Sindhi language.

One story takes him far from Bulri. An anecdote relates that he was taught 'the one crooked word', OM, the sacred syllable of the Hindus, by an ascetic in Ahmadabad. The anecdote is told in connection with a Hindu reading of the symbolism of the Arabic letters *alif* and *mim* in Shah Abdul Latif's verse, a reading that has been set aside as too far fetched, with no parallels in his descendant's poetry.

## The Shrine

Tradition holds that Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai himself stayed two years at Bulri and supervised the building of his ancestor's shrine, laying the foundation of the tomb and of its mosque of three domes about 1741, the year 1154 of the Islamic calendar.

By 1940 he was spoken of as the famous Sayid Abdul Karim, his name was still held in reverence in Lower Sind, the south of the province, and his *dargah* at Bulri, then counted in the Hyderabad district, was still a great place of yearly pilgrimage. The gathering had its own Sindhi name: the Shah Karim fair, or *mero*, held on the day of the saint's *ʿurs*. It remains so today: the *dargah* is a vibrant place of devotion, and thousands of pilgrims come to its annual *ʿurs*.

Elsewhere in Tando Muhammad Khan district, at Tando Saindad near Tando Muhammad Khan, the *gaddi nashin*, or holder of the seat of spiritual authority, was Mohsin Shah, a Sufi affiliated to the Qalandariyya, the order of the Qalandars, wandering dervishes.

## The Poet

Shah Abdul Karim stands at the head of a Sindhi tradition. It seems that in Sindh, as in other parts of the Muslim world, the Sufis were responsible for the development of the spoken language into a literary one, and he composed some of the pioneering Sufi poems in Sindhi.

His sayings and verses were first gathered by a disciple, Mir Daryai Tharawi, in a lengthy Persian memoir, the *Bayan al-Arifin*, completed in 1630, seven years after his death. This book of his *malfuzat*, the recorded sayings of a Sufi master, preserves 93 verses in Sindhi, and Shah Abdul Latif is known to have treasured them. A printed edition, under a title that names Bulri, was edited by Dr Omar Muhammad Daudpota and published in Bombay by the Qayyimah Press in 1937, the year 1356 of the Islamic calendar. Judgements of the merit of the verse that survives differ, but it is most often counted pioneering, and it has been said to contain all the ingredients of later mystical poetry.

He was among the first to weave the folk romances of the land, *Sasui and Punhun*, *Sohni and Mehar*, *Umar and Marui* and *Leela and Chanesar*, into poetry expressing the soul's longing for the Divine, a method his descendant Shah Abdul Latif later brought to its summit. Early allusions to such tales appear, veiled, in the verse of Qadi Qadan; they become more obvious in Shah Abdul Karim's short verses and reach full bloom in the *Risalo*, the collected poetry of Shah Abdul Latif. His verses allude to Sasui, and one of them names Bhambhore:

*Nobody ever took with himself / two things at once from Bhambhore, / Yearning for the beloved, / and attachment with one's world*

Another of his verses is a picture of village life:

*Like a jar poised on woman-water-carrier, / and a bird on the water, / Our beloved in the same way / has been close to our soul*

Another, on the swan that dives deep for pearls while others play in the shallows, uses an image his descendant also took up:

*A swan feeds on pearls, / he dives deep down, / He who plays in the shallows*

The image of the swan must have been popular in Sindh for a long time, for Shah Abdul Karim used it more than a century before Shah Abdul Latif. A line of his also survives inside a verse of his descendant's: the second line of one of Shah Abdul Latif's verses is a quotation from him, and his own verse continues:

*The beloved is not separated from you, turn only your face inside*

Several of the motifs of Shah Abdul Latif's poetry begin with him. The phrase *tuhnjo Allah hekro*, 'Your God is One', appears first in his verses and then in Shah Abdul Latif's. The figure of the *jogi*, the Hindu ascetic, can be found in his poetry, though it is fully expressed only in his descendant's verses, and the motif of the thief is already present in his poems. It was probably he who invented a type of verse that mocks the curriculum of the *madrasa*, the school of religious learning, a type that became very popular in later times; among the later poets who carried it on were Sachal Sarmast and Bedil of Rohri. His poems, and those of Shah Inat, are closely related to Shah Abdul Latif's poetry.

## Legacy

His verse outlived him in his descendant's hands. Shah Abdul Latif kept three books constantly by him: the Qur'an, Jalaluddin Rumi's long mystical poem the *Masnavi*, and the Sindhi verses of Shah Karim. He also inserted some of his ancestor's lines into his own poetry.

Shah Abdul Karim is one of the grounds for rejecting the picture of Shah Abdul Latif as an unlettered genius. With Shah Inat Rizvi, who died in 1711, he was one of Shah Abdul Latif's forerunners, and they show that there was already an established culture of vernacular Sufi poetry in Sindh, although it tends to be overshadowed by Shah Abdul Latif's unique reputation in the literary histories.

He has also been the subject of modern study. A monograph by Motilal Jotwani, *Shah Abdul Karim*, was published in New Delhi by Kumar Brothers in 1970; a study of him as a mystic poet of Sindh was published in Karachi by Sindi Kitab Ghar and Indus Publications in 1986; and a work by Jotwani of 1996 includes a complete translation of his Sindhi verses.

At Bulri, the town that bears his name, the shrine that tradition says his descendant raised still draws pilgrims to his yearly *ʿurs*, while in the poetry of Shah Abdul Latif his images of the swan, the *jogi* and the thief, and some of his own lines, live on.
