Name: Shrine of Shah Inayat Qadiri
Location: Mozang Chungi, Queens Road, Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: 18th century (c. 1728, per figure's death; a field survey separately gives 1141 AH)
Sufi Saint: Shah Inayat Qadiri (murshid of Bulleh Shah)
Events: Annual urs (25-27 Jamadi al-Thani / Jumāda al-Ākhira): zikr, qawwali and langar
Description:
## Overview

At Mozang Chungi on Queens Road in Lahore, not far from Fatima Jinnah Medical University, lies the shrine of Shah Inayat Qadiri. He is one of the most historically consequential Sufi figures of Mughal Punjab, less for his own writings, considerable though they were, than as the *murshid*, the spiritual guide, of Bulleh Shah, arguably the most celebrated of all Punjabi Sufi poets. His shrine and its adjoining mosque remain an active place of pilgrimage, and his yearly *ʿurs*, the commemoration of the saint's death, draws thousands of devotees.

He came to Lahore from Kasur, served as imam of a mosque near Bhati Gate, founded a school of his own and wrote Persian works of mystical philosophy. His acceptance of the young Syed Bulleh Shah as a disciple, across the lines of caste, became one of the most retold episodes in Punjabi Sufi lore, and Bulleh Shah's songs name him again and again, in joy, in longing and in the pain of separation.

## The Saint

Shah Inayat was born around 1643 at Kasur, into a farming family of the Arain community, a caste of gardeners and small cultivators who worked their own land. Accounts of his origins differ, but most tie him to Kasur, and he is described as "of Kasur, then of Lahore". His father was Pir Muhammad. His full name, as it stands in his own works *Zail al-Aghlat* and *Ghayat al-Hawashi*, was Hafiz Abu al-Maarif Muhammad Inayat Allah Hanafi Qadiri Shattari; he is also called Shah Inayat Allah Qadiri and Inayat Shah. *Hafiz* is the title of one who has memorised the whole Qur'an, and he is said to have known it by heart by the age of five. He also bears the titles Sheikh-ul-Mashaikh, master of masters, Shah-e-Lahore, king of Lahore, and Mufakkir-e-Pakistan, thinker of Pakistan.

He studied the outward sciences with Maulana Sayyid Abu al-Nasr, called Sayyid Ilyas, and with Maulvi Abdul Hadi Lahori, and took inner guidance from Shah Ali Raza Faruqi, a great-grandson of the Mujaddid Alf-e Sani, the renewer of the second millennium, and from Shaikh Muhammad Sultan Bukhari. Accounts of his master differ; the one most often named is Shah Raza Qadri Shattari of Lahore, to whom he attached himself after 1111 AH and who died in 1118 AH (1707 CE). Shah Inayat became one of his *khalifas*, his deputies, and was counted a man of great rank, versed in both the outward and the inward sciences.

He combined the Qadiri and Shattari orders in his own practice, and his full name carries both, though he is often counted simply a Qadiri, a follower of the order of Sheikh Abdul Qadir of Baghdad. Within the Shattari order the doctrine of *fanā fī 'l-shaiḳh*, the obliteration of the self in the master, was given particular importance. His learning in Arabic and Persian was overlaid with an acceptance of the mystical traditions of the people of the subcontinent, an openness that one writer has called ironical, since the creed of the Qadiri order's Hanbali founder was originally opposed to innovative adjustments of that kind. His life spanned, it has been said, the Mughal rule from Aurangzeb to Mohammad Shah.

At Kasur he fell out with Husain Khan, the ruler of Kasur, and left to settle in Lahore. Local tradition attributes part of the friction to the ruler's ill intent towards Shah Inayat's wife, who is described as unusually beautiful and of noble family. In Lahore he served as imam, the leader of the prayers, of the Oonchi Masjid near Bhati Gate and founded his own *madrasa*, a religious school, where he taught students without regard to caste or class. In one of Bulleh Shah's lyrics Lahore, the seat of royal authority in the Punjab and hence called *taḳhat lahor*, the throne of Lahore, is celebrated as Shah Inayat's home.

He wrote several Persian works of mystical philosophy, among them the *Dastur-ul-Amal* and the *Lata'if-e-Ghaibiya*. Sixteen of his works have been traced, of which *Ghayat al-Hawashi* is the largest. In the *Dastur-ul-Amal*, it has been argued, he pointed to a Hindu origin for the mystical doctrines and to their reappearance in Greek thought centuries later, and he is said to have believed in the Hindu origin of Islamic mysticism, a knowledge carried, in his view, by the Greek soldiers of Alexander the Great and borrowed from Greece by the mystics of Islam.

## Bulleh Shah, the Disciple

His acceptance of Bulleh Shah as a disciple became one of the most retold episodes in Punjabi Sufi lore, because it crossed rigid social boundaries. Bulleh Shah came from a Syed family, descendants of the Prophet, of higher perceived status, yet he sought out and remained devoted to a teacher of humbler, land tilling background, an Arain of lower rank. It is said that he faced religious decrees, *fatwas*, from his own family over the choice, and that he answered only "what I have seen in him, you cannot perceive." One of his lyrics has been read as casting the master as Ranjha of the romance of Hir: just as Ranjha was despised by Hir's family, so Shah Inayat was disparaged for being an Arain. The relationship, immortalised in Bulleh Shah's own verses, is still cited in Pakistan as an example of Sufism's disregard for caste hierarchy.

Tradition holds that Bulleh Shah was sent to him by another master. Abd al-Hakim Qadiri declined to take the young man as his disciple and told him that his share lay with Shah Inayat Qadiri, and that he should go to him and take it. With his father's leave Bulleh Shah went to Lahore to take *bai'at*, the oath of initiation, and entered Shah Inayat's service.

The master, it is said, set a price on the initiation: he would give *bai'at* only if the young man first brought five hundred rupees in cash, a horse worth five hundred rupees, a pair of gold bangles worth five hundred rupees and a suit of clothes worth five hundred rupees. When all four had been delivered exactly, he honoured Bulleh Shah with *bai'at*, and afterwards with the *khirqa* of succession, the robe that marks a master's successor. In the town, the story goes, people would say that these clothes and this horse were Shah Inayat's. From him Bulleh Shah received the word, or *kalmā*, of his Sufi teaching.

After several years, master and disciple parted. Accounts of the cause differ, but most tell that Shah Inayat disapproved of his disciple's verse. He himself, as one writer on Bulleh Shah put it, worked under "the careful camouflage of sophisticated Persian metaphor", and he was dismayed by the rough vernacular of a disciple whose poetry was too outspoken against the priestly class, openly critical on matters of gender, class and caste, and mocking of institutional religion. He advised Bulleh Shah to stop railing against the orthodox postures that the political might of the Mughal court upheld, and Bulleh Shah did not listen. These were, it has been argued, hard times for the Qadiri order: in Aurangzeb's time the Qadiri mystics of Lahore were on the defensive, careful not to offend an orthodoxy inclined to take severe punitive measures against heretics. Afraid of the political forces of the time, Shah Inayat shut his rebellious disciple out of his spiritual company. It is said that he withdrew his disciple's *wilayat*, his sainthood, and later restored it, as though it were a grant that could be revoked.

The separation lives on in Bulleh Shah's songs. His *kafi*, or short mystical lyric, *Teray Ishq nachaya* has been read as an expression of his desolation and helplessness before an unavoidable passion, and of his estrangement from his master, and a line of one famous *kafi* as symbolising the gloom created by the master's departure. Bulleh Shah knew that Shah Inayat was fond of music. It is said that, turned out of his master's house, he took up the *sarangi*, the stringed instrument associated with the wandering dervish, and, aware of the Qadiri custom of *samaʿ*, spiritual listening, and devotional dance, began to sing and dance. In time, the story continues, seeing that his disciple's heterodoxy had a divine source, the teacher took him back, and the reunion was dramatic. In the most popular tale, Bulleh Shah reappeared in Lahore one day dressed as a dancing girl, and danced and sang before Shah Inayat.

Tradition also tells of a dramatic encounter between the two in Lahore, each outdoing the other in a display of miraculous powers. Waris Shah is said to have been a second prominent disciple of this period.

## In Bulleh Shah's Verse

Bulleh Shah names his master again and again, and most often he calls on him at the end of a whole train of suffering caused by separation. A true parallel to that closing invocation, it has been said, is found only in Rumi. Where Shah Husain makes no reference to his beloved Madho Lal in his *kafis*, as has been observed, Bulleh Shah's invocation of Shah Inayat is constant. The poet as a saint's disciple is a common figure in Sufi poetry, and one with no counterpart in Western literature. In the lyrics the master is where the search ends:

*I have found Shah Inayat.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

*I got caught in its whirlpools, but Shah Inayat delivered me to the other side.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

*With every breath I have remembered Inayat.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

He holds the secret, and he is the stone that transmutes:

*If Shah Inayat reveals the secret, then all mysteries are solved.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

*Bullha, Shah Inayat is a master mystic, he is the lord of my heart. I am iron and he is the philosopher's stone.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

One poem places him in the royal city:

*Baghdad is the place of the Pir of Pirs; our guide is in royal Lahore* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

Within a few lines the same poem has:

*Shah Inayat has set out his hooks, and without being seen he tugs the line* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

He is the poet's faith and his very being:

*Shah Inayat is my religion, the one whom we accept in this world and the next* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

*My whole being became Inayat; then it got the name Bullha* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

*Leaving my parents, I have clung to your skirt, oh my lord Shah Inayat.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

Another poem closes on a profession of the mystical identity between the disciple and the master standing directly before him.

In absence and in longing the poems call him by his order's name:

*With the departure of Inayat Qadiri, my story has again become difficult* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

*Come, Inayat Qadiri, my heart desires you* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

And the poems go to his gate:

*Bullha, let us go and sit at the gate of Shah Inayat* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

Elsewhere the disciple burns with love, waits at the door, and holds that only the master can lead the way:

*The flames engulfing my house, Bulleh, only love can douse. Inayat calls up the aisle* (translated by Taufiq Rafat)

*I'm waiting, pass this way once more, Inayat Shah, my eyes are sore with looking for you at the door.* (translated by Taufiq Rafat)

*Who will lead me to the place of my master, so by his grace he may my heart and body restore.* (translated by Taufiq Rafat)

*not Bulleh, but Inayat must steer.* (translated by Taufiq Rafat)

*Only the proper guide can lead you to His side; and unless you choose Inayat, you will lose.* (translated by Taufiq Rafat)

Elsewhere the guide goes unnamed: "then help there will be none till you call on Bulleh's guide." In the end the master is the lord who shows himself:

*As Shah Inayat, you show yourself to Bullha all the time.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

*See how my lord Shah Inayat flirts with me.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

*Bullha, he lets himself be found. Shah Inayat is discovered.* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

One poem also plays on his name: *Inayat* means grace or favour in Arabic. He is the one addressed in a lyric as "Oh you with a great family", *vaḍ parvāriā*, and another line is read as telling how the divine light entered Shah Inayat.

## The Shrine

Accounts of the year of his death differ; the year the shrine keeps is around 1728. Shah Inayat is buried at Mozang alongside two of his sons, Zamanaullah, a Sufi poet who left no descendants, and Zahidullah, through whom the family line continued. A daughter is buried alongside him as well. In the 1870s his *mazar*, the tomb of a saint, was spoken of as radiant, and his descendants were still living in Lahore.

The administration of the shrine and its adjoining mosque has passed from the family's own descendants to the Auqaf Department, the government department of religious endowments.

## Devotion and Festivals

The *ʿurs* is observed from the 25th to the 27th of Jamadi al-Thani and draws thousands of devotees for nights of *zikr*, the remembrance of God, and *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis; some 40,000 to 60,000 people come during the festival. The five daily prayers are said at the attached mosque, and a corner of the shrine is set aside for lighting oil lamps. Every Thursday there is a Mehfil-e-Milad, a gathering in celebration of the Prophet's birth, with *langar*, the free communal kitchen. Some 300 to 500 visitors come each day, rising to 1,500 to 3,000 on Thursday nights.

His memory is also sung far from his own tomb. Of six compositions that one party of qawwals, the singers of *qawwali*, sang at the shrine of Bulleh Shah, five were narratives of the stages of Bulleh Shah's spiritual growth as a mystic and of his relationship with Shah Inayat, singing of the disciple, the *murid*, and the mentor, the *murshid*, through female and male representations. A song that Bulleh Shah composed for his master, *Merā pīyā ghar āyā o lālnī*, "Celebrate thou, for my beloved has come home", is also sung at weddings.

## Legacy

Shah Inayat is the key to his disciple's poetry. As one translator of Bulleh Shah has put it, he is the most important focus of the poet's love, "now as the present source of his joy, now as the absent cause of his pain, now as the master who is mysteriously both different from and identical to his adoring disciple." The signature verse of a *kafi*, the verse that carries the poet's name, often proclaims Bulleh Shah's powerful identification with his master, who is frequently alluded to as "the lord", and the poems tell of the love between the human and the divine as lived out between the poet and his lord. Behind that bond stands the Sufi pattern in which spiritual disciplines passed within the circle of disciples formed around a master, while poetry carried the Sufi message to a wider audience.

His own life has its literature in Urdu. A life of Shah Inayat was being completed in 1974, and Muhammad Iqbal Mujaddidi prepared a *Hayat-e Shah Inayat Qadri*. His titles, and the thousands who come for his *ʿurs*, show a saint remembered in his own right as well as through the verse of his disciple.

Name: Shrine of Shah Jamal
Sufi Saint: Syed Shah Jamal Uddin Naqvi Bukhari (Baba Shah Jamal)
Events: Annual urs (3-5 Rabi al-Thani); weekly Thursday-night dhamal
Description:
## Overview

The shrine of Baba Shah Jamal stands in the Lahore locality that now carries his name, beside Ichhra and opposite Forman Christian College. It honours Syed Shah Jamal, a Sufi of Hussaini Syed descent who lived in Lahore in the reign of the Mughal emperor Akbar, and the site is known as his *Damdama*, the building he is said to have raised and named in his own lifetime. Today the shrine is famous above all for its Thursday nights, when dhol drummers drive crowds of devotees, students, musicians and curious visitors into hours of *dhamal*, ecstatic devotional dancing to the beat of the drum. That weekly spectacle has made Shah Jamal one of the most written about expressions of popular Sufi devotion in the Punjab.

The place has long been famous. In the nineteenth century the tomb was already known as the *Damdama*, the story of its sinking tower was already told, and the shrine had its keepers, its offerings and an annual festival.

## The Saint

Syed Shah Jamal was a Hussaini Syed, a descendant of the Prophet, and the shrine traces his ancestry to Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari of Uch Sharif; his full name is given as Syed Shah Jamal Uddin Naqvi Bukhari. His father is remembered as Syed Ahmad Shah, and the family is said to have moved from Kashmir to Sialkot and from Sialkot to Lahore, where Shah Jamal and his brother were both born. The link with Sialkot lasted: in the 1870s his descendants were still said to be living there.

He was one of two brothers who are both counted among the saints of Lahore. His brother, Baba Shah Kamal, is buried close by, and Shah Jamal is said to have come to Ichhra to see him and to have pitched his camp a short distance from his brother's house. Shah Kamal, like his brother, was remembered as devout and ascetic, a man of spiritual rapture and devotional practice, and the marvels of both were widely known. In the nineteenth century Shah Kamal's tomb stood right beside the lodge, or *khanqah*, of Shah Jamal.

Tradition places Shah Jamal's birth in 1587, and he lived in Lahore under Akbar. He is remembered for resisting the emperor's syncretic creed, the Din-i-Ilahi, and for working instead to draw people back towards orthodox Islamic practice. In his lifetime many came to him in search of blessing. Devotees know him for his open hand as *Sakhi Sarwar*, the generous lord, a title that in the Punjab more usually belongs to Sultan Sakhi Sarwar of Dera Ghazi Khan.

There is no settled view of which Sufi order he belonged to; he is most often counted a Suhrawardi, though he is also remembered as a Qadiri. Accounts differ over who his own master was and how his spiritual chain, or *silsila*, ran; the shrine remembers him as a special disciple of Sheikh Khokar Baig Suhrawardi, and his Suhrawardi line is most often traced back to Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan. He is also counted with Shah Hussain and Mian Mir among the great saints of Lahore with whom the city's Qalandars, wandering dervishes, are still associated.

Among his disciples was Hassu Teli of Lahore, Shah Jamal's *murid*, his pledged disciple. Shah Jamal is also remembered as the guide of a Lahore grain merchant whose weights he set right. The shrine's tradition also tells of a disciple born into a Hindu family, Sheikh Fakhr-ud-Din; he stayed in the saint's service all his life, and his grave lies inside the shrine. A house bought for him was still known in the nineteenth century as the house of Shah Jamal, and his descendants made over the rent of a house and four shops as an offering in the saint's name, dedicated to Shaikh Ahmad Bakhsh.

Accounts of the year of his death differ; the year the shrine keeps is 1671. His death is commemorated on the 4th of Rabi-ul-Sani, and a Thursday is remembered as the day he died. The manner of his death is told as one with his devotions. Tradition holds that, coming out of a *chilla*, a retreat of forty days in seclusion, he died when the roof of his cell collapsed. As people struggled to free him, a voice from within is said to have commanded that he should not be pulled out, but that his grave should be raised over that very spot, and so it was.

## The Damdama and Its Legends

Legends gather thickly around the *Damdama*. The best known tells of a princess, the sister of the emperor Akbar, whose palace stood nearby. Annoyed that the saint's tall tower overlooked her palace, she demanded that he lower it. Shah Jamal answered by performing *dhamal* on the topmost floor, and as he danced the building sank into the earth, storey after storey, until only two remained above ground. He then foretold that her palace would not outlast his own, a prophecy that, it is said, came true when Sikh forces later destroyed it. The sinking of the building was already counted among the saint's marvels in the nineteenth century.

Another version, told at the shrine itself, makes the saint's anger larger still: in his wrath he is said to have buried an entire city under his foot. As one writer has observed, the story was told "long before it was discovered that the location of his shrine could be the site of a mound with archaeological importance".

The shrine's tradition preserves another story. A dishonest Hindu merchant was given a cantaloupe by the saint to feed to his wife. Twin sons followed, and one of them, named Sheikh Fakhr-ud-Din by Shah Jamal himself, became his devoted lifelong disciple. The saint is also said to have saved the same family by calling them out of their house moments before its roof fell in.

## The Shrine

Shah Jamal is said to have overseen the building of the *Damdama* himself. It is said to have been one of several places of his austerities. By the 1870s the place was already known as Shah Jamal's *damdama*, his tomb lying in Lahore beside the village of Ichhra, and by the 1880s it was counted among the Muslim sites outside the city, with a *madrasa*, a religious school, beside it. Today the site lies in Shah Jamal Colony, Ichhra, on Achhra Road, facing west.

In the nineteenth century the tomb stood south of the city, towards the Sarai Goliyan Wali, near Ichhra. In that century the tower's story also told of labourers brought from the Sarai, of a building of several storeys, of a *haveli*, a great mansion, and of the objection raised against the building. At the shrine itself there was a square platform with a stair on its southern side, a domed brick cell, a flight of nine brick steps, small towers, and a brick terrace ten *gaz* across, the old yard measure, with a niche for a lamp. There were also a mosque, a *madrasa* and a well. The platform served as the graveyard of the family of the keeper, Shaikh Amir Bakhsh: his mother lay there, and Fateh Bibi was also buried there. Shaikh Amir Bakhsh had built an enclosure at the shrine, and an inscription recording the enclosure wall honoured the saint as Hazrat Shaikh Jamal Sahib Qadiri and named Fazl Bakhsh and Shaikh Ghulam Mustafa among those who raised it. That walled enclosure measured six and a quarter by five and a quarter *gaz*, with four small towers. The marker over the saint's grave was a handsome white.

The shrine has since been rebuilt. The tomb is now enclosed within a mosque of relatively modern construction, crowned by a single dome and four minarets, with a graveyard beside it; what the visitor sees reflects rebuilding rather than preserved Mughal fabric. The shrine follows the Suhrawardi line and the Ahl-e-Sunnat, the Sunni tradition, and since 1960 it has been in the care of the government's Auqaf Department. Before that, its upkeep and adornment fell first to Shah Jamal himself and afterwards to the kings, maharajas and devotees who came after him.

## Keepers of the Shrine

In the nineteenth century the shrine was kept by a family of Shaikhs. Its *sajjada nashin*, the hereditary custodian who sits on the saint's prayer carpet, was Shaikh Amir Bakhsh, son of Shaikh Roshan Ali; Roshan Ali's father in law was a Shah Sharaf. The men of the family included Shaikh Ramzani, Qudratullah, Mehr Bakhsh, Hafiz Amanullah, Saifullah and Haidar Bakhsh.

The shrine also had its own family of sweepers. In the nineteenth century the sweeper was a woman newly converted to Islam. Her daughter was married to Hidayatullah, and her granddaughter was betrothed to Mir Taqi. Mir Taqi's son was Qasim Ali, whose son Sayyid Ahmad was the father of Sultan Shah and Fateh Ali Shah. A woman who had swept the shrine was buried within the enclosure, and so was Mir Taqi. Their place was not uncontested. The keeper, Shaikh Amir Bakhsh, and another man complained that the sweepers came only on Thursdays, for the *chadhat*, the offerings, and declared that they would appoint someone else or sit there themselves. The income was put at about three hundred rupees a year.

Today the *sajjada nashin*, a descendant of the saint, continues to hold ceremonies of *Khatam Khawajgan*.

## Thursday Nights and the Urs

Today the shrine is known not for quiet contemplation but for its exuberant Thursday nights. From dusk until the early hours devotees, students, musicians and curious visitors gather as dhol drummers beat out the rhythm and the crowd gives itself to *dhamal*. The most famous of those drummers was the late Pappu Sain, whose successors carry on his tradition. Alongside the drumming there is *qawwali*, the devotional music of the shrines, there is *langar*, the free communal kitchen, and there is the lighting of lamps.

Thursday was already the shrine's day in the nineteenth century, when offerings came in every week in cash and in kind. The crowds today are large, on the order of 10,000 to 15,000 visitors a day, rising to 200,000 to 250,000 for the annual *ʿurs*, the festival that marks the anniversary of the saint's death. The *ʿurs* is held from the 3rd to the 5th of Rabi-ul-Sani, with the ritual washing, or *gusal*, of the tomb, the offering of the *chadar*, the sheet of cloth laid over the grave, and drumming and *dhamal*. In the nineteenth century, too, the *ʿurs* drew Hindus and Muslims alike.

Besides his cell at the *Damdama*, the shrine's tradition holds that Shah Jamal kept *chillas* at Sheikhupura, Shah Rehman, Shahdara in Lahore and Chanpatpur in India. In the nineteenth century vows were still being offered at Sheikhupura, one of these places of retreat, where there was also a grave.

The shrine shows both the vitality of devotion centred on Lahore's shrines and its shadows. The city's homeless rely on its *langar* and offerings, while noise, crowding and drug use in the surrounding streets, a real concern for the safety of pilgrims, have from time to time drawn official scrutiny.

## Ichhra and the Canal

Ichhra, the village where Shah Jamal is said to have pitched his camp, also appears in Mughal history. In the seventeenth century Ichhra was a halting place outside Lahore. After Dara Shikoh had left the city for Multan, the emperor, on his return, camped on the open ground of Ichhra, received there the nobles who had been in the city, and the next day rode on towards Lahore.

The locality that took the saint's name also lived through the violence of Partition. Mary, a widow of eighty three, remembered how her family had "used to live near Shahjamal on the canal that now divides Lahore into two parts". Before Partition she played on its banks; as Partition came, she saw "mutilated bodies floating in the water".

## Legacy

Shah Jamal's *Damdama* has been a living shrine for as long as anyone has written about it. By the 1870s it already carried the name it still bears; in the nineteenth century it also had its keeper, its family of sweepers and its Thursday offerings, and its *ʿurs* drew Hindus and Muslims alike. In the early twenty first century one scholar of Sufism could call the tomb "still a popular pilgrimage place". Its legends of a tower sunk by a dancing saint and an imperial princess rebuked, and its Thursday nights of drumming and *dhamal*, have made it one of the most written about expressions of popular Sufi devotion in the Punjab, and the neighbourhood that grew up around it still bears his name.

In 1875 a book on the saints of the Punjab gave Shah Jamal a notice of his own. The book closes with a chronogram, a verse written to mark the year of its completion, by the author's son, Mufti Ghulam Safdar, and its couplet names the book's subject: the friends of God in the Punjab, whose story the book makes plain.

Name: Shrine of Shah Rukn-e-Alam
Events: Annual urs; qawwali; daily langar
Description:
## Overview

In Multan, on the mound of the old fort, rises the shrine of Hazrat Shah Rukn-e-Alam (1251 to 1335), at once the tomb of a great saint of the Suhrawardi order of Sufis, or Muslim mystics, and one of the supreme masterpieces of Islamic architecture in South Asia. Rukn-ud-Din Abu al-Fath, known by the honorific Rukn-e-Alam, "Pillar of the World", was the grandson and spiritual heir of Bahauddin Zakariya, and under him the Suhrawardi order of Multan reached the height of its fame. His towering domed tomb is the emblem of Multan and among the most beautiful buildings raised in the subcontinent before the Mughal age, and pilgrims crowd to it to honour a saint whose blessing is felt to guard the city.

He was a shaikh who moved among sultans. One sultan gave him sums of hundreds of thousands of *tankas*, or coins, on each visit to Delhi, another granted a hundred villages for his *khanqah*, his Sufi lodge, and the petitions of the needy travelled to the throne in his palanquin. Yet he saved nothing of what came to him, and the people called him *Qibla-e Hajat*, "the Qibla of needs", the qibla being the direction a Muslim faces in prayer, because no one who came to him in need went away empty.

## The Saint

Rukn-ud-Din was born in Multan in 1251 into the leading Suhrawardi family of the region; accounts of the year of his birth differ. He is said to have been born on a Friday, the ninth of Ramadan, the month of fasting. His father was Shaikh Sadr al-Din Arif, son of Bahauddin Zakariya. His grandfather gave him the name Rukn al-Din; his *kunya*, the name of honour formed with Abu, "father of", was Abu al-Fath, and his *laqab*, or title, Fazl Allah. He is also called Shaikh Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath Suhrawardi and Shaikh Rukn al-Din Multani, and in a saying reported by Shaikh Nasir al-Din Chiragh Dihlawi he is named Shaikh al-Islam Rukn al-Haqq wa al-Din. Among the praises given him, he is called the sun of the sky of guidance. A different man of almost the same name, Sayyid Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath, son of Sayyid Hamid Kabir, belonged to Uch.

His mother, Bibi Rasti, was a saint in her own right, called the Rabia of her time, after Rabia, the woman saint of early Islam. She was a *hafiza*, a woman who has memorised the whole Quran, a worshipper and an ascetic who feared God, and her practice was to complete a reading of the Quran every day. She was a *murid*, a disciple, of Bahauddin Zakariya, and she died in the year 695 of the Hijri calendar.

It is told that his grandfather foresaw his greatness before he was born. When Bibi Rasti, carrying her child, came into Bahauddin Zakariya's presence, he would rise to his feet, against the custom of the elders. Asked why, he said that the respect was not for her but for the one in her womb, who would be a sun at the height of sainthood and a moon of nobility.

He had a brother, Shaikh Imad al-Din Ismail. Once the brother put a question of doctrine to him: what was the wisdom in the Prophet's *hijra*, his emigration from Mecca to Medina? Rukn-ud-Din's answer turned on the *ashab-e suffa*, the Companions of the Bench, and Nizam al-Din Auliya's answer on the poor of Medina, who could not otherwise have reached the Prophet's company. Rukn-ud-Din himself had no children.

He was raised in the great *khanqah* his grandfather had founded at Multan, and his education and upbringing were under his grandfather's supervision. He was schooled in the religious sciences and the discipline of the order, and he was bound to prayer and fasting from the age of seven. He prayed in congregation and kept *tahajjud*, the prayer of the night, and the voluntary prayers of *ishraq* and *chasht*, after sunrise and in the forenoon; besides Ramadan he fasted in the Ashura of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic year; and he practised *zikr*, the remembrance of God, both silent and spoken, with *muraqaba*, meditation, and *muhasaba*, the reckoning of one's own soul. From the age of ten, it is said, he was distinguished in reading hearts and in the folding of earth and tongue, by which, Sufis hold, a saint crosses great distances or says much in a moment; and from the age of twenty five he possessed the outward and inward perfections. At table he ate little, but he ate well.

His succession was marked by a turban. It is told that when he was four he found his grandfather's turban lying on the leg of a bed and, at play, put it on his own head. His father, Sadr al-Din Arif, forbade him, but Bahauddin Zakariya, calling his son Baba Sadr al-Din, told him not to forbid the boy, for he had put the turban on as of right, and it was Bahauddin himself who had given it to him.

He was his father's disciple, though accounts of his master differ. On his father's death he succeeded him as *sajjada nashin*, the hereditary custodian who sits on the saint's prayer carpet, and he sat on his grandfather's *sajjada*, the prayer carpet of the house, for fifty two years. On his accession he put on that same turban, and he wore the *khirqa*, the patched cloak of the Sufi, of Shaikh Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi, which had come to him from his father. He gave himself to teaching, to *talqin*, the instruction of disciples, and to guidance. He was granted outward and inward wealth, and the sultans of his time counted it their pride to serve him. He became the foremost shaikh of the Suhrawardis in India, guiding a vast body of disciples.

## The Saint and the Sultans

He was held in the highest honour by the Delhi Sultanate, and he moved between Multan and the capital as a figure of immense spiritual and moral authority, interceding with rulers. Sultan Ala al-Din Khalji was a great devotee of his. The shaikh visited Delhi twice in Ala al-Din's reign, and when, at the sultan's request, he went to meet him, the sultan himself came out to receive him. On each visit Ala al-Din presented two lakh *tankas*, a lakh being a hundred thousand, on the day he arrived, and five lakh on the day he left. The shaikh distributed the entire amount among the people of Delhi, and his visits were a source of great jubilation to them.

Sultan Qutb al-Din, too, held him in great faith and honoured him greatly. The shaikh came to Delhi three times in Qutb al-Din's reign, on visits the sultan sponsored in the hope that the shaikh's presence might eclipse that of Nizam al-Din Auliya, the Chishti master of Delhi. But the close friendship between the two shaikhs frustrated the sultan's hopes, and the sultan could not arouse the least jealousy between them. Nizam al-Din came out of his *khanqah* to receive him, and they met in the congregational mosque, the Jami Masjid, of that time. When the sultan asked who had been the first to receive him, the shaikh answered that the first to receive him had been the best man of the city, meaning Nizam al-Din.

Although he had a serious problem with his leg, he ordered his men to lift him from his palanquin so that he could show his respect for Nizam al-Din, but Nizam al-Din prevented him. After a meal at Nizam al-Din's, Nizam al-Din's servant Iqbal laid several bolts of silk and a hundred *ashrafis*, gold coins, wrapped in a fine cloth, at his feet; he would not accept them, and they were given instead to his brother, Imad al-Din Ismail. When Nizam al-Din fell ill, he came from Multan to Delhi to visit him, led his funeral prayer, and afterwards returned to Multan.

He was a broker of petitions to the throne. On his palanquin lay a pile of papers, and he explained that they were petitions from the needy, given to him so that he could recommend them to the sultan. Whenever he went to the court of Sultan Qutb al-Din, the people of Delhi would place petitions inside his *takht-i rawan*, a palanquin like a movable throne; the petitions were then brought in, and the sultan read them and wrote sympathetic replies. A Sufi tradition holds that the shaikh would remain at court until every request had been granted, the sultan meanwhile squatting respectfully at his feet.

With the Tughluq sultans his ties were close, and they in particular revered him. His relations with Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq were most cordial. When the sultan marched towards Multan, the shaikh met him. The sultan granted him a hundred villages for the upkeep of his *khanqah*. In a battle, as a ruse to confuse the enemy, Muhammad bin Tughluq placed the shaikh's brother, Shaikh Imad al-Din, who closely resembled the sultan, under the royal canopy, and Imad al-Din was killed; accounts of the brother's fate differ.

When Multan rebelled against Muhammad bin Tughluq, the saint is remembered as having saved the city. In 1327 or 1328 Bahram Aiba Kishlu Khan, the governor of Multan, rose in revolt; the sultan defeated him, flayed the *qazi*, the judge, alive, and ordered a general massacre of the people. Accounts of what followed differ, but the shaikh went to the sultan soon after he learned of the sultan's intention and asked for clemency, and the sultan relented.

He went to receive Sultan Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq at the village of Afghanpur and lunched with him in a specially built palace. At the suggestion of the sultan's son, Muhammad bin Tughluq, he left to perform the afternoon prayer, and after he had gone the palace collapsed and Sultan Ghiyath al-Din was crushed to death under its roof. Accounts of the episode differ.

## Life at Multan

Following the tradition set by his father and grandfather, his *khanqah* at Multan was a busy meeting place for distinguished visitors from many countries west of the Indus. His fame reached as far as Alexandria, spread by the merchants who came to Multan, and the traveller Ibn Battuta was advised to see him. In 1333 Ibn Battuta reached Multan and stayed with one of the shaikh's disciples, and his conversation with the shaikh reached even to political matters. A *murid* occupied in worship in a cell of the *khanqah* was told by the shaikh that the *hajj*, the pilgrimage to Mecca, was not obligatory on him, because he was a *faqir*, one who has embraced poverty.

What came in went out again. Whatever offering came to him he spent, saving nothing of it, and when Sultan Ala al-Din presented lakhs of *tankas* on his visits to Delhi he spent the whole sum. Whoever came to him in need of this world or the next did not go away empty, and so the people called him the *Qibla-e Hajat*. When he went out in his palanquin, both his hands hung outside it, so that perhaps the hand of some forgiven soul might touch his and he too might be forgiven. He took great care of scholars, learned men and dervishes, honouring and entertaining them.

He defended a shaikh's wealth in so many words. Shaikh Nasir al-Din Chiragh Dihlawi related that when Rukn-ud-Din visited Delhi, *qalandars*, wandering dervishes, asked him for sherbet and other dervishes asked him for money, and that he satisfied them and said: "The leaders of the community should possess three things." The first was property, to satisfy such demands; the second knowledge, to hold scholarly discussions with the *ulama*, the scholars of religion; and the third *hal*, mystical enlightenment, to impress dervishes. To this Nasir al-Din added that money was not necessary, and that only knowledge and *hal* were essential. His grandfather could not tolerate *qalandars*, but Rukn-ud-Din did, for he considered that their persistent demands, and those of other visitors, justified Sufi shaikhs in possessing wealth.

Works holding his teaching, among them his *malfuzat*, the record of his discourses, were known, but accounts differ over whether any of them survives; his teaching is also found in the works of his *khalifas*, his deputies. He urged his disciples to abandon cruelty, oppression, avarice and greed, for he believed that such vices brought human beings down to the level of beasts. Purification of the self, he held, came only through humility and prayer, as in the verse: "I do not exculpate myself. Lo! the (human) soul enjoineth unto evil, save whereon my Lord hath mercy. Lo! My Lord is Forgiving and Merciful." In the final analysis, he taught, that purification depended on divine grace, as another verse says: "Had it not been for the grace of Allah and His mercy unto you, not one of you would ever have grown pure." The mark of divine grace and mercy, in his view, lay in an insight into one's own faults.

Two more of his teachings concern form and attribute, and conformity in deeds. Judgement, he taught, rests on a person's attribute and not on his form, and the truth of this appears only in the hereafter, where each person is gathered in the form that answers to his attribute. Conformity in deeds means that the limbs are to be held back, in word and deed, from whatever the *sharia*, the religious law, forbids or dislikes, and idle gatherings and the company of idlers are to be avoided.

Among his *khalifas* were Maulana Zahir al-Din, Sultan Hamid al-Din Hakim, Shaikh Fakhr al-Din Iraqi, Makhdum Jahaniyan Jahangasht Bukhari and Shaikh Sama al-Din Dehlvi, though accounts of the list differ. Shaikh Usman Sayyah of Sunnam was enrolled as his disciple near Kilukhari, on the banks of the Jumna, and taught the *Awarif al-Ma'arif*, the Sufi manual of Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi, at Multan; when he returned from seven years of travel, he was given the honour of being presented with the shaikh's own garment and turban.

Makhdum Jahaniyan Jahangasht, Sayyid Jalal al-Din Bukhari, was initiated by Rukn-ud-Din into the Suhrawardi order and completed his training under him and under Nasir al-Din Chiragh Dihlawi. He lived at Multan in the *madrasa*, the school, by the shaikh's permission. When there was friction between Makhdum Jahaniyan's father and Shaikh Jamal al-Din Khandan, the shaikh put the young man on his own boat and sent him to Uch, and on receiving the message the father went at once to Jamal al-Din Khandan and embraced him. The shaikh conferred on him in person the *khirqa* of *khilafat*, the cloak that marks a deputy's authority to guide others, and, it is told, conferred another on him in a dream, which Makhdum Jahaniyan found on his head when he woke. When Makhdum Jahaniyan held the office of *Shaikh al-Islam*, the chief religious dignitary, and the seat of the Khanqah-e Muhammadi at Sehwan, he resigned the post at Rukn-ud-Din's command. Once he lay down below the threshold so that the shaikh might step down upon him, and the shaikh took his hand and pressed him to his breast; and once he bathed in the water that ran off from the shaikh's *ghusl*, the ritual bath, and when the shaikh learned of it he honoured him with a special favour.

He prepared for his own death. For three months beforehand he shut himself in his *hujra*, his cell, day and night, coming out only for the five obligatory prayers. On his last day, after the afternoon prayer, he called Maulana Zahir al-Din and ordered him to make ready what was needed for his burial and his shroud; then he led the sunset prayer as *imam*, the leader of the prayer, and died in the prostration of the last *rak'a*, or cycle, of the supererogatory prayers. He died in 1335. Accounts of the day differ; it is most often given as the sixteenth of Rajab, in the year 735 of the Hijri calendar.

After his death his seat passed to his brother's family, though accounts differ over who took it.

## The Shrine

He was buried in Multan, in the tomb that is said to have been built originally for Sultan Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq and then given over to the saint. Raised in the early fourteenth century, it is one of the glories of the age. It is octagonal in plan, built of red brick banded with timber and dressed with carved and glazed tilework in blue and white, and it rises in three tapering tiers to a high white dome, a colossal structure that dominates the skyline of Multan from its perch on the mound of the old fort. It stands next to the shrine of his grandfather, Bahauddin Zakariya.

The tomb is counted among the earliest and finest monuments of the Tughluq style, a model that influenced the architecture of tombs across the region for generations. It has been repaired and restored over the centuries, and in modern times it has received awards for its conservation. For the people of Multan it is not only a shrine but the very symbol of their city.

By the 1870s his tomb was a place of pilgrimage for the people, and in the twentieth century it drew high and low alike. It is a centre of continuous devotion, thronged by pilgrims who come to recite the *Fatiha*, the opening chapter of the Quran, to seek his intercession, and to honour a saint whose *baraka*, or blessing, is felt to guard the city. The daily prayers, *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, and the *langar*, the free communal kitchen, are kept there, and his *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, draws great crowds from across southern Punjab.

## Legends

It is told that when the Mughals, as the Mongols were then called, came near Multan, the people asked him for prayers. He went into *muraqaba*, meditation, and then said that the Mughals had gone. On reaching the river they had scattered, and when he was asked why, he said that God Most High had sent an army of angels and scattered them.

A devotee used to receive four loaves from his house. The story goes that he went to Mecca and complained that there he received none, and a dervish told him that the shaikh came there every Friday night, and showed him the spot. He found the shaikh there and saluted him, and from then on, the story ends, four loaves and two bowls of curry reached him without fail.

A *murid*, it is told, dreamed that he was told to go on *hajj*, and the shaikh, on seeing him, said at once that the dream came from Satan, who wished to deprive him of his devotions.

Before one battle, it is told, a sultan kissed the shaikh's feet, and he in turn foretold victory; the battle took place near Abuhar. In Sindh his name enters a birth legend, which in some tellings makes him, rather than his grandfather Bahauddin Zakariya, the Sufi master of the story.

## The Setting

Multan was a strategic commercial centre of the Punjab, and by the middle of the eleventh century Sufism had reached the lands around it. The governors of Multan were bound up with the Tughluqs: Ghazi Beg Tughluq, the governor of Multan, raised an army, killed Khusrau Malik and took the throne as Ghiyath al-Din. By the time Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith, came to Multan, the city was famous as a major centre of Sufi learning and philosophy. It was then one of the biggest cities of the Punjab, known for the shrines of Muslim saints and for its Jain and Hindu temples, a sacred space for people of all religious denominations. In Aurangzeb's reign it was counted among the ancient cities, with a fort of brick; people of every kind lived there, and many saints rested in that blessed city.

In Multan and Bahawalpur, musicians performed in the family shrines of the Syeds, supported by the Syeds' large landholdings, and the Syeds arranged annual rituals such as the Eid and the Muharram ceremonies marking the tragedy of Kerbala. For the Sindhi and Punjabi poets, Multan, like Mecca and Medina, was inside the heart. The city's fame enters the verse of the poet Madho Lal Hussain too, where a dress bought in Multan is one item in a bride's trousseau:

*The dress / someone carried across the snows / all the way from Kashmir. The dress / someone brought from Gujarat… The dress bought in Multan* (translated by Naveed Alam)

## Legacy

As the heir of Bahauddin Zakariya and the most celebrated of the Suhrawardis of Multan, Rukn-e-Alam carried the order to its height, and through his tomb, at once a place of pilgrimage and a wonder of architecture, the sanctity of the "City of Saints" finds its most visible expression. After his death the Suhrawardi order declined in Multan, only to be rejuvenated in Uch.

In 1875 a book on the saints of the Punjab gave him a notice of his own. The book closes with chronograms, verses whose letters, read as numbers, give the year of its completion, and one of them, by the author's son, Mufti Ghulam Safdar, names the book's subject, the friends of God in the Punjab:

جو خدا کے دوست تھے پنجاب میں
حال ان کا اس سے ہوتا ہے عیان

*A chronogram for the completion of the book, on its subject, the saints of the Punjab*

Name: Shrine of Shah Shams-ud-Din Sabzwari
Events: Annual urs; qawwali and langar
Description:
## Overview

In Multan, the ancient "City of Saints", stands the shrine of Shah Shams-ud-Din Sabzwari, known as Shah Shams or Pir Shams, *pir* being the title of a Sufi spiritual guide. He was a saint of the thirteenth century, remembered as one of the most powerful and colourful holy figures of the region. Renowned for spectacular miracles, and associated in tradition with the spread of a form of the faith through the Ismaili *daʿwa*, the mission or call to the faith, Shah Shams gave Multan one of its oldest and most storied shrines, and his memory is bound up with the very sun and heat of the city.

## The Saint

Shah Shams is said to have come to the Indian subcontinent from Sabzwar, in the Persian lands, in the thirteenth century, as a preacher and missionary of extraordinary spiritual power. His life is more legend than chronicle, and it is famous above all for the miracle from which his name, *Shams*, "the sun", is popularly explained. It is told that, having no fire to cook a fish, the saint commanded the sun itself to come down and roast it, and that the sun drew so near that Multan has been scorched by an intense heat ever since. Such tales made him one of the great saints of the popular imagination, a worker of wonders.

He is connected with the Ismaili mission in Sindh and Multan, part of the complex religious currents of the medieval Indus valley, though today he is venerated broadly across communities. He died in Multan in the thirteenth century.

## The Shrine and Its Devotion

The shrine of Shah Shams Sabzwari is a domed tomb by the old bank of the river. It is among the oldest *darbars*, or shrines, of the city and a continuous centre of pilgrimage. Devotees come to seek the blessing of a saint famed for miraculous power, to recite the *Fatiha*, the opening chapter of the Qur'an, and to fulfil vows. The annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, draws crowds in the customary manner of Multan's shrines, with *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, and *langar*, the free communal kitchen. The shrine forms part of the dense sacred landscape that has made Multan the "City of Saints".

## The Shams of Multan

The shrine knows him as Shah Shams-ud-Din Sabzwari, of Sabzwar, and other names linked with a Shams of Multan have no settled connection with him. A saint called Shams was already honoured in Multan in the reign of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, when a Persian history composed in his reign counted a Shams al-Din, under the name Tabrizi rather than Sabzwari, among the saints buried in the city. The tomb of each of these saints, a place where divine lights are made manifest, was a place of pilgrimage for the people, and many friends of God, it was said, rested in that city in felicity. The name and the city are the only link between this Shams al-Din and the saint of this shrine.

Multan's history also remembers a tomb of a Shah Shams in the city. Nawab Shahnawaz Khan, killed in a disturbance in Multan, was buried beside it, and in the nineteenth century that tomb still stood.

The name Shams is linked with Multan in another way too. An Indian tradition holds that Shams-i Tabriz, the spiritual beloved of Maulana Rumi, was flayed alive by the mullahs in Multan, where his shrine is still venerated. It is not settled whether the Hazrat Shams Tabrizi honoured at a shrine in Multan is that renowned figure or another local Sufi of the same name, and as one scholar who was taken to that shrine observed, "Multiple shrines to the same person are not unusual." None of these traditions identifies its Shams with Shah Shams Sabzwari.

## The Setting

The history of Multan helps to place the currents with which tradition connects Shah Shams. In 711 the Arabs conquered Sindh and the provinces to the north of it up to Multan. The Carmathians, an Ismaili movement, ruled not only Bahrain but also northern Sindh and Multan, and tradition holds that the mystic Hallaj was in touch with them there. Multan became a dependency of the Fatimids of Egypt, and Sultan Mahmud dealt Ismaili power there a blow. By the middle of the eleventh century Sufism had reached the country around Multan, and in 1175 Muʿizzu'd-Din Muhammad bin Sam seized the city.

The heat that the legend of the sun explains belongs to the city's older history as well. Multan's winter is mild, its summer excessively hot, and its rain scarce. On Sultan Mahmud's second campaign, his soldiers could not bear the hot air of Multan in that season and begged to go back, so that the sultan turned back to Ghazni.

Tradition sets Shah Shams in the thirteenth century. During the twelfth century many Sufi scholars had made Multan their base, and conversion gained momentum in the early thirteenth century. The city was a strategic commercial centre in the Punjab, and by the time Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith, came to Multan, it was famous as a major centre of Sufi learning and philosophy. It was known for the shrines of Muslim saints and for its Jain and Hindu temples, a sacred space for people of all religious denominations.

Around the shrines of Multan and Sahiwal, performers sing to earn a living. Not everyone approves of the devotion of the region's shrines. One devotee of the Tableeghi Jamaat, a movement of Islamic revival, has complained that at several shrines in the Multan region and in Sindh people "light lamps, present offerings to the shrine and even bow down to the grave", which he condemns as an act of *shirk*, the sin of associating others with God.

A book of the saints of the Punjab carries a chronogram, a poem in which letters, read as numbers, give a year:

جو خدا کے دوست تھے پنجاب میں
حال ان کا اس سے ہوتا ہے عیان

*A verse of the chronogram written for the book by the author's son; its subject is the saints of the Punjab whom the book describes*

## Legacy

Shah Shams Sabzwari endures in memory as one of the great saints of medieval Multan who worked wonders, a figure of legend whose miracles, above all the calling down of the sun, have entered the folklore of the region, and whose shrine remains one of the oldest and most visited in the city. He belongs to the founding age of Sufism in the Indus valley, and his *darbar* is a fixed point in Multan's ancient devotion. In the reign of Aurangzeb a Shams was already counted among the saints whose tombs made Multan a place of pilgrimage, and who the Shams of Multan was remains an open question.

Name: Shrine of Shah Yusaf Gardez
Events: Annual urs
Description:
## Overview

In the old city of Multan stands the shrine of Hazrat Shah Yusuf Gardez, a Sufi, or Muslim mystic, who is counted among the earliest saints of the region and, by tradition, was a founding figure in the Islamisation of Multan. Coming from Gardez, in what is now Afghanistan, he settled in Multan when Islam was still taking root there, and founded the line of the Gardezi sayyids, a family descended from the Prophet Muhammad and long among the leading religious families of the city. His shrine, a low tomb famed for its exquisite blue tilework, is one of the most distinctive and revered monuments of Multan, the ‘City of Saints’, and it is a place of continuous pilgrimage.

## The Saint

Sayyid Yusuf, called Shah Yusuf Gardez, is remembered as having come from Gardez to Multan at a time when Islam was still taking root in the region. Tradition places his arrival in the years around 1088 and his death in the first half of the 1100s. A sayyid of the family of the Prophet, he is honoured as one of the first great saints of Multan.

He is remembered as a preacher whose presence helped make the city a centre of the faith even before the coming of the great Suhrawardi masters, the Sufis of the order founded by Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi. He founded the Gardezi sayyid family, which remained prominent in the religious and civic life of Multan for centuries. He died at Multan and was buried there.

## The Shrine

The shrine of Shah Yusuf Gardez is celebrated for its architecture as much as for its sanctity. It is a low, rectangular tomb sheathed in the brilliant blue and white glazed tilework of Multan known as *kashi*, one of the loveliest of the city's many shrines and among the oldest of its sacred monuments. It is kept by the Gardezi family.

The tomb is a place of continuous pilgrimage. Devotees come to recite the Fatiha, the opening chapter of the Quran, and to seek the blessing of one of Multan's founding saints, and his *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, gathers the faithful in the customary manner. In the reign of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, Multan was a city where many saints lay at rest, and Shah Yusuf Gardez was counted among the saints buried there whose tombs were places of pilgrimage.

## The Setting

In 711 the Arabs conquered Sind and the neighbouring provinces to the north as far as Multan. At one time the city was a dependency of the Fatimids of Egypt, and by the middle of the eleventh century Sufism had made its way into the country around Multan. It was into this world, tradition holds, that Shah Yusuf Gardez came. In the twelfth century many Sufi scholars made Multan their base. In 1175 Mu'izzu'd-Din Muhammad bin Sam seized the city, and in the early thirteenth century conversion gained momentum.

Multan also had its place in the region's pilgrimage and in its poetry. On reaching Multan, one sultan made the circuit of the tombs of its shaikhs, the Sufi masters of the city. For the poets of the vernacular languages, Mecca and Medina are inside the heart, and for the Sindhi and Punjabi poets, so is Multan.

## Legacy

Shah Yusuf Gardez holds an honoured place as one of the earliest saints of Multan, the founder of the Gardezi sayyids and a pioneer of Sufism in the Indus valley, whose coming, tradition holds, helped turn Multan toward the faith it would come to embody as the ‘City of Saints’. His tiled shrine remains a jewel of the old city and a living centre of devotion.

Name: Shrine of Syed Musa Pak
Events: Annual urs; qawwali; langar
Description:
## Overview

The shrine of Hazrat Syed Musa Pak Shaheed stands in Multan, the 'City of Saints', where his *darbar*, or shrine, is counted among the city's notable shrines. Syed Musa Pak was a revered saint of the sixteenth century in the Qadiri order, the Sufi order founded by Abd al-Qadir Jilani, and the ancestor of the Gilani (Musa Pak) sayyids, one of Multan's most eminent religious families. The shrine is a continuous place of pilgrimage, where devotees come to recite the Fatiha, the opening chapter of the Quran, to seek intercession and to honour the saint.

He is honoured with the titles *Pak*, "the pure", and *Shaheed*, "the martyr". Musa Pak carried the Qadiri order of Abd al-Qadir Jilani in Multan and founded a spiritual line that remained influential in the city for centuries.

## The Saint

Syed Musa, called Musa Pak Shaheed, was a Sayyid of the Gilani line, the descendants of the great Baghdad saint Shaikh Abd al-Qadir Jilani, and he flourished in Multan in the sixteenth century. He was the beloved son of Sayyid Hamid Ganj Bakhsh Gilani Uchi, a father praised as the exemplar of the noble Sayyids and the choicest of the great shaikhs. When Musa had completed his training before his father, he was given the title Jamal al-Din Abu al-Hasan, and his name at full length is Sayyid Jamal al-Din Abu al-Hasan Musa Pak Shaheed Gilani Multani.

Learned and devout, he was a shaykh of the Qadiri order and a guide of many disciples, and he is remembered for a life of piety and for the sanctity that earned him the epithet *Pak*, "the pure". He is said to have had a special *nisbat*, an inner bond, with the spirituality of Ghaus al-Azam, "the greatest helper", so that its presence was constant with him, and to have been blessed hundreds of times with visions of the Prophet, waking and sleeping. His whole life, it is said, passed in austerity, struggle, worship, teaching and instruction.

Accounts of how he came to his father's seat differ, but he is remembered as having succeeded to the *masnad*, the seat of spiritual authority, after his father's death. Through him and his descendants the presence of the Qadiri order and of the Gilani line was firmly established in Multan, and the Musa Pak Gilani family became one of the leading religious and landed houses of the region.

## Disciples and Writings

Great *ulama*, scholars of religion, became his disciples, and Shaikh Abdul Haq Muhaddith Dehlvi, too, was his sincere disciple. Abdul Haq became attached to him on 6 Shawwal 985 AH (1577 CE). He took the *bai'at*, the oath of allegiance by which a disciple enters a Sufi order, at Musa Pak's hand, and the shaikh gave his disciple special attention. After the saint's death Abdul Haq went on to Shaikh Abd al-Wahhab, the *khalifa*, or deputy, of Shaikh Ali Muttaqi, and received from him *faiz*, spiritual grace, and a *khirqa-e tabarruk*, a robe given as a blessing.

Musa Pak left a work of his own, *Taisir al-Thaqalain*, on litanies and observances (*awrad* and *ma'mulat*), which was printed at Ferozepur in 1309 AH. Another work, *Bahr al-Sarair*, is devoted to his conditions and practices.

## His Martyrdom

Tradition honours Musa Pak as a *shaheed*, a martyr, and he is said to have been martyred at the hands of ill-wishers of the Langah tribe. Accounts of the year of his death differ, and there is no settled view; it is placed between 998 and 1001 AH. His disciple Shaikh Abdul Haq Muhaddith Dehlvi marked the death with a chronogram, a phrase whose letters, read as numbers, give a year, and from it he derived the year 998 AH. The chronogram is a phrase of three words:

شمع جمع سیادت

*The chronogram on the saint's death by his disciple Shaikh Abdul Haq Muhaddith Dehlvi, from which he derived the year 998 AH.*

He was buried in Multan, where his shrine arose.

## The Shrine and Its Devotion

The shrine of Syed Musa Pak in Multan is kept by his Gilani descendants. It maintains the customary devotions of a Multan *darbar*: prayer, *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, and the free kitchen. Its annual *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of the saint's death, gathers the faithful. In the 1870s his *rauza*, or tomb, in Multan was a place of pilgrimage for God's creatures, and today it forms part of the great constellation of shrines that gives Multan its identity.

Another building, at Uch Sharif rather than at Multan, may bear on this saint. Next to the Gilani shrine at Uch stands a fifteenth century structure, octagonal, built in the typical Multani fashion with blue tiles, and now in a dilapidated condition. A board beside it, put up by the Department of Archaeology, says that the grave of Moosa Pak Shaheed once lay there and that his body was later shifted to Multan. The link with the saint of Multan rests on the name and on the board's statement that the body went to Multan; the structure at Uch is a separate building from the shrine in Multan.

## The Setting

The first of the Qadiri line to arrive in the Punjab was Sayyid Muhammad Ghaus Uchi Jili Gilani, whose ancestors had left Baghdad in the time of Hulagu Khan. He came to Multan by way of Khurasan and settled at Uch, which he entered in 887 AH. This is the story of the order, not of Musa Pak's own household. In the age of Guru Nanak, in one historian's words, the Qadiris had "made the Panjab the main centre of their activities". Sind and the Punjab also produced hymns in praise of the great masters of the mystical orders, with Abd al-Qadir Gilani above them all.

The Langah, the tribe named in the story of Musa Pak's martyrdom, once ruled Multan. In Multan the Langah raised the banner of sovereignty. Their chief seized the fort of Multan from Shaikh Yusuf Qureshi by a ruse and took a royal title, and Langah sultans followed him. Their rule ended with the Arghun conquest.

Of Multan in Guru Nanak's time one writer has said that "Multan was one of the biggest cities of Punjab and was known for the religious shrines of Muslim saints, and Jain and Hindu temples. It was a sacred space for people of all religious denominations". In another writer's words, by the time Nanak came to Multan "the city was famous as a major centre of Sufi learning and philosophy".

Multan had its place in the region's poetry as well. Of the vernacular poets, one scholar of mystical poetry wrote that "Mecca and Medina (and for the Sindhi and Panjabi, also Multan) are inside the heart". In a poem by Madho Lal Hussein the city appears as a market, in a bride's trousseau:

*The dress / someone carried across the snows / all the way from Kashmir. The dress / someone brought from Gujarat… The dress bought in Multan* (translated by Naveed Alam)

## Legacy

Syed Musa Pak Shaheed is remembered as a chief bearer of the Qadiri order in Multan and the founder of the distinguished Musa Pak Gilani line, a saint whose purity and martyrdom won him lasting veneration and whose family carried his influence through the later history of the city. Among his disciples was Shaikh Abdul Haq Muhaddith Dehlvi, and his own *Taisir al-Thaqalain* was printed at Ferozepur in 1309 AH. In the 1870s his tomb in Multan was a place of pilgrimage, and his shrine remains a revered *darbar* of the 'City of Saints'.

Name: Sial Sharif
Location: Sial Sharif, Sial Sharif (Sargodha District), Punjab
Events: Annual urs; naat and qawwali; daily langar
Description:
## Overview

At Sial Sharif, in the Sargodha district of the Punjab, stands the shrine of Hazrat Khwaja Muhammad Shamsuddin Sialvi, a leading saint of the nineteenth century in the Chishti order, an order of Sufis, or Muslim mystics, that was founded by Moinuddin Chishti and is prominent in South Asia. His *khanqah*, the Sufi lodge where disciples gather, became one of the most influential centres of the order in the region. An heir to the great Chishti revival that flowed from Taunsa Sharif, he guided a wide following and trained saints of the first rank, among them Pir Meher Ali Shah of Golra, and his *darbar*, or shrine, at Sial Sharif remains a major place of pilgrimage in central Punjab.

## The Saint

Khwaja Muhammad Shamsuddin was born in 1799 at Sial Sharif into a devout family, and from his youth he pursued the religious sciences and the Sufi path. He was initiated into the Chishti order and became a spiritual heir within the line of Khwaja Sulaiman Taunsvi, rising to be among the foremost Chishti *shaykhs*, or masters, of his age. From his *khanqah* at Sial Sharif he taught and guided disciples and kept a great *langar*, the free communal kitchen of a shrine, and his spiritual authority drew seekers from across the Punjab.

Among those who took his guidance was Pir Sayyid Meher Ali Shah of Golra Sharif, whose direct *pir*, or spiritual guide, he was. Through Meher Ali Shah the line of Sial Sharif reached into the next generation of Punjabi Sufism. Shamsuddin Sialvi died in 1883, though accounts of the year of his death differ, and he was buried at Sial Sharif.

## The Shrine and Its Devotion

His shrine at Sial Sharif is a large complex kept by his successors, who have continued as prominent religious figures and as its *sajjada-nashins*, custodians whose title means those who sit on the prayer carpet. The shrine maintains the daily prayers and the free kitchen, and gatherings of *naat*, poetry in praise of the Prophet, and of *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis. Its annual *urs*, the commemoration of the saint's death, gathers great crowds of devotees. The town of Sial Sharif takes its identity from the *darbar*, a continuing seat of Chishti teaching and devotion.

More widely, the Punjab is one of the two principal regions of the *qawwali* tradition, the other being Uttar Pradesh; the tunes of the two can be told apart mainly by their rhythmic setting, and Punjabi tunes tend to be organised rhythmically by stress.

## The Chishti Line in the Punjab

The line of Khwaja Sulaiman Taunsvi, to which Shamsuddin Sialvi belonged, is part of the Chishti revival in the Punjab. The Chishti order is usually counted among the most powerful Sufi orders of northern India and the Punjab. Its Nizami branch came to prominence in the eighteenth century, principally in Delhi, the Deccan and the Punjab, through masters who were related to local political leaders but in tension with them.

The wider spread of the Chishti Nizami Fakhri line in the Punjab came through Hazrat Khwaja Sulaiman Taunsvi, who was born in 1184 and died in 1267 of the Hijri, or Islamic, calendar. He consolidated the order by stressing learning through the founding of institutions: not only the academy called Dar al-'Ulum at Taunsa on the upper Indus, but also other religious schools throughout the Punjab. He urged his followers to take part in resistance against Sikh aggression in the Punjab, yet he worked to keep cordial relations with Punjabi Hindus even while he opposed their Sikh neighbours. In the nineteenth century the Nizami branch of the Chishti order spread through the upper Punjab by way of his disciples.

In the colonial period the history of this lineage, the Chishti Nizami Sulaymaniyya, included battles over shrines in the Punjab, Taunsa among them. Struggles for power within the Sulaymaniyya can be traced to British manipulation and to the rivalry of local Sikhs, Hindus and Muslim reformers, but political contest is only part of its story.

## The Setting

Sial Sharif is a settlement in the Sargodha district, distinct from the city of Sargodha. More generally, the cult of the holy man, the *pir*, and the folk piety associated with him are particularly evident in the countryside, where major landlords and large concentrations of land are crucial features, especially in the Punjab and Sindh. In many cases the local *pir* represents the local landlord or is at least closely related to him.

The district also has a place in the Punjab's most famous romance. In the tale of Hir and Ranjha, Ranjha, the son of a landlord of the Sargodha district, falls in love with Hir, the daughter of the ruler of Jhang.

In the city of Sargodha itself, a man from the city has told of a *fakir*, a wandering mystic, who roams Sargodha all day long surrounded by dogs, refuses to talk to any human being, and offers his food to the dogs first. In one Muslim family's ancestral house in the city the arches had three cusps, which marked them as Sikh. In the early twenty first century sectarian conflict at the processions of Eid Milad-Un-Nabi, the celebration of the Prophet's birthday, remained a problem in cities such as Sargodha, Faisalabad and Dera Ismael Khan, where ultra orthodox Sunni organisations had a large base of support, though the incidents had so far been minor.

## Legacy

Khwaja Shamsuddin Sialvi holds an important place in the Chishti revival of the Punjab in the nineteenth century. He was a master whose *khanqah* at Sial Sharif carried the tradition forward and trained saints, above all Meher Ali Shah of Golra, who would shape the religious life of the region into the twentieth century. His shrine remains a great Chishti centre of central Punjab.

Name: Swami Dharmdas Darbar, Larkana (Kennedy Market)
Location: Kennedy Market area, Larkana, Larkana District, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: No events documented
Description:
The darbar of Swami Dharmdas at Larkana is one of the *Nanakpanthi* shrines of the Larkana country of upper Sindh, recorded by the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro in his survey of the region's Hindu–Sikh saints. Swami Dharamdas is remembered as a disciple of Sant Bhai Wasan Shah of Rohri; according to Kalhoro he first established a darbar at the village of Mena and afterwards founded the shrine at Larkana with which his name is chiefly associated, said to lie in the Kennedy Market quarter of the town. He was a contemporary of Sain Vali Vilayat Rai of Kambar (a separate entry in this dataset), one of a group of nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century *sants* who spread a message of love, harmony and tolerance among the Hindu, Muslim and Sikh communities of Sindh. In the Nanakpanthi manner, such darbars house a copy of the *Guru Granth Sahib* alongside images of Hindu deities, and honour Baba Guru Nanak without a firm confessional boundary. The saint's dates and the darbar's detailed history are only thinly documented in accessible sources, and — as with most Sindhi Hindu shrines — the size and present condition of the site are uncertain; the entry is offered on the authority of Kalhoro's fieldwork and should be treated as provisional. Kalhoro records this lineage directly, writing that "Swami Dharamdas was a disciple of Sant Bhai Wasan Shah in Rohri. First, he established a darbar in Mena village and later in Larkana," and identifying him as "Swami Dharmdas who founded a darbar in Kennedy Market in Larkana." Beyond this single account, no second independent source, and no dates for the founder or the darbar, could be located.
