Founded/Opened: Traditional founding date uncertain/legendary (accounts range from antiquity to the 11th–12th century CE); abandoned 1947
Events: None - abandoned since 1947
Description:
## Overview

Tilla Jogian, the "Hill of the Ascetics", crowns the highest peak of the eastern Salt Range in the Jhelum District of the Punjab, rising to some 975 metres above sea level. On its summit lie the ruins of an ancient temple and monastic complex that was, before 1947, the foremost centre of Hindu yogis in the whole of the Punjab. Cooler and greener than the parched country below, the hilltop has for many centuries been a retreat for renunciants seeking solitude, and its long association with the *Nath* order of yogis, with Guru Nanak and with the lovers of Punjabi legend has made it one of the most storied heights in the region.

The hill was the headquarters of the order of *Kanphata*, or 'split-eared', yogis, and the most important place of pilgrimage for jogis in the Punjab. In the reign of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, great crowds of people and bands of jogis gathered there for the festival of Shivrat. And in Heer and Ranjha, the romance of the poet Waris Shah, Tilla is the hill to which Ranjha comes to take *jog*, the discipline of renunciation, from the ascetic Bal Nath.

## Gorakhnath and the Nath Yogis

Tradition traces the sanctity of Tilla Jogian back some two thousand years and links its foundation to *Gorakhnath*, the revered yogi and organiser of the *Nath* tradition. That chronology is best read as legend rather than settled history, for Gorakhnath himself is usually placed centuries later, in about the eleventh or twelfth century. He was the head of the *Kanphata* yogis, and he is believed to be an avatar, an earthly form, of the god Shiva.

The Naths, or Nathpanthis, a school of renunciants devoted to Shiva, were the followers of Gorakhnath. They lived in forests and wandered in towns, and they also established permanent monasteries. The word *jogi*, the popular form of yogi, usually means one of them: a wandering ascetic devoted to Shiva who meditates on the One.

Gorakhnath's name also reaches well beyond this hill. One tradition tells that he sent an invisible army to help Goga Pir against Rai Pithora. Another holds that the goddess Hinglaj was very fond of the Nath community, and especially of Guru Gorakhnath, so that she waited day after day in Thatta for him to come to meet her. Two texts, the *Gorakh Caritra* and the *Gorakhpurāṇa*, describe his pilgrimage to Hinglaj, and the fireplace, or *dhuni*, of Guru Gorakhnath goes back to the long tradition of Nath yogis who made that journey.

Sikh tradition, too, brings him together with Guru Nanak. The Puratan Janamsakhis, early collections of stories of Guru Nanak's life, set Gorakhnath in conversation with Guru Nanak in their account of the anointment of Guru Angad, though historically Gorakhnath lived and preached long before Nanak's time.

## The Seat of the Jogis

Tilla Jogian became the principal seat of the *Kanphata* yogis, the 'split-eared' ascetics, so called from the great rings inserted through the cartilage of their ears at initiation, an order that looked to Gorakhnath as its master. On the hilltop the *jogis* maintained shrines, cells and reservoirs of water, and at its height the complex is said to have sheltered hundreds of ascetics who came to meditate there. The site formed the easternmost of a string of ancient Hindu sanctuaries along the Salt Range, a chain that also includes the temples of Katas Raj and, at its western end, the Amb temples above the Soon Valley.

In the reign of Aurangzeb the hill was the place of austerity of a jogi. It stood on top of the salt mountain, as the range was called, seven *kos*, an old measure of distance, from the fort of Rohtas. On the appointed days, and above all on the day of Shivrat, the festival of Shiva, great crowds of people and bands of jogis gathered there and put on displays.

## Guru Nanak and the Hill

Such was its renown as a place of Hindu spiritual power that it drew, in the early sixteenth century, *Guru Nanak*, the founder of the Sikh faith, who is remembered in tradition as having spent forty days in meditation upon the hill during his travels. The episode became part of the sacred memory of the site for Sikhs, adding another layer to a place already venerated by yogis and by Hindu pilgrims from across the Punjab.

The hill enters Guru Nanak's story by another road as well. It is told that Tripta came with her husband to Tilla Jogian, the most important place of pilgrimage for jogis in the Punjab, and that there the couple paid for the jogis' food for one day, as a result of which the jogis prayed all night to bless the young couple.

## Ranjha Takes Jog

Tilla Jogian holds a special place in Punjabi folklore through the tragic romance of *Heer and Ranjha*, immortalised in the eighteenth century by the Sufi poet *Waris Shah*, who dated his poem to the year 1180 of the Hijri, or Islamic, calendar. In the tale Ranjha, parted from his beloved Heer, climbs to Tilla Jogian in his grief and there renounces the world. Accounts differ over who initiated him, but the guru most often named is the ascetic *Bal Nath*, master of the hill, who pierces his ears and initiates him into the order of the *jogis*, granting him *jog*. Through this episode the hill entered the imaginative life of the Punjab as the very emblem of the lover turned ascetic, and generations who never climbed its slopes knew its name from the recitation of Waris Shah's verses.

Ranjha sets out for Tilla sure that Bal Nath knows the way of salvation, and after many days' journeying he reaches the hill on which Bal Nath lives. He bows his head, places before the guru a piece of *gur*, raw sugar, well known as a ceremonial offering in the Punjab countryside, and clasps the feet of all the jogis. The guru is the Hindu holy man and teacher, the Hindu counterpart of the Muslim *murshid*, or spiritual guide, and tradition counts Bal Nath as the fourth guru of the hill, which it also calls Tilla Guruan, the mound of the gurus.

The guru's *chelas*, his disciples, keep his house and kitchen. When Ranjha arrives, "They were all engaged in religious contemplation and prayers. They were reading Gayan Gita Bhagvat and Bharat." They have served Bal Nath for eighteen years, giving up all, living by begging and remembering God day and night, and still he has not given them jog. The tale sets caste against the vocation: "You Jats cannot attain Jog", and "What can a Jat do with a beggars bowl or horn, whose heart is set only on ploughing?" Ranjha's own name is that of a well known caste of the Jats, the farming and herding people of the old Punjab.

Bal Nath sets out the conditions of *jog*. Ranjha will have to dress as a jogi, wear dirty clothes, long hair and a cropped skull, and beg his way through life. He will have to give up the pleasures of birth, cease to rejoice when friends come or to grieve when they die, and abstain from casting eyes on women. He will have to become divinely intoxicated with opium and other narcotic drugs, and go on long pilgrimages to Jagannath, Godavari, Ganges and Jamna. The poem defines *jog* in its own terms:

*Jog means to be dead while alive. One has to sing the song of nonentity using ones meagre body as a guitar. One's self has to be entirely absorbed. It is no child's play.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

*God has made his abode in this body of dust He is in every thing as a thread runs through the beads.* (translated by Charles Frederick Usborne)

A commentator on the poem reads its song of nonentity as the doctrine of annihilation in God, *fana fillah*, as practised by the Sufis, the Muslim mystics, a doctrine with strong spiritual affiliations with the Nirvana of the Hindus and Buddhists. The poem also names a degree of *jog* called Chit Akas, reached after passing through the stages of Bhut Kas and Juda Kas, the three planes of the philosophy of jog.

Ranjha, for his part, admits that the vocation is a means to his love: "Hir has captivated my heart. That is why I have become a Jogi." Then comes the rite of initiation. At their guru's order the chelas bring the earrings and the razor. Bal Nath takes off Ranjha's clothes, rubs him in ashes, embraces him and seats him by his side; then with the razor of separation he shaves him completely, bores his ears and puts the earrings on him. He places in his hands the beggar's bowl, the rosary, the horn and the shell, and last of all he teaches him the word Allah. With the rite comes a moral rule: "An old woman should be treated as your mother and a young woman as your sister."

So Ranjha, a Muslim, becomes the spiritual disciple of a Hindu yogi. As the same commentator observes, "This may seem strange today, but was by no means unusual at the time."

The chelas turn on their guru, leaving the jogi's house and kitchen and piercing him with shameless taunts. When they rebel, Bal Nath rebukes them, his anger blazing from his eyes; so powerful is the enchantment he lays upon them that they obey at once, and all ill feeling vanishes from their minds. Yet Bal Nath himself comes to regret his gift: "Verily I repent and am sorry for having given Jog to this youth. He has got the treasures of jog without spending a single farthing."

At the hill, too, a prayer is answered aloud. Bal Nath prays, pours ashes over his body and plunges his soul into the deep waters of meditation, and a reply comes from the *Darbar*, the court, of God: "Hir has been bestowed on Ranjha and his boat has been taken ashore." A popular belief of the Punjab countryside holds that fakirs, the wandering mystics, and jogis can, by the force of their piety, make the Moving Finger of Destiny cancel what it has written.

One cry of protest names the hill once more: "Had I known that you would try to keep me from my Love, I would never have set foot on your hill of Tilla." At last Ranjha makes haste to leave Tilla, gathering strange herbs and potent roots from the woods. The boring of the ears is the act that makes a jogi, and the tale returns to it again and again after Ranjha leaves the hill, until at the end the jogi's rings are taken out of his ears.

## The Hill in Sufi Poetry

The Sufi poet Bulleh Shah, too, follows the initiate to Tilla step by step in one of his lyrics:

*Casting aside his drum, he goes toward Tilla, he sits and meditates on his name. He has his ears split and the earrings inserted, and is initiated by the guru* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

The lyric then names the authority a *pir*, a Sufi spiritual guide, must satisfy:

*My Pir gains the approval of guru Gorakh. He keeps crying 'Hir, Hir.'* (translated by Christopher Shackle)

Bulleh Shah's verse draws on the yogis' own world. Its yogi has his ochre dress, his deerskin, skull cup, matted hair and ashes, his forehead mark, and his horn, bowl and beads; yogis sit before a bonfire and rub its ashes on their bodies. Its vocabulary is theirs too. The 'unstruck music' is the mystical sound heard at the climax of the yogic process, the 'circle of nectar' is a traditional image for the ecstatic state that is the goal of yoga, and the 'tenth door' is the hidden aperture in the skull that is opened at that climax. To 'make the Ganges flow backward', an idiom for doing the opposite of the usual, here means the drawing up of psychic energy during the yogic process, and the 'fourth state' is the state of liberation reached by transcending the three *gunas*, the qualities that govern worldly existence.

## The Salt Range

The Salt Range, on whose eastern heights the hill stands, is the line of mountains dividing the plains of the Punjab from the slightly elevated plateau of the Potwar. There is no irrigation in the range.

In the reign of Aurangzeb, rock salt was dug at the foot of the hills near Shamsabad, in the Sind Sagar doab, a *doab* being the land between two rivers, and it was famous above all other salts. Each miner went into the tunnels naked, with a lamp in his hand and a pick on his shoulder, cut a lump of about three maunds, an old measure of weight, and carried it out on his back. The miners were paid wages by the overseers of the work and felt no fear, and the tunnels, it was held, were by divine wisdom neither hot in summer nor cold in winter. Two large tunnels near Shamsabad yielded many lakhs, that is hundreds of thousands, of maunds of salt every year, and their revenue, with that of other places, went into the imperial treasury. Craftsmen made trays, dishes, covers and lampstands of salt, and the sweet gypsum found next to it was used for whitewash inside the houses of the great.

Hindus held that a pool in the range, whose depth no one could tell, was an ancient temple, and on great days such as the sun's entry into Aries they crowded there. They believed that the earth has two eyes: the right is a pool near Ajmer, and the left is this pool. The range was also called the mountain of Jud. Jud was the chief of the Janjua tribe, whose descendants still lived and ruled at the foot of the hills.

## Ruin and Legacy

The complex flourished until the Partition of 1947, when the departure of its Hindu and yogi custodians for India left it without a resident community. Though accounts of its later state differ, deprived of care the buildings fell into decay: the reservoirs silted, the shrines crumbled, and in the decades since the site has been steadily overgrown. By the early twenty first century much of it lay beneath a spread of wild olive and scrub, its masonry slipping into ruin. Conservationists and writers have repeatedly warned that this remarkable monument, at once archaeological site, sacred summit and literary landmark, risks being lost altogether without deliberate protection. Its remoteness has spared it the crowds that press upon lower shrines, but that same isolation has hastened its neglect.

Tilla Jogian gathers into one windswept hilltop several of the great strands of Punjabi religious and cultural history: the antiquity of the *Nath* yogis and their Kanphata order, the pilgrim memory of Guru Nanak, and the deathless romance of Heer and Ranjha. As one of the trio of Salt Range sanctuaries alongside Katas Raj and the Amb temples, it testifies to a landscape once dense with Hindu holiness. For the modern traveller it offers a rare and melancholy grandeur, ruined shrines amid olive groves commanding a vast prospect over the Jhelum plains, and stands as a reminder of a plural sacred past that survives now chiefly in stone and in song.

The romance of Heer and Ranjha lives on in song. It is the greatest of the local legends of the Punjab, set in the world of the Jat pastoral tribes of the western Punjab. Elaborated in more than a hundred versions in Punjabi, Urdu, Sindhi and Persian, it was given its final form in the late eighteenth century by Waris Shah, and it is his verse that is sung, time and again, wherever Punjabis meet; a visitor who stays in a Punjabi village will certainly find somebody to sing it in the classical form he gave it. Waris Shah is said to have recited it with great emotion among the people of his own speech, and many renowned folk artists in the Punjab have sung it, among them Reshma, Zahida Parvin, Nazir Begum, Sabiha Khanum, Tufail Niazi and Iqbal Bahu.

Punjabi poets and their eager audiences poured into Heer and Ranjha the same erotic emotion that was invested in Radha and Krishna in regions closer to the Ganges, and the story became a favourite Sufi device for conveying the value of erotic passion in spiritual life. Already in the reign of Aurangzeb, wonderful verses and designs on the love of Heer and Ranjha were composed and sung in the province of Lahore.

Name: Tomb of Allama Iqbal (Mazar-e-Iqbal)
Events: Iqbal Day (9 November); death anniversary (21 April); daily changing of the guard
Description:
## Overview

Mazar-e-Iqbal is the tomb of Allama Muhammad Iqbal (1877 to 1938), the poet, philosopher and jurist honoured across Pakistan as its ideological father, the Mufakkir-e-Pakistan, or Thinker of Pakistan. It stands in the Hazuri Bagh, the walled garden between the great Badshahi Mosque and the Lahore Fort, in the monumental heart of the old city and within sight of the Minar-e-Pakistan. It is not a Sufi shrine in the traditional sense, the tomb of a Muslim mystic, but the resting place of a modern thinker; yet Pakistanis approach it as a place of pilgrimage and national homage, coming to recite the Fatiha, the opening chapter of the Qur'an, and to honour the man whose verse and vision gave the Muslims of South Asia the idea of a homeland of their own.

It is one of the most revered sites in the country, and to understand it is above all to understand the life, the poetry and the thought of the man who lies within it.

## The Poet's Life

Muhammad Iqbal was born on 9 November 1877. Accounts of his birthplace differ, but it is generally given as the city of Sialkot, in the Punjab, and it was in Sialkot that he spent his boyhood. His family descended from Kashmiri Brahmins who had embraced Islam some generations before and settled in the plains, a descent the tomb's records still register, in the old style, as "Sheikh/Brahman". His father, Sheikh Noor Muhammad, was a tailor of modest means but of unusual spiritual depth, a man remembered for his piety and his love of the Qur'an.

Devotional tradition tells that before Iqbal's birth his father dreamed of a radiant white bird descending from the sky, sought after by many hands, which at last settled in his own lap, and that he woke convinced a remarkable child was coming to his house. It was Sheikh Noor Muhammad who first shaped his son's inner life. He urged the boy to recite the holy book slowly and with attention, as though it had been revealed for him to understand, and that counsel left in Iqbal a lifelong intimacy with the Qur'an.

Near the family home the boy was placed in the care of the learned Sayyid Mir Hassan, an imam, or prayer leader, and a teacher of rare gifts, who taught him Arabic, Persian and Urdu and quickened in him a hunger to understand rather than merely to memorise. Recognising his pupil's promise, Mir Hassan guided him on to the Scotch Mission High School in Sialkot, a Christian school, where the young Iqbal is said to have completed two classes in a single year. In these years too, at his elders' wish and against his own inclination, he was married as a boy of about sixteen to Karim Bibi, of a family from Gujrat. The marriage, entered so young, did not endure happily, and through his life Iqbal's deepest energies were drawn away from a settled home towards learning, poetry and the cause of his people.

From Sialkot Iqbal moved to Lahore to study at Government College, then the foremost seat of learning in the province. There he read philosophy and English literature and came under the influence of the Orientalist Sir Thomas Arnold, a teacher whose learning and friendship shaped him profoundly and who later drew him towards Europe. Even as a student his poetry began to circulate, and when some of his verses were shown to the celebrated Delhi master Dagh Dehlvi, a connoisseur of Urdu, Dagh is said to have marvelled that whoever had written them was no ordinary poet. After taking his degree Iqbal joined the Oriental College, Lahore, in 1899 as a reader in Arabic and taught philosophy, already known in the city's *mushairas*, the literary gatherings where poets recite, for verse of unusual power. From this period, too, dates his long association with his devoted household servant Ali Baksh, who served him faithfully to the end and who, after the poet's death, would tell of the private wonders of his master's life.

In 1905 Iqbal sailed for Europe, where he spent three transforming years. He read philosophy at Trinity College, Cambridge, qualified as a barrister at Lincoln's Inn in London, and took a doctorate at the University of Munich with a dissertation on *The Development of Metaphysics in Persia*, published in 1908. In Europe he came to know Western philosophy at first hand, meeting the currents of thought associated with Nietzsche, Bergson and others, and he saw, too, the spiritual emptiness he believed lay beneath the material power of the modern West. He returned to India in 1908 with a settled conviction: that the Muslims of the world had fallen from greatness through the loss of their own inner vitality, and that they must be reawakened, not by imitating Europe, but by recovering the dynamism, faith and selfhood of their own tradition.

Back in Lahore he took up the practice of law and taught for a time, but he was candid that the law was for him a means and not an end: he practised, he said, only so far as it secured his independence and left him free to serve his nation with his true instruments, which were poetry and thought. After the estrangement of his first marriage he married Sardar Begum and Mukhtar Begum, in the years around 1910 to 1913, and became the father of children, among them his son Javid, to whom the great Persian poem the *Javid Nama* is addressed. In 1922 the British Crown knighted him, and he became Sir Muhammad Iqbal, though the title sat lightly on a man who lived simply and counted his books and his verse his truest companions. He could bestow a title as well: it was Iqbal who started to call the writer Hasan Nizami "Khwaja", or master, a title with ancient resonance in the tradition of the Chishtis, the Sufi order prominent in South Asia.

Iqbal did not hold himself aloof from public affairs. He served as a member of the Punjab Legislative Council and took part in the Round Table Conferences convened in London to debate the constitutional future of India, lending to practical politics the moral authority of a thinker whose deepest labour lay elsewhere. His boldness of thought sometimes drew fire: when he argued that the inherited interpretation of Islamic law must be rethought for the modern age, some among the orthodox turned against him and issued condemnations. In his last years his health declined, and in his final illness he is said to have refused heavy treatment, explaining that he did not wish to be dulled into unconsciousness but to meet death fully aware. He died in Lahore in 1938, on 21 April, the date the nation observes, though accounts of the day differ. To his people he is known by titles that between them capture the range of the man: Shair-e-Mashriq, the Poet of the East; Hakeem-ul-Ummat, the Sage of the Community; and Mufakkir-e-Pakistan, the Thinker of Pakistan.

## The Poet of the East

Iqbal is, before all else, one of the supreme poets of the Urdu and Persian languages, and his verse is the true foundation of his fame. His Urdu collections, *Bang-e-Dara* ("The Call of the Marching Bell"), *Bal-e-Jibril* ("Gabriel's Wing") and *Zarb-e-Kalim* ("The Rod of Moses"), stand beside his great Persian works, among them *Asrar-e-Khudi* ("The Secrets of the Self"), *Rumuz-e-Bekhudi* ("The Mysteries of Selflessness"), *Payam-e-Mashriq* ("The Message of the East") and the visionary *Javid Nama*, in which the poet ascends through the heavens in the company of Rumi. Together they are gathered for readers as the *Kulliyat-e-Iqbal*, the collected works, and it is in this collection that his poetry is most widely read today. His verse ranges from devotion to the most demanding philosophy, and its lines are known by heart, quoted in ordinary speech and sung across the subcontinent.

His books of verse followed one another: the *Asrar-e-Khudi* in 1915, the *Rumuz-e-Bekhudi* in 1917, the *Payam-e-Mashriq* in 1923, the *Bang-e-Dara* in 1924, the Persian *Zabūr-i ʿAjam* in 1927, the *Javid Nama* in 1932, *Musafir* in 1934, the *Bal-e-Jibril* in 1935, the *Zarb-e-Kalim* and *Pas che bāyad kard* in 1936, and the *Armaghān-i Ḥijāz* in 1938. The title *Bang-e-Dara* names the part he took for himself: the caravan bell that helps guide the travellers to the central sanctuary in Mecca.

From his early period comes the children's morning prayer that generations have sung at school assembly:

لب پہ آتی ہے دعا بن کے تمنا میری
زندگی شمع کی صورت ہو خدایا میری

*My longing comes to my lips as a prayer: O God, may my life be like a candle, that it may give light to the world.*

From the same early collection comes the anthem that first made his name a household word, *Tarana-e-Hindi*:

سارے جہاں سے اچھا ہندوستاں ہمارا
ہم بلبلیں ہیں اس کی، یہ گلستاں ہمارا

*Better than the entire world is our land; we are its nightingales, and it is our garden.*

And in one famous *ghazal*, a short lyric poem, from *Bang-e-Dara*, the longing that runs through all his work, the yearning of the servant for the vision of God, finds one of its most quoted forms:

کبھی اے حقیقتِ منتظر نظر آ لباسِ مجاز میں
کہ ہزاروں سجدے تڑپ رہے ہیں مری جبینِ نیاز میں

*O awaited Reality, appear but once in the garb of the material world; for a thousand prostrations writhe in longing upon my brow of supplication.*

Over time his vision widened from the love of the homeland to the love of the whole Muslim community, and finally to a summons addressed to all humanity before God. In *Bang-e-Dara* the long and daring poem *Shikwa* ("The Complaint") gives voice to a believer's plaintive reproach to God at the fallen state of the Muslims, and its companion *Jawab-e-Shikwa* ("The Answer to the Complaint") supplies the divine reply: not consolation but a challenge, calling the community to make itself worthy of its inheritance once more. Recited from public platforms, these poems electrified their hearers and remain among the most famous in the language. The same summons rings through *Tulu-e-Islam* ("The Dawn of Islam"), whose lines became a kind of watchword for Muslim revival:

یقیں محکم، عمل پیہم، محبت فاتحِ عالم
جہادِ زندگانی میں ہیں یہ مردوں کی شمشیریں

*Firm certainty, ceaseless action, and a love that conquers the world: these are the swords of true men in the struggle of life.*

In poems such as *Khizr-e-Rah* ("Khizr, the Guide of the Way") he turned the same searching gaze on the poverty and bondage of his age, on labour and capital and empire, insisting that the message of faith was also a demand for justice in the world of men. Old figures served him too. Farhad, the luckless lover, became in his work, as in other modern progressive writing, the representative of the oppressed working class, while Sultan Mahmud, the king transformed into the ideal lover who finally became the slave of his slave, remained a theme of his poetry.

If any single image belongs to Iqbal, it is the *shaheen*, the eagle or royal falcon: his emblem of the free and austere spirit that relies on itself, scorns comfort, keeps no store and makes its home upon the heights. Against every temptation to ease and every limit set upon human aspiration, he summoned the young especially to a life of soaring effort:

نہیں تیرا نشیمن قصرِ سلطانی کے گنبد پر
تو شاہیں ہے، بسیرا کر پہاڑوں کی چٹانوں میں

*Your nest is not on the dome of the royal palace; you are an eagle: make your dwelling in the crags of the mountains.*

Another couplet carries the same summons further still:

ستاروں سے آگے جہاں اور بھی ہیں
ابھی عشق کے امتحاں اور بھی ہیں

*Beyond the stars there are yet other worlds; there are still more trials of love to be met.*

Nowhere is his union of art and thought more complete than in *Masjid-e-Qurtuba* ("The Mosque of Córdoba"), composed after he visited the great mosque in Spain: a sustained meditation on time, love and the deathless work of the man of God, widely held to be among the finest poems in the Urdu language. Another of his emblems is the tulip, *lāla*, the independent, vigorous plant that appears in the middle of the desert, resembling in its shape and colour the flames that Moses saw on Mount Sinai. Set against the traditional rose that lives in carefully trimmed gardens, it becomes a symbol of man's striving against heavy odds to realise himself.

Iqbal praised the Prophet Muhammad most eloquently, although he never wrote a formal *naʿt*, a poem in praise of the Prophet, in the traditional style. Even his early Urdu poems, such as *Jawab-e-Shikwa*, contain verses in praise of the Prophet, and there he sang: *Light the world, too long in darkness, / With Muhammad's radiant name.* A few years later, in the *Asrar-e-Khudi* of 1915, his first revolutionary Persian *mathnawi*, a long poem in rhyming couplets, he devoted some of his finest lines to Muhammad and claimed: *All our glory is from the name of Muhammad.* In the *Rumuz-e-Bekhudi*, the collection that turns his social and political ideals into Persian verse, the Prophet appears as the lamp in the darkness of existence.

His last verses are devoted to the Hijaz, the country he never visited, and among them stands the line *For us Mustafa is enough*, calling the Prophet by his title Mustafa, the Chosen One. In the *Javid Nama* he had gone further still, in the daring line *You can deny God, but you cannot deny the Prophet!* For Iqbal the Prophet was a leader in this world as well as the next, the political leader able to guide people towards their destiny even here, a view reflected in the complaint of Abu Jahl, one of the Prophet's grimmest enemies, who defends narrow patriotism and the distinction of races and castes. In a passage of the *Javid Nama* he defines the Prophet's state as more than human, in a poem he puts in the mouth of the mystic Hallaj, whose hymn in honour of the Prophet forms the beginning of the mystics' teaching on the Prophet, a poem turning on the word *ʿabduhu*, His slave. In Iqbal's thought Muhammad is both the political leader of his community and the scent of the mystic rose.

In 1936, hoping to be cured of an ailment, he wrote a poem in praise of the Prophet, the Arabian friend, as he called him like many Indian Muslim poets before him. He tells in a letter that he had been advised to write it by a dream apparition of Sir Sayyid Ahmad Khan, an episode that recalls the healing quality remembered of al-Būṣīrī's *Burda*, the poem in praise of the Prophet whose copies were still being sold in the shops of Lahore in the 1970s.

The *Javid Nama*, printed in 1932, takes the form of the heavenly journey made in the company of a spiritual preceptor, in Iqbal's case the spirit of Rumi, who leads the poet through the spheres and into the presence of the divine as Virgil led Dante. The poem is built from the old materials of the mystics. Imitating the title of Hallaj's *Tawasin*, Iqbal invented the *tawasin* of the Prophets, the dwelling places of the prophetic spirits in the Sphere of the Moon, and a section of the poem bears the title "Tāsīn of Muhammad". He took over Rumi's story of the Zoroastrian, where it serves to assert the spiritual strength of the Islamic religion and of true Muslims. And in the poem's Heaven of Jupiter he treated Hallaj as a sort of medieval forerunner of himself, holding up his dynamic idea of love and faith as an ideal for every free Muslim.

## The Thinker

At the centre of Iqbal's thought lies the idea of *khudi*, selfhood, or the realisation of the ego, which he set out first in the Persian *Asrar-e-Khudi* and its companion *Rumuz-e-Bekhudi*. By *khudi* he meant not selfishness but the awakening, disciplining and strengthening of the individual self through love, action and nearness to God, until the human being becomes a conscious fellow worker in the unfolding of creation. Against what he saw as the passivity and weariness of a decayed mysticism, a Sufism that counselled the annihilation of the self, and against the soulless materialism he had observed in the modern West, he preached striving, mastery of the self and the forging of the *mard-e-momin*, the complete believer who unites inward faith with outward power. He cast much of his deepest thought in Persian so that it might address the entire Muslim world. His most famous couplet fixes the height to which he believed the self could rise:

خودی کو کر بلند اتنا کہ ہر تقدیر سے پہلے
خدا بندے سے خود پوچھے، بتا تیری رضا کیا ہے

*Raise your selfhood so high that, before issuing each decree, God Himself asks His servant: 'Tell me, what is it that you wish?'*

And of that complete believer, in whom the human will becomes an instrument of the divine, he wrote in *Bal-e-Jibril*:

ہاتھ ہے اللہ کا بندۂ مومن کا ہاتھ
غالب و کار آفریں، کار کشا، کار ساز

*The hand of the true believer is the hand of God: triumphant and creative, resolving all difficulty, accomplishing all things.*

The doctrine draws on the older vocabulary of the mystics. Iqbal never tired of describing the long way of development from a drop to the ocean, from sperm to man, and eventually to the Perfect Man, the crown and apex of creation. Shabistari's *Gulshan-i raz*, in its form and content, inspired his *Gulshan-i raz-i jadid*, "The New Rose Garden of Mystery", published in 1927 and appended to his Persian *Zabūr-i ʿAjam*; in it he follows Shabistari's notions and offers his own answers to the questions of the Perfect Man, one of his central ideas, of God, and of destiny. He held that the trust spoken of in the Qur'an is the possibility of individuation. And he spoke of a higher predestination, *jabr mahmud*, reached not simply by accepting a given situation but by actively conforming with God's will through love and prayer. He claimed that he would call a people to spiritual resurrection, and in this he took on, in a sense, the role of the *qutb*, the axis or pole of the saints, the highest spiritual station. The three angelic figures Sarosh, Israfil and Gabriel occur very frequently in his poetry.

Iqbal set out his ideas not in verse alone but in searching prose. His English lectures, printed at Lahore in 1930 as *Six Lectures on the Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam* and many times since as *The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam*, remain among the most ambitious modern attempts to rethink Islamic philosophy in dialogue with modern science, evolutionary biology and Western metaphysics. In them he argued for the reopening of *ijtihad*, independent reasoning in the interpretation of Islamic law, so that the community might meet the demands of a changing world without losing its spiritual core, and he reflected on the nature of the self, of time, of prayer and of religious experience. It was these bold arguments that drew the censure of some traditional scholars in his lifetime, and the book continues to be studied, taught and debated wherever the future of Islamic thought is discussed.

In the fifth chapter of the lectures he follows the saints of medieval Islam in drawing the difference between mystical and prophetic religion, and he found that difference expressed in a nutshell in a remark of ʿAbdul Quddūs Gangohī about the Prophet's ascension: the Prophet returned in order to work in the world, while the true mystic would never like to return. In his modern reading of mystical symbols he understood the Prophet's saying "I have a time with God in which no created being has access, not even Gabriel who is pure spirit" as a reference to the moment at which serial time, "the infidel's girdle", is torn and the mystic establishes direct contact with God in an encounter of person with person.

His thought was forged in a lifelong dialogue between two worlds. His spiritual master across the centuries was Jalaluddin Rumi, the thirteenth century Persian mystic, whom he took as his guide in the fullest sense, and from whom he drew his conviction that love, *ishq*, is the engine of the self and of the cosmos, a force higher than mere intellect. He read Rumi's "I died as mineral" passage as a statement of evolution, a reading that reached him through the Indian scholar Maulana Shibli's Urdu biography of Rumi of 1903, which deeply influenced his ideas, and he gave the idea of constant development a new interpretation in his poetry. He inserted many of Rumi's lines into his own works, chiefly into his *mathnawis*, which he wrote in the same metre as Rumi's *Mathnawi*. Rumi's contrast of Intellect and Love, in which Intellect still looks for a camel to make the pilgrimage when Love has already reached the hill of Safa, he took up in his lyrical poetry, above all in the *Payam-e-Mashriq*. There too stands his poem contrasting Avicenna and Rumi, with the bookworm that dwells in Avicenna's pages and so lacks real experience of life and love. He admitted, too, his indebtedness to Bedil's poetry for the formation of his thought.

Yet Iqbal had also mastered European philosophy at first hand, and much of his originality lies in how he answered it. He admired the dynamism of Western thought, its science, its energy, its worship of will and action, while rejecting what he saw as its spiritual bankruptcy. Nietzsche's vision of the *Übermensch*, the superman who creates his own values in a world without God, fascinated and repelled him. Iqbal's own ideal, the *mard-e-momin*, is a figure of immense will, but one whose power is surrendered to God and disciplined by love, not a lonely idol of the self, and his idea of the Perfect Man, the one who has developed his individual possibilities to the fullest bloom, is not derived from the Nietzschean superman. From Bergson he took a vivid sense of time as living duration and of the universe as an unfinished, creative becoming, which he wove into his dynamic understanding of *khudi*. He turned a fierce moral gaze on the political forms of the modern West, on a narrow territorial nationalism that set brother against brother and on an imperial capitalism that ground down the poor and the colonised. His counsel to the East was neither to imitate Europe nor to shun it, but to take its fire while keeping its own soul, marrying action to faith and knowledge to love, so that the reawakened Muslim might be at once modern and whole.

He quarrelled with the Sufism of his own day. He attacked what he called pirism: the absolute sway of the spiritual master, the *pir*, over his followers, and the exploitation of ignorant peasants and villagers that went with it. He counted it one of the most dangerous aspects of Islam, a wall that closes off large groups of Muslims from a new and vital interpretation of Islamic values, and more than once he attacked the backwardness of those who passed for spiritual leaders in the subcontinent. He reacted sharply, too, to the poetry of *wahdat al-wujud*, the unity of being, with its imagery of indifference to ritual and its sweeping generalisations that seemed to leave no room for truly Islamic values, and, taking over Hali's verdict on mystical poetry, he claimed that mystical poetry after Hafiz might prove utterly dangerous for the morals of a people. Yet he admitted in the *Javid Nama*: *If the purpose of poetry is to form men, / Poetry is the heir of prophecy.*

The attack has its counterweight, for he himself followed the Sufi thought of the classical period quite closely. As a thinker he turned from the pantheism of Hegel and of Ibn ʿArabi to what seemed to him true Islam, and in fact relied heavily upon the heritage of the great masters of early Sufism. Much as he detested the enthralling, otherworldly mysticism he thought was hidden behind Hafiz's beautiful verses, he used the whole fabric of Sufi imagery in his own poetry, though he often reinterpreted it. Like Bedil, he criticised Sufi gluttony, making a fake *murid*, a pledged disciple, explain that God, though closer than the jugular vein, as the Qur'an has it, is not closer to man than his stomach.

Hallaj stayed with him from his youth onward. In his youth Iqbal described the great mystic as a pantheist, as he had seen him through hundreds of Persian, Urdu and Panjabi poems, but he later recognised Hallaj's strong personal religious commitment and saw in him one of the few who had attained to an experience of the divine higher than that of ordinary people: a man who had called the slumbering Muslims to a personal realisation of the truth, and so came into conflict with religious authorities who were afraid of any ardent witness for the living God. He came to know Hallaj's work through Louis Massignon's books. A former critic of Hallaj, he finally understood his cry *ana al-haqq*, "I am the Truth", as the Infinite entering into the loving embrace of the Finite.

The many aspects of Satan that the Sufis developed over the centuries live on in his work, in a picture of Satan of many colours. He sees in him the lover as well as the intellectual, the monotheist, and the spirit of evil who longs to be overcome by the perfect man and to be broken in order to find salvation, so that in the end he will prostrate himself before man, who proves stronger than he. Iqbal also used the more common image of Satan the seducer, the materialist and the destroyer, and his Satan sadly complains that it is much too easy for him to seduce people.

Prayer and longing run through his work. For him true prayer is constant: it cannot be limited to a number of *rak'as*, the cycles of ritual prayer, and portions of the Qur'an, but permeates man's whole being, an idea in which he follows Rumi. He often speaks of the miraculous power of true prayer, which ends in a complete conformity of the human to the divine will. He interpreted the song of the nightingale through his philosophy of unfulfilled union and longing: only longing gives the soul bird the capacity to sing. In his thought, longing is the highest state the soul can reach, for it results in creativity, whereas union brings about silence and annihilation.

For all his reservations about the legacy of institutional Sufism, which he judged medieval and opposed to progress, his poet's heart produced a *ghazal* in praise of the paragon of Chishti spirituality, Shaykh Nizam ad-Din Awliya': "Iltija-ye Musafir", "A Pilgrim's Plea". Two of its lines, in the English of Shantanu Phukan, turn on the circling of a grave: "A step around your grave's a step into the life within", and, of a saint the poem does not name, "Grant that I step, just once, around his tomb."

## The Idea of Pakistan

Iqbal's enduring place in the history of the subcontinent rests, finally, on his political vision. In his presidential address to the annual session of the All-India Muslim League at Allahabad in 1930, he argued that the Muslims of the northwest of India, of the Punjab, the North-West Frontier, Sindh and Baluchistan, formed a distinct nation with its own culture, law and moral order, and that their destiny would be best secured in a consolidated Muslim state, governing itself, within or without the British Empire. The address is remembered as the intellectual seed from which the demand for Pakistan would grow.

In the last years of his life Iqbal corresponded closely with Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the Quaid-e-Azam, or Great Leader, urging him to return from London to lead the Muslims of India and pressing upon him the case for a separate homeland; their letters are treasured as a founding document of the Pakistan Movement. He and Jinnah are said to have become involved in the Shaheed Ganj riots as they tried to calm the Muslims, a case that the Lahore High Court heard in the British era and again around 1957 and 1958. Iqbal's concern was never merely territorial: he insisted that a true Islamic polity must also be a just one, freeing the poor and the labouring from exploitation, and he saw the proposed state as a place where the ethical vision of his faith might be lived out.

He did not live to see it. He died in 1938, nine years before Pakistan came into being in August 1947, and before the Muslim League presented in Lahore, in March 1940, the Lahore Resolution, drafted by Sir Zaffarullah Khan. The new nation enshrined him as its ideological founder, one of the founding fathers of Pakistan, and its highest honours and its very image of itself are bound up with his name.

## The Tomb

Iqbal was laid to rest on a raised platform in the Hazuri Bagh, in the narrow but hallowed ground between the steps of the Badshahi Mosque and the wall of the Lahore Fort, a site of the utmost symbolic dignity at the ceremonial heart of Mughal Lahore. His mausoleum was raised in the years after his death and completed around 1951, its design a dignified fusion of Afghan with Moorish and Mughal styles. Built chiefly of red sandstone, it is grave and elegant rather than grand. The fine marble within and the two headstones of lapis lazuli are traditionally said to have been gifts from Afghanistan, whose rulers claimed a special reverence for the poet who had sung of the Muslim world beyond India's borders, and verses of Iqbal's own composition are inscribed inside.

The tomb is a protected national monument, maintained by the Government of Punjab, and a ceremonial guard furnished by the Pakistan Rangers is posted at its entrance; the changing of the guard is itself a small daily ceremony that visitors gather to watch. Its placement is deliberate and eloquent: the poet of Islamic revival rests for ever between the greatest mosque and the greatest fort of the old Mughal capital, and close by the Minar-e-Pakistan, raised to mark the demand for the country he imagined.

Iqbal has a second memorial. By the 1970s a *maqam* of Muhammad Iqbal, a place bearing his name, had been raised in the garden of Rumi's tomb at Konya, so that the poet who took Rumi as his guide is remembered in the garden of his master's tomb as well as in his own city.

## Homage and Remembrance

Hemmed in by the Badshahi Mosque, the Lahore Fort and the Minar-e-Pakistan, the mausoleum lies within the single most visited heritage precinct in the country. It draws a great and constant stream of Pakistani and foreign visitors, some forty to fifty thousand a day, and on national days and the poet's anniversaries the numbers swell towards a hundred thousand. Many come first to see the mosque, the fort and the gardens and turn aside to recite the Fatiha at Iqbal's grave; others come expressly to pay homage.

On Pakistan's national days and on Iqbal's death anniversary, floral wreaths and a ceremonial *chadar*, the sheet of cloth laid over a grave, are placed upon the grave, as they are on religious and celebratory occasions through the year, and the Army mounts a parade, rendering a formal guard of honour and a ceremonial salute, the *salami*. Because Iqbal was at once a devout Muslim thinker and a poet of vast popular reach, his tomb has gathered a quiet devotional aura not unlike that of the older shrines of the city: visitors recite the Fatiha there as at a *darbar*, a saint's shrine, and folk memory preserves stories of the poet's nearness to the saints.

Pakistan keeps Iqbal's memory as a kind of national trust. His death anniversary on 21 April, and above all Iqbal Day on his birthday, 9 November, are observed across the country with ceremonies, seminars and recitations of his verse. At the mausoleum, heads of state and visiting foreign dignitaries lay wreaths, and the site serves as a place of national remembrance as much as of private prayer. His poetry is set to music and sung, though in Pakistan *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, became the one musical genre with a clear Muslim identity, overshadowing even the sung poetry of Iqbal. His lines are quoted by leaders and inscribed on public buildings, his works are taught in every school, and his portrait travels with Jinnah's on the country's everyday surfaces, from a Pakistani flag at the Kallar Kahar cable car, with the two men on its green section, to an office wall at a school in Makhdoom Pur Pahuran.

## Legends

Among the folk stories of Iqbal's nearness to the saints, one is told on the word of his faithful servant Ali Baksh. One night, it is said, the poet bade him fetch *lassi*, a yoghurt drink, for guests who were coming, though it was the dead of night and the bazaar was shut. Setting out, the servant found the lane bathed in an unearthly light and an old man with a luminous face selling lassi where no shop had ever stood, who took no payment, saying, "I have an old account with Iqbal." When Ali Baksh later pressed his master to explain, Iqbal is said to have revealed, under a promise of secrecy kept until the poet's death, that the guests had been Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti of Ajmer, and the seller of lassi none other than Data Ganj Bakhsh, Ali Hujwiri, the patron saint of Lahore.

Hujwiri died in Lahore in 1071, and his shrine, called that of Data Ganj Bakhsh, is still a popular place of pilgrimage in the city. Such stories, whatever the historian may make of them, bind the modern thinker to the ancient sacred landscape of Lahore, and they are part of why ordinary people cherish his memory as they do that of a saint.

Another story of the poet among the saints is told by Ghulam Muhammad, a dervish at a crow shrine in Gujrat. Allama Iqbal, he says, once came to see the saint there, and one of the saint's devotees told him that the Allama wished to speak to him. "All of them are Allamas for me," the saint replied, meaning his crows.

## The Setting

The Roshani Gate, one of the thirteen gateways that lead into the ancient walled city of Lahore, stands between the Alamgiri Gate and the Royal Mosque; lamps were lit all along its passageway, hence its name, the gate of lights. Behind it is the Heera-Mandi bazaar, the area once reserved for the city's prostitutes, before they dispersed all over Lahore after a crackdown on them during the Islamist government of General Zia-ul-Haq. The musicians remain: it is still one of the largest markets for traditional instruments in the city, and the area is famous too for the food street that runs parallel to the wall of the Badshahi Masjid.

The River Ravi, which once flowed next to the fort, has changed its course and moved a few kilometres away. The Parsi community buries its dead in a graveyard next to the Minar-e-Pakistan, facing the ancient walled city. The Lahore Fort was a fort where only royalty stayed, and at the end of Sikh rule, with the British annexation of the Punjab, the troops left the Badshahi Mosque.

Lahore itself became the first centre in the subcontinent of a Muslim culture inspired by Persia, and it was in this city that Hujwiri composed his famous Persian treatise on Sufism; his tomb still provides a place of pilgrimage for the people of the Punjab.

## Legacy

More than a grave, Mazar-e-Iqbal is a meeting place of literature, faith and national identity. It honours a man who reawakened a people through poetry, who dared to rethink his religious tradition for the modern age, and who imagined into being a country he would never see. His verse is recited from schoolrooms to state ceremonies; his philosophy of *khudi* remains a living argument about the self, freedom and faith; his image of the *shaheen* still summons the young to a life of striving. Whole institutions and an entire field of scholarship, *Iqbaliyat*, the study of Iqbal, are devoted to his thought.

His poetry has been translated into many languages, carrying the Poet of the East to readers far beyond the subcontinent. Reynold A. Nicholson translated the *Asrar-e-Khudi* as *The Secrets of the Self*. The *Javid Nama* was translated into English by Shaikh Mahmud Ahmad (Lahore, 1961) and by A. J. Arberry (London, 1966), into Italian by Alessandro Bausani in 1955 and into French by Eva Meyerovitch in 1962, and Arberry also translated part of the *Zabūr-i ʿAjam* as *Persian Psalms* (Lahore, 1948). Annemarie Schimmel rendered the *Javid Nama* into German verse in 1957 and into Turkish prose in 1958.

Studies of his thought followed in several languages, among them Schimmel's *Gabriel's Wing: A Study into the Religious Ideas of Sir Muhammad Iqbal* (Leiden, 1963), Hafeez Malik's edited volume *Muhammad Iqbal: Poet-Philosopher of Pakistan* (New York, 1971), Rais Ahmad Jaʿfri's Urdu study of his love for the Prophet, *Iqbāl aur ʿishq-i rasūl* (Lahore, 1956), Bausani's articles on Satan in his work and on the *Gulshan-i raz-i jadid*, and Bürgel's "The Pious Rogue" (1979). His reach extended into the study of Sufism itself: Annemarie Schimmel's own interest in the eighteenth century mystic Khwaja Mir Dard (1721 to 1785) developed during her studies on Iqbal's work.

Because his verse gave the Pakistan Movement much of its emotional and moral vocabulary, his tomb is not a relic of the past but a living focus of the nation's understanding of itself, where the memory of the man and the idea of the country are renewed together. In the shadow of the Badshahi Mosque and within sight of the Minar-e-Pakistan, it endures as one of the places where Pakistan goes to remember who it is, and who it once hoped to become.

Location: Uch Sharif, Bahawalpur District, Punjab, Pakistan

Description:
The Tomb of Baha'al-Halim is one of the celebrated cluster of medieval shrines at the south-western edge of Uch Sharif, the ancient town in Bahawalpur district that was for centuries a great centre of the Suhrawardi order and of the Bukhari Sayyids. Together with the neighbouring tombs of Bibi Jawindi and Ustad Nuriya and the tomb and mosque of Jalaluddin Bukhari, the shrine forms the ensemble that Pakistan placed on the UNESCO World Heritage tentative list in 2004 as an outstanding example of Islamic funerary architecture. Baha'al-Halim is remembered as a revered spiritual guide of Uch, and his tomb is traditionally said to have been raised in his honour by the great saint Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht; the exact dates of his life are not securely recorded and are best treated with caution. The mausoleum is an octagonal, three-tiered structure of glazed brick, crowned by a dome and adorned with the brilliant blue, turquoise and white tilework for which Uch and Multan are famous — a fusion of Central Asian, Persian and local Multani decorative traditions. Though damaged over the centuries, it remains among the most admired monuments of the town and, like its companion shrines, is honoured with an annual *urs*. Per UNESCO's own tentative-list submission (Ref. 1883, filed 30 January 2004 by Pakistan's Department of Archaeology and Museums), the tomb is the earliest of the ensemble's three domed mausolea, raised for Baha' al-Halim by his pupil Jahaniyan Jahangasht (1307-1383 AD) during or shortly after the latter's lifetime, predating the tomb of Bibi Jawindi, built around 1494. Dawn reported in 2011 that "most of the old shrines in Uch Sharif are in massive need of restoration," and in 2025 that the Walled City of Lahore Authority had begun a conservation plan covering ten monuments — including "Hazrat Bahaul Halim" — at a cost of over Rs653 million.

## Overview

The Tomb of Bibi Jawindi at Uch Sharif, in southern Punjab, is among the most beautiful and most poignant monuments of Islamic architecture in Pakistan. A jewel of blue and white glazed tilework, half ruined by the flooding of the river, it has become the very emblem of Uch Sharif's medieval glory. Bibi Jawindi was a saintly woman of the great Bukhari family of sayyids, descendants of the Prophet Muhammad, and her ornate tomb, raised in the late fifteenth century, stands within the famous cluster of tombs in the Bukhari quarter of the town. Pilgrims honour it as the resting place of a holy woman, and together with the tombs around it, it draws lovers of architecture and history as much as pilgrims.

The tomb is the finest of a group of contiguous mausolea that together form one of the most important surviving ensembles of funerary architecture from before the Mughals in the subcontinent, and the monuments of Uch Sharif have been placed on UNESCO's Tentative List of World Heritage sites. Uch itself is called the city of saints.

## Bibi Jawindi and Her Tomb

Bibi Jawindi is remembered as a pious woman of the Jalali Bukhari line, venerated for her holiness. Accounts of her place in the family differ, but by tradition she was a great-granddaughter of the celebrated saint Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht.

Tradition holds that her tomb was built around 1493, in her honour, by an Iranian prince named Dilshad. It is an octagonal, tiered building crowned by a dome and adorned with turrets at its corners. Its surfaces are sheathed in exquisite *kashi*, glazed tilework, of cobalt blue, turquoise and white, the work for which Uch and Multan are famed. The tomb is a masterpiece of the regional style that flourished around the tombs of the Suhrawardi saints, followers of one of the orders of Sufis, or Muslim mystics.

Over the centuries the changing course of the river undermined the building, and tradition holds that a great part of it collapsed in a flood. There is no settled view of when that flood came; it is placed as early as the sixteenth century and as late as the nineteenth. What remains is the ravishing half of a tomb that visitors see today, a fragment whose surviving beauty only sharpens the sense of what has been lost.

## The Monuments of Uch Sharif

Bibi Jawindi's tomb does not stand alone. Among its neighbours in the Bukhari quarter of Uch are the tombs associated with Baha al-Halim, a teacher of the line, and with the tomb's own builder. So exceptional are these monuments that they have been the subject of international conservation efforts.

In the early twenty first century the tomb stood on a mound used as a graveyard, reached through the market, and hers was arguably the most important of the three buildings on it. Half the structures had been razed, and iron rods protected them. What remained was made of glazed Multani tiles, the tiles of Multan, coloured in blue and white, with a white dome on top. Several graves on the mound were covered, haphazardly, with blue and white tiles recovered from these historic shrines.

The river Sutlej once flowed past these buildings. It is called the lost river of Pakistan, for it was lost for ever after the Indus Water Treaty was signed between India and Pakistan in 1960.

## The Setting

Uch Sharif lies in the southern region of Punjab, near Bahawalpur, where the cultures of Punjab and Sindh merge and the language is Siraiki. The name Uch means high or great. An ancient centre of learning, trade and pilgrimage, with magnificent blue and white tiled mosques and desolate tombs, the town is built on a hill overlooking the confluence of the Sutlej and Chenab rivers. The older city stands on a mound, with the massive *havelis*, or great mansions, of the Gilanis and the Makhdooms, the families who keep the town's shrines. The south of the Punjab keeps more traces of religious and cultural syncretism, the blending of faiths and customs, than its northern and central regions.

Armies passed through Uch again and again. Shihab al-Din took it on his first campaign and came back by way of Multan and Uch on his second; Mirza Pir Muhammad brought the fortresses of Uch and Multan into his possession; and Khawas Khan's pursuit went as far as Multan and Uch. In the reign of the emperor Aurangzeb the place was known as the township of Uch, and the bounds of Multan and Uch formed one of the limits of the *suba*, or province, of Thatta.

## The Saints of Uch

Uch has its own founding legend, told in connection with Shaikh Safiu'd-Din Kaziruni. A shaikh, a Sufi master, was ordered to mount a camel and travel wherever the animal led him, and to remain where it finally halted. The camel halted in the middle of a desert, and there the shaikh founded the town later called Uch. It is a tale typical of the medieval stories told of Sufis. Other tales tell of a flying contest with a yogi, a Hindu ascetic, at Uch, and the stories of three generations of the Sufis of Uch all recount conflicts with Hindu yogis.

The first Bukhari saint of Uch was Jalaluddin Surkhposh Bukhari, who died in 1291. For a while Uch was the centre of the Suhrawardi order, thanks chiefly to the active and pious Jalaluddin Makhdum-i Jahaniyan, who died in 1383. It was at Uch, too, that Farid ad-Din is said to have kept his inverted fast of forty days, in the well of the town's Hajj mosque: every night for forty days he was suspended from a branch of the tree that overhung the well, and at daybreak he was pulled out.

Uch was also the gate by which the Qadiri order, the Sufi order founded by Abd al-Qadir Gilani, entered the subcontinent. Its first missionaries settled at Uch in the late fifteenth century, and from there the order spread. Hazrat Sayyid Muhammad Ghaus Uchi Jili Gilani is remembered as the first of this line to come to the Punjab; he came by way of Khurasan to Multan and settled at Uch. The four sons of Hazrat Muhammad Ghaus lie at rest at Uch Sharif, beside the tomb of Shah Muhammad Ghaus. The first Qadiri *khanqah*, or Sufi lodge, at Uch was founded by Shaykh Muhammad al-Husseini al-Jilani, a native of Turkey who settled there with his family, and his son, 'Abd al-Qadir Jilani Thani, is the famous Qadiri saint of Uch Sharif. In the nineteenth century the sayyids of Uch were famous, and on any disputed descent their word was final.

Uch has a place, too, in the story of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith, who is said to have come to Uch from Kartarpur at a time when Uch Sharif was one of the most famous Muslim shrines in southern Punjab. In the early twenty first century a well hidden in a field, abandoned, with juice cartons and wrappers floating in its black water, was shown as one of his traces, and beside it a grassy mound marked the site of the Gurdwara of Nanak, a Sikh place of worship, of which nothing remained.

Uch is linked, too, with the poet Bulle Shah, whose mentor, Inayat Shah, belonged to Uch. At Kasur, Muhammad Bakhsh, of a hereditary family of *qawwals*, singers of *qawwali*, the devotional music of the Sufis, said of his family: "We came with Bulle Shah's family from Uch Sharif, and we have learned his poetry from our ancestors, who have always sung here."

## Devotion and Legacy

As the resting place of a holy woman of the revered Bukhari line, Bibi Jawindi's tomb is honoured by pilgrims who come to Uch to visit the shrines of the sayyids, and it forms part of the sacred fabric of the town. Its fame today, though, is above all as a monument: a breathtaking, wounded masterpiece that stands for the vanished splendour of medieval Uch and for the artistry of the tile workers who adorned the shrines of the Punjab's saints. It is at once a place of devotion, a heritage treasure and an elegy in brick and glaze.

The tomb is also the place where one modern book on Sufism in Pakistan begins. In April 1996 its author was at the *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of a saint's death, at Allahabad, a rural village sixty miles southwest of Bahawalpur in southern Punjab, and on a day's journey from there he wandered through Uch Sharif with his companions. Near the crumbling tomb of Bibi Jawindi an elderly gentleman approached them, and the author photographed him. Disciples in Lahore later identified the man in the photograph as the deceased spiritual master Shaykh Wahid Bakhsh Sial Rabbani; in the author's telling, the shaykh had been dead for more than a year when the photograph was taken.

Name: Tomb of Qutbuddin Aibak
Location: Aibak Road, Anarkali, Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: None - heritage site, no devotional programme
Description:
## Overview

Tucked amid the crowded lanes of Aibak Road in the Anarkali quarter of Lahore, a modest garden tomb marks the burial place of Sultan Qutb ud-Din Aibak, founder of the Mamluk, or Slave, dynasty and the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate, the realm of the Muslim sultans who ruled from Delhi. A slave who rose through service to the Ghurid ruler Muhammad Ghori, he established independent rule based in Lahore after Ghori's death, laying the foundations of Muslim dynastic government in the subcontinent, and he is remembered too as the patron who commissioned Delhi's Qutb Minar. The tomb is not the shrine of a Sufi, or Muslim mystic: it hosts no *ʿurs*, the yearly commemoration of a saint's death, no pilgrimage tradition and no ongoing devotional practice. It is maintained as a protected historical monument, valued for marking the thirteenth century founding moment of Muslim dynastic rule in South Asia, centred, briefly, on Lahore itself.

Aibak died in Lahore in 1210 after a fall from his horse while playing *chaugan*, an early form of polo. The tomb's own history has been anything but continuous: for long the site was a simple, informal grave hemmed in by the houses of the Anarkali bazaar, and the structure visitors see today is essentially a reconstruction of the 1970s.

## The Sultan

Aibak was born around 1150 in Turkestan and sold into slavery as a child. He was called Aibak, it is said, because his little finger was broken. Bought by the Ghurid ruler Muhammad Ghori, also known as Sultan Shihab al-Din and as Muʿizz al-Din Muhammad bin Sam, he rose through his master's service, and after the decisive Second Battle of Tarain in 1192 he came to command the Ghurid territories in northern India.

When Ghori went back to Ghazni, he left Aibak, his chosen slave, behind as his deputy to govern Hindustan. Accounts differ over where Aibak was first posted, whether at the head of the forces in Delhi itself or as viceroy at Kuhram, a small town seventy *kos* from Delhi, the *kos* being an old measure of distance. As deputy he took the fort of Meerut in the shortest time and set governors in every place; in the second year he took the fort of Kol, and then Gwalior, Budaun and other forts. His troops, stationed at Indraprastha near Delhi, had to make several invasions into the Doab, the land between two rivers, and the regions around Ajmer to consolidate their power, and over the area he appointed Saiyid Husain Mashhadi as *darogha*, or military governor. The Saiyid served the Khwaja, a title given to Sufi saints, with great devotion.

He marched on Gujarat and took revenge on Rai Bhim Dev of Gujarat for Ghori's earlier defeat; he plundered the country, returned to Delhi, and had the *khutba*, the Friday sermon, read and coins struck in Ghori's name. When Ghori made his tenth campaign, against the Khokhars near Lahore, Aibak came from Delhi to join him, and together they chastised the tribe. His captains carried the conquest east: the beginning of Islam in Bengal is traced to Malik Muhammad Bakhtiyar, one of Aibak's great *amirs*, or nobles. A general who sent his booty from Bihar to his master at Delhi is remembered too, in a story that takes in a rutting elephant, the governorship of Bihar and an order to take Bengal.

Delhi was his seat, and he lived, as did his eventual successor Iltutmish, in the fort of Rai Pithora. He is remembered as the patron who commissioned the famous Qutb Minar there, and in Ajmer he erected a beautiful mosque, not far from which Muʿinuddin died in 1236. He is not to be confused with another Qutbuddin, Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki of Farghana, who died in 1235 and whose modest compound at Merauli, near the Qutb Minar in Delhi, is usually filled with pious pilgrims.

Iltutmish was Aibak's slave before he was his son-in-law. Aibak, himself a former slave, took a fancy to him during a visit to Ghazni after his expedition to Anhilwara in 1196, and was able to buy him in Delhi. He adopted Iltutmish and married him to his daughter. After the conquest of Gwalior he gave Iltutmish its command, and then a district with its region and, step by step, Budaun, until Iltutmish rose to be *amir al-umara*, the chief of the nobles, and received from the Sultan his letter of manumission, the deed that set him free. His rise to prominence came between 1197 or 1198 and 1206.

## Sultan in His Own Right

Ghori was assassinated in 1206 and died without a son. Aibak then established independent rule based in Lahore, though accounts differ over whether his reign began there or at Delhi. Coming out of Delhi, he reached Lahore, took the throne in his own right, and on the eleventh of Rabiʿ al-Awwal, a month of the Islamic calendar, had coins struck and the *khutba* read in his own name. From Firozkoh, Ghori's nephew, Sultan Ghiyas al-Din, sent him the parasol, an emblem of royalty, and the trappings of kingship and addressed him by the title of Sultan.

His rival for the Ghurid inheritance was Taj al-Din Yildiz, another of Ghori's special slaves, who had been given the title of sultan at Ghazni after his master's death and came on to the Punjab to take the throne of Hind. The two quarrelled over Lahore and fought a pitched battle, and Yildiz was routed. Accounts differ over what followed, but for a time Aibak's power reached as far as Ghazni itself, and after his victory he gave himself to rule in complete independence.

He ruled with great ability. In all he governed Hindustan for twenty years, and he reigned as sultan from 1206 until his death in 1210. Because he gave lakhs, hundreds of thousands, to the needy, he was called in Hind Lakh Bakhsh, the giver of lakhs. His giving was praised at length in Persian: the hand of his generosity, it was said, brushed the dust of poverty from the faces of the poor. That praise closes with a couplet in his honour:

باهمت او حوصله دریا تنگ
بارفعت او مرتبه گردون پست

## Death and Succession

He died in Lahore in November 1210, though accounts of the year differ. He was playing *chaugan* when he fell from his horse; as one chronicler writing in Persian put it, he carried the ball of his life to the field of the hereafter. The game had come to the subcontinent with the Central Asian armies, and a polo match is the scene of a *kafi*, a short mystical lyric, by the poet Madho Lal Hussein, though the poem does not name the Sultan:

*Let me stand and watch for a few days / the polo tournament. Who wins, who loses, / whose brisk horse makes a clever move? … Let's see who hits the ball / across the field. The crowd cheers and jeers* (translated by Naveed Alam)

He was succeeded, eventually, by his son-in-law Shams al-Din Iltutmish. At first the nobles seated his heir, Aram Bakhsh, on the throne in Lahore as Sultan Aram Shah, and for a short while Lahore was a royal seat again; accounts differ over whether Aram Shah was Aibak's own son or an adopted one. Under Aram Shah the affairs of state did not prosper, and after a year Iltutmish deposed him: when Iltutmish came, Aram Shah moved from Lahore towards Delhi, drew up his ranks and fled after little fighting. Iltutmish, himself remembered as a slave king, went on to rule from Delhi, and under him *muftis*, jurists of Islamic law, were appointed for Lahore. In his reign Yildiz rose again; he took Multan, came to Lahore and plundered the Punjab freely.

## The Tomb

Accounts differ over what stood over the grave in the centuries after Aibak's death, and historians dispute whether a substantial mausoleum ever stood there in the medieval period. At first, it is said, there was only the grave. Iltutmish is said to have ordered a simple small room, barely able to enclose it; built at first of mud, it was bricked in during Akbar's reign. Later a marble tomb stood there, until it was pulled down by Ranjit Singh.

In the nineteenth century the grave lay outside the Lahori Gate, on the north side, in the Sadr Bazaar of Anarkali. A house stood on its land, and courtesans occupied the place. Under Sikh rule lofty buildings of stone had stood there, until the Maharaja demolished them all and sent them off to Amritsar, and only a single grave on a raised platform remained. Old people still remembered a dome of marble two storeys high, unmatched anywhere round Lahore. For long the site was a simple, informal grave hemmed in by the houses of the Anarkali bazaar.

The tomb visitors see today is essentially a reconstruction of the 1970s by Pakistan's Department of Archaeology and Museums, though accounts of its date differ. It was built in 1972 at the order of Prime Minister Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto, given after the Bangladesh war, and Bhutto remarked that Aibak "was a great and kind ruler and deserved the respect of the poor"; the design was led by the architect Kamil Khan Mumtaz. Deliberately evoking the style of the early Sultanate period, it stands within a small walled garden and is maintained purely as a protected historical monument.

## The Setting

The tomb stands in Anarkali, whose market is named after the legendary lover of the Mughal emperor Jahangir. By the 1880s Anarkali was a cantonment, or military station, and a bazaar. In the early twenty first century the area had become the largest tyre market in the city, and the Pak Tea House, just a few shops away, once famed for its gatherings of the city's leading intelligentsia, was on its way to becoming yet another tyre shop.

Aibak's Lahore was a city the Ghurids had only lately taken. Khusraw Shah, son of Bahram Shah, driven from Ghazni by the Ghurids, took Lahore and died there, and his son Khusraw Malik held it for twenty eight years while Ghori attacked the city again and again. In the end Khusraw Malik submitted and was taken to Ghazni, where he died, and Ghori set his own deputy in Lahore. With that surrender the rule of the Ghurid sultans in Hind began, and the Ghaznavid government came to its end.

Old Lahore lost many of its monuments in the Sikh period. In Ranjit Singh's time red, black and marble stones in the neighbourhood of Lahore were torn down, and when the cantonments of his armies were built, the bricks of old tombs and houses were pulled out.

## Legacy

The tomb is valued chiefly for its symbolic role, marking the founding moment of Muslim dynastic rule in South Asia, centred, briefly, on Lahore itself. From Aibak's time Delhi was fixed as the capital of the Muslim sultans. In the nineteenth century one historian of the city held Aibak's grave to be older than any other building near Lahore, and wrote that before the Sultan the land of Hindustan had been without a lamp.

Aibak is also said to have wanted Lahore's dead buried together, setting aside land south of the village of Mozang as a graveyard for at least 150,000 dead, the origin of the present Miani Sahib graveyard.

Bhutto's tribute to a great and kind ruler who deserved the respect of the poor stands beside an older memory, that of the Lakh Bakhsh, whose giving was praised in Persian prose and verse.

Location: Bukhari mound, Uch Sharif, Bahawalpur District, Punjab, Pakistan

Description:
The Tomb of Ustad Nuriya is the smallest and plainest of the celebrated funerary monuments clustered on the Bukhari mound at Uch Sharif, an ancient town in the Bahawalpur district of southern Punjab long renowned as a centre of Suhrawardi Sufism. It stands beside the far more famous tombs of Bibi Jawindi and Baha'al-Halim (both octagonal and blue-tiled) and the flat-roofed brick tomb-and-mosque of Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari, with which it forms an ensemble of five monuments placed on UNESCO's tentative list of World Heritage Sites. Tradition holds that the tomb honours Ustad Nuriya — the master-builder, or ustad, credited with designing the exquisite tomb of Bibi Jawindi, itself usually dated to the late fifteenth century. Because it was raised for a craftsman rather than a saint, the tomb departs from the octagonal, tiered form of its neighbours: it is smaller and broadly rectangular in plan, and it lacks the lavish glazed-tile revetment for which Uch is famous. Like the rest of the group it has suffered severe structural loss over the centuries — a great flood in 1817 is traditionally blamed for the collapse of much of the complex — and part of its rear structure is gone. Its interest lies precisely in its dedication: in an architectural tradition that seldom named its makers, the survival of a monument to the builder himself is remarkable, and it underlines the extraordinary artistic reputation of the Uch workshops. Filed here under the Muslim-shrine category as an integral part of the Suhrawardi funerary complex, the tomb draws the heritage traveller and the historian of Indo-Islamic architecture rather than the pilgrim.

An academic study of the Uch Sharif funerary complex places the tomb specifically in the northwest corner of the town, on the sloping side of a hill that was once the site of a historic fortress, amid the ruins of other architecturally significant shrines — among them those of Bibi Jawindi and Baha'al-Halim. The tomb is also listed as a protected monument in the Punjab Directorate General of Archaeology's register of religious monuments, where it is classified under the heading "Early Muslim Period (8th–12th Century)."
